note: The Servant made 'a light to the nations/world' — direct background for 'you are the light of the world,' extending Israel's vocation to the disciples.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: The Servant given 'as a light to the nations'; reinforces the light-to-the-world commission.
sourceText: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations;

note: Zion's light arises and nations come to its brightness; a city/light that cannot be hidden draws on this eschatological imagery.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

note: The mountain of the LORD's house lifted up, with nations streaming to it; 'a city set on a hill cannot be hidden' evokes the eschatological Zion.
sourceText: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of Yahweh’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.

note: The wise 'shall shine like the brightness of the firmament'; the radiance of the righteous behind 'let your light shine.'
sourceText: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: The path of the righteous is like the dawning light that grows brighter; wisdom image of righteous luminance.
sourceText: But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light, that shines more and more until the perfect day.

note: When justice is done, 'your light shall break forth like the dawn'; light as visible righteous deeds (cf. 'see your good works').
sourceText: Then your light shall break out as the morning, and your healing shall spring out speedily; and your righteousness shall go before you; Yahweh’s glory shall be your rear guard.

note: Doing good to the afflicted causes one's light to rise in darkness — coheres with light shining through good works.
sourceText: and if you draw out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul: then your light shall rise in darkness, and your obscurity be as the noonday;

note: Do not add to or take from the commandment; 'not one jot or tittle shall pass' affirms the law's inviolability in the same spirit.
sourceText: You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it, that you may keep the commandments of Yahweh your God which I command you.

note: Warning against adding to or diminishing God's commands; background to the permanence of every least commandment.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder,

note: 'The grass withers... but the word of our God stands forever'; heaven-and-earth-may-pass-but-the-law-endures echoes the abiding word.
sourceText: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”

note: 'The heavens shall vanish... but my salvation shall be forever' — direct background for 'until heaven and earth pass away, not one letter shall pass from the law.'
sourceText: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.

note: 'Forever, O LORD, your word is settled in the heavens'; the eternal stability of Torah affirmed in v.18.
sourceText: Yahweh, your word is settled in heaven forever.

note: 'Every one of your righteous ordinances endures forever'; coheres with the permanence of the least commandments.
sourceText: All of your words are truth. Every one of your righteous ordinances endures forever.

note: 'The law... endures forever' — Second Temple affirmation of Torah's eternity behind v.18.
sourceText: This is the book of the commandments of God, and the law that endures for ever: all those who hold it fast are appointed to life; but such as leave it shall die.

note: Call to keep and not depart from God's statutes; resonates with not breaking the least commandments.
sourceText: From the days of your fathers you have turned aside from my ordinances, and have not kept them. Return to me, and I will return to you,” says Yahweh of Armies. “But you say, ‘How shall we return?’

note: 'You shall not murder' — verbatim citation of the sixth commandment (Decalogue) introduced by the antithesis formula.
sourceText: “You shall not murder.

note: Parallel Decalogue form of 'You shall not murder'; the cited commandment stands in both Exodus and Deuteronomy.
sourceText: “You shall not murder.

note: Bloodshed brings judgment ('whoever sheds man's blood...'); background for 'whoever murders shall be liable to judgment.'
sourceText: Whoever sheds man’s blood, his blood will be shed by man, for God made man in his own image.

note: Mosaic law on the murderer being put to death by the court; 'liable to the judgment/council' draws on this judicial framework.
sourceText: “‘Whoever kills any person, the murderer shall be slain at the mouth of witnesses; but one witness shall not testify against any person that he die. “‘Moreover you shall take no ransom for the life of a murderer who is guilty of death; but he shall surely be put to death.

note: Hard cases of bloodshed brought before judges/priests; the escalating tribunal (judgment, council) reflects Israel's courts.
sourceText: If there arises a matter too hard for you in judgment, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, being matters of controversy within your gates; then you shall arise, and go up to the place which Yahweh your God chooses. You shall come to the priests who are Levites, and to the judge who shall be in those days. You shall inquire, and they shall give you the verdict.

note: 'You shall not hate your brother in your heart' — the interiorizing of murder into anger toward 'your brother' draws on the Holiness Code.
sourceText: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.

note: Prohibition of grudge-bearing against one's kin; coheres with reconciling before offering one's gift.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: Cain's anger toward his brother culminating in murder is the archetype of the anger-to-murder continuum Jesus expounds.
sourceText: but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell. Yahweh said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen? If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.” Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, […]

note: Wisdom on settling with one's adversary before wrath/ruin; background for 'agree with your adversary quickly... lest he hand you to the judge.'
sourceText: For jealousy arouses the fury of the husband. He won’t spare in the day of vengeance. He won’t regard any ransom, neither will he rest content, though you give many gifts.

note: 'Do not hastily bring to court... settle your case with your neighbor'; coheres with vv.25-26's counsel to reconcile en route.
sourceText: Don’t be hasty in bringing charges to court. What will you do in the end when your neighbor shames you? Debate your case with your neighbor, and don’t betray the confidence of another;

note: God rejects sacrifice from those whose hands are unjust until they do right; prophetic priority of reconciliation over cultic gift (vv.23-24).
sourceText: “What are the multitude of your sacrifices to me?”, says Yahweh. “I have had enough of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed animals. I don’t delight in the blood of bulls, or of lambs, or of male goats. When you come to appear before me, who has required this at your hand, to trample my courts? Bring no more vain offerings. Incense is an abomination to me; new moons, Sabbaths, and convocations: I can’t bear with evil assemblies. My soul hates […]

note: God despises offerings divorced from justice; background to leaving one's gift to be reconciled first.
sourceText: I hate, I despise your feasts, and I can’t stand your solemn assemblies. Yes, though you offer me your burnt offerings and meal offerings, I will not accept them; neither will I regard the peace offerings of your fat animals. Take away from me the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps. But let justice roll on like rivers, and righteousness like a mighty stream.

note: 'You shall not commit adultery' — verbatim citation of the seventh commandment.
sourceText: “You shall not commit adultery.

note: Parallel Decalogue form of the adultery prohibition.
sourceText: “You shall not commit adultery.

note: 'You shall not covet your neighbor's wife' — the interiorizing of adultery into lustful looking draws directly on the coveting commandment.
sourceText: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”

note: 'I made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?' — the closest parallel to lustful looking already being sin.
sourceText: “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?

note: If my heart followed my eyes — the eye-heart link Jesus develops ('looks with lust... in his heart').
sourceText: if my step has turned out of the way, if my heart walked after my eyes, if any defilement has stuck to my hands,

note: 'Do not desire her beauty in your heart, nor let her capture you with her eyelashes' — wisdom on lust of the eyes/heart.
sourceText: Don’t lust after her beauty in your heart, neither let her captivate you with her eyelids.

note: Potiphar's wife 'cast her eyes' on Joseph; the gaze-leading-to-adultery motif.
sourceText: After these things, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph; and she said, “Lie with me.”

note: 'Turn away your eyes from a shapely woman... many have been led astray by a woman's beauty' — Second Temple wisdom on the lustful gaze.
sourceText: Turn away your eye from a comely woman, And gaze not on another’s beauty: By the beauty of a woman many have been led astray; And herewith love is kindled as a fire.

note: Prayer against the lust of the eyes and sinful desire; coheres with guarding the eye against lust.
sourceText: O Lord, Father and God of my life, Give me not a proud look, And turn away concupiscense from me. Let not greediness and chambering overtake me; And give me not over to a shameless mind.

note: Even a beloved relation must be cut off if leading to sin; background to the radical 'pluck out the eye, cut off the hand.'
sourceText: you shall not consent to him, nor listen to him; neither shall your eye pity him, neither shall you spare, neither shall you conceal him; but you shall surely kill him. Your hand shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterwards the hands of all the people.

note: 'Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce' — direct citation of the Mosaic divorce provision Jesus qualifies.
sourceText: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house.

note: The fuller divorce-and-remarriage statute; Jesus reframes its concession around the cause of immorality.
sourceText: When she has departed out of his house, she may go and be another man’s wife. If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter husband die, who took her to be his wife; her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before Yahweh. You shall not cause the land to sin, which Yahweh your […]

note: 'The two become one flesh' — the creation order of marriage underlies Jesus' restriction of divorce (made explicit in Mt 19).
sourceText: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.

note: God hates divorce / the treacherous putting-away of a wife; prophetic background to Jesus' tightening of the divorce concession.
sourceText: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For I hate divorce”, says Yahweh, the God of Israel, “and him […]

note: 'You shall not swear by my name falsely' — direct source for 'you shall not swear falsely.'
sourceText: “‘You shall not swear by my name falsely, and profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh.

note: 'When a man vows a vow to the LORD... he shall do all that proceeds from his mouth' — basis for 'but shall perform to the Lord your vows.'
sourceText: When a man vows a vow to Yahweh, or swears an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.

note: Vows to the LORD must be paid and not delayed; reinforces the obligation-to-perform clause Jesus cites.
sourceText: When you vow a vow to Yahweh your God, you shall not be slack to pay it; for Yahweh your God will surely require it of you; and it would be sin in you. But if you refrain from making a vow, it shall be no sin in you. You shall observe and do that which has gone out of your lips. Whatever you have vowed to Yahweh your God as a freewill offering, which you have promised with your mouth, you must do.

note: 'You shall not take the name of the LORD in vain' — the Decalogue prohibition behind false/empty swearing.
sourceText: “You shall not take the name of Yahweh your God in vain, for Yahweh will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.

note: Who has not 'sworn deceitfully' — the false-oath concern of the oath antithesis (and ties to the pure in heart of v.8).
sourceText: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.

note: 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool' — direct source for swearing 'neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God; nor by the earth, his footstool.'
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what kind of house will you build to me? and what place shall be my rest?

note: Zion 'the city of the great King' — direct source for 'nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.'
sourceText: Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion, on the north sides, the city of the great King.

note: 'The LORD's throne is in heaven'; coheres with heaven as God's throne, making oaths by it oaths by God.
sourceText: Yahweh is in his holy temple. Yahweh is on his throne in heaven. His eyes observe. His eyes examine the children of men.

note: Better not to vow than to vow and not pay; wisdom critique of rash vows behind 'swear not at all.'
sourceText: When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow. It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay.

note: 'Do not accustom your mouth to oaths' — Second Temple wisdom counseling against habitual swearing, closely parallel to v.34.
sourceText: Accustom not your mouth to an oath; And be not accustomed to the naming of the Holy One. For as a servant that is continually scourged will not lack a bruise, So he also that swears and names God continually will not be cleansed from sin. A man of many oaths will be filled with iniquity; And the scourge will not depart from his house: If he shall offend, his sin will be upon him; And if he disregard it, he has sinned doubly; And if he has sworn in vain, […]

note: Human powerlessness to effect things by one's word; coheres with 'you cannot make one hair white or black' (v.36).
sourceText: Who is he who says, and it comes to pass, when the Lord doesn’t command it?

note: 'Eye for eye, tooth for tooth' — verbatim citation of the lex talionis Jesus sets in antithesis.
sourceText: eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,

note: 'Fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth' — parallel talion formula behind the citation.
sourceText: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; as he has injured someone, so shall it be done to him.

note: 'Eye for eye, tooth for tooth' — third Pentateuchal statement of the talion principle.
sourceText: Your eyes shall not pity: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.

note: 'Let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him' — close parallel to 'turn the other cheek.'
sourceText: Let him give his cheek to him who strikes him; let him be filled full with reproach.

note: The Servant 'gave my back to those who strike, my cheeks to those who pull the beard' — nonretaliatory suffering behind turning the cheek.
sourceText: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.

note: 'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD' — wisdom renunciation of retaliation behind 'do not resist the evildoer.'
sourceText: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.

note: 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me' — direct rejection of tit-for-tat, paralleling the non-resistance teaching.
sourceText: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”

note: Feed your enemy, give him drink; the generous-to-the-aggressor ethic extending into giving coat and cloak.
sourceText: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.

note: The cloak taken in pledge must be returned; legal background sharpening 'let him have your cloak also.'
sourceText: If you take your neighbor’s garment as collateral, you shall restore it to him before the sun goes down, for that is his only covering, it is his garment for his skin. What would he sleep in? It will happen, when he cries to me, that I will hear, for I am gracious.

note: Do not harden your heart but open your hand to the poor and lend freely; direct background to 'give to him who asks, do not refuse the borrower.'
sourceText: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks.

note: Give freely and open your hand to the needy; reinforces v.42's command to give.
sourceText: You shall surely give, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him; because that for this thing Yahweh your God will bless you in all your work, and in all that you put your hand to. For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.

note: 'The righteous is generous and gives'; coheres with the giving/lending ethic of v.42.
sourceText: The wicked borrow, and don’t pay back, but the righteous give generously.

note: 'He is ever lending generously'; the open-handed righteous of v.42.
sourceText: All day long he deals graciously, and lends. His seed is blessed.

note: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' — direct citation of the love command, the cited half of the antithesis.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: Commands not to seek the welfare of Ammon/Moab; one strand behind the popularly inferred 'hate your enemy' (no OT verse commands hatred per se).
sourceText: An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter into Yahweh’s assembly; even to the tenth generation shall no one belonging to them enter into Yahweh’s assembly forever; because they didn’t meet you with bread and with water on the way, when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse you. Nevertheless Yahweh your God wouldn’t listen to Balaam; but Yahweh your God turned the curse into a […]

note: 'Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? ... I hate them with perfect hatred' — the scriptural posture of hating enemies Jesus overturns.
sourceText: Yahweh, don’t I hate those who hate you? Am I not grieved with those who rise up against you? I hate them with perfect hatred. They have become my enemies.

note: 'Love the sojourner as yourself' — the love command already stretched beyond kin in the Holiness Code, anticipating love of enemies.
sourceText: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.

note: Return your enemy's stray ox; help the donkey of one who hates you — Torah's seed of active goodwill toward enemies.
sourceText: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again. If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him, you shall surely help him with it.

note: 'If your enemy is hungry, give him bread' — direct wisdom command to do good to enemies, behind 'love your enemies, do good.'
sourceText: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink:

note: 'Do not rejoice when your enemy falls' — renunciation of enmity coherent with loving enemies.
sourceText: Don’t rejoice when your enemy falls. Don’t let your heart be glad when he is overthrown;

note: Job claims he never rejoiced at his enemy's ruin nor cursed him — pious refusal of vengeance behind the enemy-love ethic.
sourceText: “If I have rejoiced at the destruction of him who hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him; (yes, I have not allowed my mouth to sin by asking his life with a curse);

note: 'Be holy, for I am holy' — the imitatio Dei formula directly behind 'be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect.'
sourceText: For I am Yahweh your God. Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am holy: neither shall you defile yourselves with any kind of creeping thing that moves on the earth.

note: 'You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy' — the Holiness Code's call to imitate God, reframed as perfection in v.48.
sourceText: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.

note: 'You shall be blameless/perfect (tamim) before the LORD your God' — the LXX 'teleios' here closely matches 'be perfect.'
sourceText: You shall be perfect with Yahweh your God.

note: 'Walk before me and be blameless (tamim)' — the call to integrity before God behind 'be perfect.'
sourceText: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless.

note: 'The LORD is good to all, his mercy over all he has made' — God's indiscriminate goodness behind 'he makes his sun rise on evil and good.'
sourceText: Yahweh is good to all. His tender mercies are over all his works.

note: 'Upon whom does his light not arise?' — God's light/sun given universally, paralleling v.45.
sourceText: Can his armies be counted? On whom does his light not arise?

note: God waters the earth and provides rain abundantly; background to 'sends rain on the just and the unjust.'
sourceText: You visit the earth, and water it. You greatly enrich it. The river of God is full of water. You provide them grain, for so you have ordained it. You drench its furrows. You level its ridges. You soften it with showers. You bless it with a crop. You crown the year with your bounty. Your carts overflow with abundance. The wilderness grasslands overflow. The hills are clothed with gladness. The pastures are covered with flocks. The valleys also are clothed […]

note: God gives the rains in season for all; coheres with rain on just and unjust as common grace.
sourceText: Neither do they say in their heart, ‘Let us now fear Yahweh our God, who gives rain, both the former and the latter, in its season; who preserves to us the appointed weeks of the harvest.’

note: 'You are children of the LORD your God' — divine-sonship language behind 'that you may be children of your Father.'
sourceText: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.

note: Be like a father to orphans and you will be like a son of the Most High — deuterocanonical sonship-through-mercy parallel to v.45.
sourceText: Be as a father to the fatherless, And instead of a husband to their mother: So will you be as a son of the Most High, And he will love you more than your mother does.

note: The command to give generously to the poor ('open wide your hand to your brother') is the Torah background for Jesus' presupposition that disciples 'do merciful deeds'; almsgiving is assumed righteousness, not optional.
sourceText: For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.

note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him' — the logic of God himself repaying the secret almsgiver (v.4) closely matches this proverb's reward-from-God motif.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

note: Ben Sira: a person's almsgiving is 'like a signet ring' kept with God who guards it as a treasure — Second Temple development of almsgiving stored with God who rewards, paralleling the Father who sees in secret.
sourceText: With him the alms of a man is as a signet; And he will keep the bounty of a man as the apple of the eye.

note: Tobit's instruction to give alms from one's substance, that almsgiving 'delivers from death' and 'stores up a good treasure,' is the closest Second Temple parallel to Jesus' theology of hidden, God-rewarded charity.
sourceText: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]

note: 'Prayer with fasting and almsgiving... is better than to lay up gold' and 'almsgiving saves from death' — the same triad of almsgiving/prayer/fasting that structures Mt 6:1-18, suggesting a shared piety pattern.
sourceText: Good is prayer with fasting, alms, and righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold. Alms delivers from death, and it purges away all sin. Those who give alms and do righteousness will be filled with life;

note: Isaiah's true fast as sharing bread with the hungry links almsgiving and fasting as authentic versus performative piety, the very contrast Jesus draws.
sourceText: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the bands of the yoke, and to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke? Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?

note: Elisha 'shut the door' and prayed to the LORD in private before raising the child — a possible OT precedent for entering one's room and shutting the door (v.6) to pray unseen.
sourceText: He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh.

note: 'Enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you' — striking verbal overlap with 'enter into your inner room, and having shut your door,' though the contexts differ (hiding from wrath vs. private prayer).
sourceText: Come, my people, enter into your rooms, and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourself for a little moment, until the indignation is past.

note: The prophets of Baal cried aloud 'from morning until noon' with no answer — a possible backdrop for the Gentiles' 'much speaking' (v.7) imagining they are heard for many words.
sourceText: They took the bull which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, “Baal, hear us!” But there was no voice, nor any who answered. They leaped about the altar which was made. At noon, Elijah mocked them, and said, “Cry aloud; for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he has gone aside, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he sleeps and must be awakened.” They cried aloud, and cut themselves in […]

note: 'Let your words be few' before God in heaven — a wisdom warning against verbose prayer that closely matches the rebuke of 'vain repetitions' and 'much speaking.'
sourceText: Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few.

note: 'Do not babble in the assembly of the elders, and do not repeat yourself in your prayer' — almost a direct Second Temple parallel to the warning against vain repetition.
sourceText: Prate not in the multitude of elders; And repeat not your words in your prayer.

note: God knows the word on the tongue before it is spoken — grounds Jesus' claim that 'your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him' (v.8).
sourceText: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.

note: 'I will sanctify my great name... and the nations will know that I am the LORD' — the divine self-hallowing of God's name is the OT engine behind 'hallowed be your name'; God hallows his name by his eschatological act, which the petition invokes.
sourceText: I will sanctify my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, which you have profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am Yahweh, says the Lord Yahweh, when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes.

note: 'They will sanctify my name... and stand in awe of the God of Israel' — sanctifying/hallowing the divine Name as eschatological hope, the conceptual root of the first petition.
sourceText: But when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in the midst of him, they will sanctify my name. Yes, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and will stand in awe of the God of Israel.

note: 'You shall not profane my holy name, but I will be hallowed among the children of Israel' — the covenantal duty to hallow the Name underlies 'hallowed be your name.'
sourceText: You shall not profane my holy name, but I will be made holy among the children of Israel. I am Yahweh who makes you holy,

note: 'The God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed' — the prayer 'Let your Kingdom come' draws directly on Daniel's vision of God's everlasting kingdom breaking into history.
sourceText: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.

note: 'Your God reigns!' — the proclamation of God's kingship/reign that 'your Kingdom come' petitions to be realized.
sourceText: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

note: 'And the kingdom will be the LORD's' — terse OT articulation of the coming divine kingdom echoed in the second petition.
sourceText: Saviors will go up on Mount Zion to judge the mountains of Esau, and the kingdom will be Yahweh’s.

note: 'As may be the will in heaven, so let him do' — a Second Temple formula of submission to heaven's will closely paralleling 'your will be done.'
sourceText: Nevertheless, as may be the will in heaven, so shall he do.

note: The heavenly hosts 'do his will' (v.20-21) — the angelic obedience in heaven is the model for 'your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.'
sourceText: Praise Yahweh, all you armies of his, you servants of his, who do his pleasure.

note: 'Whatever the LORD pleased, that he has done, in heaven and in earth' — the heaven/earth scope of God's will echoes in the third petition's cosmic frame.
sourceText: Whatever Yahweh pleased, that he has done, in heaven and in earth, in the seas and in all deeps;

note: 'Feed me with the food that is needful for me' (Agur's prayer for neither poverty nor riches, just the daily portion) — the closest OT analogue to 'Give us today our daily bread,' both asking for sufficient daily provision.
sourceText: Remove far from me falsehood and lies. Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me;

note: The manna gathered 'a day's portion every day' is the typological pattern for daily bread: God provides enough for today, teaching dependence rather than hoarding (cf. anxiety section vv.25-34).
sourceText: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.

note: The manna could not be stored overnight without rotting — reinforces the day-by-day reliance behind 'give us today our daily bread' and against laying up earthly treasure.
sourceText: Moses said to them, “Let no one leave of it until the morning.” Notwithstanding they didn’t listen to Moses, but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and became foul: and Moses was angry with them.

note: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray' — a remarkably close Second Temple parallel to the reciprocal forgiveness of the fifth petition and vv.14-15.
sourceText: Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray.

note: The sabbatical 'release' (remission) of debts colors 'forgive us our debts' — debt-remission language drawn from Torah jubilee/release practice applied to sins.
sourceText: This is the way it shall be done: every creditor shall release that which he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not require payment from his neighbor and his brother; because Yahweh’s release has been proclaimed.

note: 'Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered' — the divine forgiveness of sin/debt sought in 'forgive us our debts.'
sourceText: Blessed is he whose disobedience is forgiven, whose sin is covered.

note: Petitions for God to deliver from the enemy/evildoer underlie 'deliver us from the evil one'; the Psalter's deliverance language saturates the final petition.
sourceText: For you will light my lamp, Yahweh. My God will light up my darkness. For by you, I advance through a troop. By my God, I leap over a wall. As for God, his way is perfect. Yahweh’s word is tried. He is a shield to all those who take refuge in him. For who is God, except Yahweh? Who is a rock, besides our God,

note: 'Incline not my heart to any evil thing' — a prayer not to be led toward evil that parallels 'bring us not into temptation.'
sourceText: Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips. Don’t incline my heart to any evil thing, to practice deeds of wickedness with men who work iniquity. Don’t let me eat of their delicacies.

note: 'Yours, O LORD, is the greatness, the power... the kingdom... and the glory' — David's doxology is the verbatim source of the prayer's traditional closing ascription of kingdom, power, and glory to God.
sourceText: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.

note: David asks God to keep his people's hearts directed toward him — continues the doxological context (29:11) from which the Lord's Prayer ending is drawn.
sourceText: Yahweh, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Israel, our fathers, keep this forever in the imagination of the thoughts of the heart of your people, and prepare their heart for you;

note: 'Forgive your neighbor... and then your sins will be pardoned'; the wrathful man who holds anger cannot expect healing from God — the strongest Second Temple statement of conditional, reciprocal forgiveness mirroring vv.14-15.
sourceText: Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins? He being himself flesh nourishes wrath: Who will make atonement for his sins?

note: 'You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge... but you shall love your neighbor' — the Torah ground for releasing others' trespasses as a condition of one's own standing before God.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: Joseph's brothers beg him to forgive their trespass and Joseph forgives — a narrative model of human forgiveness as the channel of restored relationship.
sourceText: ‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.

note: Wrath and anger are abominations that the sinner holds tight, and 'the Lord will take vengeance' on the unforgiving — the immediate context preceding the forgiveness teaching of Sir 28:2.
sourceText: Wrath and anger, these also are abominations; And a sinful man will possess them. He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins.

note: Isaiah's polemic against fasting done for show ('to be heard on high'... bowing the head like a reed) versus the fast God chooses — the prophetic template for Jesus' contrast between hypocritical and hidden fasting.
sourceText: ‘Why have we fasted,’ say they, ‘and you don’t see? Why have we afflicted our soul, and you take no knowledge?’ “Behold, in the day of your fast you find pleasure, and exact all your labors. Behold, you fast for strife and contention, and to strike with the fist of wickedness: you don’t fast this day so as to make your voice to be heard on high. Is such the fast that I have chosen? the day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow down his head as a […]

note: 'Rend your heart, and not your garments' — true fasting is inward not performative, the same heart-versus-display contrast Jesus presses against disfigured faces.
sourceText: “Yet even now,” says Yahweh, “turn to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.” Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity.

note: 'When you fasted... did you at all fast to me, even to me?' — God's challenge that ritual fasting may be self-directed rather than God-directed, paralleling fasting 'to be seen by men.'
sourceText: “Speak to all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, ‘When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and in the seventh month for these seventy years, did you at all fast to me, really to me? When you eat, and when you drink, don’t you eat for yourselves, and drink for yourselves?

note: 'Wash yourself, anoint yourself' — anointing and washing as ordinary grooming (the opposite of mourning), the gesture Jesus prescribes to mask fasting (v.17).
sourceText: Therefore wash yourself, anoint yourself, get dressed, and go down to the threshing floor, but don’t make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking.

note: David washes and anoints himself when he ceases mourning — the cultural background for anointing the head and washing the face to appear un-fasting.
sourceText: Then David arose from the earth, and washed, and anointed himself, and changed his clothing; and he came into Yahweh’s house, and worshiped: then he came to his own house; and when he required, they set bread before him, and he ate.

note: The triad 'prayer with fasting and almsgiving' commends fasting as genuine piety, paralleling the assumed practice of fasting that Jesus purifies of display.
sourceText: Good is prayer with fasting, alms, and righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold.

note: Daniel mourns and does NOT anoint himself while fasting — the very mourning-fast convention Jesus reverses by telling disciples to anoint themselves.
sourceText: I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine into my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all, until three whole weeks were fulfilled.

note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments... store up almsgiving in your treasuries, and it will rescue you from every misfortune' — the most direct Second Temple parallel to laying up treasure in heaven through righteous use of wealth.
sourceText: Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all affliction:

note: 'Don't weary yourself to be rich... riches sprout wings like an eagle and fly away' — the transience of earthly wealth behind 'treasures on earth, where... thieves break through and steal.'
sourceText: Don’t weary yourself to be rich. In your wisdom, show restraint. Why do you set your eyes on that which is not? For it certainly sprouts wings like an eagle and flies in the sky.

note: The wicked heaps up silver like dust but the just will wear it — the futility of hoarded wealth that another takes, echoing treasure consumed or stolen.
sourceText: Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare clothing as the clay; he may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver.

note: The rich man 'carries nothing away' at death; his glory does not descend with him — undergirds the worthlessness of earthly treasure.
sourceText: Don’t be afraid when a man is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased. For when he dies he shall carry nothing away. His glory shall not descend after him.

note: Riches kept by their owner to his hurt, perishing by misfortune, leaving nothing in hand — Qoheleth's meditation on perishable wealth.
sourceText: There is a grievous evil which I have seen under the sun: wealth kept by its owner to his harm. Those riches perish by misfortune, and if he has fathered a son, there is nothing in his hand. As he came out of his mother’s womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, which he may carry away in his hand.

note: Almsgiving lays up 'a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity' — explicit treasure-storing-with-God language behind treasures in heaven.
sourceText: for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity;

note: Bringing tithes into God's storehouse so that heaven's windows pour out blessing — a heaven-versus-earth economy of giving that resonates faintly with heavenly treasure.
sourceText: Will a man rob God? Yet you rob me! But you say, ‘How have we robbed you?’ In tithes and offerings. You are cursed with the curse; for you rob me, even this whole nation. Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this,” says Yahweh of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough for.

note: Kindness to the poor 'lends to the LORD' who repays — the mechanism by which earthly generosity becomes heavenly treasure.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

note: 'He who has a generous eye (bountiful eye) will be blessed' — the Hebrew idiom of the 'good/generous eye' versus the stingy eye underlies the 'sound' (single) eye and the 'evil eye,' linking the lamp saying to generosity (cf. surrounding treasure/mammon).
sourceText: He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.

note: 'A man with an evil eye hastens after riches' — the 'evil eye' as greed/stinginess, the very vice contrasted with the sound eye between the treasure and mammon sayings.
sourceText: A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn’t know that poverty waits for him.

note: Warning against a 'wicked' (mean/evil) eye toward the needy brother — the evil eye as ungenerous miserliness, contextually fitting the eye/lamp logion's placement amid wealth teaching.
sourceText: Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing; and he cry to Yahweh against you, and it be sin to you.

note: 'The commandment is a lamp... the way of life' — light/lamp as moral illumination, the metaphor field Jesus uses for the eye as the body's lamp.
sourceText: For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light. Reproofs of instruction are the way of life,

note: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet' — lamp/light as inner moral guidance, the imagery undergirding the eye as the lamp of the body.
sourceText: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.

note: 'An evil eye is grudging of bread' — Ben Sira's stingy 'evil eye' that begrudges sharing, fitting the generosity reading of the evil eye versus sound eye.
sourceText: An evil eye is grudging of bread, And he is miserly at his table

note: 'The spirit of man is the LORD's lamp, searching all his innermost parts' — inner illumination imagery related to the lamp of the body.
sourceText: The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.

note: 'Love the LORD your God with all your heart' — the Shema's demand of undivided love is what divided service to two masters (God and Mammon) violates; one cannot love both wholly.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: 'Choose this day whom you will serve' — the exclusive either/or of covenant allegiance behind 'no one can serve two masters.'
sourceText: If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose this day whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”

note: 'How long will you waver between two opinions?' — Elijah's demand to choose between the LORD and Baal, the prophetic either/or pattern of single-master service.
sourceText: Elijah came near to all the people, and said, “How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” The people answered him not a word.

note: 'You shall have no other gods before me' — making wealth a rival master is functional idolatry, the first commandment's exclusivity reframed as God versus Mammon.
sourceText: “You shall have no other gods before me.

note: The lover of gold cannot be justified; gold has been a stumbling block and ruin to many — Ben Sira on wealth as an idol-like snare, paralleling serving Mammon.
sourceText: He that loves gold shall not be justified; And he that follows destruction shall himself have his fill of it. Many have been given over to ruin for the sake of gold; And their perdition meets them face to face. It is a stumbling block to those who sacrifice to it; And every fool shall be taken therewith.

note: 'Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you' — the antidote to anxiety is entrusting provision to God, the heart of 'don't be anxious for your life.'
sourceText: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.

note: 'I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging bread' — God's reliable provision for the righteous undergirds 'your heavenly Father feeds them... how much more you.'
sourceText: I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging for bread.

note: God brings forth food and 'satisfies' creation — the Creator's provision for plants, beasts, and people grounds the argument from birds and lilies to human care.
sourceText: He causes the grass to grow for the livestock, and plants for man to cultivate, that he may produce food out of the earth: wine that makes glad the heart of man, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man’s heart.

note: 'These all wait for you... you give them their food in due season' — God feeds all creatures, directly behind 'your heavenly Father feeds' the birds.
sourceText: These all wait for you, that you may give them their food in due season. You give to them; they gather. You open your hand; they are satisfied with good.

note: 'He gives to the animals their food, and to the young ravens which cry' — God feeding the birds is the precise image of 'See the birds of the sky... your heavenly Father feeds them.'
sourceText: He provides food for the livestock, and for the young ravens when they call.

note: 'Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry?' — the divine-speech argument that God feeds wild birds, paralleling the lesson of v.26.
sourceText: Who provides for the raven his prey, when his young ones cry to God, and wander for lack of food?

note: 'Ask the animals... the birds of the sky' — they teach that God's hand holds all life; the pedagogy of learning providence from birds matches 'See the birds of the sky.'
sourceText: “But ask the animals, now, and they shall teach you; the birds of the sky, and they shall tell you. Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach you. The fish of the sea shall declare to you. Who doesn’t know that in all these, the hand of Yahweh has done this, in whose hand is the life of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind?

note: Ravens feed Elijah at God's command — a narrative enactment of God using birds in provision, faintly behind the birds-fed-by-the-Father motif.
sourceText: It shall be, that you shall drink of the brook. I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.” So he went and did according to Yahweh’s word; for he went and lived by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan. The ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook.

note: Solomon's surpassing glory and splendor (the queen of Sheba's awe) is the explicit comparison: 'even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these' (v.29).
sourceText: When the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, and the house that he had built, and the food of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their clothing, and his cup bearers, and his ascent by which he went up to Yahweh’s house; there was no more spirit in her. She said to the king, “It was a true report that I heard in my own land of your acts, and of your wisdom. However I didn’t believe the words, […]

note: The daily manna ('a day's portion') typifies the day-at-a-time trust of 'don't be anxious for tomorrow'; Israel's wilderness schooling in non-hoarding dependence.
sourceText: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.

note: God let Israel hunger then fed with manna 'that he might teach you that man does not live by bread alone' — provision as a lesson in dependence, behind seeking the Kingdom first over food.
sourceText: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.

note: Solomon seeks wisdom (God's priority) and is given riches and honor 'as well' — the exact pattern of 'seek first God's Kingdom... and all these things will be added.'
sourceText: God said to him, “Because you have asked this thing, and have not asked for yourself long life, neither have asked riches for yourself, nor have asked the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern justice; behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a wise and an understanding heart; so that there has been no one like you before you, neither after you shall any arise like you. I have also given you […]

note: 'Commit your works to the LORD, and your plans will be established' — entrusting one's concerns to God rather than anxious self-provision.
sourceText: Commit your deeds to Yahweh, and your plans shall succeed.

note: 'All flesh is grass... the grass withers' — the transience of grass that today is and tomorrow is burned (v.30) draws on Isaiah's grass-and-flower imagery of human frailty.
sourceText: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”

note: Humanity 'like grass which grows up. In the morning it flourishes... in the evening it is cut down' — the grass-of-the-field's day-long life behind v.30.
sourceText: You sweep them away as they sleep. In the morning they sprout like new grass. In the morning it sprouts and springs up. By evening, it is withered and dry.

note: 'As for man, his days are like grass... the wind passes over it, and it is gone' — reinforces the perishable grass imagery applied to the field's clothing.
sourceText: As for man, his days are like grass. As a flower of the field, so he flourishes. For the wind passes over it, and it is gone. Its place remembers it no more.

note: Toil for bread and the field's produce under the curse — the labor of sowing/reaping and anxious provision that Jesus relativizes by pointing to birds that neither sow nor reap.
sourceText: It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

note: Manna provision teaches that 'it is not the production of crops that feeds humankind but your word that sustains those who trust in you' — Second Temple reflection on God-given sustenance versus anxious labor.
sourceText: Therefore at that time also, converting itself into all forms, It ministered to your all-nourishing bounty, According to the desire of those who made supplication; That your sons, whom you loved, O Lord, might learn That it is not the growth of the earth’s fruits that nourishes a man, But that your word preserves those who trust you.

note: 'Anxiety brings on premature old age' — Ben Sira on the harm of worry, faintly paralleling 'which of you by being anxious can add to his lifespan?'
sourceText: Envy and wrath shorten a man’s days; And care brings old age before the time.

note: The ant gathers in summer — a nature-observation wisdom form ('consider the ant'); Jesus inverts the genre with 'consider the lilies' which do NOT toil, yet are clothed.
sourceText: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest.

note: The Holiness Code's demand for righteous, unbiased judgment ('you shall not be partial... but in righteousness shall you judge') underlies Jesus' critique of hypocritical, self-exempting judging.
sourceText: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.

note: Reproof of 'your brother/neighbor' without bearing sin or grudge frames the speck-and-beam logic: correction must be cleansed of self-righteousness; 'brother' language matches Lev's love-of-neighbor unit.
sourceText: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him. “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: Nathan's 'You are the man!' — David condemns another's sin while blind to his own — is the narrative archetype of judging with a beam in one's eye.
sourceText: David’s anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As Yahweh lives, the man who has done this is worthy to die! He shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity!” Nathan said to David, “You are the man. This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.

note: Measure-for-measure principle ('with the merciful you show yourself merciful... with the crooked, shrewd'): God deals back in kind, echoed in 'with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.'
sourceText: With the merciful you will show yourself merciful. With the perfect man, you will show yourself perfect. With the pure, you will show yourself pure. With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.

note: 'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD' — leaving recompense to God, the disposition behind 'judge not, that you be not judged.'
sourceText: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.

note: God judges with measured forbearance so the righteous learn to be kind; a Second Temple articulation of the reciprocal-measure ethic.
sourceText: While therefore you do chasten us, you scourge our enemies ten thousand times more, To the intent that we may ponder your goodness when we judge, And when we are judged may look for mercy.

note: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong... and then your sins will be pardoned' — the reciprocity of judgment/forgiveness in wisdom tradition closely parallels 7:1-2.
sourceText: He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins. Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins? He being himself flesh nourishes wrath: Who will make atonement for his sins? Remember your […]

note: 'Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words' — withholding precious teaching from those who will only scorn it parallels not casting pearls before swine.
sourceText: Don’t speak in the ears of a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words.

note: Correcting a scoffer brings abuse ('reprove a scoffer and he will hate you'); the rebuffing 'dogs' who 'turn and tear you' echoes the futility of instructing scorners.
sourceText: He who corrects a mocker invites insult. He who reproves a wicked man invites abuse. Don’t reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you. Reprove a wise man, and he will love you.

note: A gold ring in a swine's snout — wisdom tradition's pairing of something precious with a pig as image of incongruity.
sourceText: Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout, is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion.

note: 'That which is holy' (qodesh) — sacred offerings forbidden to the unconsecrated/profane — supplies cultic background for not giving the holy to dogs.
sourceText: “‘No stranger shall eat of the holy thing: a foreigner living with the priests, or a hired servant, shall not eat of the holy thing. But if a priest buys a slave, purchased by his money, he shall eat of it; and such as are born in his house, they shall eat of his bread. If a priest’s daughter is married to an outsider, she shall not eat of the heave offering of the holy things. But if a priest’s daughter is a widow, or divorced, and has no child, and has […]

note: Sacred meat is to be thrown to the dogs as the antithesis of holy use; the dog as the unclean recipient of holy things underlies the saying's logic.
sourceText: “You shall be holy men to me, therefore you shall not eat any flesh that is torn by animals in the field. You shall cast it to the dogs.

note: 'You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart' — the seek/find promise behind 'Seek, and you will find.'
sourceText: You shall seek me, and find me, when you shall search for me with all your heart.

note: 'From there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search with all your heart' — covenantal seek-and-find assurance.
sourceText: But from there you shall seek Yahweh your God, and you shall find him, when you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.

note: Wisdom: 'those who seek me diligently find me' — the wisdom-tradition seek/find topos applied to prayer.
sourceText: I love those who love me. Those who seek me diligently will find me.

note: 'Seek the LORD while he may be found, call upon him while he is near' — seeking and calling that meet divine availability.
sourceText: Seek Yahweh while he may be found; call you on him while he is near:

note: 'The LORD is near to all who call on him... he fulfills the desire of those who fear him' — the Father's reliable response to those who ask.
sourceText: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him. He also will hear their cry, and will save them.

note: A mother cannot forget her nursing child — the a fortiori of parental compassion ('how much more your Father') has prophetic precedent.
sourceText: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!

note: 'As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion' — the very father-to-children analogy of 7:11.
sourceText: Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him.

note: God hears the prayer of the wronged and does not ignore supplication — Second Temple confidence in answered petition.
sourceText: He will not accept any person against a poor man; And he will listen to the prayer of him that is wronged. He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall?

note: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' — the Golden Rule reformulates the command Jesus elsewhere names as summing the Law (Mt 22:39-40), here explicitly 'the law and the prophets.'
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'What you hate, do to no one' — the negative form of the Golden Rule in the deuterocanon; the closest verbal precedent to 7:12's reciprocity maxim.
sourceText: And what you yourself hate, do to no man. Don’t drink wine to drunkenness, and don’t let drunkenness go with you on your way.

note: Extension of neighbor-love to the resident alien ('love him as yourself') broadens the rule's scope to 'men' generally.
sourceText: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.

note: 'Judge your neighbor's feelings by your own' — wisdom-tradition empathic reciprocity anticipating the Golden Rule.
sourceText: Consider your neighbor’s liking by your own; And be discreet in every point.

note: The Mosaic 'two ways' — life and good vs. death and evil, with the call to 'choose life' — is the foundational template for the two gates/ways leading to life or destruction.
sourceText: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]

note: 'I set before you the way of life and the way of death' — the explicit prophetic 'way of life / way of death' formula behind 7:13-14.
sourceText: To this people you shall say, Thus says Yahweh: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.

note: 'The LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish' — the two-ways frame (the same Psalm informs 7:17-19 on trees/fruit).
sourceText: For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.

note: The path of the righteous vs. the way of the wicked who stumble in darkness — wisdom's contrasted ways.
sourceText: But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light, that shines more and more until the perfect day. The way of the wicked is like darkness. They don’t know what they stumble over.

note: 'There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death' — the broad way that 'leads to destruction.'
sourceText: There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.

note: 'The way of sinners is smoothly paved... but at its end is the pit of Hades' — Second Temple two-ways with a broad/smooth road to destruction.
sourceText: The way of sinners is made smooth with stones; And at the last end thereof is the pit of Hades.

note: The blessing-and-curse alternative set before Israel reinforces the binary-choice structure.
sourceText: Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse: the blessing, if you listen to the commandments of Yahweh your God, which I command you this day; and the curse, if you do not listen to the commandments of Yahweh your God, but turn aside out of the way which I command you this day, to go after other gods, which you have not known.

note: Israel's princes are 'like wolves tearing the prey' for gain — the predatory-wolf image for corrupt leaders, here the false prophets 'inwardly ravening wolves.'
sourceText: Her princes in its midst are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.

note: Judah's officials are 'roaring lions,' her judges 'evening wolves,' her prophets 'treacherous' — prophets/leaders as wolves cloaking treachery.
sourceText: Her princes in the midst of her are roaring lions. Her judges are evening wolves. They leave nothing until the next day. Her prophets are arrogant and treacherous people. Her priests have profaned the sanctuary. They have done violence to the law.

note: Warning against false prophets who speak from their own minds, not the LORD; the test of true vs. false prophecy frames 'beware of false prophets.'
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh of Armies, Don’t listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you: they teach you vanity; they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of Yahweh. They say continually to those who despise me, Yahweh has said, You shall have peace; and to everyone who walks in the stubbornness of his own heart they say, No evil shall come on you. For who has stood in the council of Yahweh, that he should perceive and hear his […]

note: The Torah test for a false prophet who leads astray though signs come true — background to discerning prophets 'by their fruits.'
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul. […]

note: The criterion for distinguishing the prophet who speaks presumptuously — judging the prophet by outcome/fruit.
sourceText: But the prophet who speaks a word presumptuously in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.” You may say in your heart, “How shall we know the word which Yahweh has not spoken?” When a prophet speaks in Yahweh’s name, if the thing doesn’t follow, nor happen, that is the thing which Yahweh has not spoken. The prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You shall not be afraid of him.

note: The righteous as a tree yielding its fruit in season vs. the wicked as chaff — the good-tree/good-fruit and judgment imagery of Ps 1 underlies 7:17-19.
sourceText: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.

note: The one trusting the LORD is a tree by water that 'does not cease to bear fruit' — fruitfulness as the mark of right relation to God.
sourceText: For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and shall not fear when heat comes, but its leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.

note: The vineyard yielding wild/bad grapes instead of good is judged and destroyed — bad fruit signaling false standing and impending judgment.
sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]

note: Ephraim 'blighted, their root dried up, they shall bear no fruit' — fruitlessness as ground for being cut off.
sourceText: Ephraim is struck. Their root has dried up. They will bear no fruit. Even though they give birth, yet I will kill the beloved ones of their womb.”

note: The coming day burns the evildoers like stubble; 'every tree that doesn't grow good fruit is... thrown into the fire' shares the burning-judgment image.
sourceText: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

note: Trees whose fruit is for food, leaves for healing — the eschatological good-tree image as foil to the corrupt tree.
sourceText: By the river on its bank, on this side and on that side, shall grow every tree for food, whose leaf shall not wither, neither shall its fruit fail: it shall produce new fruit every month, because its waters issue out of the sanctuary; and its fruit shall be for food, and its leaf for healing.

note: 'The fruit discloses the cultivation of a tree, so the expression of a thought discloses the heart' — wisdom maxim that fruit reveals inner character.
sourceText: The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man.

note: 'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity' — verbatim source of Jesus' dismissal sentence in 7:23.
sourceText: Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for Yahweh has heard the voice of my weeping.

note: Prophets prophesy lies 'in my name' though the LORD did not send them — 'didn't we prophesy in your name?' echoes false prophecy claiming the divine name.
sourceText: Then Yahweh said to me, The prophets prophesy lies in my name; I didn’t send them, neither have I commanded them, neither spoke I to them: they prophesy to you a lying vision, and divination, and a thing of nothing, and the deceit of their own heart.

note: 'They prophesy falsely in my name' — the divine repudiation of those who invoke God's name without commission.
sourceText: For I have not sent them, says Yahweh, but they prophesy falsely in my name; that I may drive you out, and that you may perish, you, and the prophets who prophesy to you.

note: 'The LORD will make known who is his' — the motif of God knowing/owning his own, inverted in 'I never knew you.'
sourceText: He said to Korah and to all his company, “In the morning, Yahweh will show who are his, and who is holy, and will cause him to come near to him. Even him whom he shall choose, he will cause to come near to him.

note: 'The LORD knows the way of the righteous' — divine 'knowing' as covenantal acknowledgment, denied to the iniquitous in 7:23.
sourceText: For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.

note: Israel cries 'My God, we know you!' yet has spurned the good — claiming acquaintance with God while doing iniquity, repudiated.
sourceText: They cry to me, ‘My God, we Israel acknowledge you!’ Israel has cast off that which is good. The enemy will pursue him.

note: 'When the storm passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever' — the storm that sweeps away the unfounded vs. the firmly founded, the core contrast of the two builders.
sourceText: When the whirlwind passes, the wicked is no more; but the righteous stand firm forever.

note: 'The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand' — the standing vs. falling house image.
sourceText: The wicked are overthrown, and are no more, but the house of the righteous shall stand.

note: False prophets build a wall and daub it with whitewash; rain, hailstones and wind break it down so it falls — the rain/flood/wind destroying a poorly founded structure, directly behind the collapsing house. (Links the false-prophet warning of 7:15 to its judgment.)
sourceText: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there is no peace; and when one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash: tell those who plaster it with whitewash, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and you, great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall tear it. Behold, when the wall has fallen, shall it not be said to you, Where is the plaster with which you have plastered it? Therefore […]

note: God lays a tested foundation stone; hail sweeps away the refuge of lies, waters overflow the shelter — the secure foundation vs. the false refuge swept by flood.
