note: 'The vats shall overflow with wine.' The eschatological abundance of new wine in the prophets colors Jesus' 'new wine' as the inbreaking new age incompatible with old structures.
sourceText: The threshing floors will be full of wheat, and the vats will overflow with new wine and oil.

note: 'The mountains shall drip sweet wine.' Like Joel, an eschatological new-wine motif faintly resonant with Jesus' claim that the new cannot be poured into the old.
sourceText: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the one treading grapes him who sows seed; and sweet wine will drip from the mountains, and flow from the hills.

note: 'When you fasted and mourned... was it for me?' Zechariah's critique of fasting that misses God anticipates Jesus' relativizing of John's-disciples' fasting in light of the bridegroom's presence.
sourceText: “Speak to all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, ‘When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and in the seventh month for these seventy years, did you at all fast to me, really to me?

note: 'He was taken away.' Jesus' ominous 'the bridegroom will be taken away' foreshadows the passion; the Servant who is 'taken away' is a plausible typological reservoir, though the verbal link is slight.
sourceText: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?

note: The woman touches 'the fringe (kraspedon/tzitzit) of his garment.' The tassels commanded in Numbers mark the wearer as a Torah-keeping Israelite; Matthew specifies the fringe, framing the healing power as flowing through Jesus' faithful Israelite dress.
sourceText: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;

note: The statute on a woman with a chronic 'discharge of blood' renders her and what she touches unclean. The twelve-year hemorrhage and her touching Jesus directly engage this purity law; rather than contracting impurity, Jesus communicates cleansing health.
sourceText: “‘If a woman has a discharge of her blood many days not in the time of her period, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her period; all the days of the discharge of her uncleanness shall be as in the days of her period: she is unclean. Every bed whereon she lies all the days of her discharge shall be to her as the bed of her period: and everything whereon she sits shall be unclean, as the uncleanness of her period. Whoever touches these things […]

note: Elijah raises the widow's dead son. The prophetic raising of a dead child is the primary type for Jesus entering, taking the girl by the hand, and raising her; Matthew presents Jesus as greater than Elijah.
sourceText: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]

note: Elisha raises the Shunammite's daughter, entering the room, acting on the child's body, and restoring her. The closest structural type (a girl, an anxious parent, prophet enters and revives), illuminating Jesus' act in the ruler's house.
sourceText: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (kanaf)' — kanaf also meaning the garment-corner/fringe. The pun links the healing 'fringe' the woman grasps to the messianic promise of healing in the 'wings,' a suggestive but disputed resonance.
sourceText: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.

note: 'Many who sleep in the dust... shall awake.' Jesus' 'the girl is not dead but sleeping' frames death as sleep, the idiom Daniel uses for resurrection, hinting that the raising prefigures eschatological awakening.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: The martyr's hope: 'the King of the universe will raise us up.' Second Temple resurrection hope forms the conceptual horizon for the daughter's restoration being read as more than resuscitation; relevant but not a verbal borrowing.
sourceText: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.

note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened.' The opening of the two blind men's eyes enacts the signature sign of Isaiah's coming-of-God salvation oracle; Matthew uses it programmatically (cf. 11:5) to identify Jesus' deeds with the promised restoration.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.

note: The Davidic covenant promising David an everlasting offspring/throne is the root of the title 'Son of David' the blind men cry. Matthew's recurring Davidic christology (1:1) is voiced precisely by those seeking mercy and sight.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]

note: 'Out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see.' A second Isaianic blindness-reversal oracle reinforcing that restored sight is the mark of God's eschatological visitation now effected by Jesus.
sourceText: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.

note: The Servant is called 'to open the eyes that are blind.' The opening of eyes as the Servant's commissioned task links Jesus' healing to Isaiah's servant-of-the-LORD vocation.
sourceText: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: 'The LORD opens the eyes of the blind.' The psalm ascribes eye-opening to the LORD himself; Jesus performing it implies the same divine agency the crowd marveled at in 9:8.
sourceText: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.

note: 'Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy.' The blind men's cry 'Have mercy on us' echoes the standard psalmic appeal for divine mercy, now addressed to the Son of David.
sourceText: Have mercy on us, Yahweh, have mercy on us, for we have endured much contempt.

note: Tobit's blindness is cured and 'his eyes were opened.' The deuterocanonical healing-of-blindness narrative is a Second Temple precedent for restored sight as a sign of divine favor; thematically apt though not directly quoted.
sourceText: Raphael said, “I know, Tobias, that your father will open his eyes. Therefore anoint his eyes with the gall, and being pricked therewith, he will rub, and willl make the white films fall away. Then he will see you.” Anna ran to him, and fell upon the neck of her son, and said to him, “I have seen you, my child! I am ready to die.” They wept both. Tobit went toward the door and stumbled; but his son ran to him, and took hold of his father. He rubbed the […]

note: 'The tongue of the mute shall sing for joy.' The mute man speaking when the demon is cast out completes the Isaiah 35 cluster (blind see in 9:30, mute speak here), presenting Jesus' miracles as the bundled signs of Isaiah's restoration.
sourceText: Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.

note: 'Who makes him mute... Is it not I, the LORD?' God's claim to sovereignty over speech and its impairment frames Jesus' loosing of the mute tongue as a divine prerogative exercised.
sourceText: Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?

note: 'Like a mute man who does not open his mouth... but for you, O LORD, do I wait.' The psalmic muteness-then-divine-help pattern faintly underlies the restoration of speech, though no verbal borrowing is present.
sourceText: But I, as a deaf man, don’t hear. I am as a mute man who doesn’t open his mouth. Yes, I am as a man who doesn’t hear, in whose mouth are no reproofs. For in you, Yahweh, do I hope. You will answer, Lord my God.

note: Moses asks for a successor so the congregation 'may not be as sheep that have no shepherd.' Matthew's 'harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd' directly takes up this idiom; Jesus' compassion answers Israel's perennial need for a true shepherd-leader.
sourceText: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”

note: Micaiah sees 'all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd.' The leaderless, scattered flock under failed kings is exactly Matthew's diagnosis of the crowds, with Jesus stepping into the vacant shepherd role.
sourceText: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let them each return to his house in peace.’”

note: 'They were scattered because there was no shepherd.' Ezekiel's indictment of Israel's negligent shepherds and promise that God himself will shepherd the flock is the richest backdrop: Jesus' compassion enacts the LORD's pledge to seek the scattered sheep.
sourceText: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered.

note: The people 'wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd.' Zechariah's shepherdless, afflicted flock parallels Matthew's 'harassed' crowds, adding a prophetic voice to the shepherd-deficit motif.
sourceText: For the teraphim have spoken vanity, and the diviners have seen a lie; and they have told false dreams. They comfort in vain. Therefore they go their way like sheep. They are oppressed, because there is no shepherd.

note: The Chronicler's parallel to 1 Kings 22:17 repeats 'all Israel scattered... as sheep that have no shepherd,' a second canonical attestation of the formula behind 9:36.
sourceText: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let them return every man to his house in peace.’”

note: 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.' Jesus' 'the harvest is plentiful' picks up the prophetic harvest image; where Joel's harvest is judgment, Matthew turns it toward ingathering, asking for laborers from the Lord of the harvest.
sourceText: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”

note: 'The LORD will thresh... and you will be gathered one by one.' The eschatological gathering-harvest of Israel is a faint resonance behind the plentiful harvest needing laborers.
sourceText: It will happen in that day, that Yahweh will thresh from the flowing stream of the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt; and you will be gathered one by one, children of Israel.

note: 'I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David.' The promise of a single Davidic shepherd is figurally fulfilled as Jesus (the Son of David of 9:27) responds to the shepherdless crowds, binding this pericope to the Davidic christology of the chapter.
sourceText: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.

note: The number Twelve is the structuring datum of the apostle list. Jacob's twelve sons becoming the twelve tribes is the obvious typological template: Jesus constitutes a renewed Israel of twelve, an eschatological re-founding of the people (cf. Mt 19:28, the Twelve judging the twelve tribes). The figural reading is widely held.
sourceText: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his blessing.

note: Moses builds an altar with twelve pillars 'according to the twelve tribes of Israel' at the covenant ratification. The setting-apart of twelve representatives at a covenant moment is a thematic analogue to the appointment of the Twelve; faint and dependent on the broader twelve-tribe pattern.
sourceText: Moses wrote all Yahweh’s words, and rose up early in the morning, and built an altar under the mountain, and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.

note: The census appoints twelve tribal leaders, 'every one for the house of his fathers.' A possible background for the twelve named representatives commissioned for a task on Israel's behalf, but the link is purely numerical and structural.
sourceText: These are those who were numbered, whom Moses and Aaron numbered, and the princes of Israel, being twelve men: they were each one for his fathers’ house.

note: 'My people have been lost sheep' (Jer 50:6) supplies the exact image and idiom behind 'the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (10:6). The phrase is a deliberate scriptural designation of Israel as a flock gone astray under failed shepherds, which the mission of the Twelve is sent to gather.
sourceText: My people have been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray; they have turned them away on the mountains; they have gone from mountain to hill; they have forgotten their resting place.

note: Ezekiel's flock 'scattered because there was no shepherd' and the sheep that 'wandered through all the mountains' is the controlling background for Israel-as-lost-sheep. Ezek 34:16, 'I will seek that which was lost,' frames the apostolic mission as God's promised search for the strays.
sourceText: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.

note: Israel as a congregation 'as sheep which have no shepherd,' Moses' prayer for a successor. Matthew uses this very phrase at 9:36 immediately before this commissioning, so it bleeds directly into the 'lost sheep' rationale for sending the Twelve.

note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray.' Reinforces the lost-sheep idiom for Israel's straying, though without the verbal specificity of Jeremiah or Ezekiel.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: 'Sodom and Gomorrah' (10:15) names the archetypal city of judgment whose destruction by fire becomes the proverbial worst-case fate. Jesus says it will be 'more tolerable' for them than for a town that rejects the apostles — a direct invocation of the Genesis paradigm of inhospitality and overthrow.
sourceText: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky. He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground.

note: The hospitality/inhospitality axis governing the worthy-household and shake-off-the-dust instructions (10:11-15) culminates in the Sodom comparison; Abraham's reception of the visitors vs. Sodom's refusal is the implicit contrast. The sin of Sodom as failed hospitality (cf. Ezek 16:49) underlies the whole judgment logic.

Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]

note: The Passover departure 'with your staff in your hand' and sandals on, ready to travel light, sits in ironic counterpoint to the mission's stripping away of staff, sandals (in the Markan form), and provisions. A possible inversion of the exodus travel kit, but the parallel is contested and the Matthean list differs.
sourceText: This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.

note: Elisha sends Gehazi with staff and the urgent command not to greet anyone on the road — a prophetic-commission travel instruction with the same terse, single-minded haste as the mission charge. Faint and disputed.
sourceText: Then he said to Gehazi, “Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my staff in your hand, and go your way. If you meet any man, don’t greet him; and if anyone greets you, don’t answer him again. Then lay my staff on the face of the child.”

note: Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his garment as a prophetic sign-act of rejection and curse against those who break faith. A possible cultural background for 'shake off the dust from your feet' (10:14) as a gesture of testimony against, though the dust-of-the-feet gesture is not identical.
sourceText: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.

note: 'Be wise as serpents' (10:16) trades on the serpent of Eden being 'more subtle/cunning than any beast of the field.' Jesus redeems the proverbial shrewdness of the serpent for the disciples' survival among hostile men; the verbal link to the Genesis serpent's craftiness is the most natural source.
sourceText: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”

note: Israel's predatory leaders are 'like wolves ravening the prey.' Combined with Zeph 3:3 this supplies the biblical 'wolves' menacing the flock, now the danger the sheep-disciples are sent into the midst of (10:16).
sourceText: Her princes in its midst are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.

note: 'Her princes within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves.' Reinforces the wolves-among-the-flock danger and specifically locates the threat in officials and judges — apt for 10:17-18, the councils, governors, and kings before whom disciples are dragged.
sourceText: Her princes in the midst of her are roaring lions. Her judges are evening wolves. They leave nothing until the next day.

note: 'What fellowship has the wolf with the lamb? No more has the sinner with the godly.' Second Temple wisdom uses the wolf/lamb pairing precisely for the irreconcilable hostility between the righteous and the wicked — close to the 'sheep among wolves' logic of the persecuted mission.
sourceText: What fellowship shall the wolf have with the lamb? So is the sinner to the godly.

note: God's promise to the prophet sent to kings and nations — 'I have put my words in your mouth' — is the prophetic-call template behind 10:19-20: do not be anxious what to say, for it will be given you in that hour; it is the Spirit of your Father speaking in you. The handing-over of words to a divinely commissioned spokesman before hostile rulers is the same scene.
sourceText: But Yahweh said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak. Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh. Then Yahweh stretched out his hand, and touched my mouth; and Yahweh said to me, “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.

note: 'I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.' Moses' commissioning, where God overrides the inadequate speaker by supplying the very words, is the foundational background for 'it will be given you in that hour what you will say' and 'it is not you who speak' (10:19-20).
sourceText: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”

note: 'The Spirit of the LORD spoke by me, and his word was in my tongue.' David's last words present the same pattern of the Spirit speaking through a human mouth, a faint background for the Spirit of the Father speaking in the disciples (10:20).
sourceText: “The Spirit of Yahweh spoke by me. His word was on my tongue.

note: 'The son dishonoreth the father... a man's enemies are the men of his own house.' Micah's portrait of the collapse of household loyalty in a day of distress stands behind 10:21 ('brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child; children will rise up against parents'). The same text is quoted more fully at 10:35-36; here it surfaces in the persecution context of intra-familial betrayal unto death.
sourceText: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.

note: 'Blessed is he that waiteth and cometh... thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days.' Daniel's eschatological endurance-to-the-end-and-be-vindicated theme underlies 10:22, 'he who endures to the end will be saved,' set amid tribulation.
sourceText: Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days. But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.

note: 'One like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven.' 10:23, 'until the Son of Man has come,' draws its title and its coming-in-judgment expectation from Daniel's vision; the apocalyptic horizon of the persecution sayings is Danielic.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: 'Beelzebul' (10:25) derives from Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron whom Ahaziah consults. The name of the rejected foreign deity becomes the slander hurled at 'the master of the house'; the disciples should expect the same naming, 'how much more those of his household.'

note: 'Neither fear ye their fear... Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear.' Isaiah's command to fear God rather than the conspiracy of men is the precise logic of 10:28: do not fear those who kill the body, but fear him who can destroy soul and body. The double 'do not fear / rather fear' structure is Isaianic.
sourceText: “Don’t say, ‘A conspiracy!’ concerning all about which this people say, ‘A conspiracy!’ neither fear their threats, nor be terrorized. Yahweh of Armies is who you must respect as holy. He is the one you must fear. He is the one you must dread.

note: 'Gehenna' (10:28) is the valley of Hinnom (Topheth), the site of child-sacrifice that Jeremiah declares will become 'the valley of slaughter.' The OT condemnation of this valley as the place of fiery judgment supplies the term for the place where God can destroy both soul and body.
sourceText: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind. Therefore behold, the days come”, says Yahweh, “that it shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter; for they shall bury in Topheth, until there is no place to bury.

note: Josiah defiles Topheth in the valley of the children of Hinnom so none could pass a child through fire to Molech. Reinforces the Gehenna background as the defiled valley of fire that becomes the figure of final destruction (10:28).
sourceText: He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.

note: 'There shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground.' The idiom of every hair guarded as a token of total providential protection (cf. 2 Sam 14:11; 1 Kgs 1:52) lies directly behind 10:30, 'the very hairs of your head are all numbered,' assuring the disciples of God's exhaustive care amid persecution.
sourceText: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God this day!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.

note: God keeps count of the sufferer's wanderings and bottles his tears. A thematic analogue to the divine bookkeeping of hairs and the fall of sparrows (10:29-31) — God's minute attention to the afflicted — though without verbal overlap.
sourceText: You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren’t they in your book?

note: 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.' The wisdom maxim that proper fear is owed to God alone undergirds the redirection of fear in 10:28, but the connection is general rather than verbal.
sourceText: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.

note: 'I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.' A faint analogue to confessing Christ before men without shame (10:32), continuous with the 'testimony before governors and kings' of 10:18. Disputed and thematic only.
sourceText: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.

note: 10:35-36 is a near-verbatim rendering of Micah 7:6: 'the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house.' Matthew reproduces the three paired antagonisms (father/son here as father, daughter/mother, daughter-in-law/mother-in-law) and the climactic 'a man's foes will be those of his own household' almost word for word. This is the strongest, formula-grade allusion in the chapter.
sourceText: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.

note: Levi 'said unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him; neither did he acknowledge his brethren... for they have observed thy word.' The blessing praises placing covenant loyalty above family bonds — the same demand as 10:37, loving God above father, mother, son, daughter. A recognized OT precedent for cult loyalty overriding kinship.
sourceText: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.

note: The Levites slay brother, companion, and neighbor at Moses' command and are thereby 'consecrated.' A harsh background for loyalty to God dividing even kin (10:34-37); thematically apt but lexically distant and contested.

note: The man who brings provisions to Elisha and 'the servant of the prophet' setting it before the people — a faint analogue to ministering to God's agents and not losing one's reward (10:42), within the same Elisha hospitality cycle.
sourceText: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]

note: Giving the thirsty water to drink as a rewarded act of mercy is a wisdom analogue to 'a cup of cold water... he will in no way lose his reward' (10:42), though the proverb concerns an enemy. Thematic and disputed.
sourceText: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.

note: Jesus' catalog of signs answers John by weaving Isaiah's vision of the redeemed: 'the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped' — 'the blind receive sight, the deaf hear' borrows verbatim imagery, marking the dawning kingdom.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.

note: 'Then shall the lame man leap as a hart' directly underlies 'the lame walk'; Isaiah 35 is the controlling subtext for Jesus' reply, signaling that the eschatological restoration has arrived.
sourceText: Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.

note: 'to preach good news to the poor' (anointed Servant) supplies the climactic 'the poor have good news preached to them' — the same verb/theme Jesus claims as his own programmatic mission (cf. Luke 4:18).
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

note: 'the dead are raised up' echoes Isaiah's resurrection hope, 'Your dead shall live... the earth shall give birth to the dead,' folded into the kingdom-signs list.
sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

note: 'In that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see' — a parallel Isaianic oracle reinforcing the deaf/blind reversal, part of a recurring Isaianic cluster.
sourceText: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.

note: The Servant 'to open the blind eyes' resonates with restoring sight; strengthens the Servant-mission reading of Jesus' self-presentation.
sourceText: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: 'Hear, you deaf; and look, you blind, that you may see' — further Isaianic deaf/blind language drawn into the answer to John.
sourceText: “Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see.

note: 'the lepers are cleansed' presumes the Torah cleansing rite for the healed leper; the only OT framework for leprosy cleansing, evoked figurally as fulfilled.
sourceText: “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest,

note: Naaman's cleansing is the paradigmatic prophetic leprosy healing; a faint precedent for 'lepers are cleansed' as a sign of prophetic power.
sourceText: Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.

note: 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you' is a formula citation ('of whom it is written') of Mal 3:1, 'Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me,' identifying John as the eschatological forerunner.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'Behold, I send a messenger before you' (LXX wording 'before your face') is conflated with Mal 3:1 in the citation; the second-person 'before your face' tracks Exodus more closely than Malachi's 'before me.'
sourceText: “Behold, I send an angel before you, to keep you by the way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.

note: 'this is Elijah, who is to come' directly invokes Mal 4:5, 'I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD,' interpreting John as the returning Elijah.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: The Elijah identification draws on the whole Elijah cycle; the wilderness/mantle prophet of austere dress stands behind the contrast with 'soft clothing' and the desert setting.
sourceText: It was so, when Elijah heard it, that he wrapped his face in his mantle, and went out, and stood in the entrance of the cave. Behold, a voice came to him, and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

note: Elijah 'a hairy man, with a leather belt' grounds the John-as-Elijah figure and the contrast with kingly 'soft clothing'; cf. Matthew's own description of John's garb.
sourceText: They answered him, “He was a hairy man, and wearing a leather belt around his waist.” He said, “It is Elijah the Tishbite.”

note: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see?' evokes the wilderness-voice preparing the way, the same way-preparation motif as the Mal 3:1 citation.
sourceText: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.

note: 'born of women' as a marker of mortal human descent is biblical idiom (cf. Job 14:1; 15:14; 25:4); the phrase frames John as the greatest of mortals.
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: 'Man who is born of a woman is of few days' supplies the idiom 'born of women' for finite humanity, against which John's greatness and the kingdom's superiority are measured.
sourceText: “Man, who is born of a woman, is of few days, and full of trouble.

note: 'wisdom is justified by her children' personifies Wisdom as in Proverbs 8, where Lady Wisdom calls and her children/sons heed her; Jesus and John are vindicated as Wisdom's offspring.
sourceText: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways.

note: 'Wisdom exalts her sons and lays hold of those who seek her' — Second Temple Wisdom personification standing directly behind 'wisdom is justified by her children.'
sourceText: Wisdom exalts her sons, And takes hold of those who seek her.

note: 'a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance' faintly underlies the children's complaint about piping/dancing and mourning/lament.
sourceText: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;

note: Wisdom's banquet invitation supports the wider Wisdom-vindicated theme; contested as a specific source.
sourceText: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars.

note: The oracle against Tyre (and Sidon, v.4) is the prophetic backdrop for naming Tyre/Sidon as proverbially judged Gentile cities now declared less culpable than the unrepentant Galilean towns.
sourceText: The burden of Tyre. Howl, you ships of Tarshish! For it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in. From the land of Kittim it is revealed to them.

note: Ezekiel's extended judgment on Tyre ('I am against you, O Tyre') makes Tyre the type of a doomed city; invoked to shame Chorazin and Bethsaida.
sourceText: therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, Behold, I am against you, Tyre, and will cause many nations to come up against you, as the sea causes its waves to come up.

note: 'Set your face against Sidon' — the companion oracle completing the Tyre/Sidon judgment pair Jesus names.
sourceText: Son of man, set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against it,

note: Sodom's fiery overthrow is the archetypal divine judgment; 'more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment' presupposes Genesis 19 as the benchmark of destroyed wickedness.
sourceText: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky.

note: 'You, Capernaum, exalted to heaven, you will go down to Hades' reworks the taunt against Babylon's king: 'I will ascend into heaven... yet you shall be brought down to Sheol' (Isa 14:13-15).
sourceText: You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north!

note: 'brought down to Sheol' is the direct verbal pattern behind 'go down to Hades'; the proud-exaltation-then-abasement form is borrowed wholesale.
sourceText: Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.

note: Ezekiel compares Jerusalem unfavorably to Sodom ('Sodom your sister has not done as you'), the same rhetorical move — guilty Israel worse than proverbial Sodom — Jesus makes against Capernaum.
sourceText: As I live, says the Lord Yahweh, Sodom your sister has not done, she nor her daughters, as you have done, you and your daughters.

note: 'the punishment of my people is greater than the punishment of Sodom' parallels the comparative-judgment logic; contested as direct source.
sourceText: For the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom, That was overthrown as in a moment, and no hands were laid on her.

note: 'repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes' echoes Nineveh's repentance in sackcloth and ashes, the model Gentile-repentance the Galilean towns failed to match.
sourceText: The news reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.

note: Sodom and Gomorrah's overthrow as covenant-curse paradigm reinforces 'the land of Sodom' as judgment shorthand.
sourceText: and that all of its land is sulfur, salt, and burning, that it is not sown, doesn’t produce, nor does any grass grow in it, like the overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which Yahweh overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath;

note: 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth' echoes Daniel's blessing of the God who 'gives wisdom to the wise' yet reveals hidden things — the same revelation-to-the-lowly, concealment-from-the-wise pattern.
sourceText: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;

note: 'I thank you... you have given me wisdom... made known to us the king's matter' supplies the thanksgiving-for-revelation form behind Jesus' prayer.
sourceText: I thank you, and praise you, you God of my fathers, who have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we desired of you; for you have made known to us the king’s matter.

note: 'the wisdom of their wise men shall perish' grounds the reversal in which God hides 'these things from the wise and understanding' — the same Isaianic critique of human wisdom.
sourceText: therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people, even a marvelous work and a wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men will perish, and the understanding of their prudent men will be hidden.”

note: Sirach 51 opens 'I will give thanks to you, O Lord and King' — a sage's thanksgiving immediately preceding the Wisdom-yoke invitation (Sir 51:23ff) that Matthew 11:28-30 reworks; the thanksgiving + invitation sequence parallels Matthew's.
sourceText: I will give thanks to you, O Lord, O King, And will praise you, O God my Saviour: I do give thanks to your name:

note: 'What is his name, and what is his son's name?' faintly anticipates the exclusive Father-Son mutual knowing of v.27; contested.
sourceText: Who has ascended up into heaven, and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has bound the waters in his garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if you know?

note: The righteous one 'calls himself a child of the Lord' and claims knowledge of God, a Second Temple anticipation of the Son's unique knowledge of the Father.
sourceText: He professes to have knowledge of God, And names himself servant of the Lord.

note: Wisdom's invitation 'Draw near to me, you who are untaught... Put your neck under the yoke, and let your souls receive instruction' is the closest analogue: 'Come to me... Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me.' Jesus speaks as incarnate Wisdom issuing her summons.
sourceText: Draw near to me, you unlearned, And lodge in the house of instruction.

note: 'Put your neck under her yoke, and let your soul receive instruction... See with your eyes how I have labored little and found for myself much rest' — supplies yoke + labor + rest in the same cluster Jesus uses.
sourceText: Put your neck under the yoke, And let your soul receive instruction: She is hard at hand to find.

note: 'I have labored little and found for myself great rest' lies directly behind 'I will give you rest' / 'rest for your souls' joined to taking up the yoke.
sourceText: Behold with your eyes, How that I laboured but a little, And found for myself much rest.

note: 'ask for the old paths... and you will find rest for your souls' is verbatim behind 'you will find rest for your souls' (Mt 11:29); Jesus offers the rest Jeremiah's generation refused.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, “Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths, ‘Where is the good way?’ and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls. But they said, ‘We will not walk in it.’

note: 'Put your feet into her fetters, and your neck into her collar/yoke... at last you will find her rest' — Sirach's earlier Wisdom-yoke passage doubling the yoke-and-rest motif.
sourceText: And bring your feet into her fetters, And your neck into her chain.

note: 'at last you will find the rest she gives, and she will be changed into joy for you' reinforces the Wisdom-yoke-rest pattern adopted in vv.28-30.
sourceText: For at the last you will find her rest; And she will be turned for you into gladness.

note: 'My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest' is the foundational divine promise of rest; 'I will give you rest' assumes God as the giver of rest.
sourceText: He said, “My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.”

note: 'gentle and lowly in heart' echoes the humble/meek king who comes 'lowly and riding on a donkey' (Mt 21:5 cites it); the same praus self-description.
sourceText: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

note: 'the man Moses was very meek, above all men' offers a precedent for 'I am gentle (meek) and lowly,' figuring Jesus as a new Moses giving an easy yoke.
sourceText: Now the man Moses was very humble, above all the men who were on the surface of the earth.

note: 'his yoke shall depart... his burden depart from off their shoulder' — the relief-from-yoke/burden imagery faintly contrasts with Jesus' light yoke and easy burden.
sourceText: that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and tread him under foot on my mountains. Then his yoke will leave them, and his burden leave their shoulders.

note: 'Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters' is the open invitational form ('Come to me, all') of prophetic Wisdom-summons.
sourceText: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

note: David, hungry, enters the house of God and eats the bread of the Presence (showbread), unlawful for any but priests. Jesus cites this episode by name ('what David did') as the controlling precedent for need overriding cultic restriction. Strong verbal and narrative borrowing: David + companions + hunger + eating the consecrated bread.
sourceText: Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came to meet David trembling, and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no man with you?” David said to Ahimelech the priest, “The king has commanded me a business, and has said to me, ‘Let no man know anything of the business about which I send you, and what I have commanded you; and I have appointed the young men to such and such a place.’ Now therefore what is under your hand? Give me five loaves […]

note: The legislation behind the showbread: twelve loaves set before the LORD, to be eaten only by Aaron and his sons 'in a holy place.' Jesus' phrase 'not lawful... but only for the priests' depends directly on this statute, which makes David's act a transgression that incurs no condemnation.
sourceText: “You shall take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes of it: two tenth parts of an ephah shall be in one cake. You shall set them in two rows, six on a row, on the pure gold table before Yahweh. You shall put pure frankincense on each row, that it may be to the bread for a memorial, even an offering made by fire to Yahweh. Every Sabbath day he shall set it in order before Yahweh continually. It is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting […]

note: The Sabbath burnt offerings (two lambs, with grain and drink offerings) — the legally mandated priestly labor on the Sabbath. This is the 'work' Jesus means when he says priests 'profane the Sabbath and are guiltless,' an a fortiori argument that the temple service licenses Sabbath labor.
sourceText: “‘On the Sabbath day, two male lambs a year old without defect, and two tenth parts of an ephah of fine flour for a meal offering, mixed with oil, and its drink offering: this is the burnt offering of every Sabbath, besides the continual burnt offering, and its drink offering.

note: Formula-marked, near-verbatim citation: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' Matthew uniquely inserts this Hosea line (cf. 9:13) as the hermeneutical key to the whole controversy; condemning the 'guiltless' violates God's own stated priority of mercy over cult.
sourceText: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

note: The Decalogue Sabbath command is the implicit law under dispute ('not lawful to do on the Sabbath'); the entire pericope is a halakhic argument over its proper scope.
sourceText: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]

note: The second Decalogue's Sabbath command, grounding the rest in liberation; relevant background to the dispute over what the Sabbath is for and whom it serves.
sourceText: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]

note: 'In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest' — the specific Sabbath rule sometimes read to forbid reaping; the disciples' plucking of grain would be construed as reaping under this line. Contested as the precise statute the Pharisees invoke.
sourceText: “Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest: in plowing time and in harvest you shall rest.

note: Plucking grain heads by hand from a neighbor's standing crop is explicitly permitted (gleaning by hand, not sickle); the disciples' act is lawful as such — the dispute is only the Sabbath, not theft. Explains why the Pharisees object to the day, not the deed.
sourceText: When you come into your neighbor’s standing grain, then you may pluck the ears with your hand; but you shall not move a sickle to your neighbor’s standing grain.

note: 'Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath' — the title carries the dominion granted to the Danielic 'one like a son of man,' here extended over the Sabbath itself. Contested whether the title here is titular-Danielic or generic 'man.'
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The Sabbath's creational institution: God rests and hallows the seventh day. Jesus' lordship over the Sabbath claim resonates against the divine origin and purpose of the day.
sourceText: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.

note: Ahimelech the priest at Nob is the figure who gives David the bread; Matthew's general 'house of God' (not yet the Jerusalem temple) tracks the Nob sanctuary setting of the source.
sourceText: Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came to meet David trembling, and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no man with you?”

note: The withered/restored hand motif: Jeroboam's hand dries up and is restored at the man of God's word. Closest OT precedent for a 'withered hand' miraculously made whole, providing the verbal-thematic template Matthew's healing fulfills.
sourceText: When the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar in Bethel, Jeroboam put out his hand from the altar, saying, “Seize him!” His hand, which he put out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back again to himself. The altar also was split apart, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by Yahweh’s word. The king answered the man of God, “Now entreat the favor […]

note: 'You shall not see your brother's ox or sheep fallen by the way and hide yourself; you shall help him lift them up.' The rescue-of-fallen-animal obligation underlies Jesus' a fortiori: if you lift a sheep from a pit, how much more do good for a man.
sourceText: You shall not see your brother’s donkey or his ox fallen down by the way, and hide yourself from them. You shall surely help him to lift them up again.

note: Obligation to relieve even an enemy's overburdened or straying animal — Torah's positive duty of mercy to beasts, which Jesus leverages to argue that doing good cannot be a Sabbath violation.
sourceText: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again. If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him, you shall surely help him with it.

note: Again the Sabbath command is the contested law; the healing is staged as a deliberate test case of what 'lawful to do on the Sabbath' includes.
sourceText: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]

note: The mercy-over-cult principle just cited (12:7) governs this scene too: 'it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath' enacts 'I desire mercy.' Thematic continuity links the two Sabbath controversies.
sourceText: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

note: 'How much more value is a man than a sheep' presupposes humanity's higher worth, rooted in creation in God's image; faint background to the lesser-to-greater argument.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: Matthew's longest formula quotation, explicitly marked 'fulfilled... through Isaiah.' The Servant Song: 'Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul delights; I will put my Spirit on him; he will proclaim justice to the nations... a bruised reed he will not break, a smoldering wick he will not quench... and in his name the nations will hope.' Matthew adapts the LXX/Hebrew to interpret Jesus' withdrawal, healing, and command to silence as the meek, non-clamorous Servant's mission.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations. note: 'My chosen... in whom my soul delights, I will put my Spirit on him' verbally underlies the baptismal voice (Matt 3:17) and the Spirit endowment; Matthew here makes explicit the Servant-Christology already signaled at the baptism.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.

sourceText: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit. The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: Servant Song extending the servant's mission to the nations ('a light to the nations'); thematically reinforces 12:18/21 'justice to the nations... the nations will hope.'

note: The crowd's 'Can this be the son of David?' invokes the Davidic-messianic hope of the dynastic promise; Matthew frames Jesus' exorcisms as evidence of Davidic/messianic identity.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. note: 'Shall the prey be taken from the mighty?... I will contend... and save your children.' The strong-man-bound-and-plundered image directly draws on Isaiah's promise that the spoil will be wrested from the tyrant — Jesus binding 'the strong man' (Satan) to plunder his house.
sourceText: Shall the plunder be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captives be delivered?
