note: 'This is the finger of God' — Pharaoh's magicians concede the plagues' divine origin. Luke's parallel reads 'finger of God'; Matthew's 'Spirit of God cast out demons, then the Kingdom of God has come' carries the same Exodus echo: God's power directly at work signals the kingdom's arrival.
sourceText: Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God:” and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them; as Yahweh had spoken.

note: Satan as the adversary rebuked by the LORD; background to the 'If Satan casts out Satan' / kingdom-of-Satan logic.
sourceText: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”

note: The kingdom of God that breaks and supplants all other kingdoms; 'the Kingdom of God has come upon you' resonates with Daniel's eschatological kingdom overthrowing rival dominions (here Satan's).
sourceText: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.

note: 'He who is not with me is against me' carries the covenantal either/or of choosing allegiance ('choose this day whom you will serve'); faint thematic resonance of forced decision.
sourceText: If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose this day whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”

note: 'They rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit; therefore he turned to be their enemy.' Background to the unforgivable 'blasphemy against the Holy Spirit' — opposing the Spirit's manifest work (the exorcisms just performed) provokes irrevocable judgment.
sourceText: But they rebelled, and grieved his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them.

note: The sin done 'with a high hand' that despises the LORD's word and finds no atonement ('that person shall be cut off'); OT precedent for a sin beyond forgiveness, coherent with blasphemy against the Spirit.
sourceText: “‘But the soul who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native-born or a foreigner, the same blasphemes Yahweh. That soul shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised Yahweh’s word, and has broken his commandment, that soul shall utterly be cut off. His iniquity shall be on him.’”

note: 'If a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?' — a sin against God himself leaving no mediation; faint resonance with the unpardonable blasphemy.
sourceText: If one man sin against another, God shall judge him; but if a man sin against Yahweh, who shall entreat for him?” Notwithstanding, they didn’t listen to the voice of their father, because Yahweh intended to kill them.

note: 'The fruit discloses the cultivation of a tree; so a person's speech discloses the cultivation of his mind.' Striking parallel to 'the tree is known by its fruit' applied to speech ('out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks'). Second Temple wisdom on word-as-fruit.
sourceText: The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man.

note: 'From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good' — wisdom linking words to fruit and to one's standing (justification/condemnation by speech), undergirding 'by your words you will be justified.'
sourceText: A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth. The work of a man’s hands shall be rewarded to him.

note: 'Death and life are in the power of the tongue' — words carry decisive judicial weight, coherent with 'by your words... justified... condemned.'
sourceText: Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

note: 'A gentle tongue is a tree of life' — wisdom's tree-and-speech imagery; faint background to the good/corrupt tree and its fruit of words.
sourceText: A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.

note: 'God will bring every deed into judgment... whether good or evil' — background to 'every idle word... in the day of judgment,' extending judgment to speech.
sourceText: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.

note: 'Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the fish' — Jesus quotes this near-verbatim ('three days and three nights in the belly of the whale') as the type of 'the Son of Man... three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.' Figural fulfillment of Jonah's burial-and-deliverance.
sourceText: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

note: Jonah's prayer 'out of the belly of Sheol' and deliverance on the third day is the typological pattern for Jesus' descent into 'the heart of the earth' and resurrection. The whole Jonah-in-the-deep scene is read as a sign of death and rising.
sourceText: Then Jonah prayed to Yahweh, his God, out of the fish’s belly. He said, “I called because of my affliction to Yahweh. He answered me. Out of the belly of Sheol I cried. You heard my voice. For you threw me into the depths, in the heart of the seas. The flood was all around me. All your waves and your billows passed over me. I said, ‘I have been banished from your sight; yet I will look again toward your holy temple.’ The waters surrounded me, even to the […]

note: 'The men of Nineveh... repented at the preaching of Jonah.' Jesus cites Nineveh's repentance as testimony against 'this generation' that refuses the greater preacher. Direct narrative borrowing from Jonah 3.
sourceText: The people of Nineveh believed God; and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from their greatest even to their least. The news reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. He made a proclamation and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, “Let neither man nor animal, herd nor flock, taste anything; let them not feed, […]

note: The queen of Sheba comes 'from the ends of the earth' to hear Solomon's wisdom. Jesus invokes 'the queen of the south' as a witness who sought wisdom, contrasting 'something greater than Solomon.' Verbal and narrative dependence on 1 Kings 10.
sourceText: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning Yahweh’s name, she came to prove him with hard questions. She came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bore spices, and very much gold, and precious stones; and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him of all that was in her heart. Solomon told her all her questions: there was not anything hidden from the king which he didn’t tell her. When the queen of Sheba had […]

note: Parallel account of the queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon; reinforces the 'queen of the south' allusion, drawn from the Chronicler's as well as the Kings narrative.
sourceText: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to prove Solomon with hard questions at Jerusalem, with a very great train, and camels that bore spices, and gold in abundance, and precious stones: and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him of all that was in her heart. Solomon told her all her questions; and there was not anything hidden from Solomon which he didn’t tell her. When the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of […]

note: 'Out of the belly of Sheol I cried' — 'heart of the earth' language for the realm of death echoes Jonah's Sheol/deep imagery specifically.
sourceText: He said, “I called because of my affliction to Yahweh. He answered me. Out of the belly of Sheol I cried. You heard my voice.

note: 'On the third day he will raise us up' — the 'third day' resurrection schema possibly informs Jesus' 'three days' beyond the Jonah figure alone. Contested as a contributing intertext.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: 'A perverse and crooked generation' — the Song of Moses' indictment lies behind Matthew's recurrent 'evil and adulterous generation'; covenantal-prophetic language for a faithless people.
sourceText: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.

note: 'A perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness' — reinforces the 'evil and adulterous generation' charge as a Mosaic Song echo.
sourceText: He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.

note: 'Adulterous' for the unfaithful covenant people draws on the prophetic marriage metaphor (Israel as faithless spouse); grounds 'adulterous generation' in Hosea's idiom.
sourceText: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts; Lest I strip her naked, and make her bare as in the day that she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst. Indeed, on her children I will have no mercy; for they are children of unfaithfulness; For their mother has played […]

note: Israel's 'adultery' / divorce for unfaithfulness; further prophetic backdrop to 'adulterous generation.'
sourceText: I saw, when, for this very cause that backsliding Israel had committed adultery, I had put her away and given her a bill of divorce, yet treacherous Judah, her sister, didn’t fear; but she also went and played the prostitute. Because she took her prostitution lightly, the land was polluted, and she committed adultery with stones and with wood.

note: The breadth and fame of Solomon's wisdom that drew rulers from afar; background to why the queen came and why 'greater than Solomon' is a weighty claim.
sourceText: God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and very great understanding, even as the sand that is on the seashore. Solomon’s wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east, and all the wisdom of Egypt. For he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol: and his fame was in all the nations all around. He spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs were one thousand five. […]

note: Desert/waterless ruins as the haunt of demons and wild creatures ('goat-demons will dance there'); background to the unclean spirit roaming 'waterless places' as the abode of demons.
sourceText: But wild animals of the desert will lie there, and their houses will be full of jackals. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will frolic there.

note: Lilith and desert demons resting in the desolate waste; reinforces 'waterless places, seeking rest' as the conventional demonic wilderness habitat in prophetic imagery.
sourceText: The wild animals of the desert will meet with the wolves, and the wild goat will cry to his fellow. Yes, the night creature shall settle there, and shall find herself a place of rest.

note: Azazel/the scapegoat driven into the wilderness; the desert as the place to which uncleanness is dispatched, faint background to the spirit's wilderness wandering.
sourceText: But the goat, on which the lot fell for the scapegoat, shall be presented alive before Yahweh, to make atonement for him, to send him away for the scapegoat into the wilderness.

note: The demon Asmodeus flees to 'the remotest parts of Egypt' / the desert and is bound; Second Temple narrative of a routed demon driven to desolate regions, parallel to the unclean spirit expelled to waterless places.
sourceText: When the demon smelled that smell, it fled into the uppermost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him.

note: 'As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly' — wisdom proverb on relapse to a worse state, thematic kin to the spirit's return making 'the last state worse than the first.'
sourceText: As a dog that returns to his vomit, so is a fool who repeats his folly.

note: Levi 'disowned his brothers and ignored his children' for covenant loyalty — kin-ties subordinated to obedience to God. Background to Jesus redefining family by doing 'the will of my Father' over natural kinship.
sourceText: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.

note: The Levites side with Moses against their own kin at the golden calf, gaining a 'blessing' for putting covenant before family; faint resonance with kinship redefined by allegiance to God's will.
sourceText: then Moses stood in the gate of the camp, and said, “Whoever is on Yahweh’s side, come to me!” All the sons of Levi gathered themselves together to him. He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and […]

note: 'I delight to do your will, O my God' — doing the Father's will as the mark of true belonging coheres with 'whoever does the will of my Father.'
sourceText: I delight to do your will, my God. Yes, your law is within my heart.”

note: 'I will tell of your name to my brothers' — the messianic figure naming the faithful as kindred ('brothers'); faint background to Jesus' new-family declaration.
sourceText: I will declare your name to my brothers. In the midst of the assembly, I will praise you.

note: The word/seed that goes out from God's mouth and does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, yielding seed and bread; the sower-and-word matrix governs the parable, made explicit in the later interpretation (v.19, 'the word of the Kingdom').
sourceText: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: 'Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns' — the contrast of receptive ground vs. thorn-choked soil maps directly onto Jesus' soils; thorns that choke recur in v.7, 22.
sourceText: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.

note: 'Sow righteousness... break up your fallow ground' — agricultural sowing-and-reaping imagery for response to God's word; thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.

note: Isaac sows and reaps a hundredfold (LXX 'hekatosteuousan') in the same year — the only clear OT 'hundredfold' agricultural blessing, possible backdrop for the good soil's hundredfold yield (v.8).
sourceText: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.

note: Second Temple (4 Ezra): the farmer sows much seed but not all that is sown takes root or is saved — a near-contemporary Jewish sower parable of differential reception; cf. also 2 Esdras 9:31.
sourceText: For as the husbandman sows much seed upon the ground, and plants many trees, and yet not all that is sown shall come up in due season, neither shall all that is planted take root: even so those who are sown in the world shall not all be saved.

note: The Song of the Vineyard: God plants/sows expecting fruit and is disappointed by a barren yield; thematic kinship with fruit-bearing soils but no verbal overlap.
sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]

note: Formal fulfillment quotation (v.14-15): 'hearing you will hear and not understand, seeing you will see and not perceive... this people's heart has grown callous.' Verbatim LXX citation explaining why parables both reveal and harden.
sourceText: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: 'The LORD has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, ears to hear' — the same eyes/ears/heart triad governing whether revelation is 'given' (v.11); the verb 'given/not given' echoes Deuteronomy's grant-of-perception language.
sourceText: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.

note: 'Foolish people without understanding, who have eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear' — close parallel to v.13's 'seeing they do not see, hearing they do not hear.'
sourceText: ‘Hear now this, foolish people, and without understanding; who have eyes, and don’t see; who have ears, and don’t hear:

note: 'A rebellious house, who have eyes to see but do not see, ears to hear but do not hear' — the same idiom of perceptual organs that fail in the obstinate.
sourceText: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of the rebellious house, who have eyes to see, and don’t see, who have ears to hear, and don’t hear; for they are a rebellious house.

note: 'There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries (mysteria)' — the only OT source of the technical 'mysteries' disclosed to the elect, behind 'to know the mysteries of the Kingdom' (v.11).
sourceText: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these: as for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter; and he who reveals secrets has made known to you what shall happen.

note: 'The wicked shall not understand, but the wise shall understand' — an eschatological have/have-not of understanding paralleling v.11-12.
sourceText: Many shall purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked shall do wickedly; and none of the wicked shall understand; but those who are wise shall understand.

note: 'Give to a wise man and he will be wiser still' — the principle of v.12, 'to him who has, more will be given,' resembles wisdom's accumulative reward.
sourceText: Instruct a wise man, and he will be still wiser. Teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.

note: 'Open my eyes that I may behold wondrous things' — the blessing on eyes that see (v.16) inverts the prayer for opened perception; thematic only.
sourceText: Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.

note: The interpretation names the seed 'the word of the Kingdom' (v.19), confirming the Isaiah 55 word-as-seed substrate that bears or fails to bear fruit.
sourceText: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: Sowing among thorns reappears interpretively (v.22, thorns = cares and riches that choke the word), echoing Jeremiah's warning not to sow among thorns.
sourceText: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.

note: 'Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth' — the cursed ground's thorns as the agents of unfruitfulness; faint thematic backdrop to thorns choking the word.
sourceText: It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field.

note: 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe' — harvest as the set time of eschatological judgment and separation, directly behind 'at the harvest time I will tell the reapers' (v.30).
sourceText: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”

note: The coming day burns like an oven, consuming the wicked as stubble; the burning of bundled weeds (v.30) anticipates this fiery consumption of evildoers.
sourceText: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

note: God will utterly sweep away / gather and remove the wicked from the land; gathering-for-removal imagery parallels gathering the weeds first.
sourceText: I will utterly sweep away everything off of the surface of the earth, says Yahweh. I will sweep away man and animal. I will sweep away the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea, and the heaps of rubble with the wicked. I will cut off man from the surface of the earth, says Yahweh.

note: 'Those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same' — the enemy who sows evil seed and its harvest of judgment; proverbial sowing/reaping morality.
sourceText: According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity, and sow trouble, reap the same.

note: The planted sprig becomes a noble cedar 'and birds of every kind will nest in it, in the shade of its branches' — the closest verbal source for 'the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches'; a Kingdom-tree sheltering the nations.
sourceText: in the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it; and it shall produce boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches shall they dwell.

note: Nebuchadnezzar's great tree under which the beasts find shade and 'the birds of the air dwelt in its branches' (cf. 4:21) — a world-empire tree image transposed to the Kingdom of Heaven.
sourceText: The leaves of it were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all: the animals of the field had shadow under it, and the birds of the sky lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.

note: Assyria as a towering cedar in whose boughs 'all the birds of the air made their nests' — reinforces the prophetic tree-of-empire-sheltering-birds motif.
sourceText: All the birds of the sky made their nests in its boughs; and under its branches all the animals of the field gave birth to their young; and all great nations lived under its shadow.

note: 'Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell; they sing among the branches' — birds nesting in branches as an image of creational shelter.
sourceText: The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.

note: Abraham tells Sarah to take 'three measures (seahs) of fine flour' and make cakes for the divine visitors — the specific 'three measures of meal' is a distinctive verbal echo, a generous/hospitality-scaled quantity now hiding the Kingdom's leaven.
sourceText: Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Quickly prepare three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.”

note: Gideon prepares an ephah of flour (roughly three seahs) for the angelic visitor — another theophany-meal of this large measure.
sourceText: Gideon went in, and prepared a young goat, and unleavened cakes of an ephah of meal. He put the meat in a basket and he put the broth in a pot, and brought it out to him under the oak, and presented it.

note: Hannah brings an ephah of flour to the house of the LORD — large-measure meal in a sacred context; faint.
sourceText: When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, with three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and a bottle of wine, and brought him to Yahweh’s house in Shiloh. The child was young.

note: The leaven left to rise by the baker; one of the few OT uses of leavening as a process working through dough, here neutral-to-positive rather than the usual negative valence.
sourceText: They are all adulterers. They are burning like an oven that the baker stops stirring, from the kneading of the dough, until it is leavened.

note: Formal fulfillment quotation: 'I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.' Asaph's didactic psalm of Israel's history is cited as prophecy of Jesus' parabolic teaching.
sourceText: I will open my mouth in a parable. I will utter dark sayings of old,

note: 'I will incline my ear to a proverb (mashal); I will open my riddle (hidah) on the harp' — parallel 'open my mouth / utter hidden things' diction; wisdom disclosing concealed truth.
sourceText: I will incline my ear to a proverb. I will open my riddle on the harp.

note: To understand 'a proverb (mashal) and a figure, the words of the wise and their riddles' — the mashal/riddle pairing underlying parabolic, hidden speech.
sourceText: to understand a proverb, and parables, the words and riddles of the wise.

note: 'Hidden things you have not known' newly declared — disclosure of things hidden, faint backdrop to 'things hidden from the foundation of the world.'
sourceText: You have heard it; see all this; and you, will you not declare it? “I have shown you new things from this time, even hidden things, which you have not known.

note: 'Those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars' — the direct source of 'the righteous will shine like the sun in the Kingdom of their Father' (v.43).
sourceText: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: The 'furnace of blazing fire' (kaminos tou pyros) into which the disobedient are cast — verbal source for casting the wicked 'into the furnace of fire' (v.42).
sourceText: and whoever doesn’t fall down and worship shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace.

note: LXX: God will remove the lawless and 'the stumbling-blocks (ta skandala) together with the wicked' — strikingly close to 'gather out of his Kingdom all things that cause stumbling (ta skandala) and those who do iniquity' (v.41).
sourceText: I will sweep away man and animal. I will sweep away the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea, and the heaps of rubble with the wicked. I will cut off man from the surface of the earth, says Yahweh.

note: The day burning like a furnace that consumes the wicked as stubble — the fiery end-of-age judgment behind the burning of the weeds (v.40-42).
sourceText: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

note: The Son of Man receiving an everlasting kingdom — Jesus self-identifies as 'the Son of Man' who has a Kingdom from which his angels gather the wicked (v.37, 41); the Danielic Son-of-Man/kingdom matrix.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: Harvest = judgment reaffirmed: 'the harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels' (v.39) interprets the harvest motif drawn from Joel.
sourceText: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”

note: Second Temple: 'In the time of their visitation the righteous will shine forth and run like sparks through the stubble' — a near-contemporary parallel to the righteous shining (v.43), pairing radiance with the burning of the wicked.
sourceText: And in the time of their visitation they will shine forth, And as sparks among stubble they will run to and fro.

note: 'Let those who love him be like the sun rising in its might' — solar radiance as the destiny of the faithful; faint verbal kinship with shining 'like the sun.'
sourceText: “So let all your enemies perish, Yahweh, but let those who love him be as the sun when it rises in its strength.” Then the land had rest forty years.

note: Seek wisdom 'as silver and search for it as hidden treasures' — the joyful search-and-sell-all for hidden treasure mirrors wisdom literature's treasure-hunt for the supreme good.
sourceText: If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures:

note: Second Temple: 'Hidden wisdom and unseen treasure — what use is either?' — wisdom imaged as concealed treasure, faint backdrop to the field's hidden treasure.
sourceText: Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is out of sight, What profit is in them both?

note: 'I will give you the treasures of darkness and hoards in secret places' — God-given hidden treasure imagery; thematic only.
sourceText: I will give you the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that you may know that it is I, Yahweh, who call you by your name, even the God of Israel.

note: 'The price of wisdom is above pearls/jewels' — wisdom surpassing precious gems; the pearl of supreme value for which all is sold echoes wisdom's incomparable worth.
sourceText: No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal. Yes, the price of wisdom is above rubies.

note: Wisdom 'is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire compares with her' (cf. 8:11) — the surpassing-value formula behind the one pearl worth selling everything.
sourceText: She is more precious than rubies. None of the things you can desire are to be compared to her.

note: Seeking wisdom as for hidden treasure; the merchant's diligent seeking (v.45) parallels the wisdom-seeker's quest.
sourceText: If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures:

note: Men caught like fish in a net and dragnet, drawn up and gathered — the dragnet (sagene) cast into the sea collecting people is anticipated by Habakkuk's image of catching humanity in a net.
sourceText: and make men like the fish of the sea, like the creeping things, that have no ruler over them? He takes up all of them with the hook. He catches them in his net, and gathers them in his dragnet. Therefore he rejoices and is glad. Therefore he sacrifices to his net, and burns incense to his dragnet, because by them his life is luxurious, and his food is good. Will he therefore continually empty his net, and kill the nations without mercy?

note: Fishermen spread nets and catch 'fish of very many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea' in the river from the temple — close to the dragnet gathering 'fish of every kind' (v.47).

note: The fiery end-of-age judgment recurs: the wicked separated and cast 'into the furnace of fire' (v.50), reusing the Malachi furnace motif.

sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

sourceText: The mandrakes produce fragrance. At our doors are all kinds of precious fruits, new and old, which I have stored up for you, my beloved.

sourceText: You shall eat old store long kept, and you shall move out the old because of the new.

sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, “Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths, ‘Where is the good way?’ and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls. But they said, ‘We will not walk in it.’

note: 'I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's children' — rejection by one's own family, paralleling 'in his own house' (v.57) where brothers and sisters are named.
sourceText: I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s children.

sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.

note: Herodias driving the execution of the prophet John echoes Jezebel, who pursues the prophet Elijah's life after he confronts the royal house. note: Ahab is the king whom 'Jezebel his wife stirred up' to do evil; Herod likewise acts at the prompting of Herodias and her daughter ('being prompted by her mother'). The motif of a king led into killing by his wife reinforces the Ahab/Jezebel typology.
sourceText: But there was no one like Ahab, who sold himself to do that which was evil in the sight of Yahweh, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.

note: John's charge, 'It is not lawful for you to have her,' rests directly on the Torah prohibition against uncovering the nakedness of one's brother's wife; Lev 20:21 specifies the explicit ban on taking a brother's wife. John's rebuke is a halakhic citation of this statute.
sourceText: “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife. It is your brother’s nakedness.

note: 'If a man takes his brother's wife, it is impurity... they shall be childless.' This is the precise legal ground for John's 'It is not lawful for you to have her' against Herod's marriage to Herodias, his brother Philip's wife.
sourceText: “‘If a man takes his brother’s wife, it is an impurity. He has uncovered his brother’s nakedness. They shall be childless.

note: The killing of a righteous prophet/messenger who rebukes the ruling house belongs to the deuteronomistic pattern of the murdered prophet (cf. Jer 26:20-23), which Matthew thematizes elsewhere (23:29-37). John's death extends this pattern of Israel slaying its prophets.

sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]

note: Prophetic commission 'to pluck up and to plant' — the plucking/planting polarity Jesus invokes in 15:13.
sourceText: Behold, I have this day set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”

note: 'Oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD' — God's planting motif resonant with Mt 15:13.
sourceText: to appoint to those who mourn in Zion, to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of Yahweh, that he may be glorified.

note: 'Who is blind but my servant... blind as the LORD's messenger?' — prophetic 'blind' leadership behind 'blind guides of the blind' (Mt 15:14).
sourceText: Who is blind, but my servant? Or who is as deaf as my messenger whom I send? Who is as blind as he who is at peace, and as blind as Yahweh’s servant?

note: 'His watchmen are blind, they are all without knowledge' — blind Israelite leaders, a strong source for the 'blind guides' charge.
sourceText: His watchmen are blind, they are all without knowledge; they are all mute dogs, they can’t bark; dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber.

note: 'The leaders of this people cause them to err, and those led are destroyed' — guides leading the people to ruin, paralleling both falling into the pit (15:14).
sourceText: For those who lead this people lead them astray; and those who are led by them are destroyed.

note: 'Whoever digs a pit will fall into it' — wisdom topos of falling into the pit echoed in 'both will fall into a pit' (Mt 15:14).
sourceText: Whoever digs a pit shall fall into it. Whoever rolls a stone, it will come back on him.

note: 'Hear but do not understand... lest they understand with their heart' — the hearing/understanding/heart cluster ironically inverted in Jesus' 'Hear and understand' (15:10) and the disciples' dullness (15:16).
sourceText: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: 'Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it are the springs of life' — heart as the wellspring from which everything proceeds, paralleling 'out of the heart come...' (15:18-19).
sourceText: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

note: 'My sheep were scattered... they wandered, lost.' Jesus' mission 'to the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Mt 15:24) draws directly on Ezekiel's scattered/lost flock that God himself will seek and shepherd.
sourceText: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.

note: 'My people have been lost sheep; their shepherds have led them astray' — close verbal source for 'the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Mt 15:24).
sourceText: My people have been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray; they have turned them away on the mountains; they have gone from mountain to hill; they have forgotten their resting place.

note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray' — the lost/straying sheep image behind 15:24.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' — individual lost-sheep language resonant with Mt 15:24.
sourceText: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.

note: The Davidic covenant promising an eternal son/throne — basis for the Gentile woman's address 'Lord, you son of David' (Mt 15:22), a messianic title.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]

note: 'A shoot from the stump of Jesse' — Davidic-messianic hope behind the 'son of David' acclamation in 15:22.
sourceText: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.

note: Elijah sent to the Gentile widow of Zarephath, in the region of Sidon, whose son he heals — a typological precedent for Jesus in 'the region of Tyre and Sidon' (15:21) granting mercy and healing to a Gentile woman's child.
sourceText: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]

note: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn' — Israel's status as God's children illumines 'the children's bread' (Mt 15:26) reserved first for Israel before Gentiles.
sourceText: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,

note: 'You are the children of the LORD your God' — Israel as God's children, background to the children-vs-dogs (Israel-vs-Gentiles) contrast of 15:26.
sourceText: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.

note: Rahab the Canaanite who confesses Israel's God and is saved — a figural precedent for a Canaanite woman whose faith Jesus praises (Mt 15:28); Matthew has already named Rahab in the genealogy.
sourceText: Joshua the son of Nun secretly sent two men out of Shittim as spies, saying, “Go, view the land, including Jericho.” They went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab, and slept there. The king of Jericho was told, “Behold, men of the children of Israel came in here tonight to spy out the land.” The king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, “Bring out the men who have come to you, who have entered into your house; for they have come to […]

note: The curse on Canaan to be servant — the Canaanite woman's reversal (faith commended) stands against the Canaanite-as-cursed-outsider background flagged by Matthew's pointed label 'a Canaanite woman'.
sourceText: He said, “Canaan is cursed. He will be a servant of servants to his brothers.” He said, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Shem. Let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth. Let him dwell in the tents of Shem. Let Canaan be his servant.”

note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped; the lame man shall leap, and the tongue of the mute sing.' Mt 15:30-31's catalogue of mute speaking, lame walking, blind seeing reproduces Isaiah's portrait of eschatological restoration almost item for item.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.

note: 'The deaf shall hear... the eyes of the blind shall see... the meek shall obtain fresh joy' — recurrence with the Isaiah 29 already quoted in 15:8-9 binds the chapter; the healings fulfill the same oracle.
sourceText: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness. The humble also will increase their joy in Yahweh, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.

note: 'They will sanctify... the God of Israel' — the crowd's response 'they glorified the God of Israel' (15:31) echoes Isaiah 29's promised honoring of Israel's God, reversing the lip-service of 15:8-9.
sourceText: But when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in the midst of him, they will sanctify my name. Yes, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and will stand in awe of the God of Israel.

note: 'Who makes the mute, the deaf, the seeing, or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD?' — the divine prerogative over these very disabilities, now exercised by Jesus, prompting glory to 'the God of Israel'.
sourceText: Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?

note: Jesus 'went up into the mountain, and sat there' (15:29) before the crowds and the feeding — a faint Sinai/Moses-on-the-mountain coloring.
sourceText: Moses wrote all Yahweh’s words, and rose up early in the morning, and built an altar under the mountain, and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.

note: 'The LORD opens the eyes of the blind; the LORD raises up those who are bowed down' — the God of Israel as healer of these conditions, glorified in 15:31.
sourceText: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.

note: The manna in the wilderness: God feeds a vast multitude in a 'deserted place' (Mt 15:33) where there is nothing to eat, and all 'ate and were filled' (15:37). The feeding of the four thousand is patterned on the wilderness provision.
sourceText: They took their journey from Elim, and all the congregation of the children of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departing out of the land of Egypt. The whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron in the wilderness; and the children of Israel said to them, “We wish that we had died by the hand of Yahweh in the land of Egypt, […]

note: Elisha feeds a hundred men with a few loaves, who 'ate and had some left over' — the closest prophetic precedent: limited loaves, a doubting servant ('how can I set this before a hundred?'), eating to satisfaction, and leftovers, all mirrored in 15:34-37.
sourceText: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]

note: 'Can God spread a table in the wilderness?... he rained down manna... they ate and were well filled.' The doubting question of 15:33 and the satisfied eating of 15:37 echo this recital of the wilderness feeding.
sourceText: Yes, they spoke against God. They said, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Behold, he struck the rock, so that waters gushed out, and streams overflowed. Can he give bread also? Will he provide flesh for his people?” Therefore Yahweh heard, and was angry. A fire was kindled against Jacob, anger also went up against Israel, because they didn’t believe in God, and didn’t trust in his salvation. Yet he commanded the skies above, and opened the doors […]

note: Moses' concern that the congregation not be 'as sheep without a shepherd' — behind Jesus' compassion on the hungry multitude (15:32) he refuses to send away; pastoral provision for a leaderless flock.
sourceText: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”

note: God the shepherd will feed his flock in good pasture and seek the lost — recurrence with 15:24's lost sheep; the feeding enacts the shepherd's provision of food.
sourceText: I will feed them with good pasture; and on the mountains of the height of Israel shall their fold be: there shall they lie down in a good fold; and on fat pasture shall they feed on the mountains of Israel. I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will cause them to lie down, says the Lord Yahweh. I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which […]

note: The hungry and thirsty fainting in the wilderness whom God satisfies: 'he satisfies the longing soul, and fills the hungry with good things' — resonant with the fainting-on-the-way concern and the filling of 15:32-37.
sourceText: Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted in them. Then they cried to Yahweh in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses, he led them also by a straight way, that they might go to a city to live in. Let them praise Yahweh for his loving kindness, for his wonderful works to the children of men! For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good.

note: 'You prepare a table before me' — the shepherd providing a meal, faint background to the wilderness feeding.
sourceText: You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil. My cup runs over.

note: 'You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD' — the eat-and-be-satisfied formula echoed in 'they all ate, and were filled' (15:37), with Jesus giving thanks.
sourceText: You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless Yahweh your God for the good land which he has given you.

note: 'You open your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing' — God satisfying the hungry, faint resonance with the multitude filled in 15:37.
sourceText: The eyes of all wait for you. You give them their food in due season. You open your hand, and satisfy the desire of every living thing.

note: The 'sign of the prophet Jonah' is a typological pointer: Jonah three days and nights in the belly of the great fish prefigures the Son of Man's burial and resurrection (made explicit in Matthew 12:40). Volume and recurrence are strong; Jesus names Jonah directly.
sourceText: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

note: Beyond the three-days motif, Jonah's preaching of repentance to Nineveh stands behind the rebuke of 'this generation': a pagan city repented at a sign, but the present generation will receive only Jonah's sign. Thematic coherence with Matthew's wider Jonah typology.
sourceText: Jonah began to enter into the city a day’s journey, and he cried out, and said, “In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown!” The people of Nineveh believed God; and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from their greatest even to their least.

note: 'An evil and adulterous generation' draws on the prophetic idiom of Israel as an adulterous people ('sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer'), where covenant infidelity is figured as adultery/idolatry.
sourceText: “But draw near here, you sons of the sorceress, the seed of the adulterer and the prostitute.

note: The 'adulterous generation' charge echoes Hosea's sustained metaphor of faithless Israel as an adulterous spouse. Faint and one of several possible prophetic backgrounds.
sourceText: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts; Lest I strip her naked, and make her bare as in the day that she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst. Indeed, on her children I will have no mercy; for they are children of unfaithfulness;

note: Demanding 'a sign from heaven' to validate Jesus inverts the Deuteronomic test of a prophet: a sign alone does not authenticate; covenant fidelity does. Conceptual rather than verbal.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.

note: The Pharisees and Sadducees 'testing' Jesus by demanding a sign recalls Israel testing the LORD at Massah; the verb of testing carries the wilderness-rebellion overtone. Faint thematic.
sourceText: Therefore the people quarreled with Moses, and said, “Give us water to drink.” Moses said to them, “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test Yahweh?”

note: The warning against 'the yeast/leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees' trades on the Passover/Unleavened Bread association of leaven with pervasive corruption that must be purged from the house. The metaphor's intelligibility presupposes this cultic background.
sourceText: “‘Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even the first day you shall put away yeast out of your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel.

note: Reinforces the leaven-as-defilement imagery from the Feast of Unleavened Bread, where no leaven may be seen within the borders. Secondary to Exodus 12:15.
sourceText: Unleavened bread shall be eaten throughout the seven days; and no leavened bread shall be seen with you, neither shall yeast be seen with you, in all your borders.

note: The disciples' anxiety over bread and the rebuke 'you of little faith' recall Israel's distrust over daily provision in the wilderness, where the LORD rained bread from heaven to test their faith. Thematic coherence with Matthew's two feeding miracles invoked here.
sourceText: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.

note: The grumbling-over-food motif behind the disciples' worry resonates with Israel's complaint about manna; the contrast is between miraculous provision already witnessed and persistent forgetfulness. Faint.
sourceText: but now we have lost our appetite. There is nothing at all except this manna to look at.” The manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like the appearance of bdellium. The people went around, gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in mortars, and boiled it in pots, and made cakes of it. Its taste was like the taste of fresh oil. When the dew fell on the camp in the night, the manna fell on it.

note: 'I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven... bind... loose' draws on the Eliakim oracle: 'I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David; he shall open and none shut, shut and none open.' The key-of-stewardship granting authority to admit and exclude is the controlling image. Strong verbal and conceptual borrowing.
sourceText: I will lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder. He will open, and no one will shut. He will shut, and no one will open.

note: 'The gates of Hades will not prevail' echoes 'Have the gates of death been revealed to you?' — the underworld as a fortified city whose gates symbolize the realm and power of death. Verbal touchpoint ('gates' of death/Hades).
sourceText: Have the gates of death been revealed to you? Or have you seen the gates of the shadow of death?

note: 'You who lift me up from the gates of death' supplies the same 'gates of death/Hades' idiom; deliverance from death's gates is precisely what Jesus' resurrection-grounded assembly will enjoy. Reinforces Job 38:17.
sourceText: Have mercy on me, Yahweh. See my affliction by those who hate me, and lift me up from the gates of death;

note: Hezekiah's 'I shall go through the gates of Sheol' offers another close instance of the 'gates of the underworld' figure standing behind 'gates of Hades.'
sourceText: I said, “In the middle of my life I go into the gates of Sheol. I am deprived of the residue of my years.”

note: Peter's confession of Jesus as 'the Son of the living God' employs the covenant title 'the living God,' contrasting Israel's God with lifeless idols. The epithet recurs across the OT and grounds the confession in covenant monotheism.
sourceText: For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?

note: 'Sons of the living God' supplies the specific collocation 'living God' with sonship language that Peter's title brings together. Faint verbal overlap.
sourceText: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’

note: The popular identification of Jesus with Elijah ('some say... Elijah') depends on Malachi's promise that Elijah would return before the day of the LORD, an expectation Matthew engages elsewhere (11:14; 17:10-13).
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: 'On this rock I will build' may play on the 'rock from which you were hewn' (Abraham) imagery for the founding of the people of God on a chosen progenitor. Disputed; rock-foundation imagery is diffuse.
sourceText: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, and I blessed him, and made him many.

note: Jeremiah being named among the guesses for Jesus' identity reflects his stature as the suffering, rejected prophet of judgment on Jerusalem; the allusion is to Jeremiah as a prophetic type rather than a specific text. Faint.
sourceText: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”

note: Jesus 'must... suffer many things... and be killed' draws on the Suffering Servant who was despised, rejected, and stricken; the divine necessity ('must') of the Messiah's suffering reflects Matthew's Servant Christology.
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.

note: 'The third day be raised up' echoes 'on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him,' the OT text most plausibly underlying the recurrent 'third day' resurrection formula.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: 'Get behind me, Satan!' as a rebuke of the adversary echoes 'The LORD rebuke you, O Satan' — Peter unwittingly plays the satan/accuser opposing God's purpose. Thematic and verbal resonance with the rebuke-of-Satan formula.
sourceText: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”

note: The figure of 'the satan' as the adversary who would divert God's servant from his path stands behind naming Peter 'Satan' for setting his mind on human things. Faint, conceptual.
sourceText: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]

note: 'He will render to everyone according to his deeds' closely cites 'to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love, for you render to a man according to his work.' Near-verbatim formula of eschatological recompense; the clearest source-citation in the chapter.
sourceText: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.

note: Parallel near-verbatim source for 'render to everyone according to his deeds': 'will he not repay each according to his work?' Matthew's wording fuses the Psalms and Proverbs recompense formula. Together with Psalm 62:12 this is a high-confidence citation.
sourceText: If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this”; doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not render to every man according to his work?

note: 'The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels... coming in his Kingdom' draws directly on the 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds to whom dominion, glory, and an everlasting kingdom are given. Strong verbal ('Son of Man,' 'coming,' 'kingdom,' 'glory') and conceptual borrowing.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'What will a man give in exchange for his life?' echoes 'no man can ransom his brother or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly.' The futility of buying back one's soul with wealth is the shared logic, sharpened by 'gains the whole world but forfeits his life.'
sourceText: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough, That he should live on forever, that he should not see corruption.

note: 'Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life' resonates with the rhetorical 'what will a man give in exchange for his life?' — the supreme value placed on life. Faint, possibly coincidental proverbial overlap.
sourceText: Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life.

note: 'With his angels' / 'in the glory of his Father' resonates with 'the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him,' a theophany of the divine coming with the heavenly host that informs the parousia imagery.
sourceText: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*

note: 'I the LORD search the heart... to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds' is a further OT recompense text reinforcing the Psalm 62 / Proverbs 24 citation of judgment according to works.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: The deuterocanonical 'he will repay to man according to his deeds' continues the Second Temple development of the recompense formula behind 16:27, attesting the currency of the idea in Jesus' milieu.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: Individual accountability — each judged for his own conduct, 'the soul who sins shall die' — undergirds the 'render to everyone according to his deeds' principle. Faint, conceptual.
sourceText: The soul who sins, he shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be on him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be on him.

note: The glory of the LORD settles on Sinai and the cloud covers it 'six days,' and on the seventh day God calls Moses out of the cloud. Matthew's opening 'after six days' plus the high mountain, the cloud, and the divine voice from the cloud reproduce this Sinai theophany sequence with striking specificity; the strongest structural anchor for the new-Sinai reading.
sourceText: Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.

note: Coming down Sinai Moses' face shone (LXX dedoxastai) so that he had to veil it. Jesus' face 'shone like the sun' figurally surpasses Moses: where Moses reflected borrowed glory, Jesus radiates his own. The shining-face motif is a deliberate Mosaic borrowing.
sourceText: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him. When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him. Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned to him; and Moses spoke to them. […]

note: 'You are my Son' — the royal-enthronement decree. The heavenly voice 'This is my beloved Son' weaves the Davidic/messianic sonship of Ps 2 into the composite oracle; widely recognized as one of the three texts fused at the baptism and transfiguration.
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.

note: 'My chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him.' 'In whom I am well pleased' (eudokesa) echoes the Servant designation. The voice fuses royal Son (Ps 2) with Servant (Isa 42), framing the glorified Son as the suffering Servant on the way to the cross.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.

note: 'The LORD will raise up for you a prophet like me... you shall listen to him' (autou akousesthe). The command 'Listen to him' is verbatim from the prophet-like-Moses promise; appended to the voice it identifies Jesus as the eschatological prophet, the climactic clause of the composite oracle.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: Elijah sent before the great Day. His appearance with Moses on the mountain anticipates the Elijah-must-come discussion of vv.10-13 and frames the scene eschatologically.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

note: Moses ascends a high mountain (Nebo), is shown the land, and dies in a manner the LORD conceals; later tradition held God buried/took him. His reappearance pairs with Elijah (who never died, 2 Kings 2) as the two who left earth extraordinarily, hence fit witnesses of glory.
sourceText: Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho. Yahweh showed him all the land of Gilead, to Dan, and all Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah, to the western sea, and the south, and the Plain of the valley of Jericho the city of palm trees, to Zoar. Yahweh said to him, “This is the land which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to […]

note: Elijah taken up to heaven in a whirlwind/chariot of fire — never tasting death. His presence on the mountain trades on the tradition of his heavenly translation, qualifying him to appear in glory alongside Moses.
sourceText: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

note: The bright cloud (the kabod/Shekinah) overshadowing and filling the tent of meeting. 'A bright cloud overshadowed them' (episkiazo) draws on the tabernacle-cloud of divine presence, reinforced by Peter's wish to build three skenai (tents).
sourceText: Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle. Moses wasn’t able to enter into the Tent of Meeting, because the cloud stayed on it, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle.

note: The Feast of Booths (Sukkot): dwelling in tents to recall the wilderness. Peter's instinct to erect three skenai may evoke the festival of God dwelling with Israel; some read an eschatological-ingathering nuance. Faint and disputed.
sourceText: You shall dwell in booths seven days. All who are native-born in Israel shall dwell in booths, that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.’”

note: 'The wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky... like the stars.' The luminous transformation ('face shone like the sun,' garments 'white as the light') draws on apocalyptic resurrection-glory imagery, anticipating the risen state foreshadowed in v.9.
sourceText: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: The Son of Man coming with clouds. The cloud plus the Son-of-Man saying in v.9 may activate the Danielic glorification motif; faint here, stronger elsewhere in Matthew.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: Moses asks to see God's glory and is hidden in the rock as the glory passes. The disciples falling on their faces in terror at the glory echoes the dangerous holiness of seeing divine glory on Sinai. Thematic.
sourceText: He said, “Please show me your glory.” He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.” He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.” Yahweh also said, “Behold, there is a place by me, and you shall stand on the rock. It will happen, while my glory passes by, that I will put you in a cleft of […]

note: 'Your son, your only/beloved son.' The 'beloved Son' (agapetos, the LXX rendering of yahid in the Aqedah) may carry an Isaac-typology overtone of the beloved son led toward sacrifice, dovetailing with the passion predictions framing the chapter.
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: God comes in radiance, 'his brightness was like the light, rays flashing from his hand.' The garments 'white as the light' may draw on theophanic light-imagery. Faint.
sourceText: God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and his praise filled the earth. His splendor is like the sunrise. Rays shine from his hand, where his power is hidden.

note: 'I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day... he will turn (restore) the hearts.' The scribal expectation 'Elijah must come first' and Jesus' 'Elijah indeed comes first and will restore all things' (apokatastesei panta) directly cite this oracle; identified with John the Baptist.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

note: 'I send my messenger to prepare the way before me.' The forerunner role attached to Elijah/John builds on the messenger of Mal 3, the companion text to 4:5 in the prophecy of the coming Day.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Of Elijah: 'destined... to calm the wrath of God, to turn the heart of the parent to the child, and to restore (katastesai) the tribes of Jacob.' This Second Temple text supplies the 'restore all things' language and shows the developed Elijah-redivivus expectation Jesus engages. Deuterocanonical.
sourceText: Who was recorded for reproofs in their seasons, To pacify anger, before it brake forth into wrath; To turn the heart of the father to the son, And to restore the tribes of Jacob.

note: Jezebel seeks Elijah's life and he flees; 'they did to him whatever they wanted' may echo the suffering/persecution of the historical Elijah, mapped onto John (and onward to the Son of Man). Thematic-typological.
sourceText: Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!” When he saw that, he arose, and went for his life, and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there. But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree: and he requested for himself that he might die, and said, […]

note: 'They did to him whatever they wanted to' — the maltreatment of the Elijah-figure (John) parallels Israel's rejection of the prophets generally; faint verbal, strong thematic continuity with the persecuted-prophet motif.
sourceText: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

note: 'Even so the Son of Man will also suffer by them' pivots to the Servant's rejection and suffering, linking the fate of the forerunner to the passion. Faint here, the Servant frame recurs in the chapter.
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.

note: 'Until the Son of Man has risen from the dead' uses the Danielic Son-of-Man title; the resurrection-secret links glory to vindication. Title-level echo.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: 'A perverse and crooked generation' (genea skolia kai diestrammene, LXX). Jesus' rebuke 'O faithless and perverse generation' (genea apistos kai diestrammene) borrows the Song of Moses' indictment of the wilderness generation, casting the unbelieving crowd as the new faithless Israel.
sourceText: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.

note: 'How long will this people despise me? How long will they refuse to believe (ou pisteuousin) in me?' The doubled 'How long...?' lament over unbelief and 'faithless' echoes God's wilderness frustration with Israel through Moses. Strengthens the Moses-typology of the descent from the mountain.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “How long will this people despise me? and how long will they not believe in me, for all the signs which I have worked among them?

note: 'They are a perverse generation, children in whom there is no faithfulness.' Continues the Song-of-Moses language behind 'faithless and perverse generation'; reinforces the Deut 32 frame.
sourceText: He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.

note: 'Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain.' The proverb of removing a mountain by God's power/Spirit may stand behind 'you will tell this mountain, Move from here.' Thematic.
sourceText: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”

note: 'Every mountain and hill made low.' The mountain-moving saying may draw on eschatological mountain-leveling imagery as a figure of God overcoming all obstacles. Faint.
sourceText: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. The uneven shall be made level, and the rough places a plain.

note: 'The righteous shall live by his faith.' The whole pericope's contrast of unbelief versus mustard-seed faith resonates with the prophetic valuation of faith, though no verbal borrowing. Thematic.
sourceText: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.

note: The wilderness generation tested God ten times and did not believe; 'How long will I bear with you?' echoes the divine forbearance toward a faithless people. Faint thematic.
sourceText: because all those men who have seen my glory, and my signs, which I worked in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tempted me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice;

note: 'The Son of Man is about to be delivered up (paradidotai) into the hands of men, and they will kill him.' The passive 'delivered up' echoes the Servant who 'was handed over for our sins' (Isa 53:6, 12 LXX paredothe), framing the death as the Servant's vicarious handing-over.
sourceText: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: 'His soul was delivered up to death... he was numbered with transgressors.' The being 'delivered into the hands of men' draws on the Servant's surrender; the divine-passive points to God's purpose behind the betrayal.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: 'On the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.' 'The third day he will be raised up' may draw on this resurrection-on-the-third-day text, a candidate source for the early 'third day' formula.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: The 'Son of Man' title carries the Danielic vindicated-one freight; the prediction couples humiliation with resurrection-vindication. Title-level echo.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: 'Three days and three nights'; Matthew elsewhere makes the Jonah-resurrection link explicit (12:40), so the 'third day' here may carry a faint Jonah resonance. Very faint.
sourceText: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

note: The half-shekel atonement-money each Israelite pays for the service of the sanctuary. The didrachma (= the temple tax, the equivalent of the half-shekel) collected in v.24 is this Mosaic census/sanctuary levy; the whole exchange presupposes Exod 30 as the legal background of the temple tax.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.
