They shall give this, everyone who passes over to those who are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary; (the shekel is twenty gerahs;) half a shekel for an offering to […]

note: The reckoning of the half-shekel (a beka) from each man counted. Confirms the fixed temple contribution behind the 'didrachma' question; the Pentateuchal institution of the sanctuary tax.
sourceText: The silver of those who were numbered of the congregation was one hundred talents, and one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary: a beka a head, that is, half a shekel, after the shekel of the sanctuary, for everyone who passed over to those who were numbered, from twenty years old and upward, for six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty men.

note: The post-exilic community pledges a third/(later half-)shekel yearly 'for the service of the house of our God.' Documents the developing annual temple-tax practice the collectors enforce, the contemporary form of the Exodus levy.
sourceText: Also we made ordinances for ourselves, to charge ourselves yearly with the third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God; for the show bread, and for the continual meal offering, and for the continual burnt offering, for the Sabbaths, for the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.

note: 'The earth is the LORD's and its fullness.' Jesus' logic that the king's own children are free, and the provision of the coin from the sea/fish, plays on God's ownership of all things — the Son not being a stranger in his Father's house (the temple). Thematic.
sourceText: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell therein.

note: 'A son honors his father.' The Father-Son / sons-of-the-king argument that the children are exempt may resonate with the sonship-over-against-temple logic; Jesus as Son is not a stranger to the Father's house. Faint.
sourceText: “A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If I am a father, then where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is the respect due me? Says Yahweh of Armies to you, priests, who despise my name. You say, ‘How have we despised your name?’

note: A fish as divine instrument/provision at sea; the miraculous coin-bearing fish may carry a faint resonance of God's sovereign use of the sea-creature, though no verbal link. Very faint.
sourceText: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

note: The reversal at the heart of the saying — 'whoever humbles himself... is the greatest' — restates the wisdom maxim that pride brings a person low while the humble in spirit obtain honor. The exaltation-through-humility logic is a sustained sapiential pattern.
sourceText: A man’s pride brings him low, but one of lowly spirit gains honor.

note: 'Before honor is humility' supplies the proverbial frame for greatness defined by lowering oneself; recurs at Prov 18:12, reinforcing thematic coherence.
sourceText: The fear of Yahweh teaches wisdom. Before honor is humility.

note: The image of becoming 'as little children' before God resonates with the psalmist's quieted, weaned-child posture of trust and renounced ambition. Verbal overlap is thin, so the link is thematic/figural rather than lexical.
sourceText: Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.

note: 'A little child shall lead them' offers an eschatological valorization of the child as figure of the messianic order, a possible backdrop to the child set 'in their midst' as model of the kingdom. Faint and disputed.
sourceText: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat; The calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together; and a little child will lead them.

note: The skandalon ('stumbling block') vocabulary draws on the Holiness Code prohibition against placing a stumbling block before the blind; Matthew moralizes the cultic-ethical image into causing 'these little ones' to fall.
sourceText: “‘You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear your God. I am Yahweh.

note: The 'Woe' (ouai) oracle form against the world and against the agent of stumbling reproduces the prophetic woe-cry, of which Isaiah 5 is the paradigmatic chain. Formal echo, not verbal borrowing.
sourceText: Woe to those who join house to house, who lay field to field, until there is no room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land!

note: Being 'sunk in the depths of the sea' may invert Micah's image of God casting sins into the depths of the sea: here it is the offender, not the sin, that is drowned. Suggestive but uncertain.
sourceText: He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

note: A stone bound to a scroll and sunk in the Euphrates as a sign of irreversible sinking judgment ('thus shall Babylon sink') parallels the millstone-and-sea image of inescapable doom. Contested.
sourceText: It shall be, when you have made an end of reading this book, that you shall bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates: and you shall say, Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise again because of the evil that I will bring on her; and they shall be weary. Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.

note: The 'eternal fire' / 'Gehenna of fire' draws directly on Isaiah's closing vision of the dead whose 'worm shall not die, nor their fire be quenched' — the classic source-image for unquenchable eschatological fire, set in the valley outside Jerusalem.
sourceText: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”

note: Gehenna = the Valley of (the son of) Hinnom (ge-hinnom), where children were burned at Topheth; Jeremiah's condemnation of that valley made it the topographic seed of the later place-of-fiery-judgment.
sourceText: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind.

note: Jeremiah renames Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom 'the Valley of Slaughter,' a judgment site; reinforces the Gehenna toponym's punitive force behind 'cast into the eternal fire.'
sourceText: and have built the high places of Baal, to burn their sons in the fire for burnt offerings to Baal; which I didn’t command, nor spoke it, neither came it into my mind: therefore, behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that this place shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter.

note: Josiah's defilement of Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom contributes to the valley's afterlife as a place of refuse and judgment underlying Gehenna. Background rather than verbal source.
sourceText: He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.

note: 'Their angels always see the face of my Father' presumes the guardian-angel motif of 'he will command his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.'
sourceText: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways.

note: Angels who 'see the face' of the Father use the royal-court idiom for the highest courtiers — those who 'saw the king's face' and had access to his presence (cf. the seven princes who saw Ahasuerus's face). The little ones' angels hold rank in the heavenly court.
sourceText: and the next to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king’s face, and sat first in the kingdom),

note: 'Those who saw the king's face' as a class of privileged courtiers parallels the access-language applied to the angels. Idiomatic background, contested.
sourceText: and out of the city he took an officer who was set over the men of war; and five men of those who saw the king’s face, who were found in the city; and the scribe, the captain of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the city.

note: V.11 ('the Son of Man came to save that which was lost') directly evokes the shepherd-God's oracle 'I will seek the lost, and bring back the strayed' — and prepares the lost-sheep parable that follows.
sourceText: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.

note: The title 'Son of Man' in v.11 ultimately reaches back to Daniel's heavenly figure, though here in a saving rather than enthroned register. Faint at this point.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: Raphael as one of the angels who 'stand and enter before the glory of the Lord' offers a Second Temple analogue to the angels who 'always see the face' of the Father. Deuterocanonical background, contested.
sourceText: I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and go in before the glory of the Holy One.”

note: The shepherd who leaves the flock to 'seek that which has gone astray' and rejoices to find it directly enacts God's oracle: 'I myself will search for my sheep... I will seek the lost, and bring back the strayed.' High volume and thematic coherence.
sourceText: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]

note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' supplies the precise pairing of straying and being sought that the parable dramatizes.
sourceText: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.

note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way' is the canonical statement of the sheep-going-astray motif underlying the one that 'goes astray.'
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: The oracle against shepherds who scatter and fail to seek the flock, with God's promise to gather the strays, shares the shepherd/lost-sheep field. Contributory background.
sourceText: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]

note: 'My sheep wandered through all the mountains... and none searched or sought' supplies the specific detail of the shepherd going 'to the mountains' to seek the strayed one.
sourceText: My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.

note: 'Go, show him his fault between you and him alone' enacts the Holiness Code command 'you shall surely reprove your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him' — private, loving rebuke that does not let sin fester into hatred.
sourceText: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.

note: 'At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established' is a near-verbatim citation of the Deuteronomic law of evidence ('on the testimony of two or three witnesses a matter shall be established'). The clearest formula-level borrowing in the chapter.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: The two-or-three-witnesses standard is doubled in Deuteronomy's capital-case law ('on the evidence of two or three witnesses he shall be put to death'), reinforcing the juridical weight of the procedure Jesus prescribes for the assembly.
sourceText: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.

note: 'Question a friend, perhaps he did not do it... reprove a neighbor before you threaten him' is the closest Second Temple parallel to the graduated, presumption-of-innocence rebuke of Mt 18:15. Deuterocanonical wisdom on fraternal correction.
sourceText: Reprove a friend; it may be he did it not: And if he did something, that he may do it no more. Reprove your neighbor; it may be he said it not: And if he has said it, that he may not say it again. Reprove a friend; for many times there is slander: And trust not every word. There is one that slips, and not from the heart: And who is he that has not sinned with his tongue? Reprove your neighbor before you threaten him; And give place to the law of the Most […]

note: Binding/loosing as authoritative juridical decision shares the open/shut imagery of the 'key of the house of David... he shall open and none shut.' The connection is firmer at Mt 16:19; here it is reasserted communally and is more diffuse.
sourceText: I will lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder. He will open, and no one will shut. He will shut, and no one will open.

note: 'Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst' resonates with those who feared the Lord speaking together while 'the Lord took note and a book of remembrance was written' — the divine presence attending the small gathered company. Contested.
sourceText: Then those who feared Yahweh spoke one with another; and Yahweh listened, and heard, and a book of memory was written before him, for those who feared Yahweh, and who honored his name.

note: The 'two or three' of v.20 re-uses the witness-count of v.16, transposing the legal quorum into a quorum of prayer and presence. The verbal carryover from the Deuteronomic formula is deliberate.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: 'Until seventy times seven' (or 'seventy-seven') deliberately reverses Lamech's boast 'If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold': the same numbers that measured escalating vengeance now measure limitless forgiveness. The LXX of Gen 4:24 reads hebdomekontakis hepta, matching Jesus' phrasing.
sourceText: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”

note: Peter's 'seven times' as a presumed limit may echo the prophetic 'for three transgressions and for four' idiom of a fixed tally of offenses before judgment; Jesus dissolves the tally. Faint formal parallel.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh: “For three transgressions of Damascus, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron;

note: The parable's logic — God forgives the one who forgives, and withholds mercy from the unmerciful — is the narrative form of Sirach's teaching: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray... Does anyone harbor anger against another, and expect healing from the Lord?' The closest extracanonical parallel to the whole pericope.
sourceText: He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins. Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins? He being himself flesh nourishes wrath: Who will make atonement for his sins? Remember your […]

note: The king who 'releases' (aphiemi) his servant and 'forgives the debt' enacts the sabbatical-year release of debts (shemittah): every creditor shall release what he has lent. The unforgiving servant violates the release he himself received.
sourceText: At the end of every seven years, you shall cancel debts. This is the way it shall be done: every creditor shall release that which he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not require payment from his neighbor and his brother; because Yahweh’s release has been proclaimed.

note: The command to sell the debtor 'with his wife and children' reflects the legal reality of debt-slavery regulated in the Jubilee laws ('if your brother becomes poor and sells himself to you'), the very bondage the king's compassion suspends.
sourceText: “‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you; you shall not make him to serve as a slave.

note: A creditor coming to seize the debtor's children as slaves (the widow's plea to Elisha) supplies the social backdrop for selling the man 'with his wife, his children, and all that he had.'
sourceText: Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets to Elisha, saying, “Your servant my husband is dead. You know that your servant feared Yahweh. Now the creditor has come to take for himself my two children to be slaves.”

note: The outcry that 'we are forcing our sons and daughters to be slaves' to pay debts parallels the parable's seizure of family for an unpayable obligation. Contributory social context.
sourceText: Yet now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children as their children. Behold, we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters have been brought into bondage. Neither is it in our power to help it; for other men have our fields and our vineyards.”

note: 'Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be answered' is the proverbial kernel of the parable: the servant who refuses his fellow's plea forfeits the mercy he had begged and received.
sourceText: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.

note: 'He who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker; he who is glad at calamity shall not go unpunished' supports the measure-for-measure judgment on the merciless servant. Faint.
sourceText: Whoever mocks the poor reproaches his Maker. He who is glad at calamity shall not be unpunished.

note: Daniel's counsel to the king to 'break off your sins by showing mercy to the oppressed' links royal forgiveness with the showing of mercy demanded of the forgiven — a possible backdrop to the king/mercy frame. Contested.
sourceText: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; if there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.

note: The setting 'beyond the Jordan' in the region of Judea/Perea uses the standard wilderness-itinerary formula for Israel encamped 'beyond the Jordan' opposite Jericho; faint geographic resonance only.
sourceText: The children of Israel traveled, and encamped in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho.

note: Jesus healing the great multitudes who follow him faintly recalls the eschatological healing of Isaiah's highway-of-the-redeemed; thematic, not verbal.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.

note: 'He who made them from the beginning made them male and female' verbatim cites Genesis 1:27 ('male and female created he them'); explicit appeal to creation order as the warrant against divorce.
sourceText: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: Genesis 5:2 repeats 'male and female created he them, and blessed them'; the doublet reinforces the 'from the beginning' creation argument and may stand behind Jesus' formulation alongside 1:27.
sourceText: He created them male and female, and blessed them. On the day they were created, he named them “Adam”.

note: 'For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall join to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh' is a verbatim quotation of Genesis 2:24, the foundational one-flesh text.
sourceText: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.

note: The Pharisees' 'Moses commanded us to give her a bill of divorce' directly cites the Mosaic divorce permission of Deuteronomy 24:1 ('let him write her a bill of divorcement'); the crux of the dispute.
sourceText: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house.

note: The full Deuteronomic divorce ordinance (vv.1-4, the prohibition of remarrying a twice-divorced wife) frames Jesus' redefinition of remarriage-after-divorce as adultery.
sourceText: If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter husband die, who took her to be his wife; her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before Yahweh. You shall not cause the land to sin, which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.

note: Malachi's covenant theology of marriage ('the wife of thy youth... did he not make one?... I hate divorce') anticipates Jesus' one-flesh-from-creation argument against putting away a wife.
sourceText: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For I hate divorce”, says Yahweh, the God of Israel, “and him […]

note: 'Bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh' establishes the one-flesh unity that 2:24 articulates and Jesus invokes as 'no more two but one flesh.'
sourceText: The man said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.”

note: Jesus' explanation that Moses permitted divorce 'because of the hardness of your hearts' draws on the Deuteronomic idiom of the uncircumcised/hardened heart of stubborn Israel.
sourceText: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.

note: Prophetic 'hardness of heart' / circumcise-your-heart language underlies Jesus' diagnosis of why the Mosaic concession was given.
sourceText: Circumcise yourselves to Yahweh, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go out like fire, and burn so that no one can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.

note: The promise to remove the heart of stone faintly contrasts with the 'hardness of heart' that necessitated the divorce concession 'from the beginning it was not so.'
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.

note: Jesus' charge that remarriage after unlawful divorce 'commits adultery' presupposes the Decalogue prohibition (Exodus 20:14 / Deuteronomy 5:18).
sourceText: “You shall not commit adultery.

note: 'Male and female' as a fixed creational pair also appears in the ark narrative; faint reinforcement of the binary-pair language Jesus cites.
sourceText: went by pairs to Noah into the ship, male and female, as God commanded Noah.

note: 'Eunuchs for the Kingdom of Heaven's sake' inverts and fulfills Isaiah's promise that faithful eunuchs receive 'a name better than of sons and daughters' within God's house; the strongest scriptural ground for valuing the eunuch in the kingdom.
sourceText: Neither let the foreigner, who has joined himself to Yahweh, speak, saying, “Yahweh will surely separate me from his people”; neither let the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” For thus says Yahweh, “To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and hold fast my covenant: to them I will give in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than of sons and of daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, […]

note: Deuteronomy bars the emasculated from the assembly of the LORD; Jesus' commendation of voluntary 'eunuchs for the kingdom' figurally reverses that exclusion, echoing the Isaian abrogation.
sourceText: He who is emasculated by crushing or cutting shall not enter into Yahweh’s assembly.

note: Wisdom blesses the eunuch 'which hath wrought no iniquity... for unto him shall be given the special gift of faith,' a Second Temple anticipation of the eunuch honored in God's kingdom.
sourceText: And happy is the eunuch which has wrought no lawless deed with his hands, Nor imagined wicked things against the Lord; For there will be given him for his faithfulness a peculiar favor, And a lot in the sanctuary of the Lord more delightsome than wife or children.

note: Jesus laying hands on the children to bless echoes Israel/Jacob laying hands on Ephraim and Manasseh to bless them; patriarchal blessing-by-imposition-of-hands prefigured.
sourceText: Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn. He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham […]

note: The kingdom belonging to little children resonates with the Psalmist's 'out of the mouth of babes' as the locus of God's praise/strength; thematic only.
sourceText: From the lips of babes and infants you have established strength, because of your adversaries, that you might silence the enemy and the avenger.
lxxText: Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou perfected praise, because of thine enemies; that thou mightest put down the enemy and avenger.

note: Laying on of hands as a means of transmitting blessing/commission (Moses on Joshua) lies behind the gesture the disciples sought to prevent.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]

note: 'You shall not murder' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:13 / Deuteronomy 5:17).
sourceText: “You shall not murder.

note: 'You shall not commit adultery' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:14 / Deuteronomy 5:18).
sourceText: “You shall not commit adultery.

note: 'You shall not steal' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:15 / Deuteronomy 5:19).
sourceText: “You shall not steal.

note: 'You shall not offer false testimony' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:16 / Deuteronomy 5:20).
sourceText: “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.

note: 'Honor your father and mother' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:12 / Deuteronomy 5:16).
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.

note: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' is a verbatim quotation of Leviticus 19:18, appended by Jesus as the summary of the second table.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: The whole sequence Jesus recites follows the second-table Decalogue as given in Deuteronomy's repetition; the Matthean order (honor-parents last, plus Lev 19:18) reflects this catechetical cluster.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.

note: 'Keep the commandments' to 'enter into life' echoes Leviticus 18:5, 'which if a man do, he shall live in them'; the Torah principle of life-by-obedience the young man invokes.
sourceText: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.

note: Doing 'all these commandments' as righteousness/life lies behind the young man's claim to have kept them and the question 'what do I still lack?'
sourceText: It shall be righteousness to us, if we observe to do all this commandment before Yahweh our God, as he has commanded us.”

note: 'Why do you call me good? No one is good but God' resonates with the recurrent confession 'the LORD is good' (Ps 118:1; 106:1; 136:1); only God is the source of the predicate 'good.'
sourceText: Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.

note: 'If you want to be perfect (teleios)' echoes the call to Abraham, 'walk before me and be thou perfect/blameless,' the Septuagint sense of wholehearted covenant integrity.
sourceText: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless.

note: 'You shall be perfect/blameless with the LORD your God' stands behind Jesus' 'if you would be perfect,' framing discipleship as covenantal completeness.
sourceText: You shall be perfect with Yahweh your God.

note: 'Give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven' enacts 'He that hath pity on the poor lendeth unto the LORD'; almsgiving as deposit with God.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

note: Tobit's counsel that almsgiving 'lays up a good treasure against the day of necessity' is the closest Second Temple parallel to 'sell what you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.'
sourceText: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]

note: Ben Sira urges 'lay up thy treasure according to the commandments... it shall bring thee more profit than gold,' directly paralleling treasure-in-heaven-through-almsgiving.
sourceText: Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all affliction:

note: 'With God all things are possible' is the strongest verbal kin to 'Is anything too hard (impossible) for the LORD?' spoken at the promise of Isaac; divine omnipotence over the humanly impossible.
sourceText: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”

note: Job's confession 'I know that thou canst do all things, and that no purpose of thine can be withheld' closely matches 'with God all things are possible.'
sourceText: “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.

note: 'If it be marvelous... should it also be marvelous in mine eyes? saith the LORD' grounds the contrast between what is impossible for men and possible for God in the restoration promise.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh of Armies: “If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my eyes?” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'There is nothing too hard for thee' (cf. 32:27, 'is there any thing too hard for me?') is a near-equivalent declaration of God's unlimited power.
sourceText: Ah Lord Yahweh! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm; there is nothing too hard for you,

note: 'Is the LORD's hand waxed short?' belongs to the same idiom of God overcoming the humanly impossible.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Has Yahweh’s hand grown short? Now you will see whether my word will happen to you or not.”

note: The difficulty of the rich entering the kingdom resonates with the Psalmist's verdict that wealth cannot ransom a life; riches as no security before God.
sourceText: Those who trust in their wealth, and boast in the multitude of their riches— none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough, That he should live on forever, that he should not see corruption.

note: The Abraham-Sodom dialogue's confidence in God ('shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?') shares the setting of the same 'too hard for the LORD?' passage Jesus echoes.
sourceText: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”

note: 'When the Son of Man will sit on the throne of his glory, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging' draws on Daniel's vision of thrones set, the Ancient of Days, and judgment convened; the throne-and-judgment imagery.
sourceText: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.

note: 'The Son of Man... on the throne of his glory' alludes to the Danielic 'one like a son of man' given dominion and an everlasting kingdom.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'Judgment was given to the saints of the Most High' grounds the disciples' role of sitting in judgment over the twelve tribes.
sourceText: until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom.

note: 'There are set thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David'—Jerusalem as the seat where the tribes are judged—stands behind the twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
sourceText: where the tribes go up, even Yah’s tribes, according to an ordinance for Israel, to give thanks to Yahweh’s name. For there are set thrones for judgment, the thrones of David’s house.

note: 'They shall judge the nations, and have dominion over the peoples' is the Second Temple promise that the righteous will share God's eschatological judging rule, paralleling the disciples on thrones.
sourceText: They will judge nations, and have dominion over peoples; And the Lord will reign over them for evermore.

note: 'In the regeneration (palingenesia)'—the renewed cosmos—echoes Isaiah's 'I create new heavens and a new earth'; the eschatological re-creation in which the thrones are set.
sourceText: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.

note: 'The new heavens and the new earth which I will make shall remain' reinforces the 'regeneration' framework of the promised renewal.
sourceText: “For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me,” says Yahweh, “so your seed and your name shall remain.

note: 'Will inherit eternal life' echoes Daniel's resurrection to 'everlasting life,' the OT locus for that phrase informing the disciples' reward.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: 'Many first will be last, and last first' resonates with Hannah's reversal song—the LORD raises the poor from the dust and seats them with princes.
sourceText: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up. He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.

note: The hundredfold restoration to those who left all faintly recalls Job's twofold/restored fortunes after loss; reward-after-renunciation pattern.
sourceText: Yahweh turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends. Yahweh gave Job twice as much as he had before. Then came there to him all his brothers, and all his sisters, and all those who had been of his acquaintance before, and ate bread with him in his house. They comforted him, and consoled him concerning all the evil that Yahweh had brought on him. Everyone also gave him a piece of money, and everyone a ring of gold. So Yahweh blessed the […]

note: Leaving 'houses... father, mother... lands' for Jesus' name's sake to inherit reward retraces Abraham's call to leave country and kindred for a promised inheritance.
sourceText: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Get out of your country, and from your relatives, and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you. I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing.

note: The vineyard (ampelon) is the master's estate where laborers are hired; Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard establishes the vineyard as Israel/God's people under his care and reckoning. Matthew reuses this stock symbol (cf. the next parable, 21:33-41, which quotes Isa 5 directly), framing the kingdom under the imagery of God's vineyard.
sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]

note: The vine/vineyard brought out of Egypt and tended by God is part of the same symbolic field; faint thematic resonance behind the kingdom-as-vineyard image rather than verbal borrowing.
sourceText: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]

note: The Torah commands paying a hired laborer his wages the same day, before sundown: 'When evening had come... pay them their wages' (20:8) directly enacts this hired-laborer wage law, giving the parable its legal verisimilitude and its concern with what is 'right' (dikaion).
sourceText: You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates. In his day you shall give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down on it; for he is poor, and sets his heart on it; lest he cry against you to Yahweh, and it be sin to you.

note: Parallel wage-law ('the wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning'); reinforces the same-day payment background of 20:8.
sourceText: “‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.

note: 'Is your eye evil because I am good?' (20:15) uses the Semitic idiom of the 'evil eye' (ophthalmos ponēros) for grudging stinginess; Deut 15:9 warns against the eye being 'evil' (begrudging) toward a needy brother — the exact moral idiom Jesus inverts (here it is the workers who begrudge the master's generosity).
sourceText: Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing; and he cry to Yahweh against you, and it be sin to you.

note: 'Do not eat the bread of him who has an evil eye' — same 'evil eye'=miserly idiom standing behind 20:15; faint, idiomatic rather than allusive.
sourceText: Don’t eat the food of him who has a stingy eye, and don’t crave his delicacies:

note: 'It is my desire to give... Isn't it lawful for me to do what I want with what I own?' (20:14-15) echoes God's sovereign freedom in mercy ('I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious'); thematic, disputed.
sourceText: He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.”

note: 'The burden of the day and the scorching heat' (20:12) faintly recalls the scorching east wind/heat motif; very weak, likely just realistic detail of agricultural labor.
sourceText: When the sun arose, God prepared a sultry east wind; and the sun beat on Jonah’s head, so that he fainted, and requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”

note: The Son of Man 'will be delivered/handed over' (paradothēsetai) to the authorities and Gentiles; paradidōmi is the verb the Greek of Isaiah 53 uses for the Servant being 'handed over' for sins (Isa 53:6,12 LXX), coloring the passion prediction with Servant theology.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: 'to mock, to scourge' (20:19) corresponds to the Servant who gives his back to those who strike and his face to mocking/spitting; the catalog of mistreatment draws on the third Servant Song.
sourceText: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.

note: 'the third day he will be raised up' (20:19) echoes 'on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him'; widely read as the scriptural background for the 'third day' resurrection formula.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: 'the Son of Man' (20:18) carries the Danielic title; here paradoxically the exalted Danielic figure is the one delivered up to death, a Matthean recurrence of the title.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: 'the cup that I am about to drink' (20:22) is the prophetic 'cup of wrath/staggering' that Jerusalem drinks (Isa 51:17,22); Jesus takes upon himself the cup of judgment, the dominant OT background for the passion-cup.
sourceText: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.

note: The cup of foaming wine of God's wrath that the wicked drink to the dregs; supplies the 'cup' = divine judgment imagery behind 20:22-23.
sourceText: For in the hand of Yahweh there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.

note: 'Take this cup of the wine of wrath from my hand, and make all the nations drink it' — the cup of wrath passed to the nations; reinforces the cup-of-judgment field Jesus says he must drink.
sourceText: For thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, to me: take this cup of the wine of wrath at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it.

note: The cup of horror and desolation that Jerusalem must drink to the dregs; same cup-of-wrath motif, fainter parallel.
sourceText: You have walked in the way of your sister; therefore will I give her cup into your hand. Thus says the Lord Yahweh: You will drink of your sister’s cup, which is deep and large; you will be ridiculed and held in derision; it contains much. You shall be filled with drunkenness and sorrow, with the cup of astonishment and desolation, with the cup of your sister Samaria. You shall even drink it and drain it out, and you shall gnaw the broken pieces of it, […]

note: The request to sit at Jesus' right hand and left in his kingdom faintly invokes enthronement-at-the-right-hand language; weak, the verbal contact is only 'right hand.'
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: The 'baptism' of overwhelming suffering pairs with the cup; the engulfing-waters imagery of the righteous sufferer ('the waters have come up to my neck') is a faint background for being 'baptized' with suffering.
sourceText: Save me, God, for the waters have come up to my neck! I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold. I have come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.

note: KEY allusion. 'The Son of Man came... to give his life as a ransom for many' (20:28) compresses the fourth Servant Song: the Servant 'pours out his soul to death' and 'bears the sin of many' (Isa 53:12), making his life an offering (asham, 53:10). 'Give his life' (dounai tēn psychēn) + 'for many' (anti pollōn) maps onto the LXX Servant who is handed over for the 'many' (polloi, Isa 53:11-12). Vicarious, substitutionary death — the figural fulfillment of the Servant.
sourceText: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]

note: Jesus identifies himself as the one who came 'to serve' (diakonēsai); the title 'Son of Man' is overlaid on the exalted 'my Servant' (pais) of Isaiah, framing his whole mission as the Servant of YHWH who suffers and is exalted.
sourceText: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.

note: 'The rulers of the nations lord it over them... it shall not be so among you' (20:25-26) inverts the false shepherds of Israel who 'with force and harshness ruled them'; Jesus contrasts domineering rule with self-giving service in the shepherd-leadership idiom of Ezek 34.
sourceText: You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither have you bound up that which was broken, neither have you brought back that which was driven away, neither have you sought that which was lost; but with force and with rigor you have ruled over them.

note: Rehoboam's choice to make his yoke heavier and rule harshly over against serving the people is a narrative type of lordly domination Jesus repudiates; thematic, disputed.
sourceText: Rehoboam went to Shechem: for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king. When Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was yet in Egypt, where he had fled from the presence of king Solomon, and Jeroboam lived in Egypt, and they sent and called him), Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came, and spoke to Rehoboam, saying, “Your father made our yoke grievous: now therefore make you the grievous service of your father, and his heavy yoke which […]

note: God 'gave Egypt as your ransom (LXX allagma/lytron), Cush and Seba in exchange for you... I give people in return for your life'; supplies the ransom-in-exchange-for-life logic of lytron anti pollōn in 20:28.
sourceText: For I am Yahweh your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior. I have given Egypt as your ransom, Ethiopia and Seba in your place. Since you have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you; therefore I will give people in your place, and nations instead of your life.

note: Each Israelite gives a 'ransom (lytra) for his life' at the census so that no plague falls; background to the ransom-price (lytron) vocabulary, though Jesus' self-gift transcends the cultic fee.
sourceText: “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.

note: 'No man can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him, for the redemption of their life is costly'; Jesus' ransom answers the impossibility the psalm laments — faint, ironic counterpoint.
sourceText: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough,

note: 'the Son of Man' (20:28) again carries the Danielic title; the one given dominion and service by the nations is here the one who himself comes to serve, a deliberate Matthean inversion of the Danielic enthronement.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'that our eyes may be opened... their eyes received their sight' (20:33-34) enacts the messianic-age promise 'then the eyes of the blind shall be opened'; the healing functions as a sign that the awaited deliverance has arrived (cf. Matt 11:5).
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.

note: The Servant is called 'to open the eyes that are blind'; the blind men's healing realizes the Servant's commission — tying this episode back to the Servant theme just sounded in 20:28.
sourceText: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: 'Son of David, have mercy on us!' (20:30-31) invokes the Davidic covenant promise of an everlasting throne to David's seed; the blind confess Jesus as the messianic Son of David.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]

note: The 'shoot from the stump of Jesse' stands behind the Son-of-David / Davidic-messiah confession; thematic support for the title in 20:30.
sourceText: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.

note: 'the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity' — additional eschatological sight-restoration promise reinforcing the Isaianic background of the healing.
sourceText: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.

note: 'Have mercy on us (eleēson hēmas), O LORD, have mercy on us' — the doubled cry of the blind (20:30-31) reuses the stock psalmic plea for mercy; idiomatic rather than a specific citation.
sourceText: Have mercy on us, Yahweh, have mercy on us, for we have endured much contempt.

note: Matthew's formula citation (21:4-5) of the prophesied king who comes 'humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.' Matthew uniquely reads the Hebrew parallelism woodenly, producing two animals (donkey and colt), which shapes his narrative of two beasts (21:7).
sourceText: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

note: The opening of the citation, 'Tell the daughter of Zion, behold...,' is drawn from Isaiah 62:11 ('Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold, your salvation comes') rather than from Zechariah, whose own opening is 'Rejoice greatly.' Matthew blends Isaiah 62:11 with Zechariah 9:9 into a single quotation.
sourceText: Behold, Yahweh has proclaimed to the end of the earth, “Say to the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your salvation comes. Behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him.’”

note: The crowd's cry (21:9) quotes Psalm 118:25-26: 'Hosanna' transliterates the Hebrew 'hoshia-na' ('save now,' Ps 118:25), and 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD' is verbatim from Ps 118:26 (LXX), a Hallel pilgrimage acclamation.
sourceText: Save us now, we beg you, Yahweh! Yahweh, we beg you, send prosperity now. Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.

note: Spreading garments on the road as an act of royal acclamation: at Jehu's anointing the men 'took every man his garment, and put it under him... and blew the trumpet, saying, Jehu is king.' The crowd's gesture (21:8) enacts an enthronement.
sourceText: Then they hurried, and took every man his garment, and put it under him on the top of the stairs, and blew the trumpet, saying, “Jehu is king.”

note: Solomon is mounted on the king's mule and led to be made king amid rejoicing; the royal son of David enters his city riding a humble mount to acclamation, the pattern Jesus' entry evokes.
sourceText: The king said to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon. Let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him there king over Israel. Blow the trumpet, and say, ‘Long live king Solomon!’ Then you shall come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne; for he shall be king in my place. I have appointed him to be prince over Israel and over Judah.” Benaiah the […]

note: The repeated acclamation 'son of David' (21:9) invokes the Davidic covenant promise of an everlasting throne to David's offspring, framing Jesus' entry as the coming of the promised Davidic king.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]

note: Jacob's blessing on Judah, 'binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine,' was read messianically (donkey + colt motif) in Jewish tradition and may stand behind the donkey imagery alongside Zechariah 9:9.
sourceText: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.

note: 'Rejoice, daughter of Zion... the King of Israel, even the LORD, is in your midst': a 'daughter of Zion' oracle announcing the arrival of the divine king, thematically resonant with the entry.
sourceText: Sing, daughter of Zion! Shout, Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. Yahweh has taken away your judgments. He has thrown out your enemy. The King of Israel, Yahweh, is in your midst. You will not be afraid of evil any more.

note: The crowd's identification of Jesus as 'the prophet' (21:11) may echo the promise of a prophet like Moses whom the people must heed.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: Simon's entry into the Jerusalem citadel 'with praise and palm branches' provides a Second Temple template for entering the holy city with branches and acclamation, paralleling the multitude cutting and spreading branches (21:8).
sourceText: And he entered into it on the three and twentieth day of the second month, in the hundred and seventy and first year, with praise and palm branches, and with harps, and with cymbals, and with viols, and with hymns, and with songs: because a great enemy was destroyed out of Israel.

note: At the temple's rededication the people carried 'branches and beautiful boughs and palms' with hymns, a Hanukkah-style festal procession resembling the branch-waving acclamation of Jesus.
sourceText: Wherefore bearing wands wreathed with leaves, and fair boughs, and palms also, they offered up hymns of thanksgiving to him that had prosperously brought to pass the cleansing of his own place.

note: Jesus' citation 'My house shall be called a house of prayer' (21:13) quotes Isaiah 56:7 verbatim, an oracle of the temple as a house of prayer for all peoples; the act of cleansing enacts the eschatological temple ideal.
sourceText: even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”

note: 'But you have made it a den of robbers' (21:13) quotes Jeremiah 7:11 from the Temple Sermon, where cultic activity masks injustice and invites judgment; the borrowed indictment imports Jeremiah's threat of the temple's destruction.
sourceText: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” says Yahweh.

note: Jesus answers the indignant priests by citing Psalm 8:2 (21:16): 'Out of the mouth of babes and nursing babies you have perfected praise' (the LXX form 'perfected praise' rather than MT 'established strength'), legitimating the children's Hosanna as God-ordained praise.
sourceText: From the lips of babes and infants you have established strength, because of your adversaries, that you might silence the enemy and the avenger.
lxxText: Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou perfected praise, because of thine enemies; that thou mightest put down the enemy and avenger.

note: 'There shall no longer be a trader (Canaanite/merchant) in the house of the LORD of hosts on that day': the eschatological purging of commerce from the temple is the closest prophetic charter for driving out sellers and money-changers.
sourceText: Yes, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to Yahweh of Armies; and all those who sacrifice will come and take of them, and cook in them. In that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple... he will purify the sons of Levi': the messenger/Lord coming to purify temple worship undergirds Jesus' purifying intervention.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and […]

note: The proverb that 'the blind and the lame' shall not come into the house is pointedly reversed: 'the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them' (21:14), so that the excluded are restored at the purified temple.
sourceText: David said on that day, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites, let him get up to the watercourse, and strike the lame and the blind, who are hated by David’s soul.” Therefore they say, “The blind and the lame can’t come into the house.”

note: The doves/pigeons sold (21:12) are the offering prescribed for the poor (also Lev 12:8); their sellers' tables being overthrown touches the cult of the poor at the temple.
sourceText: “‘If he can’t afford a lamb, then he shall bring his trespass offering for that in which he has sinned, two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, to Yahweh; one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering.

note: Nehemiah's expulsion of Tobiah's goods and his cleansing of the temple chambers offers a precedent of zealous reform purging defilement from the temple precincts.
sourceText: and I came to Jerusalem, and understood the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, in preparing him a room in the courts of God’s house. It grieved me severely: therefore I threw all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the room. Then I commanded, and they cleansed the rooms: and there brought I again the vessels of God’s house, with the meal offerings and the frankincense.

note: 'When I would gather them... there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf is withered': a judgment oracle on fruitless Israel whose figs and leaves fail, the closest prophetic backdrop to the cursed, leafy-but-fruitless fig tree (21:19).
sourceText: I will utterly consume them, says Yahweh: no grapes shall be on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall fade; and the things that I have given them shall pass away from them.

note: 'I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the first ripe in the fig tree,' followed by their apostasy and barrenness; the fig tree symbolizes Israel's spoiled fruit, the figural sense Matthew gives the withered tree.
sourceText: I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the first ripe in the fig tree at its first season; but they came to Baal Peor, and consecrated themselves to the shameful thing, and became abominable like that which they loved.

note: 'There is no cluster to eat; my soul desired the first-ripe fig' — the prophet finding no fruit on Israel, mirroring Jesus hungry and 'finding nothing on it but leaves' (21:19).
sourceText: Misery is mine! Indeed, I am like one who gathers the summer fruits, as gleanings of the vineyard: There is no cluster of grapes to eat. My soul desires to eat the early fig.

note: The fig tree laid waste and withered in the day of judgment supplies the imagery of a suddenly dried-up fig tree as a sign of devastation.
sourceText: He has laid my vine waste, and stripped my fig tree. He has stripped its bark, and thrown it away. Its branches are made white.

note: The 'first-ripe fig' that is quickly consumed/fails contributes to the prophetic stock of fig imagery for judgment on Israel.
sourceText: The fading flower of his glorious beauty, which is on the head of the fertile valley, shall be like the first-ripe fig before the summer; which someone picks and eats as soon as he sees it.

note: 'Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain': prophetic precedent for the leveling of a mountain by faith/divine word, paralleling 'tell this mountain, Be taken up and cast into the sea' (21:21).
sourceText: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”

note: 'Though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea' supplies the very image of a mountain cast into the sea used in Jesus' saying on faith.
sourceText: Therefore we won’t be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas;

note: 'Though the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines' — a fruitless fig tree as a figure of scarcity and testing, a faint resonance.
sourceText: For though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines; the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food; the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls:

note: The challenge 'By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?' (21:23) faintly recalls the recurring biblical motif of authority contested ('Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?'), the leader's commission questioned by his own people.
sourceText: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”

note: Korah's challenge to Moses and Aaron, 'Why do you lift yourselves up above the assembly?,' is a paradigmatic disputing of divinely given authority, distantly resonant with the priests' interrogation.
sourceText: They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron, and said to them, “You take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy, everyone of them, and Yahweh is among them! Why do you lift yourselves up above Yahweh’s assembly?”

note: The father's command 'go work today in my vineyard' (21:28) uses the standing prophetic image of the vineyard as Israel and its work as covenant obedience, preparing for the explicit vineyard parable that follows.

note: 'John came to you in the way of righteousness' (21:32) employs the Wisdom/sapiential idiom 'the way of righteousness' (cf. Prov 12:28; 21:16) for the path of life that the hearers refused.
sourceText: I walk in the way of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of justice;

The whole parable presupposes Isaiah's allegory of the vineyard as Israel/Judah and its expected fruit.
sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. note: Jesus cites Psalm 118:22-23 verbatim (21:42): 'The stone which the builders rejected, the same was made the head of the corner. This was from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes,' interpreting the rejected/vindicated son as the rejected/exalted cornerstone (same Psalm 118 quoted at the entry, 21:9).
sourceText: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This is Yahweh’s doing. It is marvelous in our eyes.

note: 21:44, 'He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but on whomever it will fall, it will scatter him as dust,' draws on Daniel's stone cut without hands that smashes the kingdoms and whose fragments become chaff blown away — the stone that both judges and inaugurates God's kingdom.
sourceText: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.

note: Isaiah's 'stone of stumbling and rock of offense' on which many 'shall fall, and be broken' supplies the first half of 21:44 ('he who falls on this stone will be broken'), fusing with the Psalm 118 cornerstone into a composite stone-testimonium.
sourceText: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”

note: The tenants' deliberation, 'This is the heir. Come, let's kill him, and seize his inheritance' (21:38), closely echoes Joseph's brothers: 'Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now, let us kill him' — the heir/beloved son plotted against by his own.
sourceText: They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him. They said one to another, “Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.”

note: 'I sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them, yet they did not listen' (cf. Jer 25:4) is the prophetic pattern behind the householder repeatedly sending servants who are beaten and killed (21:34-36).
sourceText: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.

note: Zechariah son of Jehoiada, sent by God to the people, was stoned to death in the court of the temple — a concrete instance of a divine messenger stoned, matching 'stoned another' (21:35).
sourceText: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.

note: Israel's confession that 'they slew your prophets which testified against them to turn them to you' summarizes the rejected-and-killed-emissaries pattern the parable allegorizes.
sourceText: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.

note: The vine brought out of Egypt and planted, whose hedges God then breaks down so passers-by pluck it, is a second vineyard-as-Israel song reinforcing Isaiah 5 and the threat to remove the vineyard's protection (21:43).

note: 'The LORD testified against Israel... by all the prophets... yet they would not hear, but hardened their necks' — the deuteronomistic summary of prophets sent and rejected, paralleling the servants' fate.
sourceText: Yet Yahweh testified to Israel, and to Judah, by every prophet, and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.” Notwithstanding, they would not listen, but hardened their neck, like the neck of their fathers, who didn’t believe in Yahweh their God.

note: The 'precious cornerstone' laid in Zion as a sure foundation belongs to the same stone-testimonia cluster (with Ps 118:22) that early Christians combined to interpret Christ as the cornerstone.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: 'You have eaten up the vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your houses' — Israel's leaders arraigned for plundering the vineyard, resonant with the tenants who seize the produce and inheritance.
sourceText: Yahweh will enter into judgment with the elders of his people, and their leaders: “It is you who have eaten up the vineyard. The plunder of the poor is in your houses.

note: 'Strike the shepherd' as the divinely sent figure who is struck may faintly inform the killing of the beloved son, though the imagery differs.
sourceText: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.

note: The kingdom given to 'a nation producing its fruit' (21:43) faintly recalls Daniel's everlasting kingdom given to the people of the saints, the transfer of dominion to a faithful nation.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The eschatological banquet — the LORD makes 'a feast of fat things' (fatlings/oxen killed, 22:4) for all peoples on his mountain. sourceText: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.

note: The LORD 'has prepared a sacrifice' and bids his guests, and on that day will punish 'all such as are clothed with strange apparel' — a striking double parallel to the prepared feast (22:4) AND the man cast out for improper garment (22:11-13). Likely source for the wedding-clothing judgment.
sourceText: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests. note: Wisdom builds her house, 'kills her beasts,' mixes her wine, and sends out maidservants to invite the simple to her feast — close structural echo of slaughtered cattle (22:4) and servants sent to call guests (22:3-4,9).

note: Open invitation to come freely to a banquet of rich food — thematic echo of the wide call to the highways (22:9), the unworthy invited replaced by all comers.

note: Prophets/servants sent to call Israel back are seized and killed (Zechariah stoned in the temple court) — the king's servants beaten and murdered (22:6) figure the rejected prophets, a deuteronomistic pattern Matthew develops (cf. 23:34-37).

note: God 'sent unto you all my servants the prophets... yet they hearkened not' but treated them shamefully — the repeated sending of servants who are spurned and killed (22:3-6) reuses this prophetic-rejection schema.
sourceText: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.

note: Israel 'slew thy prophets which testified against them' — same servants-as-prophets motif behind the murdered messengers (22:6).
sourceText: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.

note: Burning of the rebellious city (Jerusalem by Babylon) — the king sends armies, destroys the murderers and burns their city (22:7), echoing the prophetic-historical pattern of a city torched in judgment.
sourceText: He burnt Yahweh’s house, and the king’s house; and all the houses of Jerusalem, even every great house, burnt he with fire.

note: 'He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation... as a bridegroom decketh himself' — wedding-garment imagery (22:11-12) as the required clothing of righteousness/salvation for the marriage feast.
sourceText: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

note: 'Many have been created, but few shall be saved' (Fourth Ezra) — a near-formulaic Second Temple parallel to 'many are called, but few are chosen' (22:14).
sourceText: There be many created, but few shall be saved.

note: Jesus' question 'whose image (eikon) and inscription?' (22:20) plays on imago Dei: the coin bears Caesar's image and is owed to Caesar, but humanity bears God's image and is owed wholly to God — 'render to God the things that are God's' (22:21).
sourceText: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: 'The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof' — undergirds the claim that what is God's (everything, including the bearer of his image) belongs to God (22:21).
sourceText: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell therein.

note: Counsel to keep the king's commandment because of one's oath to God — faint wisdom backdrop to the dual obligation to Caesar and to God (22:21).
sourceText: I say, “Keep the king’s command!” because of the oath to God.

note: The Sadducees quote the levirate law nearly verbatim: 'If a man die, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed for his brother' (22:24) = Deuteronomy 25:5-6.
sourceText: If brothers dwell together, and one of them dies, and has no son, the wife of the dead shall not be married outside to a stranger. Her husband’s brother shall go in to her, and take her as his wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her.

note: Judah commands Onan to 'go in unto thy brother's wife... and raise up seed to thy brother' — the narrative instance of levirate duty behind the Sadducees' test case (22:24-28).
sourceText: Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her, and raise up seed to your brother.”

note: Jesus' clinching scriptural proof, formula-cited ('that which was spoken to you by God'): 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' (22:32) — verbatim from God at the bush; Jesus argues the patriarchs live to God.
sourceText: Moreover he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God.
