note: The same divine self-naming as 'the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' is repeated and declared God's everlasting memorial name — reinforces the citation in 22:32.
sourceText: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.

note: 'Many of them that sleep in the dust shall awake' — the canonical OT resurrection text behind the whole resurrection controversy the Sadducees deny (22:23,28-31).
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: Sarah had been given to seven husbands, each killed before consummation (Tobit 3:8; 7:11) — a Second Temple narrative of a woman successively wed to seven men, strikingly close to the Sadducees' seven-brothers scenario (22:25-27).
sourceText: because that she had been given to seven husbands, and Asmodaeus the evil spirit killed them, before they had lain with her. And they said to her, “Do you not know that you strangle your husbands? You have had already seven husbands, and you haven’t borne the name of any one of them.

note: The martyred brothers' hope that 'the King of the world shall raise us up... unto everlasting life' — a Second Temple affirmation of bodily resurrection contested by the Sadducees here (22:23-32).
sourceText: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.

note: 'Sons of God' / angels — faint backdrop to 'they are as the angels of God in heaven' (22:30); largely thematic and disputed.
sourceText: God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives.

note: The Shema's love command quoted as the first and great commandment: 'Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind' (22:37).
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: The second commandment quoted verbatim: 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself' (22:39).
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'To love him, to serve the LORD thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul' — reinforces the whole-being love demanded in 22:37.
sourceText: Now, Israel, what does Yahweh your God require of you, but to fear Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him, and to serve Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul,

note: Command to 'love the LORD your God... with all your heart and with all your soul' — another canonical restatement standing behind 22:37.
sourceText: Only take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law which Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, to love Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”

note: Formula-cited as David speaking 'in the Spirit': 'The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool' (22:44) — the crux for showing the Christ is more than David's son.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: The Davidic covenant promising David a 'seed' whose throne God establishes and who will be God's son — the basis for the crowd's answer that the Christ is the son of David (22:42).
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;

note: 'Thou art my Son' — royal/messianic sonship that, paired with Psalm 110, presses Jesus' question of how David's son can also be David's Lord (22:43-45).
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.

note: The messianic 'rod out of the stem of Jesse' — Davidic-descent expectation underlying 'whose son is he? ... Of David' (22:42).
sourceText: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.

note: "Moses' seat" (v2) as the locus of teaching/judging authority evokes Moses sitting to adjudicate for the people; the chair becomes a metaphor for inherited Mosaic teaching office.
sourceText: On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening.

note: The duty to do all that the Levitical judges 'at that place' tell you, not turning aside, underlies Jesus' 'observe and do whatever they tell you' (v3) even while condemning their conduct.
sourceText: You shall do according to the decisions of the verdict which they shall give you from that place which Yahweh chooses. You shall observe to do according to all that they shall teach you: according to the decisions of the law which they shall teach you, and according to the judgment which they shall tell you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the sentence which they shall show you, to the right hand, nor to the left.

note: "They make their phylacteries broad" (v5) directly references tefillin, the binding of the words 'as a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes'; Jesus targets the ostentatious enlargement of this commanded practice.
sourceText: You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.

note: Parallel phylactery command ('a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes') stands behind the broadened phylacteries of v5.
sourceText: It shall be for a sign on your hand, and for symbols between your eyes: for by strength of hand Yahweh brought us out of Egypt.”

note: "Enlarge the fringes of their garments" (v5) references the commanded tassels (tzitzit) on the corners of garments, given as a reminder of the commandments; the abuse is enlarging them for show.
sourceText: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;

note: "They love the place of honor at feasts, the best seats" (v6) inverts the wisdom counsel not to claim the place of the great but to be invited up; same banqueting-status imagery Jesus uses elsewhere (Luke 14).
sourceText: Don’t exalt yourself in the presence of the king, or claim a place among great men; for it is better that it be said to you, “Come up here,” than that you should be put lower in the presence of the prince, whom your eyes have seen.

note: "Call no man your father... one is your Father" (v9) echoes 'Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?' — the prophetic insistence on a single divine paternity over the covenant community.
sourceText: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?

note: "You, O LORD, are our Father" supports the one-Father claim of v9 against human honorifics.
sourceText: For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us: you, Yahweh, are our Father; our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.

note: "All your children shall be taught by the LORD" undergirds 'one is your teacher' (v8); divine, not rabbinic, instruction is the eschatological norm.
sourceText: All your children shall be taught of Yahweh; and great shall be the peace of your children.

note: Hannah's song ('The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and exalts') anticipates the reversal of v12, that the self-exalting are humbled and the humble exalted.
sourceText: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up.

note: "A man's pride will bring him low, but the humble in spirit will obtain honor" is the proverbial substrate of v12's exaltation/humiliation reversal.
sourceText: A man’s pride brings him low, but one of lowly spirit gains honor.

note: "Exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high" supplies the prophetic reversal formula behind v12.
sourceText: thus says the Lord Yahweh: Remove the turban, and take off the crown; this will not be as it was; exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.

note: "He saves the humble... God saves the lowly" parallels the exalt/humble logic of v12.
sourceText: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.

note: The Day of the LORD theme that 'the haughtiness of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone exalted' resonates with v12.
sourceText: The lofty looks of man will be brought low, the haughtiness of men will be bowed down, and Yahweh alone will be exalted in that day. For there will be a day of Yahweh of Armies for all that is proud and haughty, and for all that is lifted up; and it shall be brought low: For all the cedars of Lebanon, that are high and lifted up, for all the oaks of Bashan, For all the high mountains, for all the hills that are lifted up, For every lofty tower, for every […]

note: "Son of Gehenna" (v15) presupposes the Valley of Hinnom (ge-hinnom), defiled by Josiah, as the topographic origin of the eschatological place of judgment.
sourceText: He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.

note: The renaming of the Valley of the Son of Hinnom as 'the Valley of Slaughter' supplies the dark connotation behind 'son of Gehenna' (v15).
sourceText: therefore, behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that this place shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter.

note: "Blind guides" / 'his watchmen are blind' — the prophetic indictment of sightless religious leaders stands behind the repeated 'blind guides, blind fools' (vv16-19,24).
sourceText: His watchmen are blind, they are all without knowledge; they are all mute dogs, they can’t bark; dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber.

note: "You shall not swear by my name falsely" grounds the whole oath casuistry of vv16-22; the Pharisaic gradations of binding vs. non-binding oaths violate the simple seriousness of vowing.
sourceText: “‘You shall not swear by my name falsely, and profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh.

note: The law that a vow to the LORD must be paid and is not to be trifled with underlies Jesus' attack on evasive oath distinctions (vv16-22).
sourceText: When you vow a vow to Yahweh your God, you shall not be slack to pay it; for Yahweh your God will surely require it of you; and it would be sin in you. But if you refrain from making a vow, it shall be no sin in you. You shall observe and do that which has gone out of your lips. Whatever you have vowed to Yahweh your God as a freewill offering, which you have promised with your mouth, you must do.

note: "The altar... whatever touches the altar shall be holy" is the precise principle Jesus invokes in v19: the altar sanctifies the gift, so swearing by the altar binds by all on it.
sourceText: Seven days you shall make atonement for the altar, and sanctify it: and the altar shall be most holy; whatever touches the altar shall be holy.

note: Solomon's temple as the 'place for you to dwell in forever' undergirds v21, swearing 'by him who dwells in it'; cf. the tension with 8:27 that heaven cannot contain God.
sourceText: I have surely built you a house of habitation, a place for you to dwell in forever.”

note: "Heaven is my throne" directly grounds v22: to swear by heaven is to swear by the throne of God and by him who sits on it.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what kind of house will you build to me? and what place shall be my rest?

note: "The LORD has established his throne in the heavens" supports the heaven-as-throne identification of v22.
sourceText: Yahweh has established his throne in the heavens. His kingdom rules over all.

note: "The tithe of the land... is the LORD's" grounds v23; the Pharisees scrupulously tithe even garden herbs (mint, dill, cumin), extending the produce-tithe to the smallest plants.
sourceText: “‘All the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is Yahweh’s. It is holy to Yahweh.

note: "The weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith(fulness)" (v23) closely echoes 'to do justice, and to love mercy (hesed), and to walk humbly' — the prophetic distillation of true Torah.
sourceText: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

note: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice" — Matthew's signature prophetic text (cf. 9:13; 12:7) — underlies the priority of mercy over ritual scruple in v23.
sourceText: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

note: "Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy" parallels the triad of justice/mercy/faith as the weightier matters of v23.
sourceText: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother.

note: "Do justice and righteousness... do no wrong" reinforces the justice/mercy demand neglected in v23.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh: Execute justice and righteousness, and deliver him who is robbed out of the hand of the oppressor: and do no wrong, do no violence, to the foreigner, the fatherless, nor the widow; neither shed innocent blood in this place.

note: The camel is explicitly named unclean; 'strain out a gnat and swallow a camel' (v24) plays on the largest and (via Lev 11:23,41) the smallest unclean creatures, an absurd inversion of purity scruple.
sourceText: “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is unclean to you.

note: Touching a grave or human bones renders one unclean seven days; the 'whitewashed tombs... full of dead men's bones' (v27) trades on corpse-impurity, the very thing graves were whitewashed to warn passersby against.
sourceText: “Whoever in the open field touches one who is slain with a sword, or a dead body, or a bone of a man, or a grave, shall be unclean seven days.

note: The false prophets who 'whitewash' a flimsy wall to make it look sound, only for it to be torn down, supply the controlling image of v27's whitewashed tombs concealing inner corruption.
sourceText: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there is no peace; and when one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash: tell those who plaster it with whitewash, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and you, great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall tear it. Behold, when the wall has fallen, shall it not be said to you, Where is the plaster with which you have plastered it? Therefore […]

note: Purity rules for vessels (cups, dishes) that contract uncleanness stand behind the inside/outside-of-the-cup imagery of vv25-26.
sourceText: On whatever any of them falls when they are dead, it shall be unclean; whether it is any vessel of wood, or clothing, or skin, or sack, whatever vessel it is, with which any work is done, it must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it will be clean. Every earthen vessel, into which any of them falls, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it. All food which may be eaten, that on which water comes, shall be […]

note: God 'sent persistently to them by his messengers... but they kept mocking the messengers... and scoffing at his prophets' — the Chronicler's summation of prophet-rejection frames vv29-37's prophet-killing generation.
sourceText: Yahweh, the God of their fathers, sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.

note: "They killed your prophets who had warned them" — the confessional memory of slain prophets undergirds vv30-31,34-37.
sourceText: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.

note: Elijah's complaint 'they have killed your prophets with the sword' is part of the prophet-martyr tradition behind vv31,37.
sourceText: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

note: The prophet Uriah son of Shemaiah killed by the king is a concrete instance of the prophet-killing the woe presupposes (vv31,34).
sourceText: There was also a man who prophesied in Yahweh’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: and when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt: and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son […]

note: "The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete" supplies the 'measure not yet full' logic of v32, 'fill up the measure of your fathers.'
sourceText: In the fourth generation they will come here again, for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.”

note: "When the transgressors have reached their full measure" parallels the filling-up-of-iniquity idiom of v32.
sourceText: In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up.

note: "You serpents" (v33) may evoke the primeval serpent and its 'seed,' casting the opponents as offspring of the deceiver.
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: "From the serpent's root comes forth an adder, and its fruit a flying serpent" supplies the viper-offspring image of 'offspring of vipers' (v33; cf. 3:7; 12:34).
sourceText: Don’t rejoice, O Philistia, all of you, because the rod that struck you is broken; for out of the serpent’s root an adder will emerge, and his fruit will be a fiery flying serpent.

note: The wicked who 'hatch adders' eggs' parallels the 'offspring of vipers' charge (v33), linking venomous brood to deeds of bloodshed (Isa 59:7).
sourceText: They hatch adders’ eggs, and weave the spider’s web: he who eats of their eggs dies; and that which is crushed breaks out into a viper.

note: "Their wine is the poison of serpents and the cruel venom of asps' from the Song of Moses colors the serpent/viper invective of v33.
sourceText: Their wine is the poison of serpents, the cruel venom of asps.

note: "He sent prophets among them to bring them back to the LORD... they would not listen" stands directly before the Zechariah martyrdom and parallels 'I send to you prophets' (v34).
sourceText: Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again to Yahweh; and they testified against them: but they would not give ear.

note: "I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets... yet they did not listen' parallels the divine sending of prophets, wise men, and scribes in v34.
sourceText: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.

note: "The blood of righteous Abel" (v35) cites the first murder, whose blood 'cries to me from the ground' — the inaugural shed innocent blood opening the canonical span of martyrdom.
sourceText: Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him. Yahweh said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.

note: Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest, stoned 'in the court of the house of the LORD' (between sanctuary and altar), dying with 'May the LORD see and avenge' — the closing martyrdom of the Hebrew canon (Chronicles last); v35's Abel-to-Zechariah spans Genesis to Chronicles. The patronym 'son of Berechiah' likely conflates with the prophet of Zech 1:1.
sourceText: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house. Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his […]

note: "A crooked and twisted generation" from the Song of Moses lies behind the verdict on 'this generation' (v36).
sourceText: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.

note: The deuterocanonical plot of the wicked conspiring to condemn the righteous one to a shameful death anticipates the persecution/killing of the sent righteous in vv34-35.
sourceText: But let us lie in wait for the righteous man, Because he is of disservice to us, And is contrary to our works, And upbraids us with sins against the law, And lays to our charge sins against our discipline. He professes to have knowledge of God, And names himself servant of the Lord. He became to us a reproof of our thoughts. He is grievous to us even to behold, Because his life is unlike other men’s, And his paths are of strange fashion. We were accounted […]

note: God waiting 'until they have reached the full measure of their sins' parallels the filling-up of the fathers' measure (v32).
sourceText: For in the case of the other nations the Sovereign Lord does with longsuffering forbear, until that he punish them when they have attained to the full measure of their sins; but not so judged he as touching us,

note: "They stoned him... in the court of the house of the LORD" — Zechariah's stoning is a concrete referent for 'Jerusalem... who stones those sent to her' (v37).
sourceText: They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.

note: The confession that they 'killed your prophets' frames the apostrophe to prophet-killing Jerusalem (v37).
sourceText: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.

note: The eagle that 'spreads its wings... catches them, bears them on its pinions' from the Song of Moses is the maternal bird-protection image behind 'as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings' (v37).
sourceText: As an eagle that stirs up her nest, that flutters over her young, he spread abroad his wings, he took them, he bore them on his feathers.

note: "He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge" supplies the sheltering-wings imagery of v37 directly.
sourceText: He will cover you with his feathers. Under his wings you will take refuge. His faithfulness is your shield and rampart.

note: "Under whose wings you have come to take refuge" is part of the wing-shelter cluster behind v37.
sourceText: May Yahweh repay your work, and a full reward be given you from Yahweh, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”

note: "Hide me in the shadow of your wings" belongs to the protective-wings imagery gathered in v37.
sourceText: Keep me as the apple of your eye. Hide me under the shadow of your wings,

note: "Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem' — a bird-protection-of-Jerusalem image poignantly inverted when Jerusalem refuses gathering (v37).
sourceText: As birds hovering, so Yahweh of Armies will protect Jerusalem. He will protect and deliver it. He will pass over and preserve it.”

note: "This house shall become a desolation" — the LORD's oath against the royal house — is closely echoed in 'your house is left to you desolate' (v38).
sourceText: But if you will not hear these words, I swear by myself, says Yahweh, that this house shall become a desolation.

note: "I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my heritage" supplies the abandonment/desolation of the house in v38.
sourceText: I have forsaken my house, I have cast off my heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies.

note: The warning that the temple will become 'a heap of ruins' and Israel a byword if they forsake the LORD informs the desolation pronounced in v38.
sourceText: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’

note: "May their camp be a desolation; let no one dwell in their tents" parallels the desolate-house verdict of v38.
sourceText: Let their habitation be desolate. Let no one dwell in their tents.

note: The departure of the glory of the LORD from the temple is the theological backdrop to the house being 'left desolate' in v38.
sourceText: Yahweh’s glory went out from over the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubim. The cherubim lifted up their wings, and mounted up from the earth in my sight when they went out, and the wheels beside them: and they stood at the door of the east gate of Yahweh’s house; and the glory of the God of Israel was over them above.

note: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD" is quoted verbatim in v39 — the Hallel acclamation (already shouted at the entry, 21:9) whose future utterance conditions Jerusalem's seeing of Jesus again.
sourceText: Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.

note: The prophecy that not one stone of the temple will be left on another reprises Micah's oracle that 'Zion shall be plowed as a field, Jerusalem shall become heaps,' the classic prophetic word of the temple's destruction; Jeremiah cites Micah 3:12 in his temple sermon (Jer 26:18), making it the paradigmatic temple-doom text.
sourceText: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.

note: Jeremiah's temple sermon threatens to do to the Jerusalem house what was done to Shiloh; Jesus' prediction of the temple's total demolition stands in this prophetic tradition of judgment on a temple presumed inviolable.
sourceText: therefore will I do to the house which is called by my name, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.

note: Jeremiah's recitation of Micah's temple-destruction oracle before the elders forms the precedent for a prophet announcing the razing of the temple and being threatened for it.
sourceText: Micah the Morashtite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah; and he spoke to all the people of Judah, saying, Thus says Yahweh of Armies: Zion shall be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest.

note: Jesus delivers the discourse seated on the Mount of Olives, the very mountain on which Zechariah says the LORD's feet will stand on the day of judgment, splitting it in two; the eschatological setting is deliberately Zecharian.
sourceText: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.

note: The glory of the LORD departs the temple and rests on 'the mountain east of the city' (the Mount of Olives); Jesus leaving the temple and seating himself on that mountain to pronounce its doom evokes the departure of the divine presence.
sourceText: Yahweh’s glory went up from the midst of the city, and stood on the mountain which is on the east side of the city.

note: The disciples' question about the sign of 'the end of the age' uses the apocalyptic 'time of the end' vocabulary that pervades Daniel 8-12, framing the whole discourse in Danielic eschatological terms.
sourceText: But you, Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end: many shall run back and forth, and knowledge shall be increased.”

note: 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom' closely matches 2 Chronicles 15:6, 'nation was crushed by nation and city by city,' a description of the LORD troubling them with every distress; the verbal pairing is the source idiom for the upheaval motif.
sourceText: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.

note: 'I will stir up Egyptian against Egyptian... city against city, kingdom against kingdom' supplies the same nation-against-nation / kingdom-against-kingdom formula for divine judgment producing internal strife.
sourceText: I will stir up the Egyptians against the Egyptians, and they will fight everyone against his brother, and everyone against his neighbor; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.

note: 'the beginning of birth pains' draws on the prophetic figure of the Day of the LORD as labor pangs; Isaiah 13:8 has the doomed seized by 'pangs and agony... like a woman in labor' in the oracle against Babylon, a passage Matthew 24:29 mines again for cosmic darkening.
sourceText: They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame.

note: The 'birth pains' metaphor for the onset of judgment is a recurring Jeremianic figure (also Jer 4:31; 6:24; 13:21), reinforcing 'beginning of birth pains' as prophetic shorthand for the throes preceding the end.
sourceText: Inhabitant of Lebanon, who makes your nest in the cedars, how greatly to be pitied you will be when pangs come on you, the pain as of a woman in travail!

note: 'all this must happen' (Greek dei genesthai) echoes Daniel's 'what must take place' / 'what will be in the latter days,' the apocalyptic language of divinely fixed events; the necessity (dei) is Danielic determinism.
sourceText: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:

note: 'rumors' troubling the king and the eschatological wars of Daniel 11 stand behind the 'wars and rumors of wars' that must occur before the end without yet being the end.
sourceText: But news out of the east and out of the north shall trouble him; and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and utterly to sweep away many.

note: 'See that you aren't troubled' recalls Isaiah's 'do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread,' the prophetic reassurance not to be terrified by the threats of the nations.
sourceText: “Don’t say, ‘A conspiracy!’ concerning all about which this people say, ‘A conspiracy!’ neither fear their threats, nor be terrorized.

note: The triad of sword (war), famine, and pestilence/plague is the standard prophetic judgment cluster (sword-famine-pestilence) found throughout Jeremiah and Ezekiel; 'famines, plagues, and earthquakes' draws on this covenant-curse vocabulary.
sourceText: ‘If evil comes on us—the sword, judgment, pestilence, or famine—we will stand before this house, and before you, (for your name is in this house), and cry to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.’

note: The sword-famine-pestilence triad that Jesus lists as preliminary woes is Ezekiel's signature judgment formula (also Ezek 6:11-12; 7:15; 14:21), the covenant curses unleashed on Jerusalem.
sourceText: A third part of you shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in your midst; and a third part shall fall by the sword around you; and a third part I will scatter to all the winds, and will draw out a sword after them.

note: The handing over to tribulation and the promise that 'he who endures to the end will be saved' echoes Daniel 12:1, where after a time of unequaled trouble 'your people shall be delivered, everyone found written in the book'; deliverance comes through, not around, the tribulation.
sourceText: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.

note: 'they will deliver you up... and will kill you' matches Daniel 11:33, where 'those who are wise... shall fall by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder' during the persecution, the maskilim suffering before vindication.
sourceText: Those who are wise among the people shall instruct many; yet they shall fall by the sword and by flame, by captivity and by plunder, many days.

note: The wise who 'stumble' so as to be refined 'until the time of the end' (Dan 11:35) stands behind 'many will stumble' under persecution before the end comes.
sourceText: Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.

note: 'will deliver up one another, and will hate one another' draws on Micah 7:6, where son dishonors father and a man's enemies are his own household, the eschatological breakdown of kinship loyalty Jesus cites explicitly in Matthew 10:21,35-36.
sourceText: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.

note: 'many will be purified... but the wicked shall act wickedly' (Dan 12:10) parallels the sifting in which many stumble and love grows cold while some endure to be saved.
sourceText: Many shall purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked shall do wickedly; and none of the wicked shall understand; but those who are wise shall understand.

note: The refining of a remnant through fire so that those who endure are saved while two-thirds perish (Zech 13:8-9) supplies the testing-and-remnant pattern behind enduring to the end for salvation.
sourceText: I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”

note: The gospel 'preached in the whole world for a testimony to all the nations' before the end resonates with the Servant being given as 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.'
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: Proclaiming God's glory and salvation 'among all the nations' anticipates the worldwide witness to the nations that must precede the end.
sourceText: Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples.

note: The intensifying judgments and the universal hatred for the name belong to the prophetic scenario of covenant judgment poured on a faithless world, of which Ezekiel's four deadly acts are emblematic.
sourceText: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: How much more when I send my four severe judgments on Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the evil animals, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and animal!

note: 'the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of through Daniel the prophet' is an explicit, attributed citation; Daniel 9:27 reads that 'on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate' (LXX bdelygma ton eremoseon), the precise phrase Jesus quotes.
sourceText: He shall make a firm covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease; and on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate; and even to the full end, and that determined, shall wrath be poured out on the desolate.

note: The same 'abomination that makes desolate' is set up in the temple in Daniel 11:31, the historical referent in the Antiochene desecration; Jesus' explicit Danielic citation conflates 11:31 with 9:27 and 12:11 as the prophetic source.
sourceText: Forces shall stand on his part, and they shall profane the sanctuary, even the fortress, and shall take away the continual burnt offering, and they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.

note: Daniel 12:11 dates 'the abomination that makes desolate' set up after the daily sacrifice is taken away; together with 9:27 and 11:31 this is the named Danielic prophecy Jesus invokes for the desecration standing in the holy place.
sourceText: From the time that the continual burnt offering shall be taken away, and the abomination that makes desolate set up, there shall be one thousand two hundred ninety days.

note: Daniel 8:13's 'transgression that makes desolate' giving over the sanctuary and host to be trampled is part of the same Danielic abomination complex underlying the desecration of the holy place.
sourceText: Then I heard a holy one speaking; and another holy one said to that certain one who spoke, How long shall be the vision about the continual burnt offering, and the disobedience that makes desolate, to give both the sanctuary and the army to be trodden under foot?

note: 'great oppression, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, nor ever will be' is a near-verbatim rendering of Daniel 12:1, 'a time of trouble such as never has been since there was a nation till that time'; this is the controlling source for the unequaled-tribulation clause.
sourceText: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.

note: 1 Maccabees 1:54 narrates the fulfillment of Daniel: Antiochus 'erected a desolating sacrilege (bdelygma eremoseos) on the altar of burnt offering,' the deuterocanonical realization of the abomination phrase Jesus reuses for a future desecration.
sourceText: And on the fifteenth day of Chislev, in the hundred and forty and fifth year, they built an abomination of desolation upon the altar, and in the cities of Judah on every side they built idol altars.

note: The 'such as has never been... nor ever will be' formula is itself a stock superlative of unprecedented disaster (Exod 9:18, the hail; 10:14, the locusts; 11:6, the death of the firstborn), reinforcing the tribulation's incomparability.
sourceText: Behold, tomorrow about this time I will cause it to rain a very grievous hail, such as has not been in Egypt since the day it was founded even until now.

note: Joel's Day of the LORD is 'a day of darkness... such as has never been, nor will be again after them through the years,' the same unequaled-distress superlative attached to the eschatological day.
sourceText: A day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness. As the dawn spreading on the mountains, a great and strong people; there has never been the like, neither will there be any more after them, even to the years of many generations.

note: 'flee to the mountains' and do not turn back to take anything echoes the angelic command to Lot, 'Flee to the hills... do not look back,' the paradigm of urgent escape from a doomed place before destruction falls.
sourceText: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”

note: Mattathias and his sons 'fled to the mountains' to escape the persecution and desecration, a Maccabean precedent for fleeing to the hills when the abomination stands in the holy place.
sourceText: And he and his sons fled into the mountains, and forsook all that they had in the city.

note: 'those who survive shall escape and be on the mountains' when judgment falls on the land parallels the command to flee to the mountains in the day of desolation.
sourceText: But those of those who escape shall escape, and shall be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, every one in his iniquity.

note: The warnings not to go down from the housetop or turn back in the field for one's goods recall Lot's wife, who looked back toward Sodom and perished; the danger of delay for possessions is the Sodom-escape topos.
sourceText: But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.

note: The woe to pregnant and nursing women in those days resonates with Lamentations' horrors of the siege of Jerusalem, where mothers and infants suffer the extremity of the city's fall.
sourceText: The hands of the pitiful women have boiled their own children; They were their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people.

note: The special woe to pregnant women and the dashing of infants in the day of judgment (Hosea 13:16) underlies the lament for those with child and nursing mothers in the days of tribulation.
sourceText: Samaria will bear her guilt; for she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women will be ripped open.”

note: The covenant-curse siege horrors falling especially on the tender and pregnant (Deut 28:53-57) form the Deuteronomic backdrop for the woe to mothers in those days.
sourceText: You will eat the fruit of your own body, the flesh of your sons and of your daughters, whom Yahweh your God has given you, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemies will distress you.

note: The days being 'shortened for the sake of the chosen ones' so that some flesh is saved echoes the prophetic logic of God preserving a remnant 'for my servants' sake' rather than destroying all.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, “As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one says, ‘Don’t destroy it, for a blessing is in it:’ so will I do for my servants’ sake, that I may not destroy them all.

note: 'false christs and false prophets will show great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray' draws on Deuteronomy 13:1-3, the warning about a prophet who gives a sign or wonder to lead Israel astray after other gods; the criterion is fidelity, not the marvel.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder,

note: The Deuteronomic insistence that even a wonder-working prophet who leads astray must be rejected reinforces 'don't believe it' against the seductive signs of false messiahs.
sourceText: That prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death, because he has spoken rebellion against Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to draw you aside out of the way which Yahweh your God commanded you to walk in. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.

note: The deceivers leading astray 'even the chosen ones, if possible' parallels Daniel's wise being tested and some falling away amid the deceits of the end-time tribulation.
sourceText: Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.

note: Expectation of the eschatological prophet/messiah in the wilderness or hidden chamber plays against authentic prophetic anticipation; the 'wilderness' rumor (v.26) trades on Elijah-style wilderness expectation.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: 'wherever the carcass is, there is where the vultures gather' evokes the swift birds of prey swooping to the kill in Habakkuk's vision of judgment, the inevitability and visibility of the coming devastation.
sourceText: Their horses also are swifter than leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves. Their horsemen press proudly on. Yes, their horsemen come from afar. They fly as an eagle that hurries to devour.

note: 'where the slain are, there is he' (the eagle/vulture over the carcass, Job 39:30) is a likely source for the proverb of the gathering vultures, an image of unmistakable, inevitable convergence.
sourceText: His young ones also suck up blood. Where the slain are, there he is.”

note: The birds gathering to the great slaughter-sacrifice in the day of the LORD (Ezek 39:4,17-20) lies behind the carcass-and-vultures image of eschatological judgment that none will miss.
sourceText: You, son of man, thus says the Lord Yahweh: Speak to the birds of every sort, and to every animal of the field, Assemble yourselves, and come; gather yourselves on every side to my sacrifice that I do sacrifice for you, even a great sacrifice on the mountains of Israel, that you may eat flesh and drink blood.

note: 'the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light' is a near-quotation of Isaiah 13:10, 'the stars of the heavens... will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising and the moon will not shed its light,' the cosmic collapse in the Day-of-the-LORD oracle against Babylon.
sourceText: For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.

note: 'the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken' renders Isaiah 34:4, 'all the host of heaven shall rot away... all their host shall fall, as leaves fall from the vine,' the dissolution of the heavenly host in judgment.
sourceText: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.

note: Joel 2:10 (and 3:15) 'the sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining' supplies the same triad of darkened sun, moon, and stars as the heralds of the Day of the LORD.
sourceText: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.

note: 'the sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD' is part of the Joel cluster behind the cosmic-portent language of the Son of Man's coming.
sourceText: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: Ezekiel 32:7-8, 'I will cover the heavens and make their stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light,' is a direct parallel to the darkening of sun, moon, and stars over a fallen power.
sourceText: When I shall extinguish you, I will cover the heavens, and make its stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light.

note: 'they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of the sky with power and great glory' is a strong allusion to Daniel 7:13, 'one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven,' to whom dominion and glory are given; the title and the cloud-coming are Danielic.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: The 'power and great glory' and the gathering of all peoples reflects Daniel 7:14, where the son of man receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples should serve.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'all the tribes of the earth will mourn' draws on Zechariah 12:10-14, 'they shall look on him whom they have pierced, and mourn... the land shall mourn, each family by itself,' the eschatological mourning of the tribes/families at the appearance of the one they pierced.
sourceText: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

note: The enumeration of mourning 'families/tribes' in Zechariah 12:12-14 is specifically behind 'all the tribes (phylai) of the earth will mourn,' Matthew's universalizing of Zechariah's clan-by-clan lament.
sourceText: The land will mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of David apart, and their wives apart; the family of the house of Nathan apart, and their wives apart;

note: 'they will gather together his chosen ones from the four winds, from one end of the sky to the other' echoes Deuteronomy 30:4, 'though you are driven to the farthest parts of heaven, from there the LORD your God will gather you,' the promise of regathering the scattered elect.
sourceText: If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of the heavens, from there Yahweh your God will gather you, and from there he will bring you back.

note: 'I have spread you abroad like the four winds of heaven' (Zech 2:6) supplies the 'four winds' as the dispersion-points from which the elect are gathered at the end.
sourceText: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.

note: 'a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost... will come and worship the LORD' (Isa 27:13) is the source for the trumpet that summons the dispersed elect to be gathered at the Son of Man's coming.
sourceText: It will happen in that day that a great trumpet will be blown; and those who were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and those who were outcasts in the land of Egypt, shall come; and they will worship Yahweh in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

note: The LORD raising a signal/sign and 'gathering the dispersed of Israel... from the four corners of the earth' (Isa 11:12) parallels both the 'sign of the Son of Man' and the gathering of the elect from the four winds.
sourceText: He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

note: 'the Lord GOD will sound the trumpet' in the day of his appearing (Zech 9:14) reinforces the eschatological trumpet that accompanies the gathering.
sourceText: Yahweh will be seen over them; and his arrow will go flash like lightning; and the Lord Yahweh will blow the trumpet, and will go with whirlwinds of the south.

note: The 'powers of the heavens shall be shaken' specifically draws on the shaking and dissolution of the heavenly host in Isaiah 34:4, distinct from the falling stars, emphasizing cosmic powers undone.
sourceText: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.

note: 'I will shake the heavens and the earth' (Hag 2:6) is part of the prophetic shaking-of-the-cosmos tradition behind 'the powers of the heavens will be shaken.'
sourceText: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;

note: Isaiah 24:23, the moon abashed and the sun ashamed when the LORD reigns in glory on Zion, belongs to the same Isaianic cluster of luminaries failing at the LORD's appearing.
sourceText: Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed; for Yahweh of Armies will reign on Mount Zion, and in Jerusalem; and before his elders will be glory.

note: The gathering of the chosen and the kingdom given to the saints (Dan 7:27) underlies the assembling of the elect at the Son of Man's coming.
sourceText: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.

note: The trumpet sounded so that Israel is remembered and gathered/delivered (Num 10:9; cf. Lev 23:24) supplies the cultic trumpet-of-assembly background to the angels' trumpet gathering the elect.
sourceText: When you go to war in your land against the adversary who oppresses you, then you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets. Then you will be remembered before Yahweh your God, and you will be saved from your enemies.

note: 'Gather my faithful ones to me' as God comes in judgment with consuming fire (Ps 50:3-5) parallels the gathering of the chosen at the Son of Man's glorious advent.
sourceText: “Gather my saints together to me, those who have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.”

note: The fig tree (and vine) yielding its fruit as a sign of the turning season (Joel 2:22) lies loosely behind the fig-tree parable's reading of budding branches as the nearness of the appointed time.
sourceText: Don’t be afraid, you animals of the field; for the pastures of the wilderness spring up, for the tree bears its fruit. The fig tree and the vine yield their strength.

note: 'The fig tree puts forth its figs... arise, my love' (Song 2:13) marks the fig's leafing as the herald of the season's arrival, the natural sign-reading the parable trades on.
sourceText: The fig tree ripens her green figs. The vines are in blossom. They give out their fragrance. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.” Lover

note: 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away' draws on Isaiah 40:8, 'the grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever,' contrasting transient creation with God's enduring word.
sourceText: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”

note: Isaiah 51:6, 'the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out... but my salvation will be forever,' parallels the passing of heaven and earth set against the permanence of Jesus' word.
sourceText: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.

note: Psalm 102:26-27, 'they will perish, but you remain... they will pass away, but you are the same,' contributes to the heaven-and-earth-pass-away / my-words-remain antithesis.
sourceText: They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed.

note: 'As the days of Noah were... eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ship, and they didn't know until the flood came and took them all away' is a sustained allusion to Genesis 6-7, the flood narrative; the unsuspecting world swept away while Noah enters the ark is the controlling typology.
sourceText: Noah went into the ship with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives, because of the floodwaters.

note: The flood that 'took them all away' (every living thing blotted out, only Noah and those with him remaining, Gen 7:23) is the precise source for the sudden, total, unexpected sweeping-away that figures the Son of Man's coming.
sourceText: Every living thing was destroyed that was on the surface of the ground, including man, livestock, creeping things, and birds of the sky. They were destroyed from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ship.

note: The heedless eating, drinking, and marrying corresponds to the corrupt complacency of Noah's generation (Gen 6:5,11-12), heightening the contrast with the abrupt judgment.
sourceText: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.

note: 'the day that Noah entered the ark' (Gen 7:13) marks the decisive divide between the saved and the swept-away that the parable applies to the day of the Son of Man.
sourceText: In the same day Noah, and Shem, Ham, and Japheth—the sons of Noah—and Noah’s wife and the three wives of his sons with them, entered into the ship—

note: The withholding of the precise time even from heavenly beings, known only to God, resonates with Daniel sealing the appointed time until the end, knowledge reserved to God alone.
sourceText: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished.

note: 'a day known to the LORD' alone (Zech 14:7) parallels 'no one knows of that day and hour... but my Father only,' the day's timing reserved to God.
sourceText: It will be a unique day which is known to Yahweh; not day, and not night; but it will come to pass, that at evening time there will be light.

note: The sudden, unanticipated arrival of the Lord who 'will suddenly come to his temple' (Mal 3:1) resonates with the Lord coming at an unexpected hour for which one must be ready.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: The thief-in-the-night image of unexpected nocturnal plunder (cf. Jer 49:9; Obad 5, thieves who take only what they want by night) supplies the figure of the thief whose hour the householder cannot predict.
sourceText: If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, wouldn’t they destroy until they had enough?

note: The thief/murderer who rises in the dark and breaks into houses (Job 24:14,16) furnishes the burglary imagery for the unexpected coming for which one must keep watch.
sourceText: The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief.

note: The faithful and wise servant whom the master sets over his household to provision it recalls Joseph set over Potiphar's house and over all Egypt's storehouses to give out food in due season (Gen 39:4-6; 41:40-41), the trusted-steward type.
sourceText: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.

note: Giving the household 'their food in due season' echoes the providential idiom of Psalm 104:27 (and 145:15), 'you give them their food in due season,' applied to the steward's faithful provisioning.
sourceText: These all wait for you, that you may give them their food in due season.

note: The wise household manager who rises to provide food/portions for the household (Prov 31:15) parallels the faithful and wise servant dispensing the household's food at the right time.
sourceText: She rises also while it is yet night, gives food to her household, and portions for her servant girls.

note: The faithful, wise servant being promoted to be set 'over all that he has' resembles the wise Daniel exalted to rule the whole province as reward for faithful discernment.
sourceText: Then the king made Daniel great, and gave him many great gifts, and made him to rule over the whole province of Babylon, and to be chief governor over all the wise men of Babylon.

note: The wicked servant's reasoning that 'my lord is delaying' so that he turns to abuse and drunkenness reflects Qoheleth's observation that when judgment is delayed the heart is emboldened to do evil.
sourceText: Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.

note: The unfaithful steward thrust from his office and his place given to another (Shebna deposed, Isa 22:15-19) parallels the evil servant cut off and assigned his portion with the hypocrites.
sourceText: I will thrust you from your office. You will be pulled down from your station.

note: 'the wicked will see it and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and melt away' (Ps 112:10) lies behind the recurring Matthean punishment-formula 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' assigned to the evil servant.
sourceText: The wicked will see it, and be grieved. He shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away. The desire of the wicked will perish.

note: The bridegroom motif organizing the whole parable draws on the prophetic image of God/Messiah as bridegroom: 'as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.' Matthew makes the coming bridegroom the figure for the returning Son of Man, joining the eschatological wedding feast to messianic arrival.
sourceText: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.

note: God's betrothal of Israel ('I will betroth you to me forever') stands behind the bridegroom-and-attendants imagery; the marriage covenant is the controlling metaphor for the eschatological union the wise virgins enter and the foolish miss.
sourceText: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.

note: The nocturnal coming of the bridegroom in procession, the cry going up, and the wedding of King Solomon supply a scriptural scene of a bridegroom arriving by night to be met by attendants. Verbal contact is thematic rather than lexical.
sourceText: Who is this who comes up from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all spices of the merchant? Behold, it is Solomon’s carriage! Sixty mighty men are around it, of the mighty men of Israel. They all handle the sword, and are expert in war. Every man has his sword on his thigh, because of fear in the night. King Solomon made himself a carriage of the wood of Lebanon. He made its pillars of silver, its bottom of […]

note: The reversal whereby those who presume entry are shut out ('Lord, Lord, open to us' / 'I don't know you') resonates with the prophetic Day of the LORD warning that the day will be darkness for the complacent, not the light they expected.
sourceText: “Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! Why do you long for the day of Yahweh? It is darkness, and not light. As if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him; Or he went into the house and leaned his hand on the wall, and a snake bit him. Won’t the day of Yahweh be darkness, and not light? Even very dark, and no brightness in it?

note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple... but who can endure the day of his coming?' supplies the pattern of a sudden, testing arrival of the Lord for which one must be prepared; the delay-then-sudden-cry structure of the parable echoes this.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap;

note: 'Though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not delay' frames the theme of the bridegroom's delay (v.5) and the call to keep ready through the apparent postponement of the appointed time.
sourceText: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
lxxText: For the vision is yet for a time, and it shall shoot forth at the end, and not in vain: though he should tarry, wait for him; for he will surely come, and will not tarry.

note: The provision of pure oil to keep the lamp burning continually 'from evening to morning' supplies the cultic background for oil-as-fidelity that keeps the light alive through the night of waiting.
sourceText: “You shall command the children of Israel, that they bring to you pure olive oil beaten for the light, to cause a lamp to burn continually. In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil which is before the testimony, Aaron and his sons shall keep it in order from evening to morning before Yahweh: it shall be a statute forever throughout their generations on the behalf of the children of Israel.

note: The royal wedding psalm, with virgin companions led in procession to the king's palace amid gladness, provides a scriptural template for virgins escorting a bridegroom into the marriage feast.
sourceText: The princess inside is all glorious. Her clothing is interwoven with gold. She shall be led to the king in embroidered work. The virgins, her companions who follow her, shall be brought to you. With gladness and rejoicing they shall be led. They shall enter into the king’s palace.

note: Joseph entrusted with all his master's goods and proving faithful as a steward supplies a narrative type of the trusted servant set over his lord's property, rewarded with greater authority.
sourceText: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand. From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. Yahweh’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field. He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he […]

note: The condemnation of the 'slothful' servant (v.26) and the praise of diligent gain echoes wisdom's contrast between the industrious and the sluggard whose laziness brings ruin.
sourceText: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.

note: 'A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich; he who gathers in summer is a prudent son' undergirds the parable's reward of the productive servants and reproach of the one who buried his trust.
sourceText: He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth. He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during the harvest is a son who causes shame.

note: The judgment-language of the parable's frame (joy of the lord vs. outer darkness) participates in the apocalyptic two-fold destiny of the wise who shine and others who go to shame, the eschatological backdrop Matthew assumes.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: The motif of being cast into darkness as judgment ('you shall lie down in torment') faintly underlies the 'outer darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth' fate of the unprofitable servant.
sourceText: Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who adorn yourselves with torches around yourselves; walk in the flame of your fire, and among the brands that you have kindled. You shall have this of my hand; you shall lie down in sorrow.

note: The Son of Man coming in glory and seated on his throne, before whom all nations/peoples are gathered to serve him, is the direct backbone of v.31-32. Daniel's 'one like a son of man' receives dominion, glory, and kingdom over all peoples, nations, and languages; Matthew transposes this enthronement into the scene of universal judgment.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'I judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats' is the explicit verbal and conceptual source for 'he will separate them... as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats' (v.32-33). The shepherd-judge distinguishing the flock animals is unmistakable.
sourceText: As for you, O my flock, thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, the rams and the male goats.

note: The LORD 'will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep,' saving the weak from those who shove with side and shoulder. This grounds the criterion of judgment on treatment of the vulnerable and the shepherd-king's vindication of the mistreated, mirrored in care for the hungry, naked, sick, and imprisoned.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh to them: Behold, I, even I, will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep. Because you thrust with side and with shoulder, and push all the diseased with your horns, until you have scattered them abroad; therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between sheep and sheep.

note: The promise of one shepherd, 'my servant David,' set over the flock as prince, is typologically fulfilled in the Son of Man / King who shepherds and judges the nations. The Davidic shepherd-king of Ezekiel 34 is the figure Matthew casts Jesus as embodying.
sourceText: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. I, Yahweh, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken it.

note: 'I will gather all the nations... and I will enter into judgment with them there' supplies the assize of the nations gathered before the throne (v.32), where they are judged on how they treated God's people.
sourceText: I will gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat; and I will execute judgment on them there for my people, and for my heritage, Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations. They have divided my land,

note: 'Let the nations be roused and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.' The enthroned divine Judge seated to judge the assembled nations directly parallels the Son of Man sitting on the throne of his glory to judge all the nations.
sourceText: “Let the nations arouse themselves, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat; for there will I sit to judge all the surrounding nations.

note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.' This supplies the retinue of v.31, 'the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him,' for the day of the LORD's appearing.
sourceText: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*

note: The acts of true fasting/righteousness — 'share your bread with the hungry, bring the homeless poor into your house, when you see the naked, cover him' — closely match the King's catalog of hungry/stranger/naked in v.35-36. Isaiah 58 is the strongest verbal parallel for the works that mark the righteous.
sourceText: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?

note: Job's oath of innocence — feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, caring for the needy ('if I have not given the poor their portion... if I have seen any perish for lack of clothing') — supplies a near-checklist of the deeds of mercy that define the sheep.
sourceText: “If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (no, from my youth he grew up with me as with a father, her have I guided from my mother’s womb); if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or that the needy had no covering; if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been warmed with my sheep’s fleece; if I have lifted up my hand […]

note: 'If you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness' reinforces the same Isaian ethic of self-giving to the afflicted as the substance of righteousness rewarded by God.
sourceText: and if you draw out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul: then your light shall rise in darkness, and your obscurity be as the noonday;

note: The righteous man 'gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with a garment' — Ezekiel's catalog of the deeds that mark the just from the wicked closely parallels the King's criteria and reinforces the Ezekielian frame already operative in the sheep/goats image.
sourceText: and has not wronged any, but has restored to the debtor his pledge, has taken nothing by robbery, has given his bread to the hungry, and has covered the naked with a garment;

note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.' This is the precise theology of v.40 — kindness to the least is rendered to the King himself, who repays. The identification of the needy with the divine creditor is the conceptual hinge.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

note: 'Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.' The principle that treatment of the poor is treatment of God himself underwrites 'you did it to me' / 'you did not do it to me.'
sourceText: He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for his Maker, but he who is kind to the needy honors him.

note: 'The LORD will come with fire... by fire will the LORD enter into judgment with all flesh' faintly underlies the 'eternal fire' prepared for the cursed and the universal judgment of all flesh/nations.
sourceText: For, behold, Yahweh will come with fire, and his chariots shall be like the whirlwind; to render his anger with fierceness, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire will Yahweh execute judgment, and by his sword, on all flesh; and the slain of Yahweh shall be many.

note: The closing image of the unquenched fire / undying worm for the rebellious provides scriptural background for the 'eternal fire' and 'eternal punishment' of v.41, 46.
sourceText: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”

note: 'Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' This two-fold eternal destiny is the source for v.46, 'these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.'
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: The enthronement of the messianic Lord at God's right hand, with subjugation of enemies, underlies the royal session of the Son of Man on the throne of his glory and the placing of subjects at the right and left.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: The royal psalm's portrait of the king who delivers the needy, the poor, and those who have no helper, redeeming their life from oppression, supplies the ideal of the just king whose rule is measured by care for the vulnerable — the standard the King applies.
sourceText: For he will deliver the needy when he cries; the poor, who has no helper. He will have pity on the poor and needy. He will save the souls of the needy. He will redeem their soul from oppression and violence. Their blood will be precious in his sight.

note: The eschatological banquet on the mountain for all peoples, where death is swallowed up, faintly informs the inheritance/eternal-life reward into which the blessed are welcomed when all nations are gathered.
sourceText: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines. He will destroy in this mountain the surface of the covering that covers all peoples, and the veil that is spread over all nations. He has swallowed up death forever!
