Volume is maximal and the wilderness/way motif structures the whole prologue (John baptizes 'in the wilderness,' 1:4). The new-Exodus comfort-of-Zion context is highly coherent with Mark's gospel announcement.
sourceText: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.

note: John's garb of camel's hair and a leather belt around the waist deliberately mirrors Elijah, 'a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist' (2 Kings 1:8 LXX, zōnēn dermatinēn perthan identical phrase). High volume in a distinctive sartorial detail; recurrence at Mark 9:13 ('Elijah has come') confirms the identification. Coherence is strong: John is the returning Elijah of Malachi.
sourceText: They answered him, “He was a hairy man, and wearing a leather belt around his waist.” He said, “It is Elijah the Tishbite.”

note: Malachi 4:5 (3:23 MT) promises Elijah's return 'before the great day of the LORD'; Mark casts John in this role, fusing it with the messenger of Malachi 3:1. Verbal volume in 1:2-8 is indirect, but the Elijah dress (v.6) and Mark 9:11-13 make the figural identification explicit and recurrent. Coherence is the engine of the whole prologue.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: Zechariah 13:4 mentions prophets wearing 'a hairy mantle' as a deceptive sign; some see John's camel-hair garment drawing on the generic prophetic-mantle convention rather than Elijah specifically. Volume is low and the negative valence in Zechariah weakens coherence; included as a contested alternate source for the prophet's dress.
sourceText: It will happen in that day, that the prophets will each be ashamed of his vision, when he prophesies; neither will they wear a hairy mantle to deceive:

note: John's diet of locusts reflects the one insect category Leviticus 11:22 permits as clean food, anchoring his wilderness asceticism in Torah dietary law. The contact is a single permitted-food detail with no verbal borrowing, so the echo is faint and contested; it functions mainly to authenticate his wilderness piety.
sourceText: Even of these you may eat: any kind of locust, any kind of katydid, any kind of cricket, and any kind of grasshopper.

note: The heavenly voice 'You are my beloved Son' echoes the royal enthronement decree 'You are my Son' of Psalm 2:7. Volume is high (the opening clause is near-verbatim) and recurrence is strong (Mark 9:7; the title frames the Gospel). Coherence is maximal: the baptism functions as a messianic enthronement, declaring Jesus the Davidic king-son.
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.

note: 'In whom I am well pleased' draws on the Servant of Isaiah 42:1, 'my chosen, in whom my soul delights,' paired with the Spirit resting on him (v.10). Volume is high on the 'well pleased / delight' clause and the Spirit-endowment, and the fusion of royal Son (Ps 2) with suffering Servant (Isa 42) is a load-bearing Markan Christology. Coherence is high.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.

note: Mark's distinctive 'the heavens being torn' (schizomenous) recalls Isaiah 64:1 LXX, 'O that you would rend the heavens and come down.' Volume rests on the violent verb 'tear,' which Mark uniquely chooses (vs. Matthew/Luke's 'opened') and reuses at the temple veil (15:38). Coherence is high: God rends the heavens to descend in the Spirit upon Jesus.
sourceText: Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence,

note: 'Beloved Son' (agapētos) may invoke Isaac, 'your only/beloved son,' in the Aqedah of Genesis 22:2 LXX, foreshadowing the offered son. Volume is the single distinctive adjective agapētos (which LXX uses for Isaac), giving real verbal contact; recurrence at 9:7 and the passion's sacrificial logic raise coherence. Genuinely contested—agapētos may simply intensify 'Son.'
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: The Spirit descending over the baptismal waters may evoke the Spirit/wind hovering over the primordial waters of Genesis 1:2, framing the baptism as new creation. Volume is conceptual only (no 'dove' in Genesis), so the link is faint; some rabbinic traditions compared the Genesis Spirit to a bird, which marginally supports it. Contested.
sourceText: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.

note: Ezekiel's inaugural vision opens with 'the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God,' a prophetic-commission topos that Mark's heaven-rending and Spirit-descent may share. Volume is low and the verb differs (open vs. tear), so this is a generic apocalyptic-opening echo rather than a targeted citation; included for completeness.
sourceText: Now in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth of the month, as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.

note: Isaiah 63 recalls God putting his Holy Spirit among his people at the Exodus through the sea, a new-Exodus matrix coherent with Jesus' Spirit-anointing at the Jordan. The contact is thematic (Spirit + water + sonship of Israel) rather than verbal, so volume is low; it strengthens the new-Exodus reading of the whole prologue.
sourceText: Then he remembered the days of old, Moses and his people, saying, Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? where is he who put his holy Spirit in their midst? who caused his glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moses? who divided the waters before them, to make himself an everlasting name? who led them through the depths, as a horse in the wilderness, so that they didn’t stumble? As the livestock that go down into […]

note: Jesus' forty days 'tempted' in the wilderness recapitulates Israel's forty years in which the LORD led them to test (peirazō) them. Volume is thematic (forty + wilderness + testing) rather than verbal, but the typology of the new Israel re-running the wilderness probation is coherent and recurrent in early Christian reading. Mark, unlike Q, gives no scriptural debate, so the link is figural.
sourceText: You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments, or not.

note: Moses' forty days and forty nights on Sinai (also Exodus 24:18) supplies one of the canonical 'forty days' fasts that Jesus' wilderness sojourn evokes. Volume is the shared numeral and wilderness setting; the Moses typology is coherent with Mark's broader new-Exodus framing, though Mark's brevity keeps it allusive rather than verbal.
sourceText: He was there with Yahweh forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, nor drank water. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.

note: Elijah's forty days in the wilderness, sustained by an angel who 'served' him with food, closely parallels Mark's 'forty days... and the angels were serving him.' Volume includes the shared forty days plus angelic ministration, a distinctive combination; given Mark's heavy Elijah typology (John as Elijah, 1:6), recurrence and coherence are notable.
sourceText: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!” He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again. Yahweh’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty […]

note: Psalm 91 promises angelic guardianship and treading on lion and serpent unharmed; Mark's pairing of 'wild animals' and 'angels serving him' may reflect this protection motif. Volume is low and indirect (the psalm is explicit in the Q temptation, not Mark), so for Mark this is a contested thematic echo rather than a citation.
sourceText: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways. They will bear you up in their hands, so that you won’t dash your foot against a stone. You will tread on the lion and cobra. You will trample the young lion and the serpent underfoot.

note: Jesus 'with the wild animals' may evoke the eschatological peace where beasts no longer harm, marking him as inaugurator of restored creation. Volume is purely thematic and the wild beasts in Mark could equally signal danger (cf. Ps 91), so the irenic-Eden reading is contested; included for the new-creation typology.
sourceText: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat; The calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together; and a little child will lead them. The cow and the bear will graze. Their young ones will lie down together. The lion will eat straw like the ox. The nursing child will play near a cobra’s hole, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den. They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for […]

note: The new-Adam reading sees Jesus, tempted by Satan yet among the beasts and served by angels, reversing Adam's failure in the garden among the animals. Volume is conceptual (Satan as tempter, the beasts, paradise restored) with no verbal borrowing, so this Adam-Christ typology is faint and contested in Mark, who never names Adam.
sourceText: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”

note: 'The kingdom of God is at hand' announced as 'good news' fulfills the herald of Isaiah 52:7 who proclaims good news and says 'Your God reigns.' Volume couples the distinctive verb euangelizō with the reign of God, both present here; recurrence binds it to 1:1's euangelion. Coherence is maximal—this is Mark's thesis statement drawn from Isaiah's gospel of God's kingship.
sourceText: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

note: The expectation that 'the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed' supplies the apocalyptic content of Jesus' 'kingdom of God.' Volume is conceptual but the specific phrase 'kingdom of God/heaven' has its clearest Second-Temple anchor in Daniel; coherence with Mark's 'the time is fulfilled' (an apocalyptic timetable) is strong.
sourceText: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.

note: The everlasting dominion given to the 'one like a son of man' is the kingdom Mark's Jesus proclaims and later claims (Mark 13:26; 14:62). In 1:15 the contact is thematic—the inbreaking eternal kingdom—rather than verbal, but the recurrence of Daniel 7 across Mark gives the echo real weight here.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'The time is fulfilled' resonates with Isaiah 61:2's 'the acceptable year of the LORD,' the proclamation of the eschatological jubilee by the Spirit-anointed herald (cf. Jesus' anointing at 1:10). Volume is moderate on the 'favorable/fulfilled time' motif; coherence with the gospel-of-God framing is good, though Mark does not quote it as Luke does.
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind; to declare the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompence; to comfort all that mourn;

note: Ezekiel 7:7,12 declare 'the time has come, the day is near,' a near-formula for Mark's 'the time is fulfilled.' Volume is the shared 'the time has come' idiom, but Ezekiel's announcement is judgment, not gospel, weakening coherence; included as a faint, contested verbal parallel.
sourceText: Your doom has come to you, inhabitant of the land: the time has come, the day is near, a day of tumult, and not of joyful shouting, on the mountains.

note: 'I will make you into fishers for men' draws on Jeremiah 16:16, 'I will send for many fishers... and they shall fish them.' Volume rests on the distinctive 'fishers of men' image, which is rare in scripture; coherence is the chief question because Jeremiah's fishers gather for judgment while Jesus' gather for salvation, a deliberate transvaluation. Distinctiveness makes the allusion likely.
sourceText: Behold, I will send for many fishermen, says Yahweh, and they shall fish them up; and afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks.

note: Ezekiel's vision of fishermen spreading nets along the life-giving temple river offers a more positive 'fishers' background than Jeremiah's judgment. Volume is low (no verbal contact beyond 'fishermen/nets') and the link is thematic, so it is a contested alternate backdrop to the call of the fishermen.
sourceText: It shall happen, that fishermen shall stand by it: from En Gedi even to En Eglaim shall be a place for the spreading of nets; their fish shall be after their kinds, as the fish of the great sea, exceeding many.

note: Amos 4:2 threatens that the people will be taken away 'with fishhooks,' another OT fishing-for-people image. Volume is faint and, like Jeremiah, the valence is judgment; included for maximal coverage of the 'catching people' metaphor though coherence with Jesus' summons is weak.
sourceText: The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his holiness that behold, “The days shall come on you that they will take you away with hooks, and the last of you with fish hooks.

note: The abrupt prophetic call—Jesus passing by, the brothers immediately leaving father and livelihood—mirrors Elijah's call of Elisha, who left his oxen and his father to follow. Volume lies in the shared call-narrative form (summons in the midst of work, leaving family/trade), and Mark's pervasive Elijah typology raises coherence and recurrence for the pattern, even without direct quotation.
sourceText: So he departed there, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing, with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed over to him, and cast his mantle on him. He left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?” He returned from following him, and took the yoke of oxen, and killed them, […]

note: The demon's confession 'the Holy One of God' uses a title applied in Psalm 106:16 (LXX 105:16) to Aaron, 'the holy one of the LORD.' Volume is the shared distinctive title, but its referent differs sharply (Aaron vs. Jesus), so the link is contested; it may simply mark Jesus as the consecrated agent of God whose holiness repels the unclean spirit.
sourceText: They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron, Yahweh’s saint.

note: Samson is to be 'a Nazirite/holy one of God from the womb' (Judges 13:7; 16:17 LXX 'hagios theou'), the closest verbal match to the demon's 'Holy One of God.' Volume on the exact phrase is real, but the Samson connection is thematically thin, so this is a contested lexical parallel for the title rather than a developed allusion.
sourceText: but he said to me, ‘Behold, you shall conceive, and bear a son; and now drink no wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing; for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.’”

note: 'The Holy One of Israel,' Isaiah's signature divine title, may stand behind 'the Holy One of God' as a claim to Jesus' divine identity recognized by the demon. Volume is partial (Holy One + God/Israel) and the genitive differs, so coherence is suggestive but the link remains faint and contested.
sourceText: Ah sinful nation, a people loaded with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children who deal corruptly! They have forsaken Yahweh. They have despised the Holy One of Israel. They are estranged and backward.

note: Jesus taking the sick woman 'by the hand' and raising her up loosely follows the Elijah/Elisha healing pattern (Elijah revives the widow's son). Volume is purely formal (prophet restores a stricken person), with no verbal borrowing in Mark's terse account, so this is a contested figural echo riding on Mark's broader Elijah typology.
sourceText: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]

note: Elisha's raising of the Shunammite's son by personal touch offers another prophetic-healing template for Jesus' gesture of taking the hand and 'raising' the feverish woman. The contact is thematic and the language non-distinctive, so the echo is faint; included to register the prophet-healer typology underlying the miracle.
sourceText: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]

note: Mark's summary of Jesus healing 'all who were sick' and casting out demons resonates with the Servant who 'bore our infirmities,' the verse Matthew explicitly cites at this point. For Mark the link is unmarked and thematic, so volume is low and it is contested whether Mark intends the Servant-of-Isaiah reading here, though it coheres with the Isa 42 Servant motif of 1:11.
sourceText: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.

note: Jesus rising 'early in the morning' to a solitary place to pray faintly echoes the Servant who is wakened 'morning by morning' to hear and speak God's word. Volume is minimal (the morning-prayer motif) with no verbal borrowing, so this is a contested, low-confidence echo; it coheres only loosely with Mark's Servant Christology.
sourceText: The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary: he wakens morning by morning, he wakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.

note: Jesus' command to 'show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing the things which Moses commanded' directly invokes the leper's purification rite of Leviticus 14, where the cleansed person presents himself to the priest with the prescribed offerings. Volume is high (Mark names 'the things Moses commanded' for cleansing), coherence total, and the reference is explicit Torah citation in substance.
sourceText: “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him, and behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper, then the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two living clean birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop.

note: The leper's condition—ritual uncleanness and exclusion from the community—presupposes the diagnostic law of Leviticus 13, the necessary backdrop to the cleansing of v.42. Volume is conceptual but the legal framework is unmistakably in view (the leper must be declared clean by a priest), and it coheres tightly with the offering command of v.44.
sourceText: “The leper in whom the plague is shall wear torn clothes, and the hair of his head shall hang loose. He shall cover his upper lip, and shall cry, ‘Unclean! Unclean!’ All the days in which the plague is in him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall dwell alone. Outside of the camp shall be his dwelling.

note: The cleansing of a leper evokes Elisha's healing of Naaman, the paradigmatic OT leprosy cure by a prophet. Volume is the shared distinctive event (only Elisha cleanses a leper in the OT narratives) plus Mark's Elijah/Elisha typology; coherence is strong, and Luke 4:27 makes the Naaman link explicit, supporting its availability and recurrence in the tradition.

note: Miriam's leprosy and Moses' intercession, with the priestly/Mosaic handling of her exclusion and restoration, sits in the background of leprosy as a divinely-managed impurity. Volume is low and the contact thematic rather than verbal, so this is a contested supporting echo to the Levitical leprosy frame.
sourceText: The cloud departed from over the Tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow. Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. Aaron said to Moses, “Oh, my lord, please don’t count this sin against us, in which we have done foolishly, and in which we have sinned. Let her not, I pray, be as one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb.” Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “Heal her, God, I beg you!” Yahweh […]

note: The scribes' objection "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (v.7) presupposes the prophetic axiom of Isa 43:25, "I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake." High volume on the distinctive theology that pardon of sin is God's sole prerogative; Mark stages Jesus' authority precisely against this exclusive divine claim. Recurrence is strong in Isaiah's forgiveness oracles (44:22).
sourceText: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.

note: The covenant self-revelation of YHWH as the God "forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin" is the foundational text behind the scribes' assumption that forgiveness belongs to God alone. Thematic coherence is high: Jesus' pronouncement of forgiveness enacts a divine attribute scripturally reserved to the LORD. The verbal contact is via the shared lexeme of forgiving sin rather than direct quotation.
sourceText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth, keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”

note: "The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" (v.10) draws on Dan 7:13-14, where "one like a son of man" is given dominion and authority before the Ancient of Days. High distinctiveness in the title plus the keyword "authority" (exousia), which Mark recurs at 2:28 and the eschatological discourse (13:26). Mark transposes the heavenly investiture into earthly authority.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: "Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases" pairs forgiveness and healing exactly as Mark 2:1-12 does, where pardon is demonstrated by the cure of the paralytic. Thematic coherence is strong: the psalm makes the two divine acts a single benefaction, which is the logic of Jesus' "which is easier" challenge (v.9). Verbal volume is modest, carried by the forgiveness/healing pairing.
sourceText: who forgives all your sins; who heals all your diseases;

note: "Then shall the lame man leap like a deer" anchors the healing of the paralytic in Isaiah's eschatological restoration, where bodily wholeness signals the inbreaking reign of God. Thematic coherence with Mark's miracle is high; the crowd's astonishment ("We never saw anything like this!", v.12) fits the new-thing motif of Isaiah 35 and 43. Verbal repetition is limited, so this is an echo rather than allusion.
sourceText: Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.

note: 'I delight to do your will, O my God' anchors the climactic criterion of kinship: doing the will of God. The will-of-God obedience theme has strong recurrence in the Psalter and high coherence with Jesus' redefinition of family.
sourceText: I delight to do your will, my God. Yes, your law is within my heart.”

note: 'I will declare your name to my brothers' supplies a Davidic-righteous-sufferer model of a community of brothers gathered around the one who does God's will. Faint, but Psalm 22 is heavily mined by Mark's passion, raising recurrence.
sourceText: I will declare your name to my brothers. In the midst of the assembly, I will praise you.

note: Isaiah's image of rain and seed that gives bread and accomplishes God's purpose underwrites the sower parable's logic that the sown word inevitably bears fruit. Thematic coherence is strong (word = seed that does not return empty), and the harvest-yield climax in 4:8 mirrors Isaiah's effective word. Volume is moderate since Mark does not cite, but the recurrence of the word-as-seed motif across early Christian tradition supports availability.
sourceText: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: Jeremiah's 'Break up your fallow ground, and don't sow among thorns' supplies the precise agricultural antithesis of good soil versus thorn-choked ground seen in 4:7-8. The shared sowing-among-thorns image gives thematic coherence, though volume is faint and the wording is conventional farming language widely available in the prophets.
sourceText: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.

note: Hosea's 'Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness; break up your fallow ground' joins sowing and reaping as a covenant-fruit metaphor coherent with the parable's yield. The connection is thematic rather than verbal, and the sowing/harvest pairing is a stock prophetic idiom, so it remains faint.
sourceText: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.

note: Qoheleth's counsel to sow seed without knowing which will prosper resonates with the indiscriminate scattering across four soils in 4:4-8. The thematic coherence (uncertain outcome of sowing) is real but the image is proverbial, lowering volume and distinctiveness.
sourceText: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both will be equally good.

note: Isaac's hundredfold harvest as a sign of divine blessing offers a scriptural precedent for the climactic 'one hundred times' yield in 4:8. The hundredfold motif is distinctive enough to register, though Mark gives no other Isaac signals, keeping recurrence and volume low.
sourceText: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.

note: The summons 'Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear' inverts Deuteronomy's complaint that the LORD has not given Israel 'ears to hear,' setting up the hardening theme made explicit at 4:12. Thematic coherence with the eyes/ears-of-perception tradition is strong and recurs across Isaiah and Jeremiah, supporting the link even without verbatim citation.
sourceText: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.

note: Ezekiel's rebellious house 'which have ears to hear, and don't hear' supplies nearly the exact idiom of the call to hearing in 4:9 and 4:23. The verbal overlap (ears to hear) and shared context of obstinate non-perception give good volume and coherence with Mark's hardening motif.
sourceText: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of the rebellious house, who have eyes to see, and don’t see, who have ears to hear, and don’t hear; for they are a rebellious house.

note: Jeremiah's 'who have eyes, and don't see; who have ears, and don't hear' belongs to the same prophetic cluster Mark draws on for the ears-to-hear refrain. It reinforces recurrence within the Isaiah 6 family of hardening texts that frames the whole parables discourse.
sourceText: ‘Hear now this, foolish people, and without understanding; who have eyes, and don’t see; who have ears, and don’t hear:

note: Mark 4:12 directly quotes Isaiah's commission ('seeing they may see, and not perceive; hearing they may hear, and not understand; lest they should turn and be forgiven'), with the wording closer to the Targum's 'be forgiven' than the MT/LXX 'be healed.' This is the chapter's central formal citation: high volume, explicit, and thematically governing the entire purpose-of-parables saying.
sourceText: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: The disclosure of 'the mystery of the Kingdom of God' in 4:11 echoes Daniel's revealed 'mystery' (raz) of the coming kingdom that God makes known to the elect while it stays hidden from outsiders. The apocalyptic mystery-revelation vocabulary is distinctive and coherent with Mark's insider/outsider divide, giving solid thematic and verbal warrant.
sourceText: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:

note: Daniel's vision of the God of heaven setting up an indestructible kingdom underlies Mark's 'Kingdom of God' language as a revealed eschatological secret. Recurrence of the Danielic kingdom motif throughout Mark strengthens the coherence even though 4:11 cites no text.
sourceText: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.

note: Isaiah's theme of God sealing prophetic vision and giving a spirit of stupor so the people cannot understand parallels the deliberate withholding of perception in 4:11-12. It belongs to the same hardening tradition as Isaiah 6 and reinforces its recurrence, though Mark does not draw on its specific wording.
sourceText: For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers. All vision has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one who is educated, saying, “Read this, please”; and he says, “I can’t, for it is sealed:” and the book is delivered to one who is not educated, saying, “Read this, please”; and he says, “I can’t read.” The Lord said, “Because […]

note: The psalmist's 'I will open my mouth in a parable' connects parabolic speech with hidden things 'from of old' (so used in Matthew's redaction of this material). For Mark the link is faint and indirect, registering only as thematic coherence between parable-speech and concealed mysteries.
sourceText: I will open my mouth in a parable. I will utter dark sayings of old,

note: The interpretation that 'the farmer sows the word' (4:14) makes explicit the Isaianic identification of God's effective word with seed that produces fruit. The allegory's insistence that the word bears thirty/sixty/hundredfold (4:20) coheres tightly with Isaiah's word that accomplishes its purpose and does not return empty.
sourceText: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: The thorn-choked seed that 'becomes unfruitful' (4:18-19) recalls Jeremiah's warning not to sow among thorns, here moralized into the cares and riches that choke the word. The agricultural antithesis is coherent but the language is conventional, keeping it faint.
sourceText: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.

note: Ben Sira's warning that the lover of gold will not be justified and that riches are a stumbling block coheres with 'the deceitfulness of riches' that chokes the word in 4:19. The wisdom-tradition critique of wealth supplies a Second-Temple backdrop, though the connection is thematic rather than cited.
sourceText: He that loves gold shall not be justified; And he that follows destruction shall himself have his fill of it. Many have been given over to ruin for the sake of gold; And their perdition meets them face to face. It is a stumbling block to those who sacrifice to it; And every fool shall be taken therewith.

note: Proverbs' 'The spirit of man is the LORD's lamp, searching all his innermost parts' supplies a lamp-as-revelation image coherent with the saying that what is hidden must come to light (4:22). The lamp metaphor for disclosure of inner things gives thematic coherence, though Mark cites nothing and lamp imagery is widespread.
sourceText: The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.

note: Qoheleth's conviction that God will bring every hidden work into judgment matches the principle 'there is nothing hidden, except that it should be made known' (4:22). The eschatological disclosure of the concealed is thematically coherent, though the wording is independent.
sourceText: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.

note: Daniel's praise that God 'reveals the deep and secret things' and that 'light dwells with him' resonates with the hidden-to-be-revealed/come-to-light pairing in 4:22, continuing the chapter's Danielic mystery-revelation vocabulary. The link is thematic and reinforces recurrence within the discourse.
sourceText: he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.

note: The measure-for-measure principle that 'with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you' (4:24) draws on the wisdom logic of reciprocal recompense found in Proverbs' teaching that what one gives the LORD repays. The retributive-measure motif is coherent though proverbial and not specifically cited.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

note: The saying 'to him who has, more will be given' (4:25) parallels Proverbs' wisdom-multiplication theme ('Give to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser'). The principle that receptivity yields increase is thematically coherent with the surrounding hearing-discourse, though faint.
sourceText: Instruct a wise man, and he will be still wiser. Teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.

note: Daniel's God who 'gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding' offers a Second-Temple precedent for the have/have-not multiplication of 4:25. The connection is thematic and reinforces the chapter's Danielic coloring, but remains faint.
sourceText: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;

note: The harvest climax 'he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come' (4:29) closely echoes Joel's 'Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe.' The verbal overlap of sickle-and-ripe-harvest is distinctive (high volume) and coheres with Mark's eschatological framing of the kingdom's arrival as a reaping, making this the pericope's strongest link.
sourceText: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”

note: The earth bearing fruit 'of itself' (automate)—blade, ear, full grain (4:28)—recalls the creation account of the earth bringing forth vegetation yielding seed after its kind. The motif of the earth's God-given autonomous fertility is thematically coherent, though Mark gives no verbal citation.
sourceText: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so. The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.

note: The image of grain ripening to harvest draws on the broader Torah harvest framework, but the link is generic. Included for maximality; volume and distinctiveness are low and the coherence is only with the agricultural setting.
sourceText: “‘When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not wholly reap the corners of your field, neither shall you gather the gleanings of your harvest.

note: The mustard plant that puts out 'great branches, so that the birds of the sky can lodge under its shadow' (4:32) reworks Ezekiel's noble cedar planted on the mountain under which 'all birds of every wing' dwell in the shadow of its branches. The branches-shadow-birds-nesting cluster is verbally and thematically tight (high volume), and the imperial-tree-as-kingdom motif coheres with Mark's kingdom parable.
sourceText: in the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it; and it shall produce boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches shall they dwell.

note: Nebuchadnezzar's tree whose branches shelter the beasts and in which 'the birds of the sky lived' supplies the proverbial great-tree-with-nesting-birds image behind 4:32. The recurrence of this kingdom-tree topos (Daniel 4:21 repeats it) gives strong availability and coherence with the contrast between the tiny seed and the sheltering kingdom.
sourceText: The leaves of it were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all: the animals of the field had shadow under it, and the birds of the sky lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.

note: Ezekiel's Assyrian cedar in whose boughs 'all the birds of the sky made their nests' and under whose shadow great nations lived belongs to the same world-tree tradition Mark evokes. The shared birds-nest-in-the-shadow image reinforces recurrence across the prophetic kingdom-tree corpus.
sourceText: All the birds of the sky made their nests in its boughs; and under its branches all the animals of the field gave birth to their young; and all great nations lived under its shadow.

note: The reprise of the tree 'in whose branches the birds of the sky lived' restates the Danielic kingdom-tree, strengthening the topos behind 4:32 by recurrence within a single source. Its function is to confirm the availability of the great-tree-as-dominion symbol rather than to add new wording.
sourceText: whose leaves were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all; under which the animals of the field lived, and on whose branches the birds of the sky had their habitation:

note: The psalm's 'birds of the sky' that nest by the branches and sing reflects the same creation-poetic image of birds lodging in foliage. It is a faint, generic parallel that adds coherence to the nesting-birds detail but lacks the kingdom-tree distinctiveness of Ezekiel and Daniel.
sourceText: The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.

note: The summary that Jesus spoke 'without a parable he didn't speak to them' resonates with the psalmist's 'I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings of old.' The link between exclusive parabolic teaching and revealed/concealed wisdom is thematically coherent, though for Mark it is faint and uncited.
sourceText: I will open my mouth in a parable. I will utter dark sayings of old,

note: The storm-stilling sequence—seafarers in distress, a stormy wind lifting the waves, a cry to the LORD, and his making 'the storm a calm, so that its waves are still'—maps closely onto 4:37-39. The verbal echo of the LORD stilling waves into calm is distinctive (high volume) and thematically frames Jesus exercising divine prerogative over the sea.
sourceText: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their […]

note: The scene of a prophet asleep in the boat during a great storm, woken by terrified sailors fearing death, with the sea growing calm once he acts, closely parallels 4:37-41. The shared narrative structure (sleeping figure, fear of perishing, calmed sea, awe-struck question) gives strong volume and coherence, with Jesus surpassing Jonah by commanding rather than being thrown overboard.
sourceText: But Yahweh sent out a great wind on the sea, and there was a mighty storm on the sea, so that the ship was likely to break up. Then the mariners were afraid, and every man cried to his god. They threw the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten the ship. But Jonah had gone down into the innermost parts of the ship, and he was laying down, and was fast asleep. So the ship master came to him, and said to him, “What do you mean, sleeper? Arise, […]

note: 'You rule the pride of the sea. When its waves rise up, you still them' attributes to YHWH precisely the sea-rebuking power Jesus wields in 4:39. The distinctive divine-warrior motif of mastering the chaotic sea makes this a strong echo undergirding the disciples' question 'Who then is this?'
sourceText: You rule the pride of the sea. When its waves rise up, you calm them.

note: God's stilling of 'the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves' supplies the same sea-mastery vocabulary applied to Jesus in 4:39. It reinforces the recurrence of the YHWH-stills-the-sea topos across the Psalter that frames the miracle's Christological force.
sourceText: who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, and the turmoil of the nations.

note: God's 'rebuke' of the Red Sea so that it dried up supplies the rebuke-of-the-sea verb (epitimao) used in 4:39, framing the calming as a divine-warrior subjugation of chaotic waters. The shared rebuking-the-sea motif gives good coherence with Mark's exodus-tinged sea command.
sourceText: He rebuked the Red Sea also, and it was dried up; so he led them through the depths, as through a desert.

note: Nahum's God who 'rebukes the sea, and makes it dry' provides another instance of the divine rebuke of the waters behind Jesus' command 'Peace! Be still!' (4:39). It strengthens the recurrence of the sea-rebuke tradition, though it is not specifically cited.
sourceText: He rebukes the sea, and makes it dry, and dries up all the rivers. Bashan languishes, and Carmel; and the flower of Lebanon languishes.

note: The LORD's setting bounds for the sea—'thus far shall you come, but no further; and here shall your proud waves be stayed'—portrays the creator's unique authority over the deep that Jesus assumes in 4:39-41. The coherence with the disciples' awe at one who commands wind and sea is strong, supporting the figural Christology.
sourceText: “Or who shut up the sea with doors, when it broke out of the womb, when I made clouds its garment, and wrapped it in thick darkness, marked out for it my bound, set bars and doors, and said, ‘Here you may come, but no further. Here your proud waves shall be stayed?’

note: The waters fleeing at God's rebuke in the creation-psalm adds to the cluster of texts where the deity's voice masters the sea, coherent with Jesus' verbal command. It is a faint reinforcement of the sea-rebuke topos rather than a distinct source.
sourceText: At your rebuke they fled. At the voice of your thunder they hurried away.

note: The psalmist's peaceful sleep in trust—'I will both lay down and sleep in peace'—offers a faint counterpoint to Jesus asleep amid the storm (4:38), portraying serene confidence in God. The link is thematic and weak, included for maximality.
sourceText: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety.

note: Wisdom's portrait of God's providence guiding the sea-voyager safely through the waves provides a Second-Temple backdrop to deliverance from a storm at sea (4:37-39). It contributes thematic coherence and availability, but the connection is general rather than verbal.
sourceText: Again, one preparing to sail, and about to journey over raging waves, Calleth upon a piece of wood more rotten than the vessel that carries him; For that vessel the hunger for gains devised, And a craftsman, even wisdom, built it; And your providence, O Father, guideth it along, Because even in the sea you gave a way, And in the waves a sure path, Shewing that you can save out of every danger, That so even without are a man may put to sea;

note: Isaiah indicts the rebellious people who 'sit among the graves and lodge in the secret places, who eat swine's flesh.' Mark's demoniac dwelling among the tombs (vv.2-3,5) coupled with the herd of swine (vv.11-13) gives a remarkably dense convergence of both motifs — graves and pigs — that no other OT text combines. High Volume and Thematic Coherence: both passages concern unclean, rebellious figures marked off from covenant life, met by a God who reveals himself to those not seeking him (Isa 65:1).
sourceText: who sit among the graves, and lodge in the secret places; who eat pig’s flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;

note: Continues the Isaiah 65 oracle: a people 'who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens.' The demoniac's defiant, self-destructive crying out night and day (v.5) coheres with Isaiah's portrait of provocation and cultic impurity. Strengthens the recurrence of the Isaiah 65 background already secured by v.4.
sourceText: a people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens, and burning incense on bricks;

note: The unclean of Isaiah say 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you' — a perverse holiness that defiles. The demoniac's cry 'What have I to do with you... do not torment me' (v.7) and the swine's contagion echo the ironic uncleanness-as-holiness of Isa 65:5, where God calls such people 'a smoke in my nostrils.' Thematic coherence within the same oracle reinforces the allusion.
sourceText: who say, Stand by yourself, don’t come near to me, for I am holier than you. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burns all the day.

note: The drowning of the unclean spirits in the sea (v.13) and the larger Markan motif of mastering the deep (preceding stilling of the storm) draws on the chaos-waters over which God's spirit broods at creation. The sea as the locus into which disorder is cast is faintly evocative of the primeval deep, but the connection is thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.

note: 'Legion' — a Roman military term — and the herd's headlong rush into the sea where they are drowned (v.13) figurally re-enacts the destruction of Pharaoh's host swallowed by the sea. The numbering ('about two thousand'), the military diction, and the drowning of an enemy army in water echo the Exodus deliverance. Mark casts Jesus' exorcism as a new-Exodus liberation from an occupying force, a coherence many read in the Gerasene narrative.
sourceText: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its strength when the morning appeared; and the Egyptians fled against it. Yahweh overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea. The waters returned, and covered the chariots and the horsemen, even all Pharaoh’s army that went in after them into the sea. There remained not so much as one of them.

note: The Song of the Sea celebrates that horse and rider were thrown into the sea. The drowning of Legion's host (v.13) resonates with this triumph-song over a defeated army cast into the waters, supporting the new-Exodus reading; faint and thematic, dependent on the Exodus 14 figural link.
sourceText: Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to Yahweh, and said, “I will sing to Yahweh, for he has triumphed gloriously. The horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.

note: The demoniac addresses Jesus as 'Son of the Most High God' (v.7), using El Elyon, the divine title first given by Melchizedek (Gen 14:18-20). The Septuagintal 'God Most High' is a recurrent OT designation (Ps 78:35; Dan 3:26) and here, on Gentile lips, signals recognition of Israel's God by an outsider/unclean source. Strong Availability and Volume for the title.
sourceText: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High.

note: Nebuchadnezzar calls the three 'servants of the Most High God' — the same Greek title used by the demoniac (v.7) and characteristic of Gentile recognition of Israel's God in the LXX. The pattern of a pagan figure confessing 'the Most High God' coheres with Mark's setting in Gentile Decapolis. Recurrence of the title in Daniel strengthens the figural background.
sourceText: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace: he spoke and said, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, you servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here. Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out of the midst of the fire.

note: Psalm 107 describes those who 'sat in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in affliction and irons,' whom God delivers. The demoniac bound with chains and fetters, dwelling in deathly tombs and broken loose (vv.3-4), evokes this portrait of the captive freed by divine mercy. The same Psalm's later stilling of the storm (107:29) parallels Mark's preceding pericope, supporting recurrence; nonetheless verbal contact is faint.
sourceText: Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron,

note: The Torah's gravest corpse-uncleanness law marks anyone touching a grave or the dead as defiled seven days. The demoniac's permanent residence among the tombs (vv.2-3,5) renders him maximally unclean by this standard, which Mark heightens by adjoining the swine. Thematic coherence with the wider Markan concern for purity boundaries crossed by Jesus.
sourceText: “Whoever in the open field touches one who is slain with a sword, or a dead body, or a bone of a man, or a grave, shall be unclean seven days.

note: Swine are the paradigmatic unclean animal: 'of their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch.' The great herd of pigs (vv.11-13) signals the Gentile, unclean territory and supplies the fitting receptacle for unclean spirits. The legal designation of swine grounds the narrative's purity logic and reinforces the Isaiah 65:4 swine motif.
sourceText: The pig, because he has a split hoof, and is cloven-footed, but doesn’t chew the cud, he is unclean to you. Of their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch; they are unclean to you.

note: The woman 'with an issue of blood' (v.25) embodies the Levitical zavah: a woman with a discharge beyond her period is unclean all the days of the flow, and whatever and whoever she touches becomes unclean. Her touching Jesus' garment (v.27) inverts the expected contagion — purity flows outward rather than impurity inward. Very high Volume and Thematic Coherence; the legal background is essential to the scene's meaning.
sourceText: “‘If a woman has a discharge of her blood many days not in the time of her period, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her period; all the days of the discharge of her uncleanness shall be as in the days of her period: she is unclean. Every bed whereon she lies all the days of her discharge shall be to her as the bed of her period: and everything whereon she sits shall be unclean, as the uncleanness of her period. Whoever touches these things […]

note: The baseline menstrual-impurity law ('seven days she shall be in her impurity, and whoever touches her shall be unclean') frames the chronic twelve-year condition (v.25). Establishes that the woman is perpetually outside normal social and cultic contact, deepening the audacity of her approach in the crowd.
sourceText: “‘If a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood, she shall be in her impurity seven days: and whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening.

note: The law's resolution requires the priest to make atonement 'for her unclean discharge,' after which she is clean. Jesus' word 'be cured of your disease' (v.34) functions as the priestly declaration of restored cleanness, the discharge being 'dried up' (v.29). Thematic coherence: Jesus enacts the role the Levitical system assigns to atonement and priestly verdict.
sourceText: The priest shall offer the one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering; and the priest shall make atonement for her before Yahweh for the uncleanness of her discharge.

note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (kanaph)' — the same term denotes the hem/corner of a garment. The woman seeks healing by touching the edge of Jesus' clothes (vv.27-28), and Matthew/Luke specify the kraspedon (tassel). Faint but evocative: healing located in the garment's edge resonates with Malachi's healing 'in the wings.'
sourceText: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.

note: The command to wear tassels on the corners of garments as reminders of the commandments stands behind the Synoptic detail of touching the hem (here generalized as 'his clothes,' v.27). The healing power located in the garment's fringe gains resonance from the sanctity Torah attaches to the tassel; faint in Mark, who omits the tassel itself.
sourceText: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;

note: Contact with Elisha's bones revives a corpse — power transmitted by touch from a holy person even involuntarily. The woman's cure by touching Jesus' garment, with power 'gone out from him' (v.30), echoes the prophetic motif of healing virtue conveyed through physical contact. Thematic, supporting the Elijah-Elisha typology that pervades the chapter.
sourceText: As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.

note: Elijah raises the widow of Zarephath's son: he goes in to where the child lies, acts privately, and 'the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived,' then Elijah presents the living child. Mark's raising of Jairus' daughter — entering where the child lay (v.40), the restoring word, the return to life (v.42) — is patterned on this paradigmatic prophetic resurrection. Strong Volume and recurrence within the chapter's Elijah-Elisha typology.
sourceText: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. This is the other classic seeing-not/hearing-not oracle, paired with hardness; its conjunction with rebellion coheres with Mark's hardened-heart charge in v.17.
sourceText: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of the rebellious house, who have eyes to see, and don’t see, who have ears to hear, and don’t hear; for they are a rebellious house.

note: Moses tells Israel they saw the signs in Egypt 'yet to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears to hear.' This explicitly links failure to perceive God's mighty works (the feedings) with an ungiven heart—exactly Jesus' point that the disciples fail to remember the loaves.
sourceText: Moses called to all Israel, and said to them: Your eyes have seen all that Yahweh did in the land of Egypt to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land; the great trials which your eyes saw, the signs, and those great wonders. But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.

note: 'Why do you harden our hearts so that we do not fear you?' supplies the hardened-heart vocabulary that Jesus levels at the disciples ('Is your heart still hardened?'). The motif is recurrent in Mark (6:52), grounding the charge in prophetic lament over insensate Israel.
sourceText: O Yahweh, why do you make us to err from your ways, and harden our heart from your fear? Return for your servants’ sake, the tribes of your inheritance.

note: 'Harden not your hearts' carries forward from the sign-seeking pericope; the disciples' hardened hearts place them within the same warned-against wilderness generation that fails to read God's provision (the manna/loaves).
sourceText: Don’t harden your heart, as at Meribah, as in the day of Massah in the wilderness,

note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened'—the healing of the blind man at Bethsaida enacts Isaiah's promise of eschatological restoration. Mark positions this sign as a figural opening of eyes that frames the disciples' partial sight; volume and coherence with the surrounding seeing/not-seeing motif are high.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.

note: 'In that day...out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see'—paired in Isaiah with the deaf hearing, this restoration oracle undergirds the staged healing. The Isaianic blindness/sight complex is the controlling intertext for the whole pericope's placement.
sourceText: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.

note: The Servant is given 'to open the eyes that are blind,' a commissioning that Mark sees fulfilled in Jesus' physical opening of blind eyes as a sign of his servant-messiahship—coherent with the suffering Son of Man developed just after (v.31).
sourceText: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations; to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: The two-stage cure—first blurred ('men like trees walking'), then clear sight—dramatizes the half-perceiving condition diagnosed by Isaiah's seeing-but-not-perceiving oracle. Mark figures the disciples' gradual, incomplete recognition of Jesus through the man's gradual healing; the structural coherence is strong even without verbal quotation.
sourceText: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: 'The eyes of those who see will not be closed, and the ears of those who hear will listen' belongs to the cluster of restoration-of-sight oracles that Mark's healing actualizes. Faint but within the recurrent Isaianic field.
sourceText: The eyes of those who see will not be dim, and the ears of those who hear will listen.

note: The popular guess that Jesus is 'Elijah' draws directly on Malachi's promise to send Elijah before the great day of the LORD; the expectation of Elijah redivivus frames the crowd's christological speculation. Mark develops Elijah typology around John the Baptizer.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: The opinion that Jesus is 'one of the prophets' resonates with the promise of a prophet 'like Moses' whom God would raise up; the prophet-like-Moses expectation is part of the matrix the crowd's answers reflect, sharpened by Mark's Moses/wilderness typology in the feedings.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: Peter's confession 'You are the Christ' (the Anointed) actualizes the royal vocabulary of Psalm 2, where the nations rage against 'the LORD and his Anointed.' Mark's Christ-title carries the Davidic-king freight of this enthronement psalm, which surfaces explicitly at Jesus' trial and baptism.
sourceText: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,

note: The title 'Christ' invokes the Davidic covenant promise of an anointed son whose throne is established forever. Coherence with Mark's Son-of-David theme (10:47) supports reading the confession against the Nathan oracle, though the link here is conceptual rather than verbal.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;

note: That 'the Son of Man must suffer many things... and be killed' draws on the Servant who was 'despised and rejected,' 'a man of sorrows,' who bore suffering and was 'cut off.' The necessity (dei) of redemptive suffering coheres with Isaiah 53's vicarious death; this is the foundational suffering-text behind Mark's passion predictions.
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we […]

note: 'Be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes' anticipates the rejected-stone of Psalm 118, which Mark quotes explicitly at 12:10 ('the stone the builders rejected'). The specific language of rejection by the leadership maps onto the builders' rejection, making this a deliberate, recurrent intertext.
sourceText: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.

note: The self-designation 'Son of Man' derives from Daniel's vision of 'one like a son of man' who comes with the clouds and receives dominion. Mark's title is recurrent and load-bearing; though here paired paradoxically with suffering, the Danielic figure of vindicated dominion underlies the whole Son-of-Man complex.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The motif of the righteous one despised and rejected ('a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind') feeds the suffering-Son-of-Man pattern; Mark draws heavily on Psalm 22 for the passion (15:34, 15:24), so its presence behind the first prediction is coherent and recurrent.
sourceText: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”

note: 'After three days rise again' may echo Hosea's 'after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up.' The third-day-resurrection language is plausibly drawn from this oracle of restoration, a connection later interpreters made explicit.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: 'Get behind me, Satan!' resonates with Zechariah's vision where 'the LORD rebuke you, O Satan' is spoken against the accuser. The act of rebuking the satan/adversary who opposes God's purpose coheres verbally and conceptually with Jesus' rebuke of Peter as voicing 'the things of men.'
sourceText: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”

note: 'When he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels' renders the Son of Man's coming in Daniel's vision, where the one like a son of man comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days to receive glory and an everlasting kingdom. The conjunction of Son of Man, coming, and glory is a direct appropriation.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him' supplies the entourage of 'holy angels/holy ones' accompanying the divine advent. Mark's coming Son of Man 'with the holy angels' draws on this theophany of God arriving with his holy retinue for judgment.
sourceText: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*

note: The throne-and-myriads scene—'thousand thousands served him'—reinforces the angelic-attendant imagery of the Son of Man's glorious advent in v.38. Coherent with the Danielic court of judgment that frames being 'ashamed' before the coming one.
sourceText: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.

note: 'For what will a man give in exchange for his life?' closely parallels the psalm's reflection that no one can 'give to God a ransom for his life... for the redemption of their soul is costly.' The wisdom logic that life cannot be bought back with wealth underlies vv.36-37.
sourceText: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough, That he should live on forever, that he should not see corruption.

note: 'What does it profit a man, to gain the whole world?' echoes Qoheleth's recurring 'What profit (yitron) has a man of all his toil?'—the wisdom idiom of weighing profit against the vanity of worldly gain. Faint but coherent with the saying's sapiential cast.
sourceText: What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?

note: 'This adulterous and sinful generation' reprises the Song of Moses' 'perverse and crooked generation,' tying the audience of Jesus' words to the faithless wilderness cohort already invoked in the sign-seeking pericope. The recurrence of the 'generation' label within Mark 8 strengthens the link.
sourceText: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.

note: The charge 'adulterous... generation' draws on the prophetic figure of Israel as an unfaithful, adulterous spouse (Hosea's central metaphor), framing the present generation's unbelief as covenant infidelity. Faint, but within the prophetic adultery-as-apostasy tradition.
sourceText: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts;

note: Jesus' promise that some standing here will see 'the Kingdom of God come with power' draws on Daniel's vision of dominion, glory, and an everlasting kingdom given to the one like a son of man. The conjunction of kingdom and divine power coheres with Daniel's eschatological enthronement scene. Recurrence of Danielic son-of-man and kingdom language throughout Mark strengthens the allusion.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The God of heaven setting up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed and that breaks all others supplies the apocalyptic backdrop for a kingdom arriving 'with power.' The volume is faint and the verbal overlap general, but the coherence with Mark's kingdom proclamation is real.
sourceText: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.

note: The good news that 'your God reigns' lies behind Markan kingdom-arrival language. The link to 9:1 specifically is faint and rests on the shared royal-reign theme rather than verbal contact.
sourceText: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

note: The Sinai theophany supplies Mark's frame: the glory of the LORD settled on the mountain, the cloud covered it six days, and on the seventh day God called to Moses out of the cloud. Mark's 'after six days,' the high mountain, the overshadowing cloud, and the voice from the cloud reproduce this cluster with high volume and tight coherence. The Transfiguration is staged as a new Sinai.
sourceText: Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.

note: Moses goes up the mountain and the cloud covers it, the immediate setting for the giving of the covenant. Mark's ascent of three named companions onto a high mountain into a cloud reactivates this Sinai ascent. The recurrence of mountain-and-cloud theophany makes the availability and coherence criteria strong.
sourceText: Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain.

note: When Moses came down from Sinai the skin of his face shone because he had talked with God, so that the people were afraid. Jesus' garments becoming dazzling white and the disciples' fear echo the transfigured radiance of Moses, while transposing the glory from reflected to inherent. The Moses-glory pattern is reinforced by Moses' actual presence on the mountain.
sourceText: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him.

note: The LORD descended in the cloud and stood with Moses and proclaimed his name. The descending cloud and the divine voice in Mark cohere with this Sinai descent, reinforcing the Moses typology already active through Moses' appearance.
sourceText: Yahweh descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed Yahweh’s name.

note: The heavenly voice 'This is my beloved Son' draws on the royal-enthronement decree 'You are my Son.' The divine sonship language frames Jesus as the messianic king. Recurrence of Psalm 2 at the baptism (Mark 1:11) and here establishes a Markan inclusio of divine attestation.
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.

note: Moses promises a prophet like himself whom God will raise up, and commands 'to him you shall listen.' The heavenly 'Listen to him' verbally echoes this command, and the presence of Moses on the mountain makes the prophet-like-Moses identification pointed. Volume and coherence are both strong.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: 'Behold my servant, my chosen, in whom my soul delights' stands behind the beloved-Son acclamation, blending servant election with sonship. The Markan voice fuses Psalm 2 royal sonship with Isaianic servant language. The servant motif coheres with the suffering Son of Man that immediately follows.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.

note: God's command to Abraham regarding 'your son, your only son, whom you love' supplies the Aqedah resonance behind 'my beloved Son.' The Greek agapetos echoes the Septuagint of Isaac, linking divine sonship to sacrificial offering, which coheres with Mark's passion theme. The connection is suggestive rather than verbally exact.
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: Elijah's appearance on the mountain activates the expectation that Elijah will come before the day of the LORD, made explicit in 9:11-13. His presence beside Moses pairs Law and Prophets as witnesses to Jesus. The motif is developed verbally in the following pericope.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: The messenger sent to prepare the way contributes to the Elijah-forerunner complex evoked by Elijah's presence. The link here is indirect, mediated through Mark's broader Elijah typology.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Elijah's being taken up to heaven by chariot explains why he, like Moses (whose death and burial were hidden), is available to appear on the mountain rather than being among the dead. The translation traditions of both figures underwrite their eschatological reappearance. Coherence with Jewish expectation is strong though the verbal contact is nil.
sourceText: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

note: Moses' death on Mount Nebo with no known grave fed traditions of his assumption, making his appearance alongside Elijah intelligible. The faint link supports the availability of Moses as a heavenly witness. It rests on later interpretive tradition rather than the text alone.
sourceText: So Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab, according to Yahweh’s word.

note: The clothing white as snow in Daniel's vision of the Ancient of Days lies behind Mark's description of garments dazzling white beyond any launderer's whitening. The apocalyptic-glory vocabulary transfers heavenly radiance onto Jesus. Volume is moderate and coheres with Mark's son-of-man Christology.
sourceText: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire.

note: The glory of the LORD appearing in the cloud in the wilderness contributes to the cloud-glory motif overshadowing the disciples. The general theophanic cloud is shared, though Exodus 24 is the primary source. A faint reinforcing echo.
sourceText: As Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, Yahweh’s glory appeared in the cloud.

note: Peter's proposal to make three booths (skenai) may draw on the Feast of Booths command to dwell in temporary shelters, evoking eschatological feast and divine dwelling. The link is contested and may be incidental to Peter's confusion. If intended, it ties the theophany to Sukkot's hope of God's tabernacling presence.
