sourceText: You shall dwell in booths seven days. All who are native-born in Israel shall dwell in booths,

note: Zechariah's vision of all nations keeping the Feast of Booths when the LORD becomes king supplies a possible eschatological-Sukkot backdrop to Peter's tents. The connection is faint and depends on reading the booths motif eschatologically. It coheres with the kingdom-with-power saying of 9:1.
sourceText: It will happen that everyone who is left of all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up from year to year to worship the King, Yahweh of Armies, and to keep the feast of tents.

note: The scribal teaching that 'Elijah must come first' directly reflects Malachi's promise to send Elijah before the great and terrible day of the LORD. Jesus affirms and reinterprets this expectation, identifying the returned Elijah with John the Baptist. Verbal and thematic volume is high.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: Elijah's task to 'turn the hearts' and so restore relationships underlies Jesus' phrase that Elijah 'restores all things.' The restoration motif is drawn directly from Malachi's commission. Coherence with the forerunner role is exact.
sourceText: He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

note: Sirach interprets Malachi, saying Elijah is ready to calm wrath, turn the heart of the father to the son, and restore the tribes of Jacob. Jesus' wording that Elijah 'restores all things' tracks Sirach's restorationist gloss more closely than Malachi alone, demonstrating Second-Temple availability. This is a key deuterocanonical witness to the expectation Mark engages.
sourceText: Who was recorded for reproofs in their seasons, To pacify anger, before it brake forth into wrath; To turn the heart of the father to the son, And to restore the tribes of Jacob.

note: Jesus' question 'how is it written about the Son of Man, that he should suffer many things and be despised' draws on the servant who is despised and rejected by men. The suffering-and-despised pairing matches Isaiah's fourth servant song closely. Mark grounds the passion in this Scripture as 'written.'
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.

note: The servant who bears griefs and is esteemed stricken reinforces the 'suffer many things' clause. The vicarious-suffering theme coheres with Mark's repeated passion predictions. Volume is moderate alongside the stronger 53:3 contact.
sourceText: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.

note: The sufferer 'despised by the people' supplies a scriptural template for the Son of Man being 'despised.' Mark's passion narrative repeatedly draws on Psalm 22, making its recurrence a strong coherence indicator. The verbal contact on contempt strengthens the echo.
sourceText: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people.

note: Jezebel's threat to kill Elijah, who flees for his life, stands behind 'they have also done to him whatever they wanted,' applied to John the Baptist's persecution and death. The historical Elijah's suffering at royal hands prefigures the returned Elijah's fate. Coherence with the rejected-prophet pattern is strong.
sourceText: Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!”

note: Elijah's lament that the Israelites have killed the prophets and seek his life reinforces the pattern that the forerunner suffers as the prophets did. The link to 'done to him whatever they wanted' is thematic. It supports reading John's death through an Elijah lens.
sourceText: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

note: The title 'Son of Man,' twice used in this pericope, derives from Daniel's heavenly figure, here paradoxically joined to suffering. Mark fuses Danielic exaltation with Isaianic suffering. The recurrence of the title throughout Mark anchors the Danielic source.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: The rejected stone supplies a scriptural pattern of the chosen one being despised and rejected, coherent with the Son of Man being 'set at nought.' Mark cites this psalm later (12:10), making its availability and recurrence plausible. The contact here is faint.
sourceText: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.

note: Jesus descending the mountain to find a disordered crowd and disputing scribes parallels Moses descending Sinai to find Israel corrupted around the golden calf. The 'faithless generation' rebuke echoes the wilderness apostasy. The narrative staging reinforces the Moses-on-the-mountain typology of the preceding scene.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses, “Go, get down; for your people, who you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves!

note: Jesus' address 'O faithless generation' draws on the Song of Moses, which calls Israel a 'perverse and crooked generation' that has dealt corruptly and is not faithful. The generation-rebuke vocabulary is distinctively Deuteronomic. Mark frames the unbelieving crowd in covenant-lawsuit terms.
sourceText: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.

note: God hides his face from 'a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness,' precisely the charge of faithlessness Jesus levels. The pairing of 'generation' with unbelief tracks this verse closely. It deepens the Song-of-Moses backdrop to the rebuke.
sourceText: He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.

note: God's lament 'how long will this people despise me, and how long will they not believe' matches Jesus' double 'how long shall I be with you... how long shall I bear with you' aimed at unbelief. The wilderness-unbelief motif coheres with the faithless-generation theme. Volume is moderate.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “How long will this people despise me? and how long will they not believe in me, for all the signs which I have worked among them?

note: God's 'how long shall I bear with this evil congregation' supplies the bearing-with-unbelief vocabulary in Jesus' complaint. The wilderness murmuring pattern reinforces the Deuteronomy 32 frame. A faint reinforcing echo.
sourceText: “How long shall I bear with this evil congregation, that murmur against me? I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel, which they murmur against me.

note: The boy 'like one dead' so that bystanders said 'He is dead,' followed by being raised up, faintly evokes the psalm of one poured out like water and brought to the dust of death yet vindicated. The death-to-life movement coheres with the resurrection foreshadowing of the chapter. Contact is thematic and low-volume.
sourceText: I am poured out like water. All my bones are out of joint. My heart is like wax; it is melted within me.

note: Elijah raising the widow's apparently dead son, after which the child revived, supplies an Elijah-resurrection template behind Jesus taking the boy by the hand and raising him so that he arose. Given the chapter's Elijah typology, the link has some coherence. Verbal contact is slight.
sourceText: He stretched himself on the child three times, and cried to Yahweh, and said, “Yahweh my God, please let this child’s soul come into him again.”

note: Elisha reviving the Shunammite's dead son extends the prophetic resuscitation pattern that frames Jesus' raising of the boy. The motif of a prophet restoring a child reinforces the scene's prophetic resonance. The connection is faint and pattern-based.
sourceText: He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm.

note: The Son of Man being 'handed over to the hands of men' echoes the servant whom the LORD delivered up for iniquity; the Septuagint's language of being given over underlies Mark's passion prediction. The vicarious handing-over coheres with Mark's Isaianic passion theme. Recurrence across the passion predictions strengthens it.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: The servant 'poured out his soul to death' and 'was numbered with the transgressors,' having been delivered up. Mark's 'delivered into the hands of men... they will kill him' tracks the servant's being given over to death. The betrayal-and-death sequence aligns with the song's climax.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up' is the most likely scriptural source for 'on the third day he will rise again.' The third-day resurrection timing coheres with the formulaic passion predictions. Volume is moderate; the verbal 'third day' contact is notable.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: The title 'Son of Man' carries Danielic weight even when joined to betrayal and death, fusing exaltation with suffering. The recurrence across Mark's passion predictions establishes the Danielic source. Here the paradox of the heavenly figure killed is sharpest.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: The dispute about who is greatest and Jesus' reversal that the first must be last and servant of all coheres with wisdom warnings that pride goes before destruction and humility precedes honor. The link is thematic rather than verbal. It situates the teaching in the OT wisdom reversal of status.
sourceText: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.

note: 'Before honor is humility' provides a wisdom backdrop to the last-shall-be-first saying and the embrace of the child. The contact is general and pattern-based. It reinforces the OT roots of Jesus' status reversal.
sourceText: The fear of Yahweh teaches wisdom. Before honor is humility.

note: The servant who justifies many through humble service supplies a faint figural backdrop to 'servant of all.' The connection is thematic and depends on Mark's wider servant Christology. Low volume.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

note: John's complaint about an outsider casting out demons in Jesus' name, and the demand to forbid him, closely parallels Joshua's plea that Moses forbid Eldad and Medad from prophesying outside the tent. Jesus' refusal to forbid mirrors Moses' magnanimous reply. The structural and thematic parallel is striking.
sourceText: A young man ran, and told Moses, and said, “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp!”

note: Joshua's 'My lord Moses, forbid them' is answered by Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets. Mark casts the disciples as Joshua and Jesus as the larger-hearted Moses who will not restrict the Spirit's work. The parallel reinforces the Moses typology running through the chapter.
sourceText: Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his chosen men, answered, “My lord Moses, forbid them!”

note: Moses' 'Would that all the LORD's people were prophets' anticipates Jesus' inclusive 'whoever is not against us is for us.' The generous expansion of authorized agency is shared. The echo completes the Eldad-and-Medad parallel.
sourceText: Moses said to him, “Are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all Yahweh’s people were prophets, that Yahweh would put his Spirit on them!”

note: The thrice-repeated 'where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched' is a near-verbatim quotation of Isaiah's closing vision of the corpses of rebels, an undying worm and unquenchable fire. This is the strongest OT contact in the chapter and supplies the imagery of Gehenna. The repetition underscores the volume and centrality.
sourceText: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”

note: 'Every sacrifice will be seasoned with salt' draws directly on the law that every grain offering be salted, never omitting the salt of the covenant. Mark's pairing of fire and salt with sacrifice reflects this cultic prescription. The verbal contact on salting the sacrifice is high.
sourceText: Every offering of your meal offering you shall season with salt; neither shall you allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be lacking from your meal offering. With all your offerings you shall offer salt.

note: The 'covenant of salt forever' between the LORD and the priests illuminates 'have salt in yourselves, and be at peace,' linking salt to enduring covenant fidelity. The covenant-of-salt motif undergirds the call to mutual peace. It strengthens the cultic-covenantal reading of the salt sayings.
sourceText: All the wave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer to Yahweh, have I given you, and your sons and your daughters with you, as a portion forever. It is a covenant of salt forever before Yahweh to you and to your seed with you.”

note: The kingship given to David by 'a covenant of salt' reinforces salt as a symbol of permanent covenant, supporting Jesus' exhortation to keep salt and peace. The contact is general and reinforcing. It corroborates the covenant-of-salt background.
sourceText: Ought you not to know that Yahweh, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?

note: The priests casting salt on the offerings before the LORD adds to the salted-sacrifice background of 9:49. The cultic salting of offerings coheres with Mark's 'every sacrifice salted with salt.' A reinforcing low-volume echo.
sourceText: You shall bring them near to Yahweh, and the priests shall cast salt on them, and they shall offer them up for a burnt offering to Yahweh.

note: Topheth prepared with fire and a great pile of wood, kindled by the breath of the LORD, contributes to the fiery-judgment imagery behind Gehenna and 'everyone salted with fire.' The link reinforces the burning-judgment theme. Volume is modest beside Isaiah 66.
sourceText: For his burning place has long been ready. Yes, for the king it is prepared. He has made its pyre deep and large with fire and much wood. Yahweh’s breath, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.

note: The valley of the son of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom), site of child sacrifice condemned by Jeremiah, is the geographical and historical root of 'Gehenna.' Mark's term presupposes this defiled valley as the image of fiery judgment. The connection is etymological and background rather than a verbal citation.
sourceText: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind.

note: Jeremiah renames Topheth the 'valley of slaughter,' deepening the Hinnom-valley associations behind Gehenna. The judgment-in-the-valley motif underlies Mark's hell imagery. A reinforcing background echo.
sourceText: therefore, behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that this place shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter.

note: The resurrection of some to everlasting contempt provides an apocalyptic frame for the unending punishment evoked by the undying worm and unquenchable fire. The shame-and-punishment of the wicked coheres with Mark's warnings. The contact is thematic and reinforces the Isaiah 66 quotation.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: Judith's hymn warns that the Lord will give fire and worms to the flesh of the nations, weeping in pain forever, a Second-Temple development of Isaiah 66:24. Its availability shows the worm-and-fire judgment circulating in the period Mark writes. It corroborates the deuterocanonical reception of the Isaiah imagery.
sourceText: “Woe to the nations who rise up against my race! The Lord Almighty will take vengeance on them in the day of judgement, to put fire and worms in their flesh; and they will weep and feel their pain forever.”

note: Bringing the remnant through the fire to refine them lies faintly behind 'everyone will be salted with fire,' if the fire is read as purifying rather than only punitive. The refining-fire motif coheres with a disciple-formation reading of the saying. Low volume and contested.
sourceText: I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”

note: Jesus grounds marriage 'from the beginning of the creation' in 'God made them male and female,' a near-verbatim citation of the creation of humanity as male and female. High Volume and explicit appeal to creation order; the phrase functions as a formal scriptural authority over against Deuteronomy's concession. Availability and Coherence are secure within Mark's argument structure.
sourceText: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: The words 'a man will leave his father and mother, and will join to his wife, and the two will become one flesh' reproduce the etiological marriage saying nearly word-for-word. This is the load-bearing prooftext; Jesus stacks it on Genesis 1:27 to argue indissolubility. Maximal Volume and Recurrence in early Jewish marriage discourse.
sourceText: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.

note: The 'certificate of divorce' Moses 'allowed' is a direct invocation of the Mosaic divorce statute, named explicitly as Moses' command. Jesus cites it precisely in order to subordinate it as a concession to 'hardness of heart.' Explicit attribution to Moses makes this an unambiguous, high-Volume citation.
sourceText: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house. When she has departed out of his house, she may go and be another man’s wife. If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter […]

note: Malachi rebukes faithless divorce, invokes 'the wife of your covenant,' appeals to the one-flesh creation ('did he not make them one?'), and reports that God 'hates divorce.' Jesus' fusion of one-flesh creation theology with a polemic against divorce coheres strongly with Malachi's distinctive argument. The shared appeal to creation against divorce raises this above generic thematic overlap.
sourceText: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For I hate divorce”, says Yahweh, the God of Israel, “and him […]

note: The toledot restatement 'male and female he created them, and blessed them' reinforces the male-and-female creation formula Jesus cites. It is a secondary witness to the same tradition behind Genesis 1:27, strengthening Recurrence. Marked contested because Mark most plausibly draws on Genesis 1:27 directly.
sourceText: He created them male and female, and blessed them. On the day they were created, he named them “Adam”.

note: The diagnosis 'for your hardness of heart' resonates with the Pentateuch's hardened-heart vocabulary, of which the Exodus Pharaoh cycle is the paradigm. The motif frames Israel's recalcitrance as the reason for the concession. Low confidence and contested: thematic vocabulary rather than a specific citation.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “When you go back into Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders which I have put in your hand, but I will harden his heart and he will not let the people go.

note: Jacob lays his hands on Ephraim and Manasseh and blesses them, the foundational scene of patriarchal blessing by laying on of hands. Jesus 'took them in his arms, and blessed them, laying his hands on them' reenacts this gesture upon children. The verbal and ritual overlap (hands, blessing, children) gives the allusion real Volume.
sourceText: Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn. He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham […]

note: The laying on of hands to convey authority and blessing (Moses on Joshua) is the OT background for the gesture Jesus performs. It supplies the Availability of the imposition-of-hands motif. Low confidence and contested because Mark's scene is blessing, not commissioning.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.

note: The psalmist stills his soul 'like a weaned child,' modeling trustful smallness before God, which coheres with receiving the kingdom 'like a little child.' The child as image of humble dependence is the shared note. Contested and low: thematic resonance without verbal contact.
sourceText: Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.

note: Wisdom prizes virtue over many children and the immortality of the righteous, part of a Second-Temple revaluation of childhood and worth. The faint resonance lies in valuing what the world overlooks, as the disciples overlook the children. Contested; included for maximal coverage of deuterocanonical availability.
sourceText: Better than this is childishness with virtue; For in the memory of virtue is immortality: Because it is recognized both before God and before men.

note: Jesus recites the second-table Decalogue commandments against murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and to honor father and mother, citing them as 'the commandments' the man knows. The wording follows the Decalogue directly. Highest Volume and explicit appeal to the Ten Words.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.

note: The Deuteronomic recension of the same commandments is an equally valid source for Jesus' list, and the placement of 'Honor your father and mother' after the social prohibitions mirrors a known ordering. Marked as a parallel high-confidence citation alongside Exodus 20. The two Decalogue forms together secure the quotation.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.

note: Jesus' extra commandment 'Do not defraud' (not in the Decalogue) echoes the Deuteronomic prohibition against defrauding or oppressing a hired laborer and withholding wages. Mark's insertion of defrauding into a Decalogue list points to this legal tradition on economic injustice. The targeted addition to a rich landholder gives the allusion coherence.
sourceText: You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates.

note: The Holiness Code's 'you shall not defraud your neighbor nor rob him; the wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you overnight' is the strongest single source for Mark's 'Do not defraud.' Its pairing of fraud with withheld wages fits Jesus' demand that this wealthy man divest. Verbal contact on 'defraud' lifts this above generic.
sourceText: “‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.

note: Jesus' rejoinder 'No one is good except one—God' reflects the Shema's confession of God's oneness and uniqueness, here applied to the predicate of goodness. The 'one' (heis) language coheres with Deuteronomic monotheism. The link is conceptual but anchored in the distinctive 'one God' formula.
sourceText: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.

note: 'Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good' is the recurrent liturgical confession that God alone is good, the conviction behind Jesus' 'No one is good except one—God.' The refrain pervades the Psalter (106, 107, 136). Low and contested: a diffuse liturgical commonplace rather than a citation.
sourceText: Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.

note: 'He who is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him' underwrites Jesus' logic that giving to the poor yields 'treasure in heaven.' The proverb's transaction of almsgiving credited with God grounds the heavenly-treasure promise. Coherence with the divestment command is strong.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold' is the closest Second-Temple parallel to 'you will have treasure in heaven.' The instruction to convert wealth into a heavenly account, set beside almsgiving, matches Jesus' counsel precisely. Availability and verbal proximity make this a primary deuterocanonical source.
sourceText: Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold.

note: Tobit instructs giving alms from one's possessions, promising that almsgiving 'lays up a good treasure' and delivers from death. The almsgiving-as-stored-treasure theology directly parallels Jesus' 'give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.' The shared treasure-and-deliverance logic strengthens the allusion.
sourceText: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]

note: Honoring the LORD with one's wealth and firstfruits, with promised reward, lies in the background of redirecting possessions toward God. The wisdom pattern of wealth surrendered and divinely repaid coheres with the pericope. Low and contested: thematic.
sourceText: Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase: so your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine.

note: The open-handed command to give freely to the poor brother and not harden the heart frames Israel's duty to the needy, which Jesus presses to its limit. The almsgiving ethic supplies background for 'give to the poor.' Contested; a broad covenantal commonplace.
sourceText: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]

note: 'He who trusts in his riches will fall' directly underlies Jesus' qualification 'how hard is it for those who trust in riches to enter the Kingdom.' The verbal target is the verb of trusting in wealth, not merely possessing it. The proverb supplies both diagnosis and outcome, giving solid Volume.
sourceText: He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous shall flourish as the green leaf.

note: Those who 'trust in their wealth' cannot by any means ransom a person from death, exactly the impossibility Jesus presses: riches cannot purchase entry or salvation. The psalm's link between trust-in-riches and the limits of ransom coheres with the chapter's later ransom saying. Conceptual overlap is precise and recurrent.
sourceText: Those who trust in their wealth, and boast in the multitude of their riches— none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him.

note: 'Is anything too hard for the LORD?' is the canonical formula of divine possibility that Jesus restates as 'with men it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God.' Sarah's promised son against natural impossibility is the paradigm. The verbal and theological match (nothing too hard / all things possible) is strong.
sourceText: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”

note: 'I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted' is a near-formulaic source for 'all things are possible with God.' Job's confession of God's unbounded power matches Jesus' answer to 'who then can be saved?' The omnipotence formula recurs and coheres.
sourceText: “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.

note: 'If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant... should it also be marvelous in my eyes?' contrasts human limits with divine possibility in restoration. The reversal of what seems impossible to people coheres with Jesus' saying. Contested and low: thematic possibility-formula, no verbal lock.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh of Armies: “If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my eyes?” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'Nothing is too hard for you' (Jeremiah's prayer) repeats the Genesis 18:14 omnipotence formula and reinforces Recurrence behind 'all things are possible with God.' Marked contested because Genesis 18:14 is the likelier primary source. Included for completeness of the divine-possibility tradition.
sourceText: Ah Lord Yahweh! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm; there is nothing too hard for you,

note: Hannah's song declares the LORD makes poor and makes rich, raises the poor from the dust, and reverses high and low, undergirding 'many who are first will be last; and the last first.' The eschatological reversal of status and wealth coheres tightly with Jesus' promise and warning. The reversal motif is verbally and thematically apt.
sourceText: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up. He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.

note: God 'sets on high those who are lowly,' the wisdom statement of divine reversal that informs the first-last saying. It supports the reversal pattern's Recurrence. Contested and low: general reversal topos.
sourceText: so that he sets up on high those who are low, those who mourn are exalted to safety.

note: Covenant blessing promises abundance of children, livestock, and land 'a hundredfold' in plenty, faintly behind the promise of houses, family, and lands 'one hundred times more.' The hundredfold-in-the-land blessing supplies background imagery. Contested; thematic and inexact.
sourceText: Yahweh will grant you abundant prosperity, in the fruit of your body, in the fruit of your livestock, and in the fruit of your ground, in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers to give you.

note: Isaac sows and reaps 'a hundredfold' because the LORD blessed him, a concrete OT instance of the hundredfold blessing language Jesus uses. It supplies Availability for 'one hundred times more.' Contested and low: a single lexical resonance.
sourceText: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.

note: The third Servant Song's 'I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pluck out the hair; I did not hide my face from shame and spitting' supplies the specifics of Jesus' passion forecast: mocking, spitting, and scourging. The catalogue of indignities matches Mark's verbs closely. High Volume and Coherence with Mark's Servant Christology.
sourceText: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.

note: The Servant despised, oppressed, and led to death, then vindicated, frames the rejection-suffering-vindication shape of the passion prediction. Mark's 'condemn him to death... and on the third day he will rise' tracks the Servant's humiliation-and-exaltation arc. Recurrence of Isaiah 53 across the passion narrative strengthens this.
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we […]

note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up' is the principal OT source for the 'third day' resurrection formula. The phrase's distinctive temporal marker matches 'on the third day he will rise again.' Second-Temple use of Hosea 6:2 for resurrection timing raises its plausibility.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: 'The Son of Man' as Jesus' self-designation derives from the one 'like a son of man' who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion. Mark fuses this exalted figure with the suffering of the Servant. The title's repeated appearance in Mark and its Danielic root make the allusion strong.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: The scorned and mocked sufferer ('all who see me mock me') anticipates 'they will mock him,' linking the prediction to the passion psalm Mark cites at the cross. The mockery motif coheres with Mark's later use of Psalm 22. Contested here because the contact is anticipatory and thematic.
sourceText: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying,

note: The Servant who 'pours out his soul to death,' 'bears the sin of many,' and makes his life a guilt offering 'for many' is the controlling source for 'to give his life as a ransom for many.' The distinctive vicarious 'for many' (rabbim) and the substitutionary death match decisively. This is the chapter's major Servant allusion, high in Volume and Coherence.
sourceText: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]

note: Jerusalem has drunk 'the cup of his wrath... the bowl of staggering,' the cup-of-judgment imagery behind 'the cup that I drink.' Jesus takes upon himself the cup of divine wrath the city must drink. The cup as wrath to be consumed coheres with the passion's substitutionary logic.
sourceText: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.

note: 'In the hand of the LORD there is a cup... and he pours it out; surely all the wicked of the earth shall drain it' establishes the cup as the draught of God's judgment. Jesus' question 'are you able to drink the cup that I drink' draws on this judicial cup. The wrath-cup motif's Recurrence (Jeremiah 25, Isaiah 51) supports it.
sourceText: For in the hand of Yahweh there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.

note: The prophet makes the nations drink 'the cup of the wine of wrath,' the most extended OT development of the wrath-cup that Jesus alludes to. It strengthens the Recurrence of the cup-of-judgment tradition behind Mark 10:38. Marked contested only as to which cup-text is primary; Isaiah 51 and Psalm 75 are nearer.
sourceText: For thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, to me: take this cup of the wine of wrath at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it. They shall drink, and reel back and forth, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them. Then took I the cup at Yahweh’s hand, and made all the nations to drink, to whom Yahweh had sent me: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and its kings, and its princes, to make them a desolation, an […]

note: James and John request seats 'in your glory,' echoing the dominion and glory given to the son of man, while the right-and-left thrones evoke enthronement in the Danielic kingdom. The petition presupposes the Son of Man's coming glory. Coherence with the Daniel 7 background of Mark's Son of Man title supports the link.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The request to sit 'at your right hand' draws on the royal enthronement of the king at God's right hand. The right-hand seat of honor is the Psalm 110 image Mark elsewhere applies to Jesus. The single-side request makes the echo partial but apt; marked contested as to directness.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: The 'anointed one' cut off and atonement made 'for iniquity' resonates faintly with the ransoming death 'for many.' It supplies a Second-Temple frame for a representative figure's atoning death. Low and contested: conceptual, no verbal lock.
sourceText: Seventy weeks are decreed on your people and on your holy city, to finish disobedience, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy. Know therefore and discern, that from the going out of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem to the Anointed One, the prince, shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks: it shall be […]

note: Dominion is given to the saints, yet the kingdom's authority is from God, against which the Gentile kings who 'lord it over' their nations are contrasted. Jesus' antithesis between Gentile rulers' domination and servanthood draws on this kingdom-of-God-versus-beastly-empires schema. The contrast of empires coheres with Daniel 7.
sourceText: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.

note: The atonement-money 'ransom for his life' paid at the census supplies cultic background for lytron, 'ransom.' It frames a life-price offered to redeem. Contested and low: Mark's ransom is more directly Isaianic (53:10-12), but the redemption-price vocabulary is available here.
sourceText: “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.

note: The kinsman-redeemer who pays a price to redeem (gaal/lytron) supplies the OT economy of ransom behind 'a ransom for many.' It contributes Availability for the redemption metaphor. Contested; background vocabulary rather than citation.
sourceText: after he is sold he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him; or his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any who is a close relative to him of his family may redeem him; or if he has grown rich, he may redeem himself.

note: No one can 'ransom' a brother or give God 'the price of his life,' for the ransom of a soul is costly, sharpening the surprise that the Son of Man does give exactly such a ransom 'for many.' The psalm sets up the impossibility Jesus' death answers. Contested and low: an inverted thematic contact.
sourceText: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough,

note: Bartimaeus hails Jesus as 'Son of David,' invoking the Davidic covenant promise of an everlasting throne to David's offspring. The acclamation is messianic, identifying Jesus as the promised royal heir as he approaches Jerusalem. The title's covenantal weight and its placement before the entry give the allusion high Volume.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]

note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened' is the prophetic sign of the coming salvation, fulfilled as Bartimaeus 'received his sight.' The opening of blind eyes marks the in-breaking of God's redemptive reign, coherent with Mark's framing of Jesus' mighty works. Strong Volume and a recurrent Isaianic restoration motif.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.

note: 'The LORD opens the eyes of the blind,' a direct attribution to God of the act Jesus performs, framing the healing as divine work. The psalm's catalogue of the LORD's saving deeds for the afflicted coheres with the beggar's restoration. The verbal match on opening blind eyes raises the allusion above generic.
sourceText: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.

note: The Servant is given 'to open the eyes that are blind,' tying the sight-giving to the Servant's commission Mark develops in this chapter. The healing thus enacts the Servant program alongside the ransom saying. Coherence with the chapter's Servant theology supports the link.
sourceText: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: 'Have mercy on me, O LORD' is the recurrent psalmic cry for mercy that Bartimaeus repeats ('have mercy on me'). The petition voices the lament-form plea for divine compassion now directed to the Son of David. The Recurrence of 'have mercy on me' across the Psalter (Pss 6, 9, 41, 51) supports the echo; marked contested as a liturgical commonplace.
sourceText: Have mercy on me, Yahweh, for I am faint. Yahweh, heal me, for my bones are troubled.

note: 'The eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity and out of darkness' adds to the Isaianic chorus of restored sight behind the healing. It reinforces Recurrence of the opened-eyes promise. Contested and low: secondary to Isaiah 35:5.
sourceText: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.

note: 'Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love' is the best-known of the mercy-pleas and shapes the form of Bartimaeus' cry. It supplies the penitential-petition register. Contested and low: the cry is a stock liturgical phrase rather than a citation of this psalm specifically.
sourceText: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.

note: The deliberate procurement and riding of a young donkey into Jerusalem evokes Zechariah's humble king who comes 'lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt the foal of a donkey.' Mark does not quote it (unlike Matthew/John), but the staged colt-riding has high coherence with the messianic peace-king imagery, and the theme recurs across the entry tradition. Volume is strong despite the missing citation.
sourceText: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

note: Jacob's blessing of Judah, 'binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine,' supplies an old messianic-royal association of the bound colt that Second-Temple readers connected to the coming ruler of Judah (Gen 49:10). Mark's emphatically tied, never-ridden colt that is untied coheres with this figural Judahic kingship, though the link is mediated and contested.
sourceText: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.

note: The crowd's cry 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!' formally cites the Hallel pilgrimage acclamation, where 'Hosanna' (hoshia-na, 'save now') is Ps 118:25 and the blessing is 118:26. This is a verbatim liturgical quotation with maximal volume; the same psalm recurs as the rejected-stone text in Mark 12:10-11, strengthening recurrence.
sourceText: Save us now, we beg you, Yahweh! Yahweh, we beg you, send prosperity now. Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.

note: Spreading garments on the road as Jesus rides echoes the acclamation of Jehu, where the people 'took every man his garment, and put it under him... and blew the trumpet, saying, Jehu is king.' The shared royal-enthronement gesture of garments under the new king gives coherence to reading the entry as a kingmaking, though Mark adds the cut branches.
sourceText: Then they hurried, and took every man his garment, and put it under him on the top of the stairs, and blew the trumpet, saying, “Jehu is king.”

note: The crowd hails 'the coming kingdom of our father David,' invoking the Davidic covenant promise of an enduring throne and kingdom for David's offspring. The Davidic-dynastic frame of the entry coheres with Nathan's oracle, the foundational text for messianic kingship, though Mark cites no words from it.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]

note: The king's approach to Jerusalem and entry into the temple faintly recalls the processional liturgy of the King of glory entering the gates. The coherence is thematic (royal advent into the sanctuary), but there is no verbal contact, so the echo is faint and contested.
sourceText: Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is the King of glory? Yahweh strong and mighty, Yahweh mighty in battle. Lift up your heads, you gates; yes, lift them up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is this King of glory? Yahweh of Armies is the King of glory! Selah.

note: Mark situates the entry at the Mount of Olives, the very site where Zechariah says the LORD's feet will stand on the day of his eschatological coming. The geographic note may be loaded with this Day-of-the-LORD coherence, but the topographic detail is also simply realistic, so the allusion is contested.
sourceText: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.

note: Jesus' cursing of the fruitless fig tree enacts Jeremiah's judgment oracle, 'there shall be no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall fade,' where Israel's barrenness brings consuming judgment. The fig-tree-as-Israel symbolism has high coherence and recurs throughout the prophets, framing the act as a prophetic sign against the temple it brackets.
sourceText: I will utterly consume them, says Yahweh: no grapes shall be on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall fade; and the things that I have given them shall pass away from them.

note: The prophet's lament 'there is no cluster to eat; my soul desired the firstripe fig' supplies the disappointed seeking of early fruit and finding none, a precise match for Jesus hungering and finding only leaves. The coherence is strong with Micah's portrait of a fruitless, faithless people awaiting judgment.
sourceText: Misery is mine! Indeed, I am like one who gathers the summer fruits, as gleanings of the vineyard: There is no cluster of grapes to eat. My soul desires to eat the early fig.

note: Hosea recalls finding Israel 'like the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time,' a metaphor of early promise turned to apostasy and barrenness (Hos 9:16, 'their root is dried up, they shall bear no fruit'). The dried-up-root motif coheres tightly with the tree withered from the roots in 11:20, reinforcing the figural reading.
sourceText: I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the first ripe in the fig tree at its first season; but they came to Baal Peor, and consecrated themselves to the shameful thing, and became abominable like that which they loved.

note: Joel's judgment imagery includes the LORD laying waste the vine and barking the fig tree so that its branches are made white, part of a Day-of-the-LORD agricultural desolation. The shared fig-tree-judgment field adds recurrence, though the verbal contact is faint and the theme is widely diffused, so the link is contested.
sourceText: He has laid my vine waste, and stripped my fig tree. He has stripped its bark, and thrown it away. Its branches are made white.

note: Jeremiah's vision of good and bad figs sorts Judah for blessing or judgment, supplying a prophetic precedent for figs symbolizing the nation's fate before the LORD. The coherence with Mark's fig sign-act against the temple is thematic rather than verbal, hence faint and contested.
sourceText: Yahweh showed me, and behold, two baskets of figs set before Yahweh’s temple, after that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and the princes of Judah, with the craftsmen and smiths, from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon. One basket had very good figs, like the figs that are first-ripe; and the other basket had very bad figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad. Then Yahweh […]

note: Jesus' teaching 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations' is a verbatim citation of Isaiah's oracle gathering foreigners and outcasts to worship at the temple. Mark uniquely preserves 'for all the nations,' heightening the inclusion theme; the formal quotation has maximal volume and frames the cleansing as eschatological restoration.
sourceText: even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”

note: The charge 'you have made it a den of robbers' formally quotes Jeremiah's temple sermon, where the people treat the LORD's house as a robbers' hideout while presuming on its protection. The citation imports Jeremiah's threat of the temple's destruction (Jer 7:14), giving the act prophetic-judgment force; high volume and tight coherence.
sourceText: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” says Yahweh.

note: Zechariah closes with the promise that on the day of the LORD 'there shall be no more the Canaanite (trader/merchant) in the house of the LORD of hosts.' Jesus' expulsion of the buyers, sellers, and money-changers enacts this eschatological purging of commerce from the temple, a strong coherence often noted as the act's interpretive key.
sourceText: Yes, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to Yahweh of Armies; and all those who sacrifice will come and take of them, and cook in them. In that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of Yahweh of Armies.

note: Malachi's Lord who 'shall suddenly come to his temple' to purify the sons of Levi and refine worship until offerings are again acceptable supplies the pattern of a sudden temple-cleansing visitation. Jesus' inspecting (11:11) then purging the temple coheres with this messenger-of-the-covenant judgment, though Mark cites no words.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and […]

note: Hosea's 'I will drive them out of my house' for their wickedness offers a verbal parallel to Jesus driving out the temple traffickers. The link is faint and the phrase generic, but it adds to the prophetic-expulsion field around the act.
sourceText: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal; for there I hated them. Because of the wickedness of their deeds I will drive them out of my house! I will love them no more. All their princes are rebels.

note: Nehemiah's reforming expulsion of profane goods from the temple chambers furnishes a historical precedent for a zealous leader cleansing the sanctuary of misuse. The coherence is typological rather than verbal, so the echo is faint and contested.
sourceText: and I came to Jerusalem, and understood the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, in preparing him a room in the courts of God’s house. It grieved me severely: therefore I threw all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the room. Then I commanded, and they cleansed the rooms: and there brought I again the vessels of God’s house, with the meal offerings and the frankincense.

note: Jeremiah 7, which Jesus quotes, indicts oppression of the alien, fatherless, and widow alongside temple abuse, a complex echoed in prophetic calls for justice over cult. This widens the den-of-robbers charge into Mark's social critique, though the specific text is faint here.
sourceText: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother. Don’t oppress the widow, nor the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor; and let none of you devise evil against his brother in your heart.’

note: The fig tree 'withered away from the roots' closely matches Hosea's judgment, 'Ephraim is smitten, their root is dried up, they shall bear no fruit,' completing the barren-Israel sign begun in 11:14. The root-withering verbal contact strengthens the figural reading of the temple's coming judgment with strong coherence.
sourceText: Ephraim is struck. Their root has dried up. They will bear no fruit. Even though they give birth, yet I will kill the beloved ones of their womb.”

note: 'Whoever says to this mountain, Be taken up and cast into the sea' is most pointed if 'this mountain' is the Temple Mount/Mount of Olives, which Zechariah 14 says the LORD will split and move on the day of his coming. The eschatological mountain-moving coheres with Zechariah's geography (the entry's Mount of Olives), giving the saying a temple-judgment edge.
sourceText: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.

note: The psalmist's confidence though 'the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea' supplies the image of mountains hurled into the sea as a figure of God's overturning power amid which the faithful do not fear. Jesus' mountain-into-the-sea saying coheres with this faith-not-fear motif, though the contact is thematic and faint.
sourceText: Therefore we won’t be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas; though its waters roar and are troubled, though the mountains tremble with their swelling. Selah.

note: Isaiah's 'the mountains shall depart and the hills be removed, but my kindness shall not depart' offers another prophetic image of removable mountains contrasted with steadfast faith in God. The link to Jesus' 'have faith in God' plus mountain-removal is faint and one of several candidate backgrounds, hence contested.
sourceText: For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed; but my loving kindness shall not depart from you, neither shall my covenant of peace be removed,” says Yahweh who has mercy on you.

note: Jesus' demand to forgive while praying so the Father may forgive (11:25) closely tracks Ben Sira's 'Forgive thy neighbour the hurt that he hath done unto thee, so shall thy sins also be forgiven when thou prayest.' The deuterocanonical maxim's near-identical conditional reciprocity gives this strong availability and coherence as a Second-Temple background.
sourceText: Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray.

note: The authorities' challenge 'By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?' recalls the recurring biblical pattern of questioning a deliverer's mandate, as in 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?' against Moses. The coherence is typological (the rejected commissioned agent), so the echo is faint and contested.
sourceText: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”

note: Korah's challenge to Moses and Aaron, disputing who authorized their elevation over the assembly, is another scriptural instance of leaders contesting a divinely given authority. It supplies a faint typological backdrop to the priests' question, with low volume and no verbal anchor.
sourceText: They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron, and said to them, “You take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy, everyone of them, and Yahweh is among them! Why do you lift yourselves up above Yahweh’s assembly?”

note: Jesus' counter-question about whether John's baptism was 'from heaven' rests on the people regarding John as a true prophet, evoking Malachi's promised Elijah who turns hearts before the day of the LORD, the figure Mark identifies with John. The Elijah-prophet background gives the baptism's heavenly origin coherence, though it is implicit here.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

note: The parable's opening reproduces the Song of the Vineyard nearly clause for clause: a man plants a vineyard, sets a hedge/fence around it, digs a pit for the winepress, and builds a tower. The verbal volume is overwhelming (LXX Isaiah supplies phragmos 'hedge,' hypolenion 'winepress pit,' pyrgos 'tower'), and coherence is total since both texts indict Israel's leadership through the vineyard image. This is the load-bearing intertext of the pericope.
sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes.

note: Isaiah identifies the vineyard explicitly as 'the house of Israel' and looks for justice but finds bloodshed; Mark's parable likewise turns on the owner seeking fruit and finding murderous tenants. The interpretive key Mark assumes — that the vineyard is the covenant people and the owner is God — is supplied directly by Isaiah 5:7, making the allusion not merely scenic but thematic.
sourceText: For the vineyard of Yahweh of Armies is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for justice, but, behold, oppression; for righteousness, but, behold, a cry of distress.

note: Mark 12:10-11 quotes verbatim from LXX Psalm 117(118): 'The stone which the builders rejected, the same was made the head of the corner; this was from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.' This is a formal citation introduced by 'Have you not read this Scripture,' and it functions as the parable's vindication of the slain son. The Volume and explicitness are maximal.
sourceText: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This is Yahweh’s doing. It is marvelous in our eyes.

note: Isaiah's tested cornerstone laid in Zion belongs to the same Second-Temple 'stone' testimony cluster that Mark draws on via Psalm 118. While Mark quotes only the Psalm, the messianic-stone catena that early readers heard behind 'head of the corner' typically braided Isaiah 28:16 (precious cornerstone) and Daniel 2 with it, so its availability and coherence support a faint echo.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: Daniel's stone, cut without hands, that destroys the kingdoms and fills the earth feeds the wider stone-testimonia tradition that Christian and Jewish readers associated with Psalm 118's rejected stone. The link here is associative rather than verbal and rests on the established recurrence of these texts together in the Second-Temple stone catena.
sourceText: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.

note: The owner's 'one beloved son' (huion agapeton) whom he sends last echoes the Aqedah language where God names Isaac 'your beloved son.' Mark has already used 'beloved Son' at the baptism and transfiguration, so recurrence within the Gospel raises the volume; the figural resonance of a beloved son sent to death sharpens the parable's pathos.
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: The tenants' deliberation, 'Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours,' verbally mirrors Joseph's brothers' plot, 'Come, let us kill him... and we shall see what becomes of his dreams.' The conspiratorial cohortative 'Come, let us kill' is distinctive enough to register as a faint Joseph echo, reinforcing the motif of a beloved son betrayed by his own.
sourceText: They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him. They said one to another, “Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.”

note: Psalm 80 is the other major vineyard-as-Israel poem, lamenting that God brought a vine out of Egypt, broke down its hedges, and prays for the 'son' he made strong. Its pairing of vineyard imagery with a 'son of man at God's right hand' coheres with Mark's parable and its sequel, making it a plausible secondary scriptural matrix alongside Isaiah 5.
sourceText: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]

note: The motif of God repeatedly sending his servants the prophets, who are beaten and killed, is a Deuteronomistic commonplace that Mark's sequence of mistreated servants dramatizes. Jeremiah's 'I sent you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them, yet they did not listen' supplies the theology of the rejected-servant chain.
sourceText: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.

note: Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned to death in the temple court for prophesying, is the paradigmatic murdered messenger of the Chronicler. The tenants who 'threw stones' at and 'killed' the sent servants enact this Deuteronomistic pattern of prophet-killing, which Jesus elsewhere frames as Israel's history of rejecting its messengers.
sourceText: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.

note: Jesus' question 'Whose image (eikon) and inscription is this?' and the verdict 'render to God the things that are God's' trades on the assumption that, as the coin bears Caesar's image, the human person bears God's image and so is owed to God. The image-of-God theology of Genesis 1 supplies the unspoken second half of the antithesis; the eikon vocabulary strengthens the link.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: The provocative display of a coin bearing the emperor's graven image in temple precincts plays on Israel's aniconic commitment against making images. The Decalogue's prohibition of graven images lurks behind the trap, since possessing Caesar's image already compromises the questioners, but the connection is thematic rather than cited.
sourceText: “You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:

note: Proverbs' counsel to 'fear the Lord and the king, and do not associate with those who change' offers a wisdom precedent for distinguishing honor due to God from honor due to the sovereign. The conceptual parallel to 'render to Caesar and to God' is real but diffuse, with no verbal overlap.
sourceText: My son, fear Yahweh and the king. Don’t join those who are rebellious:

note: The Sadducees cite the levirate law almost verbatim: 'If a man's brother dies and leaves a wife and no child, his brother should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.' Mark frames it as 'Moses wrote to us,' a formal scriptural citation that sets up the resurrection test case.
sourceText: If brothers dwell together, and one of them dies, and has no son, the wife of the dead shall not be married outside to a stranger. Her husband’s brother shall go in to her, and take her as his wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her. It shall be that the firstborn whom she bears shall succeed in the name of his brother who is dead, that his name not be blotted out of Israel.

note: The earliest narrative enactment of levirate duty is Onan, commanded to 'go in to your brother's wife and raise up offspring for your brother' — the precise idiom the Sadducees use. Genesis 38 is the practical backdrop to the Deuteronomic statute and likely shapes the wording of their hypothetical.
sourceText: Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her, and raise up seed to your brother.”

note: Jesus' decisive proof of resurrection is the formal quotation of God's self-identification at the bush: 'I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' He explicitly cites 'the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush,' and argues God is God of the living, not the dead. This is the pericope's load-bearing citation.
sourceText: Moreover he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God.

note: Sarah's seven successive husbands who die before consummation (each taken by the demon Asmodeus) is the closest Second-Temple analogue to the Sadducees' woman with seven husbands. Availability is strong (Tobit was widely read), and the shared number-seven serial-marriage motif suggests the deuterocanonical tale may color the construction of the test case.
sourceText: The same day it happened to Sarah the daughter of Raguel in Ecbatana of Media, that she also was reproached by her father’s maidservants; because that she had been given to seven husbands, and Asmodaeus the evil spirit killed them, before they had lain with her. And they said to her, “Do you not know that you strangle your husbands? You have had already seven husbands, and you haven’t borne the name of any one of them.

note: Daniel's promise that many who sleep in the dust will awake, and the wise will shine like the stars, is the clearest OT resurrection text and grounds the doctrine the Sadducees deny. Jesus' claim that the risen are 'like angels in heaven' coheres with Daniel's astral/angelic glorification of the righteous dead.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: Jesus charges the Sadducees with not knowing 'the power of God,' the same divine power that, per Genesis, makes the barren conceive and does what is humanly impossible. The 'power of God' that raises the dead resonates with the patriarchal narratives of God overriding natural limits, though the link is conceptual.
sourceText: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”

note: Jesus names the greatest commandment by quoting the Shema in full: 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength.' This is a formal, explicit citation of Israel's central confession, the pericope's anchor text.
sourceText: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: The second commandment, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' is quoted verbatim from the Holiness Code. Mark's pairing of Deuteronomy 6 and Leviticus 19 as the summary of the Law is a formal double citation that the scribe affirms.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: The scribe's approving gloss, 'he is one, and there is no other but he,' echoes Deuteronomy's monotheistic confession 'the Lord is God; there is no other besides him.' This buttresses the Shema's 'the Lord is one' with the classic Deuteronomic affirmation of God's uniqueness.
sourceText: It was shown to you so that you might know that Yahweh is God. There is no one else besides him.

note: Deutero-Isaiah's repeated 'there is no other God besides me' supplies the same monotheistic formula the scribe uses ('there is none other but he'). Given the recurrence of this oneness language across Deuteronomy and Isaiah, the scribe's confession may draw on the broader prophetic monotheism as well as the Shema.
sourceText: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me.

note: The scribe declares that loving God and neighbor is 'more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices,' echoing Samuel's rebuke that 'to obey is better than sacrifice.' The prioritizing of covenant love and obedience over cultic offering is a prophetic commonplace the scribe deliberately invokes.
sourceText: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.

note: Hosea's 'I desire mercy/steadfast love, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings' lies directly behind the scribe's ranking of love above 'whole burnt offerings.' The pairing of love-of-God with the relativizing of burnt offerings closely matches Hosea's formula.
sourceText: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

note: Micah's contrast between multiplied burnt offerings and the real requirement to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God supplies the same prophetic logic the scribe applies. It belongs to the recurrent prophetic critique that ethical love outweighs sacrifice, reinforcing the scribe's verdict.
sourceText: How shall I come before Yahweh, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will Yahweh be pleased with thousands of rams? With tens of thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience? The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

note: Joshua's exhortation to love the Lord, walk in his ways, and serve him 'with all your heart and all your soul' echoes the Shema's totalizing love-language that Jesus quotes. As a near-verbatim restatement of Deuteronomy's command, it shows the formula's currency but adds little beyond the primary citation.
sourceText: Only take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law which Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, to love Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”

note: Jesus quotes verbatim 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet,' attributing it to David 'in the Holy Spirit.' This is the pericope's formal citation, the entire argument about the Messiah being David's Lord turns on it.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: The premise that the Christ is 'the son of David' rests on the Davidic covenant promise that God will raise up David's offspring and be a father to him. The scribal expectation Jesus interrogates is generated by Nathan's oracle, making it the necessary background to the riddle even though it is not quoted.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
