note: The 'footstool' / subjugation-of-enemies-under-the-feet motif overlaps with Psalm 8's 'you have put all things under his feet.' The enthronement imagery of dominion beneath the feet belongs to a recurring royal/messianic cluster that interpreters frequently read alongside Psalm 110.
sourceText: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:

note: Jesus condemns scribes who 'devour widows' houses,' invoking the covenant's strict protection of widows: God hears the cry of any widow afflicted and his wrath burns against the oppressor. The exploitation of widows is precisely the sin the Torah threatens with divine vengeance, grounding the prophetic 'greater condemnation.'
sourceText: “You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child. If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.

note: Isaiah pronounces woe on those who make widows their prey and rob the needy of justice, the same predatory devouring of widows Jesus denounces. The prophetic woe-against-widow-plunderers tradition supplies both the indictment and the eschatological judgment Jesus announces.
sourceText: Woe to those who decree unrighteous decrees, and to the writers who write oppressive decrees; to deprive the needy from justice, and to rob the poor among my people of their rights, that widows may be their plunder, and that they may make the fatherless their prey!

note: The Torah's prohibition against perverting justice due the widow or taking her garment in pledge frames widows as the paradigmatic protected class. Jesus' charge that the scribes devour widows' houses presupposes this legal duty of care that they have inverted.
sourceText: You shall not deprive the foreigner or the fatherless of justice, nor take a widow’s clothing in pledge;

note: Malachi names those who oppress the widow among the wrongdoers God will swiftly judge. The pairing of widow-oppression with imminent divine reckoning parallels Jesus' 'these will receive greater condemnation,' reinforcing the prophetic-judgment frame.
sourceText: I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against the perjurers, and against those who oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and who deprive the foreigner of justice, and don’t fear me,” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Ben Sira insists God does not ignore the supplication of the widow nor her tears running down her cheek, and will repay her oppressor. This Second-Temple wisdom text, available to Mark's milieu, coheres with the indictment of those who profit from widows.
sourceText: He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall?

note: The poor widow who gives 'all that she had to live on' strongly recalls the widow of Zarephath who, at Elijah's word, spends her last handful of meal trusting God for provision. The shared figure of a destitute widow giving her entire remaining sustenance makes this the closest narrative analogue and likely a deliberate typological echo.
sourceText: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]

note: The treasury-offering setting and the contrast between giving from abundance versus giving all evoke the Torah's regulation of dedicated gifts and tithes. The widow's total gift outdoes proportional giving, implicitly measuring devotion against the cultic baseline of the tithe.
sourceText: “‘All the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is Yahweh’s. It is holy to Yahweh.

note: Deuteronomy's gleaning laws structurally cast the widow as a recipient of charity, not a donor; Mark inverts the expectation by showing the widow as giver, which heightens the pathos of her poverty against the Torah's assumption that widows need provision rather than provide it.
sourceText: When you reap your harvest in your field, and have forgotten a sheaf in the field, you shall not go again to get it. It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow; that Yahweh your God may bless you in all the work of your hands. When you beat your olive tree, you shall not go over the boughs again. It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow. When you harvest your vineyard, you shall not glean it after […]

note: The temple treasury chest where money was cast, established in Jehoiada's reform, is the institutional backdrop of the scene. Mark's 'treasury' and the act of casting coins into it presuppose this cultic apparatus, a faint but concrete OT realia echo.
sourceText: But Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one comes into Yahweh’s house: and the priests who kept the threshold put therein all the money that was brought into Yahweh’s house.

note: Jesus' oracle that not one stone of the temple will be left on another reprises the classic prophetic threat that Zion will be plowed as a field and the temple mount become a wooded height. Micah's word is itself remembered in Jeremiah 26:18 as a precedent for temple-doom prophecy, giving recurrence; the volume (a prophet announcing the sanctuary's ruin) is strong and the coherence with Jeremiah 7 below is tight.
sourceText: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.

note: Jeremiah's temple sermon threatens to make 'this house like Shiloh' and Jerusalem a curse, the OT template for a prophet predicting the sanctuary's destruction and being put on trial for it. Mark frames Jesus in exactly this Jeremianic role, and the temple-saying becomes evidence at his trial (Mark 14:58), so the figural coherence is high.
sourceText: then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.

note: The threat to do to 'this house which is called by my name' as was done to Shiloh undergirds the prediction that the great buildings will fall. Mark elsewhere quotes Jeremiah 7:11 ('den of robbers') at the temple cleansing, establishing recurrence of this chapter in the temple-confrontation narrative.
sourceText: therefore will I do to the house which is called by my name, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.

note: The disciples' marveling at 'what stones, what buildings' inverts Haggai's prophecy of glory for the rebuilt house ('stone laid upon stone'); Jesus' reversal of stone-on-stone may play against the temple-construction language of the post-exilic prophets. Faint and contested.
sourceText: Now, please consider from this day and backward, before a stone was laid on a stone in Yahweh’s temple.

note: The Deuteronomistic warning that if Israel forsakes the LORD 'this house will become a heap of ruins; everyone who passes will be appalled' supplies the covenantal logic for the temple's fall as judgment. Coherence with the prophetic temple-doom tradition is strong, though the specific 'stone on stone' idiom comes from Micah.
sourceText: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’

note: Jesus delivers the apocalyptic discourse seated on the Mount of Olives 'opposite the temple,' the very mountain where Zechariah says the LORD's feet will stand on the day of the LORD and the mount will split. The setting is freighted with eschatological geography, lending figural coherence to a discourse about the day of the LORD, though Mark does not cite the verse.
sourceText: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.

note: Ezekiel's glory of the LORD departs the doomed temple and halts on 'the mountain east of the city,' i.e., Olivet; Jesus pronouncing the temple's destruction from that same eastern mountain may echo the departure-of-the-glory motif. Faint and dependent on topographical identification.
sourceText: Yahweh’s glory went up from the midst of the city, and stood on the mountain which is on the east side of the city.

note: The disciples' double question — 'when will these things be, and what is the sign that all is about to be accomplished?' — closely tracks Daniel's question to the man clothed in linen, 'how long until the end of these wonders?' and the answer measuring the time of the end. Mark's eschatological timetable is structured by Daniel 12, giving this opening question strong Danielic coherence.
sourceText: One said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, How long shall it be to the end of these wonders? I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be […]

note: Daniel's 'I will tell you what will happen at the latter end of the indignation, for it pertains to the appointed time of the end' parallels the disciples' request to be told the sign of the consummation. The vocabulary of an 'appointed time of the end' shapes the whole discourse.
sourceText: He said, Behold, I will make you know what shall be in the latter time of the indignation; for it belongs to the appointed time of the end.

note: 'These things must happen' (Greek dei genesthai) verbally echoes Daniel 2:28 LXX, 'what must come to pass in the latter days,' the programmatic statement of apocalyptic necessity. Mark adopts Daniel's deterministic 'must' to frame the wars and disasters as the divinely fixed sequence before the end.
sourceText: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:

note: 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom' closely reproduces Isaiah's oracle, 'I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians... kingdom against kingdom.' The paired idiom of nation/kingdom conflict is distinctive enough (high volume) to mark deliberate use of Isaiah's day-of-the-LORD imagery of internecine collapse.
sourceText: I will stir up the Egyptians against the Egyptians, and they will fight everyone against his brother, and everyone against his neighbor; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.

note: 'Nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every distress' supplies the same nation-against-nation formula combined with God-sent 'trouble,' matching Mark's 'troubles.' The Chronicler's portrait of God-ordained civil chaos coheres with the apocalyptic catalogue.
sourceText: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.

note: 'The beginning of birth pains' draws on Isaiah's day-of-the-LORD oracle against Babylon where men are 'in anguish like a woman in labor.' Birth-pang imagery for eschatological tribulation is a recurrent prophetic topos (Isaiah 26:17; Jeremiah 22:23; Hosea 13:13), and Isaiah 13 also supplies the cosmic darkening cluster echoed later in 13:24, strengthening coherence.
sourceText: They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame.

note: 'Like a woman with child... cries out in her pangs, so were we before you, O LORD' is part of the proto-apocalyptic Isaiah Apocalypse (chs. 24-27) that supplies Mark with resurrection-and-tribulation imagery. The labor-pang figure for the people's distress before deliverance coheres tightly with Mark's 'beginning of birth pains.'
sourceText: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh.

note: 'How you will groan when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor' applies the birth-pang figure specifically to Jerusalem/Judah's coming judgment, the very referent of Mark 13. The recurrence of the labor metaphor across the prophets for the city's doom supports its presence here.
sourceText: Inhabitant of Lebanon, who makes your nest in the cedars, how greatly to be pitied you will be when pangs come on you, the pain as of a woman in travail!

note: 'The pangs of childbirth come for him' as an image of Ephraim's crisis adds to the prophetic stock of birth-pang imagery behind Mark's phrase. Faint, included for recurrence within the tradition rather than distinctive verbal contact.
sourceText: The sorrows of a travailing woman will come on him. He is an unwise son; for when it is time, he doesn’t come to the opening of the womb.

note: The warning 'do not be led astray' by 'many who come in my name' echoes Deuteronomy's law against the prophet or dream-diviner who arises to 'lead you astray' (LXX planao) from the LORD. The same planao verb and the testing-of-Israel motif recur in 13:22, indicating Deuteronomy 13 as a structuring subtext for the deception warnings.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.

note: 'Wonders in the heavens and on the earth' before the day of the LORD lies behind the catalogue of cosmic and terrestrial signs (wars, earthquakes); Joel is quoted heavily in early Christian eschatology and resurfaces in Mark's darkening of sun and moon in 13:24. Faint here, marked for recurrence.
sourceText: I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: 'I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land, and all nations' supplies a prophetic precedent for cosmic-political upheaval (kingdoms, shaking) preceding the end. The 'shaking' language returns in 13:25 ('powers shaken'), giving the cluster coherence.
sourceText: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land; and I will shake all nations. The precious things of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Daniel's little horn that 'wears out the saints of the Most High' for an appointed time supplies the apocalyptic pattern of the faithful handed over to persecuting authorities before vindication. Mark's councils, beatings, and kings before whom believers stand instantiate the saints' tribulation under hostile rulers, a Danielic frame the discourse repeatedly invokes.
sourceText: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.

note: 'Brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child; children will rise against parents' is a near-verbatim use of Micah 7:6, 'the son treats the father with contempt... a man's enemies are the men of his own household.' The family-rending of the eschatological crisis is drawn directly from Micah's lament over a society in moral collapse; high volume and distinctiveness.
sourceText: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.

note: 'The gospel must first be preached to all the nations' draws on the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth,' the Isaianic universalism behind the worldwide proclamation. The 'must' (eschatological necessity) plus the nations theme coheres with Isaiah's mission oracles.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: The mandate that the good news be proclaimed 'to all the nations' echoes the dominion given to the one like a son of man, that 'all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him.' Since Mark 13:26 explicitly invokes Daniel 7:13, the universal-nations note here likely draws on the same vision's worldwide scope.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'I will speak of your testimonies before kings and not be ashamed' faintly parallels standing 'before rulers and kings... for a testimony.' The righteous-sufferer-before-rulers motif is diffuse in the Psalter; low confidence, included for the testimony-before-kings overlap.
sourceText: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.

note: The promise 'do not be anxious what you will say... it is not you who speak but the Holy Spirit' echoes the LORD's commission to Jeremiah, 'do not say I am only a youth... I have put my words in your mouth,' the prophetic-inspiration topos. The assurance of divinely given speech before hostile powers follows the call-narrative pattern.
sourceText: But Yahweh said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak. Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh. Then Yahweh stretched out his hand, and touched my mouth; and Yahweh said to me, “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.

note: 'I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak' is the foundational promise of God-supplied speech for a reluctant messenger, directly behind 'say whatever is given you in that hour.' The Moses-commissioning of inspired speech reinforces the Jeremiah parallel.
sourceText: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”

note: 'He who endures to the end will be saved' resonates with Daniel's beatitude on the one who waits and reaches the end of the days ('blessed is he who waits... you shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days'). The endurance-to-the-end-yields-deliverance logic is Danielic apocalyptic, coherent with Mark's framework.
sourceText: Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days. But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.

note: Daniel's promise that 'your people shall be delivered, everyone found written in the book' stands behind the eschatological 'will be saved.' The deliverance of the faithful remnant through the unequaled tribulation (cited explicitly at 13:19) frames the salvation of the endurer here.
sourceText: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.

note: 'The abomination of desolation' is a formal citation, named as 'spoken of by Daniel the prophet.' Daniel 9:27's 'abomination that makes desolate' upon the wing of the temple is the source phrase; Mark's masculine participle 'standing where it ought not' personalizes the desolator. The highest-volume Danielic anchor of the discourse.
sourceText: He shall make a firm covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease; and on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate; and even to the full end, and that determined, shall wrath be poured out on the desolate.

note: Daniel 11:31's forces that 'profane the temple... and set up the abomination that makes desolate' supplies the historical referent (Antiochus' altar to Zeus) reapplied to a future profanation. Mark's 'standing where it ought not' (i.e., in the holy place) directly tracks this temple-desecration sense.
sourceText: Forces shall stand on his part, and they shall profane the sanctuary, even the fortress, and shall take away the continual burnt offering, and they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.

note: Daniel 12:11 dates 'the abomination that makes desolate set up' to the countdown of the end (1,290 days), tying the phrase to the eschatological timetable Mark is expounding. The recurrence of the exact phrase across Daniel 9, 11, and 12 underwrites Mark's explicit appeal to 'Daniel the prophet.'
sourceText: From the time that the continual burnt offering shall be taken away, and the abomination that makes desolate set up, there shall be one thousand two hundred ninety days.

note: 1 Maccabees 1:54 narrates the fulfillment of Daniel, 'they erected a desolating sacrilege on the altar of burnt offering,' giving the concrete Second-Temple referent for the phrase. As a deuterocanonical witness to how 'abomination of desolation' was understood, it supplies the interpretive backdrop ('let the reader understand') for Mark's reuse.
sourceText: And on the fifteenth day of Chislev, in the hundred and forty and fifth year, they built an abomination of desolation upon the altar, and in the cities of Judah on every side they built idol altars.

note: 'Mattathias and his sons fled to the mountains' at the persecution provides the precise precedent for 'let those in Judea flee to the mountains.' The Maccabean flight from the desolating sacrilege is the paradigmatic response Mark commands, making this a strong situational echo within the same desolation script.
sourceText: And he and his sons fled into the mountains, and forsook all that they had in the city.

note: 'Flee to the mountains... do not look back, do not stop' (the angels to Lot at Sodom) underlies the urgent flight commands — not going back from the roof or field for possessions. The Sodom-escape pattern of immediate, possession-abandoning flight before judgment coheres with Mark's instructions (cf. Luke's explicit 'remember Lot's wife').
sourceText: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”

note: 'Tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of creation... and never will be' closely renders Daniel 12:1, 'a time of trouble such as never has been since there was a nation till that time.' The unequaled-distress formula is distinctive and explicitly Danielic, the climactic tribulation before the deliverance of the elect.
sourceText: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.

note: Joel's day of the LORD is 'a day of darkness... such as has never been from of old, nor will be again after,' an unequaled-day formula parallel to Daniel 12:1 and reused by Mark. Joel supplies both the superlative-distress idiom and (in 2:10, 31) the sun-moon darkening cluster Mark deploys at 13:24, strengthening coherence.
sourceText: A day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness. As the dawn spreading on the mountains, a great and strong people; there has never been the like, neither will there be any more after them, even to the years of many generations.

note: 'A great cry... such as there has never been, nor ever will be again' (the plague of the firstborn) is an early instance of the unequaled-event formula that Daniel and Joel inherit. Faint, included as the deep background of the 'never before, never again' superlative.
sourceText: There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has not been, nor shall be any more.

note: The shortening of the days 'for the sake of the elect, whom he chose' resonates with Isaiah's promise to preserve a remnant 'for my servants' sake, that I may not destroy them all.' The mercy-for-the-chosen logic that mitigates total destruction parallels Mark's 'unless the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh would be saved.'
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, “As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one says, ‘Don’t destroy it, for a blessing is in it:’ so will I do for my servants’ sake, that I may not destroy them all. I will bring a seed out of Jacob, and out of Judah an inheritor of my mountains; and my chosen shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there.

note: 1 Enoch speaks of the days being shortened/disordered in the time of the sinners, a Second-Temple apocalyptic motif of cosmic time foreshortened in the last crisis. The pseudepigraphal parallel to 'he shortened the days' suggests a shared apocalyptic idiom rather than direct dependence; marked contested.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: 'False prophets will arise and show signs and wonders to lead astray' reproduces Deuteronomy's test: the prophet who 'gives a sign or wonder' and it comes to pass, yet leads you after other gods, is testing whether you love the LORD. The pairing of 'signs and wonders' with seductive false prophecy and the verb 'lead astray' (planao) is distinctively Deuteronomic.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.

note: Deuteronomy's verdict that such a prophet has 'spoken to lead you astray from the LORD your God' underlies Mark's 'that they may lead astray, if possible, even the elect.' The danger to even the faithful elect echoes the law's concern that the whole community could be seduced by validated false signs.
sourceText: That prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death, because he has spoken rebellion against Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to draw you aside out of the way which Yahweh your God commanded you to walk in. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.

note: The law on the presumptuous prophet who speaks in the LORD's name without commission supplements the false-prophet warning. Less verbally specific than Deuteronomy 13, included for the recurrent false-prophet legislation behind Mark's 'false christs and false prophets.'
sourceText: But the prophet who speaks a word presumptuously in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.” You may say in your heart, “How shall we know the word which Yahweh has not spoken?” When a prophet speaks in Yahweh’s name, if the thing doesn’t follow, nor happen, that is the thing which Yahweh has not spoken. The prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You shall not be afraid of him.

note: Jeremiah's polemic against prophets who 'have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying peace, peace, when there is no peace' supplies the prophetic stock of deceiving prophets in a doomed Jerusalem. Faint and thematic rather than verbal; coheres with Mark's setting of false messianic claims amid the city's crisis.
sourceText: “For from their least even to their greatest, everyone is given to covetousness; and from the prophet even to the priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed also the hurt of my people superficially, saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ when there is no peace.

note: 'The sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light' is near-verbatim from Isaiah 13:10, 'the sun will be dark at its rising and the moon will not shed its light,' the day-of-the-LORD oracle against Babylon. The catastrophic dimming of the luminaries is the lead element of Mark's cosmic-collapse cluster; highest volume in the constellation.
sourceText: For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.

note: 'The stars will be falling from heaven and the powers of the heavens will be shaken' draws on Isaiah 34:4, 'all the host of heaven shall rot away, the skies roll up like a scroll, all their host fall.' Mark's falling stars and shaken heavenly powers reproduce Isaiah's cosmic-judgment imagery (LXX 'the powers of the heavens shall melt').
sourceText: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.

note: 'The sun and moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining' (also 2:31, 3:15) is a primary source for Mark's three-element luminary collapse. Joel's day-of-the-LORD theophany combines earth-quaking, heaven-trembling, and darkened sun/moon/stars, matching Mark's whole cluster and reinforcing the multiply-attested character of the imagery.
sourceText: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.

note: Ezekiel's lament over Pharaoh: 'I will cover the heavens and darken their stars; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of heaven I will darken,' supplies the exact 'moon shall not give its light' phrase Mark shares with Isaiah 13. A fourth witness in the darkening cluster, demonstrating Hays' recurrence.
sourceText: When I shall extinguish you, I will cover the heavens, and make its stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of the sky will I make dark over you, and set darkness on your land, says the Lord Yahweh.

note: 'They will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory' directly cites Daniel 7:13, 'one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven.' This is the christological centerpiece of the discourse; Mark adds 'power and glory' from the dominion granted in 7:14, and the title 'Son of Man' is the load-bearing self-designation throughout Mark.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: 'With great power and glory' renders the gift to the son of man of 'dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples should serve him.' Mark fuses 7:13's coming-on-clouds with 7:14's enthronement glory, so the Son of Man's parousia carries the universal dominion of Daniel's vision.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'Gather the elect from the four winds' echoes Zechariah 2:6, 'I have spread you abroad as the four winds of heaven, declares the LORD,' a regathering-of-the-dispersed oracle. The eschatological ingathering of the scattered people from the four winds is the conceptual core of Mark's angelic harvest of the elect.
sourceText: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.

note: 'If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the LORD will gather you' undergirds gathering the elect 'from the ends of the earth to the ends of the sky.' Deuteronomy's covenant promise of regathering the exiled from the extremities of earth and heaven matches Mark's double horizon precisely.
sourceText: If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of the heavens, from there Yahweh your God will gather you, and from there he will bring you back.

note: Isaiah's promise that the LORD will 'assemble the banished of Israel and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth' supplies the messianic-age ingathering behind Mark's gathering of the elect. The 'four corners/four winds' regathering is a recurrent restoration motif, here applied to the Son of Man's harvest.
sourceText: It will happen in that day that the Lord will set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant that is left of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

note: 'A great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost... will come and worship the LORD' from the Isaiah Apocalypse provides the trumpet-summoned ingathering of the scattered; Matthew's parallel makes the trumpet explicit. Mark's angelic gathering coheres with this Isaianic regathering even without naming the trumpet.
sourceText: It will happen in that day that a great trumpet will be blown; and those who were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and those who were outcasts in the land of Egypt, shall come; and they will worship Yahweh in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

note: 'They will look on him whom they have pierced' and the mourning of the tribes lies behind 'they will see the Son of Man'; the seeing-and-mourning at the coming one is more explicit in Matthew 24:30 and Revelation 1:7 but may color Mark's 'they will see.' Faint in Mark, marked contested.
sourceText: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn. In that day there will be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon. The land will mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of […]
lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son. In that day the lamentation in Jerusalem shall be very great, as the mourning for the pomegranate grove cut down in the plain. And the land shall lament in separate families, the […]

note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him' parallels the Son of Man sending out his angels at the parousia. The accompanying-holy-ones motif of the day of the LORD coheres with Mark's angelic retinue; included for recurrence of the Zecharianic day-of-the-LORD material in this pericope.
sourceText: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*

note: 'He makes the clouds his chariot, riding on the wings of the wind' is part of the OT cloud-rider theophany tradition (cf. Isaiah 19:1; Psalm 18:9-12) that informs the Son of Man's coming 'in clouds.' The divine-prerogative of cloud-borne arrival lends figural weight to Daniel 7's cloud-coming as Mark applies it.
sourceText: He lays the beams of his rooms in the waters. He makes the clouds his chariot. He walks on the wings of the wind.

note: The fig-tree parable ('the fig tree puts forth... you know summer is near') faintly recalls Joel's restoration imagery, 'the fig tree and vine give their full yield,' as a sign-bearing tree marking the season's turn. The fig tree elsewhere in Mark (11:13-21) carries judgment symbolism; here its budding signals nearness, a season-discernment topos. Contested.
sourceText: Don’t be afraid, you animals of the field; for the pastures of the wilderness spring up, for the tree bears its fruit. The fig tree and the vine yield their strength.

note: 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away' draws on Isaiah 51:6, 'the heavens will vanish like smoke, the earth wear out like a garment... but my salvation will be forever.' The contrast between the perishing cosmos and the enduring divine word is distinctively Isaianic and high in volume.
sourceText: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.

note: 'The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever' is the closest source for the permanence of God's word over against transient creation. Mark transfers the abiding-word of Isaiah 40 to 'my words,' an implicit christological claim; the verbal contrast (pass away / not pass away vs. wither / stand forever) is strong.
sourceText: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”

note: 'They will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment... but you are the same' grounds 'heaven and earth will pass away.' The Psalm's contrast of the perishable heavens-and-earth with the unchanging LORD supplies the theological warrant Mark applies to the abiding word.
sourceText: Of old, you laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same. Your years will have no end.

note: 'All the host of heaven shall rot away and the skies roll up like a scroll' reinforces 'heaven and earth will pass away,' connecting this declaration to the cosmic-dissolution imagery already cited at 13:25. Recurrence of Isaiah 34 across the discourse supports its faint presence here.
sourceText: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.

note: 'All these things' coming to pass before 'this generation' passes resonates with Daniel's assurance that 'the saints shall receive the kingdom... forever, forever and ever'; the certainty that the decreed events will be accomplished is Danielic. Faint, included for the apocalyptic guarantee that frames 'most certainly I say.'
sourceText: But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.

note: 'A unique day... known to the LORD' on which the timing is hidden faintly parallels 'of that day or hour no one knows... but only the Father.' Zechariah's day-of-the-LORD whose timing belongs to God alone coheres with Mark's reservation of the hour to the Father; contested.
sourceText: It will be a unique day which is known to Yahweh; not day, and not night; but it will come to pass, that at evening time there will be light.

note: Daniel is told 'the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end' — the timing of the consummation is withheld even from the seer. Mark's 'no one knows the day or hour' continues this Danielic concealment of the appointed time, the necessary counterpart to the timetable expounded throughout the chapter.
sourceText: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished. I heard, but I didn’t understand: then I said, my lord, what shall be the issue of these things? He said, Go your way, […]

note: The watchman who stations himself to keep watch (2:1) and the vision that 'awaits its appointed time... if it seems slow, wait for it' (2:3) supplies the watching-for-a-delayed-coming posture behind the doorkeeper commanded to keep watch and the repeated 'watch.' The waiting-watchman for an appointed-yet-delayed arrival is the Habakkuk pattern.
sourceText: I will stand at my watch, and set myself on the ramparts, and will look out to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer concerning my complaint. Yahweh answered me, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it. For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.

note: 'Go, set a watchman... he calls, Upon a watchtower I stand continually by day, and at my post whole nights' provides the prophetic figure of the sentinel keeping watch through the night-watches. Mark's doorkeeper told to 'keep watch' and the listing of evening/midnight/cockcrow/morning watches draw on this watchman tradition.
sourceText: For the Lord said to me, “Go, set a watchman. Let him declare what he sees. When he sees a troop, horsemen in pairs, a troop of donkeys, a troop of camels, he shall listen diligently with great attentiveness.” He cried like a lion: “Lord, I stand continually on the watchtower in the daytime, and every night I stay at my post.

note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple' parallels the master who returns 'suddenly,' lest he find the servants sleeping. The sudden, unannounced arrival of the lord coheres with Malachi's suddenly-coming Lord; faint and contested, but Malachi is a recurrent source in Mark.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Ezekiel's watchman charged with sounding the alarm and held accountable if he fails to keep watch supplies the responsibility-of-the-sentinel theme behind 'commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch.' Faint relative to Isaiah 21 and Habakkuk 2; included for the recurrent watchman motif.
sourceText: Son of man, speak to the children of your people, and tell them, When I bring the sword on a land, and the people of the land take a man from among them, and set him for their watchman; if, when he sees the sword come on the land, he blow the trumpet, and warn the people; then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet, and doesn’t take warning, if the sword come, and take him away, his blood shall be on his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet, and […]

note: The parable of the man who goes abroad, leaves his house, and assigns each servant authority over his work faintly recalls the trusted-steward-over-an-absent-master's-household pattern (e.g., Joseph over Potiphar's house). A diffuse OT household-management topos rather than a specific text; low confidence.
sourceText: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.

note: The four night-watches (evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning) draw on the OT/Second-Temple reckoning of the night's divisions; Proverbs' 'in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness' attests the watch-segmented night. Marked contested as a cultural-temporal echo rather than a quoted text.
sourceText: in the twilight, in the evening of the day, in the middle of the night and in the darkness. Behold, there a woman met him with the attire of a prostitute, and with crafty intent.

note: Mark times the whole Passion by 'the Passover and the unleavened bread,' invoking the foundational deliverance festival of Exodus 12 as the calendrical and theological frame. The recurrence of Passover language across the chapter (vv. 1, 12, 14, 16) raises the volume, and the coherence is total since Mark presents Jesus' death as a new exodus. The availability is secure as the institution narrative of Israel's central feast.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]

note: The chief priests and scribes who 'sought how they might seize him by deception, and kill him' enact the rulers who 'take counsel together against the Lord and against his anointed.' Mark has already cited Psalm 2 at the baptism, so recurrence supports a faint conspiratorial echo, though there is no verbal quotation here.
sourceText: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,

note: The plot to take Jesus' life 'by deception' resonates with the lament psalmist's complaint that his enemies 'scheme together against me, plotting to take my life.' The motif of conspiratorial counsel against the righteous sufferer belongs to the psalmic matrix Mark draws on throughout the Passion, but the link is thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: For I have heard the slander of many, terror on every side, while they conspire together against me, they plot to take away my life.

note: Jesus' saying 'you always have the poor with you' reproduces Deuteronomy's declaration that 'the poor will never cease out of the land,' which grounds the command to open one's hand to the needy. The verbal volume is high and the coherence sharp: Jesus does not dismiss the poor but cites the very text that mandates perpetual generosity, contrasting that standing obligation with the unrepeatable moment of his own burial.
sourceText: For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.

note: The woman's costly nard (nardos) poured on the reclining Jesus closely matches the bride's line, 'while the king sat at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.' The rare term nard and the banquet setting give real verbal volume, and the figural reading of the beloved anointing the king coheres with Mark's messianic scene, though Mark does not cite it.
sourceText: While the king sat at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance.

note: The pouring of oil over the head as an act that designates a king (Jehu anointed by Elisha's servant) supplies background for reading this anointing as royal/messianic. The connection is conceptual, drawing on Israel's anointing rites generally rather than a specific verbal parallel.
sourceText: Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets, and said to him, “Put your belt on your waist, take this vial of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth Gilead. When you come there, find Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi, and go in, and make him arise up from among his brothers, and carry him to an inner room. Then take the vial of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, ‘Thus says Yahweh, “I have anointed you king over Israel.”’ Then […]

note: Samuel pouring a flask of oil on Saul's head and kissing him as the Lord's anointed offers the paradigmatic royal anointing on the head that Mark's scene quietly evokes (Christos = 'anointed'). The echo is thematic, suggesting kingship, with no direct verbal borrowing.
sourceText: Then Samuel took the vial of oil, and poured it on his head, and kissed him, and said, “Isn’t it that Yahweh has anointed you to be prince over his inheritance?

note: Jesus interprets the anointing as preparation 'for the burying,' resonating with Israelite burial customs of anointing the dead with spices, as at Asa's funeral with its bed of spices. This supplies the cultural background for the burial reading, though it is a custom-echo rather than a cited text.
sourceText: They buried him in his own tombs, which he had dug out for himself in the city of David, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odors and various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumers’ art: and they made a very great burning for him.

note: Judas going to the priests who 'promised to give him money' to deliver Jesus evokes the shepherd-prophecy where the people 'weighed out thirty pieces of silver' as the price of the rejected shepherd. Mark, unlike Matthew, does not specify the sum, so the volume is lower, but the motif of betraying the shepherd for a priced payment coheres with Mark's shepherd-citation in v. 27.
sourceText: I said to them, “If you think it best, give me my wages; and if not, keep them.” So they weighed for my wages thirty pieces of silver.

note: The intimate associate who turns to hand Jesus over begins the betrayed-friend motif that Mark develops at the table (v. 18); Psalm 41's 'my close friend who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me' is the controlling subtext. Here the link is anticipatory and thematic, with the verbal force concentrated in the meal scene that follows.
sourceText: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

note: Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor who defected to Absalom, is the classic Old Testament type of the intimate betrayer, traditionally paired with Psalm 41 in readings of treachery against the anointed. Judas' defection coheres with this Ahithophel pattern, though the echo is typological rather than verbal.
sourceText: Someone told David, saying, “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” David said, “Yahweh, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”

note: The disciples prepare 'on the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover,' directly enacting Exodus 12's prescription that the lamb be killed at twilight on the appointed day. The volume is high and the coherence total as Mark stages the Last Supper as a Passover meal, drawing the institution narrative into the Passion frame.
sourceText: and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening.

note: The instruction to 'prepare' the Passover and to eat it in a guest room invokes the Exodus regulation that the lamb be eaten roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs that same night. The preparatory action presupposes the full Exodus rubric, supplying the meal's content even where Mark abbreviates.
sourceText: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.

note: Jesus' detailed prediction that the disciples will meet a man carrying a water jar who leads them to a prepared place mirrors Samuel's sequence of precise sign-predictions to Saul ('you will meet... you will come... you will find'). The form of foreknown encounters fulfilled to the letter resonates, though there is no verbal citation.
sourceText: When you have departed from me today, then you shall find two men by Rachel’s tomb, in the border of Benjamin at Zelzah; and they will tell you, ‘The donkeys which you went to seek have been found; and behold, your father has stopped caring about the donkeys, and is anxious for you, saying, “What shall I do for my son?”’ “Then you shall go on forward from there, and you shall come to the oak of Tabor; and three men shall meet you there going up to God to […]

note: Jesus' words 'one of you will betray me—he who eats with me' and 'he who dips with me in the dish' draw their pathos directly from 'my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.' The shared scene of table fellowship turned to treachery gives high coherence, and the deliberate emphasis on shared eating supplies strong verbal volume for this load-bearing subtext.
sourceText: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

note: The lament over betrayal by 'a man my equal, my companion and familiar friend, with whom I kept pleasant company... in the house of God' parallels the intimate-betrayer motif of the meal. Its recurrence alongside Psalm 41 in the suffering-righteous tradition makes it a strong secondary subtext for the betrayed table-companion.
sourceText: For it was not an enemy who insulted me, then I could have endured it. Neither was it he who hated me who raised himself up against me, then I would have hidden myself from him. But it was you, a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend. We took sweet fellowship together. We walked in God’s house with company.

note: Jesus' self-designation 'the Son of Man goes, even as it is written about him' presupposes the scriptural Son-of-Man figure that Mark will name explicitly in v. 62, framing his death as the destined path of that figure. The phrase 'as it is written' signals a scriptural script even though no single text is quoted, with Daniel 7 as the governing Son-of-Man matrix.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: The notion that 'the Son of Man goes as it is written' — a suffering and death foreordained in Scripture — coheres with the Servant who is led to slaughter according to God's purpose. Mark gives no quotation here, but the Servant Song is a leading candidate for the scriptural 'writing' about the Son of Man's fated suffering.
sourceText: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth. He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people? They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he […]

note: 'This is my blood of the covenant' formally echoes Moses' words at Sinai, 'Behold the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you,' as he dashes sacrificial blood on the people. The verbal correspondence (haima tes diathekes) is exact and the coherence high: Jesus enacts a covenant-ratifying blood rite that recapitulates and surpasses Sinai. This is the load-bearing intertext of the cup-word.
sourceText: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”

note: The blood 'poured out for many' draws on the Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and 'bore the sin of many,' where the rare 'many' (rabbim/polloi) language is distinctively Isaianic. The combination of pouring-out unto death and vicarious 'for many' gives strong volume and coheres with Mark's ransom saying at 10:45, making Isaiah 53 a controlling subtext.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: The covenant sealed in Jesus' blood evokes Jeremiah's promised 'new covenant' that the Lord will make with the house of Israel, written on the heart. Even in Mark's shorter 'blood of the covenant' reading, the eschatological covenant-renewal theme makes Jeremiah 31 a natural subtext; the explicit 'new' is firmer in the parallel traditions, lowering the volume slightly here.
sourceText: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:

note: Zechariah's 'because of the blood of my covenant with you, I will set your prisoners free' joins covenant-blood to eschatological release, matching Jesus' cup-word that looks ahead to the Kingdom (v. 25). The shared phrase 'blood of the covenant' in a deliverance context makes this a plausible secondary allusion within the same covenant-blood cluster.
sourceText: As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I have set free your prisoners from the pit in which is no water.

note: Within a Passover meal, the saving power of the lamb's blood smeared on the doorposts stands behind the cup of Jesus' blood that delivers 'many.' The Passover-blood and covenant-blood motifs fuse in Mark's scene, so Exodus 12 supplies the festal-blood resonance alongside the explicit Sinai citation.
sourceText: They shall take some of the blood, and put it on the two door posts and on the lintel, on the houses in which they shall eat it.

note: Jacob's blessing of Judah, who 'washes his garments in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes,' was read messianically in Second-Temple tradition and links wine, blood, and the coming ruler. Jesus' 'fruit of the vine' and 'blood' in a kingdom-context may faintly evoke this royal vine-and-blood imagery, though the connection is associative.
sourceText: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.

note: Jesus' vow to drink the fruit of the vine 'anew in the Kingdom of God' evokes the eschatological banquet on Zion where the Lord makes 'a feast of well-aged wines' for all peoples. The messianic-feast horizon coheres with Mark's kingdom-cup, supplying the festal-wine background for the eschatological pledge.
sourceText: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.

note: The promise that in the restored kingdom 'the mountains shall drip sweet wine' and replanted vineyards yield abundance supports the eschatological vine-imagery of Jesus' pledge to drink anew in the Kingdom. The link is thematic, part of the prophetic vision of restored vintage in the age to come.
sourceText: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the one treading grapes him who sows seed; and sweet wine will drip from the mountains, and flow from the hills. I will bring my people Israel back from captivity, and they will rebuild the ruined cities, and inhabit them; and they will plant vineyards, and drink wine from them. They shall also make gardens, and eat their fruit.

note: 'When they had sung a hymn' refers to the Hallel psalms sung at Passover, the fixed liturgical conclusion of the seder. The volume rests on established liturgical practice rather than a quoted line, but the coherence is strong: Mark places the praise of God's deliverance on Jesus' lips immediately before Gethsemane, and Psalm 118 in particular (already cited at 12:10-11 and the triumphal entry) frames his approaching vindication.
sourceText: Praise Yah! Praise, you servants of Yahweh, praise Yahweh’s name. Blessed be Yahweh’s name, from this time forward and forever more. From the rising of the sun to the going down of the same, Yahweh’s name is to be praised. Yahweh is high above all nations, his glory above the heavens. Who is like Yahweh, our God, who has his seat on high, Who stoops down to see in heaven and in the earth? He raises up the poor out of the dust. Lifts up the needy from the […]

note: Jesus going out to the Mount of Olives in the night of betrayal evokes David ascending the Mount of Olives weeping as he flees Absalom's conspiracy, with Ahithophel's treachery in view. The geographical and situational parallel (the anointed crossing Olivet amid betrayal) supports a faint Davidic typology.
sourceText: David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and wept as he went up; and he had his head covered, and went barefoot: and all the people who were with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up.

note: The Mount of Olives is the site where, in Zechariah, the Lord's feet stand on the day of eschatological battle and deliverance. Mark's repeated staging of decisive moments on Olivet (chs. 11, 13, 14) may quietly trade on this prophetic geography, though the link is locational rather than verbal.
sourceText: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.

note: Mark introduces with 'it is written' and quotes 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered,' a formal citation of Zechariah's sword-against-the-shepherd oracle. The volume is maximal and the coherence total: God himself strikes the shepherd, the disciples are the scattered flock, and the surrounding Zecharian context (the refining of the remnant) frames the Passion. Mark adapts the verb to a divine-passive/first-person form fitting his theology.
sourceText: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.

note: Ezekiel's image of the flock 'scattered because there is no shepherd,' wandering over the mountains, reinforces the shepherd-and-sheep motif of the citation. Mark elsewhere casts the crowds as sheep without a shepherd (6:34), so this prophetic scattered-flock tradition coheres strongly and supplies depth to the Zechariah quotation.
sourceText: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.

note: The continuation of the struck-shepherd oracle — the remnant passed through fire, refined, and restored as God's people — coheres with Jesus' immediate promise of restoration after he is 'raised up' (v. 28). Reading the quotation in its Zecharian context illuminates the scattering-then-regathering pattern Mark builds into Peter's failure and recovery.
sourceText: It shall happen that in all the land,” says Yahweh, “two parts in it will be cut off and die; but the third will be left in it. I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”

note: The shepherd-flock imagery and the dark valley of the night's events faintly evoke the shepherd psalm, though here the shepherd is struck rather than protecting. The connection is associative within the broader shepherd motif rather than a cited parallel.
sourceText: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.

note: Jesus' words 'My soul is exceedingly sorrowful' closely echo the refrain 'Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me?' of the downcast psalmist. The verbal correspondence (perilypos / he psyche mou) is strong, and the coherence is high: Mark voices Gethsemane's anguish in the idiom of the lament psalms, casting Jesus as the suffering-yet-hoping righteous one.
sourceText: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him for the saving help of his presence. My God, my soul is in despair within me. Therefore I remember you from the land of the Jordan, the heights of Hermon, from the hill Mizar.

note: The repeated refrain 'Why are you cast down, O my soul?' continues into Psalm 43, the twin lament of 42, and undergirds Jesus' 'my soul is sorrowful even to death.' Its recurrence as a fixed refrain strengthens the allusion, and the psalmist's longing for God's deliverance coheres with Jesus' prayer that the hour might pass.
sourceText: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him: my Savior, my helper, and my God.

note: The third occurrence of the cast-down-soul refrain reinforces that Mark frames Jesus' sorrow through this specific psalmic complaint. The triple repetition across Psalms 42-43 mirrors the threefold prayer of Gethsemane, deepening the recurrence and coherence of the allusion.
sourceText: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him, the saving help of my countenance, and my God.

note: Jonah's 'I am angry enough to die' (lit. 'sorrowful unto death') supplies a verbal precedent for Jesus being grieved 'even to death.' The phrase 'unto death' as an intensifier of grief makes this a plausible secondary verbal echo, though Jonah's resentment differs sharply from Jesus' obedient sorrow.
sourceText: God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the vine?” He said, “I am right to be angry, even to death.”

note: Jesus' plea 'remove this cup from me' draws on the prophetic 'cup' of God's wrath and judgment, here Psalm 75's cup of foaming wine that the wicked must drink to the dregs. The metaphor of drinking a divinely appointed cup of suffering gives real volume and coheres with Mark's earlier cup-saying (10:38-39).
sourceText: For in the hand of Yahweh there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.

note: Isaiah's 'cup of his wrath,' the 'cup of staggering' that Jerusalem has drunk to the dregs, is a leading source for the cup Jesus prays to have removed. The strong prophetic-cup tradition of divine judgment-wine coheres with Jesus drinking the cup on behalf of the 'many,' reinforcing the wrath-cup reading.
sourceText: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.

note: Jeremiah's cup of wrath, which the nations must drink at God's hand, belongs to the same prophetic cluster that informs Jesus' 'cup.' Its recurrence across the prophets establishes the cup as a fixed symbol of appointed judgment, supporting the figural reading of Gethsemane's prayer.
sourceText: For thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, to me: take this cup of the wine of wrath at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it. They shall drink, and reel back and forth, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them. Then took I the cup at Yahweh’s hand, and made all the nations to drink, to whom Yahweh had sent me: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and its kings, and its princes, to make them a desolation, an […]

note: The saying 'the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak' resonates with the penitential psalm's prayer for a willing/steadfast spirit ('uphold me with a willing spirit'). The spirit-versus-weak-flesh contrast may draw on this psalmic anthropology, though the link is conceptual rather than a direct citation.
sourceText: Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me with a willing spirit.

note: The agonized obedience of the son who submits to the father's will ('not what I desire, but what you desire') faintly recalls the Aqedah, where Abraham obeys God's command to offer his beloved son. The figural resonance of obedient surrender of a son's life coheres with Mark's beloved-Son theology, though there is no verbal borrowing.
sourceText: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and […]

note: Jesus' announcement that 'the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners' continues Mark's Danielic Son-of-Man thread, here in its suffering aspect. The title carries the Daniel 7 background even as Mark inverts the figure's exaltation into delivery to sinners, anticipating the explicit citation at v. 62.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: Judas, 'one of the twelve,' identifying Jesus with a kiss completes the intimate-betrayer motif governed by Psalm 41's friend who shared bread and 'lifted his heel.' The treacherous gesture of affection from a close companion gives the arrest its psalmic depth, consummating the theme opened at the meal.
sourceText: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

note: Joab's murderous kiss of Amasa — 'he took him by the beard with his hand to kiss him' before stabbing him — is the Old Testament archetype of the deadly false kiss that Judas reenacts. The pairing of a feigned greeting-kiss with betrayal gives this a strong typological coherence, though Mark does not cite it.
sourceText: Joab said to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand. So he struck him with it in the body, and shed out his bowels to the ground, and didn’t strike him again; and he died. Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri.

note: The proverb 'the kisses of an enemy are deceitful' (LXX) supplies a wisdom commentary on Judas' kiss, contrasting the faithful wounds of a friend with an enemy's profuse kisses. The conceptual fit is exact, but the connection is gnomic rather than a quoted source.
sourceText: Faithful are the wounds of a friend; although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.

note: Jesus' protest that they come 'as against a robber' and his arrest among the violent faintly anticipate the Servant 'numbered with the transgressors.' The motif of the innocent treated as a criminal coheres with Mark's Servant-shaped Passion, though here it is allusive and undeveloped.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: The arrest that precipitates the disciples' flight ('they all left him, and fled,' v. 50) enacts the scattering of the sheep foretold by the struck-shepherd oracle just quoted in v. 27. The narrative fulfills the citation, tying the arrest scene back to Zechariah's prophecy.
sourceText: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.

note: The young man who 'left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked' closely matches Amos' oracle that 'he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day.' The distinctive image of fleeing naked in a day of judgment gives real verbal volume, and the coherence fits Mark's depiction of total abandonment as the day of reckoning falls on Jesus' followers.
sourceText: and he who is courageous among the mighty will flee away naked on that day,” says Yahweh.

note: The flight in which a garment is left behind in the grasping hands recalls Joseph fleeing Potiphar's wife, who 'caught him by his garment... and he left his garment in her hand, and fled.' The shared motif of escaping by abandoning the seized cloth supports a faint verbal echo, though the contexts differ.
sourceText: She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!” He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.

note: The wider Amos context of inescapable judgment, where none can flee the Lord's hand, reinforces the day-of-reckoning resonance of the naked flight. This strengthens the Amos 2:16 reading by establishing the prophet's recurring theme of futile flight in the day of judgment.
sourceText: I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, and he said, “Strike the tops of the pillars, that the thresholds may shake; and break them in pieces on the head of all of them; and I will kill the last of them with the sword: there shall not one of them flee away, and there shall not one of them escape. Though they dig into Sheol, there my hand will take them; and though they climb up to heaven, there I will bring them down. Though they hide themselves in the […]

note: Peter following 'from a distance' while Jesus is led to the high priest faintly echoes the lament psalmist's complaint that 'my friends and companions stand aloof from my affliction, and my kinsmen stand far off.' The motif of associates keeping their distance from the suffering righteous one coheres with Peter's hesitant, fearful following.
sourceText: My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my plague. My kinsmen stand far away.

note: The psalmist's 'you have caused my companions to shun me' belongs to the same lament tradition of friends who withdraw in the hour of suffering. Peter warming himself among the officers, distanced and soon to deny, fits this isolation motif, though the connection is thematic.
sourceText: You have taken my friends from me. You have made me an abomination to them. I am confined, and I can’t escape.

note: The council seeking testimony as 'false witnesses rose up against him, breathing out violence' is precisely Mark's scene of those who 'gave false testimony against him.' The volume is strong (pseudomartyres), and the coherence is high: Mark casts Jesus as the persecuted righteous one of the psalms, hemmed in by lying witnesses, confident in God's vindication.
sourceText: Don’t deliver me over to the desire of my adversaries, for false witnesses have risen up against me, such as breathe out cruelty.

note: 'Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things that I do not know' matches the false testimony and incoherent accusations leveled at Jesus. The recurrence of the false-witness motif across the lament psalms (27, 35) strengthens the allusion and frames the trial as the persecution of the innocent sufferer.
sourceText: Unrighteous witnesses rise up. They ask me about things that I don’t know about.

note: The psalmist surrounded by 'lying tongues' and 'words of hatred' who 'attack me without cause' coheres with the conspiratorial false testimony of Mark's council. As another suffering-righteous psalm prominent in the Passion tradition, it reinforces the false-accusation matrix Mark draws on.
sourceText: for they have opened the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of deceit against me. They have spoken to me with a lying tongue. They have also surrounded me with words of hatred, and fought against me without a cause.

note: The plotters who seek a charge against the blameless Daniel and find none parallel the council that 'sought witnesses against Jesus... and found none.' The motif of conspirators unable to fault the righteous man until they manufacture a charge resonates, though the link is situational rather than verbal.
sourceText: Then the presidents and the satraps sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion nor fault, because he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him. Then these men said, We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God.

note: Susanna's ordeal by false witnesses whose testimony does not finally agree offers a Second-Temple type of the righteous condemned on perjured evidence that fails to cohere. Mark's note that the witnesses' testimony 'did not agree' echoes this exposure-of-false-witness pattern, supplying a deuterocanonical parallel.
sourceText: Then the two elders stood up in the midst of the people, and laid their hands upon her head. And she weeping looked up toward heaven: for her heart trusted in the Lord. And the elders said, As we walked in the garden alone, this woman came in with two maids, and shut the garden doors, and sent the maids away. Then a young man, who there was hid, came to her, and lay with her. And we, being in a corner of the garden, saw this wickedness, and ran to them. […]

note: Jesus' silence — 'he stayed quiet, and answered nothing' before his accusers — directly enacts the Servant who 'was oppressed and afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter... so he opened not his mouth.' The volume is high and the coherence total: Mark portrays Jesus' refusal to answer as the deliberate fulfillment of the silent Servant.
sourceText: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.

note: The psalmist who, surrounded by accusers, becomes 'like a deaf man... like a mute man who does not open his mouth' offers a psalmic parallel to Jesus' silence under interrogation. This lament-psalm motif of the righteous keeping silence before false charges reinforces the Isaianic Servant-silence Mark foregrounds.
