sourceText: But I, as a deaf man, don’t hear. I am as a mute man who doesn’t open his mouth. Yes, I am as a man who doesn’t hear, in whose mouth are no reproofs.

note: 'I was mute; I did not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it' supplies a further psalmic instance of the sufferer's silent submission to God's hand. The connection deepens the lament-psalm coloring of Jesus' silence, though Isaiah 53 remains the controlling text.
sourceText: I was mute. I didn’t open my mouth, because you did it.

note: The high priest's question 'Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?' joins the titles 'anointed' and 'son' that Psalm 2 fuses ('the Lord and his anointed... you are my Son'). Mark's Christology trades on this royal-messianic psalm, lending the interrogation its scriptural charge even without quotation.
sourceText: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,

note: Jesus' 'you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power' fuses the enthronement oracle 'Sit at my right hand,' which Mark has just expounded at 12:36. The volume is maximal and the coherence climactic: the accused declares his coming vindication as the one seated at God's right hand, making this the decisive scriptural self-claim of the Gospel.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: 'Coming with the clouds of the sky' quotes Daniel's vision of 'one like a son of man' who comes 'with the clouds of heaven' and is given everlasting dominion before the Ancient of Days. Mark fuses this with Psalm 110 into a single declaration, so that the Son of Man both sits enthroned and comes in glory; the conflation is the theological summit of Mark's Christology.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: Jesus' bare 'I am' (ego eimi) in answer to the high priest may carry an overtone of the divine self-naming 'I AM' of the burning bush, especially given Mark's other ego-eimi sayings. The reading is contested, since the phrase functions primarily as a plain affirmative, but the loaded context invites the figural divine-name resonance.
sourceText: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

note: 'Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you made strong for yourself' uniquely joins 'son of man' with God's 'right hand,' the two elements Jesus combines. As a psalm that already braids these motifs, it may stand among the scriptural matrix behind the fused declaration.
sourceText: Let your hand be on the man of your right hand, on the son of man whom you made strong for yourself.

note: Zechariah's oracle that 'they shall look on him whom they have pierced' anticipates the council 'seeing' the vindicated Son of Man, a connection drawn explicitly elsewhere in the NT. The verb of seeing the rejected-yet-coming one resonates with Jesus' 'you will see,' lending an eschatological-recognition overtone.
sourceText: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

note: The spitting, blindfolding, and beating — 'some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to beat him' — enact the Servant who said 'I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting.' The specific cluster of spitting and striking the face gives high volume and coherence, casting the abuse as fulfillment of the third Servant Song.
sourceText: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.

note: The high priest tearing his clothes at the alleged blasphemy ironically transgresses the Levitical rule that the high priest 'shall not tear his clothes.' Mark's readers attuned to Torah would register the violation, sharpening the irony that the one charged with blasphemy is condemned by a priest breaking his own consecration law. The allusion turns on the prohibition's reversal.
sourceText: “‘He who is the high priest among his brothers, upon whose head the anointing oil is poured, and that is consecrated to put on the garments, shall not let the hair of his head hang loose, nor tear his clothes;

note: Micah's 'they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek with a rod' (LXX 5:1) offers a prophetic image of the smitten ruler that resonates with the blows to Jesus' face. The motif of striking Israel's appointed judge/ruler coheres with Mark's mocked-king theme, though it is a faint secondary echo to Isaiah 50:6.
sourceText: Now you shall gather yourself in troops, daughter of troops. He has laid siege against us. They will strike the judge of Israel with a rod on the cheek.

note: The taunt 'Prophesy!' mockingly tests the messianic gift of discerning judgment that Isaiah ascribes to the shoot of Jesse, who judges not by what his eyes see. The irony of demanding prophecy from the blindfolded Messiah plays on this expectation, though the connection is thematic and undeveloped.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh. note: Zedekiah striking the prophet Micaiah on the cheek and challenging his prophetic word ('How did the Spirit pass from me to speak to you?') parallels the officers striking Jesus and jeering 'Prophesy!' The pattern of slapping and taunting a true prophet supplies a faint Old Testament precedent.
sourceText: Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near, and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, “Which way did the Spirit of Yahweh go from me to speak to you?”

note: Peter's threefold denial, capping the abandonment by the inner circle, extends the Passion's betrayed-by-intimates theme rooted in the psalm of the friend who lifted his heel. While Judas is the primary referent, Peter's failure broadens the motif of the righteous sufferer forsaken even by his closest companions.
sourceText: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

note: The psalmist who has become 'a horror to my acquaintances; those who see me in the street flee from me' resonates with Peter's recoil and the disciples' flight from association with Jesus. The lament motif of acquaintances disowning the afflicted one colors Peter's denials, though without verbal citation.
sourceText: Because of all my adversaries I have become utterly contemptible to my neighbors, A fear to my acquaintances. Those who saw me on the street fled from me.

note: Peter's denial that he 'knows' Jesus enacts the lament theme of friends and kinsmen who 'stand far off' from the sufferer's affliction. The repeated psalmic image of withdrawn intimates frames Peter's failure as a further instance of the righteous one's abandonment, deepening Mark's lament-shaped Passion.
sourceText: My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my plague. My kinsmen stand far away.

note: Jesus' refusal to answer Pilate's repeated questions ('Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate marveled') enacts the Servant who 'was oppressed and afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.' The volume is high because Mark twice underscores the silence (vv. 4-5) precisely where defense is expected, and the Servant coherence runs through the whole passion. This is the load-bearing intertext of the trial.
sourceText: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.

note: The suffering psalmist becomes 'like a deaf man' who 'hears not, and in whose mouth are no reproofs,' opening not his mouth before his accusers. The same psalm supplies later passion details (friends standing far off, v. 11), and its portrait of the afflicted righteous one mute before those who 'seek my hurt' coheres with Jesus' silence before Pilate.
sourceText: But I, as a deaf man, don’t hear. I am as a mute man who doesn’t open his mouth. Yes, I am as a man who doesn’t hear, in whose mouth are no reproofs.

note: 'I was mute, I opened not my mouth, because you have done it' offers a further psalmic instance of the righteous sufferer's deliberate silence under affliction interpreted as God's doing. The link is conceptual rather than verbal but belongs to the same cluster of silent-sufferer texts available behind Mark's twice-noted silence.
sourceText: I was mute. I didn’t open my mouth, because you did it.

note: The third Servant Song's defendant who 'set my face like a flint,' confident that 'he who vindicates me is near' and asks 'who will contend with me?', frames the silent, composed bearing of the accused before a hostile tribunal. Its juridical setting coheres with Jesus standing wordless before Pilate's questions.
sourceText: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed. He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me.

note: Pilate's 'handing over' (paredoken) of Jesus to be crucified continues the Servant motif that 'the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all' and that he was 'given up' for transgressions; the Greek paradidomi recurs across Mark's passion as the technical Servant-handing-over verb. The crowd's choice of a murderer-insurrectionist over the innocent one sharpens the substitution coherence.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: The release of Barabbas alongside the condemnation of Jesus has long been read figurally against the Day of Atonement's two goats: one released, one bearing sin to death. The pairing of a freed prisoner and a doomed one invites the scapegoat typology, though Mark makes no explicit citation and the connection rests on conceptual coherence.
sourceText: He shall take the two goats, and set them before Yahweh at the door of the Tent of Meeting. note: The innocent 'righteous one' delivered up while a guilty insurrectionist goes free echoes the Servant who 'bore the sin of many' and was 'numbered with transgressors.' The contrast between Barabbas the murderer and the sinless Jesus dramatizes the vicarious exchange the Servant Song announces.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. note: The soldiers' mockery — striking Jesus' head, spitting on him, and abusing him — closely tracks the third Servant Song: 'I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled out the beard; I hid not my face from shame and spitting.' The combination of striking and spitting (v. 19) is distinctive enough, and Isaiah 50 is so embedded in Mark's passion, that the allusion registers strongly.
sourceText: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.

note: The mock-coronation — purple robe, thorn-crown, the sarcastic 'Hail, King of the Jews,' and homage — enacts the psalmist who is 'scorned by men and despised by the people,' mocked by all who see him. Psalm 22 is the controlling passion psalm in Mark 15, and the derisive royal homage coheres tightly with its portrait of the righteous sufferer made an object of contempt.
sourceText: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”

note: 'You know my reproach, and my shame and my dishonor... reproaches have broken my heart' supplies the other great passion psalm's vocabulary of public humiliation. Mark draws heavily on Psalm 69 (esp. v. 21), so the soldiers' degrading mockery resonates with this psalm's catalogue of shame as well.
sourceText: You know my reproach, my shame, and my dishonor. My adversaries are all before you. Reproach has broken my heart, and I am full of heaviness. I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; for comforters, but I found none.

note: The plotters in Wisdom resolve to 'test him with insult and torture, that we may find out how gentle he is, and make trial of his forbearance.' The soldiers' systematic insult and physical abuse of the mock-king enacts precisely this testing of the righteous one through outrage; the Wisdom passage is a key Second-Temple template for the mocked-righteous-sufferer that Mark's scene embodies.
sourceText: With outrage and torture let us put him to the test, That we may learn his gentleness, And may prove his patience under wrong.

note: The piercing thorn-crown and abuse of the one who is 'King' faintly anticipate Zechariah's 'they shall look on me whom they have pierced' and the mourning for a smitten royal figure. The link is thematic and contested, resting on the broader Zecharian shepherd-king matrix Mark uses elsewhere.

lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

note: The compelled bearing of the cross-beam out to the place of execution has been read figurally against Isaac, who 'carried the wood of the burnt offering... laid it on Isaac his son,' as the son bears the wood of his own sacrifice. The connection is typological and unmarked in Mark, resting on the Aqedah's availability as a beloved-son-to-sacrifice pattern.
sourceText: Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. He took in his hand the fire and the knife. They both went together.

note: Simon of Cyrene compelled to 'bear' (airo) the cross can echo the Servant who 'has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows,' the burden-bearing language at the heart of the Song. The link is faint and lexical, but it belongs to the Servant coherence that pervades the chapter.
sourceText: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.

note: The drink offered at the cross — here 'wine mixed with myrrh' — and again the vinegar of v. 36 derive from the psalmist's complaint, 'they gave me also gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.' Matthew sharpens the link to 'gall,' but Mark's offered drugged/bitter wine already evokes the psalm's hostile offering. Psalm 69 is one of the two governing passion psalms here, so the volume and coherence are high.
sourceText: They also gave me gall for my food. In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.

note: 'Give strong drink to him who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress, let him drink and forget his poverty' provides a sapiential rationale for offering a numbing draught to the dying. The custom of a stupefying wine to the condemned may stand behind the gesture Jesus refuses, though the connection is conceptual.
sourceText: Give strong drink to him who is ready to perish; and wine to the bitter in soul: Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more.

note: The motif of drinking 'the wine of the condemned' in a context of injustice offers a faint prophetic resonance with the bitter cup pressed on the crucified. The link is associative and contested.
sourceText: and they lay themselves down beside every altar on clothes taken in pledge; and in the house of their God they drink the wine of those who have been fined.

note: 'They parted his garments among them, casting lots on them, what each should take' reproduces the psalm nearly verbatim: 'they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.' This is a formal-level allusion (near-quotation of LXX Psalm 21:19) embedded in the crucifixion narration itself, and it is the clearest single proof that Mark narrates the cross through Psalm 22. Volume and explicitness are maximal.
sourceText: They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.

note: Crucifixion between 'two robbers,' one on the right and one on the left, fulfills the Servant 'numbered with transgressors' — a link Mark (or the early textual tradition) makes explicit in v. 28, 'The Scripture was fulfilled, which says, He was numbered with transgressors.' This is a formal citation of Isaiah 53:12, even if v. 28 is text-critically secondary; the scene itself enacts the Servant being reckoned among the lawless.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: 'A company of evildoers encircle me; they have pierced my hands and feet' resonates with the crucifixion act and the criminals flanking Jesus. The LXX reading and the surrounding-by-the-wicked motif cohere with the scene, though Mark does not cite it directly here.
sourceText: For dogs have surrounded me. A company of evildoers have enclosed me. They have pierced my hands and feet.

note: The passersby who 'blasphemed him, wagging their heads' and the chief priests' taunt 'He saved others, he cannot save himself... let him come down' directly enact the psalm: 'All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me, they wag their heads: He committed himself to the Lord; let him deliver him, let him rescue him, since he delights in him.' Both the head-wagging gesture and the 'let God save him' challenge are present, making this a high-volume, double-feature allusion.
sourceText: All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”

note: The mockers' logic — 'let the Christ come down... that we may see and believe' and 'he saved others, he cannot save himself' — closely matches Wisdom's ungodly: 'Let us see if his words are true... for if the righteous man is God's son, he will help him and deliver him from his adversaries. Let us condemn him to a shameful death, for he will be protected, according to what he says.' This deuterocanonical righteous-sufferer text is the strongest non-Psalmic intertext for the mockery, supplying the taunt's 'son of God / let God deliver him' shape.
sourceText: Let us see if his words be true, And let us try what shall befall in the ending of his life. For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries. With outrage and torture let us put him to the test, That we may learn his gentleness, And may prove his patience under wrong. Let us condemn him to a shameful death; For he will be visited according to his words.

note: 'I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they wag their heads' supplies a second head-wagging derision text reinforcing Psalm 22:7. Psalm 109 is an imprecatory suffering psalm whose mocking accusers cohere with the crowd's gestures, raising the recurrence of the head-wagging motif.
sourceText: I have also become a reproach to them. When they see me, they shake their head.

note: 'All who pass along the way clap their hands at you; they hiss and wag their heads at daughter Jerusalem' applies the passers-by-wagging-the-head gesture to the destroyed temple/city. Mark's mockers — who taunt the destroyer-of-the-temple as they pass by and wag their heads — fold the temple-destruction theme into the head-wagging derision, making Lamentations a coherent secondary echo.
sourceText: All that pass by clap their hands at you. They hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men called The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?

note: 'Zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me' resonates with the temple-destruction taunt hurled at Jesus ('you who destroy the temple'). The passion psalm's fusion of temple-zeal and reproach coheres with the mockery's content.
sourceText: For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.

note: The taunt that God will not save the sufferer anticipates and frames the cry of dereliction (v. 34); the mockers unwittingly voice the psalm's opening abandonment that Jesus will quote. The recurrence of Psalm 22 across the scene strengthens this proleptic echo.
sourceText: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning?

note: Darkness over the whole land from the sixth to the ninth hour (noon to mid-afternoon) enacts the day-of-the-Lord oracle: 'I will make the sun go down at noon, and darken the earth in broad daylight.' The midday darkening is distinctive and eschatologically loaded, and Amos's following line about turning feasts into mourning over an 'only son' coheres with the death of the beloved Son.
sourceText: It will happen in that day,” says the Lord Yahweh, “that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day.

note: The plague of darkness over the land of Egypt — 'a darkness to be felt' for three days — supplies the exodus-judgment template for supernatural midday darkness. The coherence is strong (a divine darkness signaling judgment and deliverance) and the motif is widely available, reinforcing the cosmic-sign reading of the cross.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.” Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days. They didn’t see one another, neither did anyone rise from his place for three days; but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.

note: Joel's day-of-the-Lord darkening — 'the sun and the moon are darkened' — belongs to the prophetic cluster of cosmic gloom at divine judgment that Mark draws on (cf. Mark 13:24, quoting Joel/Isaiah). The crucifixion darkness signals the eschatological day breaking in, cohering with Joel's imagery.
sourceText: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.

note: 'A day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness' adds another day-of-the-Lord text to the matrix of judgment-darkness behind the noon gloom. The link is general but reinforces the prophetic recurrence of cosmic darkening at the day of wrath.
sourceText: That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,

note: 'The sun will be dark at its rising' in Isaiah's oracle of cosmic upheaval contributes to the same prophetic darkening-of-the-luminaries tradition. Its availability strengthens the eschatological coloring of the crucifixion darkness, though it is not specifically cited here.
sourceText: For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.

note: Jesus' cry 'Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?' — interpreted 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' — is a formal quotation of the psalm's opening line, given in Aramaic (a Targum-like rendering of the Hebrew). This is the climactic citation that retrospectively unlocks the whole chapter's reliance on Psalm 22, and it is the highest-volume, most explicit OT use in Mark 15.
sourceText: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning?

note: The same psalm Jesus cites turns from abandonment to a plea for help and ends in vindication and praise; readers who hear v. 1 are meant to hear the whole arc. The trajectory toward deliverance frames the dereliction cry as something other than final despair, supplying the coherence of the broader psalm.
sourceText: But don’t be far off, Yahweh. You are my help: hurry to help me. Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of the dog. Save me from the lion’s mouth! Yes, from the horns of the wild oxen, you have answered me.

note: 'One ran, and filling a sponge full of vinegar... gave it to him to drink' directly enacts 'in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.' The Greek oxos ('sour wine/vinegar') matches LXX Psalm 68:22 exactly, making this the chapter's second strong contact with Psalm 69 and a near-quotation of the offered drink.
sourceText: They also gave me gall for my food. In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.

note: The bystanders' guess that Jesus is 'calling Elijah' and the wait to 'see whether Elijah comes' trade on the expectation, from Malachi, that 'Elijah the prophet' would come before the great day of the Lord. The Elijah-redivivus hope is the Second-Temple backdrop that makes the misheard 'Eloi' into a question about eschatological rescue.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: Elijah's translation to heaven without dying underlies the popular belief that he could return to intervene; the bystanders imagine him coming 'to take him down.' The link is to the Elijah-rescue tradition rather than a verbal parallel, but it grounds the crowd's expectation.
sourceText: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

note: The veil (katapetasma) of the temple torn in two evokes the curtain Exodus commands to be made, separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy and screening the divine presence. Mark's tearing of this barrier at Jesus' death signals access to God and/or judgment on the sanctuary; the specific cultic vocabulary makes the allusion firm.
sourceText: “You shall make a veil of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cherubim. The work of the skillful workman shall it be made. You shall hang it on four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold; their hooks shall be of gold, on four sockets of silver. You shall hang up the veil under the clasps, and shall bring the ark of the testimony in there within the veil: and the veil shall separate the holy place from the most holy for you.

note: The veil 'before the mercy seat' that only the high priest may pass on the Day of Atonement defines what the torn curtain guarded. Its rending at the moment of death coheres with an atonement reading — the way into the holiest opened — making Leviticus 16 a coherent secondary intertext to the Exodus veil.
sourceText: and Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother, not to come at all times into the Most Holy Place within the veil, before the mercy seat which is on the ark; lest he die: for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat.

note: The tearing open of the sacred boundary recalls Sinai's theophany where God descends in cloud and the mountain is wrapped in awe; some read the rent veil as a renewed theophanic disclosure paralleling the heavens 'torn' (schizomenous) at Jesus' baptism, the same verb. The Sinai echo is faint but coheres with Mark's tearing-open inclusio.
sourceText: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lower part of the mountain. Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked […]

note: 'Oh that you would tear open (LXX) the heavens and come down' uses the same dramatic rending language for divine self-disclosure that Mark applies to the heavens at the baptism and arguably to the veil here. The verbal resonance of 'tearing' for God breaking through reinforces the theophanic reading.
sourceText: Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence,

note: The centurion's confession 'Truly this man was the Son of God' answers the mockers' Wisdom-shaped taunt: 'if the righteous man is God's son, God will help him.' What the ungodly proposed as a test, the Gentile soldier declares as truth at the moment of death, so the deuterocanonical righteous-son motif frames the irony of the climactic recognition.
sourceText: For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries.

note: The psalm Jesus quotes ends with 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord; all the families of the nations shall worship.' The Gentile centurion's confession at the cross can be read as the first-fruits of that promised turning of the nations, cohering with the psalm's universal-worship climax.
sourceText: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Yahweh. All the relatives of the nations shall worship before you. For the kingdom is Yahweh’s. He is the ruler over the nations.

note: The women 'watching from afar' echoes the lament 'My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my kinsmen stand far off.' Mark's distinctive note that the followers observe 'from a distance' (apo makrothen) matches the psalm's portrait of the afflicted righteous one abandoned to watch alone, fitting the chapter's suffering-psalm weave.
sourceText: My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my plague. My kinsmen stand far away.

note: 'You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them' adds a second psalm of the friendless sufferer whose acquaintances are removed far off. Its bleak isolation coheres with the women keeping their distance at the cross.
sourceText: You have taken my friends from me. You have made me an abomination to them. I am confined, and I can’t escape.

note: Burial by Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy and prominent councillor who lays Jesus in his own rock-cut tomb, fulfills 'they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence.' The Servant's honorable burial 'with a rich man' coheres precisely with the rich Joseph's intervention, sealing the chapter's Servant frame.
sourceText: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

note: The urgency to take the body down and bury it before nightfall on the Preparation Day reflects the law that a man hanged on a tree 'shall not remain all night... you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God,' lest the land be defiled. This statute drives the same-day burial and carries the theology of the curse borne on the tree.
sourceText: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree; his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God; that you don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.

note: Joshua's taking down of the hanged kings at sunset and laying them in a cave, sealed with great stones, offers a narrative precedent for the same-day removal of a hanged body and burial behind a rolled stone. The link is conceptual but coheres with the Deuteronomic same-day-burial command and the stone at the tomb.
sourceText: Afterward Joshua struck them, put them to death, and hanged them on five trees. They were hanging on the trees until the evening. At the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down off the trees, and cast them into the cave in which they had hidden themselves, and laid great stones on the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.

note: Abraham's burial of Sarah in a purchased cave-tomb hewn for the family establishes the patriarchal pattern of honorable interment in a rock-cut sepulchre. The dignity of Jesus' rock-tomb burial faintly recalls this venerable practice, though there is no verbal contact.
sourceText: After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre (that is, Hebron), in the land of Canaan.

note: The 'young man' (neaniskos) sitting in the tomb dressed in a white/dazzling robe matches the Second-Temple convention of angelic figures appearing as young men in bright apparel; in 2 Macc 3 two glorious young men in splendid robes (and elsewhere five) appear at the temple. Volume is moderate (shared vocabulary of youthful angelic messengers in shining garb) and the convention is widely available in Jewish literature of the era, supporting an angelophany reading of Mark's 'amazement.'
sourceText: Two other also appeared to him, young men notable in their strength, and beautiful in their glory, and splendid in their apparel, who stood by him on either side, and scourged him unceasingly, inflicting on him many sore stripes.

note: A heavenly horseman in white apparel leads the Maccabean army, reinforcing the deuterocanonical topos of angelic deliverers clothed in white. The echo is faint and corroborative rather than a direct source, supporting the figural identification of Mark's white-robed youth as angelic.
sourceText: And as they were there, close to Jerusalem, there appeared at their head one on horseback in white apparel, brandishing weapons of gold.

note: The dazzling-white garment recalls Daniel's vision where the Ancient of Days' clothing is white as snow, the apocalyptic register from which heavenly whiteness derives; Mark's restrained 'white robe' partakes of this imagery cluster. Coherence with Mark's transfiguration whiteness (9:3) supports the link, though the specific divine throne setting is absent here.
sourceText: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire.

note: Hosea's 'after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up' is the most plausible scriptural matrix for early Christian 'third day' resurrection language; though Mark does not say 'third day' here, the dawn-of-the-first-day raising participates in that pattern. Recurrence is high across the NT (1 Cor 15:4), but Mark 16's silence on explicit third-day phrasing keeps the volume low and the link contested.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: Three days and nights in the fish became a stock figure for death-and-deliverance, invoked elsewhere in the Jesus tradition (the sign of Jonah). The empty-tomb scene enacts the emergence-from-the-deep pattern figurally, but Mark 16 makes no verbal contact, so the connection is thematic and faint.
sourceText: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

note: 'You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor let your holy one see corruption' became the foundational psalm-text for resurrection proclamation (cited at Acts 2:27). The empty tomb dramatizes the body not seeing corruption, but Mark supplies no citation, so the resonance is conceptual and low-volume.
sourceText: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.

note: The women's 'trembling and astonishment' and fear follows the conventional human response to theophany and divine deliverance, as in the Song of the Sea where trembling seizes the nations. The pattern of fear before God's saving acts is widely available; the link is to a topos rather than a specific text.
sourceText: Terror and dread falls on them. By the greatness of your arm they are as still as a stone— until your people pass over, Yahweh, until the people pass over who you have purchased.

note: Daniel's companions are seized by great trembling and flee at an angelic vision, closely paralleling the women who flee in trembling from the white-robed messenger. This fear-and-flight response to an angelophany is a coherent Second-Temple convention that Mark's ending deploys, though no shared wording fixes the source.
sourceText: I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; for the men who were with me didn’t see the vision; but a great quaking fell on them, and they fled to hide themselves.

note: The longer ending's notice that Jesus 'had risen early on the first day of the week' reasserts the third-day/restoration pattern crystallized in Hosea's revival oracle. The connection remains a low-volume conceptual echo, since the appended ending narrates rather than cites Scripture.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: Jesus 'revealed in another form' to the two travelers evokes the biblical pattern of divine/angelic visitants appearing in altered or unrecognized guise to wayfarers, as the LORD appears to Abraham as travelers. The motif of hospitality-with-a-stranger-who-is-more-than-he-seems is available in the patriarchal narratives, though the link here is thematic and faint.
sourceText: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth,

note: The promise that believers 'will take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will in no way hurt them' directly recalls Psalm 91's pledge that the faithful will tread on the serpent and the adder and be guarded from harm. Volume is moderate (shared serpent-and-protection imagery) and the psalm's protective register coheres with the signs-following-believers theme, making this the strongest OT echo in the longer ending.
sourceText: You will tread on the lion and cobra. You will trample the young lion and the serpent underfoot.

note: The eschatological vision of the infant playing over the adder's den, harm undone in the messianic age, underlies the promise that serpents and poison will not hurt believers. The connection is to Isaiah's new-creation peace between humans and venomous creatures, a coherent backdrop for the signs, though no verbal citation is present.
sourceText: The nursing child will play near a cobra’s hole, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den.

note: The bronze-serpent episode, where looking to the lifted serpent neutralizes deadly snakebite, supplies a scriptural precedent for serpents made harmless to the faithful. The link is figural and low-volume, mediated by the wider tradition of God's people delivered from serpent venom.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.

note: The commission to 'go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation' echoes the Servant's mandate to be a light to the nations reaching to the end of the earth. The universalizing scope coheres with Isaianic mission theology, but the appended ending offers no quotation, keeping the volume low.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: The call to declare God's glory and salvation among all nations stands behind the worldwide preaching commission. The enthronement-psalm summons to proclaim to every people is a coherent matrix for the universal mission, though the contact is thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples.

note: 'Sat down at the right hand of God' is a formal allusion to Psalm 110:1, 'Sit at my right hand,' the most-cited OT verse in the NT and Mark's own christological touchstone (Mark 12:36; 14:62). Volume and recurrence are high, and the enthronement coheres with Mark's exaltation theology, making this an unmistakable, near-quotation reuse of the psalm.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: Jesus being 'received up into heaven' echoes Elijah's bodily assumption, the paradigmatic OT ascent narrative that shapes early Christian ascension language. The motif of a prophet taken up to heaven is coherent and available, supplying the narrative grammar for Mark's ascension notice, though the wording is shared with the Elijah cycle only loosely.
sourceText: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

note: Enoch's being 'taken' by God, with the Second-Temple expansion of his heavenly ascent, contributes to the assumption tradition behind 'received up into heaven.' The echo is faint and corroborative of the broader taken-up-to-God pattern rather than a direct source.
sourceText: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.

note: The one like a son of man brought up to the Ancient of Days and given dominion provides an apocalyptic backdrop for Jesus' heavenly enthronement and the subsequent worldwide proclamation. Coherence with Mark's son-of-man enthronement language (14:62) supports the link, though the ascension verb here points more directly to Psalm 110 and the Elijah motif.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: Luke's literary preface (orderly account, careful tracing, dedication) most closely resembles the Greek prefatory conventions of Second-Temple Jewish writers; the grandson's prologue to Sirach offers the nearest scriptural analogue of an author explaining his method and aim. Volume is low (no shared diction) but thematic coherence and availability are strong, so it registers as a genre echo rather than a citation.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: The epitomist's preface in 2 Maccabees, in which the writer describes condensing and ordering his material for readers' benefit, parallels Luke's claim to have 'traced the course of all things accurately' and written 'in order.' A deuterocanonical, pre-Lukan model for the historiographic-preface form; verbal overlap is slight, so the link is a formal echo only.
sourceText: Now the things concerning Judas Maccabaeus and his kindred, and the purification of the great temple, and the dedication of the altar, and further the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes, and Eupator his son, and the manifestations that came from heaven to those that vied with one another in manful deeds for the religion of the Jews; so that, being but a few, they rescued the whole country, and chased the barbarous multitudes, and recovered again the temple […]

note: 'The priestly division of Abijah' names the eighth of the twenty-four courses assigned by lot in 1 Chronicles 24:10. The distinctiveness of the proper name and the technical priestly-rota system give high volume; Luke grounds Zechariah in the precise Chronicler's order, signaling continuity with Israel's temple cult.
sourceText: the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah,

note: Elizabeth (Elisabet) bears the name of Aaron's wife Elisheba in Exodus 6:23, and Luke explicitly makes her 'of the daughters of Aaron.' The onomastic match plus the priestly-lineage framing is distinctive and deliberate, casting the Baptist's parents as an idealized Aaronic couple.
sourceText: Aaron took Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab, the sister of Nahshon, as his wife; and she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.

note: That the priest Zechariah has a wife 'of the daughters of Aaron' reflects the priestly marriage regulations of Leviticus 21:7,13-14, which restrict whom a priest may marry. Thematic coherence with the Aaronic-purity theme is strong; the diction is not quoted, so it functions as a halakhic echo.
sourceText: “‘They shall not marry a woman who is a prostitute, or profane; neither shall they marry a woman divorced from her husband; for he is holy to his God.

note: 'Righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments' echoes the Lord's charge to Abraham, 'walk before me and be blameless' (Genesis 17:1). The pairing of walking + blamelessness before God is distinctive covenant language, reinforcing the Abrahamic typology that pervades the chapter.
sourceText: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless.

note: The double descriptor 'righteous... blameless' matches the verdict on Noah, who was 'a righteous man, blameless' and 'walked with God' (Genesis 6:9). Septuagintal vocabulary (dikaios, amemptos) recurs; the echo enrolls Zechariah and Elizabeth among Scripture's exemplary righteous.
sourceText: This is the history of the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God.

note: 'They both were well advanced in years' and 'Elizabeth was barren' reproduces almost verbatim the description of Abraham and Sarah, who 'were old, advanced in years,' with Sarah barren (Genesis 11:30; 18:11). High volume and recurrence (the motif returns at 1:18, 36) establish the Abraham-Sarah type-scene as the controlling frame.
sourceText: Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age. Sarah had passed the age of childbearing.

note: 'Elizabeth was barren' directly recalls 'Sarai was barren; she had no child' (Genesis 11:30), the opening of the matriarchal barrenness theme. Shared diction (steira / 'barren') and the no-child clause make this a focused contributor to the type-scene.
sourceText: Sarai was barren. She had no child.

note: Hannah, who 'had no children' because she was barren (1 Samuel 1:2), is a second barren-mother template standing behind Elizabeth; the Samuel narrative will be quarried repeatedly in the canticles. Recurrence across the chapter strengthens an otherwise moderate-volume link.
sourceText: and he had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of other Peninnah: and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.

note: Manoah's wife was 'barren and had no children' (Judges 13:2) before the annunciation of Samson, a Nazirite. Luke's John narrative leans on this Judges 13 type-scene (cf. the Nazirite diction at 1:15), so the barrenness notice here primes that allusion.
sourceText: There was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah; and his wife was barren, and didn’t bear.

note: Zechariah's duty 'to enter into the temple of the Lord and burn incense' enacts the priestly incense ordinance of Exodus 30:7-8, where Aaron burns incense on the golden altar morning and evening. Distinctive cultic vocabulary (altar of incense, burning) gives high volume; Luke situates the scene in exact Pentateuchal liturgy.
sourceText: Aaron shall burn incense of sweet spices on it every morning. When he tends the lamps, he shall burn it. When Aaron lights the lamps at evening, he shall burn it, a perpetual incense before Yahweh throughout your generations.

note: 'The whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense' presupposes the equation of incense with prayer voiced in Psalm 141:2, 'let my prayer be set before you as incense.' Thematic coherence is strong; the link is conceptual rather than verbally quoted.
sourceText: Let my prayer be set before you like incense; the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice.

note: Gabriel comes to Daniel 'at the time of the evening oblation' while Daniel prays (Daniel 9:21); here Gabriel appears at the hour of incense amid the people's prayer. The convergence of angel + appointed sacrificial/prayer hour is distinctive and recurs in the Gabriel-naming at 1:19, marking deliberate Danielic patterning.
sourceText: yes, while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening offering.

note: The 'angel of the Lord' standing by the altar is, per 1:19, Gabriel, the interpreting angel of Daniel 8:16. Even before he is named, the apocalyptic visitation at the sanctuary is shaped by Daniel; high distinctiveness given Gabriel appears only in Daniel within the canon.
sourceText: I heard a man’s voice between the banks of the Ulai, which called, and said, Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision.

note: 'Zacharias was troubled... and fear fell upon him' reproduces Daniel's terror before Gabriel, when Daniel 'was frightened and fell on my face' (Daniel 8:17; cf. 10:7-9). The stock prophetic dread-at-theophany reaction, paired with the Gabriel context, makes this a coherent Danielic allusion.
sourceText: So he came near where I stood; and when he came, I was frightened, and fell on my face: but he said to me, Understand, son of man; for the vision belongs to the time of the end.

note: Manoah's fear at the angel ('We will surely die, for we have seen God,' Judges 13:22) is a possible secondary model for Zechariah's terror, given the Samson type-scene already in play. Volume is low and the fear-reaction is conventional, so it is a faint contributing echo.
sourceText: Manoah said to his wife, “We shall surely die, because we have seen God.”

note: 'Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John' follows the exact pattern of God's promise to Abraham: 'Sarah your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac' (Genesis 17:19). The bear-a-son + name-the-child formula has high volume and anchors the Abrahamic frame.
sourceText: God said, “No, but Sarah, your wife, will bear you a son. You shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant for his seed after him.

note: 'Your request has been heard... you shall call his name John' replays the angelic birth-announcement to Hagar: 'the Lord has heard your affliction... you shall call his name Ishmael' (Genesis 16:11). The hearing + naming clause is the formal core of the OT annunciation type-scene.
sourceText: Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Behold, you are with child, and will bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction.

note: The annunciation to a barren wife that she 'will conceive and bear a son' who is to abstain from wine and be set apart from the womb (Judges 13:3-5) is the closest single template for Gabriel's speech, supplying both the structure and the Nazirite content. High volume and tight thematic coherence.
sourceText: Yahweh’s angel appeared to the woman, and said to her, “See now, you are barren, and don’t bear; but you shall conceive, and bear a son. note: 'Your request has been heard' echoes Eli's word to Hannah, 'the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked' (1 Samuel 1:17), followed by the granting of the longed-for son. The petition-heard motif coheres with the Hannah substratum that drives the Magnificat.
sourceText: Then Eli answered, “Go in peace; and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him.”

note: 'He will drink no wine nor strong drink' quotes the Nazirite statute of Numbers 6:3, which forbids wine and strong drink to the consecrated. The distinctive paired prohibition gives high volume and marks John as a lifelong Nazirite-like figure.
sourceText: he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink. He shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of fermented drink, neither shall he drink any juice of grapes, nor eat fresh grapes or dried.

Both diction and the from-the-womb consecration recur, giving high volume.
sourceText: Now therefore please beware and drink no wine nor strong drink, and don’t eat any unclean thing: for, behold, you shall conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head; for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb: and he shall begin to save Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.” Then the woman came and told her husband, saying, “A man of God came to me, and his face was like the face of the angel of God, very awesome; and I […]

note: Hannah's vow that no razor and (in the LXX) no wine or strong drink shall touch her son (1 Samuel 1:11) supplies a third Nazirite-from-birth model behind John. Recurrence of the Samuel narrative across the chapter raises an otherwise medium-volume link.
sourceText: She vowed a vow, and said, “Yahweh of Armies, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your handmaid, and remember me, and not forget your handmaid, but will give to your handmaid a boy, then I will give him to Yahweh all the days of his life, and no razor shall come on his head.”

note: 'Filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb' echoes prophetic pre-natal consecration: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you... I appointed you a prophet' (Jeremiah 1:5). Coheres with John's prophetic calling (1:76) and the from-the-womb motif.
sourceText: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”

note: The Servant 'called from the womb' and named while in his mother's body (Isaiah 49:1,5) provides a further model for John's womb-consecration and prophetic vocation. Thematic coherence is good; verbal overlap is partial, so it reads as a supporting echo.
sourceText: Listen, islands, to me; and listen, you peoples, from far: Yahweh has called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother has he made mention of my name:

sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

note: 'To prepare a people prepared for the Lord' and John's going 'before him' draw on Malachi 3:1, the messenger sent to prepare the way before the Lord, fused with the Elijah promise of 4:5-6. Recurrence (cited again at 1:76) confirms Malachi as a structural source.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

sourceText: Who was recorded for reproofs in their seasons, To pacify anger, before it brake forth into wrath; To turn the heart of the father to the son, And to restore the tribes of Jacob.

note: 'He will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God' echoes the ideal of Levi, who 'turned many from iniquity' (Malachi 2:6). The turning-many language reinforces the Malachi matrix already supplying the Elijah oracle.
sourceText: The law of truth was in his mouth, and unrighteousness was not found in his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and turned many away from iniquity.

note: 'To prepare a people prepared for the Lord' anticipates the Baptist's later identification with Isaiah 40:3, 'prepare the way of the Lord.' Here the preparation language is more Malachian, so Isaiah 40 is a secondary, partly anticipatory echo.
sourceText: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.

sourceText: He said, “Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?”

sourceText: Then Abraham fell on his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, “Will a child be born to him who is one hundred years old? Will Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”

note: 'I am Gabriel' explicitly names the angel of Daniel 8:16 and 9:21, the only OT figure to bear this name. The self-identification is effectively a citation of the Danielic character, confirming the apocalyptic frame retroactively over the whole scene.
sourceText: I heard a man’s voice between the banks of the Ulai, which called, and said, Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision.

note: Gabriel 'who stands in the presence of God' and is 'sent' recalls Daniel 9:21, where Gabriel is dispatched to Daniel at prayer; the sent-to-explain function matches. Recurrence with 1:11,19 makes Daniel 9 a sustained source.
sourceText: yes, while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening offering.

sourceText: I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and go in before the glory of the Holy One.”

sourceText: and when he had spoken to me according to these words, I set my face toward the ground, and was mute.

sourceText: and I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth, that you shall be mute, and shall not be to them a reprover; for they are a rebellious house.

sourceText: She conceived, bore a son, and said, “God has taken away my reproach.”

note: Hannah's plea that God 'look on the affliction of your handmaid' and grant a child (1 Samuel 1:11) stands behind Elizabeth's sense that 'the Lord... looked at me' to remove her shame. The look-upon-the-barren motif coheres with the pervasive Hannah substratum.
sourceText: She vowed a vow, and said, “Yahweh of Armies, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your handmaid, and remember me, and not forget your handmaid, but will give to your handmaid a boy, then I will give him to Yahweh all the days of his life, and no razor shall come on his head.”

note: Isaiah 54 promises the barren woman that she will 'forget the shame... and the reproach... remember no more' (Isaiah 54:1,4). Elizabeth's reproach-removal participates in this prophetic reversal of barren-Israel's disgrace; the link is thematic and figural rather than verbatim.

sourceText: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

sourceText: Yahweh’s angel appeared to him, and said to him, “Yahweh is with you, you mighty man of valor!”

sourceText: “Jael shall be blessed above women, the wife of Heber the Kenite; blessed shall she be above women in the tent.

sourceText: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.

sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.

sourceText: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
