sourceText: yet I will rejoice in Yahweh. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!

note: 'My soul shall rejoice in the Lord, exulting in his salvation' (Psalm 35:9) supplies the soul-rejoices-in-salvation diction underlying 1:47. A coherent psalmic echo within the cluster of rejoicing-in-God's-deliverance texts.
sourceText: My soul shall be joyful in Yahweh. It shall rejoice in his salvation.

note: 'My soul shall exult in my God' (Isaiah 61:10) within the Spirit-anointed-good-news passage contributes to the rejoicing diction of the canticle's opening. Thematic coherence with eschatological salvation supports the echo.
sourceText: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

note: 'He has looked at the humble state (tapeinosin) of his handmaid' quotes Hannah's prayer that God would 'look on the affliction (tapeinosin) of your handmaid' (1 Samuel 1:11 LXX). The shared rare-noun + handmaid combination is high-volume and ties the canticle's singer to Hannah.
sourceText: She vowed a vow, and said, “Yahweh of Armies, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your handmaid, and remember me, and not forget your handmaid, but will give to your handmaid a boy, then I will give him to Yahweh all the days of his life, and no razor shall come on his head.”

note: 'He has looked at the humble state' also echoes Leah's 'the Lord has looked upon my affliction' at Reuben's birth (Genesis 29:32 LXX). The look-on-affliction-of-the-lowly motif coheres with the matriarchal reversal theme; a supporting echo to the Hannah primary.
sourceText: Leah conceived, and bore a son, and she named him Reuben. For she said, “Because Yahweh has looked at my affliction. For now my husband will love me.”

note: 'From now on, all generations will call me blessed' takes up Leah's 'the women will call me blessed' (Genesis 30:13 LXX), spoken at the birth of a son. The call-me-blessed formula is distinctive matriarchal speech, here universalized to all generations.
sourceText: Leah said, “Happy am I, for the daughters will call me happy.” She named him Asher.

note: 'Holy is his name' quotes Psalm 111:9, 'holy and awesome is his name' (cf. Psalm 99:3). The fixed liturgical predication of the divine name gives high volume; Psalm 111 also feeds the Benedictus (1:68), showing recurrence.
sourceText: He has sent redemption to his people. He has ordained his covenant forever. His name is holy and awesome!

note: 'He who is mighty has done great things for me' echoes 'The Lord has done great things for us; we are glad' (Psalm 126:2-3). The great-things-the-Lord-has-done formula is a coherent psalmic source for the canticle's praise.
sourceText: Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing. Then they said among the nations, “Yahweh has done great things for them.” Yahweh has done great things for us, and we are glad.

note: 'He... has done great things for me' also recalls 'He is your praise; he is your God, who has done for you these great and awesome things' (Deuteronomy 10:21). A further great-deeds source coherent with the doxological tone.
sourceText: He is your praise, and he is your God, who has done for you these great and awesome things, which your eyes have seen.

note: 'His mercy is for generations of generations on those who fear him' quotes Psalm 103:17, 'the steadfast love of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him.' The mercy + on-those-who-fear-him + perpetual-generations combination is high-volume and distinctive.
sourceText: But Yahweh’s loving kindness is from everlasting to everlasting with those who fear him, his righteousness to children’s children;

note: 'His mercy is for generations... on those who fear him' echoes the Decalogue's promise of steadfast love 'to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments' (Exodus 20:6; Deuteronomy 5:10). The covenant mercy-to-generations formula coheres with Psalm 103.
sourceText: and showing loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.

note: 'He has shown strength with his arm. He has scattered the proud' echoes Psalm 89:10, 'you scattered your enemies with your mighty arm.' The arm + scatter combination is distinctive, and Psalm 89 (Davidic covenant) coheres with the chapter's throne themes; high volume.
sourceText: You have broken Rahab in pieces, like one of the slain. You have scattered your enemies with your mighty arm.

note: 'He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts' draws on Hannah's warning, 'Talk no more so very proudly... the bows of the mighty are broken' (1 Samuel 2:3-4). The humbling-of-the-arrogant motif is structurally central to Hannah's Song, the canticle's master text.
sourceText: “Talk no more so exceeding proudly. Don’t let arrogance come out of your mouth, For Yahweh is a God of knowledge. By him actions are weighed. “The bows of the mighty men are broken. Those who stumbled are armed with strength.

note: 'He has put down princes from their thrones, and has exalted the lowly' directly reworks Hannah: 'The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts. He raises up the poor from the dust... to make them sit with princes' (1 Samuel 2:7-8). High volume; the great-reversal heart of the Magnificat.
sourceText: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up. He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.

note: 'He has filled the hungry with good things. He has sent the rich away empty' reworks Hannah's 'those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but the hungry have ceased to hunger' (1 Samuel 2:5). The hungry-filled / sated-emptied antithesis is high-volume and distinctive.
sourceText: Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread. Those who were hungry are satisfied. Yes, the barren has borne seven. She who has many children languishes.

note: 'He has filled the hungry with good things' quotes Psalm 107:9, 'he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things.' Near-verbatim; a strong psalmic doublet to the Hannah hunger-reversal.
sourceText: For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good.

note: 'He has put down princes from their thrones' echoes Job 12:19, 'he leads priests away stripped and overthrows the mighty.' Job 12's catalogue of God's reversal of the powerful (12:14-25) coheres with the Magnificat's social inversion; a focused supporting allusion.
sourceText: He leads priests away stripped, and overthrows the mighty.

note: 'He has put down princes from their thrones' closely matches Sirach 10:14, 'The Lord has cast down the thrones of rulers, and has seated the lowly in their place.' A deuterocanonical near-parallel with the throne-down / lowly-up structure; strong coherence, moderate independent volume.
sourceText: The Lord cast down the thrones of rulers, And set the meek in their stead.

note: 'Has exalted the lowly' reflects Psalm 113:7-8, 'He raises the poor from the dust... to make them sit with princes.' Psalm 113 (a Hallel psalm) shares both the lifting-the-lowly motif and its own debt to Hannah; high volume within the reversal cluster.
sourceText: He raises up the poor out of the dust. Lifts up the needy from the ash heap; that he may set him with princes, even with the princes of his people.

note: 'Put down princes from their thrones... exalted the lowly' echoes Ezekiel 21:26, 'exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.' The abase-the-high / exalt-the-low formula coheres with the inversion theme as a prophetic supporting echo.
sourceText: thus says the Lord Yahweh: Remove the turban, and take off the crown; this will not be as it was; exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.

note: 'He has given help to Israel, his servant' draws on Isaiah 41:8-9, 'But you, Israel, my servant... whom I have taken... I have chosen you and not cast you off.' The Israel-my-servant designation plus God's helping/upholding (Isaiah 41:10) gives high volume for the canticle's turn to corporate Israel.
sourceText: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend, You whom I have taken hold of from the ends of the earth, and called from its corners, and said to you, ‘You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you away;’

note: 'That he might remember mercy' quotes Psalm 98:3, 'He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel.' The remembered-mercy-to-Israel formula is distinctive and rounds off the canticle's covenant-faithfulness theme.
sourceText: He has remembered his loving kindness and his faithfulness toward the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.

note: 'As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his seed forever' echoes Micah 7:20, 'You will show faithfulness to Jacob and steadfast love to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old.' The mercy-to-Abraham-as-sworn-to-the-fathers structure is high-volume and concludes both hymns (cf. 1:73).
sourceText: You will give truth to Jacob, and mercy to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old.

note: 'To Abraham and his seed forever' takes up the Abrahamic covenant, 'to be God to you and to your offspring after you... an everlasting covenant' (Genesis 17:7; cf. 13:15). The to-Abraham-and-his-seed-forever formula is distinctive covenant language; high volume.
sourceText: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.

note: 'And his seed forever' also recalls the oath at the Aqedah, 'I will surely multiply your offspring' (Genesis 22:17), the same sworn promise the Benedictus names explicitly at 1:73. A coherent supporting echo binding Magnificat and Benedictus.
sourceText: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies.

note: 'Mary stayed with her about three months' parallels the ark of God remaining 'in the house of Obed-edom... three months' (2 Samuel 6:11). Combined with the ark allusions of 1:43-44, the three-month notice supports the Mary-as-ark typology; figural and contested.
sourceText: Yahweh’s ark remained in the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite three months: and Yahweh blessed Obed-Edom, and all his house.

note: 'The time that Elizabeth should give birth was fulfilled, and she gave birth to a son' echoes 'When her days to give birth were fulfilled' (Genesis 25:24, Rebekah; cf. 21:1-2, Sarah). The fulfilled-days birth formula situates John's birth within the patriarchal-birth pattern.
sourceText: When her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb.

note: 'Her neighbors and her relatives... rejoiced with her' recalls Sarah at Isaac's birth, 'God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh (rejoice) with me' (Genesis 21:6). The community-rejoices-with-the-mother motif coheres with the Isaac typology running through the John narrative.
sourceText: Sarah said, “God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.”

note: The neighbor-women's joy and involvement in acclaiming and naming the child echoes Ruth 4:14-17, where 'the women of the neighborhood gave him a name.' The communal naming scene is a coherent supporting echo for 1:58-61.
sourceText: The women said to Naomi, “Blessed be Yahweh, who has not left you this day without a near kinsman; and let his name be famous in Israel. He shall be to you a restorer of life, and sustain you in your old age, for your daughter-in-law, who loves you, who is better to you than seven sons, has borne him.” Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse to it. The women, her neighbors, gave him a name, saying, “There is a son born to Naomi”; […]

note: 'On the eighth day, they came to circumcise the child' enacts the Abrahamic covenant requirement, 'He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised' (Genesis 17:12). The precise eighth-day specification gives high volume and roots John in covenant fidelity.
sourceText: He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed.

note: The eighth-day circumcision also fulfills the Levitical statute, 'on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised' (Leviticus 12:3). High-volume legal citation reinforcing the family's Torah observance.
sourceText: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.

note: 'What then will this child be?' echoes Manoah's question about Samson, 'What is to be the child's rule of life, and what is he to do?' (Judges 13:12). The wonder-about-the-destined-child question coheres with the Samson birth type-scene already shaping John.
sourceText: Manoah said, “Now let your words happen. What shall the child’s way of life and mission be?”

note: 'The hand of the Lord was with him' uses the idiom for prophetic empowerment, e.g. 'the hand of the Lord was on Elijah' (1 Kings 18:46; cf. Ezekiel 1:3; 3:14). Given the explicit Elijah typology of 1:17, the hand-of-the-Lord notice fittingly marks John's prophetic endowment.
sourceText: The hand of Yahweh was on Elijah; and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.

note: 'Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel' quotes the berakah formula of Psalm 41:13, 'Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting' (cf. 72:18; 106:48). The fixed liturgical benediction opening gives high volume; it is the canonical doxology closing Books of the Psalter.
sourceText: Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting and to everlasting! Amen and amen.

note: 'Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel' equally matches Psalm 106:48; Psalm 106 also supplies 1:71-72 (saved from enemies, remembered covenant), so its presence here strengthens recurrence across the Benedictus.
sourceText: Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting even to everlasting! Let all the people say, “Amen.” Praise Yah!

note: 'He has visited and worked redemption for his people' quotes Psalm 111:9, 'He sent redemption to his people; he has commanded his covenant forever.' The redemption-to-his-people + everlasting-covenant pairing (cf. 1:72) gives high volume; Psalm 111 also undergirds 'holy is his name' at 1:49.
sourceText: He has sent redemption to his people. He has ordained his covenant forever. His name is holy and awesome!

note: 'He has visited (epeskepsato)... his people' echoes the Exodus visitation, 'the Lord had visited the people of Israel' to deliver them (Exodus 4:31; cf. Genesis 50:24-25). The divine-visitation-for-rescue idiom frames the redemption as a new exodus.
sourceText: The people believed, and when they heard that Yahweh had visited the children of Israel, and that he had seen their affliction, then they bowed their heads and worshiped.

note: 'Raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David' draws on Psalm 132:17, 'There I will make a horn to sprout for David.' The horn + David-my-servant combination is distinctive royal-messianic imagery; high volume.
sourceText: There I will make the horn of David to bud. I have ordained a lamp for my anointed.

note: The 'horn of salvation' echoes Hannah's closing line, 'he will... exalt the horn of his anointed' (1 Samuel 2:10). The horn-of-the-anointed image binds the Benedictus to Hannah's Song as the Magnificat was bound; strong recurrence.
sourceText: Those who strive with Yahweh shall be broken to pieces. He will thunder against them in the sky. “Yahweh will judge the ends of the earth. He will give strength to his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed.”

note: 'Horn of salvation' also matches David's 'the horn of my salvation' (Psalm 18:2; 2 Samuel 22:3). A coherent Davidic echo within the horn cluster, fitting the in-the-house-of-David context.
sourceText: Yahweh is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge; my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my high tower.

note: 'Salvation from our enemies, and from the hand of all who hate us' quotes Psalm 106:10, 'he saved them from the hand of the foe and redeemed them from the power of the enemy.' The saved-from-the-hand-of-haters/enemies formula is high-volume and new-exodus in tone.
sourceText: He saved them from the hand of him who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.

note: 'Salvation from our enemies' echoes 'He delivered me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me' (Psalm 18:17; 2 Samuel 22:18), a Davidic deliverance text coherent with the horn-of-David context.
sourceText: He delivered me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me; for they were too mighty for me.

note: 'To remember his holy covenant' echoes Leviticus 26:42, 'then I will remember my covenant with Jacob... Isaac... Abraham.' The God-remembers-his-covenant-with-the-patriarchs formula gives high volume and leads directly into the Abraham oath of 1:73.
sourceText: then I will remember my covenant with Jacob; and also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham; and I will remember the land.

note: 'To remember his holy covenant' also quotes Psalm 106:45, 'For their sake he remembered his covenant.' Combined with 1:71's debt to Psalm 106:10, this confirms Psalm 106 as a sustained source of the Benedictus.
sourceText: He remembered for them his covenant, and repented according to the multitude of his loving kindnesses.

note: 'To remember his holy covenant' recalls 'God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob' at the Exodus (Exodus 2:24). The remembered-covenant-precipitating-deliverance motif coheres with the new-exodus framing.
sourceText: God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.

note: 'The oath which he spoke to Abraham, our father' names the sworn promise of Genesis 22:16-17, 'By myself I have sworn... I will surely bless you and multiply your offspring.' The oath-to-Abraham reference is distinctive and high-volume, fulfilling the Magnificat's 'to Abraham and his seed forever' (1:55).
sourceText: and said, “I have sworn by myself, says Yahweh, because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son, that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies.

note: 'The oath which he spoke to Abraham' echoes Psalm 105:9, 'the covenant he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac.' Psalm 105 rehearses covenant + oath + remembering (105:8-9), tightly coherent with 1:72-73; high volume.
sourceText: the covenant which he made with Abraham, his oath to Isaac,

note: 'The oath which he spoke to Abraham, our father' recalls Micah 7:20, the steadfast love sworn 'to Abraham... to our fathers from the days of old.' Recurrence with 1:55 (which leans on the same verse) reinforces the Micah source across both canticles.
sourceText: You will give truth to Jacob, and mercy to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old.

note: 'The oath which he spoke to Abraham' echoes Jeremiah 11:5, 'that I may confirm the oath that I swore to your fathers.' The confirm-the-oath-to-the-fathers diction coheres with the covenant-remembrance theme as a supporting echo.
sourceText: that I may establish the oath which I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as at this day. Then answered I, and said, Amen, Yahweh.

note: 'That we... should serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness' echoes the covenant summons to 'serve the Lord in sincerity and in faithfulness' (Joshua 24:14). The serve-God-faithfully ideal coheres with the exodus-deliverance-unto-worship logic of 1:74-75.
sourceText: “Now therefore fear Yahweh, and serve him in sincerity and in truth. Put away the gods which your fathers served beyond the River, in Egypt; and serve Yahweh.

note: 'In holiness and righteousness before him' closely matches Wisdom 9:3, that humankind should 'rule... in holiness and righteousness.' The paired virtue-formula (hosiotes + dikaiosyne) is distinctive and Second-Temple; the link is a strong-coherence but contested deuterocanonical echo.
sourceText: And rule the world in holiness and righteousness, And execute judgement in uprightness of soul;

note: 'Delivered out of the hand of our enemies, should serve him' reflects the exodus pattern 'let my son go that he may serve me' (Exodus 4:23; 8:1), where rescue is for the purpose of worship. The deliverance-unto-service logic coheres, but the diction is generic, so it is a faint echo.
sourceText: and I have said to you, “Let my son go, that he may serve me”; and you have refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”

note: 'You will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways' cites Malachi 3:1, 'Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me.' Near-verbatim go-before + prepare-the-way language; recurrence with 1:17 confirms Malachi as the defining text for the Baptist's role.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'To prepare his ways' draws on Isaiah 40:3, 'prepare the way of the Lord, make straight... a highway,' the prophecy Luke later applies explicitly to John (Luke 3:4). High volume; the prepare-the-way-of-the-Lord motif fuses with Malachi 3:1 here.
sourceText: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.

note: 'To give knowledge of salvation to his people by the remission of their sins' echoes the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:34, 'they shall all know me... I will forgive their iniquity.' The knowledge-of-God + forgiveness-of-sins pairing coheres with the covenant-fulfillment theme of the Benedictus.
sourceText: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin will I remember no more.

note: 'Salvation to his people by the remission of their sins' echoes Psalm 130:7-8, 'with him is plentiful redemption. And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.' The redeem-Israel-from-its-sins formula is a coherent psalmic source for the forgiveness clause.
sourceText: Israel, hope in Yahweh, for with Yahweh there is loving kindness. With him is abundant redemption. He will redeem Israel from all their sins.

note: 'The dawn (anatole) from on high will visit us, to shine on those who sit in darkness' draws on Malachi 4:2, 'the sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in its wings.' The rising-light-of-salvation imagery, distinctive and eschatological, gives high volume to the anatole metaphor.
sourceText: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.

note: 'The dawn from on high' plays on the messianic rising-star/sceptre of Numbers 24:17, 'a star shall come out of Jacob' (LXX 'a star shall rise/anatelei'). The anatole wordplay activates this Balaam oracle as a messianic-advent source; moderate volume via the LXX cognate.
sourceText: I see him, but not now. I see him, but not near. A star will come out of Jacob. A scepter will rise out of Israel, and shall strike through the corners of Moab, and break down all the sons of Sheth.

note: The noun anatole ('dawn'/'branch') evokes 'my servant the Branch' (anatole, Zechariah 3:8; 6:12), the Davidic shoot. The double meaning of anatole lets Luke fuse dawn and Davidic-branch messianism; a coherent allusion via shared LXX vocabulary.
sourceText: Hear now, Joshua the high priest, you and your fellows who sit before you; for they are men who are a sign: for, behold, I will bring out my servant, the Branch.

note: 'The dawn (anatole) from on high' specifically echoes Zechariah 6:12, 'Behold, the man whose name is the Branch (anatole)... he shall build the temple of the Lord.' The exact LXX noun for the Davidic Branch strengthens the messianic reading; moderate volume.
sourceText: and speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple;

note: 'The dawn from on high' may also evoke the 'righteous Branch' raised up for David in Jeremiah 23:5 (LXX anatole at 23:5/33:15). The Davidic-branch coherence is good but the link is mediated through Zechariah's clearer anatole usage, so it is a faint contested echo.
sourceText: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will raise to David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.

note: 'To shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death' draws on Isaiah 9:2, 'the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in the land of deep darkness (shadow of death), on them has light shined.' Distinctive darkness/shadow-of-death + light combination; high volume.
sourceText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: 'Those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death' quotes Psalm 107:10, 'some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death,' whom God then delivers (107:14). The verbatim sit-in-darkness-and-shadow-of-death phrase gives high volume.
sourceText: Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron,

note: 'To shine on those who sit in darkness' echoes the Servant's commission 'to bring out... from the prison those who sit in darkness' (Isaiah 42:7). The Servant-as-light-to-those-in-darkness theme coheres with the salvation-dawn imagery.
sourceText: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: 'The dawn from on high will visit us, to shine' echoes Isaiah 58:8, 'then shall your light break forth like the dawn.' The light-breaks-forth-like-dawn imagery contributes to the anatole metaphor; a coherent supporting echo.
sourceText: Then your light shall break out as the morning, and your healing shall spring out speedily; and your righteousness shall go before you; Yahweh’s glory shall be your rear guard.

note: 'The dawn... will shine on those who sit in darkness' echoes Isaiah 60:1-2, 'Arise, shine, for your light has come... darkness shall cover the earth... but the Lord will arise upon you.' The light-rising-over-darkness imagery coheres with the eschatological-dawn theme.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you.

note: 'To guide our feet into the way of peace' echoes Isaiah 59:8, 'The way of peace they do not know,' the very condition the dawn now reverses. The way-of-peace diction is distinctive enough to register as a focused echo.
sourceText: The way of peace they don’t know; and there is no justice in their goings: they have made them crooked paths; whoever goes therein does not know peace.

note: 'To guide our feet into the way of peace' faintly echoes 'He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way' (Psalm 25:9; cf. 25:4). The God-guides-in-the-way motif coheres, but the diction is generic, making this a low contested echo.
sourceText: He will guide the humble in justice. He will teach the humble his way.

note: 'The child was growing, and becoming strong in spirit' echoes the refrain about Samuel, 'the child Samuel grew... and grew in the presence of the Lord' (1 Samuel 2:21,26; 3:19). The child-grew summary, tied to the Hannah/Samuel matrix governing the chapter, gives high volume.
sourceText: Yahweh visited Hannah, and she conceived, and bore three sons and two daughters. The child Samuel grew before Yahweh.

note: 'The child was growing, and becoming strong in spirit' parallels 'the woman bore a son and called his name Samson. And the young man grew, and the Lord blessed him. And the Spirit of the Lord began to stir him' (Judges 13:24-25). The grew + Spirit notice closes the Samson-style annunciation cycle; high volume.
sourceText: The woman bore a son, and named him Samson: and the child grew, and Yahweh blessed him. The Spirit of Yahweh began to move him in Mahaneh Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.

note: Luke locates the birth in 'Bethlehem... the city of David,' the very town Micah names as the origin of the ruler 'whose goings forth are from of old.' Volume is high (the place-name itself), recurrence strong in the early-Jewish messianic reading of Micah, and thematic coherence exact: a Davidic ruler from Bethlehem. Luke leaves the citation implicit rather than quoting, but the topographic anchor is unmistakable.
sourceText: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings out are from of old, from ancient times.

note: Joseph belongs 'to the house and family of David,' and Jesus is born in David's city, activating Nathan's oracle of an everlasting Davidic throne. Coherence with Gabriel's earlier promise (1:32-33, intra-Lukan) shows Luke reading the Nathan dynastic covenant as availability; volume here is the repeated 'David' framing across vv. 4-11.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]

note: David himself was found and anointed at Bethlehem among the family of Jesse, so Bethlehem functions as the appointed site where God designates the true king over against appearances. The thematic link (humble Bethlehem origin of the LORD's chosen) is coherent, though Luke makes no verbal contact with the Samuel narrative.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.”

note: Bethlehem is the setting of Ruth, whose closing genealogy issues in David; the elders' blessing invokes building up the house of Israel in Bethlehem (Ephrathah). The connection is figural and dynastic rather than verbal, hence faint, but it belongs to the Bethlehem-David availability cluster Luke is drawing on.
sourceText: All the people who were in the gate, and the elders, said, “We are witnesses. May Yahweh make the woman who has come into your house like Rachel and like Leah, which two built the house of Israel; and treat you worthily in Ephrathah, and be famous in Bethlehem.

note: Luke pointedly calls Jesus Mary's 'firstborn son' (prototokos), the same charged term governing the consecration of every firstborn to the LORD in Exodus. The label anticipates the redemption/presentation in vv. 22-23, so its volume is reinforced by recurrence within the chapter; coherence with the firstborn-belongs-to-God theme is high.
sourceText: “Sanctify to me all of the firstborn, whatever opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and of animal. It is mine.”

note: The detail that the infant is laid in a phatne (feeding trough/manger) has long been read against Isaiah's 'the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger,' a contrast between dumb beasts who recognize and an Israel that does not. The link is interpretive rather than lexically secured by Luke, so it is faint and contested, but the manger word supplies real verbal contact.
sourceText: The ox knows his owner, and the donkey his master’s crib; but Israel doesn’t know, my people don’t consider.”

note: The shepherds 'keeping watch over their flock' near Bethlehem evoke Micah's 'tower of the flock' (Migdal Eder), traditionally located by Bethlehem and read messianically as the place where kingship returns. Verbal contact is slight in Greek, so the echo is faint, but the Bethlehem-shepherd-king geography is thematically coherent.
sourceText: You, tower of the flock, the hill of the daughter of Zion, to you it will come, yes, the former dominion will come, the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem.

note: Shepherds first receive the Davidic birth announcement, fittingly because David was taken 'from following the sheep' to shepherd Israel. The motif of the shepherd-king frames the angel's proclamation of a 'Savior... in the city of David'; coherence is high, though the link is conceptual rather than quoted.
sourceText: Now therefore you shall tell my servant David this, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “I took you from the sheep pen, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people, over Israel.

note: 'The glory of the LORD shone around them' renders the Septuagintal doxa kyriou, the visible Sinai/tabernacle glory that settled and shone. Luke uses the technical theophany vocabulary, giving real volume; coherence is high as the kabod now attends the announcement of salvation.
sourceText: Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.

note: The angel announces a child born 'this day' who is 'Savior... Christ the Lord' bringing 'great joy' and 'peace,' the cluster of Isaiah's oracle of the child born to us, called the Prince of Peace, on whose shoulder the government rests. Coherence is exact (birth, joy, peace, Davidic rule) and the theme recurs across the infancy account, giving strong volume despite no formula quotation.
sourceText: For to us a child is born. To us a son is given; and the government will be on his shoulders. His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.

note: 'Good news of great joy' echoes Isaiah's 'they rejoice before you... as men rejoice when they divide the spoil,' the joy attending the breaking of the oppressor's yoke in the same Immanuel oracle that names the child. The joy-language strengthens the broader Isaiah 9 allusion in this pericope.
sourceText: You have multiplied the nation. You have increased their joy. They rejoice before you according to the joy in harvest, as men rejoice when they divide the plunder.

note: The angel 'brings good news' (euangelizomai) of peace and salvation, the very verb-and-content of Isaiah's herald who publishes peace and announces 'your God reigns.' Septuagintal availability is direct and the salvation/peace coherence is strong; Luke universalizes it to 'all the people.'
sourceText: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

note: The Gloria's 'on earth peace' set beside the heavenly host's praise recalls the psalm in which the LORD enthroned amid the heavenly beings 'gives strength to his people' and 'blesses his people with peace.' The host-of-heaven plus peace pairing is coherent though the verbal contact is thin, so it is a faint supporting echo.
sourceText: Yahweh will give strength to his people. Yahweh will bless his people with peace.

note: The 'multitude of the heavenly army' crying 'Glory to God in the highest' resembles the seraphim antiphon 'Holy... the whole earth is full of his glory,' a heavenly liturgy proclaiming God's glory over the earth. The pattern (angelic chorus, glory, earth) is coherent though Luke's wording is independent.
sourceText: One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”

note: 'Glory to God in the highest' with the angelic host praising parallels the psalm's call to 'praise him in the heights... praise him, all his hosts/angels.' The heights/host/praise vocabulary is coherent, supplying a plausible liturgical backdrop to the Gloria, though faint as direct source.
sourceText: Praise Yah! Praise Yahweh from the heavens! Praise him in the heights! Praise him, all his angels! Praise him, all his army!

note: Naming Jesus 'Savior... Christ (anointed) the Lord' in David's city recalls the anointing of David at Bethlehem when the Spirit rushed upon him. The christos-David-Bethlehem nexus is coherent within the chapter's Davidic frame, though no verbal echo is pressed.
sourceText: Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brothers: and the Spirit of Yahweh came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up, and went to Ramah.

note: 'Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart' resembles Jacob who 'kept the saying in mind' after Joseph's dreams (LXX: dieterei to rhema). The verbal pattern (keeping/treasuring a rhema) is close and recurs at 2:51, giving recurrence, though the motif is also a general wisdom convention, so the specific source is contested.
sourceText: His brothers envied him, but his father kept this saying in mind.

note: Mary's treasuring the matter 'in her heart' parallels Daniel who 'kept the matter in my heart' (LXX) after a revelation he did not fully grasp. The apocalyptic reticence-and-treasuring motif coheres with Luke's portrayal of a not-yet-understood revelation, but the link is faint.
sourceText: Here is the end of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts much troubled me, and my face was changed in me: but I kept the matter in my heart.

note: The shepherds 'returned, glorifying and praising God' and publishing the saying recalls the psalmist's vow to 'declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will praise you.' The proclaim-and-praise pattern is coherent but generic, so a faint echo at best.
sourceText: I will declare your name to my brothers. In the midst of the assembly, I will praise you.

note: Jesus is circumcised 'when eight days were fulfilled,' the precise Abrahamic stipulation that every male be circumcised on the eighth day as the sign of the covenant. Volume is high (the eighth-day specification) and coherence exact: Jesus is incorporated into the covenant of Abraham.
sourceText: He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed.

note: The eighth-day circumcision restates the Mosaic legislation, 'on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised,' which also frames the purification timeline taken up in the next pericope. Direct legal availability and exact coherence make this a strong allusion.
sourceText: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.

note: That the child's 'name was called' as commanded by the angel before conception echoes the divine naming of Isaac ('you shall call his name Isaac') announced before his birth. The angel-given name-before-birth pattern is coherent with the Isaac annunciation type-scene Luke is reworking.
sourceText: God said, “No, but Sarah, your wife, will bear you a son. You shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant for his seed after him.

note: 'The days of their purification according to the law of Moses' are exactly Leviticus 12's prescription for the mother's purification after childbirth, culminating in a burnt offering and a sin offering. Volume and availability are maximal since Luke is paraphrasing the statute; coherence is total.
sourceText: “‘When the days of her purification are completed, for a son, or for a daughter, she shall bring to the priest at the door of the Tent of Meeting, a year old lamb for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon, or a turtledove, for a sin offering:

note: Luke quotes the offering 'a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,' the Levitical concession for those who cannot afford a lamb. This is the explicit nearer source of v. 24's citation and signals the holy family's poverty; it is a near-verbatim quotation introduced by 'as is said in the law.'
sourceText: If she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves, or two young pigeons; the one for a burnt offering, and the other for a sin offering: and the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean.’”

note: 'Every male who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord' renders the consecration of the firstborn, 'sanctify to me every firstborn that opens the womb.' Luke marks it 'as it is written,' so this is a formal quotation; the firstborn-belongs-to-God theme tracks the prototokos of v. 7.
sourceText: “Sanctify to me all of the firstborn, whatever opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and of animal. It is mine.”

note: The presentation of the firstborn to the Lord enacts the Exodus mandate to set apart every firstborn that opens the womb because the LORD spared Israel's firstborn at the Passover. Coherence is exact and the redemptive backstory (firstborn spared by blood) resonates with Luke's larger soteriology.
sourceText: that you shall set apart to Yahweh all that opens the womb, and every firstborn which you have that comes from an animal. The males shall be Yahweh’s. Every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb; and if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck; and you shall redeem all the firstborn of man among your sons. It shall be, when your son asks you in time to come, saying, ‘What is this?’ that you shall tell him, ‘By strength of hand […]

note: The redemption of the firstborn human (to be redeemed at a set price) underlies bringing Jesus 'to present him to the Lord'; Numbers spells out that every firstborn is the LORD's and must be redeemed. This is the priestly legislation completing the Exodus firstborn command Luke invokes.
sourceText: Everything that opens the womb, of all flesh which they offer to Yahweh, both of man and animal shall be yours. Nevertheless, you shall surely redeem the firstborn of man, and you shall redeem the firstborn of unclean animals. You shall redeem those who are to be redeemed of them from a month old, according to your estimation, for five shekels of money, after the shekel of the sanctuary, which weighs twenty gerahs.

note: Bringing the child up to the sanctuary and presenting him 'to the Lord' strongly recalls Hannah bringing Samuel and 'lending' him to the LORD; Luke's whole infancy narrative is patterned on 1 Samuel (Magnificat on Hannah's song). Recurrence of the Samuel template gives this real weight beyond the bare legal citations.
sourceText: When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, with three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and a bottle of wine, and brought him to Yahweh’s house in Shiloh. The child was young. They killed the bull, and brought the child to Eli. She said, “Oh, my lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to Yahweh. For this child I prayed; and Yahweh has given me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore also I have granted him […]

note: The restated covenant law that 'all that opens the womb is mine' and the firstborn must be redeemed reinforces v. 23's quotation; the doublet across Exodus 13 and 34 supplies recurrence for the firstborn-consecration theme Luke foregrounds.
sourceText: “All that opens the womb is mine; and all your livestock that is male, the firstborn of cow and sheep. The firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb: and if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck. All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. No one shall appear before me empty.

note: When 'they brought him up to Jerusalem... to the temple,' Luke begins to stage Malachi's promise that 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple,' a theme that climaxes in Simeon and Anna meeting him there. The temple-arrival coherence is strong and recurs through vv. 25-38, though it is set up rather than quoted here.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Simeon is 'looking for the consolation (paraklesis) of Israel,' the exact Septuagintal keynote of Isaiah's 'Comfort, comfort my people.' Volume is high (the noun consolation), the Isaiah background recurs throughout the Nunc Dimittis, and coherence is exact: the end of exile-comfort arrives in the child.
sourceText: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.

note: 'Now you are releasing your servant... in peace; for my eyes have seen...' draws on the promise that Abraham would 'go to his fathers in peace' once God's word was fulfilled. The depart-in-peace-after-seeing-the-promise pattern is coherent, supplying the form of Simeon's release.
sourceText: but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried in a good old age.

note: Simeon's readiness to die having seen salvation closely parallels Jacob: 'Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.' The see-then-ready-to-die formula is verbally and thematically close, a strong candidate alongside Genesis 15:15 for the source of the Nunc Dimittis opening.
sourceText: Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.”

note: 'My eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples' renders Isaiah's 'all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God,' where the LORD bares his arm 'before all the nations.' The seeing-of-God's-salvation-before-all-nations cluster is verbally and thematically exact.
sourceText: Yahweh has made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.

note: 'A light for revelation to the nations (Gentiles), and the glory of your people Israel' fuses the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' with Israel's restoration. Volume and coherence are very high; this is among the clearest OT echoes in the chapter.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: The Servant given 'as a light to the nations' (and a covenant to the people) directly informs Simeon's 'light for revelation to the nations.' The doublet with Isaiah 49:6 supplies recurrence; the universal-light-of-salvation theme coheres exactly with Luke's program of salvation reaching the Gentiles.
sourceText: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations;

note: 'I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory' supplies the second half of Simeon's couplet, 'the glory of your people Israel,' pairing salvation with Israel's glory. The salvation-and-glory-of-Israel coherence and Septuagintal availability make this a solid supporting allusion.
sourceText: I bring near my righteousness, it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not wait; and I will place salvation in Zion for Israel my glory.

note: Simeon's 'my eyes have seen your salvation... before the face of all peoples' echoes 'the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together.' The universal-seeing-of-revealed-glory theme reinforces the broader Isaiah 40-55 matrix of the Nunc Dimittis.
sourceText: Yahweh’s glory shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together; for the mouth of Yahweh has spoken it.”

note: 'This is our God; we have waited for him... let us be glad in his salvation' parallels the waiting Simeon who finally sees God's salvation. The wait-then-rejoice-in-salvation pattern is coherent, though it is a faint supporting echo within the strong Isaianic cluster.
sourceText: It shall be said in that day, “Behold, this is our God! We have waited for him, and he will save us! This is Yahweh! We have waited for him. We will be glad and rejoice in his salvation!”

note: Simeon's oracle that the child is 'set for the falling and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign spoken against' draws on Isaiah's stone that becomes 'a sanctuary, but a stone of offense... many shall stumble and fall.' The fall/rise division of Israel over the sign is verbally and thematically coherent, a key prophetic warrant for Luke's divided-Israel theme.
sourceText: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”

note: The 'sign spoken against' over which many fall and rise also draws on the tested cornerstone laid in Zion, which becomes the criterion of standing or stumbling. Paired with Isaiah 8 this supplies the stone-of-decision motif; coherence is strong though Luke does not quote it.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: The 'sword' that 'will pierce through your own soul' has been linked to Ezekiel's recurring 'a sword shall pass through the land,' a figure of sifting judgment that divides. The sword-of-division imagery coheres with the falling-and-rising oracle, though the application to Mary's soul is distinctively Lukan, so the source is faint.
sourceText: Or if I bring a sword on that land, and say, Sword, go through the land; so that I cut off from it man and animal;

note: The piercing 'sword' anticipating grief over the child has been read against Zechariah's 'they shall look on me whom they have pierced, and mourn,' associated with a future piercing of the LORD's chosen. The piercing-and-mourning link is suggestive but indirect here, hence a contested faint echo.
sourceText: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

note: 'A sword will pierce through your own soul' may color itself with the psalm's idiom that the wicked's 'sword shall enter their own heart.' The sword-into-the-soul phrasing offers verbal contact, but the sense differs (Mary's anguish vs. the wicked's self-destruction), so the echo is faint.
sourceText: Their sword shall enter into their own heart. Their bows shall be broken.

note: Simeon meets the child precisely in the temple, fulfilling 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple,' which Malachi pairs with a refining that tests Israel, coherent with the falling-and-rising oracle. The temple-coming-as-test theme recurs with Anna in the next pericope, giving it recurrence.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Anna, a long-widowed woman of great age devoted to fasting and prayer, closely matches Judith, a widow who lived chastely many years, fasted often, and feared God greatly. The pious-aged-widow type is coherent and the fasting-and-prayer detail gives real volume; Luke seems to draw on the Second-Temple ideal Judith exemplifies.
sourceText: Judith was a widow in her house three years and four months. She made herself a tent upon the roof of her house, and put on sackcloth upon her loins. The garments of her widowhood were upon her. And she fasted all the days of her widowhood, except the eves of the Sabbaths, the Sabbaths, the eves of the new moons, the new moons, and the feasts and joyful days of the house of Israel. She was of a goodly countenance, and exceeding beautiful to behold. Her […]

note: Anna is introduced as 'a prophetess' (prophetis), the same title and role given to Miriam who leads Israel's praise. The prophetess-who-leads-thanksgiving pattern is coherent, situating Anna in the line of Israel's women prophets.
sourceText: Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dances.

note: Anna 'the prophetess' also recalls Deborah, 'a prophetess... judging Israel,' another woman bearing the prophetic office at a hinge of salvation history. The title link is real but generic across the female-prophet category, so it is a faint supporting echo to Miriam.
sourceText: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, she judged Israel at that time.

note: Anna speaks of the child 'to all who were looking for the redemption (lytrosis) of Jerusalem,' echoing Isaiah's 'the LORD has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.' The redemption-of-Jerusalem phrase has direct Septuagintal availability and pairs with Simeon's 'consolation of Israel,' giving the pericope a strong Isaianic frame.
sourceText: Break out into joy, sing together, you waste places of Jerusalem; for Yahweh has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.

note: 'Looking for the redemption of Jerusalem' also resonates with Isaiah's address to Jerusalem that her warfare is ended and iniquity pardoned. It belongs to the same Isaiah 40-52 consolation matrix as Simeon's oracle; faint as an independent source but coherent with the cluster.
sourceText: “Speak comfortably to Jerusalem; and call out to her that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received of Yahweh’s hand double for all her sins.”

note: Anna's name is the Greek form of Hannah, and her temple devotion of fasting and prayer mirrors Hannah's vow and worship at the sanctuary; Luke's infancy narrative is steeped in the Hannah/Samuel story. The onomastic and devotional link is suggestive though not pressed, so a faint echo.
sourceText: She vowed a vow, and said, “Yahweh of Armies, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your handmaid, and remember me, and not forget your handmaid, but will give to your handmaid a boy, then I will give him to Yahweh all the days of his life, and no razor shall come on his head.”

note: 'The child was growing, and was becoming strong... filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him' closely follows the boy Samuel who 'continued to grow... in favor with the LORD and with men.' The growth-and-favor formula is verbally and structurally parallel, and recurs at v. 52, giving strong recurrence within the chapter.
sourceText: The child Samuel grew on, and increased in favor both with Yahweh, and also with men.

note: 'The child grew, and the LORD blessed him' (Samson) supplies the same OT growth-of-the-promised-child notice that Luke reuses; together with 1 Samuel 2:26 it shows the type-scene of the divinely favored child maturing. Coherence with the annunciation-and-birth pattern is high.
sourceText: The woman bore a son, and named him Samson: and the child grew, and Yahweh blessed him.

note: That the child is 'filled with wisdom' and grows under God's grace faintly recalls the Nazirite child set apart to God from the womb in the Samson cycle; the link is the consecrated-child motif, supportive of the Samson allusion but not independently strong.
sourceText: but he said to me, ‘Behold, you shall conceive, and bear a son; and now drink no wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing; for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.’”

note: The family's annual Passover pilgrimage to Jerusalem enacts the Torah requirement that all appear before the LORD at the appointed feasts, the first being Unleavened Bread/Passover. The pilgrimage-feast obligation gives the scene its legal frame and coherence with Luke's law-observant family.
sourceText: You shall observe the feast of unleavened bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib (for in it you came out of Egypt), and no one shall appear before me empty.

note: Going up 'every year to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover' follows the Deuteronomic centralization of Passover at the place the LORD chooses, i.e., Jerusalem. Availability is direct and coherence exact for the pilgrimage detail in vv. 41-42.
sourceText: Observe the month of Abib, and keep the Passover to Yahweh your God; for in the month of Abib Yahweh your God brought you out of Egypt by night. You shall sacrifice the Passover to Yahweh your God, of the flock and the herd, in the place which Yahweh shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there. You shall eat no leavened bread with it. You shall eat unleavened bread with it seven days, even the bread of affliction; for you came out of the land of Egypt […]

note: The explicit Passover setting frames Jesus' first recorded words against the founding redemption feast, a figural touch given Luke's later Passion-Passover. The connection is contextual rather than verbal here, so a faint echo at this point in the narrative.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. note: The closing 'Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men' restates Samuel's growth 'in favor with the LORD and with men,' an inclusio with v. 40. Strong verbal parallel and double recurrence make this the chapter's clearest growth-formula allusion.
sourceText: The child Samuel grew on, and increased in favor both with Yahweh, and also with men.

note: The boy 'filled with wisdom,' astonishing the teachers and increasing 'in wisdom,' is colored by Wisdom's call to the children who keep her ways and find favor from the LORD. The wisdom-and-favor coherence is real but the sapiential coloring is diffuse, so a faint echo.
sourceText: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways. Hear instruction, and be wise. Don’t refuse it. Blessed is the man who hears me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at my door posts. For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh.

note: The precociously wise child amazing his elders resembles the ideal in Wisdom where the speaker, 'a child of good parts,' receives wisdom as a gift sought in the sanctuary. The early-wisdom motif is coherent within Second-Temple thought, though not a verbal source.
sourceText: Now I was a child of parts, and a good soul fell to my lot; Nay rather, being good, I came into a body undefiled. note: Jesus 'sitting in the midst of the teachers, both listening and asking questions' embodies Ben Sira's counsel to stand in the assembly of elders, attach oneself to the wise, and meditate on the law. The disciple-among-the-sages image coheres, but the link is thematic and faint.
sourceText: Stand you in the multitude of the elders; And whoso is wise, cleave you to him. Be willing to listen to every godly discourse; And don’t let the proverbs of understanding escape you. Let your mind dwell upon the ordinances of the Lord, And meditate continually in his commandments: He will establish your heart, And your desire of wisdom will be […]

note: Jesus is found in the temple declaring he 'must be in my Father's house,' the Lord present in his own temple as Malachi foretold and as Simeon's temple-encounter anticipated. The temple-claim coheres with the Father-Son relation Luke develops and recurs across the chapter's temple scenes.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Jesus' devotion to being 'in my Father's house' resonates with the psalmist's one desire 'to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life.' The longing-for-God's-house theme is coherent but generic, hence a faint supporting echo.
sourceText: One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after, that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.
