note: The Nazareth scroll reading 'The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor... release to the captives... recovering of sight to the blind... to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord' is a formal citation of Isaiah 61:1-2 (LXX). Highest Volume in the chapter; explicitly introduced as 'the book of the prophet Isaiah.'
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind; to declare the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompence; to comfort all that mourn;

note: The clause 'to deliver/set at liberty those who are crushed (oppressed)' is spliced in from Isaiah 58:6 (LXX 'aphesei tethrausmenous'), not part of Isa 61. The deliberate conflation of two 'release/aphesis' texts is a recognized Lukan composite citation; high Volume and verbatim LXX wording.
sourceText: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the bands of the yoke, and to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke?

note: 'To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord' and 'release/aphesis' evoke the Jubilee of Leviticus 25, when liberty is proclaimed and debts/captives released. Isaiah 61 itself draws on Jubilee language; Luke makes the year-of-release motif programmatic, giving strong Coherence and Availability.
sourceText: You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.

note: 'Recovering of sight to the blind' and 'release to the captives' resonate with the Servant's task in Isaiah 42:7 ('to open blind eyes, to bring out prisoners'). Recurrence of the Isaianic Servant/blindness motif strengthens this, though the wording is closest to Isa 61/LXX.
sourceText: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: The opening of blind eyes and hearing of the deaf in Isaiah 29:18 belongs to the cluster of Isaianic restoration texts Luke draws on for sight-to-the-blind. Faint and secondary to Isa 61, but coherent with Luke's Isaianic program.
sourceText: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.

note: The crowd's wonder at the 'gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth' faintly echoes Psalm 45:2 (LXX 44:3), 'grace is poured upon your lips.' Low Volume; the verbal overlap (grace + mouth/lips) is suggestive but the connection is contested.
sourceText: You are the most excellent of the sons of men. Grace has anointed your lips, therefore God has blessed you forever.

note: 'No prophet is acceptable in his hometown,' and the townsmen's coming murderous rejection, reflects the prophet-rejected-by-his-own pattern, e.g. Jeremiah's own people of Anathoth seeking his life (Jer 11:21). Faint, pattern-level allusion rather than verbal citation.
sourceText: Therefore thus says Yahweh concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, saying, You shall not prophesy in Yahweh’s name, that you not die by our hand;

note: 'When the sky was shut up three years and six months... a great famine' summarizes Elijah's drought announced in 1 Kings 17:1 (and ended in 18:1). Jesus names the era explicitly ('in the days of Elijah'); high Volume narrative citation.
sourceText: Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the foreigners of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”

note: 'Elijah was sent... to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow' directly retells 1 Kings 17:8-16, the widow of Zarephath. Explicit naming of place and figure makes this a high-Volume citation deployed as Gentile-inclusion precedent.
sourceText: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]

note: 'Naaman, the Syrian' cleansed of leprosy by Elisha retells 2 Kings 5:1-14. Named figure and event; high Volume, paired with the Zarephath widow to ground Jesus' point that prophets are sent to Gentiles when Israel rejects them.
sourceText: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]

note: The synagogue's murderous rage and attempt to throw Jesus off the cliff continues the rejected-prophet motif (cf. Israel killing the prophets, 1 Kings 19:10,14). Pattern-level echo reinforcing the Elijah framing just invoked; faint verbal contact.
sourceText: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

note: The demon's title 'the Holy One of God' (ho hagios tou theou) draws on the OT 'holy one' (LXX hosios) of Psalm 16:10 (LXX 15:10), a text Luke applies messianically in Acts 2:27. Coherence with Lukan Christology; medium because 'Holy One' also has wider OT roots (e.g. consecrated figures).
sourceText: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.

note: 'Holy one of God' may also echo the Nazirite consecration language ('a Nazirite/holy one of God', Judg 13:7 LXX), faintly punning on Jesus 'of Nazareth' in the demon's cry. Faint and contested but available in the LXX tradition.
sourceText: but he said to me, ‘Behold, you shall conceive, and bear a son; and now drink no wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing; for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.’”

note: Healings gathered 'when the sun was setting' may evoke Malachi 4:2 (LXX 3:20), 'the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings.' Faint and contested word-play on sun + healing; Luke's sunset detail is plausibly incidental, hence low confidence.
sourceText: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.

note: 'I must preach the good news of the Kingdom of God... for this reason I have been sent' echoes the commissioning of the Isaiah 61:1 herald ('he has sent me to preach good news') that opened the chapter. Inclusio-like Recurrence binding the chapter to its Isaianic program; faint as a standalone allusion.
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

note: Peter's reaction, falling at Jesus' knees and crying 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man,' replays the prophet's response to theophany: confrontation with the holy provokes confession of uncleanness ('Woe is me, for I am a man of unclean lips'). Both join recognition of divine presence to commissioning ('Don't be afraid... you will be catching people'). High volume and coherence with the call-narrative form.
sourceText: Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!”

note: The 'catching people alive' commission draws on the prophetic image of God sending fishermen to gather Israel ('I will send for many fishers, and they shall fish them'). The shared metaphor of human fishers as agents of God's ingathering gives volume; the call setting supplies coherence, though Jeremiah's image is originally one of judgment.
sourceText: Behold, I will send for many fishermen, says Yahweh, and they shall fish them up; and afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks.

note: Ezekiel's temple-river vision teems with fish and stations fishers from Engedi to Eneglaim, a figure of eschatological abundance and life flowing outward. The miraculous superabundant catch may echo this image of overflowing life as a sign of the new creation, though the verbal links are faint.
sourceText: It shall happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, shall live; and there shall be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea shall be healed, and everything shall live wherever the river comes. It shall happen, that fishermen shall stand by it: from En Gedi even to En Eglaim shall be a place for the spreading of nets; their fish shall be after their kinds, as the […]

note: Habakkuk likens people gathered by the conqueror to fish caught in a net and hauled up. The fishers-of-men motif may invert this image of catching for destruction into one of catching for life. Faint and contested; offered for the recurrence of the fish-net-people complex in the prophets.
sourceText: and make men like the fish of the sea, like the creeping things, that have no ruler over them? He takes up all of them with the hook. He catches them in his net, and gathers them in his dragnet. Therefore he rejoices and is glad.

note: Abraham's self-deprecation before the LORD ('I am but dust and ashes') models the creature's recognition of unworthiness in the divine presence, paralleling Peter's 'I am a sinful man.' The motif of the human cowering before manifest holiness is widely attested; low volume here.
sourceText: Abraham answered, “See now, I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord, who am but dust and ashes.

note: Gideon's fear at having seen the angel of the LORD face to face, answered by 'Peace, do not fear,' parallels the theophanic-fear-and-reassurance pattern (Jesus' 'Don't be afraid'). The form is recurrent across call narratives, lending coherence though the link to Luke 5 is general.
sourceText: Gideon saw that he was Yahweh’s angel; and Gideon said, “Alas, Lord Yahweh! Because I have seen Yahweh’s angel face to face!” Yahweh said to him, “Peace be to you! Don’t be afraid. You shall not die.”

note: The 'man full of leprosy' invokes the priestly diagnosis of skin disease and the resulting state of ritual uncleanness and exclusion. Luke's scene presupposes this legal world; the leper's plea 'you can make me clean' uses Levitical cleanness language directly.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, “When a man shall have a rising in his body’s skin, or a scab, or a bright spot, and it becomes in the skin of his body the plague of leprosy, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons, the priests: and the priest shall examine the plague in the skin of the body: and if the hair in the plague has turned white, and the appearance of the plague is deeper than the body’s skin, it is the […]

note: Jesus' command to 'show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing according to what Moses commanded' explicitly cites the Levitical rite for cleansing the leper (Lev 14:2-32). High volume: a near-direct reference to Mosaic legislation by name.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him, and behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper, then the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two living clean birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop. The priest shall command them to kill one of the birds in […]

note: Naaman the Syrian's cleansing from leprosy is the paradigmatic OT leprosy-healing and is explicitly invoked by Luke at 4:27, just before this scene. The healing of the leper here coheres with that recently activated narrative; Naaman's restored flesh and the prophet's mediation supply the type.
sourceText: Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.

note: Miriam's leprosy and Moses' intercessory plea ('Heal her, O God') present another instance where leprosy is removed by divine power at a mediator's word. Recurrence of the leprosy-healing motif gives some coherence, though no verbal contact with Luke.
sourceText: The cloud departed from over the Tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow. Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. Aaron said to Moses, “Oh, my lord, please don’t count this sin against us, in which we have done foolishly, and in which we have sinned. Let her not, I pray, be as one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb.” Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “Heal her, God, I beg you!” Yahweh […]

note: The lepers outside Samaria's gate exemplify the social exclusion of the leper that frames Luke's scene. Faint, contextual only.
sourceText: Now there were four leprous men at the entrance of the gate. They said one to another, “Why do we sit here until we die?

note: 'I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake' grounds the scribes' premise that God alone forgives sins. Jesus' pronouncement of forgiveness, and the controversy it provokes, presuppose this divine prerogative; strong coherence with the second-Isaiah claim that pardon is God's act.
sourceText: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.

note: The covenantal self-revelation of the LORD as the one 'forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin' is the foundational scriptural warrant for God's sole authority to pardon. The scribes' objection ('who can forgive sins but God alone?') rests on this confession. Medium volume; thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth, keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”

note: 'Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases' yokes forgiveness and healing exactly as Jesus does ('which is easier: your sins are forgiven, or arise and walk?'). The Psalm's pairing supplies the logic that healing demonstrates the authority to forgive.
sourceText: who forgives all your sins; who heals all your diseases;

note: Jesus' self-designation 'the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins' draws on the one like a son of man to whom dominion and authority are given. The claim of authority bound to the Son of Man title gives volume and coherence with the Danielic vision.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow' offers the prophetic promise of divine cleansing of sin that underlies the forgiveness pronounced here. Thematic only; low volume.
sourceText: “Come now, and let us reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

note: 'Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity... he will subdue our iniquities; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea' echoes the rhetorical 'who can forgive but God?' and the pardon motif. Faint; offered for recurrence of the God-alone-pardons theme.
sourceText: Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity, and passes over the disobedience of the remnant of his heritage? He doesn’t retain his anger forever, because he delights in loving kindness. He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

note: 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice' is the prophetic warrant for Jesus' table-fellowship with tax collectors and sinners against the Pharisees' purity objection. Though the explicit citation appears in Matthew's parallel, the same logic of mercy over ritual separation governs Luke's controversy; medium coherence.
sourceText: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

note: 'Is there no balm in Gilead? is there no physician there?' supplies the physician imagery Jesus turns on his critics ('those who are sick need a physician'). The prophetic lament over an unhealed people lends thematic depth; verbal contact is the shared 'physician' figure.
sourceText: Is there no balm in Gilead? is there no physician there? why then isn’t the health of the daughter of my people recovered?

note: The LORD as shepherd who seeks the lost, binds the broken, and strengthens the sick coheres with Jesus' coming to call sinners rather than the righteous. The seek-the-sick/lost motif gives some coherence to the mission statement; low volume.
sourceText: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.

note: Ben Sira's praise of the physician, whose healing comes from the Most High, belongs to the Second-Temple physician imagery Jesus deploys. Availability within the deuterocanon; faint and contested.
sourceText: Honor a physician according to your need of him with the honors due to him: For verily the Lord has created him. For from the Most High comes healing; And from the king he shall receive a gift.

note: 'As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you' supplies the bridegroom imagery by which Jesus interprets the festal joy of his presence as incompatible with fasting. The prophetic figure of God as bridegroom of his people grounds the metaphor; medium coherence.
sourceText: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.

note: The LORD's betrothal of Israel 'in righteousness... in lovingkindness' is a primary scriptural source of the divine-bridegroom motif underlying Jesus' saying. The wedding/betrothal frame coheres with the bridegroom-present logic of the fasting question.
sourceText: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.

note: Joel's call to fasting and solemn assembly, which summons even 'the bridegroom out of his chamber,' joins fasting and bridegroom imagery in one passage. The juxtaposition makes it a plausible backdrop to Jesus' bridegroom-and-fasting saying, though the use is allusive and faint.
sourceText: “Yet even now,” says Yahweh, “turn to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.” Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity. Who knows? He may turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him, even a meal offering and a drink offering to Yahweh, your God. Blow the trumpet in […]

note: 'Your Maker is your husband' reinforces the prophetic divine-spouse motif that the bridegroom saying presupposes. Recurrence with Isa 62 and Hosea; low independent volume.
sourceText: For your Maker is your husband; Yahweh of Armies is his name: and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer; the God of the whole earth shall he be called.

note: Elihu's 'my belly is as wine which has no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles' is the closest OT parallel to the new-wine-bursting-old-skins parable. Shared imagery of new wine straining fresh versus old skins gives notable volume to the figure.
sourceText: Behold, my breast is as wine which has no vent; like new wineskins it is ready to burst.

note: 'Every bottle shall be filled with wine' belongs to the prophetic wineskin imagery and is offered for recurrence of the wineskin figure; the connection to the new/old contrast is thematic and faint.
sourceText: Therefore you shall speak to them this word: Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, Every bottle shall be filled with wine: and they shall tell you, Do we not certainly know that every bottle shall be filled with wine?

note: 'A new friend is as new wine; when it is old, you shall drink it with pleasure' uniquely parallels Jesus' closing maxim 'the old is better.' The shared old-wine-is-preferred proverb gives this Second-Temple text real coherence with v.39, though verbal contact is partial.
sourceText: Forsake not an old friend; For the new is not comparable to him: As new wine, so is a new friend; If it become old, you will drink it with gladness.

note: Jesus explicitly cites David eating the consecrated bread of the Presence when hungry, with his companions. The verbal and narrative dependence is direct (named figure, the showbread, eating what is 'not lawful except for the priests'), satisfying Volume and Availability decisively.

note: This is the legal basis for Jesus' phrase 'which is not lawful to eat except for the priests alone' — Leviticus prescribes the showbread and reserves it for Aaron and his sons. Luke's halakhic argument presupposes this statute, giving high Coherence with the David citation.

It is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting […]

note: The whole controversy is over what is 'lawful to do on the Sabbath day,' which presupposes the Decalogue Sabbath command. Jesus' claim that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath answers directly to this prohibition of work, a strong thematic echo.

You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]

note: The Deuteronomic restatement of the Sabbath command frames it humanely (rest, mercy, deliverance), coherent with Jesus' merciful reading of Sabbath law over the plucking of grain. Lower volume than Exodus 20 since Luke does not quote, but the humanitarian rationale is apt.
sourceText: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]

note: The Torah explicitly permits plucking heads of grain by hand from a neighbor's standing crop; the disciples' act is lawful in itself, so the dispute is purely about the Sabbath. This statute is the unspoken Availability that makes the Pharisees' objection narrowly Sabbatarian.
sourceText: When you come into your neighbor’s standing grain, then you may pluck the ears with your hand; but you shall not move a sickle to your neighbor’s standing grain.

note: God's own Sabbath rest at creation is the root of Sabbath theology behind the pericope and the 'lord of the Sabbath' claim. The connection is theological rather than verbal, so confidence is low and the link is figural-conceptual.
sourceText: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.

note: A second Sabbath controversy (healing the withered hand) again presupposes the Sabbath commandment; Jesus' question 'is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good?' directly engages the Decalogue prohibition of work. High Coherence with 6:1-5 and Recurrence within the chapter.

note: Jeroboam's hand withers and is then restored at the prophet's word — the closest OT parallel to a withered (LXX exēranthē) hand being healed. The shared rare motif of a withered-then-restored hand gives moderate Volume despite no quotation.

note: Moses builds an altar with twelve pillars 'according to the twelve tribes of Israel.' Jesus' deliberate choice of twelve from his disciples evokes the constitution of Israel's twelve tribes, an act of eschatological restoration. Moderate Volume; the number twelve is the load-bearing link.
sourceText: Moses wrote all Yahweh’s words, and rose up early in the morning, and built an altar under the mountain, and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.

note: The 'twelve tribes of Israel' as the patriarchal sons stand behind the symbolism of the Twelve apostles as a renewed Israel. The connection is typological rather than verbal, so confidence is medium.
sourceText: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his blessing.

note: Jesus goes up the mountain and spends the night in prayer before constituting the Twelve, recalling Moses ascending the mountain to commune with God before the covenant. The mountain-prayer setting gives a faint figural echo.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Come up to me on the mountain, and stay here, and I will give you the stone tablets with the law and the commands that I have written, that you may teach them.” Moses rose up with Joshua, his servant, and Moses went up onto God’s Mountain. note: Moses asks God to appoint a leader 'over the congregation' so Israel is not 'as sheep without a shepherd'; Jesus' night of prayer before appointing leaders echoes that pattern of God-directed appointment. Low Volume, conceptual only.
sourceText: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”

note: Crowds from Tyre and Sidon (Phoenicia) coming to be healed faintly recalls prophetic oracles concerning the nations' turning to Israel's God. The geographic detail evokes the inclusion of Gentile coastlands; low and contested.
sourceText: Don’t rejoice, O Philistia, all of you, because the rod that struck you is broken; for out of the serpent’s root an adder will emerge, and his fruit will be a fiery flying serpent.

note: 'Power came out of him and healed them all' loosely recalls the divine spirit/power resting on and going out from a mediator. Faint thematic echo of the OT idea of healing power proceeding from God's anointed.
sourceText: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more.

note: The beatitudes for the poor, the mourning (who will laugh/rejoice), and the comforted directly draw on Isaiah's good-news-to-the-poor and comfort-for-mourners, which Luke programmatically makes Jesus' manifesto (cf. Luke 4:18). High Volume, Recurrence in Luke, and strong Coherence.
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn; to appoint to those who mourn in Zion, to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of […]
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind; to declare the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompence; to comfort all that mourn; that there should be given to them that mourn in Sion glory instead of ashes, the oil of joy to the mourners, the garment of glory for the spirit of heaviness: and […]

note: Isaiah's eschatological reversal — God's servants will eat, rejoice and sing while the wicked hunger, are ashamed and wail — supplies the exact hunger/fullness and weeping/laughing antitheses structuring Luke's blessings and woes. Strong Coherence with the following woes section.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be disappointed; behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart, but you shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall wail for anguish of spirit.

note: 'Those who sow in tears shall reap with joyful shouting' is the Psalter's paradigm of weeping turned to joy, matching 'blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.' Moderate Volume via shared reversal motif.
sourceText: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.

note: 'He satisfies the hungry soul with good things' undergirds 'blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled.' Coherent with Luke's broader hunger-satisfaction theme (Magnificat, 1:53).
sourceText: For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good.

note: 'Their fathers did the same thing to the prophets' invokes the deuteronomistic tradition of Israel persecuting and killing the prophets, classically summarized in 2 Chronicles 36:16. High Coherence; Luke makes the persecuted-prophet typology explicit.
sourceText: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.

note: Jeremiah's macarism 'blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD' (tree planted by water) stands behind the OT beatitude form Luke adopts. The form-critical background gives a faint but real echo.
sourceText: Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose trust Yahweh is. For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and shall not fear when heat comes, but its leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.

note: The Psalter's opening 'Blessed is the man...' is the fountainhead of the beatitude genre Jesus employs, contrasting two ways with reward/judgment. Genre-level Availability, hence low confidence and figural.
sourceText: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.

note: Persecution endured 'for the Son of Man's sake,' with reward in heaven, draws the title and the vindication-of-the-righteous frame from Daniel's heavenly Son of Man. Coherent with Luke's pervasive Son of Man usage.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'Woe to those who are at ease... the notable men' — Amos' woe against the complacent rich is the prophetic prototype of Jesus' 'woe to you who are rich.' Shared genre (prophetic woe-oracle) and target (the comfortable wealthy) give moderate Volume.
sourceText: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel come!

note: The full/hungry and laughing/mourning reversals in the woes mirror Isaiah's oracle that the wicked who feast will hunger and those who rejoice will be put to shame and wail. Strong structural Coherence with the beatitudes that precede.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be disappointed; behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart, but you shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall wail for anguish of spirit.

note: Amos turns feasting and songs into mourning and lamentation, paralleling 'you will mourn and weep' for those who now laugh. Faint thematic echo of prophetic reversal of revelry into grief.
sourceText: It will happen in that day,” says the Lord Yahweh, “that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day. I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will make you wear sackcloth on all your bodies, and baldness on every head. I will make it like the mourning for an only son, and its end like a bitter day.

note: 'The prophets prophesy falsely... and my people love it so' grounds 'their fathers did the same thing to the false prophets' — popular acclaim is the mark of the false prophet. Coherent with the deuteronomistic false-prophet tradition (cf. Micaiah, 1 Kings 22).
sourceText: The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority; and my people love to have it so. What will you do in the end of it?

note: 'Love your enemies' radicalizes and inverts the Holiness Code's 'love your neighbor as yourself,' which forbids vengeance and grudge-bearing. The love-command and its anti-retaliation logic are directly in view; high Coherence with vv.32-36.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: The Torah already commands aiding an enemy's straying ox or fallen donkey — concrete enemy-love. This statute is the OT seedbed of 'do good to those who hate you,' giving strong Availability and Volume for the command.
sourceText: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again. If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him, you shall surely help him with it.

note: 'If your enemy is hungry, give him bread... ' is the wisdom tradition's enacted enemy-love, closely matching 'do good to those who hate you' and 'give to everyone who asks.' High Coherence with Leviticus 19 and Exodus 23.
sourceText: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.

note: 'What you hate, do to no one' is the deuterocanonical negative Golden Rule, the nearest Second-Temple antecedent to 'as you would like people to do to you, do so to them.' Direct conceptual dependence; Availability within the OT/deuterocanon is secure.
sourceText: And what you yourself hate, do to no man. Don’t drink wine to drunkenness, and don’t let drunkenness go with you on your way.

note: 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me' is the proverbial renunciation of retaliation behind 'offer also the other cheek' and not demanding goods back. Moderate Volume; reinforces the anti-lex-talionis thrust.
sourceText: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”

note: 'Let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with reproach' is a striking verbal parallel to 'to him who strikes you on the cheek, offer also the other.' Notable Volume despite being a lament rather than a command.
sourceText: Let him give his cheek to him who strikes him; let him be filled full with reproach.

note: The Servant 'gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pluck the beard' models nonretaliatory submission to assault, coherent with the cheek-turning saying. Figural link to the Suffering Servant pattern.
sourceText: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.

note: Ben Sira's teaching on lending to a neighbor and showing mercy stands behind 'lend, expecting nothing back.' Faint wisdom-tradition echo of generous lending without calculation.
sourceText: He that shows mercy will lend to his neighbor; And he that strengthens him with his hand keeps the commandments. Lend to your neighbor in time of his need; And pay you your neighbor again in due season.

note: 'Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful' is a deliberate reworking of the Holiness Code's imitatio Dei formula 'be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.' The imitation-of-God structure is unmistakable; Luke substitutes mercy for holiness. High Volume.
sourceText: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.

note: The defining self-revelation 'the LORD, a God merciful and gracious' supplies the content of the Father's mercy that disciples are to imitate, and 'kind toward the unthankful and evil' echoes God's compassion on the undeserving. Strong Coherence with the imitatio Dei.

note: 'All day long he deals graciously and lends' commends the righteous lender who gives freely, undergirding 'lend, expecting nothing back.' Faint wisdom-Psalter echo, low confidence.
sourceText: All day long he deals graciously, and lends. His seed is blessed.

note: The command to lend generously to the poor 'and your heart shall not be grieved' grounds open-handed lending without expectation of return. Coherent with Luke's generosity ethic; moderate Availability.
sourceText: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]

note: 'I will measure their former work into their bosom' supplies the measure-into-the-lap imagery behind 'good measure... running over, will be given into your bosom.' Faint but specific verbal contact with the lap/bosom measuring motif.
sourceText: your own iniquities, and the iniquities of your fathers together”, says Yahweh, “who have burned incense on the mountains, and blasphemed me on the hills; therefore will I first measure their work into their bosom.”

note: The Torah's demand for honest measures ('a just ephah') stands behind the just-recompense logic of 'with the measure you measure it will be measured back.' Conceptual echo of measure-for-measure justice.
sourceText: “‘You shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in measures of length, of weight, or of quantity. You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin. I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay' captures the give-and-it-will-be-given reciprocity of v.38. Coherent with the surrounding generosity teaching; moderate Volume.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

note: 'With the merciful you show yourself merciful... with the pure you show yourself pure' is the OT measure-for-measure principle of divine requital matching human conduct, behind 'with the measure you measure.' Low and contested.
sourceText: With the merciful you will show yourself merciful. With the perfect man you will show yourself perfect. With the pure you will show yourself pure. With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.

note: Israel's leaders are 'blind watchmen' who cannot see — the prophetic image of blind guides directly informs 'can the blind guide the blind?' Strong Coherence between Jesus' polemic against the Pharisees and Isaiah's blind shepherds.
sourceText: His watchmen are blind, they are all without knowledge; they are all mute dogs, they can’t bark; dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber.

note: 'Those who guide this people lead them astray, and those who are guided by them are swallowed up' is a close conceptual match to blind guides and their followers both falling into a pit. Moderate Volume on the leaders-lead-astray motif.
sourceText: For those who lead this people lead them astray; and those who are led by them are destroyed.

note: 'Whoever digs a pit will fall into it' supplies the pit-falling imagery of v.39. Faint proverbial echo, low confidence given how common the motif is.
sourceText: Whoever digs a pit shall fall into it. Whoever rolls a stone, it will come back on him.

note: 'The fruit discloses the cultivation of a tree; so the expression of a thought discloses the cultivation of a person's mind' is an almost exact deuterocanonical parallel to 'each tree is known by its own fruit' joined to speech from the heart's abundance. High Volume; nearest Second-Temple antecedent.
sourceText: The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man.

note: 'I the LORD search the heart... to give every man according to his fruit' fuses heart and fruit imagery exactly as Luke links the good treasure of the heart to good fruit. Coherent with the heart-fruit correspondence.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: The wider Sirach passage on sieving (chaff/refuse remaining) and a person revealed by speech, including 'do not praise anyone before he speaks,' undergirds 'out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.' Reinforces the high-confidence v.6 link.
sourceText: In the shaking of a sieve, the refuse remains; So the filth of man in his reasoning. The furnace will prove the potter’s vessels; And the trial of a man is in his reasoning. The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man. Praise no man before you hear him reason; For this is the trial of men.

note: 'From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good' connects mouth, fruit, and the good a person produces, a faint wisdom echo behind vv.44-45. Low confidence given the commonplace nature of fruit imagery.
sourceText: A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth. The work of a man’s hands shall be rewarded to him.

note: Ezekiel's wall, daubed without proper foundation, that the LORD breaks down with a flooding rain and storm until it falls, is the closest OT antecedent to the house without foundation swept away by the flood. High Volume and Coherence with the build/collapse imagery.
sourceText: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there is no peace; and when one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash: tell those who plaster it with whitewash, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and you, great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall tear it. Behold, when the wall has fallen, shall it not be said to you, Where is the plaster with which you have plastered it? Therefore […]

note: 'When the whirlwind passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever' is the proverbial two-outcomes saying behind the wise/foolish builders surviving or collapsing in the storm. Strong wisdom-tradition Coherence.
sourceText: When the whirlwind passes, the wicked is no more; but the righteous stand firm forever.

note: The tested foundation stone in Zion, with judgment as a flooding waters that sweeps away the refuge of lies, supplies the rock-foundation-versus-flood contrast. Moderate Volume; the foundation/flood pairing is apt.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily. I will make justice the measuring line, and righteousness the plumb line. The hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters will overflow the hiding place.

note: The two-ways conclusion — the righteous established versus the wicked driven away like chaff — frames the wise/foolish builders as the chapter's closing two-ways. Genre-level echo, low confidence.
sourceText: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper. The wicked are not so, but are like the chaff which the wind drives away. Therefore the wicked shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous. For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.

note: The cataclysmic flood that sweeps away all not preserved supplies the eschatological-judgment overtone of the rising stream destroying the foundationless house. Faint figural echo of flood-as-judgment.
sourceText: The flood was forty days on the earth. The waters increased, and lifted up the ship, and it was lifted up above the earth. The waters rose, and increased greatly on the earth; and the ship floated on the surface of the waters. The waters rose very high on the earth. All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered. The waters rose fifteen cubits higher, and the mountains were covered. All flesh died that moved on the earth, including […]

note: The healing of a Gentile military officer (Naaman, captain of Aram's army) at a distance through Israel's prophet supplies a strong typological precedent for the centurion whose servant Jesus heals from afar. Naaman's mediated request, his concern about the prophet's coming, and the wonder at faith found outside Israel cohere with Luke's emphasis on the believing Gentile. Recurrence is supported by Luke 4:27, where Jesus himself names Naaman as the paradigm of Gentile favor.

The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]

note: Solomon's prayer that the foreigner who hears of God's name and comes toward the temple be answered frames the God-fearing Gentile who loves Israel and builds the synagogue. The elders' plea that the centurion is 'worthy' because 'he loves our nation' echoes the Deuteronomic ideal of the righteous resident foreigner. Faint and thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: “Moreover concerning the foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, when he shall come out of a far country for your name’s sake (for they shall hear of your great name, and of your mighty hand, and of your outstretched arm); when he shall come and pray toward this house; hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and do according to all that the foreigner calls to you for; that all the peoples of the earth may know your name, to fear you, as do your people […]

note: The foreigner who joins himself to the LORD, loves his name, and is welcomed into the house of prayer resonates with the synagogue-building centurion. The coherence with Luke's Gentile-inclusion theme is strong even though there is no verbal contact, so this is a faint figural echo.
sourceText: Also the foreigners who join themselves to Yahweh, to minister to him, and to love Yahweh’s name, to be his servants, everyone who keeps the Sabbath from profaning it, and holds fast my covenant; even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”

note: The raising of the widow of Nain's son is closely modeled on Elijah's raising of the widow of Zarephath's only son. Luke 7:15, 'he gave him to his mother,' reproduces 1 Kings 17:23 LXX nearly verbatim, and the shared motifs (a widow, a dead only son, a city gate, the crowd's recognition of a great prophet) give high volume and coherence. Zarephath lies near Nain's geography of Galilee/Sidon, and the Elijah-typology pervades Luke 7.
sourceText: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]

note: Elisha's raising of the Shunammite woman's only son is the second prophetic resurrection paradigm behind Nain. The motif of a single beloved son restored to a grieving mother, and the prophet's bodily proximity to the corpse, reinforce the doubled Elijah/Elisha typology Luke deploys. Recurrence with 7:11-17 is strengthened by Luke 9:8,19 expectations of a returning prophet.
sourceText: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]

note: The clause 'and he gave him to his mother' (kai edoken auton te metri autou) matches the LXX of 1 Kings 17:23 word-for-word, making this the strongest verbal anchor for the whole pericope. The near-citation in narrative voice signals deliberate Elijah modeling rather than coincidence.
sourceText: Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the room into the house, and delivered him to his mother; and Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives.”

note: The crowd's cry 'A great prophet has arisen among us' activates the expectation of an Elijah-like prophet whose coming Malachi promises before the Day of the LORD. Coherence with the deliberate Elijah typology of the resurrection scene makes this more than incidental, though the verbal link is to the popular prophetic-return hope rather than a citation.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: Ben Sira's praise of Elijah explicitly celebrates that he 'raised a corpse from death' (Sir 48:5), the same deed Jesus performs at Nain, making the deuterocanonical encomium a Second-Temple lens that shaped the crowd's prophet-acclamation. Availability and coherence are strong; this clarifies how a first-century audience read raising-the-dead as the signature of an Elijah figure.
