sourceText: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend money for that which is not bread? and your labor for that which doesn’t satisfy? listen diligently to me, and eat you that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.

note: Wisdom 'has slaughtered her beasts, mixed her wine, set her table, and sent out her maidens' to call guests — 'Come, eat of my bread.' The sent-servant-summoning-the-invited pattern and the call to the simple closely parallel the great supper's structure and the gathering of the lowly.
sourceText: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars. She has prepared her meat. She has mixed her wine. She has also set her table. She has sent out her maidens. She cries from the highest places of the city: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” As for him who is void of understanding, she says to him, “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!

note: The gathering of outsiders — foreigners and eunuchs brought to God's house, 'others besides those already gathered' — anticipates the master sending into highways and hedges to fill the house. Coheres with Luke's Gentile-inclusion trajectory but verbally diffuse.
sourceText: Neither let the foreigner, who has joined himself to Yahweh, speak, saying, “Yahweh will surely separate me from his people”; neither let the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” For thus says Yahweh, “To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and hold fast my covenant: to them I will give in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than of sons and of daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, […]

note: Samuel's sacrificial feast where 'the people will not eat until he comes... afterward those eat who are invited' supplies the formal vocabulary of invited guests waiting on the host's bidding. A faint background to the supper's summons protocol.
sourceText: As soon as you have come into the city, you shall immediately find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat; for the people will not eat until he come, because he blesses the sacrifice. Afterwards those who are invited eat. Now therefore go up; for at this time you shall find him.”

note: 'If anyone... doesn't disregard his own father, mother, wife, children' echoes the blessing of Levi, who said of father and mother 'I have not seen him,' disowned his brothers and ignored his children — keeping covenant fidelity above kin. The radical preference of covenant loyalty over family ties is the closest scriptural precedent for Jesus' hyperbolic 'hate.'
sourceText: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.

note: The Levites' ordination by slaying brother, companion, and neighbor at Moses' command — 'each one at the cost of his son and his brother' — is the narrative behind Deut 33:9's praise of Levi. It models the disciple's willingness to set covenant allegiance above family, coherent with Jesus' demand and the cross-bearing that follows.
sourceText: He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. Moses said, “Consecrate yourselves today to Yahweh, yes, every man against his son, and against […]

note: Micah's portrait of eschatological family division — son dishonoring father, daughter against mother, 'a man's enemies are the men of his own household' — undergirds Jesus' setting discipleship against the closest kin (and is explicitly cited at Luke 12:53). Recurrence in Luke strengthens its availability here.
sourceText: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.

note: The command to show no pity even to a brother, son, daughter, or wife who entices to false worship — placing exclusive devotion to the Lord above the dearest relations — offers a Torah analogue to subordinating family to higher allegiance. Faint and contested, but coheres with the covenant-over-kin theme of Deut 33:9.
sourceText: If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom, or your friend, who is as your own soul, entices you secretly, saying, “Let us go and serve other gods,” which you have not known, you, nor your fathers; of the gods of the peoples who are around you, near to you, or far off from you, from the one end of the earth even to the other end of the earth; you shall not consent to him, nor listen to him; neither […]

note: The king who 'will not sit down first and consider' before going to war reflects the proverb 'by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in an abundance of counselors there is victory.' The counsel to deliberate before battle is the sapiential ground of Jesus' second illustration about counting the cost.
sourceText: for by wise guidance you wage your war; and victory is in many advisors.

note: 'Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war' doubles the counting-the-cost-before-war motif of vv.31-32. Recurrence of this maxim across Proverbs 20:18 and 24:6 strengthens the wisdom-deliberation background of the tower-and-war pair.
sourceText: Plans are established by advice; by wise guidance you wage war!

note: 'Prepare your work outside... and after that build your house' supplies the prudence-before-building logic behind the tower illustration ('count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it'). Faint but coherent with the sapiential planning theme.
sourceText: Prepare your work outside, and get your fields ready. Afterwards, build your house.

note: Ben Sira's 'before every action let counsel go, and before every undertaking deliberation' captures the count-the-cost-first principle of both illustrations. Deuterocanonical availability adds Second-Temple recurrence to the wisdom-deliberation reading.
sourceText: Let reason be the beginning of every work, And let counsel go before every action.

note: 'Salt is good, but if the salt becomes flat and tasteless...' draws on the covenant-of-salt requirement that every grain offering be seasoned with salt — salt as the indispensable mark of acceptable offering. Saltless disciples 'fit neither for soil nor manure pile' invert the covenant-of-salt's enduring fidelity.
sourceText: Every offering of your meal offering you shall season with salt; neither shall you allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be lacking from your meal offering. With all your offerings you shall offer salt.

note: The 'covenant of salt forever before the Lord' given to the priests defines salt as a symbol of permanent, unbreakable covenant — the very quality lost when salt goes flat. Coherent with the disqualification-from-covenant-service theme and reinforces Lev 2:13's availability.
sourceText: All the wave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer to Yahweh, have I given you, and your sons and your daughters with you, as a portion forever. It is a covenant of salt forever before Yahweh to you and to your seed with you.”

note: The Davidic kingship granted 'by a covenant of salt' extends the salt-as-perpetual-covenant idiom that gives Jesus' saltlessness saying its bite. Faint and contested, but adds recurrence to the covenant-of-salt motif across the canon.
sourceText: Ought you not to know that Yahweh, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?

note: Jeremiah's curse on the one who trusts in man — dwelling in 'a salt land not inhabited,' barren and uninhabitable — resonates with salt-spoiled ground 'fit neither for the soil nor the manure pile.' Faint figural overlap between barren salt-land and the worthless flat salt thrown out.
sourceText: For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good comes, but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, a salt land and not inhabited.

note: The Pharisees and scribes 'murmured' (diegongyzon) that Jesus eats with sinners; LXX uses gongyzo precisely for Israel's murmuring against God's provision in the wilderness. Luke evokes the recurrent grumbling motif to cast the objectors as faithless Israel resisting God's gracious feeding. Coherence is strong because the parables that follow defend a divine table.
sourceText: and in the morning, then you shall see Yahweh’s glory; because he hears your murmurings against Yahweh. Who are we, that you murmur against us?” Moses said, “Now Yahweh shall give you meat to eat in the evening, and in the morning bread to satisfy you; because Yahweh hears your murmurings which you murmur against him. And who are we? Your murmurings are not against us, but against Yahweh.”

note: The separatist who says 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am holier than you' supplies the exact posture Luke's Pharisees adopt against table fellowship with sinners. Isaiah condemns this self-segregating holiness as a stench before God, which coheres with Jesus' vindication of welcoming sinners. Availability and thematic coherence are high; verbal overlap is thematic rather than lexical.
sourceText: who say, Stand by yourself, don’t come near to me, for I am holier than you. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burns all the day.

note: The wisdom ideal that the righteous do not sit with sinners frames the Pharisees' assumption that eating with sinners defiles. Luke inverts the maxim: Jesus' table redefines blessedness as seeking rather than separating. Faint and contested, resting on shared sinner/righteous vocabulary.
sourceText: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;

note: God declares 'I myself will search for my sheep... I will seek the lost,' the precise plot of the one shepherd who leaves the flock to find the strayed (vv. 4,6,16). Volume is high (sustained seeking-shepherd oracle), recurrence strong (Ezekiel 34 is a touchstone for Luke's shepherd Christology), and coherence exact: God's own searching contrasts the failed shepherds, just as Jesus seeks sinners the Pharisees abandon.
sourceText: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]

note: The shepherd who gathers lambs and carries them in his bosom illuminates the man carrying the found sheep on his shoulders rejoicing. The tender carrying gesture is distinctive and shared, strengthening the divine-shepherd reading. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the comfort-of-God shepherd image.
sourceText: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.

note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' supplies the penitent's voice answered by the seeking shepherd. The verbal pairing of straying sheep and divine seeking is close, and coherence with the repentance emphasis (v.7) is strong. Slightly lower volume than Ezekiel 34.
sourceText: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.

note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way' is the canonical image of straying that the parable assumes for 'one sinner who repents.' Recurrence in Luke's passion theology supports availability; the echo is thematic rather than cited here. Contested as to whether Luke intends the Servant song specifically.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: The woe on shepherds who scatter and the promise that God will gather the remnant and set true shepherds over them stands behind the lost-sheep rescue. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the prophetic indictment of leaders who fail the flock, paralleling the Pharisees. Lower volume, so an echo.

note: God's promise to gather the remnant of Israel 'like sheep in a fold' supplies the regathering motif. Faint and one of several gathering oracles; included for recurrence within the shepherd-restoration cluster. Contested because no distinctive verbal link to a single lost sheep.
sourceText: I will surely assemble, Jacob, all of you; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the midst of their pasture; they will swarm with people.

note: The flock doomed to slaughter and the shepherd's care/abandonment drama belongs to the same prophetic shepherd field Luke draws on. Faint here; included as availability for the seeking-shepherd theme. Contested.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]

note: God 'searches Jerusalem with lamps' to find the complacent, a near image to the woman lighting a lamp and sweeping to find the coin. The lamp-search vocabulary is suggestive, though Zephaniah's search is judicial, here gracious. Contested and faint.
sourceText: It will happen at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are settled on their dregs, who say in their heart, “Yahweh will not do good, neither will he do evil.”

note: Seeking wisdom 'as silver, and searching for it as for hidden treasure' parallels the diligent search for the lost silver drachma until found. The seek-until-found wisdom pattern coheres with the parable's diligence, but the link is thematic. Contested.
sourceText: If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures:

note: The beloved who seeks through the night 'until I found him' and then summons others to rejoice mirrors the woman's seek-find-celebrate structure. Faint, figural, contested; included as a seek-and-find availability rather than a deliberate citation.
sourceText: By night on my bed, I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him. note: The law of inheritance giving the firstborn a double portion frames 'give me my share of your property' and the father's division between the two sons. The legal background makes the younger son's premature demand pointed and the father's later 'all that is mine is yours' (v.31) the firstborn's lawful due. Coherence high; verbal link thematic.
sourceText: but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the hated, by giving him a double portion of all that he has; for he is the beginning of his strength. The right of the firstborn is his.

note: The patriarchal pattern of departing to a far country when 'a severe famine' strikes the land underlies the son's far-country famine. The famine-driven sojourn is a recurrent Genesis motif (also 26:1; 41-47), lending availability. Contested as a specific source; an ambient echo.
sourceText: There was a famine in the land. Abram went down into Egypt to live as a foreigner there, for the famine was severe in the land.

note: The pig is declared unclean, so feeding swine and craving their husks marks the Jewish son's total degradation and ritual estrangement. For a Torah-formed audience the swine signal maximal defilement, intensifying the depth from which the father's mercy reaches. Volume modest but coherence and distinctiveness high.
sourceText: The pig, because he has a split hoof, and is cloven-footed, but doesn’t chew the cud, he is unclean to you.

note: 'Whoever loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth' compactly anticipates both the prodigal's wasteful living and the elder son's accusation of harlots (v.30). The proverb pairs squandering and harlotry with a father, exactly Luke's configuration. Coherence strong.
sourceText: Whoever loves wisdom brings joy to his father; but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.

note: 'Do not give yourself to prostitutes, lest you lose your inheritance' (deuterocanonical wisdom) joins squandering to harlotry and lost inheritance, the prodigal's exact fall. Availability within Second-Temple wisdom strengthens the moral frame. Contested and faint as a direct source.
sourceText: Give not your soul to harlots, That you lose not your inheritance.

note: Pharaoh's 'I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you' is the closest verbal template for 'I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight,' the dual against-God-and-against-you formula. The parallel sharpens the son's confession as a recognized penitential script. Contested between this and the Davidic confessions.
sourceText: Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron in haste, and he said, “I have sinned against Yahweh your God, and against you.

note: 'Against you, you only, have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight' supplies the language of sinning before God's sight that the son rehearses. As the paradigmatic penitential psalm it carries high recurrence in Jewish repentance piety, cohering with Luke's repentance theme (vv.7,10). Distinctive 'in your sight' overlap.
sourceText: Against you, and you only, have I sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight; that you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge.
lxxText: Against thee only have I sinned, and done evil before thee: that thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged.

note: David's terse 'I have sinned against the LORD' models confession answered immediately by restoration, the rhythm of the son's resolve answered by the father. Recurrence of the 'I have sinned' formula across Saul/David/Pharaoh makes any single attribution contested. Faint.
sourceText: David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against Yahweh.” Nathan said to David, “Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.

note: Esau 'ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, and kissed him, and they wept' is the precise gesture-cluster of the father who ran, fell on his neck, and kissed the returning son. Volume and verbal distinctiveness are very high (run + fall on neck + kiss in sequence), and coherence is strong: an estranged brother/son reunion of unexpected mercy.
sourceText: Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.

note: Joseph falling on his brothers' necks, weeping and kissing them, reinforces the reconciliation embrace, and the broader Joseph reunion (46:29, falling on Jacob's neck) supplies the lost-then-found-alive frame. Recurrence of the Joseph story across this pericope (robe, ring, 'dead/alive') is strong. Slightly lower verbal match than Genesis 33:4.
sourceText: He fell on his brother Benjamin’s neck, and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck. He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.

note: Pharaoh exalts Joseph by putting a ring on his hand and clothing him in fine robes, the exact pair of honors (best robe + ring) the father bestows. The Joseph parallel makes the restored son a reinstated heir, not merely a forgiven servant. Distinctive robe-and-ring combination yields high volume and coherence.

note: Joshua the high priest has his filthy garments removed and is clothed in rich robes as a sign of restored standing, illuminating the 'best robe' that re-clothes the defiled son. The figural logic of imputed honor replacing defilement coheres tightly with the swine-defiled returnee. Verbal link is the robe of restoration.
sourceText: Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and was standing before the angel. He answered and spoke to those who stood before him, saying, “Take the filthy garments off of him.” To him he said, “Behold, I have caused your iniquity to pass from you, and I will clothe you with rich clothing.” I said, “Let them set a clean turban on his head.” So they set a clean turban on his head, and clothed him; and Yahweh’s angel was standing by.

note: Abraham's slaughter of a choice, tender calf for honored guests supplies the cultural background of the fattened calf killed for celebration. Faint and one of several calf-feast scenes (1 Samuel 28:24); included for the hospitality-feast availability. Contested.
sourceText: Abraham ran to the herd, and fetched a tender and good calf, and gave it to the servant. He hurried to dress it.

note: Jacob mourns Joseph as dead and refuses comfort, so that Joseph's later disclosure that he is alive (45:26-28) is the canonical 'was dead and is alive, was lost and is found' reversal the father proclaims. The figural fit of a father's lost-and-restored son is strong and recurs across this pericope's Joseph allusions. Lower verbal volume, hence figural.
sourceText: He recognized it, and said, “It is my son’s coat. An evil animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn in pieces.” Jacob tore his clothes, and put sackcloth on his waist, and mourned for his son many days. All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, “For I will go down to Sheol to my son mourning.” His father wept for him.

note: Jonah is angry at God's mercy to the undeserving, sulks outside, and God comes out reasoning with him to the parable's open end, exactly the elder son angry at mercy whom the father comes out and entreats, ending on an unanswered appeal. Coherence is very high (resentment at grace, divine entreaty, open conclusion) and the structural parallel is distinctive. A strong figural-allusive frame for Luke's audience of grumblers.

Directly preceding the inheritance law (21:17) already echoed, strengthening recurrence. Coherence high as a subverted intertext.

For he has supplanted me these two times. He took away my birthright. See, now he has taken away my blessing.” He said, “Haven’t you reserved a blessing for me?” Isaac answered Esau, “Behold, […]

Recurrence with 15:13 makes the proverb a coherent through-line. Verbal overlap of squandering plus harlotry.

When the money was all spent in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph, and said, “Give […]

The shared logic that present generosity with money secures future, divine reception gives strong coherence with a widely available sapiential maxim.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

High coherence and Second-Temple availability make this a strong deuterocanonical echo behind 'receive you into the eternal tents.'
sourceText: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]

note: Ben Sira urges laying up alms in one's treasury as a deposit that will rescue one from misfortune, framing charity to the poor as deferred self-interest. The volume and coherence with 'make friends... so they may receive you' is high, and Sirach was demonstrably available to Luke's milieu.
sourceText: Howbeit with a man in poor estate be longsuffering; And let him not wait for your alms. Help a poor man for the commandment’s sake; And according to his need send him not empty away. note: Daniel's appeal to Nebuchadnezzar to 'redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by mercy to the poor' supplies the redemptive-almsgiving theology underlying using mammon to gain eternal welcome. Strong coherence with the verse's logic; the connection is conceptual rather than verbal.
sourceText: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; if there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.

note: The maxim 'faithful in a very little is faithful in much' coheres with Ben Sira's wisdom that integrity in small dealings with the lowly proves character, but the gnomic form is broadly diffused and no single passage controls it. Faint and contested as a specific source.
sourceText: Incline your ear to a poor man, And answer him with peaceful words in meekness. Deliver him that is wronged from the hand of him that wrongeth him; And be not faint-hearted in giving judgement. Be as a father to the fatherless, And instead of a husband to their mother: So will you be as a son of the Most High, And he will love you more than your mother does.

note: 'No servant can serve two masters... you cannot serve God and Mammon' echoes the covenantal either/or of choosing whom to serve, the LORD versus rival gods. Coherence with the exclusive-service motif is real but the diction is independent, so it is a faint figural echo at best.
sourceText: If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose this day whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”

note: The demand for undivided love of God set against love of money draws on the Shema's totalizing claim ('with all your heart'), which forbids a divided heart. The opposition of single-hearted devotion versus a rival master gives modest coherence; verbal contact is absent, so it is contested.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: 'That which is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God' closely matches the proverb that everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD. Strong verbal and conceptual coherence (the 'abomination'/divine-loathing of human self-exaltation) and high availability support an allusion.
sourceText: Everyone who is proud in heart is an abomination to Yahweh: they shall certainly not be unpunished.

note: 'You justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts' rests on Samuel's principle that man looks on outward appearance while the LORD looks on the heart. The contrast of human-facing display versus divine heart-knowledge is a coherent and well-known scriptural axiom.
sourceText: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

note: 'Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the hearts' parallels self-justification before men exposed by God's knowledge of hearts. Coherence is high and the sapiential idiom was available, though Proverbs 16:5 and 1 Samuel 16:7 are the closer touchstones.
sourceText: Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but Yahweh weighs the hearts.

note: The LORD who 'searches the heart' to repay each according to his ways undergirds 'God knows your hearts.' The heart-searching-God motif is recurrent in the prophets, giving thematic coherence but no controlling diction here.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John' presupposes the Elijah-figure who marks the close of the prophetic era and the turn to the day of the LORD. Malachi's promise of Elijah before the great day gives coherent, available background to John as the canon's hinge.
sourceText: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

note: 'Easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the Law to fall' coheres with 'the grass withers... but the word of our God stands forever,' affirming the imperishability of God's word against the transient cosmos. Strong conceptual coherence with a recurrent Isaianic theme.
sourceText: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”

note: 'Forever, O LORD, your word is settled in heaven' parallels the indestructibility of the Law's least stroke. The endurance-of-Torah motif gives thematic coherence, though the saying's imagery of a 'stroke of a pen' is independent.
sourceText: Yahweh, your word is settled in heaven forever.

note: The divorce-and-remarriage saying directly engages the Mosaic certificate-of-divorce legislation, which Jesus reads against the grain by classing remarriage as adultery. Availability and coherence are decisive; this is the legal text the dictum addresses, framed by v.17's claim on the Law.
sourceText: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house. When she has departed out of his house, she may go and be another man’s wife. If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter […]

note: The prohibition of divorce-and-remarriage as adultery rests on the creational one-flesh union that divorce cannot truly dissolve. The coherence with Genesis is high (Jesus' parallel teaching elsewhere makes the link explicit), supplying the theological ground here.
sourceText: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.

note: Malachi's oracle against faithless divorce ('the LORD hates divorce... she is your companion by covenant') coheres with Jesus' hardening of the marriage bond. The prophetic critique of casual divorce gives recurrent, available support, though no verbal quotation.
sourceText: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For I hate divorce”, says Yahweh, the God of Israel, “and him […]

note: Lazarus laid 'at the gate' desiring crumbs while the rich man feasts dramatizes the Deuteronomic command not to harden the heart against the poor brother at your gate, for the poor will never cease in the land. High coherence with the covenantal gate-and-poor topos.
sourceText: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]

note: Lazarus 'full of sores' with dogs licking him evokes Job afflicted with sores from sole to crown, scraping himself amid loss. The shared imagery of a body covered in sores as the type of the abject sufferer gives coherent, available background.
sourceText: So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head. He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes.

note: The prospering, sumptuously clothed rich man set against the afflicted poor man echoes the psalmist's scandal at the wicked who are 'always at ease' and 'clothed with violence' while the godly suffer, resolved only at their end. Strong coherence with the reversal-of-fortunes frame that the parable will enact.
sourceText: For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no struggles in their death, but their strength is firm. They are free from burdens of men, neither are they plagued like other men. Therefore pride is like a chain around their neck. Violence covers them like a garment. Their eyes bulge with fat. Their minds pass the limits of conceit. They scoff and speak with malice. In arrogance, they threaten oppression. They […]

note: The rich man 'clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting in luxury every day' matches Amos' woe on those who lie on ivory beds, eat lambs, and feast while not grieved over ruin, who go first into exile. The prophetic indictment of callous luxury gives recurrent, coherent background.
sourceText: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel come! Go to Calneh, and see; and from there go to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. are they better than these kingdoms? or is their border greater than your border? Those who put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near; Who lie on beds of […]

note: 'Whoever shuts his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard' anticipates the rich man's later unanswered cry from Hades after ignoring Lazarus at his gate. Coherence with the lex talionis of neglected mercy is real but the link is thematic, not verbal.
sourceText: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.

note: Being 'carried to Abraham's bosom' and the rich man's address 'Father Abraham' draw on the patriarchal hope of being gathered to one's fathers, with Abraham as the paradigmatic destination of the righteous dead. Coherence with the gathered-to-Abraham motif is strong, though 'bosom' as the resting place is Second-Temple development.
sourceText: but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried in a good old age.

note: 'Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will receive us' on the lips of the martyrs supplies the explicit Second-Temple picture of the righteous welcomed by the patriarchs after death, illuminating 'Abraham's bosom.' Availability and coherence with the post-mortem reception motif support the echo.
sourceText: If we suffer thus, Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob will receive us, and all the fathers will commend us.

note: The rich man's torment, flame, and anguish in Hades draws on Isaiah's closing vision of the dead whose fire is not quenched, the canonical seedbed of post-mortem fiery punishment. Coherence with the unquenched-fire judgment is high and the text was widely available.
sourceText: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”

note: Ben Sira's image of the assembly of the wicked as tow set to flame and the broad road of sinners ending in Hades coheres with the flame and fixed-gulf fate of the rich man. The link is thematic to the sapiential fate-of-the-wicked topos rather than verbal.
sourceText: The congregation of wicked men is as tow wrapped together; And the end of them is a flame of fire. The way of sinners is made smooth with stones; And at the last end thereof is the pit of Hades.

note: Enoch's tour of the hollow places of the dead, where the righteous and wicked are separated by a great division awaiting judgment, parallels the great chasm fixed between Lazarus and the rich man. As pseudepigraphal background to Second-Temple afterlife topography it is warranted but faint and contested.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: 'They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them' presses the Deuteronomic demand to heed the words spoken in God's name, with refusal entailing accountability. Coherence with the obligation to 'hear' the authoritative Mosaic word is strong, framing the sufficiency-of-Scripture point.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]

note: Abraham's verdict that those who will not hear Moses will not be persuaded even by a resurrection coheres with Deuteronomy's insistence that the word is not far off in heaven or beyond reach but near, in mouth and heart, so no extraordinary sign is needed. The sufficiency and nearness of the revealed word grounds the saying.
sourceText: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]

note: Israel's stiff-necked refusal to listen to the LORD's testimony 'by every prophet' despite warnings prefigures brothers who 'will not be persuaded' though warned by Moses and the prophets. The recurrent prophetic-rejection motif gives coherence, but the connection is thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: Yet Yahweh testified to Israel, and to Judah, by every prophet, and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.” Notwithstanding, they would not listen, but hardened their neck, like the neck of their fathers, who didn’t believe in Yahweh their God.

note: The Holiness Code commands 'you shall surely rebuke your neighbor' rather than bear sin against him, the foundational text for fraternal correction that Jesus reproduces almost as a paraphrase ('rebuke him'). High Coherence with the surrounding love-of-neighbor frame and strong recurrence of this verse in Second-Temple reproof ethics give it good standing.
sourceText: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.

note: Lamech's boast that he is avenged 'seventy-sevenfold' is the numerical foil that Jesus' sevenfold-forgiveness saying (and Matthew's seventy-seven) inverts: unlimited vengeance becomes unlimited pardon. The shared and distinctive sevenfold idiom gives moderate Volume; the figural reversal supplies Coherence.
sourceText: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”

note: The new-covenant promise that God will forgive iniquity and remember sin no more underwrites the disciples' obligation to forgive the repentant brother. The link is thematic rather than verbal, so confidence is low, but the forgiveness motif gives Coherence with the pericope.
sourceText: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin will I remember no more.

note: Ezekiel's oracle on a land that 'sins against me' and the prophet's responsibility for warning resonates faintly with the 'if your brother sins' correction logic, but the connection is diffuse and the vocabulary common, so this is a contested faint echo at best.
sourceText: Son of man, when a land sins against me by committing a trespass, and I stretch out my hand on it, and break the staff of its bread, and send famine on it, and cut off from it man and animal;

note: Jeremiah's sign-act binds a stone to the scroll and casts it into the Euphrates so Babylon will 'sink and not rise,' the closest OT image to a weight sunk in deep water as a figure of irreversible doom. The millstone-and-sea threat shares the distinctive stone-cast-into-water motif of total destruction, giving moderate Volume.
sourceText: It shall be, when you have made an end of reading this book, that you shall bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates:

note: The Song of the Sea says the enemy 'went down into the depths like a stone,' supplying the stone-sinking-in-the-sea imagery of judgment. The verbal overlap (stone, depths of the sea) is suggestive but the motif is widespread, so the echo is faint.
sourceText: The deeps cover them. They went down into the depths like a stone.

note: Nehemiah's prayer recalls the pursuers cast 'into the depths, like a stone into mighty waters,' reinforcing the same drowning-by-stone judgment topos. Low Volume and a commonplace image keep this contested.
sourceText: You divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on the dry land; and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into the mighty waters.

note: Zechariah's word that the great 'mountain' shall become a plain before Zerubbabel by the Spirit, not by might, is the canonical pairing of faith with the moving/leveling of an immovable obstacle. The mountain-removed-by-faith logic gives Coherence with 'faith like a mustard seed,' though Luke uses a sycamore-into-sea rather than a mountain, lowering Volume.
sourceText: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”

note: The psalm's confidence even 'though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea' supplies the very image of an immovable thing thrown into the sea, here recast as the work of faith. The verbal overlap (uprooted/carried into the sea) is real but the figure is proverbial, so it is faint.
sourceText: Therefore we won’t be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas;

note: The theophany that scatters the everlasting mountains coheres with the faith-moves-mountains topos behind the uprooted-tree saying. The connection is conceptual and diffuse, so confidence is low.
sourceText: He stood, and shook the earth. He looked, and made the nations tremble. The ancient mountains were crumbled. The age-old hills collapsed. His ways are eternal.

note: Isaiah's 'the mountains may depart' as a figure of cosmic upheaval feeds the same stock of immovable-object-displaced imagery that the mustard-seed/sycamore saying exploits. Faint and contested.
sourceText: For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed; but my loving kindness shall not depart from you, neither shall my covenant of peace be removed,” says Yahweh who has mercy on you.

note: Eliphaz asks whether a man can be profitable to God or whether it is gain to the Almighty that one is righteous, the wisdom premise that human service places God under no obligation. This grounds the 'we are unworthy servants, we have only done our duty' logic; moderate Coherence with the servant parable.
sourceText: “Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that you are righteous? Or does it benefit him, that you make your ways perfect?

note: Elihu's 'if you are righteous, what do you give him?' states the same theology of non-meritorious obedience underlying the unprofitable-servant saying. Recurrence of the motif across Job strengthens the Availability and Coherence, though there is no verbal quotation.
sourceText: If you are righteous, what do you give him? Or what does he receive from your hand?

note: The image of servants' eyes fixed on the hand of their master, waiting on his command, supplies the master-servant deference picture the parable assumes. Conceptual rather than verbal, hence low confidence.
sourceText: Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress; so our eyes look to Yahweh, our God, until he has mercy on us.

note: God's claim that the Israelites are his servants whom he brought out of Egypt frames Israel's whole obedience as owed service, the covenantal backdrop to 'we have only done what was our duty.' Faint, diffuse, contested.
sourceText: For to me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.

note: The Naaman narrative — a leprous Syrian foreigner cleansed who returns to the prophet to confess the God of Israel — is the structural template for the lone Samaritan leper who turns back to give thanks. The distinctive convergence of foreigner + leprosy + cleansing + grateful return gives strong Volume and Coherence, and Luke elsewhere cites Naaman explicitly (4:27), confirming Recurrence.
sourceText: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]

note: The leprosy law requires the unclean to dwell apart and cry out, explaining why the ten 'stood at a distance' and lifted their voices. The pericope presupposes this purity legislation as its narrative grammar, giving high Coherence and Availability.
sourceText: “The leper in whom the plague is shall wear torn clothes, and the hair of his head shall hang loose. He shall cover his upper lip, and shall cry, ‘Unclean! Unclean!’ All the days in which the plague is in him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall dwell alone. Outside of the camp shall be his dwelling.

note: The cleansed leper must be presented to the priest for inspection and rites of restoration, exactly what Jesus commands: 'Go, show yourselves to the priests.' The direct dependence on the priestly examination law gives high Volume and Coherence.
sourceText: “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him, and behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper, then the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two living clean birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop.

note: Miriam's leprosy, exclusion 'outside the camp' for seven days, and restoration by intercession reinforce the segregation-and-cleansing pattern shaping the leper episode. Moderate Coherence; the motif overlaps with the Leviticus laws, so it adds recurrence rather than independent Volume.
sourceText: The cloud departed from over the Tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow. Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. Aaron said to Moses, “Oh, my lord, please don’t count this sin against us, in which we have done foolishly, and in which we have sinned. Let her not, I pray, be as one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb.” Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “Heal her, God, I beg you!” Yahweh […]

note: The four lepers at the gate of Samaria who 'stood at the entrance' likewise embody the marginalized-leper-at-a-distance topos and the Samaria setting. Geographic and situational resonance, but no verbal dependence, so low.
sourceText: Now there were four leprous men at the entrance of the gate. They said one to another, “Why do we sit here until we die?

note: The psalm's call to 'bless the Lord, O my soul... who heals all your diseases' coheres with the Samaritan's loud-voiced glorifying of God for his healing. Thematic only; faint.
sourceText: Praise Yahweh, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name! Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits; who forgives all your sins; who heals all your diseases;

note: Daniel's vision that the God of heaven will set up an everlasting kingdom underlies the Pharisees' question of when the Kingdom of God would come and Jesus' redefinition of its arrival. Moderate Volume from the shared 'kingdom of God' eschatology; Daniel is the key Second-Temple source for the expectation Jesus is correcting.
sourceText: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.

note: The everlasting dominion given to the one like a son of man frames the kingdom expectation in view; the link is conceptual, anticipating the Son-of-Man material that immediately follows, so it is low here.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: Moses insists the commandment is 'not far off... but very near you, in your mouth and in your heart,' a nearness-not-distant idiom that resonates with 'the Kingdom of God is among/within you' rather than 'here' or 'there.' Suggestive but contested.
sourceText: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]

note: The title 'the Son of Man' and his sudden, heaven-spanning revelation derive from Daniel's one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. This is the controlling OT source for the entire 'days of the Son of Man' discourse, giving high Volume, Recurrence, and Coherence.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: Zechariah's theophany where 'the Lord will appear... his arrow will go out like lightning' supplies the lightning-flash imagery for the Son of Man's day. The distinctive divine-lightning-of-judgment motif gives moderate Volume.
sourceText: Yahweh will be seen over them; and his arrow will go flash like lightning; and the Lord Yahweh will blow the trumpet, and will go with whirlwinds of the south.

note: 'His lightnings light up the world' depicts the cosmic, world-illuminating theophany echoed in the lightning that shines from one part of the sky to the other. Common theophanic imagery, so low.
sourceText: His lightning lights up the world. The earth sees, and trembles.

note: The Suffering Servant 'despised and rejected by men' undergirds 'he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.' The must-suffer-and-be-rejected formula coheres strongly with Isaiah 53, giving moderate Volume to a figural reading.
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.

note: The flood narrative — humanity eating and marrying in oblivious normalcy until Noah enters the ark and the deluge destroys them all — is explicitly invoked ('as in the days of Noah'). Direct named typology gives maximal Volume and Coherence.
sourceText: Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came on the earth. Noah went into the ship with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives, because of the floodwaters. Clean animals, unclean animals, birds, and everything that creeps on the ground went by pairs to Noah into the ship, male and female, as God commanded Noah. After the seven days, the floodwaters came on the earth. In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the […]

note: The verdict that human wickedness was great and every intention only evil supplies the moral indictment implicit in the days-of-Noah comparison: heedless wickedness met by sudden judgment. Strengthens the Coherence of the flood typology.
sourceText: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.

note: Sodom's destruction by fire and sulfur rained from heaven, with Lot going out on the day of doom, is named directly ('the days of Lot'). The explicit citation of fire-and-brimstone judgment gives maximal Volume and Coherence as the paired type to Noah.
sourceText: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky. He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground.

note: The outcry against Sodom's sin that prompts the divine visitation supplies the moral premise behind the eating-buying-building-as-usual-until-judgment picture. Coheres with the Lot typology and supports its Recurrence.
sourceText: Yahweh said, “Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous, I will go down now, and see whether their deeds are as bad as the reports which have come to me. If not, I will know.”

note: The covenant curse describes the land as 'brimstone and salt... like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah,' showing Sodom's fire-and-sulfur as the standard type of sudden total ruin Luke is invoking. Adds Recurrence; faint as an independent source.
sourceText: and that all of its land is sulfur, salt, and burning, that it is not sown, doesn’t produce, nor does any grass grow in it, like the overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which Yahweh overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath;

note: Ezekiel's reading of Sodom's sin as prosperous, complacent ease before judgment matches the buying/selling/planting/building complacency Luke emphasizes. Thematic reinforcement, low Volume.
sourceText: Behold, this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and prosperous ease was in her and in her daughters; neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy. They were haughty, and committed abomination before me: therefore I took them away when I saw it.

note: 'Remember Lot's wife' explicitly names the woman who looked back and became a pillar of salt, the warning against turning back when fleeing judgment. A direct citation by name gives maximal Volume and Coherence with 'let him not turn back.'
sourceText: But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.

note: The angels' command 'do not look behind you... lest you be consumed' is the prohibition Lot's wife violated and the imperative behind 'let him not go down... not turn back.' The flee-without-looking-back instruction is closely reproduced, giving high Volume.
sourceText: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”

note: The proverb 'all that a man has he will give for his life' resonates faintly with the paradox of seeking to save one's life and losing it; the connection is thematic, not verbal, so low.
sourceText: Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life.

note: The plague on the firstborn 'from the firstborn of Pharaoh to the firstborn of the maidservant who is behind the mill' pairs sleeping/grinding social opposites singled out for judgment, a structural analogue to the two in one bed and two grinding, one taken and one left. Suggestive selective-judgment motif, but no verbal dependence, so low.
sourceText: and all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the female servant who is behind the mill; and all the firstborn of livestock.

note: Malachi's promise that you will again distinguish 'between the righteous and the wicked' on the day of judgment coheres with the sudden separation of the paired figures, one taken and one left. Thematic and faint.
sourceText: Then you shall return and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him who serves God and him who doesn’t serve him.

note: The Lord's speech on the eagle/vulture whose young suck up blood and that is wherever the slain are ('where the slain are, there is he') is the clearest source for 'where the body is, there the vultures gather.' The distinctive corpse-and-bird-of-prey proverb gives strong Volume and Coherence with the judgment scene.
sourceText: His young ones also suck up blood. Where the slain are, there he is.”

note: The Chaldean horsemen who fly 'like an eagle swift to devour' gathering to the prey supply the swooping-bird-of-prey-toward-the-doomed imagery. Moderate Volume; reinforces the judgment-by-gathering-raptors motif.
sourceText: Their horses also are swifter than leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves. Their horsemen press proudly on. Yes, their horsemen come from afar. They fly as an eagle that hurries to devour.

note: The summons to the birds to gather to God's sacrificial slaughter and eat the flesh of the slain provides an eschatological carrion-gathering image very close to the saying's apocalyptic function. Good Coherence with the day-of-judgment context, lowered only by the eagles/vultures vs. generic-birds difference.
sourceText: You, son of man, thus says the Lord Yahweh: Speak to the birds of every sort, and to every animal of the field, Assemble yourselves, and come; gather yourselves on every side to my sacrifice that I do sacrifice for you, even a great sacrifice on the mountains of Israel, that you may eat flesh and drink blood. You shall eat the flesh of the mighty, and drink the blood of the princes of the earth, of rams, of lambs, and of goats, of bulls, all of them […]

note: 'Set the trumpet to your lips! One like an eagle is over the house of the Lord' offers an eagle-as-onrushing-judgment image. Faint and contested, but adds Recurrence to the bird-of-prey-judgment topos.
sourceText: “Put the trumpet to your lips! Something like an eagle is over Yahweh’s house, because they have broken my covenant, and rebelled against my law.

note: Sirach declares the Lord will not ignore the widow's cry nor the supplication of the oppressed, the prayer that pierces the clouds, and that he will not delay nor be patient (slow) until he repays vengeance. Luke fuses the widow figure, the day-and-night crying, the question of God's delay, and the swift vindication, making this the densest Second-Temple background for the parable. High volume and coherence.
sourceText: He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall? He that serves God according to his good pleasure shall be accepted, And his supplication shall reach to the clouds. The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds; And till it come near, he will not be comforted; And he will not depart, till […]

sourceText: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

sourceText: “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.

note: The crowd cries 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord,' quoting the pilgrim blessing of Psalm 118:26 with the added royal title 'the King.' This is a direct verbal citation embedded in the Hallel context of festal approach to the temple. High volume; the quotation is explicit and load-bearing.
sourceText: Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.

note: Setting the king-to-be on a mount for a processional enthronement recalls Solomon riding David's mule to Gihon to be proclaimed king. The royal mounting and acclamation parallel the Davidic succession ritual, supporting Luke's kingship framing. Medium confidence; the mount differs (colt vs. mule) but the enthronement pattern is strong.
sourceText: The king said to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.

note: Spreading garments before the rider evokes the acclamation of Jehu, where the people put their cloaks under him on the steps and proclaimed 'Jehu is king.' The garment-strewing as royal enthronement gesture closely parallels the crowd's act here. Medium volume; the cloak ritual is a recognizable kingship sign.
sourceText: Then they hurried, and took every man his garment, and put it under him on the top of the stairs, and blew the trumpet, saying, “Jehu is king.”

note: The acclamation 'Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest' echoes the heavenly-praise summons of the Psalms to praise the Lord 'in the heights.' The vertical glory-in-the-highest language coheres with the angelic Gloria pattern Luke reprises. Low because it is diffuse liturgical idiom.
sourceText: Praise Yah! Praise Yahweh from the heavens! Praise him in the heights!

note: Jesus's claim that 'the stones would cry out' if the disciples were silent draws on Habakkuk's woe, where the stone cries out from the wall and the beam answers against injustice. The personified crying stone witnessing truth coheres with the inevitability of acclaiming the coming king. High volume; the crying-stone image is rare and distinctive.
sourceText: For the stone will cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the woodwork will answer it.

note: The summons to Zion to rejoice because 'the King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst' resonates with the rejoicing multitude hailing the coming king at the descent to Jerusalem. The Daughter-of-Zion joy at the king's arrival coheres with Luke's scene. Low confidence; Zechariah 9 is the dominant source.
sourceText: Sing, daughter of Zion! Shout, Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. Yahweh has taken away your judgments. He has thrown out your enemy. The King of Israel, Yahweh, is in your midst. You will not be afraid of evil any more.

note: The siege oracle against Ariel (Jerusalem), where the Lord encamps against her, raises siege-works, and brings her low so she speaks from the ground, supplies the language of barricade, encirclement, and being dashed to the ground. Luke's weeping prophecy closely tracks this Ariel oracle's imagery of the humbled city. High volume and coherence with the lament form.
sourceText: Woe to Ariel! Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts come around; then I will distress Ariel, and there will be mourning and lamentation. She shall be to me as an altar hearth. I will encamp against you all around you, and will lay siege against you with posted troops. I will raise siege works against you. You will be brought down, and will speak out of the ground. Your speech will mumble out of the dust. Your voice will be […]

note: Jeremiah commands to 'cast up a mound against Jerusalem' for the siege and indicts the people who 'did not know' and were not ashamed at the time of visitation. Luke's barricade, encirclement, and the charge 'you did not know the time of your visitation' draw directly on this oracle's siege-and-visitation structure. High volume; the visitation language is verbally close.
sourceText: For Yahweh of Armies said, “Cut down trees, and cast up a mound against Jerusalem: this is the city to be visited; she is wholly oppression in the midst of her. As a well produces its waters, so she produces her wickedness: violence and destruction is heard in her; before me continually is sickness and wounds. Be instructed, Jerusalem, lest my soul be alienated from you; lest I make you a desolation, a land not inhabited.” Thus says Yahweh of Armies, […]

note: Isaiah's 'what will you do in the day of visitation' undergirds Jesus's reproach that Jerusalem 'did not know the time of your visitation.' The day-of-visitation as a moment of accountability and judgment coheres with Luke's siege lament. Medium; Jeremiah 6 carries the parallel verbal weight.
sourceText: What will you do in the day of visitation, and in the desolation which will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth?

note: The prophecy that enemies 'will dash you and your children within you to the ground' echoes the imprecatory Psalm's image of dashing children against the rock. The dash-children-to-the-ground violence of urban conquest supplies the horror Luke evokes for Jerusalem's fall. Medium; the verb dashing applied to children is distinctive.
sourceText: Happy shall he be, who takes and dashes your little ones against the rock.

note: Ezekiel's sign-act lays siege to a depicted Jerusalem, building siege-works and an iron wall against the city. Luke's 'your enemies will throw up a barricade against you' draws on this prophetic siege-enactment imagery. Medium volume; the barricade/siege-wall is the shared element.
sourceText: You also, son of man, take a tile, and lay it before yourself, and portray on it a city, even Jerusalem: and lay siege against it, and build forts against it, and cast up a mound against it; set camps also against it, and plant battering rams against it all around. Take for yourself an iron pan, and set it for a wall of iron between you and the city: and set your face toward it, and it shall be besieged, and you shall lay siege against it. This shall be a […]

note: Elisha's tearful prophecy of the coming atrocities, the slain young men and the dashed little ones, parallels Jesus's weeping over the city's foreseen destruction. The weeping prophet foreseeing the slaughter of children coheres with Luke's lament tone. Low; the contact is thematic.
sourceText: Hazael said, “Why do you weep, my lord?” He answered, “Because I know the evil that you will do to the children of Israel. You will set their strongholds on fire, and you will kill their young men with the sword, and will dash in pieces their little ones, and rip up their women with child.”

note: Hosea's judgment that Samaria's infants will be dashed in pieces and her pregnant women ripped open supplies another prophetic image of children destroyed in conquest behind 'dash you and your children to the ground.' The atrocity-on-children topos coheres but Hosea concerns Samaria. Low and contested.
sourceText: Samaria will bear her guilt; for she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women will be ripped open.”

note: Nahum's depiction of conquered Thebes, whose little ones 'were dashed in pieces at the head of every street,' is another stock siege-atrocity image standing behind Luke's children-dashed-to-the-ground. The shared conquest-of-a-city horror coheres faintly. Low confidence.
sourceText: Yet was she carried away. She went into captivity. Her young children also were dashed in pieces at the head of all the streets, and they cast lots for her honorable men, and all her great men were bound in chains.

note: Jeremiah declares that at 'the time of their visitation they shall be cast down,' the very phrase Luke turns into the reproach that Jerusalem failed to know its time of visitation. The visitation-as-judgment idiom is a direct conceptual borrowing. Medium, overlapping with the broader Jeremiah 6 siege oracle.
sourceText: Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush. Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time that I visit them, they shall be cast down,” says Yahweh.

note: The covenant curse foretells the enemy besieging your towns until the high walls fall, with horrors befalling children during the siege. Luke's siege, encirclement, and destruction of the city read as the realization of the Deuteronomic covenant curse for disobedience. Medium; the curse-fulfillment frame coheres strongly with Luke's theology.
sourceText: They will besiege you in all your gates, until your high and fortified walls come down, in which you trusted, throughout all your land. They will besiege you in all your gates throughout all your land, which Yahweh your God has given you. You will eat the fruit of your own body, the flesh of your sons and of your daughters, whom Yahweh your God has given you, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemies will distress you. The man who is tender […]

note: Isaiah's vision of the land laid waste, cities burned, and Daughter Zion left desolate provides a background for Jerusalem's coming devastation. The desolation-of-Zion motif coheres with Luke's lament but is diffuse. Low confidence.
sourceText: Your country is desolate. Your cities are burned with fire. Strangers devour your land in your presence, and it is desolate, as overthrown by strangers. The daughter of Zion is left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a field of melons, like a besieged city.

note: God's warning that he will cast out Israel and make the temple a heap if they forsake him, leaving passersby astonished, anticipates the destruction Jesus foresees. The conditional ruin-of-house-and-city coheres with the visitation-judgment theme. Low and contested.
sourceText: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’

note: Jesus quotes 'My house shall be a house of prayer' from Isaiah's oracle promising that foreigners' offerings will be accepted in a house of prayer for all peoples. The citation grounds the temple's intended purpose against its corruption. High volume; an explicit, marked quotation introduced by 'it is written.'
sourceText: even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”

note: Jesus brands the temple traffickers as making it 'a den of robbers,' quoting Jeremiah's temple sermon that asks whether the Lord's house has become a den of robbers in the people's eyes. The citation imports Jeremiah's threat of the temple's destruction for covenant infidelity. High volume; explicit quotation fused with Isaiah 56:7.
sourceText: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” says Yahweh.

note: Zechariah's eschatological vision ends with 'there shall be no more a trader (Canaanite) in the house of the Lord,' coheres with Jesus expelling the buyers and sellers from the temple. The purified end-time temple free of commerce supports the cleansing act. Low confidence; the prophetic-cleansing background is suggestive but uncited.
sourceText: Yes, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to Yahweh of Armies; and all those who sacrifice will come and take of them, and cook in them. In that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of Yahweh of Armies.

note: Malachi foretells the Lord suddenly coming to his temple to purify the sons of Levi and the offerings, an oracle of temple purgation that coheres with Jesus's cleansing entry. The Lord-comes-to-purify-the-temple pattern undergirds the scene though no words are quoted. Low confidence.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? note: The zeal for God's house that consumes the psalmist faintly informs Jesus's forceful purging of the temple, a connection John makes explicit. In Luke the link is at most an echo of the zealous-for-the-house motif. Low confidence and contested.
sourceText: For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.

note: The challenge 'by what authority?' / 'who made you ruler?' echoes the perennial Israelite question put to a divinely commissioned but unrecognized agent (Moses rebuffed: 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?'). Coherent with Luke's Moses-typology of Jesus but volume is faint and the wording is not distinctive.
sourceText: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”

note: The crowd's conviction that 'John was a prophet' whom it would be deadly to dishonor draws on the deuteronomistic theme that God repeatedly sent prophets whom the people rejected, setting up the tenants parable that follows. Volume is moderate; recurrence is strong across the OT prophet-rejection tradition, and it coheres tightly with 20:9-16.
sourceText: Yahweh, the God of their fathers, sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.

note: The framing of John's baptism as 'from heaven' and the people's reckoning of John as a true prophet trades on the Deuteronomic test of the authentic prophet sent by God. Availability and coherence are good, but the link to John specifically is inferential and contested.

Volume is high (the LXX of Isaiah 5:2 supplies 'planted a vineyard' and the verb for letting/hedging), recurrence pervades the vineyard-Israel tradition, and coherence with Luke's polemic against the leaders is total.

sourceText: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. note: 'I will send my beloved son' (ton huion mou ton agapeton) verbally echoes the LXX of the Aqedah, where Isaac is the 'beloved son' whom the father gives up. Volume rests on the distinctive phrase agapetos huios, shared with Luke's baptism/transfiguration; coherent with Luke's Son Christology, though some read it merely as 'only/dear son.'
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: The tenants' deliberation 'Come, let us kill him' over the heir verbally mirrors the brothers' plot against Joseph ('Come now, let us kill him... and we shall see what becomes of his dreams'). The shared conspiratorial formula is suggestive but the wording is conventional and the connection is contested.
sourceText: They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him. They said one to another, “Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.”

note: The escalating beating and killing of successive servants (prophets) sent to the vineyard reflects the murder of Zechariah son of Jehoiada and the broader chronicle of slain prophets, the canonical endpoint of prophet-rejection in the Hebrew Bible. Coherent and recurrent with the deuteronomistic theme, supplying the parable's 'servants.'
sourceText: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper?
