sourceText: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn. In that day there will be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon. The land will mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of […]
lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son. In that day the lamentation in Jerusalem shall be very great, as the mourning for the pomegranate grove cut down in the plain. And the land shall lament in separate families, the […]

note: The 'daughter of Jerusalem' weeping over the city's ruin, with infants and sucklings fainting, supplies the lament-over-Zion register Luke evokes. Lamentations is the canonical genre-source for Jerusalem-grief; contact is atmospheric.
sourceText: My eyes do fail with tears, my heart is troubled; My liver is poured on the earth, because of the destruction of the daughter of my people, Because the young children and the infants swoon in the streets of the city.

note: People hiding 'in the caves of the rocks' from the terror of the Lord in the day of judgment parallels the cry to mountains and hills; a possible secondary source alongside Hosea 10:8 for the day-of-wrath flight motif.
sourceText: Men shall go into the caves of the rocks, and into the holes of the earth, from before the terror of Yahweh, and from the glory of his majesty, when he arises to shake the earth mightily.

note: Crucified between 'two criminals' fulfills 'he was numbered with the transgressors' (Isa 53:12), a verse Luke quotes explicitly at 22:37 and here enacts narratively. The 'forgive them' intercession likewise renders the Servant who 'made intercession for the transgressors.' Both Servant clauses converge on this scene with high volume and recurrence.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: 'Dividing his garments among them, they cast lots' directly enacts Psalm 22:18, 'they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.' Verbal correspondence is exact; this is the most secure Psalm-22 echo in the chapter.
sourceText: They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.

note: 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing' embodies the Servant who 'bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.' The dying intercession for the executioners is the narrative form of Isaiah 53:12's final clause; high coherence within Luke's Servant Christology.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: 'In return for my love they accuse me, but I give myself to prayer' colors the dying intercession 'forgive them.' The righteous sufferer who prays for his persecutors is a psalm topos; faint verbal contact, coherent with the lament cluster.
sourceText: In return for my love, they are my adversaries; but I am in prayer.

note: Joseph forgiving brothers who 'did not know' the good God intended frames the 'they know not what they do' ignorance-forgiveness pattern. A thematic Second-Temple resonance (cf. Acts 3:17 'you acted in ignorance'); offered low.
sourceText: ‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him. His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.” Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God? As for you, you meant evil against me, but God […]

note: Forgiveness for those who 'know not what they do' aligns with the Torah category of unintentional/inadvertent sin (sins of ignorance) which is atoneable. Luke may be invoking the legal distinction that makes intercession fitting; faint but available.
sourceText: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘If anyone sins unintentionally, in any of the things which Yahweh has commanded not to be done, and does any one of them:

note: The rulers scoff 'He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the Christ' — a close rendering of Psalm 22:8, 'He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him, let him rescue him, for he delights in him,' framed by 22:7's mocking head-shakers. Volume and recurrence (Luke's sustained Ps 22 use) make this high.
sourceText: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”

note: The soldiers 'offering him vinegar' enacts Psalm 69:21, 'for my thirst they gave me vinegar (sour wine) to drink' — the mocking drink of the righteous sufferer. Direct lexical correspondence (oxos); a core Passion-psalm fulfillment.
sourceText: They also gave me gall for my food. In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.

note: 'Let us see if his words are true... if the righteous man is God's son, he will help him and deliver him' — the wicked taunting the righteous one to prove divine sonship maps precisely onto 'if this is the Christ of God, his chosen one... save yourself.' Deuterocanonical and demonstrably available, this taunt-of-the-righteous text is a strong source for the mockery's logic.
sourceText: Let us see if his words be true, And let us try what shall befall in the ending of his life. For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries. With outrage and torture let us put him to the test, That we may learn his gentleness, And may prove his patience under wrong. Let us condemn him to a shameful death; For he will be visited according to his words.

note: 'the Christ of God, his chosen one' (ho eklektos) echoes Isaiah 42:1, 'my chosen, in whom my soul delights,' the Servant designation Luke favors (cf. the transfiguration 'my Chosen'). The title brings the Servant frame into the mockery scene.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.

note: God's anointed rejected and scorned ('you have renounced... cast off your anointed') resonates with the mocking of the Christ/chosen one. A royal-lament background to the messianic mockery; faint verbal contact.
sourceText: But you have rejected and spurned. You have been angry with your anointed. You have renounced the covenant of your servant. You have defiled his crown in the dust.

note: 'The people stood watching... the rulers scoffed' realizes Psalm 22:7, 'all who see me mock me; they make mouths at me, they wag their heads.' The watching-and-deriding tableau is the psalm's own scene; recurrence with v. 35 mockery is strong.
sourceText: All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying,

note: The dialogue with the two criminals continues the 'numbered with the transgressors' enactment; the penitent's confession 'this man has done nothing wrong' restates the Servant's innocence (Isa 53:9 'he had done no violence'). Luke turns the transgressor-companions into witnesses to the just sufferer.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: 'This man has done nothing wrong' echoes 'he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth' — the criminal's verdict confirms the Servant's blamelessness even among the condemned. Coherent with Luke's innocence motif (vv. 4, 14, 22, 47).
sourceText: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

note: 'Today you will be with me in Paradise' draws on Isaiah's promise that the LORD will comfort Zion and 'make her wilderness like Eden, her desert like the garden (paradeisos) of the LORD.' The eschatological-Eden 'paradise' is the availably scriptural term Luke uses for restored blessedness.
sourceText: For Yahweh has comforted Zion; he has comforted all her waste places, and has made her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of Yahweh; joy and gladness shall be found therein, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.

note: 'Paradise' (paradeisos, the LXX word for the Eden garden) frames Jesus' promise as the regained Eden — readmission to the garden and the tree of life forfeited in Genesis 3. The figural Eden-restoration reading is well grounded in the LXX vocabulary; medium because Luke does not cite Genesis directly.
sourceText: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed. Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

note: 'Eden, the garden of God' (paradeisos in LXX) supplies another availability for the restored-paradise hope. Secondary to the Genesis/Isaiah Eden language; offered as a faint lexical support.
sourceText: You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone adorned you: ruby, topaz, emerald, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and beryl. Gold work of tambourines and of pipes was in you. In the day that you were created they were prepared.

note: 'Remember me when you come into your Kingdom' invokes the bestowal of an everlasting kingdom on one like a son of man (Dan 7:14). The kingdom-coming hope draws on Danielic enthronement language; thematic rather than verbal here.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'Darkness came over the whole land' at midday fulfills Amos 8:9, 'I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in clear day' — Amos' day-of-the-Lord judgment over mourning Israel. The noon-darkness (sixth hour) verbal and temporal match is strong; the surrounding Amos context (mourning as for an only son, v. 10) reinforces it.
sourceText: It will happen in that day,” says the Lord Yahweh, “that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day.

note: 'Darkness over the whole land' recalls the ninth plague, 'thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days,' a darkness 'that may be felt.' The exodus-plague resonance casts the crucifixion as a moment of judgment/new exodus; coherent though Amos is the closer noon-darkness source.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.” Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days.

note: 'The sun was darkened' echoes Joel's day-of-the-LORD signs, 'the sun and moon are darkened' (Joel 2:10; 3:15), language Luke himself cites in Acts 2:20. Availability is confirmed by Luke's own use; the cosmic-portent register fits the crucifixion's apocalyptic framing.
sourceText: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.

note: 'The veil of the temple was torn in two' presupposes the Exodus curtain (katapetasma) that screens the Holy of Holies. The tearing dramatically signifies access/judgment upon the sanctuary; the cultic referent is unambiguously the Tabernacle/Temple veil of Exodus 26.
sourceText: “You shall make a veil of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cherubim. The work of the skillful workman shall it be made. You shall hang it on four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold; their hooks shall be of gold, on four sockets of silver. You shall hang up the veil under the clasps, and shall bring the ark of the testimony in there within the veil: and the veil shall separate the holy place from the most holy for you.

note: 'A day of darkness and gloom' as the day of the LORD's wrath supplies further prophetic backing for the noon darkness. Secondary to Amos/Joel; offered as a faint convergent witness.
sourceText: That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,

note: 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit' is a direct quotation of Psalm 31:5, 'into your hand I commit my spirit,' the explicit dying word. Luke makes the righteous sufferer's prayer of trust the climactic utterance, replacing Mark's cry of dereliction; verbatim and unmistakable.
sourceText: Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth.

note: The whole psalm of the trusting righteous sufferer ('you redeem me, O LORD, faithful God,' surrounded by enemies yet committing himself to God) frames the death-cry beyond the single quoted line. Recurrence of Psalm 31's confidence motif throughout Luke's calm passion supports a wider allusion.
sourceText: In you, Yahweh, I take refuge. Let me never be disappointed. Deliver me in your righteousness. Bow down your ear to me. Deliver me speedily. Be to me a strong rock, a house of defense to save me. For you are my rock and my fortress, therefore for your name’s sake lead me and guide me. Pluck me out of the net that they have laid secretly for me, for you are my stronghold. Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth. I hate those […]

note: 'God of the spirits of all flesh' / the giving-up of spirit may faintly evoke the biblical idiom of the breath/spirit returning to God (cf. Eccl 12:7). Thematic background for the 'breathed his last'; not a specific Lukan target.
sourceText: They fell on their faces, and said, “God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?”

note: The centurion's verdict 'Certainly this was a righteous man' (dikaios) crowns Luke's Servant-as-righteous-one theme — 'my righteous servant shall make many righteous.' Luke's distinctive dikaios (vs Mark's 'Son of God') points to Isaiah 53:11 LXX; medium-high coherence with the chapter's innocence refrain.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

note: The vindicated 'righteous man' (dikaios) recalls Wisdom's persecuted just one whom God acknowledges as son. The centurion's confession answers the mockers' Wisdom-styled taunt (v. 35); thematic inclusio rather than quotation.
sourceText: For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries.

note: 'All his acquaintances, and the women... stood at a distance, watching' enacts Psalm 38:11, 'my friends and companions stand aloof from my affliction, and my kinsmen stand far off.' The distant-onlookers detail is a precise lament motif of abandonment; strong verbal/situational match.
sourceText: My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my plague. My kinsmen stand far away.

note: The multitudes 'beating their breasts' over the crucified one resonates with the mourning of Zechariah 12:10-12, 'they shall look on him whom they pierced and mourn.' Luke's repentant breast-beating crowd (cf. 18:13) faintly draws on this Jerusalem-mourning prophecy.
sourceText: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

note: 'You have caused my companions to shun me' parallels the acquaintances standing at a distance, doubling Psalm 38:11. A secondary lament witness to the friends-kept-far motif; offered low.
sourceText: You have taken my friends from me. You have made me an abomination to them. I am confined, and I can’t escape.

note: Burial by Joseph, a rich council member, in an unused rock-cut tomb realizes Isaiah 53:9, 'they made his grave... with a rich man in his death,' the Servant honored in burial despite dying among criminals. The 'rich and righteous man' and the new tomb make this Luke's enactment of the Servant's burial; high coherence.
sourceText: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

note: Taking the body down and burying it the same day, before the Sabbath, observes Deuteronomy 21:22-23, 'his body shall not remain all night... you shall bury him the same day,' lest the land be defiled by one 'hanged on a tree.' The same-day burial urgency is governed by this law; strong availability and coherence.
sourceText: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree; his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God; that you don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.

note: 'On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment' directly invokes the Decalogue Sabbath law, Exodus 20:10 ('you shall not do any work'). Luke's editorial 'according to the commandment' is an explicit appeal to Torah; the rest also frames the third-day timing.
sourceText: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates;

note: The Sabbath rest after the finished work of the cross resonates figurally with God resting on the seventh day after creation — the new creation's Sabbath repose before resurrection. A theological-figural reading; Luke signals only the commandment, so it is offered low.
sourceText: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.

note: The Deuteronomic form of the Sabbath commandment is an equally available source for 'rested according to the commandment.' Listed alongside Exodus 20 as the alternative Decalogue text Luke's phrase could intend.
sourceText: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]

note: The 'two men in dazzling clothing' at the tomb echo Daniel's angelic figure clothed in linen with a face/body 'like lightning' and 'like the gleam of beryl.' Luke's verb 'astraptousē' (flashing/dazzling) matches the Danielic theophanic vocabulary for angelic interpreters who appear at moments of eschatological revelation. Volume and coherence are strong; Daniel is Luke's apocalyptic template.
sourceText: I lifted up my eyes, and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, whose thighs were adorned with pure gold of Uphaz: his body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as flaming torches, and his arms and his feet like burnished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.

note: The two young men of 'splendid' appearance who appear in the Jerusalem temple to Heliodorus furnish a close Second-Temple parallel to Luke's two men in dazzling clothing. The doubling of radiant angelic figures (cf. also 2 Macc 3:33-34) was a recognizable Hellenistic-Jewish topos for divine vindication and intervention. Availability and coherence support it.
sourceText: Two other also appeared to him, young men notable in their strength, and beautiful in their glory, and splendid in their apparel, who stood by him on either side, and scourged him unceasingly, inflicting on him many sore stripes.

note: 'The third day rise again' draws on Hosea's 'after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up,' the most cited prophetic warrant for third-day resurrection in early Christian and rabbinic exegesis. Luke makes the 'third day' a fixed kerygmatic formula (cf. 24:7, 21, 46), and Hosea supplies the schematic Scriptural pattern. Contested as the precise source but high recurrence.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: Jonah's 'three days and three nights' in the fish is invoked elsewhere in the Gospel tradition as the sign of resurrection (the 'sign of Jonah'), and stands behind the third-day pattern Luke repeats here. The link is typological rather than verbal in Luke 24, so confidence is low and the connection is contested.
sourceText: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

note: 'On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes' (the Aqedah) was read in early Jewish and Christian tradition as a deliverance-on-the-third-day pattern, the deliverance of the bound son. As a faint contributor to the rabbinic/Christian web of 'third day' rescue texts it may color Luke's formula, though there is no verbal contact. Contested and low volume.
sourceText: On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place far off.

note: 'Be ready for the third day, for on the third day the LORD will come down' supplies another 'third day' theophany-and-covenant text feeding the Jewish pattern of decisive divine action on the third day. Its contribution to Luke's resurrection formula is figural and faint, lacking verbal correspondence. Marked contested.
sourceText: and be ready against the third day; for on the third day Yahweh will come down in the sight of all the people on Mount Sinai.

note: Luke dates the resurrection to 'the first day of the week' (mia tōn sabbatōn), and early Christian reading saw new-creation overtones in the resurrection on the day light was first made. The echo is figural and depends on canonical placement rather than wording, so confidence is low and it is contested.
sourceText: God called the light “day”, and the darkness he called “night”. There was evening and there was morning, the first day.

note: The angels recall Jesus' words that 'the Son of Man must be delivered up... and the third day rise again.' The Son of Man title and his vindication/exaltation derive from Daniel 7, where the one like a son of man is brought before the Ancient of Days and given dominion. The vindication-after-suffering motif coheres with Luke's whole chapter.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: The risen Jesus joins the travelers unrecognized and is pressed to stay and share a meal, recalling the LORD/angels appearing to Abraham as a wayfarer who is welcomed with hospitality and food. The pattern of unrecognized divine visitor received with hospitality is a Scriptural type Luke evokes, though there is no verbal quotation. Contested, low volume.
sourceText: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]

note: The angel Raphael travels incognito with Tobias as an unrecognized companion whose true identity is disclosed only at the end (Tob 12). The Emmaus narrative's structure of a hidden divine guide on a journey parallels Tobit's traveling-angel motif, a recognizable Second-Temple type. Faint and structural rather than verbal, hence low and contested.
sourceText: He went to seek a man, and found Raphael who was an angel; and he didn’t know it. He said to him, “Can I go with you to Rages of Media? Do you know those places well?” The angel said to him, “I will go with you. I know the way well. I have lodged with our brother Gabael.” Tobias said to him, “Wait for me, and I will tell my father.” He said to him, “Go, and don’t wait. And he went in and said to his father, “Behold, I have found someone who will go with […]

note: Jesus' rebuke that the Christ 'had to suffer these things and enter into his glory' presupposes the Suffering Servant who is 'despised and rejected' yet afterward exalted (Isa 52:13; 53:11-12). Luke roots the necessity (dei) of messianic suffering in the Servant Songs, which he cites explicitly elsewhere (Lk 22:37). Coherence with the chapter's exegetical climax is strong.
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.

note: The motif of the righteous one who suffers grievously and is then vindicated, which Jesus expounds 'beginning from Moses and all the prophets,' draws on the Passion psalm Luke uses in the crucifixion scene. The suffering-and-glory pattern of Psalm 22 (lament turning to praise/vindication) is a primary text in the Scriptural 'things concerning himself.' Coherence high.
sourceText: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning? My God, I cry in the daytime, but you don’t answer; in the night season, and am not silent. But you are holy, you who inhabit the praises of Israel. Our fathers trusted in you. They trusted, and you delivered them. They cried to you, and were delivered. They trusted in you, and were not disappointed. But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of […]

note: 'Enter into his glory' echoes the enthronement of the one like a son of man who is given glory and dominion before the Ancient of Days. Luke pairs suffering with glorification, and Daniel 7 supplies the vindicated-and-glorified figure central to his messianic reading. Recurrence across the chapter supports it.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The travelers describe Jesus as 'a prophet mighty in deed and word,' and the exposition 'beginning from Moses' invokes the prophet-like-Moses whom God would raise up and to whom Israel must listen. Luke elsewhere applies this text to Jesus (Acts 3:22; 7:37), making it a likely component of the Mosaic witness here. Coherence and recurrence support medium confidence.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: The report that the chief priests 'delivered him up to be condemned to death' resonates with the Servant who was 'led like a lamb to the slaughter' and handed over. As part of the Servant subtext Jesus is about to expound, it colors the travelers' summary, though without quotation. Low and somewhat contested.
sourceText: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.

note: The hope that Jesus 'would redeem Israel' sits within the Servant's mission to restore and redeem Israel before he is given as a light to the nations. Luke's redemption-of-Israel language (cf. Lk 1:68; 2:38) draws on Deutero-Isaiah's restoration vocabulary. Faint here, hence low.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, the Redeemer of Israel, and his Holy One, to him whom man despises, to him whom the nation abhors, to a servant of rulers: “Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall worship; because of Yahweh who is faithful, even the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you.”

note: 'Their eyes were opened, and they recognized him' deliberately inverts 'the eyes of both were opened' in Eden, where opened eyes brought shame and exile; here opened eyes at the breaking of bread bring recognition of the risen Lord. The verbal correspondence (eyes opened) plus reversal is a coherent Lukan new-creation motif. Volume is moderate; the allusion is widely recognized.
sourceText: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.

note: The shared meal at which the divine guest is recognized recalls the LORD/angels eating with Abraham at Mamre, where hospitality discloses the visitor's identity. The Emmaus meal as the locus of revelation parallels the Mamre table-fellowship type. Structural and faint, so low and contested.
sourceText: He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.

note: The breaking of bread that opens their eyes carries Passover/Eucharistic overtones, the meal at which deliverance is remembered and made present. Given Luke's Passover framing of the Last Supper, the Emmaus bread figurally recalls the Passover bread of redemption. Typological rather than verbal, hence low and contested.
sourceText: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.

note: Elisha's prayer that the servant's eyes be opened to see the unseen heavenly reality offers a parallel for the divinely granted opening of eyes to perceive the risen Christ. The motif of God opening human eyes to spiritual sight is a recurring OT pattern Luke taps. Faint and contested.
sourceText: Elisha prayed, and said, “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” Yahweh opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.

note: Jesus 'vanished out of their sight' faintly echoes the sudden removal of righteous figures who are 'taken' by God (Enoch 'was not, for God took him'). As a marker of a translated/heavenly figure no longer subject to ordinary presence, it anticipates the ascension. Very faint, contested.
sourceText: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.

note: Raphael's disclosure, 'I appeared to you, but I did not eat or drink; it was a vision that you saw,' frames the Second-Temple assumption that angelic/spirit visitants only seem to eat. Luke counters precisely this by having the risen Jesus eat real food to prove he is 'not a spirit' but has flesh and bones, engaging Tobit's category. Coherence and availability are strong.
sourceText: All these days I appeared to you. I didn’t eat or drink, but you all saw a vision.

note: Jesus eating broiled fish before them to prove corporeal reality parallels the angels who 'ate' before Abraham at Mamre, the locus classicus for heavenly visitors sharing human food. Luke uses the eating motif as physical proof against the disciples' supposition of a spirit. Recurrence of the 'divine visitor eats' type supports it.
sourceText: He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.

note: The disciples suppose they see a disembodied 'spirit' (pneuma), reflecting a current view that the righteous dead exist as souls 'in the hand of God.' Luke's insistence on flesh and bones engages and corrects such a discarnate-soul expectation. Conceptual and faint, so low and contested.
sourceText: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them.

note: 'In my flesh I shall see God' anticipates an embodied vindication beyond death that resonates with Luke's emphasis on the risen Jesus' flesh and bones. As a faint OT witness to bodily hope it may color the scene, but there is no verbal contact. Contested, low.
sourceText: After my skin is destroyed, then in my flesh shall I see God,

note: That repentance and forgiveness be proclaimed 'to all the nations' fulfills the Psalter's vision that 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD,' part of the Writings (psalmoi) Jesus names as bearing witness to him. Luke roots the universal mission in the Psalms he has just cited. Coherence with the tripartite-canon statement supports it.
sourceText: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Yahweh. All the relatives of the nations shall worship before you.

note: The Servant given 'as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' is the programmatic text behind 'repentance and remission of sins... to all the nations.' Luke quotes Isa 49:6 explicitly at Acts 13:47 and alludes to it at Acts 1:8, making it the key prophetic warrant for the worldwide mission launched here. Volume and recurrence are high.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: 'Beginning at Jerusalem' enacts the eschatological pattern whereby 'out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem,' the nations streaming to and the word streaming from Zion. Luke reverses the centripetal pilgrimage into a centrifugal mission from Jerusalem. Coherence is strong.
sourceText: Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.

note: Micah's parallel oracle that 'the word of the LORD' goes forth 'from Jerusalem' to instruct the nations reinforces the Jerusalem-origin of the universal proclamation. The doubled prophetic witness (with Isa 2:3) strengthens the case that Luke draws on the Zion-mission tradition. Recurrence supports medium.
sourceText: Many nations will go and say, “Come, and let us go up to the mountain of Yahweh, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For the law will go out of Zion, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem;

note: The herald who proclaims good news of salvation from Zion underlies Luke's commissioning of witnesses to preach forgiveness beginning at Jerusalem. Luke's vocabulary of proclaiming (kēryssō) good news echoes the Isaianic herald, a text central to his mission theology. Coherence good.
sourceText: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

note: 'Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved... in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape' underwrites repentance/forgiveness proclaimed 'in his name' beginning from Jerusalem. Luke cites Joel 2 at Pentecost (Acts 2:21), making it a strong intertext for the commission. Recurrence in Luke-Acts supports it.
sourceText: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.

note: 'I send out the promise of my Father on you... until you are clothed with power from on high' anticipates Joel's outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, which Luke fulfills explicitly at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, quoting Joel). The Spirit as the Father's promise is the bridge from Luke 24 to Acts. Volume and recurrence are high.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.

note: 'Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high' supplies the very phrase 'power from on high' (ex hypsous) for the promised Spirit-endowment. Luke's 'clothed with power from on high' draws on this Isaianic image of the Spirit poured out to renew. Verbal contact ('from on high') gives medium-strong confidence.
sourceText: Until the Spirit is poured on us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is considered a forest.

note: 'I will pour my Spirit upon your descendants' reinforces the promised-Spirit theme of being clothed with power, an OT pattern of the Spirit poured out as gift and blessing. Together with Joel and Isa 32 it forms the cluster behind the Father's promise. Recurrence within the cluster supports it.
sourceText: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:

note: 'Clothed with power' (enedysasthe) recalls the idiom that the Spirit of the LORD 'clothed itself with' Gideon, the standard OT metaphor for divine empowerment of a chosen agent. Luke's clothing-with-power language may draw on this Spirit-clothing idiom. Faint verbal idiom, hence low and contested.
sourceText: But the Spirit of Yahweh came on Gideon; and he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered together after him.

note: 'All things written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms... must be fulfilled' names the threefold Hebrew canon (Torah, Prophets, Writings), and the Law of Moses as a written witness placed beside the ark to testify is the Torah pole of that witness. Luke frames the whole of Scripture, beginning with Moses' written law, as testifying to Christ. Coherence with the canon formula supports it.
sourceText: When Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished, Moses commanded the Levites, who bore the ark of the covenant of Yahweh, saying, “Take this book of the law, and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of Yahweh your God, that it may be there for a witness against you.

note: The prologue to Sirach repeatedly names 'the Law and the Prophets and the others/the rest of the books,' the earliest explicit witness to the tripartite division of Hebrew Scripture that Luke 24:44 presupposes ('law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms'). It supplies the Second-Temple canonical framework, not a content-quotation. Availability and coherence support medium.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: Jesus 'lifted up his hands and blessed them' as he departs reproduces the climactic scene of Simon the high priest who 'lifted up his hands over the whole congregation... to pronounce the blessing of the LORD,' after which the people worship. Luke casts the ascending Jesus as the great high priest performing the Aaronic benediction. Volume, coherence, and the worship response all align strongly.
sourceText: Then he went down, and lifted up his hands Over the whole congregation of the children of Israel, To give blessing to the Lord with his lips, And to glory in his name. And he bowed himself down in worship the second time, To declare the blessing from the Most High. And now bless you the God of all, Which everywhere does great things, Which exalts our days from the womb, And deals with us according to his mercy.

note: 'Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and came down' is the priestly prototype for Jesus' parting gesture of lifted hands and blessing. The lifting-hands-to-bless is the defining act of the Aaronic priesthood, which Luke transfers to the ascending Christ. Verbal and gestural correspondence is high.
sourceText: Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people, and blessed them; and he came down from offering the sin offering, and the burnt offering, and the peace offerings.

note: The Aaronic blessing ('The LORD bless you and keep you...') is the content of the priestly benediction Jesus enacts with lifted hands. Luke evokes the priest putting the divine name on the people as the risen Christ blesses them at his departure. Coherence with the Lev/Sirach cluster supports it.
sourceText: “Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying, ‘This is how you shall bless the children of Israel.’ You shall tell them, ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’ “So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them.”

note: Jesus 'was carried up into heaven' while his disciples watch, closely paralleling Elijah taken up into heaven before Elisha, whose witnessing disciple then receives a double portion of his spirit. Luke's ascension-then-Spirit sequence is modeled on the Elijah-Elisha succession, and Luke uses Elijah typology throughout. Volume and coherence are high.
sourceText: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

note: Elisha's request to inherit Elijah's spirit, granted 'if you see me taken,' parallels the disciples who witness Jesus' ascent and then await the promised Spirit. Luke ties the seeing of the departure to the bestowal of the Spirit, mirroring the Elijah-Elisha transfer. Recurrence with the prior verse supports medium.
sourceText: When they had gone over, Elijah said to Elisha, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha said, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” He said, “You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it shall be so for you; but if not, it shall not be so.”

note: 'God has gone up with a shout' supplies the enthronement-ascent motif of God ascending to his throne amid praise, fitting the disciples who 'worshiped him and returned... with great joy, praising God.' Luke's ascension-to-worship sequence draws on the Zion enthronement psalms. Coherence with the joyful praise response supports it.
sourceText: God has gone up with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a trumpet.

note: The 'gates lift up your heads' entry of the King of glory was read in early tradition as the ascent of the exalted Lord into the heavenly sanctuary, paralleling Jesus carried up into heaven. Faint and traditional rather than verbal in Luke, so low and contested.
sourceText: Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is the King of glory? Yahweh strong and mighty, Yahweh mighty in battle. Lift up your heads, you gates; yes, lift them up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is this King of glory? Yahweh of Armies is the King of glory! Selah.

note: Enoch who 'walked with God, and was not, for God took him' is an OT type of the righteous one assumed into heaven, contributing to the assumption pattern Luke narrates. As one of the canonical assumption figures (with Elijah) it faintly informs the ascension. Low, contested.
sourceText: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.

note: The ascent into heaven and the disciples' worship enact the giving of dominion and the service/worship of all peoples to the one like a son of man who comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days. Luke's exalted Christ receiving worship realizes the Danielic enthronement. Coherence with the Son of Man framing of the chapter supports it.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: After Aaron's blessing the glory of the LORD appears and the people fall down/worship; Luke's sequence of priestly blessing followed by worship in the temple mirrors this Levitical pattern of blessing-then-glory-then-worship. Structural echo reinforcing the priestly reading, so low and supportive.
sourceText: Moses and Aaron went into the Tent of Meeting, and came out, and blessed the people: and Yahweh’s glory appeared to all the people. Fire came out from before Yahweh, and consumed the burnt offering and the fat upon the altar. When all the people saw it, they shouted, and fell on their faces.

note: John opens with the exact phrase 'In the beginning' (en archē), the LXX incipit of Genesis 1:1, signaling a deliberate re-narration of creation. Volume is maximal (verbatim phrase in the most marked position of the Gospel) and recurrence strong (creation language saturates vv.1-5). Thematic coherence is total: John reads the Genesis creation through the lens of the Word as agent.
sourceText: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

note: Creation 'by the word' ('Let there be light') is recast as creation 'through him,' the Logos (v.3). The Genesis pattern of God speaking the world into being is the conceptual substrate for 'all things were made through him.' High thematic coherence between divine speech-act and the personified Word.
sourceText: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

note: 'By the word of the LORD the heavens were made' is the clearest OT text crediting creation to God's spoken word, the Jewish exegetical bridge from Genesis to a creative Logos. Strong thematic coherence with v.3 ('all things were made through him') and availability secure in Second-Temple liturgy.
sourceText: By Yahweh’s word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth.

note: Personified Wisdom, 'with' God 'in the beginning' as the agent/craftsman of creation, is the primary background for the Word who 'was with God' and through whom all things were made. Recurrence of the with-God-at-creation motif and high thematic coherence; widely recognized as John's Wisdom-Christology source.
sourceText: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was […]

note: Wisdom as the 'breath of the power of God,' a pure effulgence of glory, an unspotted mirror, and the light surpassing all light underwrites John's identification of the Word with life and light (vv.4-5). Availability secure (deuterocanonical, first century) and strong thematic coherence with the light/glory motifs of the Prologue.
sourceText: For she that is the architect of all things taught me, even wisdom. For there is in her a spirit quick of understanding, holy, Alone in kind, manifold, Subtil, freely moving, Clear in utterance, unpolluted, Distinct, unharmed, Loving what is good, keen, unhindered, Beneficent, loving toward man, Stedfast, sure, free from care, All-powerful, all-surveying, And penetrating through all spirits That are quick of understanding, pure, most subtle: For wisdom is […]

note: 'O God... who made all things by your word, and by your wisdom formed man' explicitly pairs word and wisdom as co-agents of creation, the exact fusion John performs on the Logos. Medium confidence because it is conceptual parallel rather than verbal, but thematic coherence with v.3 is high.
sourceText: O God of the fathers, and Lord who keep your mercy, Who made all things by your word; And by your wisdom you formedst man, That he should have dominion over the creatures that were made by you,

note: Wisdom's self-praise, coming forth from the mouth of the Most High and present from the beginning, is a key model for the pre-existent Word. Sirach 24 is the most sustained Wisdom-tabernacle hymn and is recurrent across the Prologue (see also v.14). High thematic coherence.
sourceText: Wisdom will praise herself, And will glory in the midst of her people. In the congregation of the Most High will she open her mouth, And glory in the presence of his power. I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, And covered the earth as a mist. I lived in high places, And my throne is in the pillar of the cloud. Alone I compassed the circuit of heaven, And walked in the depth of the abyss. In the waves of the sea, and in all the earth, And in every […]

note: The darkness over the deep before the first light is evoked by 'the light shines in the darkness' (v.5). The creation-from-darkness sequence reinforces the Genesis 1 framing; medium confidence as the verbal contact is thematic (light/darkness) rather than lexical.
sourceText: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.

note: 'For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light' fuses life and light as divine gifts, exactly the pairing of v.4 ('in him was life, and the life was the light of men'). Thematic coherence is high; flagged medium for absence of verbal borrowing.
sourceText: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.

note: 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' offers the light-shining-in-darkness topos. Low confidence and somewhat contested: the motif is broad and could derive from several light texts, but it coheres with the Prologue's darkness-versus-light contest.
sourceText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: 'Whoever finds me finds life' links personified Wisdom directly to life, supporting the life-in-the-Word claim of v.4. Faint and contested, but coherent with the broader Wisdom substrate already established.
sourceText: For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh.

note: 'Behold, I send my messenger' frames John as the divinely sent forerunner ('there came a man, sent from God'). The sending-of-the-messenger motif is the standard prophetic preparation pattern and coheres with John's witness role; medium because the verbal link is conceptual.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'A light to the nations' resonates with 'the true light that enlightens everyone' (v.9), the universal scope of illumination. Low confidence: the universalizing of light is a shared Isaianic theme rather than a direct quotation.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' supplies the divine-light identification that the Prologue transfers to the Logos. Faint and contested; included for recurrence of the light-as-God motif.
sourceText: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?

note: Wisdom seeks a resting place among the nations and is given Israel as her inheritance; the motif of the agent of creation coming to her own people who variously receive or reject her underlies vv.10-11. Thematic coherence with the Wisdom-rejection pattern is strong; medium for lack of verbal contact.
sourceText: With all these I sought rest; And in whose inheritance shall I lodge? Then the Creator of all things gave me a commandment; And he that created me made my tabernacle to rest, And said, Let your tabernacle be in Jacob, And your inheritance in Israel. He created me from the beginning before the world; And to the end I will not fail. In the holy tabernacle I ministered before him; And so was I established in Sion. In the beloved city likewise he gave me […]

note: Wisdom calls but is not received ('I called and you refused'), the rejection-of-Wisdom topos behind 'his own didn't receive him' (v.11). The motif of the personified divine agent spurned by her people coheres tightly with John's tragic note.
sourceText: Because I have called, and you have refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no one has paid attention; but you have ignored all my counsel, and wanted none of my reproof; I also will laugh at your disaster. I will mock when calamity overtakes you; when calamity overtakes you like a storm, when your disaster comes on like a whirlwind; when distress and anguish come on you. Then will they call on me, but I will not answer. They will seek me diligently, […]

note: Wisdom finds no dwelling place among humans and returns to heaven, the most pointed Second-Temple parallel to the Word coming to his own and being rejected (vv.10-11). Pseudepigraphal but genuinely warranted here: the Wisdom-withdrawal pattern matches John's reversal closely. Contested as to direct dependence.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: 'You are the children of the LORD your God' supplies the divine-sonship category recast as the 'right to become God's children' (v.12). Low confidence; the sonship-of-God-people motif is broad across the OT.
sourceText: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.

note: 'The God who gave you birth' offers a God-as-begetter image behind 'born... of God' (v.13). Faint and contested, but coheres with the divine-generation language that replaces ordinary descent.
sourceText: Of the Rock who became your father, you are unmindful, and have forgotten God who gave you birth.

note: 'You are children of the living God,' the promise of new divine sonship to those who were not a people, resonates with becoming God's children by birth from God (vv.12-13). Low confidence; thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’

note: 'The Word became flesh and lived (eskēnōsen, 'tabernacled') among us' deliberately evokes the sanctuary that God commanded so he might 'dwell among them.' The tabernacle-pitching verb is the load-bearing figural cue: the incarnate Word is the new tent of meeting. High volume and thematic coherence.
sourceText: Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them. According to all that I show you, the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all of its furniture, even so you shall make it.

note: The glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle is the template for 'we saw his glory' (v.14): the indwelling Word manifests the kabod that once filled the tent. The tabernacle-plus-glory pairing makes the figural reading near-certain. High coherence and recurrence with the Sinai cycle.
sourceText: Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle. Moses wasn’t able to enter into the Tent of Meeting, because the cloud stayed on it, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle.

note: 'Full of grace and truth' renders the LXX/Hebrew formula 'abounding in steadfast love (hesed) and faithfulness ('emet)' from God's self-revelation to Moses. This is the densest verbal-conceptual borrowing of the Prologue's climax (vv.14,17). Very high thematic coherence: the glory Israel saw at Sinai is now seen in the Word.
sourceText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,

note: Moses' request to see God's glory, granted only as a passing of God's goodness while his face remains unseen, undergirds both 'we saw his glory' and 'no one has seen God at any time' (vv.14,18). The contrast (Moses denied the face; the Son makes God known) is structured directly on this scene.
sourceText: He said, “Please show me your glory.” He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you.
