sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]

note: Nehemiah's zealous cleansing of the temple chambers of Tobiah's goods provides a scriptural model of reforming zeal that purges the temple of intrusion, resonating with Jesus' 'zeal' and his expulsion of the traders. The echo is faint and typological rather than verbal.
sourceText: and I came to Jerusalem, and understood the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, in preparing him a room in the courts of God’s house. It grieved me severely: therefore I threw all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the room. Then I commanded, and they cleansed the rooms: and there brought I again the vessels of God’s house, with the meal offerings and the frankincense.

note: 'Holiness befits your house, O LORD, forevermore' undergirds the indignation at profaning the Father's house, the principle Jesus enforces. Volume is low and the connection conceptual; included as a faint sanctity-of-the-house resonance.
sourceText: Your statutes stand firm. Holiness adorns your house, Yahweh, forever more.

note: 'The LORD looks on the heart' while man looks on outward appearance is the classic text for divine knowledge of the inner person, directly behind 'he knew what was in man.' Volume and Coherence are strong: Jesus exercises the uniquely divine prerogative of reading hearts, a Johannine claim to his deity. The conceptual contact is precise.
sourceText: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

note: 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways' ascribes heart-searching to YHWH alone; John applies this to Jesus, who 'knew everyone' and needed no testimony about man. Coherence is high within John's high Christology; the divine heart-searcher motif is the operative background.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: The psalm's confession that the LORD searches and knows everything, discerning thoughts from afar before a word is spoken, is the paradigmatic statement of omniscient knowledge of persons that John attributes to Jesus. Volume and Coherence are strong; this is a leading text for the divine knowledge Jesus possesses.
sourceText: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.

note: Solomon's temple prayer affirms that God alone 'knows the hearts of all the children of mankind.' Set against the temple context just preceding (2:13-22), Jesus' knowledge of all hearts pointedly claims the prerogative Solomon reserved to God alone, reinforcing the divine-knowledge Christology. Coherence with the chapter's temple frame strengthens it.
sourceText: then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive, and do, and render to every man according to all his ways, whose heart you know; (for you, even you only, know the hearts of all the children of men;)

note: 'O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind' is another heart-testing formula in the same cluster as 17:10; it reinforces the divine-omniscience background without distinct verbal contact of its own. Listed as a corroborating faint echo.
sourceText: But, Yahweh of Armies, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, I shall see your vengeance on them; for to you have I revealed my cause.

note: Ben Sira's praise of the Most High who 'searches out the abyss and the human heart' and from whom no thought is hidden offers a deuterocanonical parallel to Jesus knowing what is in man. Availability is good; the echo is thematic, reinforcing the omniscience motif rather than supplying a direct source.
sourceText: He searcheth out the deep, and the heart, And he has understanding of their cunning plans: For the Most High knows all knowledge, And he looks into the signs of the world, Declaring the things that are past, and the things that shall be, And revealing the traces of hidden things. No thought escapes him; There is not a word hid from him.

note: Being 'born of water and spirit' fuses the two halves of Ezekiel's new-covenant oracle: God sprinkles 'clean water' for cleansing and puts a 'new spirit' within. The water-then-spirit sequence and the regeneration theme give high volume and coherence; Jesus' rebuke that 'the teacher of Israel' should know this presumes a known prophetic text.
sourceText: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: The wind that 'blows where it wants to' and the one 'born of the Spirit' echo Ezekiel's valley vision where the ruach/breath comes from the four winds to give life. The Hebrew ruach pun (wind/spirit/breath) underlies both Ezek 37 and John 3:8; high coherence with the new-creation/resurrection motif of new birth.
sourceText: Then he said to me, Prophesy to the wind, prophesy, son of man, and tell the wind, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Come from the four winds, breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live. So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army. Then he said to me, Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel: behold, they say, Our bones are dried up, and our hope […]

note: The new-covenant promise of an inward, Spirit-written law ('I will put my law within them') coheres with regeneration 'from above.' Recurrence of new-covenant texts (alongside Ezek 36-37) strengthens the cluster, though John makes no verbal quotation.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:

note: The 'water of cleansing' / sprinkling rite for purification may stand behind 'born of water,' especially given v.25's dispute 'about purification.' Faint and contested; the water imagery is more naturally Ezekiel's, but the purification context raises availability.
sourceText: “For the unclean, they shall take of the ashes of the burning of the sin offering; and running water shall be poured into a vessel. A clean person shall take hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle it on the tent, on all the vessels, on the persons who were there, and on him who touched the bone, or the slain, or the dead, or the grave. The clean person shall sprinkle on the unclean on the third day, and on the seventh day. On the seventh day, he shall […]

note: 'As you do not know the way of the wind (ruach)... so you do not know the work of God' supplies the exact analogy of 3:8: the unknowable course of the wind/spirit mirrors the mystery of divine begetting in the womb. High coherence and a shared sapiential ruach-pun; verbal volume is moderate.
sourceText: As you don’t know what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child; even so you don’t know the work of God who does all.

note: The Psalm makes winds God's messengers and 'when you send forth your Spirit (ruach), they are created.' Resonates with wind/Spirit/new-creation in 3:5-8 but is faint and diffuse.
sourceText: He lays the beams of his rooms in the waters. He makes the clouds his chariot. He walks on the wings of the wind. He makes his messengers winds; his servants flames of fire.

note: The Spirit/wind (ruach) hovering at creation undergirds 'born of the Spirit' as new creation; coheres with John's creation framing (1:1-3) but verbal contact with ch.3 is faint.
sourceText: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.

note: God breathing the breath of life to make the man a living being stands behind Spirit-begetting as the giving of new life; low volume, drawn in by the ruach/breath cluster of 3:6-8.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: 'Who has ascended to heaven and come down? ... What is his name, and his son's name?' is strikingly answered by 3:13 ('No one has ascended... but he who descended, the Son of Man'). High volume of shared ascent/descent language plus the 'son' motif; a recognized wisdom backdrop.
sourceText: Who has ascended up into heaven, and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has bound the waters in his garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if you know?

note: 'Who will ascend to heaven for us to bring it down?' frames revelation as something no human can fetch from heaven; 3:13 inverts this — the Son of Man alone has descended bearing heavenly things. Coherent revelation-from-above theme; moderate verbal contact.
sourceText: It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?”

note: 'Son of Man' coming with the clouds of heaven supplies the title and the heaven-earth movement that John reworks as descent/ascent. Recurrent Johannine Son-of-Man usage gives coherence, though here the motion is reversed.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: 'Israel does not know, my people do not understand' may color Jesus' rebuke of 'the teacher of Israel' who does not understand (3:10). Faint thematic echo of Israel's failure to perceive.
sourceText: The ox knows his owner, and the donkey his master’s crib; but Israel doesn’t know, my people don’t consider.”

note: 'We can hardly guess at what is on earth... but who has traced out what is in the heavens? Who has learned your counsel unless you have given wisdom and sent your holy spirit?' closely parallels 3:12's earthly-vs-heavenly things and the Spirit-given knowledge of 3:8-11. Strong conceptual coherence (Second-Temple availability).
sourceText: And hardly do we divine the things that are on earth, And the things that are close at hand we find with labor; But the things that are in the heavens who ever yet traced out? And who ever gained knowledge of your counsel, except you gave wisdom, And sent your holy spirit from on high?

note: 'I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One' immediately precedes the ascent question and reinforces the human inability to grasp heavenly things (3:12); faint, drawn in with v.4.
sourceText: I have not learned wisdom, neither do I have the knowledge of the Holy One.

note: The explicit typological centerpiece: 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up.' Direct verbal and figural correspondence — the lifted bronze serpent that the snake-bitten looked to and lived prefigures the crucified Son giving eternal life to those who believe. Maximal volume and coherence.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.

note: The Wisdom midrash on Numbers 21 clarifies that 'the one who turned toward it was saved, not by what was seen, but by you, the Savior of all' — exactly John's point that the serpent saves by directing faith beyond itself to God. Strong Second-Temple interpretive parallel, high coherence with 3:15's believing-and-living.
sourceText: For even when terrible raging of wild beasts came upon your people, And they were perishing by the bites of crooked serpents, Your wrath continued not to the uttermost; But for admonition were they troubled for a short space, Having a token of salvation, To put them in remembrance of the commandment of your law: For he that turned toward it was not saved because of that which was seen, But because of you, the Saviour of all.

note: The Servant who is 'lifted up (hypsothesetai) and exalted' supplies the double sense of John's hypsoo (crucified/exalted) Son of Man. LXX verbal contact with the lifting-up vocabulary that John deploys here and in 8:28; 12:32-34.
sourceText: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.

note: Hezekiah's destruction of the bronze serpent (Nehushtan) is part of the object's canonical afterlife and may inform the careful 'not the bronze itself but faith' nuance; faint, supplementary to Num 21.
sourceText: He removed the high places, and broke the pillars, and cut down the Asherah: and he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made; for in those days the children of Israel burned incense to it; and he called it Nehushtan.

note: 'God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son' echoes the Aqedah where God says of Isaac 'your son, your only son, whom you love' and credits Abraham who 'did not withhold' him. The LXX agapetos / monogenes-equivalent and the giving of the beloved only son give strong figural volume and coherence.
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: 'The light has come into the world' and nations coming to the light coheres with Isaiah's 'Arise, shine, for your light has come.' Recurrent Johannine light-coming-into-the-world motif (cf. 1:9; 8:12); moderate verbal contact.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

note: The evildoers who 'rebel against the light,' who do their deeds in darkness and for whom 'morning is like deep darkness,' closely parallel 3:19-20: those who do evil hate the light lest their works be exposed. Strong thematic coherence of light/darkness moral exposure.
sourceText: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths. The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief. The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face. In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light. For the morning is to all of them like thick […]

note: 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' supplies the light-into-darkness frame of 3:19; faint, part of the broader Isaianic light cluster.
sourceText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: 'Whoever finds me finds life... all who hate me love death' parallels the believe-and-live / hate-the-light-love-darkness antithesis of 3:16-20 in a wisdom register; faint.
sourceText: For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh. But he who sins against me wrongs his own soul. All those who hate me love death.”

note: The salvific 'looking' that brings life carries over from 3:14-15 into the believing-for-eternal-life of 3:15-16; low independent volume here, recurrence within the pericope cluster.
sourceText: But for admonition were they troubled for a short space, Having a token of salvation, To put them in remembrance of the commandment of your law: For he that turned toward it was not saved because of that which was seen, But because of you, the Saviour of all.

note: 'Their works were evil' (3:19) faintly recalls the flood-judgment verdict that human deeds were continually evil; low volume, judgment register.
sourceText: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.

note: 'The voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride' as the sound of restored joy underlies the Baptist as 'friend of the bridegroom' who rejoices at the bridegroom's voice (3:29). Coherent eschatological-wedding-joy motif; moderate verbal contact via 'voice of the bridegroom.'
sourceText: the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voice of those who say, Give thanks to Yahweh of Armies, for Yahweh is good, for his loving kindness endures forever; who bring thanksgiving into Yahweh’s house. For I will cause the captivity of the land to return as at the first, says Yahweh.

note: 'As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you' establishes God/Messiah as bridegroom to his people; John casts Jesus as that bridegroom 'who has the bride.' Strong thematic coherence within the OT marriage-of-YHWH typology.
sourceText: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.

note: The bridegroom and his companions/'friends' at the wedding feast resonate with the 'friend of the bridegroom' figure; faint, supplies the nuptial-companion role.
sourceText: I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Friends Eat, friends! Drink, yes, drink abundantly, beloved. Beloved

note: YHWH betrothing Israel to himself stands within the marriage typology that makes the messianic-bridegroom image legible; faint background, no verbal contact.
sourceText: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.

note: 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven' (3:27) coheres with the sapiential/apocalyptic axiom that God gives and removes authority (cf. Dan 2:21,37); faint, conceptual.
sourceText: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;

note: 'He who comes from above/from heaven is above all' recapitulates the ascent/descent and heavenly-origin question of Prov 30:4 already invoked at 3:13; recurrence within the chapter strengthens the link.
sourceText: Who has ascended up into heaven, and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has bound the waters in his garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if you know?

note: 'God gives the Spirit without measure' (3:34) contrasts/develops the Spirit resting on the messianic shoot; Isaiah's lavish Spirit-endowment of the anointed coheres with the immeasurable Spirit on the sent one. Moderate thematic volume.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: 'He whom God has sent speaks the words of God' (3:34) echoes the promised prophet-like-Moses in whose mouth God puts his words. Coherent with John's sent-one-speaks-God's-words theme; moderate verbal contact.
sourceText: I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him.

note: 'The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand' (3:35) recapitulates the beloved-Son giving of 3:16 / the Aqedah; recurrence within the chapter, low independent volume.
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: 'Given all things into his hand' resonates with the Son of Man given dominion and all peoples serving him; faint, draws on the Danielic enthronement already present at 3:13-14.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The wrath that 'remains' on the one who disobeys the Son (3:36) faintly echoes 'kiss the Son lest he be angry'—submit to the Son or face wrath. Low verbal volume, coherent judgment register.
sourceText: Give sincere homage to the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish on the way, for his wrath will soon be kindled. Blessed are all those who take refuge in him.

note: 'The one who believes... has life' vs. the disobedient who 'won't see life' faintly mirrors the righteous living by faith over against the unbelieving; faint, conceptual.
sourceText: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.

note: Sychar lies near the plot of ground at Shechem that Jacob purchased; v5's 'parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph' anchors the scene in this patriarchal land-grant. High Volume (named geography) and Coherence with John's Jacob/Joseph framing.
sourceText: Jacob came in peace to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Paddan Aram; and encamped before the city. He bought the parcel of ground where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for one hundred pieces of money.

note: Jacob's deathbed gift of an extra 'portion' (shekem/Shechem) to Joseph is the explicit referent of v5, where the well stands on land Jacob gave Joseph. Strong verbal-thematic Coherence; the giving-of-portion motif underwrites the woman's later 'our father Jacob who gave us the well.'
sourceText: Moreover I have given to you one portion above your brothers, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.”

note: Joseph's bones were buried in the parcel at Shechem that Jacob bought, the same patriarchal plot John names. Availability and Coherence are strong; it reinforces the Jacob-Joseph-Shechem matrix even if John cites no text.
sourceText: They buried the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, in Shechem, in the parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. They became the inheritance of the children of Joseph.

note: The classic betrothal type-scene: a man journeys, sits/stops at a well, a woman comes to draw, water is given, she runs to tell her household. v6 'sat down by the well' mirrors Jacob meeting Rachel at the well. High Recurrence (three OT instances) and Volume; the reader primed for betrothal finds a startling inversion.
sourceText: Then Jacob went on his journey, and came to the land of the children of the east. He looked, and behold, a well in the field, and, behold, three flocks of sheep lying there by it. For out of that well they watered the flocks. The stone on the well’s mouth was large. There all the flocks were gathered. They rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone again on the well’s mouth in its place. Jacob said to them, “My […]

note: The Rebekah betrothal scene at the well: servant asks 'give me a drink,' woman draws, kinship and marriage follow. John's scene reuses the well-meeting template down to the request for water (v7). Strong Volume and Recurrence; coheres with the type-scene channel John exploits.
sourceText: The servant took ten camels, of his master’s camels, and departed, having a variety of good things of his master’s with him. He arose, and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor. He made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time that women go out to draw water. He said, “Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham, please give me success this day, and show kindness to my master Abraham. Behold, I am standing […]

note: Moses, a stranger in foreign territory (Midian), sits by a well where women come to draw; betrothal to Zipporah follows. As the third betrothal-at-well scene it raises Recurrence, strengthening the type even if the verbal contact with John is looser than Genesis 24/29.
sourceText: Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and lived in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came and drew water, and filled the troughs to water their father’s flock. The shepherds came and drove them away; but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock. When they came to Reuel, their father, he said, “How is it that you […]

note: Eliezer's 'Let me drink, I pray thee' to Rebekah at the well is verbally echoed by Jesus' 'Give me a drink' (v7), continuing the betrothal type-scene into the dialogue itself. Volume is moderate (short shared phrase) but Coherence with the well-meeting frame is high.
sourceText: The servant ran to meet her, and said, “Please give me a drink, a little water from your pitcher.”

note: Israel forsook the LORD, 'the fountain of living waters,' for broken cisterns; Jesus offers the 'living water' (hydor zon) the woman cannot draw from a deep well. High Volume (rare exact phrase 'living water/fountain of living waters') and Coherence: Jesus is the true fountain over against a cistern that cannot hold.
sourceText: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

note: Those who forsake the LORD have forsaken 'the fountain of living waters'; the doubled Jeremianic phrase raises Recurrence and makes the divine self-identification as living-water source the most likely source-pool for v10-14.
sourceText: Yahweh, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be disappointed. Those who depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken Yahweh, the spring of living waters.

note: On the eschatological day 'living waters shall go out from Jerusalem.' Jesus relocates that eschatological living water into himself given to a Samaritan, fitting John's realized-eschatology and the 'hour comes and now is' just ahead. Moderate Volume, strong thematic Coherence.
sourceText: It will happen in that day, that living waters will go out from Jerusalem; half of them toward the eastern sea, and half of them toward the western sea; in summer and in winter will it be.

note: 'With joy shall you draw water out of the wells of salvation' joins drawing water (the woman's task) to salvation (v22 'salvation is from the Jews'). Coherence is good; the drawing-water verb links the literal and figural planes.
sourceText: Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation.

note: 'Everyone who thirsts, come to the waters... without money' parallels Jesus' free 'gift of God' (v10) of water that ends thirst (v14). Strong Coherence with John's thirst/gift language; moderate Volume.
sourceText: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

note: The blessed will be 'like a spring of water, whose waters fail not' — the interior, never-failing spring matches v14's 'well of water springing up to eternal life.' Coherence high on the perpetual-inner-spring image; Volume modest.
sourceText: and Yahweh will guide you continually, and satisfy your soul in dry places, and make strong your bones; and you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters don’t fail.

note: The redeemed 'shall not hunger nor thirst,' for God leads them by springs of water — paralleling 'never thirst again' (v14). Faint, but coherent with the never-thirst promise.
sourceText: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.

note: The life-giving river flowing from the temple, deepening and bringing life, is a leading source for NT living-water imagery. John makes Jesus the temple-source of the eschatological water; moderate Volume, strong Coherence with the temple/water/life nexus.
sourceText: He brought me back to the door of the house; and behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward; (for the forefront of the house was toward the east;) and the waters came down from under, from the right side of the house, on the south of the altar. Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me round by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east; and behold, there ran […]

note: 'With you is the fountain of life' grounds the divine-fountain motif; Jesus' gift becomes 'a well of water springing up to eternal life' (v14). Coherence with the life-fountain image is high; Volume modest.
sourceText: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.

note: 'The wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook' and Proverbs' fountain-of-life sayings supply the sapiential backdrop for water = life/wisdom. Faint verbal contact; contributes to the broader well/fountain field.
sourceText: The words of a man’s mouth are like deep waters. The fountain of wisdom is like a flowing brook.

note: The beloved is 'a well of living waters' — a rare exact match to 'living water,' and, given the betrothal type-scene already in play, a thematically apt nuptial overtone. Volume on the phrase is notable but the connection is contested.
sourceText: a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing streams from Lebanon. Beloved

note: Isaac's servants find 'a well of springing water' (be'er mayim chayyim) — the same idiom rendered 'well of water springing up' in v14, set again in patriarchal well-digging. Reinforces the patriarchal-well + living-water overlap.
sourceText: Isaac’s servants dug in the valley, and found there a well of springing water.

note: Wisdom says 'those who drink me will thirst for more'; Jesus inverts it — whoever drinks his water 'will never thirst again' (v14). Likely deliberate contrast with the sapiential tradition; Availability secure as Second-Temple deuterocanon.
sourceText: They that eat me will yet be hungry; And those who drink me will yet be thirsty.

note: The Samaritans were resettled foreign peoples who 'feared the LORD and served their own gods'; the woman's 'five husbands' has long been read as a figure for this syncretism (Josephus counts five settler nations/deities). Coherence with John's Samaritan setting is high, though the allegory of the number is debated.
sourceText: The king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Avva, and from Hamath and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel; and they possessed Samaria, and lived in the cities of it. So it was, at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they didn’t fear Yahweh: therefore Yahweh sent lions among them, which killed some of them. Therefore they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying, “The […]

note: Israel as the adulterous wife pursuing many lovers/baalim supplies the prophetic marriage-and-apostasy grammar behind the husbands motif. Faint and contested, but coherent with reading the woman's marital history as covenantal figure.
sourceText: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts; Lest I strip her naked, and make her bare as in the day that she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst. Indeed, on her children I will have no mercy; for they are children of unfaithfulness; For their mother has played […]

note: The prophet as 'seer' who knows hidden things lies behind the woman's 'I perceive you are a prophet' (v19) after Jesus discloses her secret. Faint lexical contact; supports the prophet-recognition motif.
sourceText: (In earlier times in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, thus he said, “Come, and let us go to the seer”; for he who is now called a prophet was before called a Seer.)

note: The blessing was set on Mount Gerizim, the Samaritan holy mountain the woman means by 'this mountain' (v20). High Volume and Availability: the Gerizim/Jerusalem dispute is the precise OT fault-line John dramatizes.
sourceText: It shall happen, when Yahweh your God brings you into the land where you go to possess it, that you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim, and the curse on Mount Ebal.

note: Six tribes stand on Gerizim to pronounce blessing, grounding the Samaritan claim that 'our fathers worshiped in this mountain.' Coheres with v20; moderate Volume.
sourceText: “These shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people, when you have passed over the Jordan: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.

note: Worship is to be at 'the place the LORD shall choose,' the Deuteronomic charter behind the Jewish claim that 'in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship' (v20). High Coherence: Jesus transcends the very 'place' debate this text founds (v21-23).
sourceText: But to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose out of all your tribes, to put his name there, you shall seek his habitation, and there you shall come. There you shall bring your burnt offerings, your sacrifices, your tithes, the wave offering of your hand, your vows, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock. There you shall eat before Yahweh your God, and you shall rejoice in all that you put your hand to, you and […]

note: Moses promised a prophet 'like me' who would speak all God commands; the Samaritan Taheb expectation rests here, matching the woman's 'when Messiah comes he will declare to us all things' (v25). High Coherence with Samaritan messianism and Jesus' 'I am he' (v26).
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]

note: 'My people shall know my name... that I am he that speaks' supplies the divine 'I am he' (ego eimi ho lalon) Jesus uses in v26, knitting revelation-of-name to direct speech. Volume is strong on the unusual 'he that speaks / I am he' formula.
sourceText: Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore they shall know in that day that I am he who speaks; behold, it is I.”

note: The divine self-naming 'I AM' stands behind John's recurring ego eimi, here in v26. Faint at this point (the absolute uses come later in John), but Availability and Coherence with John's theme are real.
sourceText: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

note: 'The Egyptians are flesh, and not spirit' gives the flesh/spirit contrast informing 'God is spirit' (v24). Faint and contested, but a plausible OT seed for the spirit-worship claim.
sourceText: Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When Yahweh stretches out his hand, both he who helps shall stumble, and he who is helped shall fall, and they all shall be consumed together.

note: Nations stream to Zion, for 'out of Zion shall go forth the law' — backing 'salvation is from the Jews' (v22). Coherence good for the Jew-as-source-of-salvation claim; moderate Volume.
sourceText: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of Yahweh’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.

note: Rebekah 'ran and told' her household after the well encounter; the woman leaves her water pot and runs to tell the city (v28-29), completing the betrothal type-scene's go-and-announce beat. Faint verbal contact but coherent with the type-scene already established.
sourceText: The young lady ran, and told her mother’s house about these words.

note: Man lives not by bread alone but by what proceeds from God's mouth; Jesus' 'I have food you don't know about... to do the will of him who sent me' (v32-34) reuses this contrast of bodily food with God's word/will. Strong Coherence; moderate Volume.
sourceText: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.

note: 'I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food' parallels Jesus' food-as-doing-God's-will. Faint, supporting the word/will-over-food motif.
sourceText: I haven’t gone back from the commandment of his lips. I have treasured up the words of his mouth more than my necessary food.

note: The eschatological harvest where 'the plowman overtakes the reaper' — sowing and reaping collapse together — underlies 'fields white for harvest already' and sower-and-reaper rejoicing together (v35-36). High Coherence with realized harvest; Volume strong on the compressed-harvest image.
sourceText: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the one treading grapes him who sows seed; and sweet wine will drip from the mountains, and flow from the hills.

note: 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe' supplies the ripe/ready harvest call behind v35. Coherence is good, though Joel's harvest is judgment, making the transfer to mission-harvest somewhat contested.
sourceText: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”

note: Those who sow in tears reap in joy, going out and returning rejoicing — matching 'he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together' (v36). Coherence good on the joint sow/reap rejoicing; moderate Volume.
sourceText: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.

note: 'You shall sow but not reap' typifies the sow-one/reap-another proverb cited in v37. One of several covenant-curse/proverb backgrounds; faint individually.
sourceText: You will sow, but won’t reap. You will tread the olives, but won’t anoint yourself with oil; and crush grapes, but won’t drink the wine.

note: 'Let me sow, and another eat' is a close formal analogue to the proverb 'one sows and another reaps' (v37). Faint but apt for the sowing/reaping-by-different-parties saying.
sourceText: then let me sow, and let another eat. Yes, let the produce of my field be rooted out.

note: The Servant made 'salvation to the ends of the earth' / light to the nations stands behind 'the Savior of the world' confessed by Samaritans (v42), extending salvation beyond Israel. Strong Coherence with the universal-salvation theme; moderate Volume.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: 'A just God and a Savior... look unto me, all the ends of the earth' is the OT locus for God as universal Savior, reframed as 'Savior of the world.' Volume good on the Savior-for-all-earth formula.
sourceText: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.

note: 'All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God' supports the world-wide Savior confession in v42. Faint but coherent with the universalizing of salvation.
sourceText: Yahweh has made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.

note: 'After two days he will revive us' may color the deliberate 'he stayed there two days' (v40) before life/belief spreads, given John's symbolic use of time. Faint and contested.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: The men of Jeremiah's own town Anathoth sought his life, illustrating the prophet dishonored in his own country (v44). Offered as an OT exemplar of the rejected-prophet motif rather than a verbal source; faint and contested.
sourceText: Therefore thus says Yahweh concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, saying, You shall not prophesy in Yahweh’s name, that you not die by our hand;

note: Elijah revives the widow's dying son and the mother's faith follows; Jesus' word 'your son lives' (v50-53) reprises the prophet who restores a son at the point of death. High Coherence and a strong type for the life-giving prophetic word; the 'son lives' acclamation closely matches.
sourceText: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]

note: Elisha restores the Shunammite's dead son, again a prophet giving life to a child amid a parent's plea. Reinforces (with 1 Kings 17) the son-restored-by-prophetic-word type; high Recurrence strengthens the channel.
sourceText: When the child was grown, one day he went out to his father to the reapers. He said to his father, “My head! My head!” He said to his servant, “Carry him to his mother.” When he had taken him, and brought him to his mother, he sat on her knees until noon, and then died. She went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God, and shut the door on him, and went out. She called to her husband, and said, “Please send me one of the servants, and one of the […]

note: 'He sent his word, and healed them' precisely captures the healing-at-a-distance by bare word (v50-53), where the father believes 'the word that Jesus spoke.' Strong Coherence on word-as-healing-agent; moderate Volume.
sourceText: He sends his word, and heals them, and delivers them from their graves.

note: Naaman, a Gentile official, is healed at a distance through the prophet's word without the prophet's presence — paralleling the royal official whose son is healed by Jesus' remote command. Coherence good on official-faith-by-word; moderate Volume.
sourceText: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]

note: Hezekiah is 'sick unto death' and healed by the prophet's word, with the recovery confirmed by a sign tied to a precise hour — echoing the son 'at the point of death' (v47) and the verified 'seventh hour' of recovery (v52). Coherence good on the point-of-death/hour-confirmed pattern.
sourceText: In those days was Hezekiah sick to death. Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, “Thus says Yahweh, ‘Set your house in order; for you shall die, and not live.’” Then he turned his face to the wall, and prayed to Yahweh, saying, “Remember now, Yahweh, I beg you, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in your sight.” Hezekiah wept bitterly. Before Isaiah had gone out into […]

note: The man has been infirm 'thirty-eight years.' Volume: the number is exact and otherwise unmotivated, and Deut 2:14 marks precisely thirty-eight years from Kadesh-barnea until the wilderness generation that could not enter the land had died off. Coherence: John repeatedly frames Jesus' signs against an exodus/wilderness backdrop (manna in ch. 6, water in ch. 7, serpent in 3:14), so a paralytic stranded thirty-eight years beside healing water he cannot reach evokes the generation barred from the promised land's rest. Recurrence: low (the figure is unique to this scene), and many read the number as merely realistic, so contested but the coincidence with the sole OT '38 years' is striking.
sourceText: The days in which we came from Kadesh Barnea, until we had come over the brook Zered, were thirty-eight years; until all the generation of the men of war were consumed from the midst of the camp, as Yahweh swore to them.

note: Healing water by the temple/sheep gate, a pool whose stirring brings cure, faintly recalls Ezekiel's eschatological river flowing from the temple that heals all it touches. Volume is low (no shared wording) and Recurrence weak, but Coherence with John's temple-and-water typology (cf. 7:38) gives it some force. Faint and contested; the immediate Bethesda tradition is folk-medical rather than scriptural.
sourceText: He brought me back to the door of the house; and behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward; (for the forefront of the house was toward the east;) and the waters came down from under, from the right side of the house, on the south of the altar. Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me round by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east; and behold, there ran […]

note: The gathered 'blind, lame, paralyzed' and the command to the lame man to rise and walk echoes Isaiah's promise that in the day of salvation 'the lame shall leap like a deer.' Volume thematic only; Coherence high with the sign's meaning (Jesus as the one who fulfills the healing of the eschaton). Recurrence low within John. Honestly faint.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.

note: 'I am the LORD who heals you' stands behind the whole motif of God as healer at the waters; the angel-stirred pool offers a counterfeit/lesser healing that Jesus' word transcends. Volume low, Recurrence low; included as a maximal, faint candidate for the divine-healer background.
sourceText: and he said, “If you will diligently listen to Yahweh your God’s voice, and will do that which is right in his eyes, and will pay attention to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you, which I have put on the Egyptians; for I am Yahweh who heals you.”

note: The objection 'It is not lawful for you to carry the mat' on the Sabbath rests directly on the prophetic Sabbath law forbidding bearing a burden on the Sabbath day. Volume: the specific prohibition of carrying a load on the Sabbath is verbal and conceptual bedrock here; Jeremiah is the sharpest scriptural articulation. Coherence: the entire pericope turns on Sabbath legality. Recurrence: the same burden-bearing prohibition recurs (Neh 13:15-19), so the charge is grounded in available scripture, not later tradition alone.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, Be careful, and bear no burden on the Sabbath day, nor bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem; neither carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath day, neither do any work: but make the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers.

note: The Sabbath controversy ('because he did these things on the Sabbath') invokes the Decalogue Sabbath command. Volume: foundational; the legal framework the Jews enforce is the fourth commandment. Coherence: high, the dispute is explicitly about Sabbath observance. Recurrence: the parallel Deut 5:12-15 reinforces availability. This is the law Jesus is accused of breaking, making it load-bearing for the whole chapter.
sourceText: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]

note: 'My Father is still working, so I am working, too' answers the Sabbath charge by appeal to creation: God rested on the seventh day, yet (so the live Second-Temple debate, e.g. Philo, Leg. All. 1.5-6; later rabbinic discussion) God never ceases the works of giving life and rendering judgment, which alone are his prerogative even on the Sabbath. Volume: the rest of Gen 2:2-3 is exactly the premise Jesus' claim contests. Coherence: very high — it generates the equal-with-God charge in v.18 and the life/judgment exposition that follows. Recurrence: the creation Sabbath underlies the whole Bethesda-on-the-Sabbath structure. Availability: the 'God works even on the Sabbath' tradition is attested in Second-Temple/early-rabbinic sources.
sourceText: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.

note: Jesus 'called God his own Father, making himself equal with God,' provoking a death plot — closely paralleling the ungodly in Wisdom who plot against the righteous one precisely because 'he calls himself a child of the Lord' and 'boasts that God is his father.' Volume: strong conceptual and near-verbal overlap on the Father-claim provoking lethal hostility. Coherence: high with John's righteous-sufferer framing. Recurrence: the Wisdom passage informs passion narratives broadly. A deuterocanonical source, hence flagged but well-grounded.
sourceText: We were accounted of him as worthless metal, And he abstains from our ways as from uncleannesses. The latter end of the righteous he calls happy; And he vaunts that God is his father. Let us see if his words be true, And let us try what shall befall in the ending of his life. For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries.

note: The charge that Jesus made 'himself equal with God' could be heard against the background of the proud one who said 'I will make myself like the Most High' — the accusers frame Jesus' self-equation as that blasphemous presumption. Volume low and the resonance is in the accusers' mouths, not the narrator's. Coherence moderate; included as a faint, contested candidate for the 'equal with God' polemic.
sourceText: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!”

note: 'As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life' draws on the Song of Moses' exclusive divine self-claim, 'I kill and I make alive,' which makes giving life and putting to death God's sole prerogative. Volume: strong conceptual identity (raising the dead / making alive). Coherence: very high — this is the theological warrant for the equal-with-God claim, transferring the uniquely divine life-giving power to the Son. Recurrence: the make-alive formula recurs (1 Sam 2:6; cf. v.21,24-29 below).
sourceText: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.

note: Hannah's confession 'The LORD kills and makes alive; he brings down to Sheol and raises up' supplies the same death-and-resurrection-as-divine-act idiom undergirding 'the Father raises the dead.' Volume: shared raise/make-alive language. Coherence: high. Recurrence: reinforces Deut 32:39; together they establish that life-giving is an exclusively divine work now exercised by the Son.
sourceText: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.

note: 'The Father... has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son even as they honor the Father' reflects Daniel's one like a son of man to whom is given dominion and the worship/service of all peoples. Volume: conceptual (universal honor/authority granted by God to a son-of-man figure), made explicit when v.27 names him 'son of man.' Coherence: high with John's transfer of judgment and honor. Recurrence: Danielic son-of-man framing recurs across the Gospel tradition; here it grounds the demand that all honor the Son.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'All who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment' is John's closest verbal-conceptual echo of Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, some to shame and everlasting contempt.' Volume: high — the two-outcome resurrection of the dead is distinctively Daniel's. Coherence: very high with the life/judgment theme. Recurrence: Daniel 12 is the seminal OT resurrection text and is the available source for the double resurrection.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: 'He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is a son of man' explicitly grounds the Son's judging authority in the Danielic son-of-man who receives dominion and an everlasting kingdom from the Ancient of Days. Volume: the anarthrous 'son of man' plus granted judging authority is a direct Danielic signal. Coherence: very high. Recurrence: ties the resurrection-judgment scene to the dominion granted in Dan 7. This is the clearest figural citation in the discourse.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The dead hearing the life-giving voice of the Son of God and coming alive from the tombs resonates with Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, where God's word/breath summons the dead to life and opens the graves ('I will open your graves and raise you'). Volume: shared open-graves and voice-summons imagery. Coherence: high with the resurrection theme. Recurrence: Ezekiel 37 is a stock resurrection-of-Israel text; somewhat less verbally precise than Dan 12, hence medium.
sourceText: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]

note: 'Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise... the earth will give birth to the dead' is another available resurrection oracle behind 'those in the tombs will come out.' Volume thematic; Coherence high; Recurrence modest. A genuine but secondary candidate to Daniel 12, flagged faint.
sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

note: The whole witness section ('If I testify about myself, my witness is not valid... It is another who testifies about me') applies the Torah's rule that a matter is established only by two or three witnesses. Volume: the legal principle is structurally determinative — Jesus marshals multiple corroborating witnesses (John, the works, the Father, the Scriptures) precisely to satisfy this requirement. Coherence: very high. Recurrence: the two-witness rule recurs (Deut 17:6; Num 35:30) and is invoked elsewhere in John (8:17).
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: 'You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his form' inverts and presupposes the Sinai tradition that no one can see God's face/form and live, and that Israel heard the voice but saw no form (Deut 4:12). Volume: the voice/form pairing is a deliberate scriptural touchstone. Coherence: high — the point is that the accusers, unlike the Son, have no immediate access to the Father. Recurrence: the no-form motif is firmly grounded in the Sinai narratives.
sourceText: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”

note: John the Baptist as 'the burning and shining lamp' may echo the prepared 'lamp for my anointed' set before the messianic king, casting John as the lamp pointing to the coming one. Volume low (single image), Recurrence low; Coherence moderate with John's witness-to-the-light theme (cf. 1:8). Faint and contested.
sourceText: There I will make the horn of David to bud. I have ordained a lamp for my anointed.

note: 'Moses wrote about me... if you believed Moses you would believe me' centers on the Pentateuch as christological witness, with the prophet-like-Moses promise the prime text Jesus claims Moses 'wrote' concerning him. Volume: conceptual but specific — the expectation of a coming prophet whom Israel must heed. Coherence: very high; the chapter's climax makes Moses Jesus' chief scriptural witness and accuser. Recurrence: Deut 18 is the standard prophet-like-Moses proof-text in the NT (cf. Acts 3:22).
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]

note: Among the things 'Moses wrote' about Christ, the protoevangelium (the seed of the woman crushing the serpent) is a candidate text for what Jesus claims the Pentateuch foretells of him. Volume: low (not quoted); the verse names no specific passage. Coherence: moderate within a figural reading of Genesis as messianic. Recurrence: low in John. Included as a maximal, contested specification of 'he wrote about me.'
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: 'There is one who accuses you, even Moses, on whom you have set your hope' ironically reverses Moses' role as Israel's intercessor who pleaded for the people; the very mediator they trust becomes their accuser. Volume low, Recurrence low, but Coherence moderate with the reversal motif. Faint and contested.
sourceText: Moses returned to Yahweh, and said, “Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made themselves gods of gold. Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”

note: Moses as accuser fits the Torah's own provision that the book of the law be placed 'as a witness against you' because of Israel's rebellion. Volume: conceptual but apt — Moses' writings testify against unbelief, exactly Jesus' charge ('if you don't believe his writings'). Coherence: high with the witness/accusation framing. Recurrence: moderate; strengthens the figural reading of Moses-as-witness.
sourceText: “Take this book of the law, and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of Yahweh your God, that it may be there for a witness against you. For I know your rebellion, and your stiff neck. Behold, while I am yet alive with you this day, you have been rebellious against Yahweh. How much more after my death?

note: 'You don't have God's love in yourselves' and 'how can you believe, who... don't seek the glory from the only God' resonate with the Shema's call to love the one God with whole heart. Volume low (no quotation), but Coherence moderate: the indictment is that those who recite love of the one God fail to love and honor him. Faint, contested, included for completeness.
sourceText: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: The wilderness feeding of a great multitude with miraculous bread sets the controlling type that the chapter will name explicitly in v.31. High Volume and total Coherence with the manna economy (bread, gathering, leftovers, no waste); the feeding scene is the narrative enactment of the manna gift Jesus later interprets.

Strong structural and verbal Coherence: a leader confronted with an impossible crowd, mountain setting, and divine provision overriding human arithmetic.

John alone specifies 'barley loaves' and 'what are these among so many?', and adds the leftovers motif. High Volume and verbal Recurrence make this the closest single OT analogue to the miracle's mechanics.

note: Asaph's 'he rained down manna... gave them grain of heaven... bread of the angels' is the psalm John will quote at v.31; its presence governs the feeding as the eschatological manna. High Coherence: the crowd reads the sign as a renewed wilderness banquet.
sourceText: He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky. Man ate the bread of angels. He sent them food to the full.

note: 'He gave them bread from heaven in abundance' — a second psalmic celebration of the manna, reinforcing the satisfied-fullness motif ('when they were filled,' v.12). Lower distinctiveness than Ps 78 but adds Recurrence to the manna tradition active here.
sourceText: They asked, and he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of the sky.

note: The crowd's acclamation 'This is truly the prophet who comes into the world' (v.14) invokes the promised prophet-like-Moses. The Mosaic feeding miracle triggers a Mosaic-prophet expectation; high Coherence with John's prophet-and-king Christology.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: John's editorial note 'Now the Passover was at hand' (v.4) frames the whole chapter under the paschal lamb, preparing the flesh-and-blood discourse (vv.51-56). Availability and Coherence are strong; the Passover anchor is authorial, though the feeding scene itself does not verbally cite Exodus 12.

note: The crowd's move to 'take him by force, to make him king' (v.15) faintly evokes Israel's improper demand for a king, which the LORD treats as rejection of his rule. Thematic rather than verbal; offered as a contested background to Jesus' refusal of a politicized kingship.
sourceText: and they said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” But the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” Samuel prayed to Yahweh. note: Jesus' 'It is I (ego eimi); do not be afraid' atop the storm reads, in John's idiom, as the divine self-naming 'I AM.' High Coherence with the chapter's later absolute 'I am' sayings; the theophanic-on-the-water setting elevates the otherwise ordinary phrase to divine self-disclosure.
sourceText: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

note: 'who alone... treads on the waves of the sea' ascribes sea-trampling to God alone. Jesus 'walking on the sea' enacts a prerogative the OT reserves for the Creator; strong Volume and Coherence with the I-AM disclosure that accompanies it.
sourceText: He alone stretches out the heavens, and treads on the waves of the sea.

note: 'Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen' — a hymn of God's exodus march across the deep. Coheres with Jesus pathless on the water; the psalm's exodus frame fits John's Passover setting.
sourceText: Your way was through the sea; your paths through the great waters. Your footsteps were not known.

note: 'Fear not... when you pass through the waters I will be with you' pairs the precise reassurance ('Don't be afraid') with passage through threatening waters. Coherence with the disciples' deliverance; the chapter's I-AM resonates with Isaiah 43:10 below.
sourceText: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. note: 'that you may... believe me and understand that I am he (ani hu / ego eimi)' supplies the LXX 'I am' that stands behind Jesus' words on the sea. Strengthens the case that v.20's ego eimi is theophanic rather than mere identification.
sourceText: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.

note: Seafarers in a wind-tossed storm cry out and God 'made the storm a calm' and 'brought them to their desired haven' — strikingly close to the boat reaching land 'immediately' (v.21). Good Coherence though John gives stilling-by-arrival rather than rebuke of the storm.

note: 'He gave them bread out of heaven to eat' (v.31) is a formal citation ('as it is written') closest in wording to LXX Psalm 78:24 ('arton ouranou edoken autois'). The chapter's hermeneutical hinge; maximal Volume.
sourceText: He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky.

note: 'I am about to rain bread from heaven for you' is the originating text behind the v.31 citation; Jesus directly contests its meaning ('it was not Moses who gave...'). The quotation conflates Exodus 16 with Psalm 78, so both are primary sources.

sourceText: “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!

note: Wisdom says 'Come to me... those who eat me will hunger for more, those who drink me will thirst for more.' John inverts it ('will never hunger... never thirst'), a deliberate transformation signalling Jesus surpasses Wisdom/Torah. High Availability and Coherence; the inversion is the point.

note: 'They shall not hunger or thirst... he who has pity will lead them' supplies the hunger-and-thirst-abolished promise of the eschatological return. Coheres tightly with v.35's double negation; an exilic-restoration backdrop to the bread of life.
sourceText: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.

note: The repeated 'I will raise him up at the last day' (vv.39-40) draws on the clearest OT resurrection text, 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake... to everlasting life.' Provides the Availability for John's last-day raising; recurs across the discourse.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: 'The Jews therefore murmured concerning him' (v.41,43) deliberately casts the audience as the wilderness generation that 'murmured against Moses and Aaron' over bread. High Volume and Coherence: the same verb-of-grumbling against the same gift (bread from heaven).
sourceText: The whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron in the wilderness; and the children of Israel said to them, “We wish that we had died by the hand of Yahweh in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots, when we ate our fill of bread, for you have brought us out into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.” Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the […]

note: 'It is written in the prophets, They will all be taught by God' (v.45) formally cites Isaiah 54:13 ('all your children shall be taught by the LORD'). A second explicit citation in the chapter; high Volume.
sourceText: All your children shall be taught of Yahweh; and great shall be the peace of your children.

sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin […]

note: 'Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died' (v.49) recalls the wilderness generation that craved, ate, and perished. The manna's described provision (Num 11:7-9) plus the death of that generation give Volume to Jesus' contrast with bread that lets one 'not die.'

sourceText: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”

note: 'The bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh' (v.51), under the Passover frame, fuses bread with the slain paschal lamb whose flesh is eaten and whose blood saves. Typological Coherence prepares the eat-flesh scandal of the next pericope.

note: 'They shall eat the flesh that night' — the paschal lamb whose flesh is consumed. Jesus' demand to eat his flesh, set 'at Passover,' identifies him as the lamb; high typological Coherence binding the discourse to the chapter's opening note (v.4).
sourceText: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.

note: 'You shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood' is the primal Noachic blood prohibition predating Sinai, broadening the scandal of v.53 beyond Israel to a universal taboo. Adds Recurrence to the blood-prohibition background.
sourceText: But flesh with its life, that is, its blood, you shall not eat.

note: 'Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life' restates the prohibition with the life-in-the-blood rationale that John ironically affirms (the blood gives life). Reinforces the contested commandment behind the discourse.
sourceText: Only be sure that you don’t eat the blood; for the blood is the life. You shall not eat the life with the flesh.

note: Wisdom's 'those who eat me... those who drink me' returns here with literal eating and drinking, deepening the Wisdom-banquet identification of Jesus. Coheres with v.35; the eat/drink pairing strengthens the Sirach link.
sourceText: They that eat me will yet be hungry; And those who drink me will yet be thirsty.

note: 'Eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed' — Wisdom's bread-and-wine banquet underlies the flesh-as-food/blood-as-drink doubling of vv.53-56. Lower distinctiveness than the Leviticus collision but adds the sapiential meal frame.
sourceText: “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!

sourceText: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.

sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: 'The Egyptians are flesh and not spirit' supplies the flesh/spirit antithesis behind 'the flesh profits nothing' (v.63), where flesh is the weak human plane and spirit the divine. Conceptual Coherence; moderate Volume.
sourceText: Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When Yahweh stretches out his hand, both he who helps shall stumble, and he who is helped shall fall, and they all shall be consumed together.

sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: Peter's 'you are the Holy One of God' (v.69) resonates with 'you will not let your Holy One see corruption,' a key resurrection/messianic title. Coheres with the chapter's raising-on-the-last-day refrain; the holy-one designation is OT-rooted.
sourceText: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.

note: Aaron is 'the holy one of the LORD' — the only OT figure given nearly this exact title, offering a priestly alternative background to Peter's confession (v.69). Lower Volume than Psalm 16; contested as the operative source.
sourceText: They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron, Yahweh’s saint.

note: 'You have the words of eternal life' (v.68) faintly recalls Moses' 'it is no empty word for you, but your very life.' The word-as-life motif suits John's Mosaic typology; diffuse and contested.
sourceText: For it is no vain thing for you; because it is your life, and through this thing you shall prolong your days in the land, where you go over the Jordan to possess it.”

note: The whole chapter is framed by 'the Feast of the Jews, the Feast of Booths' (v.2), the pilgrimage festival Leviticus institutes with its seven days of dwelling in booths and rejoicing 'before the LORD your God.' Availability and volume are high: the named feast supplies the liturgical theater (water-libation, temple lights) that every subsequent saying exploits. John deliberately stages Jesus' self-disclosure against this Mosaic ordinance.

The Deuteronomic command to 'rejoice in your feast' undergirds the brothers' urging that Jesus 'reveal yourself to the world' at the festival. Coherence with the going-up-to-Judea motif is strong.
