note: 'Even his brothers didn't believe in him' (v.5) coheres with the psalm of the righteous sufferer, 'I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's children' — a psalm John cites elsewhere for Jesus' zeal and rejection. Recurrence of Psalm 69 in the Fourth Gospel raises the plausibility that the brothers' unbelief is read figurally through the estranged sufferer.
sourceText: I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s children.

note: 'When his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up' enacts the Deuteronomic requirement that every male 'appear before the LORD' three times a year, Booths being one. The going-up language and the search 'at the feast' (v.11) presuppose the pilgrim crowds the law gathers. Coherence with the festival frame is strong though the verbal contact is general.
sourceText: Three times in a year all of your shall males appear before Yahweh your God in the place which he chooses: in the feast of unleavened bread, in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tents. They shall not appear before Yahweh empty.

note: 'My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me' (v.16) and 'he who sent me is true' echo the prophet-like-Moses who speaks only what God commands, into whose mouth God puts his words. The sending/speaking-not-from-self language is the diagnostic mark distinguishing the true prophet (Deut 18) from one who speaks presumptuously. Strong coherence with John's prophet-Christology, reinforced by v.40 ('truly the prophet').
sourceText: I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him. It shall happen, that whoever will not listen to my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.

note: Moses' self-authentication, 'the LORD has sent me to do all these works, and I have not done them of my own accord,' supplies the precise idiom of vv.17-18 ('if I am speaking from myself... seeks his own glory'). The criterion of not seeking one's own glory but the sender's marks divine commission. Availability and verbal coherence are good even if the contact is unmarked.
sourceText: Moses said, “Hereby you shall know that Yahweh has sent me to do all these works; for they are not from my own mind.

note: 'Didn't Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law?' (v.19) directly invokes the Mosaic Torah as a body, with the Pentateuch as availability. The argument turns on the law's own internal logic, and John names Moses three times in this unit. Quotation-strength reference to Torah as institution rather than a single verse.
sourceText: Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.

note: 'On the Sabbath you circumcise a boy' (vv.22-23) rests on the law that a male child is circumcised 'on the eighth day,' which can fall on a Sabbath, overriding Sabbath rest. Leviticus 12:3 is the explicit eighth-day legislation Jesus reasons from a fortiori (if circumcision overrides Sabbath, how much more healing a whole man). High volume and coherence.
sourceText: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.

note: 'Moses has given you circumcision (not that it is of Moses, but of the fathers)' (v.22) corrects the attribution to the Abrahamic covenant, where God commands circumcision on the eighth day as the sign 'between me and you.' The patriarchal origin ('of the fathers') points precisely to Genesis 17, prior to Moses. Direct conceptual citation.
sourceText: This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed.

note: 'Don't judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment' (v.24) echoes the Holiness Code's command, 'you shall do no injustice in judgment... in righteousness you shall judge your neighbor.' The pairing of forbidden partial judgment with commanded righteous judgment matches Leviticus closely. High coherence; the verse recurs as a juridical touchstone in this chapter (cf. vv.51).
sourceText: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.

note: The charge to judges, 'judge righteously... you shall not be partial in judgment... you shall not be afraid of the face of man,' undergirds 'judge righteous judgment' (v.24) and anticipates Nicodemus' procedural appeal (v.51). Recurrence within the chapter strengthens the figural reading of impartial judgment. Verbal overlap is with the 'righteous judgment' idiom.
sourceText: I commanded your judges at that time, saying, “Hear cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother, and the foreigner who is living with him. You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be afraid of the face of man, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.”

note: The messianic shoot 'shall not judge by what his eyes see... but with righteousness he shall judge' is the prophetic mirror of v.24's 'do not judge by appearance but judge righteous judgment.' Coherence with John's messianic theme (the crowd debating whether Jesus is the Christ) makes this more than coincidental, though John gives no citation formula. Contested as an unmarked echo.
sourceText: His delight will be in the fear of Yahweh. He will not judge by the sight of his eyes, neither decide by the hearing of his ears; but with righteousness he will judge the poor, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked.

note: 'Render true judgment, show kindness and mercy' is one more prophetic locus for the impartial-justice ideal behind v.24. Volume is low and the contact is thematic rather than verbal, but Zechariah's prominence elsewhere in John 7 (rivers of living water) raises availability. Marked contested and low.
sourceText: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother.

note: 'When the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from' (v.27) reflects a strand of expectation about the Messiah's hidden origin; Isaiah's 'as for his generation, who considered it?' was read in Second-Temple sources for the servant's obscure origin. The hiddenness motif coheres with John's irony that they know Jesus' earthly origin but not his heavenly one (vv.28-29). Contested and allusive.
sourceText: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?

note: The popular belief about the Messiah's unknown origin (v.27) stands in tension with, and presupposes, the Bethlehem expectation made explicit at v.42. Micah's 'whose origins are from of old, from ancient days' could itself feed the 'no one will know where he comes from' tradition. Low volume here; the fuller Micah contact belongs to 7.6.
sourceText: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings out are from of old, from ancient times.

note: 'You will seek me, and won't find me' (v.34) inverts the Deuteronomic promise 'you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search with all your heart.' The reversal (seeking without finding) functions as covenantal judgment language. Volume and verbal contact are modest; marked contested.
sourceText: But from there you shall seek Yahweh your God, and you shall find him, when you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.

note: 'They will seek me diligently but will not find me' is Wisdom's verdict on those who spurned her, closely matching 'you will seek me, and won't find me' (v.34). The Wisdom-Christology of John (incarnate Logos withdrawing) gives strong coherence, and the verbal parallel is tight. The unmarked allusion fits John's pattern of figural Wisdom motifs.
sourceText: Then will they call on me, but I will not answer. They will seek me diligently, but they will not find me;

note: 'They shall go to seek the LORD, but they will not find him; he has withdrawn from them' parallels the seek-but-not-find judgment of v.34. Hosea casts it as God hiding because of unfaithfulness, coherent with the crowd's unbelief. Low volume, offered as an alternate prophetic source.
sourceText: They will go with their flocks and with their herds to seek Yahweh; but they won’t find him. He has withdrawn himself from them.

note: 'Will he go to the Dispersion among the Greeks?' (v.35) ironically gestures toward the prophetic ingathering of the scattered, where the messianic root 'gathers the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.' John's irony (the mission to the Greeks the speakers mock) coheres with the Diaspora-ingathering hope. Contested, thematic.
sourceText: He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

note: 'From within him will flow rivers of living water' (v.38), declared 'on the last and greatest day' of Booths, draws on Zechariah's eschatological vision read at the feast: 'living waters shall flow out from Jerusalem.' Zechariah 14 is the Tabernacles lectionary, explicitly naming the feast (14:16-19), giving maximal availability and coherence. This is the spine of John's water typology here.
sourceText: It will happen in that day, that living waters will go out from Jerusalem; half of them toward the eastern sea, and half of them toward the western sea; in summer and in winter will it be.

note: The temple-river vision, water flowing from beneath the threshold and swelling into a life-giving river, supplies the 'rivers of living water' imagery flowing from the new temple (Jesus/the believer). High volume and coherence: John casts Jesus' body as the eschatological temple source. The plural 'rivers' and life-giving flow match Ezekiel's swelling stream.
sourceText: He brought me back to the door of the house; and behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward; (for the forefront of the house was toward the east;) and the waters came down from under, from the right side of the house, on the south of the altar. Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me round by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east; and behold, there ran […]

note: 'He split the rocks in the wilderness... brought streams out of the rock and caused waters to run down like rivers' is the wilderness water-from-the-rock typology underlying 'rivers of living water' at the water-libation feast. Booths commemorated wilderness dwelling; the rock-water gift is the natural figural source. The verbal 'rivers' (potamous) coheres with John's plural.
sourceText: He split rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink abundantly as out of the depths. He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers.

note: Moses striking the rock so that 'water came out abundantly' is the foundational wilderness rock-water event behind v.38, tied to Booths' commemoration of the wilderness sojourn and its water-pouring rite. Coherence is strong; offered alongside Exodus 17:6 as the source-event for the rock typology. Medium because the contact is mediated through the Psalm/feast tradition.
sourceText: Moses lifted up his hand, and struck the rock with his rod twice, and water came out abundantly. The congregation and their livestock drank.

note: 'You shall be like a watered garden, like a spring of water whose waters do not fail' supplies the image of the believer as an unfailing inward source ('from within him will flow'), matching the interiority of v.38. Isaiah's spring-that-fails-not coheres with the Spirit's permanence (v.39). A plausible component of John's composite scriptural citation.
sourceText: and Yahweh will guide you continually, and satisfy your soul in dry places, and make strong your bones; and you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters don’t fail.

note: 'I will pour water on the thirsty land... I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring' directly joins water-outpouring to Spirit-giving, exactly the move John makes when he glosses the living water as 'the Spirit' (v.39). The water/Spirit equation gives strong coherence and supplies the interpretive key John attaches to the saying. High confidence as a Spirit-water source.
sourceText: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:

note: 'With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation' was the text sung at the Tabernacles water-libation (the Hallel/water-drawing rite). The festal water-drawing ceremony is precisely the backdrop of Jesus' invitation 'if anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink' (v.37). Coherence with the liturgical setting is high; verbal contact moderate.
sourceText: Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation.

note: 'Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters' is the closest invitation-formula to v.37, 'if anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink.' The thirst-come-drink structure and free offer match. John re-voices the prophetic summons with Jesus as the water-giver; medium confidence as an unmarked but strongly parallel allusion.
sourceText: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

note: 'The words of a man's mouth are deep waters; the fountain of wisdom is a flowing stream' may feed the 'rivers of living water... from within him' image, linking inner source to wisdom/teaching. Low volume, offered because John's living-water motif elsewhere blends Wisdom and Spirit. Contested.
sourceText: The words of a man’s mouth are like deep waters. The fountain of wisdom is like a flowing brook.

note: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' grounds v.39's note that the Spirit 'was not yet given,' since the prophetic Spirit-outpouring awaited the eschaton. The pouring-out language coheres with the water imagery and explains the deferral until Jesus is glorified. Medium as background to the editorial Spirit comment.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.

note: 'A fountain shall come forth from the house of the LORD' joins the Zechariah/Ezekiel temple-spring cluster behind the 'rivers of living water.' Joel's fountain from the temple coheres with Jesus as the eschatological temple-source on the feast day. Offered as a recurrent member of the temple-river tradition John draws on.
sourceText: It will happen in that day, that the mountains will drop down sweet wine, the hills will flow with milk, all the brooks of Judah will flow with waters, and a fountain will flow out from Yahweh’s house, and will water the valley of Shittim.

note: 'This is truly the prophet' (v.40) names the eschatological prophet-like-Moses God promised to raise up, 'to him you shall listen.' Booths' Mosaic/wilderness setting and Jesus' Moses-discourse earlier (vv.19-23) make the Deuteronomic prophet the precise referent. High coherence and recurrence of the prophet motif in John (cf. 1:21, 6:14).
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: 'The Christ comes... from Bethlehem, the village where David was' (v.42) reflects the scribal reading of Micah, 'But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah... from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel.' John presents the crowd citing Scripture ('Hasn't the Scripture said'), the nearest thing to a formal quotation in the chapter. Maximal volume and availability.
sourceText: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings out are from of old, from ancient times.

note: 'The Christ comes of the seed of David' (v.42) invokes the Davidic covenant, 'I will raise up your offspring after you... and I will establish his kingdom.' The 'seed of David' formula is the covenantal root of messianic expectation the crowd recites. Strong coherence with the Bethlehem-of-David clause and the whole is-this-the-Christ debate.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom.

note: 'I have made a covenant with my chosen one... I will establish your offspring forever' restates the Davidic 'seed' promise behind v.42. The psalm's covenant-with-David vocabulary reinforces the 'seed of David' expectation; medium because 2 Samuel 7 is the more direct source. Recurrence of the Davidic-seed theme raises coherence.
sourceText: “I have made a covenant with my chosen one, I have sworn to David, my servant, ‘I will establish your seed forever, and build up your throne to all generations.’” Selah.

note: 'The LORD swore to David... one of the fruit of your body I will set on your throne' is another locus of the Davidic-seed oath underlying 'the seed of David' (v.42). The Bethlehem/David pairing coheres with the throne-promise. Offered as a member of the Davidic-covenant cluster the crowd's scriptural objection presupposes.
sourceText: Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it: “I will set the fruit of your body on your throne.

note: Nicodemus' 'Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him personally?' (v.51) applies the Mosaic charge to judges, 'hear the cases between your brothers and judge righteously... you shall not be partial.' The duty to hear a party before condemning is the procedural core of the Deuteronomic judicial code. High coherence with the chapter's 'judge righteous judgment' (v.24).
sourceText: I commanded your judges at that time, saying, “Hear cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother, and the foreigner who is living with him. You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be afraid of the face of man, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.”

note: Nicodemus' appeal to due process (v.51) reflects the law of inquiry and witnesses, where judges 'shall inquire diligently' and a matter is established only after examination. The insistence that the law not condemn without first hearing the accused matches the diligent-inquiry requirement. Strong verbal-conceptual contact and recurrence of the fair-hearing theme.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established. If an unrighteous witness rises up against any man to testify against him of wrongdoing, then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand before Yahweh, before the priests and the judges who shall be in those days; and the judges shall make […]

note: 'No prophet has arisen out of Galilee' (v.52) is John's irony against the very prophet-like-Moses expectation (v.40); the Pharisees deny on geographical grounds what Scripture and Jonah (a Galilean prophet) would unsettle. The prophet motif from Deuteronomy frames the dismissal as mistaken. Medium; functions through dramatic irony rather than citation.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: 'Search, and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee' (v.52) is ironized by Isaiah's prophecy that 'Galilee of the nations' would see a great light — a messianic dawn from the despised region. John's reader hears the Pharisees contradicting Scripture's own honoring of Galilee. Low volume and unmarked; offered as the corrective subtext.
sourceText: But there shall be no more gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time, he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali; but in the latter time he has made it glorious, by the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: The accusers' charge presupposes the Holiness Code's death sentence for adultery, which Leviticus prescribes for both parties. High Volume and Coherence: the scene is staged as a halakhic test about applying exactly this statute, and the conspicuous absence of the male partner exposes the accusers' selective use of the law.
sourceText: “‘The man who commits adultery with another man’s wife, even he who commits adultery with his neighbor’s wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death.

note: The specific penalty of stoning (rather than unspecified execution) for a betrothed woman taken in adultery supplies the legal frame the Pharisees invoke when they say Moses commanded stoning. High Coherence with their wording; the citation of 'Moses commanded us to stone' points to the Deuteronomic form of the law.
sourceText: If a man is found lying with a woman married to a husband, then they shall both die, the man who lay with the woman and the woman. So you shall remove the evil from Israel. If there is a young lady who is a virgin pledged to be married to a husband, and a man finds her in the city, and lies with her; then you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and you shall stone them to death with stones; the lady, because she didn’t cry, being in the […]

note: Jesus' 'let him who is without sin throw the first stone' reworks the rule that the hands of the witnesses shall be first against the condemned to put away evil. High Coherence: Jesus accepts the procedure but disqualifies the witnesses morally rather than legally, turning the witness-stone rule back on the accusers.
sourceText: The hand of the witnesses shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.

note: The parallel statute that the informer's hand shall be first to execute reinforces the witness-first-stone tradition behind v.7. Lower Volume than 17:7 but the same legal motif; Recurrence within Deuteronomy strengthens that the 'first stone' formula is the intended backdrop.
sourceText: but you shall surely kill him. Your hand shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterwards the hands of all the people.

note: The prohibition of joining hands with a wicked man as a malicious witness illumines the narrator's note that they spoke 'testing him, that they might accuse him.' Moderate Coherence: the accusers function as the malicious witnesses the law forbids, an irony built on this statute.
sourceText: “You shall not spread a false report. Don’t join your hand with the wicked to be a malicious witness.

note: 'Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent' coheres with Jesus' refusal to condemn and with exposing the accusers' bad faith. Contested because the verbal contact is thematic rather than lexical, but the coherence with the pericope's concern for unjust killing is strong.
sourceText: “Keep far from a false charge, and don’t kill the innocent and righteous: for I will not justify the wicked.

note: The Susanna narrative (Greek Daniel) is the closest Second-Temple analogue: a wise judge intervenes in a capital adultery accusation, tests and discredits the accusers, and saves the accused. High Coherence and Availability; the figural pattern of a Daniel-like discerner overturning a rigged witness procedure plausibly shapes the scene, though direct dependence is debated.
sourceText: A man lived in Babylon, and his name was Joakim: and he took a wife, whose name was Susanna, the daughter of Helkias, a very fair woman, and one that feared the Lord. Her parents also were righteous, and taught their daughter according to the law of Moses. Now Joakim was a great rich man, and had a fair garden joining to his house: and to him resorted the Jews; because he was more honorable than all others. And the same year there were appointed two of […]

note: Jesus' twice-noted writing on the ground may evoke 'those who turn away from you shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water.' Coherence with John's living-water theme is suggestive, but the gesture is unexplained in the text and the link remains a classic patristic conjecture.
sourceText: Yahweh, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be disappointed. Those who depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken Yahweh, the spring of living waters.

note: The detail that Jesus wrote 'with his finger' may recall the finger of God inscribing the tablets of the law, casting the lawgiver writing afresh over against those who wield Moses' law. Low Volume and contested; the verbal hook ('finger,' 'wrote') is real but the application is speculative.
sourceText: He gave to Moses, when he finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets, written with God’s finger.

note: The two-or-three-witness requirement hovers over a scene where the accusers withdraw one by one until no valid witness remains to condemn. Faint here and developed explicitly in 8:17; flagged for Recurrence across the chapter rather than strong presence in this pericope.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: 'I am the light of the world... will have the light of life' draws on the people who walked in darkness seeing a great light. High Volume in the light/darkness antithesis and strong Coherence with John's prologue light theme; Isaiah's dawning light on those in the land of deep darkness is a primary source for Johannine light Christology.
sourceText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: The Servant given as 'a light to the nations' to open blind eyes underwrites the universal scope of 'light of the world.' High Coherence: John repeatedly casts Jesus in Servant terms, and the worldwide reach of the light matches Isaiah's covenant-to-the-peoples commission.
sourceText: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations; to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: 'I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' supplies the 'of the world' scope of Jesus' claim. High Recurrence with 42:6 and strong Coherence with John's mission to gather scattered children of God.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: 'Arise, shine, for your light has come... nations shall come to your light' frames the eschatological light to which peoples are drawn. High Coherence with the Tabernacles setting and with Jesus as the light that the world follows; the procession-to-the-light image matches 'he who follows me.'
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

note: The pillar of fire that led Israel by night so they could walk is the exodus type behind 'he who follows me will not walk in darkness but have the light of life.' High Coherence given the Tabernacles temple-lamp ceremony commemorating wilderness guidance; Jesus presents himself as the guiding light-presence for a new exodus.
sourceText: Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night:

note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' lends the divine self-designation Jesus appropriates. Moderate Volume; Coherence is strong because John's 'I am' light-claim takes up a predicate Scripture reserves for the LORD, reinforcing the chapter's high Christology.
sourceText: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?

note: Wisdom as 'a reflection of eternal light' and unspotted mirror of God supplies Second-Temple Wisdom-light language close to John's incarnate Logos-light. Good Availability and Coherence with Johannine Wisdom Christology, though the link is conceptual rather than verbal.
sourceText: For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.

note: Zechariah's Tabernacles-day vision of continuous light ('at evening time there shall be light'), read liturgically at the feast, situates Jesus' light-claim within the festival's eschatological imagery. Moderate Coherence with the temple setting of v.20.
sourceText: It will be a unique day which is known to Yahweh; not day, and not night; but it will come to pass, that at evening time there will be light.

note: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path' links walking, word, and light, themes that converge in the pericope. Low Volume and contested; offered for the walking-by-light motif rather than a distinct source.
sourceText: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.

note: 'It is written in your law that the testimony of two people is true' explicitly cites the two-or-three-witness statute. High Volume (near-quotation) and total Coherence; Jesus appeals to this rule to count himself and the Father as the two valid witnesses.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: The parallel formulation that a matter is established on the evidence of two or three witnesses reinforces the law Jesus cites in v.17. Recurrence within Deuteronomy strengthens the witness-law backdrop; slightly lower Volume than 19:15.
sourceText: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.

note: The capital-case rule requiring multiple witnesses extends the legal field Jesus invokes. Low Volume; included for Recurrence of the witness statute across the Pentateuch rather than as a primary source.
sourceText: “‘Whoever kills any person, the murderer shall be slain at the mouth of witnesses; but one witness shall not testify against any person that he die.

note: 'Unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins' and 'then you will know that I am he' deploy the absolute egō eimi rooted in God's self-revelation 'I AM WHO I AM.' High Coherence with the chapter's climactic I AM in v.58; Jesus appropriates the divine Name as the object of saving faith.
sourceText: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

note: 'That you may know and believe me and understand that I am he' (LXX hina pisteusēte... hoti egō eimi) supplies the exact 'believe that I am he' construction of v.24,28. High Volume and Coherence; Isaiah's courtroom of witnesses for the one God matches John's witness theme and 'I am he' formula.
sourceText: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.

note: 'I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he' (egō eimi) furnishes the same self-predication tied to God's sovereignty over the generations. Recurrence with 43:10 strengthens the case that John draws the absolute 'I am he' from Deutero-Isaiah's monotheistic self-declarations.
sourceText: Who has worked and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I, Yahweh, the first, and with the last, I am he.”

note: 'My servant shall be exalted and lifted up' undergirds 'when you have lifted up the Son of Man.' John's double-meaning of hypsoō (crucifixion/exaltation) coheres tightly with Isaiah's Servant who is lifted up; moderate Volume but high thematic Coherence.
sourceText: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.

note: The bronze serpent lifted on a pole so that those who look live is the lifting-up type John established in 3:14 and recalls here with 'lifted up the Son of Man.' Recurrence across John and Coherence of the look-and-live/lift-and-know pattern support a figural reading.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.

note: 'You will die in your sins' echoes Ezekiel's watchman warning that the wicked 'shall die in his iniquity' if unwarned. Moderate Coherence: John uses the prophetic death-in-sin formula for those who reject the light, and Ezekiel is its densest source.
sourceText: When I tell the wicked, You shall surely die; and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at your hand.

note: Ezekiel's repeated 'he shall die in his iniquity' for the unrepentant strengthens the prophetic background of 'die in your sins.' Lower Volume than 3:18; included for Recurrence of the formula within Ezekiel.
sourceText: As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, robbed his brother, and did that which is not good among his people, behold, he shall die in his iniquity.

note: 'You will seek me and not find me; where I am going you cannot come' resonates with Wisdom's warning that those who refused her 'will seek me diligently but will not find me.' Faint and contested, but the seek-but-not-find judgment pattern coheres with Johannine Wisdom Christology.
sourceText: Then will they call on me, but I will not answer. They will seek me diligently, but they will not find me;

note: The dispute turns on being 'Abraham's seed,' invoking the patriarchal promise that Abraham's offspring would be multiplied. High Coherence: Jesus concedes physical descent (sperma) but redefines true sonship by deeds, pressing the gap between biological seed and genuine children of Abraham.
sourceText: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies.

note: 'A slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever' alludes to Sarah's demand that the slave woman's son not inherit with the free son, the Isaac/Ishmael household division. High Coherence; the slave-vs-son contrast that grounds Jesus' freedom argument is drawn from this Genesis scene of casting out the bondservant.
sourceText: Therefore she said to Abraham, “Cast out this handmaid and her son! For the son of this handmaid will not be heir with my son, Isaac.”

note: The Abrahamic blessing-to-the-nations promise underlies the claim to do 'the works of Abraham,' i.e., faith-hospitality toward God's messenger rather than murder. Moderate Coherence; Abraham's welcome of divine visitors stands behind 'you would do the works of Abraham.'
sourceText: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”

note: Abraham's hospitable reception of the LORD and his angels at Mamre exemplifies 'the works of Abraham' that the hostile interlocutors fail to imitate by seeking to kill Jesus. Coherence is good in Jewish exegesis that paired Abraham's welcome with his descendants' murderous rejection of prophets.
sourceText: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]

note: 'You are of your father the devil... a liar and the father of lies' reads the Eden serpent's deceit as the devil's primal lie that brought death. High Coherence: the murderer-from-the-beginning and liar-from-the-beginning charges fuse the serpent's deception with the death it caused, the dominant Second-Temple reading of Genesis 3.
sourceText: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]

note: 'A murderer from the beginning' likely also evokes Cain's killing of Abel, the first human murder, traditionally traced to the devil's influence (cf. 1 John 3:12, but the OT base is Genesis 4). Moderate Coherence with 'you seek to kill me,' aligning the accusers with the archetypal fratricide.
sourceText: Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.

note: 'Through the devil's envy death entered the world' is the clearest Second-Temple bridge interpreting Genesis 3 as the devil being a murderer from the beginning. High Availability and Coherence; this verse supplies precisely the devil-as-death-bringer logic John's charge presupposes.
sourceText: But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, And those who are of his portion make trial thereof.

note: 'We were not born of sexual immorality' (porneia) may carry the prophetic charge that idolatrous Israel was born of harlotry; the interlocutors deny the very status the prophets assigned faithless Israel. Faint and contested, offered for the figural irony of the porneia denial.
sourceText: When Yahweh spoke at first by Hosea, Yahweh said to Hosea, “Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitution and children of unfaithfulness; for the land commits great adultery, forsaking Yahweh.”

note: 'Before Abraham came into existence, I AM' (egō eimi) climactically claims the divine Name revealed at the burning bush, asserting timeless self-existence over against Abraham's createdness. Highest Volume of the chapter and total Coherence; the immediate attempt to stone him for blasphemy confirms the hearers grasped a divine self-identification.
sourceText: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

note: Deutero-Isaiah's 'I am he... before me no god was formed... I am God, and also henceforth I am he' provides the absolute, eternal egō eimi that v.58 enacts. High Coherence and Recurrence (also behind 8:24,28); John draws the unqualified I AM from Isaiah's monotheistic self-declarations.
sourceText: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me. I myself am Yahweh; and besides me there is no savior. I have declared, I have saved, and I have shown; and there was no strange god among you. Therefore you are my witnesses”, says Yahweh, “and I am God. Yes, since the day was I am he; and there is no […]

note: 'Who has performed this... calling the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he' supplies the over-the-generations claim implicit in standing before Abraham. Moderate Volume; reinforces the Isaianic I AM backdrop.
sourceText: Who has worked and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I, Yahweh, the first, and with the last, I am he.”

note: 'Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day' connects to Abraham's laughter/rejoicing at the promise of Isaac, read in Jewish tradition as joy over the messianic future. Moderate Coherence; the verb of rejoicing and the forward-looking 'day' are anchored in the covenant-promise scenes of Abraham.
sourceText: Then Abraham fell on his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, “Will a child be born to him who is one hundred years old? Will Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”

note: The Aqedah, where Abraham 'saw the place afar off' and named the mount 'the LORD will provide/be seen,' was widely read as Abraham foreseeing the day of deliverance, illuminating 'he saw it and was glad.' Good Availability in Second-Temple Abraham traditions and Coherence with Abraham's prophetic sight.
sourceText: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and […]

note: 'They took up stones to throw at him' enacts the statute that one who blasphemes the Name shall be stoned by all the congregation. High Coherence: the stoning response directly judges Jesus' I AM as blasphemous use of the divine Name, so the law of Leviticus 24 is the operative legal backdrop.
sourceText: He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.

note: 'Before the mountains were brought forth... from everlasting to everlasting you are God' parallels the pre-Abrahamic eternity asserted in v.58. Low Volume and verbal contact, but coheres with the claim to existence prior to creation/patriarch.
sourceText: Before the mountains were born, before you had formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, you are God.

note: 'What man can live and never see death?' frames the dispute over Jesus' promise that one who keeps his word 'will never see death,' which the hearers measure against Abraham's death. Faint; offered for the see/taste-death motif rather than as a primary source.
sourceText: What man is he who shall live and not see death, who shall deliver his soul from the power of Sheol? Selah.

note: The prophets dying yet the patriarch's hope of seeing God's 'day' resonates faintly with prophetic 'in your days' announcements of a work to be marveled at. Highly contested and low Volume; included only for maximal coverage of the 'see my day' language.
sourceText: “Look among the nations, watch, and wonder marvelously; for I am working a work in your days, which you will not believe though it is told you.
lxxText: Behold, ye despisers, and look, and wonder marvelously, and vanish: for I work a work in your days, which ye will in no wise believe, though a man declare it to you.

note: The disciples' question 'who sinned, this man or his parents' presupposes the Decalogue principle of God visiting the iniquity of fathers upon children. The transgenerational logic is precisely what is at issue; Volume is moderate and Coherence high, since Johannine sin-theology engages the retribution framework only to overturn it.
sourceText: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,

note: Ezekiel's countervailing principle that 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father' frames the very debate the disciples raise. Jesus' answer ('neither did this man sin, nor his parents') aligns with Ezekiel's repudiation of inherited guilt, making this a coherent and available Second-Temple intertext.
sourceText: The soul who sins, he shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be on him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be on him.

note: The friends' assumption that suffering proves prior sin (Eliphaz: 'who ever perished, being innocent?') is the wisdom-debate background to the disciples' question. Job as a whole resists the suffering-equals-sin calculus; the echo is thematic and diffuse rather than verbal.
sourceText: “Remember, now, whoever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?

note: YHWH to Moses: 'Who makes a man dumb or deaf, or seeing or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?' This grounds blindness in God's sovereign purpose, exactly Jesus' reframing ('that the works of God might be revealed'). Coherence is high since the giver of sight here becomes incarnate as the light-bringer.
sourceText: Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?

note: 'I am the light of the world' resonates with Zion's eschatological illumination where YHWH's light shines on a darkened earth. The light-of-the-nations motif is available and coherent with John's worldwide scope, though no verbal citation links them.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' supplies a scriptural backdrop for Jesus' self-identification as light, especially apposite as a blind man is about to receive sight/salvation. The echo is conceptual; Volume is low and many candidates compete.
sourceText: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?

note: Jesus forms mud from spittle and the ground and applies it to make eyes whole, evoking the Creator forming the man from the dust of the ground. The clay-and-creation figure casts the healing as a new-creation act by the agent of Genesis 1's 'let there be light'; Coherence with the light-of-the-world saying is strong.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: The 'ground/dust' material of the healing recalls the adamic dust to which humanity belongs. The reversal — dust here restores rather than condemns — supports a new-creation reading, though the link rides on the same Genesis 2-3 imagery as the stronger 2:7 echo.
sourceText: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

note: John glosses Siloam as 'Sent,' and the pool's name derives from the gently-flowing 'waters of Shiloah' that Judah despised in Isaiah 8:6. The deliberate etymological note signals figural intent: the rejected waters become the means of sight, and 'Sent' identifies Jesus as the one sent by the Father. High Volume via the explicit gloss.
sourceText: “Because this people have refused the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah’s son;

note: The Hebrew 'Shiloh' ('until Shiloh comes') was read messianically in Second-Temple tradition and shares the consonantal root behind Siloam/'Sent.' John's 'Sent One' Christology may exploit this resonance, but the linguistic bridge is contested and the gloss more naturally targets Isaiah's Shiloah.
sourceText: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs. To him will the obedience of the peoples be.

note: 'Go, wash' in a specific body of water and be made whole closely patterns Elisha's command to Naaman to wash in the Jordan and be cleansed. The prophetic-healing-by-washing type, with obedience producing restoration, is coherent and the man's later confession that Jesus is 'a prophet' reinforces the Elijah/Elisha matrix.
sourceText: Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall come again to you, and you shall be clean.”

note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened' is the eschatological sign of God's coming; the actual opening of a blind man's eyes enacts it. The healing is a programmatic fulfillment-sign, and John repeatedly frames Jesus' works as the dawning of the promised age. High Coherence and Recurrence across Isaiah's sight oracles.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.

note: 'In that day...the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity' supplies the eschatological frame as neighbors marvel that the beggar now sees. The pericope is largely narrative dialogue, so the echo is ambient rather than pointed, carried over from the healing itself.
sourceText: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.

note: The conflict turns on Jesus 'making mud' and healing on the Sabbath, engaging the Decalogue's Sabbath command and its later halakhic elaborations (kneading clay was forbidden work). The Sabbath statute is the legal axis of the Pharisees' charge that Jesus is 'not from God.'
sourceText: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.

note: The healed man's verdict 'He is a prophet' invokes the Mosaic promise of a prophet like Moses whom Israel must heed. John develops the prophet-like-Moses Christology, and the sign-working healer fits the criterion of the true prophet; Coherence with John's wider Moses typology is strong.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: The interrogation of the parents to corroborate the son's testimony reflects the Torah's two-or-three-witnesses requirement that governs Johannine 'witness' motifs. The link is structural/legal rather than verbal, and the courtroom framing is broadly Deuteronomic.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: 'Give glory to God' is a near-verbatim adjuration formula: Joshua so charges Achan to confess before God in a judicial setting. The Pharisees use the identical oath-formula to pressure the man to recant, marking his testimony as sworn courtroom speech. High Volume via the fixed idiom.
sourceText: Joshua said to Achan, “My son, please give glory to Yahweh, the God of Israel, and make confession to him. Tell me now what you have done! Don’t hide it from me!”

note: 'Give glory to the God of Israel' as a confessional demand recurs in the Philistine episode, reinforcing the formula behind 9:24. It is a secondary witness to the same idiom rather than an independent source; Joshua 7:19 is the closer judicial parallel.
sourceText: Therefore you shall make images of your tumors, and images of your mice that mar the land; and you shall give glory to the God of Israel: perhaps he will lighten his hand from off you, and from off your gods, and from off your land.

note: 'We are disciples of Moses... God has spoken to Moses' echoes the Torah's claim that no prophet arose like Moses, whom YHWH knew face to face. The Pharisees stake authority on Mosaic revelation, the very framework John uses to argue Jesus surpasses Moses. Coherence high within the chapter's Moses polemic.
sourceText: Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face,

note: 'With him I speak mouth to mouth' grounds the unique standing of Moses claimed by 'God has spoken to Moses.' The Pharisees' 'we know God has spoken to Moses, but we don't know where this man is from' trades on this Mosaic-speech privilege. Available and coherent with the disciples-of-Moses boast.
sourceText: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”

note: 'If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me' is closely paraphrased by 'God does not listen to sinners, but to the worshiper who does his will.' The man invokes a wisdom-psalm axiom about answered prayer to argue Jesus is from God. High Coherence and near-propositional match.
sourceText: If I cherished sin in my heart, the Lord wouldn’t have listened.

note: 'The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous' is the proverbial doublet behind 9:31's 'God does not listen to sinners but to the worshiper who does his will.' Recurrence with Psalm 66:18 strengthens both as the wisdom substrate of the man's argument.
sourceText: Yahweh is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous.

note: 'When you spread out your hands I will hide my eyes... I will not hear' supplies the prophetic version of God refusing to hear sinners. It reinforces 9:31 alongside the psalm and proverb, broadening the 'God hears the righteous' axiom across Torah-Prophets-Writings.
sourceText: When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you. Yes, when you make many prayers, I will not hear. Your hands are full of blood.

note: 'The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous, and his ears toward their cry' is a further wisdom witness to the principle that God hears the God-fearing but not the wicked. It coheres with 9:31 and adds Recurrence, though the man's wording is closest to Psalm 66:18 and Proverbs 15:29.
sourceText: Yahweh’s eyes are toward the righteous. His ears listen to their cry.

note: Ben Sira affirms that God hears the prayer of the humble and the one who serves him with his whole heart, a deuterocanonical articulation of the doctrine in 9:31. Available within Second-Temple piety and coherent, though the canonical psalm/proverb are the nearer sources.
sourceText: He will not accept any person against a poor man; And he will listen to the prayer of him that is wronged. He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall? He that serves God according to his good pleasure shall be accepted, And his supplication shall reach to the clouds.

note: 'Since the world began it was never heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind' frames the sign as unprecedented — only God can do the eschatological eye-opening of Isaiah 35:5. The man's argument turns the prophetic sign-act into proof of divine origin. Coherence with the chapter's controlling Isaianic motif.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.

note: 'The LORD opens the eyes of the blind' names eye-opening as a distinctly divine work, undergirding 'if this man were not from God he could do nothing.' The man reasons exactly along the psalm's lines, attributing a God-only act to Jesus. Strong Coherence with John's high Christology.
sourceText: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.

note: 'I came for judgment, that those who don't see may see, and those who see may become blind' inverts and fulfills Isaiah's commission to blind the seeing and deafen the hearing. John elsewhere cites Isaiah 6:10 explicitly (12:40), making this the controlling intertext for the chapter's sight/blindness-as-judgment theme. High Recurrence and Coherence.
sourceText: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: 'Who is blind but my servant... seeing many things, but you do not observe' supplies the prophetic paradox of those who possess sight yet remain blind, mirroring the Pharisees who 'see' yet have sin remaining. Coherent with the judicial blinding motif and available within the Isaianic servant oracles.
sourceText: “Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see. Who is blind, but my servant? Or who is as deaf as my messenger whom I send? Who is as blind as he who is at peace, and as blind as Yahweh’s servant? You see many things, but don’t observe. His ears are open, but he doesn’t listen.

note: 'Bring forth the people who are blind, yet have eyes, and the deaf who have ears' reinforces the sighted-yet-blind paradox applied to the Pharisees. Secondary to Isaiah 6 and 42; adds Recurrence to the Isaianic blindness cluster but contributes little independently.
sourceText: Bring out the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears.

note: Isaiah's stupefied, blinded leaders ('they are blind... the LORD has poured on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes') parallel the self-confident Pharisees judged blind. The judicial-blinding theme coheres, though the verbal contact is faint amid the stronger Isaiah 6 link.
sourceText: Pause and wonder! Blind yourselves and be blind! They are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink. For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers.

note: 'Do you believe in the Son of Man?' (a strong textual variant for 'Son of God') invokes the Danielic Son of Man before whom worship is rendered, fitting the man's response of belief and worship in 9:38. The link depends on the variant reading, so confidence is low though the title is Danielic.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: 'In that day the deaf shall hear... and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity and darkness' frames the chapter's resolution: a blind man comes to physical and spiritual sight while the seeing are darkened. The double movement realizes Isaiah's reversal-of-perception oracle and coheres with the light/darkness frame.
sourceText: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.

note: Ezekiel 34 is the controlling subtext for the whole discourse: false shepherds who do not enter rightly and exploit the flock vs. the true shepherd. The thief/robber who climbs in 'some other way' answers Ezekiel's self-feeding shepherds, and the rightful shepherd entering by the door answers the LORD's own shepherding. High volume, recurrence across the chapter, and coherence with John's polemic against Israel's leaders.
sourceText: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and tell them, even to the shepherds, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, and you clothe yourself with the wool, you kill the fatlings; but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither […]

note: Moses asks the LORD to appoint a shepherd who leads Israel 'out' and brings them 'in,' so the congregation not be sheep without a shepherd. John's shepherd who 'leads them out' (v.3) and goes before them (v.4) echoes the leading-out/going-before language of the appointment of a shepherd over Israel.
sourceText: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”

note: 'The sheep listen to his voice' and refusal to follow strangers resonates with 'the sheep of his hand. Today, if you would hear his voice.' The motif of the flock recognizing and hearing the shepherd's voice is verbally and thematically coherent.
sourceText: for he is our God. We are the people of his pasture, and the sheep in his care. Today, oh that you would hear his voice!

note: 'We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture' supplies the flock-belonging frame behind the shepherd who knows his own and calls them by name. Faint; competes with Psalm 95 and the broader shepherd-of-Israel topos.
sourceText: Know that Yahweh, he is God. It is he who has made us, and we are his. We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.

note: Zechariah's flock 'doomed to slaughter' under worthless shepherds who do not care for the sheep, and the breaking of the bond with the flock, anticipates John's thieves/robbers contrasted with the true shepherd. Recurs more strongly at vv.11-13, but the false-shepherd indictment colors the parable here.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]

note: 'This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous will enter into it' undergirds Jesus' self-identification as the door through which one 'enters in' and 'will be saved.' Psalm 118 is a major Johannine/Synoptic source and the entering-and-being-saved language coheres with the entrance-gate motif.
sourceText: This is the gate of Yahweh; the righteous will enter into it.

note: 'All who came before me are thieves and robbers' continues the indictment of Israel's bad shepherds in Ezekiel 34, while 'find pasture' (v.9) directly echoes the LORD's promise to feed his flock in good pasture (Ezek 34:14). Strong recurrence and coherence with the governing subtext.
sourceText: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and tell them, even to the shepherds, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, and you clothe yourself with the wool, you kill the fatlings; but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither […]

note: 'Will go in and go out, and will find pasture' echoes the shepherd who leads Israel 'out' and brings them 'in' so they may be led to pasture. The go-in/go-out idiom for secure shepherded life is shared, though common in the OT.
sourceText: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”

note: 'Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep' parallels the thief who 'comes to steal, kill, and destroy.' Jeremiah promises to set up shepherds who will feed the flock so none is lacking, coherent with John's life-giving shepherd over against destroyers.
sourceText: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]

note: The LORD himself seeks, gathers, and feeds the scattered sheep, rescuing them from where they were scattered in the day of clouds. Jesus as the good shepherd who knows his own enacts the LORD's own pastoral self-commitment, making the divine claim of Ezekiel 34 the load-bearing subtext.
sourceText: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]

note: 'I will set up one shepherd over them, my servant David... and I the LORD will be their God.' This is the source of the singular good shepherd and converges with v.16's 'one flock, one shepherd.' High volume and exact thematic match to the Davidic-messianic single shepherd.
sourceText: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. I, Yahweh, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken it.

note: 'David my servant shall be king over them; and they all shall have one shepherd' is the closest verbal antecedent to 'one flock, one shepherd' (v.16). Recurs with Ezek 34:23 and reinforces the reunification of a divided flock under one Davidic shepherd.
sourceText: My servant David shall be king over them; and they all shall have one shepherd: they shall also walk in my ordinances, and observe my statutes, and do them.

note: 'He will feed his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arm' supplies the tender LORD-as-shepherd image behind the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. Coherent with John's identification of Jesus with the LORD's own shepherding care.
sourceText: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.

note: 'The LORD is my shepherd... though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death.' The good shepherd who lays down his life and faces the wolf evokes the shepherd who protects through death's shadow. Strong cultural availability, though the laying-down-of-life motif goes beyond Psalm 23.
sourceText: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.

note: The 'worthless shepherd' who deserts the flock, does not care for the perishing, and abandons them to be devoured is the negative counterpart to John's hired hand who flees the wolf and does not care for the sheep. Verbal and thematic coherence in the abandonment/devouring imagery.
sourceText: Yahweh said to me, “Take for yourself yet again the equipment of a foolish shepherd. For, behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, who will not visit those who are cut off, neither will seek those who are scattered, nor heal that which is broken, nor feed that which is sound; but he will eat the flesh of the fat sheep, and will tear their hoofs in pieces. Woe to the worthless shepherd who leaves the flock! The sword will be on his arm, and on his […]

note: Without a shepherd the flock 'became food for all the beasts of the field, and were scattered.' The wolf that snatches and scatters the sheep (v.12) replays Ezekiel's scattering and devouring of the unshepherded flock.
sourceText: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.

note: 'The Lord GOD, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, says, Yet others will I gather besides his own that are gathered.' This is the strongest antecedent for the 'other sheep... not of this fold' whom the shepherd must also bring (v.16), grounding the Gentile ingathering.
sourceText: The Lord Yahweh, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, says, “Yet will I gather others to him, besides his own who are gathered.”

note: 'I will surely gather all of you, Jacob... I will put them together like the sheep of Bozrah... they will swarm with people.' Supplies the regathering-into-one-flock image behind the 'one flock' formed from other sheep. Coherent but competes with Ezekiel/Isaiah gathering texts.
sourceText: I will surely assemble, Jacob, all of you; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the midst of their pasture; they will swarm with people.

sourceText: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.

sourceText: I said, “You are gods, all of you are sons of the Most High.

note: Beyond the quoted v.6, the whole psalm frames those 'to whom the word of God came' (v.35) as the divine council/judges called 'gods,' supplying the a-fortiori logic for the one the Father consecrated. The surrounding context, not just the citation, drives the defense.

note: 'Before you came forth out of the womb I sanctified you; I appointed you a prophet' parallels 'the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world' (v.36). The consecrate-and-send pattern of prophetic commissioning is closely echoed.
sourceText: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”

note: The consecration of Aaron and his sons to serve the LORD provides cultic resonance for the Father's 'sanctifying' of Jesus, fitting the Dedication setting where the altar itself is consecrated. Faint and competes with the prophetic-commission sense of Jer 1:5.
sourceText: You shall put them on Aaron your brother, and on his sons with him, and shall anoint them, and consecrate them, and sanctify them, that they may minister to me in the priest’s office.

note: 'He who blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death... shall stone him' grounds the crowd's move to stone Jesus 'for blasphemy' (vv.31-33). The stoning-for-blasphemy procedure is the legal backdrop the narrative presupposes.
sourceText: He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.

note: The 'sickness not unto death but for the glory of God' frames Lazarus' death as a stage on which divine life-giving will be displayed, echoing the Creator who breathes life into dust. Faint, but coheres with John's creation theology (1:1-4) and the breath-of-life motif that undergirds resurrection texts. Contested.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: Jesus' euphemism that Lazarus 'has fallen asleep' and will be awakened maps onto Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake,' the classic OT idiom for resurrection as awakening from sleep. Volume is moderate (shared sleep/awaken vocabulary) and coheres with the chapter's resurrection program. Availability secure as the seminal resurrection text.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: Job's 'man lies down and rises not till the heavens are no more; they will not awake nor be roused from their sleep' supplies the sleep-of-death idiom that Jesus inverts by awakening Lazarus. Coherence is good but volume is faint and the idiom is widely diffused. Contested as a specific source.
sourceText: so man lies down and doesn’t rise. Until the heavens are no more, they shall not awake, nor be roused out of their sleep.

note: 'Lighten my eyes lest I sleep the sleep of death' associates sleep with death and divine light, resonating with both the 'fallen asleep' euphemism and Jesus' day/night light saying (vv.9-10). Faint and idiomatic; offered honestly as low-confidence.
sourceText: Behold, and answer me, Yahweh, my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death;

note: Jesus' walking-in-the-day-versus-stumbling-in-the-dark saying echoes the prophetic 'give glory to the LORD before he brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the twilight mountains.' Shared stumble/light/darkness imagery; coherence with Johannine light theme but low volume. Contested.
sourceText: Give glory to Yahweh your God, before he causes darkness, and before your feet stumble on the dark mountains, and, while you look for light, he turns it into the shadow of death, and makes it gross darkness.

note: Martha's confession 'I know he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day' is precisely the Danielic doctrine of bodily resurrection at the end, the only OT text giving it explicit shape. High volume and recurrence; Jesus then collapses 'the last day' into his own person ('I am the resurrection'). Availability and coherence are strong.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: The whole Lazarus episode enacts Ezekiel's vision: God opens graves, raises the dead, and gives life by his Spirit/word so that 'you shall know that I am the LORD.' 'I am the resurrection and the life' figurally fulfills Yahweh's promise to raise the dead from their tombs. High volume of shared grave/raising imagery and strong coherence with the sign's purpose (that they may believe / know).

sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

sourceText: I will not die, but live, and declare Yah’s works.

note: 'You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle' frames divine attentiveness to human weeping, resonating with Jesus weeping and being deeply moved at the tomb. Faint and thematic rather than verbal; coherence with the compassion motif but low volume. Contested.
