note: 'Don't be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey's colt' is a formula-cited fulfillment of Zech 9:9 (John conflates its opening with Isa/Zeph 'fear not'). Highest Volume and explicit 'as it is written'; the humble-king-on-a-colt image is the controlling typology of the whole entry.
sourceText: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

note: John's 'Don't be afraid, daughter of Zion' more exactly matches Zeph 3:16 ('Do not fear, O Zion') and 3:15 ('the King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst') than Zech 9:9's 'rejoice greatly.' The 'King of Israel' acclaim (v.13) and the 'fear not' opening suggest a deliberate Zephaniah blend; medium for the conflation.
sourceText: Yahweh has taken away your judgments. He has thrown out your enemy. The King of Israel, Yahweh, is in your midst. You will not be afraid of evil any more. In that day, it will be said to Jerusalem, “Don’t be afraid, Zion. Don’t let your hands be weak.”

note: Jacob's blessing of Judah 'binding his colt (polos) to the vine' is the classic messianic donkey text read alongside Zech 9:9; the shared polos and royal-Judah expectation give faint background support to the colt motif. Low and contested: no verbal citation in John.
sourceText: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.

note: Simon's triumphal entry into Jerusalem 'with praise and palm branches' (also 2 Macc 10:7) shows palms as the established Second-Temple sign of liberation-procession into the holy city. Availability and Coherence make this the nearest cultural template for John's palm-waving crowd; echo, not citation.
sourceText: And he entered into it on the three and twentieth day of the second month, in the hundred and seventy and first year, with praise and palm branches, and with harps, and with cymbals, and with viols, and with hymns, and with songs: because a great enemy was destroyed out of Israel.

note: The Greeks who 'went up to worship' and seek Jesus faintly enact the pilgrimage of the nations to Zion in the last days. Coherence with John's universalizing 'I will draw all people' (v.32) gives the motif some weight; low because no verbal contact.
sourceText: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of Yahweh’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.

note: The seed-sowing wisdom of 'in the morning sow your seed... you do not know which will prosper' lies behind the grain-of-wheat agricultural maxim, though Jesus inverts it: the seed must die to bear fruit. Faint and generic; sowing imagery was broadly available.
sourceText: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both will be equally good.

note: 'Those who sow in tears... goes out weeping, bearing the seed... comes home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves' offers a death-to-harvest pattern resonant with the grain that dies to bear much fruit. Thematic Coherence only; no lexical anchor, hence low.
sourceText: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.

note: 'Now my soul is troubled... save me from this time?' echoes the lament psalter, esp. Ps 6:3-4 'my soul is greatly troubled... save my life,' the Johannine analogue to the Synoptic Gethsemane. Coherence with the psalmist's troubled-soul-then-deliverance pattern is strong; medium since John gives no citation formula.
sourceText: My soul is also in great anguish. But you, Yahweh—how long? Return, Yahweh. Deliver my soul, and save me for your loving kindness’ sake.

note: 'If I am lifted up from the earth' (hypsotho) reactivates the bronze-serpent type John named in 3:14: the lifted-up serpent that gives life when looked upon prefigures the crucified-glorified Son of Man. High Coherence and Recurrence across John; the verb 'lifted up' is the load-bearing link to Moses' standard.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.

note: John's distinctive fusion of 'lifted up' with 'glorified' tracks the LXX of the Servant Song: 'my servant shall be exalted (hypsothesetai) and glorified (doxasthesetai) exceedingly.' The pairing hypsoo + doxazo is rare and precise, giving strong Volume; John reads crucifixion as the Servant's exaltation.
sourceText: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.

note: 'Now the prince of this world will be cast out' faintly resonates with the protevangelium's defeat of the serpent. Low and contested; the casting-out of the ruler is more cosmic/apocalyptic than tied to any single verse.
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: The crowd's 'we have heard out of the law that the Christ remains forever' rests on the Davidic-covenant promise that his offspring/throne 'shall endure forever.' Coherence with messianic exegesis is strong; medium because John cites 'the law' generically rather than a fixed text.
sourceText: His seed will endure forever, his throne like the sun before me. It will be established forever like the moon, the faithful witness in the sky.” Selah.

note: 'Who is this Son of Man?' and the claim that the Christ 'remains forever' invoke Daniel's heavenly Son of Man given everlasting dominion. The crowd's puzzlement over an eternal yet 'lifted up' Son of Man trades on Dan 7's title; medium for the conceptual rather than verbal link.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The notion of the messianic king whose government and reign have 'no end' supports the crowd's 'remains forever.' Faint background to the eternal-Messiah expectation; low, with no verbal contact.
sourceText: Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, on the throne of David, and on his kingdom, to establish it, and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from that time on, even forever. The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will perform this.

note: 'Walk while you have the light... that you may become children of light' draws on the prophetic 'walk in the light of the Lord' and the wider light/darkness covenant motif. Coherence with Isaiah's light-walking and John's pervasive light theme gives medium weight; an idiom rather than a citation.
sourceText: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of Yahweh.

note: 'Lord, who has believed our report? To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?' is a formula-cited quotation ('that the word of Isaiah... might be fulfilled') of Isa 53:1 LXX verbatim. Maximal Volume; John reads Israel's unbelief at the signs through the Servant Song's lament over a rejected revelation.
sourceText: Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?

note: 'He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they should see... and turn, and I would heal them' quotes Isa 6:10, the commission-text of judicial hardening (cf. its NT recurrence). High Volume and explicit attribution to Isaiah; the divine blinding explains the unbelief just described.
sourceText: Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: 'Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him' alludes to the throne-vision of Isa 6:1, 'I saw the Lord... high and lifted up,' identifying the glory Isaiah beheld with Christ's. Strong Coherence: John binds the 'lifted up' (hypsoo) Servant to the 'high and lifted up' enthroned Lord of the call narrative.
sourceText: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.

note: 'I spoke not from myself, but the Father... gave me a commandment what I should say' and the warning that the rejected 'word' will judge in the last day echo the prophet-like-Moses who speaks only the words God commands, and whom God will hold men accountable to hear. Coherence with John's prophet christology is strong; medium absent a citation formula.
sourceText: I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him. It shall happen, that whoever will not listen to my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.

note: 'I know that his commandment is eternal life... this word is your life' resonates with Moses' charge that the law-word 'is no trifle for you, but your very life.' Faint thematic link between commandment and life; low, with only conceptual contact.
sourceText: He said to them, “Set your heart to all the words which I testify to you this day, which you shall command your children to observe to do, all the words of this law. For it is no vain thing for you; because it is your life, and through this thing you shall prolong your days in the land, where you go over the Jordan to possess it.”

note: 'I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes... may not remain in the darkness' continues the light-to-the-nations motif of Isaiah's eschatological dawn. Coherence with John's universal-light christology gives faint support; low, idiomatic rather than cited.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

note: John frames the entire farewell on the eve of 'the feast of the Passover,' deliberately situating Jesus' self-giving against the exodus deliverance. Volume and coherence are high in John, which has already cast Jesus as the lamb (1:29) and dates the crucifixion to Passover. The footwashing supper thus becomes the new Passover meal of departure.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]

note: 'The Father had given all things into his hands' echoes the giving of universal dominion to the one like a son of man. The handing-over language coheres with John's repeated Son-of-Man glorification motif and prepares for 13:31. Coherence is strong though the wording is general.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'All things into his hands' may echo the psalmist's 'you put all things under his feet/gave him dominion.' The thought-rhyme of universal subjection is present but the verbal overlap is faint and the motif is widely diffused.
sourceText: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:

note: 'Having loved his own... he loved them to the end' resonates with the LORD's everlasting love and faithful hesed toward his own people. The covenant-love register fits, but the wording is too common to claim a deliberate citation.
sourceText: Yahweh appeared of old to me, saying, Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love: therefore with loving kindness have I drawn you.

note: 'The devil having already put into the heart of Judas to betray him' echoes the Satan who 'stood up against Israel and incited David.' The pattern of the adversary inciting a human agent to a destructive deed coheres with the fuller 'Satan entered into him' of 13:27. Availability and recurrence in Second-Temple Satan-tradition support the link.
sourceText: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to number Israel.

note: The accuser figure who provokes harm against the righteous undergirds the Johannine 'devil.' The connection is thematic rather than verbal and the Job satan is a heavenly prosecutor, so the echo is faint.
sourceText: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]

note: Abraham's 'let a little water be brought and wash your feet' establishes footwashing as the host's act of hospitality, here inverted so the Lord performs the servant's task. The image is the closest patriarchal antecedent and coheres with John's reversal of status. Recurrence of the motif across Genesis strengthens availability.
sourceText: Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.

note: Abigail's 'a servant to wash the feet of my lord's servants' marks footwashing as the lowliest slave duty. Jesus assuming exactly this office dramatizes 13:16 (the servant not greater than his lord). The status-coherence is strong.
sourceText: She arose, and bowed herself with her face to the earth, and said, “Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”

note: The priestly laver where Aaron and his sons wash hands and feet to be clean for service frames footwashing as cultic purification for ministry. Jesus' 'if I don't wash you, you have no part with me' reads the act as priestly consecration. Coherence with the cleansing language is high.
sourceText: Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet in it. When they go into the Tent of Meeting, they shall wash with water, that they not die; or when they come near to the altar to minister, to burn an offering made by fire to Yahweh. So they shall wash their hands and their feet, that they not die: and it shall be a statute forever to them, even to him and to his descendants throughout their generations.”

note: The water of purification that cleanses defilement supplies the conceptual background for 'completely clean.' The transfer from ritual to christological cleansing fits John's pattern of fulfilling purification rites. The link is conceptual, not verbal.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, “This is the statute of the law which Yahweh has commanded. Tell the children of Israel to bring you a red heifer without spot, in which is no defect, and which was never yoked. You shall give her to Eleazar the priest, and he shall bring her outside of the camp, and one shall kill her before his face. Eleazar the priest shall take some of her blood with his finger, and sprinkle her blood toward the front of the […]

note: 'Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow' supplies the imagery of moral cleansing behind 'you are clean.' The penitential washing register coheres with Jesus distinguishing the bathed-and-clean from the betrayer. Wording overlaps in the wash/clean pairing.
sourceText: Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.

note: 'I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean' is the eschatological cleansing promise most verbally aligned with 'you are clean.' Its new-covenant context coheres with the new commandment of 13:34. Volume of the clean-water motif raises confidence.
sourceText: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.

note: The fountain opened 'for sin and for impurity' supplies an eschatological cleansing backdrop. The connection is thematic and the wording does not closely match. Marked faint.
sourceText: “In that day there will be a spring opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness.

note: The 'beautiful feet' of the herald is sometimes invoked behind footwashing, but the link is associative only and the volume is negligible. Listed for completeness and marked contested.
sourceText: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

note: 'A servant is not greater than his lord' restates the lord/servant hierarchy that Abigail's footwashing self-description presumes, now made the basis for mutual service. The status logic coheres tightly with the preceding act. Recurrence of the master/servant ordering across the OT supports availability.
sourceText: She arose, and bowed herself with her face to the earth, and said, “Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”

note: 'One who is sent is not greater than he who sent him' reflects the shaliach principle dramatized by Abraham's commissioned servant who acts with his master's authority. The agency concept is Second-Temple and pervasive, so the echo is conceptual and faint.
sourceText: Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had, “Please put your hand under my thigh.

note: 'Blessed are you if you do them' adopts the OT beatitude form that ties blessing to doing the will/law. The macarism cadence is biblical but generic, so the link is to a form rather than a text.
sourceText: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;

note: Explicitly introduced 'that the Scripture may be fulfilled,' Jesus cites 'He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.' This is a formal quotation, John's clearest OT citation in the chapter, applying the lament of the betrayed righteous sufferer to Judas. Volume, recurrence in the Passion tradition, and coherence are all maximal.
sourceText: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

note: 'That when it happens, you may believe that I am he' (ego eimi) draws on the divine self-naming 'I AM.' The absolute ego eimi pervades John's Christology and here is tied to prediction-and-fulfillment as proof of identity. Coherence with the Johannine I-AM sayings is very high.
sourceText: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

note: 'That you may know and believe me... that I am he' supplies the exact pattern of foretelling-so-you-may-believe-I-am-he that John reproduces in 13:19. The Deutero-Isaian 'I am he' (ani hu) is the immediate scriptural matrix for the Johannine ego eimi. Verbal and structural overlap are strong.
sourceText: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.

note: 'Declaring the end from the beginning... before it happens' grounds Jesus' 'I tell you before it happens' as the divine prerogative of predictive sovereignty. The link reinforces the I-am theme and coheres with Isaiah 43. Recurrence of this announce-beforehand motif in Isaiah raises confidence.
sourceText: Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is no one else; I am God, and there is none like me; declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things that are not yet done; saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure;

note: 'I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass... lest you say my idol did them' parallels Jesus telling them beforehand so they will believe. The fore-announcement-for-faith logic matches closely. A near-doublet of Isaiah 46, strengthening the cluster.
sourceText: therefore I have declared it to you from of old; before it came to pass I showed it to you; lest you should say, ‘My idol has done them, and my engraved image, and my molten image, has commanded them.’

note: The betrayal by 'my equal, my companion, my familiar friend' with whom 'we took sweet counsel together' reinforces the table-companion betrayal of Psalm 41 applied to Judas. It is a coherent secondary lament of intimate treachery. Offered as an alternate/reinforcing source.
sourceText: For it was not an enemy who insulted me, then I could have endured it. Neither was it he who hated me who raised himself up against me, then I would have hidden myself from him. But it was you, a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend. We took sweet fellowship together. We walked in God’s house with company.

note: The 'heel' of the lifted-heel quotation can evoke the protoevangelium's heel-bruising enmity, given Satan's role in the betrayal. The catchword link is suggestive but the underlying Hebrew terms differ and the connection is interpretive. Marked contested.
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor turned conspirator (and traditionally linked to Psalm 41/55), is a typological forerunner of the intimate betrayer. The echo is mediated through the psalm rather than direct. Faint, marked contested.
sourceText: Someone told David, saying, “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” David said, “Yahweh, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”

note: The dipped morsel handed to the betrayer at table enacts the just-quoted 'he who eats bread with me,' so the narrative dramatizes the scripture already cited. Coherence with 13:18 is exact. The shared-bread treachery is the controlling image.
sourceText: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

note: 'Satan entered into him' completes the inciting-adversary pattern begun in 13:2, recalling the Satan who moved a man to a ruinous act. The intensification from 'put into the heart' to 'entered' tracks Second-Temple demonological development. Coherence is strong.
sourceText: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to number Israel.

note: 'Dip your morsel in the wine' is the only OT scene of a dipped morsel offered at a meal, providing possible verbal coloring for the dipped piece of bread. The setting is benevolent, not treacherous, so the link is lexical and faint. Marked contested.
sourceText: At meal time Boaz said to her, “Come here, and eat of the bread, and dip your morsel in the vinegar.” She sat beside the reapers, and they reached her parched grain, and she ate, and was satisfied, and left some of it.

note: 'It was night' fits the OT topos of evildoers as those who rebel against the light and work in darkness. John's pervasive light/darkness dualism makes the closing clause symbolically charged. The echo is to a motif rather than a specific text.
sourceText: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths. The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief. The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face. In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light. For the morning is to all of them like thick […]

note: The disciples' guess that Judas should 'give something to the poor' reflects the Deuteronomic almsgiving duty toward the poor at the feast. The connection is to ordinary festal piety and only incidental to the narrative. Faint.
sourceText: For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.

note: 'Now the Son of Man has been glorified' draws on the one like a son of man who receives glory and dominion. John transposes the apocalyptic enthronement onto the hour of the cross, his signature reading of Daniel's glorification. Volume, recurrence, and coherence across John are maximal.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified' provides the servant-glorification pattern behind 'God has been glorified in him... God will glorify him.' The mutual glorifying of God and his agent coheres with John's Servant Christology. The verbal overlap on 'glorified in' is notable.
sourceText: and he said to me, “You are my servant; Israel, in whom I will be glorified.”

note: 'Love one another' restates 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself,' the OT love command Jesus calls 'new' by christological measure ('as I have loved you'). Availability and recurrence are high; the command is the explicit scriptural substrate of the new commandment. Coherence with the footwashing example is strong.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: Calling the love command 'new' evokes the new covenant with the law written on the heart, fitting the Passover/farewell setting. John presents internalized covenant love as the mark of the disciples. The conceptual coherence is strong though the wording is not quoted.
sourceText: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they broke, although I was a husband to them, says Yahweh. But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in […]

note: The Shema's 'love the LORD your God' stands behind the love command, here redirected to mutual love as the visible sign of belonging to Jesus. Pairing neighbor-love (Lev 19:18) with covenant love is a standard Second-Temple combination. Echo is conceptual.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: The promise of a new heart and spirit enabling obedience underlies the capacity to keep the 'new' commandment of love. The link is thematic to the new-covenant cluster and not verbally explicit. Faint, marked contested.
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: Peter's confident boast 'I will lay down my life for you,' answered by the prediction of a threefold denial, fits the wisdom pattern that pride precedes a fall. The connection is to a proverbial topos rather than a cited text. Faint and marked contested.
sourceText: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.

note: The chapter's frame of intimate failure (betrayal by Judas, denial by Peter) extends the trusted-companion turning-away motif of the cited psalm to the inner circle. The link is structural across the pericopes rather than to the wording here. Faint.
sourceText: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

note: Jesus' promise to receive disciples into the 'Father's house' where they will dwell forever figurally fulfills the psalmist's hope to 'dwell in the house of the LORD forever.' Coherence is strong: John repeatedly reads the temple/house of God Christologically (2:16-21), and the eternal abode (monai) recasts the psalm's permanent residence in God's house. Volume rests on the shared house-dwelling motif rather than a verbal quotation.
sourceText: Surely goodness and loving kindness shall follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in Yahweh’s house forever.

note: 'One thing I have asked... to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life' supplies the prototypical longing for permanent residence in God's house that 14:2-3 grants the disciples. Recurrence of the 'house of the LORD as abode' topos in the Psalter strengthens the case; the contestation is that John gives no verbal cue, only the dwelling theme.
sourceText: One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after, that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.

note: 'How lovely is your dwelling place... blessed are those who dwell in your house' frames the temple as the place of beatitude, the same register behind the 'many rooms' in the Father's house. Low confidence: thematically apt but adds no distinctive lexeme beyond the shared house/dwelling idea, and competes with the other Psalter echoes.
sourceText: How lovely are your dwellings, Yahweh of Armies! My soul longs, and even faints for the courts of Yahweh. My heart and my flesh cry out for the living God. Yes, the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may have her young, near your altars, Yahweh of Armies, my King, and my God. Blessed are those who dwell in your house. They are always praising you. Selah.

note: 'Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them' establishes the tabernacle as God's dwelling, the OT substrate John reworks when Jesus prepares an eternal dwelling-place and elsewhere reads his own body as the temple. Figural rather than verbal; the connection runs through John's larger temple Christology more than through 14:2 itself.
sourceText: Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them. According to all that I show you, the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all of its furniture, even so you shall make it.

note: The ark going ahead 'to seek out a resting place' for Israel offers a faint Exodus-journey backdrop to Jesus going ahead to 'prepare a place' for his followers. Volume is weak and the lexical overlap thin; flagged low and contested as a possible wilderness-itinerary resonance rather than a deliberate citation.
sourceText: They set forward from the Mount of Yahweh three days’ journey. The ark of the covenant of Yahweh went before them three days’ journey, to seek out a resting place for them. The cloud of Yahweh was over them by day, when they set forward from the camp.

note: 'Make me to know your ways, O LORD... lead me in your truth' fuses 'way' and 'truth' in a prayer for divine guidance, the very pairing Jesus claims to embody as 'the way and the truth.' Coherence is high with the Psalter's 'way of the LORD' theology; John transfers the divine path/truth that leads to God onto Jesus himself, who is now the access to the Father.
sourceText: Show me your ways, Yahweh. Teach me your paths. Guide me in your truth, and teach me, For you are the God of my salvation, I wait for you all day long.

note: 'Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth' again binds 'way' and 'truth' as the route to communion with God, paralleling 14:6's claim that the way and truth lead to the Father. Recurrence of this way/truth collocation across the Psalter raises Volume; the contestation is that John offers no formula-citation, only the absorbed idiom.
sourceText: Teach me your way, Yahweh. I will walk in your truth. Make my heart undivided to fear your name.

note: The 'Holy Way' on which the redeemed travel to Zion provides a prophetic 'way' that leads God's people home, figurally fulfilled when Jesus is the exclusive 'way' to the Father's house. Coherence with John's homecoming theme (14:2-3) is strong; the singular eschatological highway resonates with Jesus as the one road of return.
sourceText: A highway will be there, a road, and it will be called The Holy Way. The unclean shall not pass over it, but it will be for those who walk in the Way. Wicked fools will not go there.

note: Moses sets before Israel 'life' and 'the way' of obeying the LORD, the choice that is itself 'your life' and the means to dwell in the land. Jesus' self-identification as 'the way... and the life' recasts this Deuteronomic life-through-the-way into a person; Coherence is reinforced by 14:15's love-and-keep-commandments idiom drawn from the same book.
sourceText: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]

note: The LORD proclaims himself 'abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (emet/aletheia),' the covenant 'truth' that John's prologue already applied to the incarnate Word (1:14, 'full of grace and truth'). Jesus' claim to be 'the truth' thus draws on the Sinai self-revelation of God's faithfulness; medium confidence given the strong Johannine recurrence of 'truth' language.

note: Wisdom declares 'whoever finds me finds life' and blesses those who keep her 'ways,' supplying a way/life nexus mediated by a personified divine figure. Jesus as 'the way... and the life' through whom one reaches the Father parallels the Wisdom-mediator pattern; low confidence because the verbal links are diffuse and the Wisdom backdrop is more securely felt in John 1.
sourceText: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways. Hear instruction, and be wise. Don’t refuse it. Blessed is the man who hears me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at my door posts. For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh.

note: 'I have chosen the way of faithfulness (truth)' once more couples 'way' and 'truth' as the path of covenant fidelity. It adds Recurrence to the way/truth motif behind 14:6 but is too generic on its own; flagged low and contested as cumulative support rather than a discrete source.
sourceText: I have chosen the way of truth. I have set your ordinances before me.

note: Philip's 'show us the Father' directly replays Moses' 'show me your glory,' to which God replies that no one can see his face and live. John inverts the denial: the one who has seen Jesus has seen the Father, fulfilling the Sinai longing to behold God. High Volume and Coherence given the explicit 'show us'/'show me' request and John's programmatic 'no one has ever seen God; the only Son has made him known' (1:18).
sourceText: He said, “Please show me your glory.” He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.” He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.” Yahweh also said, “Behold, there is a place by me, and you shall stand on the rock. It will happen, while my glory passes by, that I will put you in a cleft of […]

note: The LORD spoke to Moses 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend,' yet 33:20 forbids seeing God's face directly; this tension is exactly what 14:9 resolves by locating the Father's visible presence in Jesus. Coherence with the surrounding Exodus 33 theophany strengthens the medium rating beyond the headline 33:18-23 allusion.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. He turned again into the camp, but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, didn’t depart from the Tent.

note: At Horeb Israel 'heard the sound of words but saw no form,' codifying that God is heard, not seen. Jesus' claim that his words are the Father's and that seeing him is seeing the Father answers this aniconic tradition. Low confidence: thematic counterpoint rather than verbal echo, supporting the 'unseen God' frame behind the pericope.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to you out of the midst of the fire: you heard the voice of words, but you saw no form; you only heard a voice.

note: God promises a prophet 'in whose mouth I will put my words... he shall speak all that I command him,' the pattern Jesus claims in 14:10: 'the words I speak are not from myself; the Father does his works.' The prophet-like-Moses speech-formula gives modest Coherence with John's sent-one Christology; low because John does not cite the prophet text here.
sourceText: I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him.

note: Moses uniquely beholds 'the form of the LORD' and speaks with him 'mouth to mouth,' a near-vision that 14:9 surpasses by granting the disciples the Father in the Son. Faint, contested support for the seeing-God motif; the lexical overlap is limited to the shared theophanic register.
sourceText: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”

note: Israel had 'seen all the great work of the LORD that he did,' framing God's redemptive deeds as 'works' the people witness; Jesus speaks of 'the works that I do' continuing in his followers. Low confidence: 'works of the LORD' is a broad Deuteronomic idiom rather than a targeted source, offering only thematic coloring to 14:12.
sourceText: but your eyes have seen all of Yahweh’s great work which he did.

note: Israel served the LORD all the days that the elders 'had known all the work of the LORD that he did for Israel,' another instance of redemptive deeds as 'works.' It reinforces the OT 'works of God' register behind Jesus' 'greater works,' but is too generic to credit as a specific allusion; flagged low and contested.
sourceText: Israel served Yahweh all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, and had known all the work of Yahweh, that he had worked for Israel.

note: 'You have indeed done all our works for us,' confessing that human works are wrought by God, resonates faintly with 14:12's promise that believers will do the works Jesus does because he goes to the Father. Low and contested: a thematic affinity about divinely-empowered works rather than a deliberate citation.
sourceText: Yahweh, you will ordain peace for us, for you have also worked all our works for us.

note: 'The LORD is near to all who call on him... he fulfills the desire of those who fear him' undergirds the answered-petition promise of 14:13-14 ('whatever you ask in my name'). The granting-of-requests motif is widespread in the Psalter; low confidence because no single verse is verbally anchored, though it situates Jesus in the role of the request-granting LORD.
sourceText: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him. He also will hear their cry, and will save them.

note: The Shema's command to 'love the LORD your God' grounds the love-of-God demanded in 14:15, now reoriented to Jesus: 'if you love me, keep my commandments.' Coherence is strong because John fuses love and obedience in the Deuteronomic manner; medium rather than high since the wording is paraphrased and reattributed to Jesus.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: God keeps covenant 'with those who love him and keep his commandments,' the precise love+keep-commandments pairing echoed in 14:15 and 14:21. Recurrence of this formula across Deuteronomy raises Volume; the contestation is that John supplies the idiom without a citation marker.
sourceText: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,

note: The Decalogue promises steadfast love 'to those who love me and keep my commandments,' the foundational love-and-obey formula behind 14:15. Strong Coherence with John's repeated linkage of loving Jesus and keeping his word; medium because it is one of several overlapping Pentateuchal sources for the same idiom.
sourceText: and showing loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.

note: 'I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes' supplies the new-covenant gift of an indwelling Spirit that produces obedience, exactly the logic of 14:15-17 where loving-and-obeying flows into the Paraclete who 'will be in you.' High Coherence: the Spirit given to dwell within and to enable commandment-keeping is Ezekiel's signature promise.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: 'The Spirit of the LORD shall rest on him, the Spirit of wisdom... and of knowledge' anchors the messianic 'Spirit of truth' the Father gives in 14:17. Coherence is good because Isaiah's endowing Spirit is a Spirit of knowledge/truth resting permanently; medium given the conceptual rather than verbal link to 'Spirit of truth.'
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: Israel 'grieved his Holy Spirit,' yet God 'put in the midst of them his Holy Spirit,' one of the rare OT uses of 'his Holy Spirit' that the Paraclete passages presuppose. The motif of God placing his Spirit among the people undergirds 14:16-17's abiding Counselor; medium for the shared 'Holy Spirit' terminology with the wider Isaianic-Spirit complex.
sourceText: But they rebelled, and grieved his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them. Then he remembered the days of old, Moses and his people, saying, Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? where is he who put his holy Spirit in their midst?

note: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' is the eschatological Spirit-bestowal that 14:16-17 promises in personalized form as the indwelling Paraclete. Coherence is solid within John's realized-eschatology of the Spirit's coming; medium because John individualizes the corporate outpouring and offers no verbal quotation.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.

note: 'My Spirit remains in your midst; do not fear' couples the abiding Spirit with the dismissal of fear, paralleling the Paraclete who abides 'forever' alongside 14:27's 'let not your heart be afraid.' Low confidence: a suggestive thematic pairing of abiding-Spirit and courage rather than a demonstrable citation.
sourceText: This is the word that I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit lived among you. ‘Don’t be afraid.’

note: The LORD takes the Spirit on Moses and places it on the seventy, with Moses wishing all the LORD's people were prophets endowed with the Spirit. This distribution of the Spirit to the community prefigures the Paraclete given to all the disciples; low and contested because the link is conceptual, lacking the 'Spirit of truth' vocabulary.

note: 'A holy and disciplined spirit will flee from deceit' and (1:7) 'the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world' offer a Second-Temple 'spirit of truth/wisdom that the deceitful world cannot hold,' resonant with 14:17's Spirit 'whom the world cannot receive.' Low confidence: deuterocanonical mood-music supporting the truth-vs-world contrast rather than a direct source.
sourceText: For a holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit. And will start away from thoughts that are without understanding, And will be put to confusion when unrighteousness has come in.

note: 'You shall no more be termed Forsaken (Azubah)... for the LORD delights in you' counters abandonment with renewed presence, faintly behind 'I will not leave you orphans (orphanous); I will come to you.' Low confidence: the not-forsaking promise is thematically apt but lacks the orphan lexeme; flagged contested as ambient consolation language.
sourceText: You shall no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall your land any more be termed Desolate: but you shall be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for Yahweh delights in you, and your land shall be married.

note: 'He will not leave you or forsake you' is the classic divine-presence assurance, recast in 14:18 as Jesus' pledge not to abandon his own. The not-forsake formula gives modest Coherence with the consolation here; low because John uses the distinctive 'orphans' image rather than the Deuteronomic wording.
sourceText: Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or scared of them; for Yahweh your God himself is who goes with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.”

note: 'I will not leave you or forsake you,' God's commissioning promise to Joshua, contributes to the OT not-forsake topos standing behind 'I will not leave you orphans.' Recurrence of this formula (Deut/Josh) raises its cumulative Volume slightly, but the link to 14:18 remains thematic; low and contested.
sourceText: No man will be able to stand before you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not fail you nor forsake you.

note: God as 'father of the fatherless (orphans)' supplies the one strong OT orphan-care motif behind Jesus' refusal to leave the disciples 'orphans.' Figural and contested: the shared orphan vocabulary is suggestive, but John applies it to bereaved disciples rather than to literal orphans, so the connection is allusive at best.
sourceText: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.

note: 'After two days he will revive us... that we may live before him,' a revival-after-a-little-while hope, lightly resonates with 14:19, 'because I live, you also will live,' and 'yet a little while.' Low confidence: the life-after-interval pattern is genuinely parallel but verbally diffuse, and the resurrection-on-the-third-day reading is contested.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him. Let us acknowledge Yahweh. Let us press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.”

note: 'I will make my dwelling among you... and I will walk among you and be your God' is the covenant indwelling formula that 14:23 personalizes: 'we will come to him and make our home (monen) with him.' High Coherence because John reuses the same divine-dwelling-with-the-people promise, now realized as Father and Son abiding with the believer.
sourceText: I will set my tent among you, and my soul won’t abhor you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.

note: 'My dwelling place shall be with them, and I will be their God,' the new-covenant restatement of God dwelling among his people, reinforces the indwelling promise of 14:23. Recurrence of the 'dwelling with them' formula (Lev/Ezek) strengthens Volume; medium because John gives the topos individual rather than national scope.
sourceText: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

note: 'I will dwell in your midst... and many nations shall join themselves to the LORD... and shall be my people,' an eschatological in-dwelling promise resonant with the Father and Son making their home with the one who loves Jesus. Low confidence: it adds Recurrence to the divine-indwelling motif but contributes no distinctive wording to 14:23.
sourceText: Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion; for, behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst,’ says Yahweh. Many nations shall join themselves to Yahweh in that day, and shall be my people; and I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that Yahweh of Armies has sent me to you.

note: 'These words that I command you... shall be on your heart,' the Shema's call to internalize God's word, undergirds 14:23-24's 'keep my word'/'the word you hear is the Father's.' Low and contested: the keep-the-word idiom is broadly Deuteronomic and not anchored to a single verse here.
sourceText: These words, which I command you this day, shall be on your heart;

note: The Aaronic blessing climaxes 'the LORD... give you peace (shalom),' the priestly bestowal of divine peace that Jesus reissues as 'Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.' High Coherence: Jesus speaks the priestly gift-of-peace formula directly, distinguishing his giving from the world's, just as the blessing conveys God's own peace.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: 'You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you,' linking peace with an untroubled, trusting heart, parallels 14:27's 'my peace I give... let not your heart be troubled.' Coherence is strong between the peace-and-undisturbed-heart pairing; medium because the connection is thematic rather than a verbal citation.
sourceText: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.

note: 'Peace, peace, to the far and to the near, says the LORD; and I will heal him' is God's gift of peace to his people, the prophetic backdrop to Jesus bestowing his own peace. Medium for the shared divine-gift-of-peace motif; John heightens it by contrasting Jesus' peace with the world's hollow giving.
sourceText: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”

note: 'In this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of hosts,' tying peace to the eschatological house/temple, resonates with the farewell peace given amid the 'Father's house' discourse. Low confidence: a thematic temple-peace link rather than a verbal one, supplementing the stronger Aaronic and Isaianic echoes.
sourceText: ‘The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former,’ says Yahweh of Armies; ‘and in this place will I give peace,’ says Yahweh of Armies.”

note: The resting 'Spirit of wisdom and understanding' that teaches and counsels stands behind the Paraclete who 'will teach you all things' (14:26). Low and contested here because the teaching-Spirit link is better located at 14:17; included for the instructive-Spirit motif that the reminder-and-teaching function of the Counselor presupposes.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: 'You gave your good Spirit to instruct them,' a rare OT statement of the Spirit as teacher of God's people, parallels the Paraclete who 'will teach you all things.' Low confidence: genuine conceptual match for the teaching-Spirit, but verbally remote and not signaled as a source by John.
sourceText: You gave also your good Spirit to instruct them, and didn’t withhold your manna from their mouth, and gave them water for their thirst.

note: 'You shall love the LORD your God' lies behind 14:28's 'if you loved me' and 14:31's 'that the world may know that I love the Father,' transposing the Shema's love onto the Father-Son relation. Low and contested: it reiterates the Deuteronomic love idiom already credited at 14:15, here governing Jesus' own filial love.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: 'The commandment... that the LORD commanded me to teach you' models the obedient mediator who does only as God commanded, the pattern Jesus claims in 14:31, 'as the Father commanded me, so I do.' Low confidence: the as-commanded obedience motif is generically Deuteronomic, supplying coloring rather than a specific source.
sourceText: Now this is the commandment, the statutes, and the ordinances, which Yahweh your God commanded to teach you, that you might do them in the land where you go over to possess it;

note: Moses commissions Joshua 'as the LORD directed... so he did,' the do-as-commanded formula echoed in Jesus' 'as the Father commanded me, even so I do.' Low and contested: a faint obedient-agent parallel without verbal anchoring; one of several Pentateuchal 'as commanded, so he did' instances.
sourceText: He laid his hands on him, and commissioned him, as Yahweh spoke by Moses.

Low confidence: it grounds the accusing-adversary figure conceptually, but John's title and the 'no claim on me' idea outrun anything verbal in Job.

note: Wisdom says 'I spread out my branches like a terebinth... like a vine I caused loveliness to bud, and my blossoms became glorious and abundant fruit.' Personified Wisdom as a fruitful vine offers a Second-Temple analogue to the 'I am the vine' self-predication, supporting the figural reading.
sourceText: As the vine I put forth grace; And my flowers are the fruit of glory and riches.

note: 'You did not choose me, but I chose you' (15:16) echoes Israel's election: the Lord chose them not for their merit but in love. Strong coherence on divine election and love; covenantal keeping of commandments (15:10) belongs to the same Deuteronomic frame.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth. Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, […]

note: 'Abraham my friend' (lit. the one who loved me) — the title 'friend of God' Jesus confers, 'I have called you friends' (15:14-15). The friendship/election language ('Israel... whom I have chosen, offspring of Abraham my friend') gives high availability and coherence to the friend motif.
sourceText: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend,

note: 'Abraham your friend' — second OT witness to the Abraham-as-friend-of-God title that 'you are my friends' (15:14) actualizes for the disciples. Recurrence with Isa 41:8 strengthens the friend-of-God tradition behind the saying.
sourceText: Didn’t you, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it to the seed of Abraham your friend forever?

note: The Lord spoke to Moses 'as a man speaks to his friend' — the paradigm of intimate friendship with God in which the friend is told the divine purposes, matching 15:15: not servants but friends, 'for everything I heard from my Father I have made known to you.'
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. He turned again into the camp, but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, didn’t depart from the Tent.

note: 'Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?' — the friend of God is not kept ignorant of the master's plans, precisely the logic of 15:15 ('the servant doesn't know what his lord does... I have made known to you'). Coherence with the friend-vs-servant distinction.
sourceText: Yahweh said, “Will I hide from Abraham what I do, since Abraham has surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth will be blessed in him? For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of Yahweh, to do righteousness and justice; to the end that Yahweh may bring on Abraham that which he has spoken of him.”

note: 'Love your neighbor as yourself' underlies the new commandment to 'love one another' (15:12,17). Availability and thematic coherence are strong, though Jesus reframes the measure as 'as I have loved you.'
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: Jonathan's covenant love for David, loving him 'as his own soul' and risking his life, is the paradigmatic OT instance of self-giving friendship behind 'greater love has no one than to lay down his life for his friends' (15:13). Faint but coherent.
sourceText: When he had made an end of speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father’s house. Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.

note: The vineyard the Beloved tends out of love continues from 15:1-8 into the love/fruit language here (15:9-16); election to 'go and bear fruit that should remain' recalls God's purpose for his loved vineyard. Secondary recurrence of the chapter's controlling image.
sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]

note: 'Let not those who hate me without cause wink the eye.' One of the two psalms behind the explicit citation 'They hated me without a cause' (15:25), introduced as 'written in their law.' Verbal correspondence to the hate-without-cause phrase is exact; a Davidic-righteous-sufferer text.
sourceText: Don’t let those who are my enemies wrongfully rejoice over me; neither let those who hate me without a cause wink their eyes.

note: 'More than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause.' The other source of 15:25's formula; Ps 69 is heavily used of Jesus' passion elsewhere, raising its likelihood here. Exact verbal match to 'hated me without a cause.'
sourceText: Those who hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of my head. Those who want to cut me off, being my enemies wrongfully, are mighty. I have to restore what I didn’t take away.

note: 'They... attack me without cause' — a further Davidic lament of causeless hatred in the same psalmic stream that supplies 15:25. A contributory background witness rather than the cited text.
sourceText: They have also surrounded me with words of hatred, and fought against me without a cause.

note: 'Those who hate me wrongfully are mighty' — another lament-of-the-righteous text echoing causeless hatred of the innocent sufferer, coherent with the world's hatred theme (15:18-25) and the citation in 15:25.
sourceText: But my enemies are vigorous and many. Those who hate me without reason are numerous.

note: 'Have you found me, O my enemy?' / hating the prophet who confronts sin parallels 15:22-24: the world hates Jesus because his coming and works expose its sin, leaving it 'no excuse.' A faint resonance with the prophetic pattern of being hated for exposing guilt.
sourceText: Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” He answered, “I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do that which is evil in the sight of Yahweh.

note: 'Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake' anticipates being persecuted 'for my name's sake' (15:21). The phrase about suffering on account of God's name gives coherence to the disciples' share in the world's hatred.
sourceText: Hear Yahweh’s word, you who tremble at his word: “Your brothers who hate you, who cast you out for my name’s sake, have said, ‘Let Yahweh be glorified, that we may see your joy;’ but it is those who shall be disappointed.

note: 'The Spirit of the Lord shall rest on him, the Spirit of wisdom... and knowledge' grounds the title 'the Spirit of truth' (15:26) in the prophetic Spirit who imparts true knowledge of God. Coherence with the Spirit's testifying/witness role; medium volume.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: 'Not by might... but by my Spirit, says the Lord' — divine action accomplished by the Spirit rather than human power, a backdrop to the Paraclete's empowering witness (15:26-27). A faint thematic echo rather than verbal.
sourceText: Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is Yahweh’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.

note: The promised outpouring of the Spirit on God's people stands behind Jesus' promise to 'send' the Spirit who, with the disciples, testifies (15:26-27). Availability of the eschatological Spirit-gift tradition; low verbal contact.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.

note: The Spirit placed on the elders so they prophesy, and Moses' wish that all the Lord's people might have the Spirit, anticipates the Spirit given so the disciples 'also testify' (15:27). Faint coherence with Spirit-enabled witness.
sourceText: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more. But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on them; and they were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran, and told […]

note: 'Whoever kills you will think that he offers service to God' figurally invokes the Phinehas-zeal pattern, where killing in defense of God's honor is reckoned righteous and brings a covenant of priesthood. John frames synagogue persecution as misdirected cultic zeal; coherence with the prophet-killing motif is high, and Phinehas was the paradigmatic Second-Temple model of lethal zeal (1 Macc 2:26, 54).
sourceText: Behold, one of the children of Israel came and brought to his brothers a Midianite woman in the sight of Moses, and in the sight of all the congregation of the children of Israel, while they were weeping at the door of the Tent of Meeting. When Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose up from the midst of the congregation, and took a spear in his hand. He went after the man of Israel into the pavilion, and thrust both of […]

note: Persecution 'for your sake' / zeal for God's house consuming the persecutor sits behind the idea that opponents act in supposed devotion. John 2:17 already cited this psalm, so recurrence within the Gospel supports a faint echo of the zeal-as-cover motif, but volume here is thin.
sourceText: Because for your sake, I have borne reproach. Shame has covered my face. I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s children. For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.

note: Isaiah 66:5 speaks of brethren who hate and cast out the faithful 'for my name's sake,' claiming it is God who is glorified — strikingly close to expulsion from the synagogue done as service to God. Volume and coherence are strong; the verb of casting out the faithful from the cultic community matches John's aposynagogos.
sourceText: Hear Yahweh’s word, you who tremble at his word: “Your brothers who hate you, who cast you out for my name’s sake, have said, ‘Let Yahweh be glorified, that we may see your joy;’ but it is those who shall be disappointed.

note: The killing of Zechariah the prophet in the temple court typifies prophets slain by the very people of God under pretense of fidelity. As a representative of the persecuted-prophets tradition it coheres with Jesus' warning that disciples will be killed by those who think they serve God.
sourceText: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house. Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his […]

note: The Paraclete as 'Spirit of truth' who convicts the world recalls the Spirit of the LORD resting on the shoot of Jesse — wisdom, counsel, and judging with righteousness, reproving the earth. The convicting/judicial function of the Spirit (krinei, elenxei) coheres tightly with Isaiah's Spirit-endowed righteous judge.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh. His delight will be in the fear of Yahweh. He will not judge by the sight of his eyes, neither decide by the hearing of his ears; but with righteousness he will judge the poor, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the […]

note: The Spirit convicting 'the world about sin, righteousness, and judgment' enacts the divine lawsuit (rib) of Deutero-Isaiah, where God prosecutes the nations and their idols, exposing their case as nothing. John's forensic vocabulary (elenchein, krisis, dikaiosyne) coheres with the Isaianic courtroom, supplying the conceptual matrix for the Paraclete's prosecutorial role.
sourceText: Produce your cause,” says Yahweh. “Bring out your strong reasons,” says the King of Jacob. “Let them announce, and declare to us what shall happen. Declare the former things, what they are, that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or show us things to come. Declare the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods. Yes, do good, or do evil, that we may be dismayed, and see it together. Behold, you are of nothing, […]

note: 'The prince of this world has been judged' figurally evokes the protoevangelium's sentence on the serpent, read in Second-Temple tradition as the crushing of the adversary. The judgment of the ruler coheres with John's wider serpent/devil typology (8:44), though the verbal link is faint.
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: Isaiah foretells the LORD punishing 'the host of the high ones' and the kings of the earth, shut up and visited after many days — a judgment of cosmic rulers that prefigures the 'prince of this world' being judged. The motif of a heavenly ruler subjected to verdict coheres with John 16:11.
sourceText: It shall happen in that day that Yahweh will punish the army of the high ones on high, and the kings of the earth on the earth. They shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison; and after many days shall they be visited.

note: The satan/accuser rebuked and condemned in the heavenly court anticipates the ruler of this world being judged. The forensic setting where the accuser is himself overruled coheres with the Paraclete (Advocate) replacing the prosecuting adversary.
sourceText: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”

note: The 'Spirit of truth' who guides into all truth draws on the Spirit of wisdom and understanding; the leading/guiding function recalls the Spirit as teacher. Recurrence of the Spirit-of-truth title in John strengthens the Isaianic resonance.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: 'Guide me in your truth and teach me' supplies the precise idiom of being led/guided into truth (hodegein + aletheia in LXX), matching 'he will guide you into all truth.' Volume is notable because the verb and noun co-occur as in John 16:13.
sourceText: Guide me in your truth, and teach me, For you are the God of my salvation, I wait for you all day long.

note: 'Your good Spirit will lead me' pairs the divine Spirit with guidance into right paths, coherent with the Paraclete leading disciples. The conjunction of Spirit and leading reinforces the guidance motif though the wording is more distant than Psalm 25.
sourceText: Teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Your Spirit is good. Lead me in the land of uprightness.

note: 'The Lord GOD will do nothing but he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets' undergirds 'he will declare to you things that are coming' — the Spirit functioning as the prophetic revealer of God's hidden future. Coherence with the disclosure-of-the-future clause is good though the allusion is diffuse.
sourceText: Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.

note: 'There is a God in heaven who reveals secrets and has made known what shall come to pass' parallels the Spirit declaring 'things that are coming.' The apocalyptic disclosure of the future coheres with the Paraclete's revelatory role.
sourceText: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these: as for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter; and he who reveals secrets has made known to you what shall happen.

note: The woman in labor whose anguish turns to deliverance, set beside resurrection ('your dead shall live'), is the controlling figure behind sorrow-turned-to-joy and 'I will see you again.' Volume is high (extended birth-pang image), recurrence strong in the prophets, and coherence with John's death-to-resurrection movement is exact.
sourceText: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh. We have been with child. We have been in pain. We gave birth, it seems, only to wind. We have not worked any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen. Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of […]

note: Zion's painless birth issuing in joy, comfort, and rejoicing hearts ('your heart shall rejoice') is closely echoed by 'your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away.' The labor-to-joy reversal and the explicit heart-rejoicing give high volume and coherence.
sourceText: “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her pain came, she delivered a son. Who has heard such a thing? who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? shall a nation be born at once? for as soon as Zion travailed, she gave birth to her children. Shall I bring to the birth, and not cause to be delivered?” says Yahweh: “shall I who cause to give birth shut the womb?” says your God. “Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who […]

note: Zion in labor 'like a woman in travail' who must groan before being delivered prefigures the disciples' pangs preceding deliverance. The eschatological birth-pang motif coheres with Jesus' 'her time has come' / 'a human being is born into the world.'
sourceText: Now why do you cry out aloud? Is there no king in you? Has your counselor perished, that pains have taken hold of you as of a woman in travail? Be in pain, and labor to give birth, daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail; for now you will go out of the city, and will dwell in the field, and will come even to Babylon. There you will be rescued. There Yahweh will redeem you from the hand of your enemies.

note: The day of distress likened to a man in the pangs of a woman in labor — Jacob's trouble out of which he is saved — supplies the tribulation-then-salvation structure of 16:20-22. Coherence with the messianic 'birth-pangs' tradition is strong.
sourceText: Ask now, and see whether a man does travail with child: why do I see every man with his hands on his waist, as a woman in travail, and all faces are turned into paleness? Alas! for that day is great, so that none is like it: it is even the time of Jacob’s trouble; but he shall be saved out of it.

note: 'Hide yourselves for a little while (mikron) until the indignation passes' is the closest LXX source for the repeated 'a little while' bracketing distress before vindication. The mikron-then-deliverance pattern coheres tightly with 16:16-19.
sourceText: Come, my people, enter into your rooms, and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourself for a little moment, until the indignation is past.

note: 'Yet once, it is a little while (mikron), and I will shake the heavens' offers an eschatological 'little while' before God's decisive intervention. It supports the 'little while' time-marker, though the shaking-the-cosmos context is only loosely coherent.
sourceText: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;

note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him' undergirds the short-interval-then-seeing-again pattern of 'a little while... and you will see me.' The revival-after-brief-interval coheres with the resurrection sense, though John does not cite it.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him. Let us acknowledge Yahweh. Let us press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.”

note: 'Weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning' is a tight aphoristic match for 'you will weep and lament... but your sorrow will be turned into joy.' The night-weeping/morning-joy reversal coheres precisely with the sorrow-to-joy promise.
sourceText: For his anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.

note: 'I will turn their mourning into joy, and will comfort them, and make them rejoice from their sorrow' is verbally close to 'your sorrow will be turned into joy.' The turning-of-mourning-to-joy in the new-covenant restoration passage gives strong coherence.
sourceText: Then shall the virgin rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old together; for I will turn their mourning into joy, and will comfort them, and make them rejoice from their sorrow.

note: 'Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart' resonates with 'whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it.' The granting-of-petitions motif coheres, though the link is generic to OT prayer theology.
sourceText: Also delight yourself in Yahweh, and he will give you the desires of your heart.

note: 'Before they call, I will answer' frames the eschatological 'in that day' when asking yields immediate granting, coherent with 16:23-24's day of unhindered prayer. The new-creation setting matches John's 'in that day' marker.
sourceText: It shall happen that, before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.

note: God speaks to Moses 'mouth to mouth, clearly (plainly), and not in dark speeches' — the plain-speech vs. figures-of-speech contrast (16:25) echoes the riddle/plain-revelation distinction. Coherence with 'no more speak in figures but tell you plainly' is suggestive.
sourceText: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”

note: 'Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered' lies behind 'you will be scattered, everyone to his own place, and you will leave me alone.' The scattering-of-the-flock-at-the-shepherd's-smiting is a recognized passion testimony; coherence is strong even without formal citation.
sourceText: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.

note: 'I have overcome the world' enacts the divine-warrior/royal-Son motif of Psalm 2, where the nations rage but the enthroned Son subdues them. The cosmic conquest coheres with John's 'ruler of this world' being judged and the Son's victory over a hostile world.
sourceText: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying, “Let’s break their bonds apart, and cast their cords from us.” He who sits in the heavens will laugh. The Lord will have them in derision. Then he will speak to them in his anger, and terrify them in his wrath: “Yet I have set my King on my holy hill of Zion.” I will tell […]
