sourceText: I lifted up my eyes, and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, whose thighs were adorned with pure gold of Uphaz: his body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as flaming torches, and his arms and his feet like burnished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.

note: Cornelius falls at Peter's feet to worship and Peter raises him: 'Stand up! I myself am also a man' — the refusal-of-veneration scene echoes Raphael's correction of Tobit and Tobias, redirecting worship from the messenger to God. Here transposed to a human apostle. Thematic coherence high.
sourceText: And they were both troubled, and fell upon their faces; for they were afraid. And he said to them, “Don’t be afraid. You will all have peace; but bless God forever. For I came not of any favor of my own, but by the will of your God. Therefore bless him forever. All these days I appeared to you. I didn’t eat or drink, but you all saw a vision. Now give God thanks, because I ascend to him that sent me. Write in a book all the things which have been done.” […]

note: Peter's 'it is unlawful for a Jew to associate with one of another nation, but God has shown me not to call any man unholy or unclean' transfers the clean/unclean categories of the dietary law (and its boundary-keeping function) to persons; recurrence of the Levitical theme from 10:9-16 within the chapter.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]

note: Cornelius's 'I was fasting until this hour, and at the ninth hour I prayed' echoes Daniel's seeking God 'by prayer and supplications, with fasting' as the disposition that precedes angelic revelation. Faint.
sourceText: I set my face to the Lord God, to seek by prayer and petitions, with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.

note: 'God doesn't show favoritism' (ou prosopolemptes) directly restates the Deuteronomic confession that God 'regards not persons (does not lift the face) nor takes a bribe.' Distinctive theological formula; the basis for the whole Gentile-inclusion argument. High volume and coherence.
sourceText: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.

note: Jehoshaphat's charge that 'with the LORD our God there is no iniquity, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts' is a second locus of the 'no partiality' formula informing v34. Recurrence strengthens the allusion.
sourceText: Now therefore let the fear of Yahweh be on you. Take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with Yahweh our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes.”

note: 'Preaching good news of peace' (euangelizomenos eirenen) reproduces the herald who 'publishes peace, brings good tidings' on the mountains. The gospel-of-peace formula in v36 is drawn from this servant-song herald text. High volume.
sourceText: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

note: 'Peace, peace, to him that is far off, and to him that is near' undergirds the proclamation of peace now extended to the far-off Gentiles in Cornelius's house; coherent with the chapter's inclusion theme.
sourceText: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”

note: 'Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that brings good tidings, that publishes peace' is a parallel herald-of-peace text reinforcing the Isaianic background of v36.
sourceText: Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.

note: 'The word which he sent to the children of Israel' faintly echoes 'he sent his word and healed them,' apt given the immediate reference to Jesus 'healing all who were oppressed.' Low volume.
sourceText: He sends his word, and heals them, and delivers them from their graves.

note: 'God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good' reflects 'the Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me' to bring good news and release. The Spirit-anointing summary of Jesus' ministry draws on this servant text. High coherence.
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

note: 'My chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him' supports v38's portrait of the Spirit-endowed servant and v41's 'witnesses chosen before by God.' Thematic coherence high; verbal moderate.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.

note: 'Whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree' (kremasantes epi xylou) deliberately invokes the law that a man 'hanged on a tree' is accursed of God and must be taken down. The xylon language is the distinctive Deuteronomic marker. High volume.
sourceText: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree; his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God; that you don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.

note: 'God raised him up the third day' resonates with 'on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.' A recurrent NT third-day intertext; figural/typological with moderate verbal touch.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: Jesus 'appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead' echoes the title 'Judge of all the earth.' Thematic.
sourceText: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”

note: 'He comes to judge the earth... the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity' undergirds the designation of the risen one as eschatological Judge in v42.
sourceText: Let them sing before Yahweh, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.

note: 'Everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins' to which 'all the prophets testify' echoes the new-covenant promise 'I will forgive their iniquity, and remember their sin no more,' the prophetic witness to forgiveness Peter invokes. Coherent.
sourceText: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin will I remember no more.

note: 'The people that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity' is among the prophetic texts of forgiveness that 'all the prophets testify' to in v43. Faint, offered maximally.
sourceText: The inhabitant won’t say, “I am sick.” The people who dwell therein will be forgiven their iniquity.

note: 'The gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles' fulfills 'I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh' — the same Joel oracle already cited at Pentecost (recurrence within Acts), now extended to 'all flesh' inclusive of Gentiles. High coherence; the pouring-out language is distinctive.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.

note: 'I will pour my Spirit upon your seed' provides a parallel outpouring-of-the-Spirit promise reinforcing the Joel intertext behind v45. Moderate verbal overlap.
sourceText: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:

note: 'I have poured out my Spirit upon the house of Israel' is a further prophetic pour-out text in the background of the Spirit falling on the hearers. Faint.
sourceText: neither will I hide my face any more from them; for I have poured out my Spirit on the house of Israel, says the Lord Yahweh.

note: 'Until the Spirit be poured upon us from on high' contributes to the prophetic expectation of the Spirit's outpouring realized here on the Gentiles.
sourceText: Until the Spirit is poured on us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is considered a forest.

note: The Gentiles 'speaking in other languages and magnifying God' figurally reverses Babel's scattering of tongues, with diverse speech now uniting in praise. Typological, no verbal borrowing.
sourceText: The whole earth was of one language and of one speech. As they traveled east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there. They said one to another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar. They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make ourselves a name, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole […]

note: The vision's core conflict — a divine command to 'kill and eat' four-footed animals, creeping things, and birds, and Peter's refusal because 'nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered into my mouth' — directly engages the Levitical taxonomy of clean and unclean creatures. Volume is high (the whole pericope turns on these dietary categories); recurrence is strong (the sister account in Acts 10 and the parallel here); thematic coherence is high. The narrative reads the Levitical food law figurally, the abolition of the clean/unclean boundary dramatizing the inclusion of Gentiles.

note: Elymas struck with mist and darkness, groping for someone to lead him, closely parallels the men of Sodom struck with blindness so they could not find the door, a divine judgment-blinding. Strong narrative recurrence with 2 Kings 6 below.
sourceText: They struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness, both small and great, so that they wearied themselves to find the door.

note: Elisha prays and the Aramean army is struck blind by the prophet's word, the OT type for a man of God blinding an enemy of the Lord's purpose; the prophet-induced judicial blindness is the operative pattern behind Paul's act.
sourceText: When they came down to him, Elisha prayed to Yahweh, and said, “Please strike this people with blindness.” He struck them with blindness according to the word of Elisha.

note: The covenant curse of blindness, groping at noonday as the blind grope in darkness, supplies the language of Elymas groping for a guide. Thematic coherence with judgment-blinding; verbal echo of groping.
sourceText: Yahweh will strike you with madness, with blindness, and with astonishment of heart. You will grope at noonday, as the blind gropes in darkness, and you shall not prosper in your ways. You will only be oppressed and robbed always, and there will be no one to save you.

note: 'The hand of the Lord is upon you' echoes the recurring Exodus formula of the LORD's hand falling in judgment (e.g., upon Pharaoh's livestock and Egypt). A stock OT idiom for divine striking; volume low.
sourceText: behold, the hand of Yahweh is on your livestock which are in the field, on the horses, on the donkeys, on the camels, on the herds, and on the flocks with a very grievous pestilence.

note: 'The hand of the LORD was heavy' upon the Philistines is another instance of the judgment-hand idiom behind 'the hand of the Lord is on you.' Generic, included for breadth.
sourceText: But the hand of Yahweh was heavy on them of Ashdod, and he destroyed them, and struck them with tumors, even Ashdod and its borders.

note: The synagogue pattern of reading the Law and the Prophets followed by exhortation reflects the post-exilic public reading of the Law with exposition; Luke's scene presupposes this liturgical inheritance. Background rather than citation.
sourceText: All the people gathered themselves together as one man into the broad place that was before the water gate; and they spoke to Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which Yahweh had commanded to Israel. Ezra the priest brought the law before the assembly, both men and women, and all who could hear with understanding, on the first day of the seventh month. He read therein before the broad place that was before the water gate from early […]

note: Paul's opening summons, 'Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen,' echoes the Asaphite call to the people to give ear, the conventional opening of a historical recital (as the sermon then becomes). Faint formulaic resonance.
sourceText: Hear my teaching, my people. Turn your ears to the words of my mouth.

note: 'The God of this people Israel chose our fathers' restates Deuteronomy's foundational election theology, that the LORD set his love on and chose the patriarchs and their seed. Strong thematic coherence and clear conceptual borrowing opening the historical resume.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth. Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, […]

note: 'The LORD set his affection on your fathers to love them and chose their descendants' is a near-synonymous parallel to the election of the fathers; reinforces the choosing language. Recurrence strengthens the Deuteronomic source pool.
sourceText: Only Yahweh had a delight in your fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them, even you above all peoples, as at this day.

note: Deliverance from Egypt 'with a strong hand' undergirds Paul's 'with uplifted arm he led them out.' The Exodus deliverance formula is unmistakable here.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh, for by a strong hand he shall let them go, and by a strong hand he shall drive them out of his land.”

note: 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm' supplies the exact 'uplifted/high arm' (brachion hypselos) by which God led Israel out of Egypt. High-volume verbal borrowing of a fixed Exodus formula.
sourceText: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:

note: God's taking a nation out of Egypt 'by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and great terrors' is the canonical Deuteronomic exodus formula behind 'with uplifted arm he led them out.' Reinforces Exod 6:6.
sourceText: Or has God tried to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, by war, by a mighty hand, by an outstretched arm, and by great terrors, according to all that Yahweh your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?

note: 'He made the people great (exalted them) during their stay in Egypt' echoes the multiplication of Israel in Egypt, who grew exceedingly numerous. Conceptual; the LXX verb differs.
sourceText: The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them.

note: Israel sojourning in Egypt where 'the LORD made his people very fruitful, and made them stronger than their foes' closely matches 'exalted the people during their stay as aliens in Egypt.' This psalm is itself a historical recital paralleling Paul's, raising recurrence.
sourceText: Israel also came into Egypt. Jacob lived in the land of Ham. He increased his people greatly, and made them stronger than their adversaries.

note: 'The forty years in the wilderness' draws on the canonical forty-year wandering during which Israel ate manna. Stock chronological datum but verbally precise.
sourceText: The children of Israel ate the manna forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They ate the manna until they came to the borders of the land of Canaan.

note: The forty years in the wilderness as the span of God's bearing with a rebellious generation supplies both the number and the note of divine forbearance ('he put up with them'). Strong thematic coherence.
sourceText: Your children shall be wanderers in the wilderness forty years, and shall bear your prostitution, until your dead bodies are consumed in the wilderness. After the number of the days in which you spied out the land, even forty days, for every day a year, you will bear your iniquities, even forty years, and you will know my alienation.’

note: 'The LORD your God carried (bore) you as a father carries his son' lies behind the well-attested variant 'he bore/nursed them' for forty years; even in the 'put up with them' reading, Deut 1:31's wilderness-forbearance is the matrix. Textual-critical note: etropophoresen vs etrophophoresen.
sourceText: and in the wilderness, where you have seen how that Yahweh your God bore you, as a man does bear his son, in all the way that you went, until you came to this place.”

note: 'For forty years I loathed that generation' supplies the forty-years-plus-divine-toleration motif behind God 'putting up with them' in the wilderness. Recurrence with Numbers 14.
sourceText: Forty long years I was grieved with that generation, and said, “It is a people that errs in their heart. They have not known my ways.”

note: 'When he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan' directly quotes the Deuteronomic catalogue of the 'seven nations greater and mightier than you' the LORD casts out before Israel. Distinctive numeral 'seven nations' is verbatim.
sourceText: When Yahweh your God brings you into the land where you go to possess it, and casts out many nations before you, the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, seven nations greater and mightier than you;

note: Joshua's recital of the nations of Canaan delivered into Israel's hand and the land given as inheritance parallels Paul's compression; Josh 24 is itself a covenant historical resume, raising recurrence.
sourceText: “‘You went over the Jordan, and came to Jericho. The men of Jericho fought against you, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite; and I delivered them into your hand.

note: 'He gave them their land for an inheritance' restates the apportioning of Canaan as inheritance by lot. Thematic coherence high; standard conquest language.
sourceText: These are the inheritances which the children of Israel took in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest, Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers’ houses of the tribes of the children of Israel, distributed to them, by the lot of their inheritance, as Yahweh commanded by Moses, for the nine tribes, and for the half-tribe.

note: The land sworn to the fathers given for possession underlies 'he gave them their land for an inheritance.' Generic land-gift formula.
sourceText: Behold, I have set the land before you. Go in and possess the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give to them and to their seed after them.’”

note: 'He drove out nations before them and apportioned them for an inheritance' compresses conquest-plus-inheritance exactly as Paul does, within another historical psalm. Recurrence reinforces.
sourceText: He also drove out the nations before them, allotted them for an inheritance by line, and made the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents.

note: 'After that he gave them judges' directly summarizes the book of Judges' refrain that the LORD raised up judges to deliver Israel. Clear thematic and verbal correspondence.
sourceText: Yahweh raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.

note: 'until Samuel the prophet' fixes the transition point at Samuel, recognized from Dan to Beersheba as a prophet of the LORD, the last of the judges. Distinctive named figure.
sourceText: All Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of Yahweh.

note: 'Then they asked for a king' directly recalls Israel's demand to Samuel, 'appoint a king to judge us like all the nations.' Strong verbal and narrative correspondence.
sourceText: and they said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.”

note: 'Here is the king you have chosen, for whom you asked' reinforces the request-for-a-king motif. Recurrence within the same Samuel narrative.
sourceText: Now therefore see the king whom you have chosen, and whom you have asked for: and behold, Yahweh has set a king over you.

note: Saul son of Kish 'of the tribe of Benjamin' is drawn from the selection-by-lot narrative naming Saul of the tribe of Benjamin and the family of Kish. Distinctive named details.
sourceText: He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by their families; and the family of the Matrites was taken; and Saul the son of Kish was taken: but when they sought him, he could not be found.

note: The introduction of Kish the Benjamite and his son Saul, a choice young man, supplies the 'Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin.' Reinforces 10:21.
sourceText: Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Becorath, the son of Aphiah, the son of a Benjamite, a mighty man of valor. He had a son, whose name was Saul, an impressive young man; and there was not among the children of Israel a better person than he. From his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people.

note: 'When he had removed him' alludes to the LORD's rejection of Saul as king ('you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has rejected you from being king'). Thematic coherence high.
sourceText: For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim. Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.”

note: God's word to Samuel, 'I have rejected Saul... I have provided for myself a king,' bridges the removal of Saul and the raising up of David. Reinforces the removal-then-David sequence.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.”

note: 'He raised up David to be their king' draws on the anointing of David at Bethlehem, whom the LORD designates and Samuel anoints. Distinctive narrative behind the David accession.
sourceText: He sent, and brought him in. Now he was ruddy, and withal of a beautiful face, and goodly to look on. Yahweh said, “Arise, anoint him; for this is he.” Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brothers: and the Spirit of Yahweh came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up, and went to Ramah.

note: 'A man after my own heart, who will do all my will' quotes Samuel's verdict to Saul that the LORD has sought out 'a man after his own heart' to be ruler. The 'man after my heart' phrase is verbatim; this is the controlling source of the composite citation.
sourceText: But now your kingdom shall not continue. Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and Yahweh has appointed him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept that which Yahweh commanded you.”

note: 'I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him' supplies the opening clause 'I have found David,' fused with 1 Sam 13:14 into Paul's composite testimony. Verbal borrowing of 'I have found David.'
sourceText: I have found David, my servant. I have anointed him with my holy oil,

note: 'The LORD looks on the heart' undergirds the 'man after my heart' verdict, reinforcing the heart-language of David's election. Conceptual support for the composite quotation.
sourceText: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

note: 'who will do all my will/pleasure' resembles the LORD's word that Cyrus 'shall fulfill all my purpose'; some see the third clause of Paul's composite drawn from this anointed-agent idiom. Faint and contested.
sourceText: Who says of Cyrus, ‘He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure,’ even saying of Jerusalem, ‘She will be built;’ and of the temple, ‘Your foundation will be laid.’”

note: 'From this man's seed God has brought salvation to Israel according to his promise' rests on the Davidic covenant promise that God will raise up David's seed after him and establish his kingdom. The promise-to-David seed theology is the backbone of the verse.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom.

note: 'The LORD swore to David... one of the fruit of your body I will set on your throne' supplies the sworn promise of a descendant, reinforcing the seed-of-David savior. Recurrence with 2 Sam 7.
sourceText: Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it: “I will set the fruit of your body on your throne.

note: The shoot from the stump of Jesse, a messianic seed of David, contributes to the seed-of-David savior expectation. Conceptual messianic background.
sourceText: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.

note: John's preparatory preaching before the Coming One echoes the messenger sent ahead to prepare the way of the Lord. Faint; the forerunner motif is operative.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: John's preparatory role and self-effacement before the one who comes after resonate with the wilderness voice preparing the way of the LORD. Background to the Baptist tradition rather than a citation here.
sourceText: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.

note: Address to 'children of the stock of Abraham' echoes the covenant designation 'offspring of Abraham his servant,' situating the hearers within the elect line. Idiomatic.
sourceText: you seed of Abraham, his servant, you children of Jacob, his chosen ones.

note: 'Children of the stock of Abraham' rests on the covenant with Abraham and his seed; the word of salvation comes first to the covenant heirs. Generic covenant background.
sourceText: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.

note: That they 'found no cause for death' yet had him killed and 'laid in a tomb' resonates with the Servant who had done no violence yet was assigned a grave; the innocence-then-burial pattern is the Servant Song's. Thematic coherence medium-high.
sourceText: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

note: 'They took him down from the tree' draws on the law that a man hanged on a tree must be taken down the same day, a text Luke and Paul repeatedly attach to the crucifixion. Distinctive 'tree' (xylon) language and the taking-down detail.
sourceText: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree; his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God; that you don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.

note: The condemnation and execution of the innocent one with the connivance of rulers faintly recalls the lament psalm of the suffering righteous appropriated for the passion. Contested, low volume here.
sourceText: For dogs have surrounded me. A company of evildoers have enclosed me. They have pierced my hands and feet. I can count all of my bones. They look and stare at me. They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.

note: 'The promise made to the fathers' includes the Abrahamic blessing-to-the-nations promise now declared fulfilled. Background to the promise theology of the verse.
sourceText: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”

note: The 'promise made to the fathers' that God has fulfilled by raising Jesus centers on the Davidic covenant, especially 'I will be his father and he shall be my son,' which dovetails with the Ps 2 citation. Reinforces the father-son sonship theme.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;

note: 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you' is quoted verbatim as the second-psalm proof that God raised up Jesus. Explicit formula citation ('as it is written in the second psalm'); maximal volume.
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.

note: 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings/mercies of David' (ta hosia Dauid ta pista) is quoted to prove the resurrection-incorruption, linking the everlasting covenant mercies promised to David to the risen Christ. Explicit LXX citation.
sourceText: Turn your ear, and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live: and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David.

note: 'You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption/decay' is quoted ('in another psalm') as the climactic resurrection proof-text, then argued to apply to Jesus and not David. Verbatim LXX quotation; the linchpin of the resurrection argument.
sourceText: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.

note: 'David... fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw decay' draws on the notice that David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, grounding Paul's argument that David did see corruption. Distinctive 'slept with his fathers' idiom.
sourceText: David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David.

note: The sworn covenant with David ('I will establish your seed forever') reinforces the 'sure mercies of David' applied to the imperishable risen one. Recurrence with Isa 55:3 covenant language.
sourceText: “I have made a covenant with my chosen one, I have sworn to David, my servant, ‘I will establish your seed forever, and build up your throne to all generations.’” Selah.

note: 'Everyone who believes is justified' faintly recalls the Servant who 'shall make many to be accounted righteous,' the OT seed of justification language. Conceptual, contested.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

note: 'Behold, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish; for I work a work in your days, a work you will not believe though one declares it' is quoted verbatim (LXX, 'scoffers/despisers') as the prophetic warning closing the sermon. Explicit citation, maximal volume.
sourceText: “Look among the nations, watch, and wonder marvelously; for I am working a work in your days, which you will not believe though it is told you.
lxxText: Behold, ye despisers, and look, and wonder marvelously, and vanish: for I work a work in your days, which ye will in no wise believe, though a man declare it to you.

note: 'I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth' is quoted verbatim (LXX) as the Lord's commission justifying the turn to the Gentiles. Explicit Servant-Song citation; maximal volume.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: 'A light for the Gentiles' also stands in the first Servant Song ('I will give you... for a light to the nations'), reinforcing the light-to-the-nations commission Paul cites. Recurrence with Isa 49:6.
sourceText: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations;

note: The Jews 'filled with jealousy' contradicting the word, leading to the turn toward the Gentiles, faintly enacts the Song of Moses' principle that God provokes Israel to jealousy by a non-people, a motif Paul develops elsewhere. Contested here.
sourceText: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

note: Shaking off the dust of the feet against the city as a sign-act of rejection has loose kinship with prophetic shaking-out gestures of repudiation (Nehemiah shaking out his lap against covenant-breakers). Very faint; the gesture is more dominical instruction than OT citation.
sourceText: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.

note: The Lord 'testified to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands' (v3). The pair 'signs and wonders' (sēmeia kai terata) is the fixed Septuagintal idiom for the Exodus deliverance, where the Lord 'showed signs and wonders' against Egypt. Thematic Coherence is strong (divine attestation of the messenger); Volume rests on the set two-word phrase. Plausibility high: Luke saturates Acts with Exodus-shaped signs-and-wonders language.
sourceText: and Yahweh showed great and awesome signs and wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh, and on all his house, before our eyes;

note: Reinforces the 'signs and wonders' idiom by tying it specifically to a commissioned human agent (Moses 'whom the Lord sent to do all the signs and wonders'), paralleling miracles done 'by their hands.' Recurrence within the Pentateuch supports the topos; Volume is faint on its own. Contested as a distinct source rather than part of the broader Exodus signs-and-wonders cluster.
sourceText: in all the signs and the wonders, which Yahweh sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land,

note: The plot to 'mistreat and stone them' (v5) presupposes the Torah's mode of execution by stoning, carried out by the community and its rulers. Volume low (no verbal borrowing), but the legal practice underlies the narrative threat. Contested: the link is conceptual to the institution of stoning rather than to this verse specifically.
sourceText: “Bring out of the camp him who cursed; and let all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and let all the congregation stone him.

note: The man 'a cripple from his mother's womb, who never had walked' is healed and 'leaped up and walked' (vv8-10). Isaiah's eschatological promise, 'then shall the lame man leap (halletai) as a hart,' supplies the rare verb and the lame-restored motif. Volume high (distinctive 'leap' for a healed lame man); Thematic Coherence strong (the dawning age of restoration enacted among the nations); Recurrence good (Isa 35 is a programmatic restoration text echoed across Luke-Acts).
sourceText: Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.

note: Paul's command 'Stand upright on your feet!' (v10) echoes the prophetic summons 'Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I will speak with you.' Volume rests on the shared imperative to stand on the feet; Thematic Coherence moderate (a word of power that raises a prostrate/incapable person). Contested whether Luke intends a prophetic-call resonance or merely a healing command.
sourceText: He said to me, Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you.

note: The crowd cries 'The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men' and the priest of Zeus prepares oxen and garlands (vv11-13). The psalm's mockery of idols 'the work of men's hands' frames the scene's irony: the living agents of God are taken for the lifeless gods of the nations. Volume nil (no verbal contact); the link is typological-thematic, exposing pagan idolatry. Contested as an intended echo.
sourceText: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.

note: The summons to turn to 'the living God, who made the sky and the earth and the sea, and all that is in them' (v15) reproduces the Sabbath-commandment formula 'the Lord made the heaven and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them.' Volume very high (the full four-membered creation list verbatim); Thematic Coherence strong (Creator vs. the 'vain things' of idolatry). The clearest scriptural backbone of the Lystra speech.
sourceText: for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.

note: Parallel source for v15: the Lord 'who made the heaven and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them,' here explicitly tied to the 'living' God who keeps faith and provides. Volume very high (same creation catalogue); Thematic Coherence strong (God as faithful provider, matching v17's rains and food). Likely conflated with Exod 20:11 in the speech's monotheistic appeal.
sourceText: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who keeps truth forever;

note: Ezra's prayer, 'You are the Lord alone; you have made heaven... the earth... the seas, and all that is in them, and you preserve them all,' is the great post-exilic monotheistic confession built on the same creation list and joined to providential preservation, both present in vv15-17. Volume moderate (creation catalogue plus preservation); Recurrence supports the formula's currency in Second Temple worship.
sourceText: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.

note: 'The sea is his, for he made it, and his hands formed the dry land' undergirds v15's pairing of sea and earth as the Creator's work and stands behind the call to worship the true God rather than idols. Volume moderate; Thematic Coherence high (creation as ground for worship, against false gods).
sourceText: The sea is his, and he made it. His hands formed the dry land.

note: 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth' is the headwater of the heaven-and-earth creation language deployed in v15. Volume moderate (foundational phrasing) but diffuse, since the speech follows the fuller Exod/Ps liturgical lists rather than Genesis directly. Recurrence very high across Scripture.
sourceText: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

note: The exhortation to 'turn from these vain things' (mataia, v15) draws on the prophetic-Pentateuchal label for idols as 'vanities' that 'provoked me with their vanities/no-gods.' Volume moderate (mataia is the LXX term for idols); Thematic Coherence strong (idols as empty nothings opposed to the living God). Contested only as to which idol-vanity text is primary.
sourceText: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

note: 'Are there any among the vanities (idols) of the nations that can cause rain? ... it is you, O Lord our God,' directly ties the 'vain things' of v15 to the rain-giving of v17: the nations' idols cannot give rain, but the living God does. Volume moderate but precise (vanities + rain), making this an unusually apt double-link. Thematic Coherence very high.
sourceText: Are there any among the vanities of the nations that can cause rain? or can the sky give showers? Aren’t you he, Yahweh our God? therefore we will wait for you; for you have made all these things.

note: 'Those who regard vain idols (mataia) forsake their own mercy' adds Recurrence to the 'vain things' (v15) idol-vocabulary in a Gentile setting (Nineveh/sailors), apt to a speech to pagans. Volume faint (single shared term). Contested as a discrete source within the broad idol-vanity cluster.
sourceText: Those who regard lying vanities forsake their own mercy.

note: 'The living God' (v15) is a fixed OT epithet distinguishing the true God from idols; Deut 5:26 ('the voice of the living God') is a Pentateuchal anchor. Volume moderate (set title); Thematic Coherence high (living God vs. dead idols, the speech's thesis). Recurrence very high across the OT.
sourceText: For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?

note: 'who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways' (v16) echoes God giving Israel 'up to their own hearts' lusts, and they walked in their own counsels.' Volume moderate (the idiom of being let to walk in one's own ways); Thematic Coherence strong (divine forbearance/handing-over of the nations). Contested between this and the Deut 32 nations-allotment tradition.
sourceText: So I let them go after the stubbornness of their hearts, that they might walk in their own counsels.

note: 'he... gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons' (v17) reflects the covenant promise 'I will give the rain of your land in its season, the early and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain.' Volume high (rain given in due season → harvest); Thematic Coherence strong (God's good gifts as witness). A core text for the natural-revelation argument.
sourceText: that I will give the rain of your land in its season, the former rain and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain, your new wine, and your oil.

note: 'I will give you rain in its season, and the land shall yield its produce' parallels the rains and 'fruitful seasons' of v17. Volume moderate; Recurrence reinforces the Pentateuchal rain-blessing topos alongside Deut 11:14.
sourceText: then I will give you your rains in their season, and the land shall yield its increase, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit.

note: 'Let us fear the Lord our God, who gives rain, both the early and the latter, in its season, who keeps for us the appointed weeks of the harvest' is the closest prophetic parallel to v17's rains and 'fruitful seasons.' Volume high (rain in season + fixed harvest seasons); Thematic Coherence strong (creation's seasons as a witness summoning to fear/turn to God).
sourceText: Neither do they say in their heart, ‘Let us now fear Yahweh our God, who gives rain, both the former and the latter, in its season; who preserves to us the appointed weeks of the harvest.’

note: The psalm of God visiting the earth with rain, enriching it, crowning the year with bounty so the valleys 'shout for joy,' matches v17's rains, fruitful seasons, and resulting 'food and gladness.' Volume moderate (rain → fertility → joy sequence); Thematic Coherence high (providence evoking gladness).
sourceText: You visit the earth, and water it. You greatly enrich it. The river of God is full of water. You provide them grain, for so you have ordained it. You drench its furrows. You level its ridges. You soften it with showers. You bless it with a crop. You crown the year with your bounty. Your carts overflow with abundance. The wilderness grasslands overflow. The hills are clothed with gladness. The pastures are covered with flocks. The valleys also are clothed […]

note: 'who covers the heaven with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who makes grass to grow on the mountains' echoes v17's rains-from-heaven-producing-food. Volume moderate; Recurrence supports the providence-praise tradition.
sourceText: who covers the sky with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who makes grass grow on the mountains.

note: God brings forth food from the earth and 'wine that gladdens the heart of man... and bread that strengthens man's heart' closely matches v17's 'filling our hearts with food and gladness.' Volume moderate-to-high (food + gladness of heart); Thematic Coherence strong (creation's provision as joy-giving witness).
sourceText: He causes the grass to grow for the livestock, and plants for man to cultivate, that he may produce food out of the earth: wine that makes glad the heart of man, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man’s heart.

note: 'You have put gladness in my heart, more than in the time their grain and wine increased' overlaps v17's 'filling our hearts with... gladness' linked to harvest abundance. Volume faint (gladness in the heart + grain/wine); contested as distinct from Ps 104.
sourceText: You have put gladness in my heart, more than when their grain and their new wine are increased.

note: 'who gives rain on the earth, and sends water on the fields' adds Recurrence to the rain-as-divine-gift motif of v17. Volume faint (general statement); contested as an intended source.
sourceText: who gives rain on the earth, and sends waters on the fields;

note: Paul is stoned and 'dragged out of the city' (v19), reflecting the Torah practice of taking the condemned 'outside the camp' to be stoned. Volume moderate (stoning + expulsion from the community space); Thematic Coherence moderate (Paul suffers the prophet's/martyr's fate at the city's edge). Contested between this and Lev 24.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “The man shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall stone him with stones outside of the camp.” All the congregation brought him outside of the camp, and stoned him to death with stones, as Yahweh commanded Moses.

note: The stoning of Paul, left for dead yet rising (vv19-20), stands in the typological line of God's messengers stoned for their witness, exemplified by Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned 'in the court of the house of the Lord.' Volume nil verbally; the link is the figural pattern of the persecuted prophet. Plausibility good given Luke's persecuted-witness theme; contested as an intended allusion.
sourceText: They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.

note: 'Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers him out of them all' fits Paul's stoning and immediate rising (vv19-20), anticipating the explicit 'many afflictions' of v22. Volume faint; contested as a deliberate echo here rather than a general providence motif.
sourceText: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.

note: 'When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly' (v23) reflects the foundational appointment of elders to share leadership of God's people, where Moses gathers seventy elders to bear the burden with him. Volume moderate (institution of elders for the community); Thematic Coherence strong (ordered leadership over the people of God). Contested between this and the Exod 18 model.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, that they may stand there with you. I will come down and talk with you there. I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you not bear it yourself alone.

note: 'through many afflictions we must enter into the Kingdom of God' (v22) restates the wisdom that 'many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers him out of them all.' Volume moderate (the phrase 'many afflictions'); Thematic Coherence strong (suffering as the path of the faithful toward deliverance).
sourceText: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.

note: God 'had opened a door of faith to the nations' (v27) realizes the Servant's mandate to be 'a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth,' a programmatic Gentile-mission text in Luke-Acts (cf. Acts 13:47). Volume nil here (no verbal contact in v27); the link is the figural fulfillment of the nations' inclusion. Contested as an echo within this verse specifically.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: The Judean teachers demand circumcision 'after the custom of Moses' as necessary for salvation; the underlying institution is the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision, the sign required of every male, where the uncircumcised is 'cut off.' The whole dispute presupposes this text as the charter of the boundary marker. Verbal coherence ('circumcised') and thematic centrality are strong.
sourceText: This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed. He who is born in your […]

note: The Mosaic codification of circumcision (eighth-day) is what 'the custom of Moses' (v.1) most directly names, distinguishing the demand here from the merely Abrahamic command; supports the phrase 'keep the law of Moses' (v.5).
sourceText: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.

note: The Torah's own rule that a foreigner must be circumcised before sharing in the Passover/community is the legal logic the circumcision party extends to Gentile believers — only the circumcised may belong. Faint, conceptual.
sourceText: When a stranger shall live as a foreigner with you, and will keep the Passover to Yahweh, let all his males be circumcised, and then let him come near and keep it; and he shall be as one who is born in the land: but no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.

note: Peter calls God the one 'who knows the heart' (kardiognostes, v.8) who 'made no distinction... cleansing their hearts.' This recalls the LORD who, unlike man looking on outward appearance, 'looks on the heart' — here applied to overturning the outward circumcision marker in favor of inward purity. Strong thematic coherence.
sourceText: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

note: Solomon's prayer addresses God who alone 'knows the hearts of all the children of men'; a recurrent OT divine epithet standing behind Peter's heart-knowing God who reads Gentile faith. Recurrence test supports the motif.
sourceText: then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive, and do, and render to every man according to all his ways, whose heart you know; (for you, even you only, know the hearts of all the children of men;)

note: 'I the LORD search the heart' — part of the same cluster of heart-searching texts informing v.8's claim that God testified about the Gentiles by reading their hearts.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: God 'cleansing their hearts by faith' (v.9) echoes the promise that the LORD will circumcise the heart — interiorized, divinely-wrought purity displacing the external rite at issue in the chapter. Thematically potent for the circumcision debate.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.

note: Heart-cleansing language (v.9) coheres with the promise to sprinkle clean water, give a new heart, and put the Spirit within — note v.8's gift of the Spirit alongside the cleansing. The Spirit + cleansed heart pairing is striking.
sourceText: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: 'Circumcise the foreskin of your heart' reinforces the inward-circumcision motif behind 'cleansing their hearts' (v.9). Faint, overlaps with Deut 30:6.
sourceText: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.

note: Peter's 'yoke... which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear' (v.10) uses yoke-as-burden imagery; OT yoke metaphor (e.g., the good of bearing the yoke) lies in the background, though Peter inverts it as an unbearable load. Figural/contested.
sourceText: It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.

note: James's formal scriptural proof (vv.16-17): 'I will... build the tabernacle of David which has fallen... that the rest of men may seek after the Lord, all the Gentiles who are called by my name.' This follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew: MT 'that they may possess the remnant of Edom' becomes LXX 'that the rest of mankind may seek' (Heb. yireshu 'possess' read as yidreshu 'seek'; 'Edom' read as 'adam, mankind) — the very reading that makes Gentile inclusion the prophetic point. Highest volume and decisive function in the argument.
sourceText: In that day I will raise up the tent of David who is fallen, and close up its breaches, and I will raise up its ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old; that they may possess the remnant of Edom, and all the nations who are called by my name,” says Yahweh who does this.
lxxText: In that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and will rebuild the ruins of it, and will set up the parts thereof that have been broken down, and will build it up as in the ancient days: that the remnant of men, and all the Gentiles upon whom my name is called, may earnestly seek me, saith the Lord who does all these things.

note: The opening of the citation, 'After these things I will return' (v.16), is not in Amos; it most closely matches 'I will return and have compassion on them,' suggesting James has conflated Amos with Jeremiah's restoration promise. A genuine secondary source spliced into the quotation.
sourceText: It shall happen, after that I have plucked them up, I will return and have compassion on them; and I will bring them again, every man to his heritage, and every man to his land.

note: 'Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God and David their king' shares the post-restoration 'seek the Lord' + Davidic motif underlying vv.16-17. Possible contributor to the catena's 'after these things... seek the Lord.' Contested.
sourceText: Afterward the children of Israel shall return, and seek Yahweh their God, and David their king, and shall come with trembling to Yahweh and to his blessings in the last days.

note: James says God 'first visited the nations, to take out of them a people for his name' (v.14). The phrase 'a people for his name/possession' reuses the election formula by which Israel was 'a people for his own possession' — now extended to Gentiles. Strong thematic reuse of covenant election language.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God, and Yahweh has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.

note: 'A people for his name' (v.14) echoes the Sinai promise that Israel would be God's 'treasured possession out of all peoples' — the foundational election text now applied to the nations. Recurrence with Deut 7:6 / 14:2.
sourceText: Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine;

note: 'Many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day and shall be my people' anticipates God taking a people from the Gentiles (v.14); part of the prophetic stream James invokes ('the words of the prophets,' v.15). Faint.
sourceText: Many nations shall join themselves to Yahweh in that day, and shall be my people; and I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that Yahweh of Armies has sent me to you.

note: The closing tag, 'known to him from eternity / who declared these things of old' (vv.17b-18), resembles Isaiah's 'Who has declared this from of old?' — supplying the 'long-known to God' coloring appended to the Amos citation. Contested wording.
sourceText: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me.

note: James's first prohibition, 'the pollution of idols' (v.20), corresponds to the resident-alien (ger) law forbidding sacrifices offered apart from the LORD — i.e., meat from idol-worship. The four-item decree as a whole derives from the laws binding on the stranger sojourning in Israel (Lev 17-18). High coherence; foundational to the decree.
sourceText: “You shall say to them, ‘Any man there is of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice, and doesn’t bring it to the door of the Tent of Meeting, to sacrifice it to Yahweh; that man shall be cut off from his people.

note: The prohibition of 'blood' (v.20) directly reuses the repeated Levitical ban applying to both Israelite and the resident alien: 'no one of you shall eat blood.' Explicitly extended to the ger, which is why it grounds rules for Gentile believers.
sourceText: “‘Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who eats any kind of blood, I will set my face against that soul who eats blood, and will cut him off from among his people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel, “No person […]

note: 'What is strangled' (v.20) reflects the requirement to drain the blood of any animal caught/killed — flesh with blood in it (a strangled animal) is forbidden, again binding on the sojourner. The 'strangled'/blood pairing in the decree mirrors this law.
sourceText: “‘Whatever man there is of the children of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who takes in hunting any animal or bird that may be eaten; he shall pour out its blood, and cover it with dust. For as to the life of all flesh, its blood is with its life: therefore I said to the children of Israel, “You shall not eat the blood of any kind of flesh; for the life of all flesh is its blood. Whoever eats it shall be cut off.” “‘Every […]

note: 'Sexual immorality' (porneia, v.20) corresponds to the forbidden-unions catalogue of Lev 18, which v.26 expressly imposes on 'the stranger that sojourns among you.' The decree's fourth item completes the set of Holiness-Code rules for resident aliens.
sourceText: “‘None of you shall approach anyone who are his close relatives, to uncover their nakedness: I am Yahweh. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, nor the nakedness of your mother: she is your mother. You shall not uncover her nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife. It is your father’s nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father, or the daughter of your mother, […]

note: The blood prohibition (v.20) also rests on the Noahic command given to all humanity — 'flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat' — which suits Gentiles since it precedes and exceeds Israel's law. Often paired with Lev 17 as the rationale for a universally-binding minimum.
sourceText: But flesh with its life, that is, its blood, you shall not eat.

note: 'Moses... read in the synagogues every Sabbath' (v.21) presupposes the Sabbath institution as the appointed day of holy convocation. Faint, institutional background to the verse.
sourceText: “‘Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation; you shall do no kind of work. It is a Sabbath to Yahweh in all your dwellings.

note: The written decree restates the prohibitions: 'things sacrificed to idols' (v.29) reuses the Levitical ban on sacrifices offered outside the LORD's worship, binding on the resident alien. Repetition of the v.20 list.
sourceText: “You shall say to them, ‘Any man there is of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice, and doesn’t bring it to the door of the Tent of Meeting, to sacrifice it to Yahweh; that man shall be cut off from his people.

note: 'Blood' (v.29) again reflects the Holiness Code's repeated prohibition extended to the sojourner.

note: 'Things strangled' (v.29) reflects the requirement to drain blood from killed animals; flesh retaining blood is forbidden to Israelite and stranger alike.
