note: 'Sexual immorality' (v.29) corresponds to the forbidden unions of Lev 18, imposed on the resident alien (v.26). The letter's four items reproduce the ger-laws of Lev 17-18.
sourceText: “‘None of you shall approach anyone who are his close relatives, to uncover their nakedness: I am Yahweh. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, nor the nakedness of your mother: she is your mother. You shall not uncover her nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife. It is your father’s nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father, or the daughter of your mother, […]

note: The blood abstention (v.29) coheres with the universal Noahic command against eating flesh with its blood, the natural basis for a rule binding on Gentiles.
sourceText: But flesh with its life, that is, its blood, you shall not eat.

note: Paul circumcises Timothy 'because of the Jews.' The act invokes the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision as the enduring sign of belonging to the covenant people; Luke presents it as missionary accommodation rather than salvific necessity, but the gesture is unintelligible apart from this foundational statute.
sourceText: God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he […]

note: The Passover rule that an uncircumcised man may not partake, while the circumcised foreigner becomes 'as one born in the land,' frames Timothy (son of a Jewess, Greek father) as a borderline figure regularized by circumcision so he can move freely among Jews. Thematic resonance; no verbal borrowing.
sourceText: When a stranger shall live as a foreigner with you, and will keep the Passover to Yahweh, let all his males be circumcised, and then let him come near and keep it; and he shall be as one who is born in the land: but no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.

note: Delivering 'the decrees... to keep' which the apostles and elders ordained echoes the Mosaic pattern of transmitting statutes and ordinances for the people to keep; the apostolic council functions as a new authoritative legislature. Structural/lexical resonance (statutes delivered to be kept).
sourceText: You shall teach them the statutes and the laws, and shall show them the way in which they must walk, and the work that they must do.

note: 'The assemblies... increased in number daily' recalls the Septuagintal language of Israel multiplying and increasing greatly in Egypt (cf. Genesis 1:28); a recurring Lukan growth-formula casting the church as the multiplying covenant people.
sourceText: The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them.

note: God speaks to Israel/Jacob 'in visions of the night,' directing his movement to a new land ('I will go down with thee') with assurance of divine purpose. The Macedonian vision in the night that redirects Paul's journey across into Europe shares the genre (night vision) and function (divine redirection of geography) closely.
sourceText: God spoke to Israel in the visions of the night, and said, “Jacob, Jacob!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “I am God, the God of your father. Don’t be afraid to go down into Egypt, for there I will make of you a great nation. I will go down with you into Egypt. I will also surely bring you up again. Joseph will close your eyes.”

note: The Spirit twice forbidding and not allowing the missionaries' chosen routes, then steering them, echoes the pillar of cloud and fire guiding Israel's route step by step; divine micromanagement of the missionary itinerary as a new wilderness leading. Thematic only.
sourceText: Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night:

note: 'A vision appeared to Paul in the night' uses the stock revelatory idiom of the word/vision of the LORD coming in the night; Abram's night vision is the paradigm of God commissioning through nocturnal revelation. Generic verbal resonance.
sourceText: After these things Yahweh’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.”

note: Mystery 'revealed in a night vision' as the medium of divine disclosure; faint Septuagintal parallel for night-vision revelation that resolves a course of action.
sourceText: Then was the secret revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.

note: Lydia, a 'seller of purple' whose household and hospitality she manages, evokes the capable woman of Proverbs 31 whose clothing is purple and who trades in fine cloth; a wealthy, industrious, God-honoring matron. Suggestive characterization, no quotation.
sourceText: She makes for herself carpets of tapestry. Her clothing is fine linen and purple.

note: Purple as the prized textile of the tabernacle offerings; Lydia's trade in purple carries an aura of dignity and devoted craft. Lexical (purple) only.
sourceText: blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair,

note: 'The Lord opened her heart to listen' is the divine-initiative idiom of the LORD circumcising/opening the heart so that Israel will hear and obey; conversion is portrayed as God's sovereign opening of the heart, the inward counterpart to covenant circumcision. Thematic coherence strong.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.

note: 'Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things' as the prayer-paradigm for God enabling perception of his word; Lydia's opened heart to attend to Paul's words is its narrative fulfillment. Conceptual parallel.
sourceText: Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.

note: The slave girl has a 'spirit of divination' (Greek: a python spirit) and earns money by fortune-telling. The Mosaic legislation expressly bans divination, soothsaying, and consulting spirits as abominations among the nations Israel dispossesses; Paul's exorcism enacts the abolition of precisely this pagan practice. Strong thematic and conceptual coherence with the core prohibition.
sourceText: There shall not be found with you anyone who makes his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, one who uses divination, one who practices sorcery, or an enchanter, or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or a consulter with a familiar spirit, or a wizard, or a necromancer. For whoever does these things is an abomination to Yahweh. Because of these abominations, Yahweh your God drives them out from before you.

note: 'Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards.' The girl's mantic spirit is the very category Israel is forbidden to consult; Paul's command silences and casts out the source. Reinforces the divination-prohibition cluster.
sourceText: “‘Don’t turn to those who are mediums, nor to the wizards. Don’t seek them out, to be defiled by them. I am Yahweh your God.

note: The penalty against souls turning after mediums and familiar spirits; the pericope dramatizes the divine verdict on a profit-driven mantic spirit. Thematic recurrence within the Holiness Code's ban on spiritism.
sourceText: “‘The person that turns to those who are mediums, and to the wizards, to play the prostitute after them, I will even set my face against that person, and will cut him off from among his people.

note: The medium of Endor as the canonical narrative instance of a woman trafficking in a familiar/divining spirit; the Philippian slave girl is its degraded Greco-Roman counterpart, here exposed and dispossessed. Narrative-typological resonance.
sourceText: Then Saul said to his servants, “Seek me a woman who has a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and inquire of her.” His servants said to him, “Behold, there is a woman who has a familiar spirit at Endor.” Saul disguised himself, and put on other clothing, and went, he and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night: and he said, “Please divine to me by the familiar spirit, and bring me up whomever I shall name to you.” The woman said to him, […]

note: The spirit's cry that these are servants of 'the Most High God' (El Elyon) uses the divine title introduced by Melchizedek, God Most High, maker of heaven and earth; a Gentile-context title for the one true God now proclaimed (ironically) by a pagan spirit. Lexical-theological link to the El Elyon title-tradition.
sourceText: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High. He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth: and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Abram gave him a tenth of all.

note: 'Servants of the Most High God' is the Septuagintal acclamation applied to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego by a pagan king; the slave girl's confession echoes this Gentile recognition of servants of God Most High. Verbal parallel to the title.
sourceText: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace: he spoke and said, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, you servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here. Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out of the midst of the fire.

note: The prophet Jeremiah is beaten and put in the stocks for proclaiming God's word; Paul and Silas, beaten with rods and fastened in stocks in the inner prison, replay the persecuted-prophet-in-stocks pattern. Strong situational coherence (beating + stocks for the word).
sourceText: Then Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper gate of Benjamin, which was in Yahweh’s house.

note: Joseph, falsely accused, is cast into the prison where the king's prisoners are bound, yet the LORD is with him; the righteous servant unjustly imprisoned and divinely vindicated prefigures Paul and Silas. Typological resonance setting up the deliverance.
sourceText: Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were bound, and he was there in custody.

note: The Mosaic regulation of judicial beating by a fixed number of stripes ('many stripes' laid on them) supplies the legal-cultural backdrop for the flogging, though here the Roman magistrates' beating is lawless. Conceptual link to the stripes motif.
sourceText: It shall be, if the wicked man is worthy to be beaten, that the judge shall cause him to lie down, and to be beaten before his face, according to his wickedness, by number. He may sentence him to no more than forty stripes. He shall not give more; lest, if he should give more, and beat him more than that many stripes, then your brother will be degraded in your sight.

note: 'Thou puttest my feet in the stocks' as the poetic image of constraint by an adversary; the securing of Paul and Silas's feet in the stocks resonates with this Joban idiom of the afflicted righteous (cf. Job 33:11). Lexical (feet in stocks).
sourceText: You also put my feet in the stocks, and mark all my paths. You set a bound to the soles of my feet,

note: God 'brought them out of darkness... and brake their bands in sunder,' for 'he hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder.' The midnight earthquake that opens all the prison doors and looses everyone's bonds is the narrative enactment of this thanksgiving for the imprisoned whom God frees. Strong volume and thematic coherence; the controlling subtext for the deliverance.
sourceText: He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke away their chains. Let them praise Yahweh for his loving kindness, for his wonderful works to the children of men! For he has broken the gates of brass, and cut through bars of iron.

note: 'The LORD looseth the prisoners' as a signature of God's saving character; the loosing of every prisoner's bonds dramatizes this divine attribute. Direct thematic match.
sourceText: who executes justice for the oppressed; who gives food to the hungry. Yahweh frees the prisoners.

note: 'At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee.' Paul and Silas praying and singing hymns to God 'about midnight' closely matches the psalmist's nocturnal praise of the righteous sufferer who blesses God at the very hour of distress.
sourceText: At midnight I will rise to give thanks to you, because of your righteous ordinances.

note: 'God my maker, who giveth songs in the night' as the wisdom theme of praise amid darkness; the midnight hymns of the prisoners embody songs given in the night. Conceptual parallel.
sourceText: But no one says, ‘Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,

note: 'The earth shook and trembled; the foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken' in God's deliverance of his servant from enemies; the 'great earthquake' shaking 'the foundations of the prison' is the theophanic-rescue earthquake of the Davidic deliverance psalm. Lexical (foundations shaken) and thematic.
sourceText: Then the earth shook and trembled. The foundations also of the mountains quaked and were shaken, because he was angry.

note: The quaking of Sinai at God's descent supplies the theophany-as-earthquake background; the prison earthquake signals God's powerful presence. Thematic resonance, generic earthquake-theophany.
sourceText: Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.

note: 'I will break in pieces the gates of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron' (to Cyrus); a second prophetic instance of God shattering prison/city barriers, reinforcing the Psalm 107 gate-breaking motif behind the opened doors. Recurrence of the broken-barriers theme.
sourceText: “I will go before you, and make the rough places smooth. I will break the doors of brass in pieces, and cut apart the bars of iron.

note: The Servant's commission 'to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house'; the liberation of the jailer's prisoners realizes this servant-mission imagery. Thematic.
sourceText: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: 'Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing'; the jailer who was about to kill himself ends 'rejoicing greatly with all his household,' the reversal-into-joy pattern of the deliverance psalms. Conceptual resonance for the turn from despair to rejoicing.
sourceText: You have turned my mourning into dancing for me. You have removed my sackcloth, and clothed me with gladness,

note: 'Go in peace' is the stock Hebrew dismissal-blessing (cf. Exodus 4:18; Judges 18:6); the jailer's 'go in peace' to the released prisoners carries this benedictory idiom. Lexical formula only.
sourceText: Then Eli answered, “Go in peace; and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him.”

note: 'The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.' The magistrates who were 'afraid when they heard that they were Romans' and came begging, while Paul stands boldly on his rights, illustrates this wisdom reversal of fear between the unjust and the vindicated righteous. Thematic.
sourceText: The wicked flee when no one pursues; but the righteous are as bold as a lion.

note: Joseph brought out of the prison and publicly vindicated before the authorities; Paul's insistence that the magistrates themselves come and bring them out continues the unjustly-imprisoned-then-honorably-released pattern. Typological resonance closing the prison sequence.
sourceText: Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon. He shaved himself, changed his clothing, and came in to Pharaoh.

note: The reversal in which fear of the formerly oppressed falls upon the officials and rulers who had moved against them; the Philippian magistrates' fear and capitulation echoes this peripeteia of vindication. Faint thematic link.
sourceText: Now in the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the month, when the king’s commandment and his decree drew near to be put in execution, on the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to conquer them, (but it was turned out the opposite happened, that the Jews conquered those who hated them), the Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the King Ahasuerus, to lay hands on those who wanted […]

note: Paul reasons 'from the Scriptures' that the Christ 'had to suffer'; the Suffering Servant is the natural scriptural ground for a suffering Messiah, a recurrent NT proof-text. Volume modest in the narrative summary itself but thematic coherence with the synagogue argument is strong.
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we […]

note: 'rise again from the dead' echoes the psalm's 'you will not abandon my soul to Sheol,' the standard apostolic resurrection proof from Scripture (cf. its explicit use in earlier Acts speeches). Recurrence high in Luke-Acts.
sourceText: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.

note: 'rise again' may glance at 'on the third day he will raise us up'; verbal contact is thin and the third-day motif is not stated here, so the link is faint and contested.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.

note: The charge that Paul proclaims 'another king, Jesus' resonates with the psalm's rulers raging against the LORD and his Anointed; Luke elsewhere cites Psalm 2, so recurrence supports a faint background, though no quotation is made here.
sourceText: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,

note: 'another king' set against Caesar's decrees may evoke the everlasting dominion given to the son of man, but verbal volume is negligible.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The Beroeans 'examining the Scriptures daily' figurally images the blessed one who meditates on the law day and night; thematic coherence only, no verbal borrowing.
sourceText: but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.

note: Daily reading and searching of the written word loosely recalls the king's charge to read the law all his days; very faint.
sourceText: It shall be, when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write himself a copy of this law in a book, out of that which is before the priests the Levites. It shall be with him, and he shall read from it all the days of his life; that he may learn to fear Yahweh his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them;

note: Paul's spirit 'provoked' (paroxynein) at a city full of idols echoes the LXX of Israel provoking God to anger with their idols, the same verb-field; thematic coherence between human and divine zeal against idolatry is strong.
sourceText: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

note: A 'city full of idols' matches Wisdom's diatribe on the proliferation of cult images; deuterocanonical idol-polemic is the closest contemporary parallel and frames the whole Athens episode.
sourceText: Therefore also among the idols of the nations will there be a visitation, Because, though formed of things which God created, they were made an abomination, And stumbling blocks to the souls of men, And a snare to the feet of the foolish. For the devising of idols was the beginning of fornication, And the invention of them the corruption of life: For neither were they from the beginning, neither will they be forever; For by the vaingloriousness of men […]

note: The lifeless 'idols' that provoke Paul evoke the classic psalm of handmade gods of silver and gold that cannot see or hear; recurrence of this polemic across the Psalter is high.
sourceText: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.

note: Parallel idol-polemic to Psalm 115; included for completeness as a recurrent OT topos behind the scene.
sourceText: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they can’t speak. They have eyes, but they can’t see. They have ears, but they can’t hear; neither is there any breath in their mouths. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.

note: Isaiah's extended mockery of the craftsman who fashions a god stands behind both Paul's revulsion here and his later argument that the divine is not 'engraved by art'; sets up vv.29.
sourceText: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]

note: Jeremiah's contrast of dead idols with the living Creator anticipates Paul's pivot from idols to the God who made all; thematic, not verbal.
sourceText: Hear the word which Yahweh speaks to you, house of Israel! Thus says Yahweh, “Don’t learn the way of the nations, and don’t be dismayed at the signs of the sky; for the nations are dismayed at them. For the customs of the peoples are vanity; for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman with the ax. They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it not move. They are like a palm tree, […]

note: 'The God who made the world and all things in it' is creation-monotheism rooted in the opening of Genesis; high volume and thematic coherence, the foundation of the whole sermon.
sourceText: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

note: Isaiah's God who 'created the heavens... gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who walk in it' tightly combines both of Paul's claims: maker of the world (v.24) and giver of life and breath (v.25). Strong verbal and conceptual overlap.
sourceText: Thus says God Yahweh, he who created the heavens and stretched them out, he who spread out the earth and that which comes out of it, he who gives breath to its people and spirit to those who walk in it.

note: 'made the heaven and the earth, the sea and all that is in them' is echoed in 'made the world and all things in it... Lord of heaven and earth'; recurrent creation formula.
sourceText: for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.

note: 'who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them' parallels v.24's creation summary; recurrence of the formula raises confidence.
sourceText: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who keeps truth forever;

note: 'You made heaven... the earth and all that is on it... and you give life to them all' parallels both creation and life-giving themes; included as a recurrent OT confession.
sourceText: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.

note: 'Lord of heaven and earth' (v.24) echoes 'God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth'; faint title-level contact.
sourceText: He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth:

note: 'heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth and all that is in it' supports 'Lord of heaven and earth'; recurrent title.
sourceText: Behold, to Yahweh your God belongs heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth, with all that is therein.

note: Solomon's 'heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house I have built' directly grounds 'does not dwell in temples made with hands.' Strong thematic coherence at the dedication of the very institution Paul relativizes.
sourceText: But will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!

note: 'Heaven is my throne and the earth my footstool; what house will you build for me?' is the prophetic charter for 'does not dwell in temples made with hands' and for needing nothing from human hands; quoted by Stephen in Acts 7, so recurrence in Acts is high.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what kind of house will you build to me? and what place shall be my rest? For all these things has my hand made, and so all these things came to be,” says Yahweh: “but to this man will I look, even to him who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word.

note: Parallel to 1 Kings 8:27, the same temple-cannot-contain-God confession behind v.24.
sourceText: “But will God indeed dwell with men on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house which I have built!

note: 'If I were hungry I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine' grounds v.25, that God is not 'served by human hands as though he needed anything'; strong thematic coherence with sacrificial critique.
sourceText: I don’t rebuke you for your sacrifices. Your burnt offerings are continually before me. I have no need for a bull from your stall, nor male goats from your pens. For every animal of the forest is mine, and the livestock on a thousand hills. I know all the birds of the mountains. The wild animals of the field are mine. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine, and all that is in it. Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of […]

note: 'He himself gives to all life and breath' echoes God breathing the breath of life into the man; foundational creation text for the life-giver claim.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: 'In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind' closely matches 'gives to all life and breath.'
sourceText: in whose hand is the life of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind?

note: 'The breath of the Almighty gives me life' parallels v.25's life and breath; recurrent wisdom motif.
sourceText: The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.

note: 'God of the spirits of all flesh' supports the universal life-giver theme of v.25.
sourceText: They fell on their faces, and said, “God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?”

note: The high and lofty One who nonetheless gives breath ('the breath that I have made') touches v.25; faint.
sourceText: For thus says the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite. For I will not contend forever, neither will I be always angry; for the spirit would faint before me, and the souls who I have made.

note: 'When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance... he fixed the boundaries of the peoples' is the key text behind v.26, God making every nation and 'fixing the boundaries of their dwellings.' Strong verbal and conceptual coherence.
sourceText: When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the children of men, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.

note: 'Made from one... every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth' draws on the creation and filling of the earth from the one human pair.
sourceText: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them. God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”

note: The Table of Nations, all peoples spreading 'from one' after the flood, underlies the unity-of-nations claim in v.26.
sourceText: These are the families of the sons of Noah, by their generations, according to their nations. The nations divided from these in the earth after the flood.

note: 'Determined appointed seasons' may glance at the luminaries set 'for seasons'; faint, since the sense here is more likely the epochs of nations.
sourceText: God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years;

note: 'He makes nations great, and destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away' parallels v.26's sovereign setting of appointed times and boundaries for peoples.
sourceText: He increases the nations, and he destroys them. He enlarges the nations, and he leads them captive.

note: 'You have fixed all the boundaries of the earth' directly supports 'the boundaries of their dwellings' in v.26.
sourceText: You have set all the boundaries of the earth. You have made summer and winter.

note: 'You will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search with all your heart' underlies v.27, that the nations 'should seek the Lord... and find him.'
sourceText: But from there you shall seek Yahweh your God, and you shall find him, when you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.

note: 'Seek the LORD while he may be found' parallels v.27's seek-and-find; recurrent prophetic summons.
sourceText: Seek Yahweh while he may be found; call you on him while he is near:

note: 'You will seek me and find me, when you seek with all your heart' parallels v.27; recurrent seek-and-find formula.
sourceText: You shall seek me, and find me, when you shall search for me with all your heart.

note: 'The LORD is near to all who call on him' grounds 'he is not far from each one of us' (v.27).
sourceText: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth.

note: 'Am I a God near at hand... and not a God far off? Do I not fill heaven and earth?' closely supports 'not far from each one of us' and the immanence of vv.27-28.
sourceText: Am I a God at hand, says Yahweh, and not a God afar off? Can any hide himself in secret places so that I shall not see him? says Yahweh. Don’t I fill heaven and earth? says Yahweh.

note: 'What nation has a god so near to it as the LORD?' supports the nearness theme of v.27; faint.
sourceText: For what great nation is there, that has a god so near to them, as Yahweh our God is whenever we call on him?

note: 'To whom will you liken God?... a craftsman casts an idol, a goldsmith overlays it with gold' directly grounds v.29, that the Divine Nature is not 'like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art.'
sourceText: To whom then will you liken God? Or what likeness will you compare to him? A workman has cast an image, and the goldsmith overlays it with gold, and casts silver chains for it. He who is too impoverished for such an offering chooses a tree that will not rot. He seeks a skillful workman to set up an engraved image for him that will not be moved.

note: The craftsman who fashions a god from wood/metal stands behind v.29's rejection of images 'engraved by art and design of man.'
sourceText: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]

note: Idols 'the work of human hands, wood and stone, which neither see nor hear' parallels v.29's gold, silver, and stone made by human craft.
sourceText: There you shall serve gods, the work of men’s hands, wood and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.

note: 'To whom will you liken me?... they hire a goldsmith who makes it into a god' parallels v.29; recurrent Isaianic idol-polemic.
sourceText: “To whom will you liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like? Some pour out gold from the bag, and weigh silver in the balance. They hire a goldsmith, and he makes it a god. They fall down—yes, they worship. They bear it on the shoulder, they carry it, and set it in its place, and it stands, from its place it shall not move: yes, one may cry to it, yet it can not answer, nor save him out of his trouble.

note: Wisdom's critique that people who admired the world's beauty failed to find its Maker, yet are 'not to be excused' because they could seek and find, closely tracks vv.24-29 (knowing the Creator from creation, seeking and finding). The deuterocanonical natural-theology bridge is the nearest analogue to the whole Areopagus argument.
sourceText: For verily all men by nature were but vain who had no perception of God, And from the good things that are seen they gained not power to know him that is, Neither by giving heed to the works did they recognize the architect; But either fire, or wind, or swift air, Or circling stars, or raging water, or luminaries of heaven, They thought to be gods that rule the world. And if it was through delight in their beauty that they took them to be gods, Let them […]

note: 'Miserable... who called gods the works of human hands, gold and silver fashioned with skill, and likenesses of animals, or useless stone' is verbally very close to v.29's gold, silver, and stone shaped by human art.
sourceText: But miserable were they, and in dead things were their hopes, Who called them gods which are works of men’s hands, Gold and silver, wrought with careful are, and likenesses of animals, Or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand.

note: 'You overlook the sins of men, that they may repent' parallels v.30, God 'overlooked' the times of ignorance and now commands repentance.
sourceText: But you have mercy on all men, because you have power to do all things, And you overlookest the sins of men to the end they may repent.

note: Faint contact with the call to overlook ignorance and turn; weak link to v.30.
sourceText: Remember the commandments, and be not angry with your neighbor; And remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.

note: 'He comes to judge the earth; he will judge the world in righteousness' is almost verbatim with v.31, that God 'will judge the world in righteousness.' High volume.
sourceText: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.

note: 'He will judge the world in righteousness' is a near-exact verbal parallel to v.31; recurrence of this formula across the Psalter strengthens the link.
sourceText: He will judge the world in righteousness. He will administer judgment to the peoples in uprightness.

note: 'He comes to judge the earth; he will judge the world with righteousness' is the third near-identical parallel to v.31, confirming a fixed liturgical formula behind Paul's words.
sourceText: Let them sing before Yahweh, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.

note: 'He will judge the peoples with equity' reinforces the universal-righteous-judgment theme of v.31.
sourceText: Say among the nations, “Yahweh reigns.” The world is also established. It can’t be moved. He will judge the peoples with equity.

note: Judgment 'by the man whom he has ordained' evokes the installed/anointed son to whom the nations are given; coherent with the appointed agent of v.31.
sourceText: “Yet I have set my King on my holy hill of Zion.” I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father. Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance, the uttermost parts of the earth for your possession. You shall break them with a rod of iron. You shall dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel.”

note: Judgment of the world entrusted to 'the man' (anthropos) recalls the son of man given everlasting dominion and judgment; supports the human appointed judge of v.31.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: 'God will bring every deed into judgment' supports the coming-judgment theme of v.31; faint, no verbal contact.
sourceText: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.

note: The Athenians' reaction to 'the resurrection of the dead' brushes the OT bodily-resurrection hope of those who 'sleep in the dust' awakening; thematic background only, no verbal borrowing in the narrative response.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: 'Your dead shall live... the earth will give birth to the dead' is the prophetic resurrection hope behind the doctrine the philosophers mock; faint.
sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

note: Paul reasons in the synagogue 'every Sabbath' (v.4); the rhythm of weekly Sabbath gathering presupposes the Decalogue's Sabbath command. Faint and institutional rather than verbal, but the Sabbath frame is the OT scaffolding for the scene.
sourceText: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.

note: Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla and works as a tentmaker (vv.2-3), earning bread by the labor of his own hands. A faint resonance with the Edenic decree of toil/sweat; the motif of apostolic self-support by manual labor draws on the dignity-and-burden-of-work theme rooted here.
sourceText: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

note: Paul 'shook out his clothing' (garment) as a prophetic sign-act against those who oppose him — directly mirroring Nehemiah shaking out the fold of his robe as a curse-gesture: 'So may God shake out everyone... who does not perform this promise.' A symbolic disavowal handing the consequences back on the offenders.
sourceText: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.

note: 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean' transposes the watchman oracle: the warned who ignore the trumpet bear their own blood, while the faithful watchman has delivered his soul. Paul casts himself as the discharged watchman, his hearers as the warned-but-unheeding.
sourceText: then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet, and doesn’t take warning, if the sword come, and take him away, his blood shall be on his own head.

note: The watchman who warns the wicked and is not heeded 'has delivered his soul' — exactly Paul's claim 'I am clean.' Recurrence with Ezekiel 33:4 strengthens the watchman frame.
sourceText: Nevertheless, if you warn the wicked of his way to turn from it, and he doesn’t turn from his way; he shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.

note: The original commissioning of the watchman: if he warns and the wicked does not turn, 'you will have delivered your soul.' Paul's 'I am clean / your blood on your heads' draws on this earlier statement of the same principle.
sourceText: When I tell the wicked, You shall surely die; and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at your hand.

note: 'Your blood be on your own head' is David's verdict on the Amalekite — the same idiom of self-incurred bloodguilt that Paul pronounces over the resisting synagogue.
sourceText: David said to him, “Your blood be on your head; for your mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I have slain Yahweh’s anointed.’”

note: The recurring legal formula 'his blood shall be upon him' (cf. vv.11-13,16,27) is the juridical source of the 'blood on your own head' idiom of self-responsibility that Paul invokes.
sourceText: “‘For everyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death: he has cursed his father or his mother; his blood shall be upon him.

note: Rahab's covenant: anyone who goes out of the house, 'his blood shall be on his own head,' while the household is held guiltless — the same shifting-of-bloodguilt formula behind Paul's declaration.
sourceText: It shall be that whoever goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood will be on his head, and we will be guiltless. Whoever is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head, if any hand is on him.

note: 'His blood shall be upon himself' in the chapter on individual responsibility reinforces the bloodguilt idiom underlying Paul's words.
sourceText: has lent on interest, and has taken increase; shall he then live? he shall not live: he has done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be on him.

note: The night-vision reassurance 'Do not be afraid... for I am with you' is the classic divine-encouragement formula, of which Isaiah 41:10 ('Fear not, for I am with you... I will strengthen you') is the paradigm. Paul stands in the line of those summoned and steadied by God's presence.
sourceText: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.

note: Jeremiah's prophetic call: 'Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you.' Paul's commission to keep speaking despite opposition echoes the prophet's reassurance against hostile hearers.
sourceText: Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh.

note: 'They will fight against you but will not prevail, for I am with you' closely matches 'no one will attack you to harm you, for I am with you' — the same promise of protected speech in a hostile city.
sourceText: They will fight against you; but they will not prevail against you; for I am with you”, says Yahweh, “to deliver you.”

note: 'I will be with you' grounds Moses' sending; the same assurance underwrites Paul's mission in Corinth. The call-narrative pattern (objection met by promise of presence) shapes the vision.
sourceText: He said, “Certainly I will be with you. This will be the token to you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain.”

note: Closest single parallel: the LORD appears to Isaac by night and says, 'Do not be afraid, for I am with you... I will multiply your offspring.' Night theophany + 'fear not' + 'I am with you' + promise of a great people maps almost point-for-point onto vv.9-10, including 'I have many people in this city.'
sourceText: Yahweh appeared to him the same night, and said, “I am the God of Abraham your father. Don’t be afraid, for I am with you, and will bless you, and multiply your seed for my servant Abraham’s sake.”

note: 'Do not be frightened... for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go' — the commissioning encouragement to a leader facing a daunting task, reused for Paul.
sourceText: Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid, neither be dismayed: for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.”

note: 'Do not fear... for the LORD your God goes with you; he will not leave you' belongs to the same 'fear not / I am with you' tradition behind the vision.
sourceText: Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or scared of them; for Yahweh your God himself is who goes with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.”

note: 'Fear not, for I am with you' paired with gathering a people resonates with both the reassurance and the promise of 'many people in this city.'
sourceText: Don’t be afraid; for I am with you. I will bring your seed from the east, and gather you from the west.

note: Paul is haled before the tribunal by accusers who 'rose up' with malicious charges — the lament motif of malicious witnesses rising against the righteous sufferer ('Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things I do not know').
sourceText: Unrighteous witnesses rise up. They ask me about things that I don’t know about.

note: The concerted false accusation 'with one accord' before the judgment seat faintly recalls the law against joining a multitude to bring a malicious/false charge.
sourceText: “You shall not spread a false report. Don’t join your hand with the wicked to be a malicious witness.

note: Paul 'shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow' — the Nazirite practice of shaving the head at the completion/discharge of a vow. Numbers 6:18 specifies shaving the consecrated head; the detail marks Paul's continued observance of Torah piety.
sourceText: The Nazirite shall shave the head of his separation at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and shall take the hair of the head of his separation, and put it on the fire which is under the sacrifice of peace offerings.

note: The Nazirite law that no razor touch the head during the vow's duration (the hair grown then shaved) underlies the haircut-as-vow-completion in v.18. Recurrence with Numbers 6:18 anchors the Nazirite frame.
sourceText: “‘All the days of his vow of separation no razor shall come on his head, until the days are fulfilled, in which he separates himself to Yahweh. He shall be holy. He shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow long.

note: Paul's resolve to 'keep this coming feast in Jerusalem' (v.21) reflects the pilgrimage-feast obligation to appear before the LORD at the appointed feasts in Jerusalem.
sourceText: Three times in a year all of your shall males appear before Yahweh your God in the place which he chooses: in the feast of unleavened bread, in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tents. They shall not appear before Yahweh empty.

note: The thrice-yearly command to appear before the Lord undergirds Paul's intention to keep the feast in Jerusalem; faint and institutional.
sourceText: Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord Yahweh.

note: Apollos, 'mighty in the Scriptures,' speaks boldly in the synagogue and publicly refutes opponents from Scripture — resonating with the psalmist's resolve to 'speak of your testimonies before kings and not be put to shame.' Faint thematic, no verbal borrowing.
sourceText: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.

note: The Spirit comes upon the twelve disciples and they prophesy and speak in other tongues. Joel's promise of the outpoured Spirit producing prophecy (Volume: shared Spirit-prophecy idiom; Recurrence: this is Luke's programmatic Pentecost text from Acts 2, re-applied here to a 'second Pentecost' at Ephesus; Thematic Coherence: strong, the Spirit poured on believers issuing in prophetic speech). Satisfaction: the Ephesian episode reads as a deliberate echo of the Joel fulfillment Luke announced in Acts 2.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.

note: When the Spirit rests on the seventy elders they prophesy; here the Spirit comes and the twelve prophesy. The corporate, derivative bestowal of the Spirit producing immediate prophecy is a close conceptual match (Volume: moderate; Recurrence: Luke elsewhere draws on Numbers 11 Moses/spirit motifs; Coherence: high). Moses' wish that all the Lord's people were prophets stands behind Luke's spreading-Spirit theology.
sourceText: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more. But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on them; and they were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran, and told […]

note: Paul lays his hands on the disciples and the Spirit comes; Moses lays hands on Joshua, a man in whom is the Spirit, transferring authority. The laying-on-of-hands-to-convey-Spirit gesture has its primary OT root here (with Deut 34:9). Low volume, contested as it may simply be a fixed cultic gesture.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]

note: Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him; here laying on of hands conveys the Spirit. Reinforces the Mosaic hand-laying/Spirit-transfer pattern. Low volume, contested.
sourceText: Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as Yahweh commanded Moses.

note: The Spirit of the Lord rushes upon Saul and he prophesies, turned into another man; here the Spirit comes and the disciples prophesy. A stock OT pattern of Spirit-onset producing ecstatic prophecy. Contested, faint verbal contact.
sourceText: and the Spirit of Yahweh will come mightily on you, and you shall prophesy with them, and shall be turned into another man.

note: Paul explains John's baptism as preparatory, pointing to the Coming One. John's whole ministry is grounded in the Isaian voice preparing the way; this verse explicitly recalls the forerunner role. Faint here since the verbal weight is minimal in this pericope.
sourceText: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.

note: Paul preaches boldly in the synagogue until some are hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way; Ezekiel is told the house of Israel will not listen because they are hard of forehead and stubborn of heart. The hardened-hearer motif of the prophet's rejected word is strongly coherent (Volume: shared hardening/refusal language; Recurrence: Luke uses Israel-hardening as a structuring theme in Acts; Coherence: high).
sourceText: But the house of Israel will not listen to you; for they will not listen to me: for all the house of Israel are obstinate and hard-hearted.

note: The hardening of those who hear the word, leading the messenger to turn elsewhere, echoes Isaiah's commission to a people whose heart is made fat and will not understand. Luke cites this text explicitly in Acts 28 as the climactic interpretation of Jewish unbelief, making it a recurring lens here. Coherence high; verbal contact in this pericope is allusive.
sourceText: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: Paul reasons and persuades about the Kingdom of God for three months. Daniel's God of heaven who sets up an everlasting kingdom is a chief OT source of the kingdom-of-God language. Faint, since the phrase is summary. Contested.
sourceText: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.

note: Over two years all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord; Isaiah's word that goes out and does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose underlies Luke's repeated 'the word spread/grew' refrain. Faint here, fuller at 19:20. Contested.
sourceText: so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: Cloths that had touched Paul's body heal the sick and expel spirits; mere contact with Elisha's bones revives a dead man. The motif of healing power mediated through physical contact with a holy person (even at a remove) is a strong conceptual parallel to the Elisha cycle (Volume: shared contact-healing logic; Recurrence: Luke models Paul/Peter on Elijah-Elisha; Coherence: high).
sourceText: As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.

note: Elisha sends his staff (an extension of himself) ahead to heal, then heals by bodily contact; here objects from Paul's body carry healing virtue. The mediating-object pattern links the two. Low volume, contested.
sourceText: Then he said to Gehazi, “Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my staff in your hand, and go your way. If you meet any man, don’t greet him; and if anyone greets you, don’t answer him again. Then lay my staff on the face of the child.” The mother of the child said, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” He arose, and followed her. Gehazi passed on before them, and laid the staff on the face of the child; but there was neither […]

note: Elijah's mantle, a garment of the holy man, works miracle when applied; Paul's handkerchiefs and aprons function similarly as charged garments. Faint, contested.
sourceText: Elijah took his mantle, and wrapped it together, and struck the waters, and they were divided here and there, so that they two went over on dry ground.

note: Jewish exorcists invoke the name of the Lord Jesus illegitimately and are violently humiliated; the prohibition against taking the divine name in vain stands behind the danger of wielding a holy name without authorization. Conceptual, low verbal contact. Contested.
sourceText: “You shall not take the name of Yahweh your God in vain, for Yahweh will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.

note: The outcome is that the name of the Lord Jesus is magnified; the psalmist's call to magnify the Lord and exalt his name supplies the idiom. Faint, formulaic. Contested.
sourceText: Oh magnify Yahweh with me. Let us exalt his name together.

note: The evil spirit overpowers the would-be exorcists who flee naked and wounded, exposing the impotence of those who presume on holy power; compare the humiliation of Dagon falling before the ark when the holy is mishandled by outsiders. Figural parallel of the sacred overpowering presumptuous handlers. Faint, contested.
sourceText: Now the Philistines had taken the ark of God, and they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. The Philistines took the ark of God, and brought it into the house of Dagon, and set it by Dagon. When they of Ashdod arose early on the next day, behold, Dagon was fallen on his face to the ground before Yahweh’s ark. They took Dagon, and set him in his place again. When they arose early on the next day morning, behold, Dagon was fallen on his face to the ground […]

note: Fear falls and the name of the Lord is magnified among Jews and Greeks alike; Malachi's vision of the Lord's name being great among the nations resonates with the name being exalted across ethnic lines at Ephesus. Faint, contested.
sourceText: For from the rising of the sun even to the going down of the same, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the nations,” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Magicians publicly renounce and burn their books of magical arts; Deuteronomy names sorcery, divination, and the practice of magic as detestable abominations to be purged from Israel. The repudiation of magic is the precise behavior the law demands (Volume: strong thematic match of magic-renunciation; Recurrence: Luke repeatedly opposes the gospel to magic, Simon in ch.8, Bar-Jesus in ch.13; Coherence: high). The book-burning enacts the Deuteronomic purge.
sourceText: There shall not be found with you anyone who makes his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, one who uses divination, one who practices sorcery, or an enchanter, or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or a consulter with a familiar spirit, or a wizard, or a necromancer. For whoever does these things is an abomination to Yahweh. Because of these abominations, Yahweh your God drives them out from before you.

note: The destruction of magical practice at Ephesus enacts the law's severe stance against sorcery, you shall not permit a sorceress to live. The Ephesians do not kill but burn the apparatus, yet the abolition of magic from the believing community is the same impulse. Coherence high; allusive.
sourceText: “You shall not allow a sorceress to live.

note: Believers turn from magical arts; Leviticus forbids turning to mediums and wizards lest one be defiled. The conversion-from-occult theme coheres strongly. Contested in that no single phrase is quoted.
sourceText: “‘Don’t turn to those who are mediums, nor to the wizards. Don’t seek them out, to be defiled by them. I am Yahweh your God.

note: Babylon's abundance of sorceries and enchantments cannot save her and will be burned like stubble; here the magicians' costly books (50,000 pieces of silver) are burned, the impotence of magic exposed before the word. A pointed figural parallel of magic consumed by fire. Contested.
sourceText: but these two things shall come to you in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood; in their full measure shall they come on you, in the multitude of your sorceries, and the great abundance of your enchantments. For you have trusted in your wickedness; you have said, No one sees me; your wisdom and your knowledge, it has perverted you, and you have said in your heart, I am, and there is no one else besides me. Therefore evil will come on […]

note: I will cut off sorceries from your hand, and you shall have no more soothsayers; the eschatological cleansing of magic from God's people is enacted at Ephesus. Faint, contested.
sourceText: I will destroy witchcraft from your hand; and you shall have no soothsayers.

note: Believers come confessing and declaring their deeds; whoever confesses and forsakes his sins obtains mercy. The open confession-and-renunciation pattern coheres. Faint, contested.
sourceText: He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.

note: So the word of the Lord grew mightily and prevailed; Isaiah's effectual word that accomplishes God's purpose underlies Luke's growth refrain. Faint, formulaic. Contested.
sourceText: so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: Paul resolves in the spirit on a journey culminating at Jerusalem and Rome, the imperial center; Daniel's vision of God's kingdom set up in the days of the Gentile empires gives a backdrop to the gospel's march toward Rome. Very faint, contested.
sourceText: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.

note: Demetrius's silversmiths make shrines of Artemis, and Paul has taught that gods made with hands are no gods; Isaiah's great satire on the craftsman who fashions an idol with his own hands and then worships it is the controlling OT polemic (Volume: strong, the made-with-hands idol-craftsman is the shared center; Recurrence: idol-polemic recurs across Isaiah and the Psalms which Luke knows; Coherence: very high, the economic self-interest of the idol-trade mirrors Isaiah's irony). Plausibility and satisfaction: this is the classic prophetic mockery of manufactured deity.
sourceText: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]

note: Idols are the work of the craftsman's hands, silver and gold, decked and unable to act; the silversmith is put to shame by his idols. Demetrius the silver craftsman and his guild embody exactly this trade. Strong thematic and lexical coherence (silver, craftsman, the work of human hands). Plausible and satisfying as the source of Paul's 'no gods made with hands.'
sourceText: Hear the word which Yahweh speaks to you, house of Israel! Thus says Yahweh, “Don’t learn the way of the nations, and don’t be dismayed at the signs of the sky; for the nations are dismayed at them. For the customs of the peoples are vanity; for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman with the ax. They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it not move. They are like a palm tree, […]

note: Can man make gods for himself? Such are no gods. Paul's words that they are no gods which are made with hands stand remarkably close to Jeremiah's rhetorical denial. Volume high for the specific phrase; contested only because it is a stock prophetic commonplace.
sourceText: Shall a man make to himself gods, which yet are no gods?

note: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands; those who make them become like them. The silver-shrine trade and the made-with-hands charge directly invoke this psalm's idol-satire. Strong coherence and recurrence (paired with Ps 135).
sourceText: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.

note: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands, mouths that cannot speak; a near-twin of Ps 115 reinforcing the made-with-hands polemic against the silver Artemis shrines. Coherence high.
sourceText: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they can’t speak. They have eyes, but they can’t see. They have ears, but they can’t hear; neither is there any breath in their mouths. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.

note: Deuterocanonical satire on the artisan who shapes a worthless image and prays to it for his livelihood; Demetrius openly admits the cult is his source of wealth (v.25). Wisdom's link between idol-craft and economic dependence on dead images is the closest ancient parallel to the silversmiths' protest. Strong coherence; Luke and Paul plausibly stand in this Hellenistic-Jewish idol-polemic tradition.
sourceText: But miserable were they, and in dead things were their hopes, Who called them gods which are works of men’s hands, Gold and silver, wrought with careful are, and likenesses of animals, Or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand. Yes and if some woodcutter, having sawn down a tree that is easily moved, Skilfully strippeth away all its bark, And fashioning it in comely form makes a vessel useful for the service of life; And burning the refuse of his […]

note: Cursed is the idol and the one who made it; the made object and its maker condemned together. Coheres with the indictment of the manufactured Artemis. Contested.
sourceText: But the idol made with hands is accursed, itself and he that made it; Because his was the working, and the corruptible thing was named a god:

note: The potter/craftsman who molds gods for gain, knowing he sins, caring only for profit; Demetrius's frank appeal to profit from the shrine-trade matches Wisdom's portrait of the mercenary idol-maker. Strong thematic coherence; contested as one of several overlapping idol texts.
sourceText: For a potter, kneading soft earth, Laboriously mouldeth each several vessel for our service: Nay, out of the same clay does he fashion Both the vessels that minister to clean uses, and those of a contrary sort, All in like manner; But what shall be the use of each vessel of either sort, The craftsman himself is the judge. And also, laboring to an evil end, he mouldeth a vain god out of the same clay, He who, having but a little before been made of earth, […]

note: They lavish gold and weigh out silver, hire a goldsmith to make a god, then bow down; it cannot move or save. The silversmith hiring out his craft to make a deity matches Demetrius's guild. Coherence high; contested among the cluster.
sourceText: Some pour out gold from the bag, and weigh silver in the balance. They hire a goldsmith, and he makes it a god. They fall down—yes, they worship. They bear it on the shoulder, they carry it, and set it in its place, and it stands, from its place it shall not move: yes, one may cry to it, yet it can not answer, nor save him out of his trouble.

note: What profit is an idol when its maker has shaped it, a teacher of lies, woe to him who says to wood Awake; the futility of the crafted image the maker trusts. Coheres with the made-with-hands theme. Contested.
sourceText: “What value does the engraved image have, that its maker has engraved it; the molten image, even the teacher of lies, that he who fashions its form trusts in it, to make mute idols? Woe to him who says to the wood, ‘Awake!’ or to the mute stone, ‘Arise!’ Shall this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in its midst.

note: There you will serve gods, the work of men's hands, wood and stone, which neither see nor hear; the made-with-hands formula. Faint, contested, part of the cluster.
sourceText: There you shall serve gods, the work of men’s hands, wood and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.

note: The crowd cries Great is Artemis of the Ephesians with one voice for about two hours; the prophets of Baal call on their god from morning until noon, O Baal hear us, raving in vain while no one answers. The prolonged, frenzied, futile invocation of a powerless deity is a striking figural parallel exposing the impotence of the idol (Volume: shared marathon-cry of pagan devotees; Coherence: high). Satisfaction: Luke's reader hears the Carmel irony behind the Ephesian shouting.
sourceText: They took the bull which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, “Baal, hear us!” But there was no voice, nor any who answered. They leaped about the altar which was made. At noon, Elijah mocked them, and said, “Cry aloud; for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he has gone aside, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he sleeps and must be awakened.” They cried aloud, and cut themselves in […]

note: The whole city is thrown into uproar and rushes together in confusion; why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain. The raging Gentile mob set against the Lord's work fits the psalm's tumult of the nations. Faint, contested.
sourceText: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?

note: A confused mass shouting and surging in devotion to a false god recalls the noise of the camp at the golden calf, a tumult of idolatrous celebration. Figural and faint. Contested.
sourceText: When Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, “There is the noise of war in the camp.” He said, “It isn’t the voice of those who shout for victory, neither is it the voice of those who cry for being overcome; but the noise of those who sing that I hear.” As soon as he came near to the camp, he saw the calf and the dancing. Then Moses’ anger grew hot, and he threw the tablets out of his hands, and broke them beneath the […]

note: The town clerk appeals to the image of Artemis that fell from heaven (Diopetes); Isaiah's satire that the idol is in truth a manufactured object stands in tension with the civic claim of a heaven-fallen image, underscoring the irony Luke wants the reader to feel. Faint here, fuller at 19:23-27. Contested.
sourceText: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]

note: The town clerk quiets and stills the roaring multitude; only God stills the roaring of the seas and the tumult of the peoples. A faint figural touch on the stilling of crowd-tumult. Contested.
sourceText: who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, and the turmoil of the nations.

note: The clerk urges them to be quiet and do nothing rash; a wise man holds back the fool's outburst of anger. Faint sapiential resonance. Contested.
sourceText: A fool vents all of his anger, but a wise man brings himself under control.

note: Luke dates the Troas voyage 'after the days of Unleavened Bread,' invoking the Passover/Massot calendar prescribed here. The festival reference is precise and structural (it anchors the chronology), though it functions as a time-marker rather than an interpretive citation; volume is moderate, recurrence in Luke-Acts of festal dating is real (cf. Pentecost in v.16).
sourceText: “‘Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even the first day you shall put away yeast out of your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel. You have not performed the duty of my holy things; but you have set performers of my duty in my sanctuary for yourselves. Thus says the Lord Yahweh, No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and […]

note: The lethal seriousness of the crowd ('trying to kill him') over an outsider entering sacred precincts reflects the Pentateuchal death sanction against the unauthorized approaching the sanctuary; thematic background to the temple's exclusion zones, low verbal volume.
sourceText: When the tabernacle is to move, the Levites shall take it down; and when the tabernacle is to be set up, the Levites shall set it up. The stranger who comes near shall be put to death.

note: The tumult in the temple courts, seizing and dragging Paul out, and the doors immediately shut faintly evoke the OT scenes of the sanctuary overrun and its gates violated; atmospheric resonance only, no verbal borrowing.
sourceText: The Lord has cast off his altar, he has abhorred his sanctuary; He has given up into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces: They have made a noise in Yahweh’s house, as in the day of a solemn assembly.

note: The crowd brands Paul the man who teaches 'against the people, and the law, and this place,' casting him as a troubler of Israel — the same accusation Ahab levels at Elijah ('troubler of Israel'). Faint thematic parallel of the faithful prophet charged with subverting the nation.
sourceText: When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, “Is that you, you troubler of Israel?” He answered, “I have not troubled Israel; but you, and your father’s house, in that you have forsaken the commandments of Yahweh, and you have followed the Baals.

note: Paul's request to address the hostile crowd, beckoning for silence before a defense, faintly recalls the OT pattern of the divinely commissioned spokesman who must speak to a resistant people; the connection is typological and weak, with no verbal borrowing.
sourceText: Moses said to Yahweh, “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.”

note: Paul's speaking 'in the Hebrew language' to the people signals covenant identity and the language of Israel; Nehemiah's concern over loss of the language of Judah supplies a faint thematic backdrop to Hebrew speech as a marker of belonging, though no quotation is involved.
sourceText: and their children spoke half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews’ language, but according to the language of each people.

note: Paul's self-description as 'zealous for God' (v3) echoes Elijah's signature self-defense, 'I have been very zealous for the LORD' — the OT idiom of cultic zeal that justified violence against deviants, which Paul applies to his persecuting career. Coherent with the chapter's portrait of misdirected zeal; verbal contact via 'zealous.'
sourceText: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

note: Phinehas' zeal that turned away wrath is the paradigm of violent piety standing behind 'zealous for God, even as you all are' — the very zealotry that drove Paul to bind men and women. Thematic only, no verbal borrowing; contested as background rather than allusion.
sourceText: “Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I didn’t consume the children of Israel in my jealousy. Therefore say, ‘Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace.
