note: 'the law of our fathers' (v3), anticipating 'the God of our fathers' in v14, draws on the patriarchal-covenant formula whose anchor is Exodus 3:15. Faint here; the formula lands more fully in the Ananias speech.
sourceText: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.

note: 'instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers' rests on the Mosaic law as the ancestral inheritance of Israel; Deut 33:4 ('the law Moses commanded, the inheritance of the assembly of Jacob') supplies the conception. Background, contested.
sourceText: Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.

note: The doubled vocative 'Saul, Saul' (v7) follows the OT pattern of urgent divine address by repeated name — 'Abraham, Abraham' at the binding of Isaac. The form signals a theophanic call/redirection. Recurs across the OT call narratives below.
sourceText: Yahweh’s angel called to him out of the sky, and said, “Abraham, Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.”

note: 'Moses, Moses' from the burning bush is the closest formal parallel: a doubled-name call out of blinding/luminous divine presence that commissions the hearer. Strong thematic and formal coherence with Paul's vocation-by-theophany.
sourceText: When Yahweh saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the midst of the bush, and said, “Moses! Moses!” He said, “Here I am.”

note: 'Samuel, Samuel' — doubled-name nocturnal call of the prophet who must learn the LORD's identity ('Speak, for your servant hears') just as Paul asks 'Who are you, Lord?' Reinforces the recurrence of the call-form.
sourceText: Yahweh came, and stood, and called as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” Then Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.”

note: The overwhelming light/glory before which Paul 'fell to the ground' (v7) reproduces Ezekiel's response to 'the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD' — 'I fell on my face.' Theophanic glory + prostration is the shared structure inaugurating prophetic commission.
sourceText: As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh’s glory. When I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard a voice of one that spoke.

note: Daniel's vision: he alone sees it, his companions flee in terror, his strength fails, he falls to the ground at the voice — closely matching v7-9 where the light fells Paul, his companions see the light and are afraid but do not grasp the voice. Notable volume.
sourceText: So I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me; for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength. Yet heard I the voice of his words; and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I fallen into a deep sleep on my face, with my face toward the ground.

note: Covenant-curse blindness ('the LORD will strike you with blindness... you shall grope at noonday') resonates with Paul struck sightless 'about noon' (v6, 11), led by the hand. Ironic inversion — judgment-blindness becomes the threshold of conversion. Contested verbal link via 'noon'/'blindness.'
sourceText: Yahweh will strike you with madness, with blindness, and with astonishment of heart. You will grope at noonday, as the blind gropes in darkness, and you shall not prosper in your ways. You will only be oppressed and robbed always, and there will be no one to save you.

note: Ananias' 'The God of our fathers has appointed you' (v14) deploys the patriarchal covenant title fixed at the burning bush ('the God of your fathers... my name forever'), grounding Paul's commission in Israel's God. Verbal formula and thematic coherence.
sourceText: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.

note: 'to see the Righteous One' (v14) draws on the Servant who 'shall make many to be accounted righteous,' titled the righteous one; the Suffering Servant title is applied christologically to the one Paul is to witness. Coheres with the chapter's commissioning frame.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

note: 'calling on the name of the Lord' (v16) quotes the Joel formula ('everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved'), already programmatic in Acts; here bound to baptism and the washing away of sins. Clear verbal contact.
sourceText: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.

note: 'wash away your sins' (v16) echoes 'Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove the evil of your deeds' — the prophetic call to cleansing. Verbal overlap on 'wash'; thematic coherence with repentance.
sourceText: Wash yourselves, make yourself clean. Put away the evil of your doings from before my eyes. Cease to do evil.

note: 'I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses' supplies the cultic-cleansing background for baptismal washing-away of sins. Contested as direct echo versus shared motif.
sourceText: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.

note: Paul's temple vision in a trance, seeing the Lord and being sent (v17-21), maps onto Isaiah's temple theophany and commission ('I saw the Lord... Whom shall I send?... Go'). Setting (temple), visionary mode, sending command, and a hardened audience that 'will not receive' all converge — a deliberate prophetic-call form.
sourceText: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was […]

note: 'I will send you out far from here to the Gentiles' (v21) reprises the Servant's mandate to be 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.' Acts elsewhere quotes this verse for the Gentile mission; here it shapes the climactic sending. High thematic coherence and recurrence.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: The Servant's call ('The LORD called me from the womb... Listen, O coastlands, from far away') underlies both Paul's vocation-by-vision and the 'far away' geography of v21. Recurs with Jer 1:5 as the womb-call topos behind Pauline self-understanding.
sourceText: Listen, islands, to me; and listen, you peoples, from far: Yahweh has called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother has he made mention of my name:

note: Jeremiah's appointment as 'a prophet to the nations' with the divine 'to all to whom I send you, you shall go' is the classic prophetic commission form mirrored in 'I will send you out... to the Gentiles' (v21). Strong formal coherence.
sourceText: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.” Then I said, “Ah, Lord Yahweh! note: The Lord's warning 'they will not receive testimony concerning me from you' (v18) reproduces Ezekiel's sending to a people who 'will not be willing to listen to you' — the prophet rejected by his own. Thematic and near-verbal.
sourceText: But the house of Israel will not listen to you; for they will not listen to me: for all the house of Israel are obstinate and hard-hearted.

note: 'I will send survivors... to the nations... to the coastlands far away, who have not heard my fame' anchors the sending-to-distant-Gentiles motif of v21. Contested as direct echo versus shared Isaianic mission theme.
sourceText: “I will set a sign among them, and I will send such as escape of them to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the islands afar off, who have not heard my fame, neither have seen my glory; and they shall declare my glory among the nations.

note: The crowd 'threw dust into the air' (v23) as a gesture of extreme distress/outrage parallels Job's friends who 'sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven.' Shared mourning/protest ritual; visible volume.
sourceText: When they lifted up their eyes from a distance, and didn’t recognize him, they raised their voices, and wept; and they each tore his robe, and sprinkled dust on their heads toward the sky.

note: The elders of Zion 'have cast dust on their heads' in grief — the OT dust gesture standing behind the mob's throwing of dust. Contested; one of several dust-ritual parallels.
sourceText: The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground, they keep silence; They have cast up dust on their heads; they have clothed themselves with sackcloth: The virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground.

sourceText: and shall cause their voice to be heard over you, and shall cry bitterly, and shall cast up dust on their heads, they shall wallow themselves in the ashes:

High Volume (formula + verbatim match) and high Thematic Coherence (Paul submits to the Torah he is accused of violating). Recurrence: the same verse underlies Eccl 10:20. Plausible and historically apt for a Pharisee.
sourceText: “You shall not blaspheme God, nor curse a ruler of your people.

Strong Volume (the rare 'whitewash'/wall image) and Thematic Coherence (Ananias, who orders an unlawful blow while presiding 'to judge by the law,' is exposed as a whitewashed hypocrite under judgment). sourceText: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.

note: The unlawful 'strike on the mouth' inverts Deut's regulation that corporal punishment follow a judicial verdict 'according to his wrongdoing' — here Paul is struck before any verdict. Low Volume; the link rests on the contrast between lawful and lawless beating rather than verbal echo.
sourceText: If there is a controversy between men, and they come to judgment, and the judges judge them; then they shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked. note: 'I have lived before God in all good conscience until this day' resonates with the biblical ideal of walking 'before God' blamelessly (Gen 17:1; cf. 1 Kgs 9:4). Faint, idiomatic echo of covenantal integrity rather than a targeted citation; Volume is low.
sourceText: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless.

note: Paul's opening claim of a clear conscience before the assembly recalls Samuel's farewell protest of blameless conduct before all Israel ('whom have I defrauded?'). Thematic parallel of a leader on trial asserting integrity; low Volume, contested.

Dan 12:2 ('many who sleep in the dust shall awake, some to everlasting life') is the clearest OT bodily-resurrection text and the touchstone of the Pharisaic 'hope.' Strong Thematic Coherence and Recurrence (Paul ties his whole defense to this hope across Acts 23-26). Volume rests on the shared, distinctive doctrine rather than wording.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: 'Your dead shall live, their bodies shall rise' is a second pillar of OT resurrection hope underlying the Pharisaic confession Paul invokes. Good Thematic Coherence; medium confidence because Daniel 12 is the more direct referent and no wording is quoted.
sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

note: The vision of dry bones revived contributed to Second Temple resurrection belief and may stand behind the Pharisees' confession of resurrection. Low Volume (no verbal contact); included maximally as a contributing OT stream.

note: 'In my flesh I shall see God' is a classic proof-text for bodily resurrection in the very debate Paul provokes. Faint echo; cited for completeness of the resurrection-hope background.
sourceText: But as for me, I know that my Redeemer lives. In the end, he will stand upon the earth. After my skin is destroyed, then in my flesh shall I see God,

note: The night vision in which the Lord stands by Paul and says 'Take courage' (be of good cheer) follows the OT pattern of God commissioning a servant for a daunting journey with the charge to be strong/unafraid, classically Josh 1:6-9 at the threshold of a new mission. Medium Thematic Coherence (divine reassurance + mandate to 'go'); Volume moderate via the 'fear not / be strong' formula.
sourceText: “Be strong and courageous; for you shall cause this people to inherit the land which I swore to their fathers to give them. Only be strong and very courageous, to observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded you. Don’t turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may […]

note: 'Do not be afraid... for I am with you to deliver you' to a prophet sent to hostile authorities closely parallels the Lord's nighttime encouragement to Paul before his testimony to kings and Rome. Good coherence with Paul's prophetic-witness role; medium confidence as a type rather than a quotation.
sourceText: Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh.

note: 'That same night the LORD appeared to him and said, Do not fear, for I am with you' (to Isaac) is a tight formal parallel: a night theophany of reassurance. Low Volume but strong formal coherence; contested as a specific source.
sourceText: Yahweh appeared to him the same night, and said, “I am the God of Abraham your father. Don’t be afraid, for I am with you, and will bless you, and multiply your seed for my servant Abraham’s sake.”

note: 'Fear not, for I am with you' — the prototypical divine encouragement formula reflected in the Lord's 'Cheer up, Paul.' Faint, generic echo; low Volume.
sourceText: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.

note: The forty-plus conspirators bind themselves 'under a curse' (anathema) to eat and drink nothing until they kill Paul. This rash self-imprecatory food-oath echoes Saul's curse that no one eat until evening/until vengeance is done — an oath that scripture frames as misguided and self-entrapping. Medium Thematic Coherence (a reckless binding oath that cannot be kept); Volume rests on the shared curse-not-to-eat structure.
sourceText: The men of Israel were distressed that day; for Saul had adjured the people, saying, “Cursed is the man who eats any food until it is evening, and I am avenged of my enemies.” So none of the people tasted food.

note: 'They scheme together against me, plotting to take my life' matches the conspiracy 'lying in wait' to kill Paul. The lament-of-the-righteous-pursued pattern (Psalm of David, used in Acts' passion typology for the suffering witness) gives good coherence; medium confidence as thematic echo.
sourceText: For I have heard the slander of many, terror on every side, while they conspire together against me, they plot to take away my life.

note: 'Let us lie in wait for blood... swift to shed blood' portrays the bloodthirsty ambush the forty plan. Sapiential portrait of murderous conspirators; low Volume, no quotation, but apt coherence.
sourceText: If they say, “Come with us, Let’s lay in wait for blood; let’s lurk secretly for the innocent without cause; let’s swallow them up alive like Sheol, and whole, like those who go down into the pit. We’ll find all valuable wealth. We’ll fill our houses with plunder. You shall cast your lot among us. We’ll all have one purse.” My son, don’t walk on the path with them. Keep your foot from their path, for their feet run to evil. They hurry to shed blood.

note: The wicked who 'lurks in ambush... to seize the poor' mirrors the men who 'lie in wait' for Paul. Generic lament imagery of the ambushing wicked; faint echo, included maximally.
sourceText: He lies in wait near the villages. From ambushes, he murders the innocent. His eyes are secretly set against the helpless. He lurks in secret as a lion in his ambush. He lies in wait to catch the helpless. He catches the helpless, when he draws him in his net.

note: Lysias' elaborate night convoy (two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen) brings Paul 'safely' to Felix, thwarting the sworn plot — a narrative enactment of 'no wisdom or counsel can avail against the LORD; the horse is made ready for battle, but victory belongs to the LORD.' Low Volume, thematic/providential coherence with the divine assurance of v.11.
sourceText: There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against Yahweh. The horse is prepared for the day of battle; but victory is with Yahweh.

note: Paul's deliverance from violent enemies by armed rescue and removal to safety faintly echoes the deliverance-from-foes language of the royal/Davidic psalms ('you delivered me from my enemies... from the violent man'). Generic providence echo; low confidence, contested.
sourceText: He rescues me from my enemies. Yes, you lift me up above those who rise up against me. You deliver me from the violent man.

note: Tertullus and the elders bring formal, hostile charges against Paul before the governor; the situation of the righteous man delivered up to the will of false, violent accusers echoes the psalmist's cry against 'false witnesses' who 'breathe out cruelty.' Thematically coherent with the Lukan figural pattern of the just sufferer hauled before rulers; verbal volume is low, so echo rather than allusion.
sourceText: Don’t deliver me over to the desire of my adversaries, for false witnesses have risen up against me, such as breathe out cruelty.

note: 'Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things I know not.' The hired orator's manufactured indictment ('a plague,' 'instigator of insurrections,' temple-profaner) fits the lament topos of the innocent assailed by lying accusers. Recurs across Luke-Acts; no direct quotation, hence echo.
sourceText: Unrighteous witnesses rise up. They ask me about things that I don’t know about.

note: Paul is denounced as ringleader of 'the sect of the Nazarenes.' The title Nazarene is widely traced to the messianic netzer ('branch') of Isaiah's stump-of-Jesse oracle; the accusation thus carries, ironically, a hidden scriptural-messianic claim. Contested and indirect, voiced by opponents, so low confidence.
sourceText: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.

note: 'Wicked and deceitful mouths are opened against me... they encircle me with words of hatred.' The choreographed, flattering-then-accusing speech of Tertullus, joined by the assembled Jews, resonates with the imprecatory lament against encircling slanderers. Faint, no shared diction.
sourceText: for they have opened the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of deceit against me. They have spoken to me with a lying tongue. They have also surrounded me with words of hatred, and fought against me without a cause.

note: Paul stresses he went up 'to worship at Jerusalem' only days before, a pious pilgrim, not an agitator; the pilgrimage-to-Zion frame faintly recalls the Songs of Ascents ('let us go to the house of the LORD'). Thematic only, no verbal borrowing.
sourceText: I was glad when they said to me, “Let’s go to Yahweh’s house!”

note: 'Nor can they prove to you the things of which they accuse me' anticipates Paul's evidentiary appeal; the Deuteronomic rule that a charge stands only on established proof / multiple witnesses underlies his demand. Developed more fully in 24:19; here only incipient, hence low.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: Paul confesses he serves 'the God of our fathers' (ho theos ton pateron), the covenant self-designation given at the burning bush, 'the God of your fathers... my memorial to all generations.' High thematic coherence and recurrent formula; standard Septuagintal idiom Paul deliberately claims to assert continuity, not novelty.
sourceText: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.

note: 'There will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust' closely tracks Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt' — the locus classicus for a two-fold resurrection of righteous and wicked. High volume and thematic coherence; the bifurcation just/unjust is distinctively Danielic.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: 'Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise... the earth will give birth to the dead.' Paul's hope of bodily resurrection draws on this prophetic resurrection text alongside Daniel; supports the claim that his hope rests on 'the law and the prophets.' Medium: real thematic match, less verbal proximity than Daniel.
sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

note: 'We cried to the LORD, the God of our fathers' — the credal recital tying worship to the ancestral God reinforces Paul's 'God of our fathers' framing as covenant fidelity. Faint, overlaps with the Exodus 3:15 idiom.
sourceText: Then we cried to Yahweh, the God of our fathers. Yahweh heard our voice, and saw our affliction, our toil, and our oppression.

note: 'They ought to have been here before you, and to make accusation' — Paul invokes the legal principle that accusers must appear and a charge requires proper witnesses; the absent Asian Jews cannot satisfy the Deuteronomic requirement. Coherent with Mosaic judicial procedure; medium.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: Paul was 'found purified in the temple' with offerings; this reflects completion of a Nazirite-style vow of purification (cf. Acts 21:23-26), the rite of Numbers 6 requiring offerings at the sanctuary. Concrete ritual referent; medium.
sourceText: “‘All the days of his vow of separation no razor shall come on his head, until the days are fulfilled, in which he separates himself to Yahweh. He shall be holy. He shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow long.

note: Paul came 'to bring gifts for the needy to my nation' — almsgiving to the poor reflects the Torah's command to open the hand to the needy. Thematic, no verbal link.
sourceText: For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.

note: Paul reiterates that he is on trial 'concerning the resurrection of the dead,' recurring to the same Danielic hope voiced in 24:15; recurrence within the chapter strengthens the link. Echo here since the topic is named without restating the just/unjust formula.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: Felix keeps Paul in custody but grants him privileges and freedom to receive his friends — the imprisoned righteous man shown favor while detained typologically recalls Joseph, to whom the LORD gave favor in the prison-keeper's sight. No verbal borrowing; figural pattern of the just one preserved in confinement.
sourceText: But Yahweh was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him, and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison.

note: As Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, the ruler Felix 'was terrified' — recalling Belshazzar, before whom the prophetic word made the king's countenance change and his knees knock. The motif of God's spokesman striking dread into a powerful but compromised ruler is typologically apt; medium for thematic coherence.
sourceText: Then the king’s face was changed in him, and his thoughts troubled him; and the joints of his thighs were loosened, and his knees struck one against another.

note: Paul's reasoning about 'the judgment to come' echoes Qoheleth's conclusion that 'God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.' Coherent with the eschatological-accountability theme that unsettles Felix; medium.
sourceText: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.

note: Felix 'hoped that money would be given to him by Paul' — a corrupt judge angling for a bribe stands in direct contrast to the Torah's prohibition, 'You shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of the righteous.' Felix embodies the very corruption the law forbids; medium thematic coherence.
sourceText: “You shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds those who have sight and perverts the words of the righteous.

note: Paul preaching righteousness and judgment to the cohabiting Felix and Drusilla (Felix's union with a Jewess he had taken) recalls the prophet confronting a ruler over righteousness and unlawful marriage, as Nathan confronted David ('You are the man'). Figural pattern of bold prophetic confrontation; low, no diction.
sourceText: Nathan said to David, “You are the man. This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.

note: The chief priests press Festus to summon Paul to Jerusalem while 'plotting to kill him on the way' (v.3). The psalter's portrait of the wicked who 'watches the righteous and seeks to slay him' supplies the scriptural type of the ambush against the innocent man; verbal contact is slight, so this is a thematic echo rather than a quotation, and contested.
sourceText: The wicked watches the righteous, and seeks to kill him.

note: The lying-in-wait imagery (the wicked 'lurks... to seize the poor') matches the planned roadside ambush of Paul. A stock motif of the persecuted-righteous psalms; flagged contested for low volume.
sourceText: He lies in wait near the villages. From ambushes, he murders the innocent. His eyes are secretly set against the helpless. He lurks in secret as a lion in his ambush. He lies in wait to catch the helpless. He catches the helpless, when he draws him in his net.

note: Jeremiah, a prophet brought as a lamb to slaughter against whom his enemies 'devise devices,' is the classic prophetic prototype of the messenger targeted by a covert plot. Luke's Paul stands in this Jeremianic line of the rejected prophet; the link is figural-thematic, contested.
sourceText: But I was like a gentle lamb that is led to the slaughter; and I didn’t know that they had devised devices against me, saying, Let us destroy the tree with its fruit, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name may be no more remembered.

note: Enemies who 'take counsel together' against the righteous, saying God has forsaken him so they may pursue and seize him, parallel the priests' conspiracy. Faint, contested.
sourceText: For my enemies talk about me. Those who watch for my soul conspire together, saying, “God has forsaken him. Pursue and take him, for no one will rescue him.”

note: 'Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things I know not.' The Jews bring 'many and grievous charges which they could not prove' (v.7) — precisely the false, unsubstantiated accusation the persecuted-righteous psalmist faces. The strongest of the chapter's faint OT resonances; the unprovable-charge motif recurs through Luke's passion-and-trial pattern, giving it some thematic coherence. Still an echo rather than a citation.
sourceText: Unrighteous witnesses rise up. They ask me about things that I don’t know about.

note: 'False witnesses have risen against me, breathing out violence.' Reinforces the accused-but-innocent posture of Paul before the tribunal. Contested, low volume.
sourceText: Don’t deliver me over to the desire of my adversaries, for false witnesses have risen up against me, such as breathe out cruelty.

note: Paul's insistence that no one can simply 'give him up' without a true case (v.11), and his demand to be tried where charges can be tested, resonates with the Torah's law of witnesses and diligent inquiry into accusation. The principle surfaces explicitly in Festus' own summary (v.16); here it is the implied legal backdrop. Contested.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established. If an unrighteous witness rises up against any man to testify against him of wrongdoing, then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand before Yahweh, before the priests and the judges who shall be in those days; and the judges shall make […]

note: Paul submits himself to judgment, willing to die if guilty but appealing for vindication if innocent (vv.10-11), echoing the psalmist's plea 'judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness.' Faint, contested.
sourceText: Yahweh administers judgment to the peoples. Judge me, Yahweh, according to my righteousness, and to my integrity that is in me. Oh let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end, but establish the righteous; their minds and hearts are searched by the righteous God.

note: Festus states the Roman rule that one is not handed over 'before the accused has met the accusers face to face, and has had opportunity to make his defense' (v.16). This due-process principle — confrontation of accuser and accused, diligent inquiry — directly mirrors Deuteronomy's law of witnesses, so that Roman custom is narrated in terms a Scripture-shaped reader recognizes. Thematic, not verbal quotation.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established. If an unrighteous witness rises up against any man to testify against him of wrongdoing, then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand before Yahweh, before the priests and the judges who shall be in those days; and the judges shall make […]

note: The deuterocanonical Susanna dramatizes the same conviction — that no one should be condemned without examination and testing of the accusers — which Festus voices. A loose thematic parallel within the Jewish wisdom-and-justice tradition; contested.
sourceText: So he standing in the midst of them said, Are you such fools, you sons of Israel, that without examination or knowledge of the truth you have condemned a daughter of Israel? Return again to the place of judgement: for these have borne false witness against her. Wherefore all the people turned again in haste, and the elders said to him, Come, sit down among us, and show it us, seeing God has given you the honor of an elder. Then said Daniel to them, Put […]

note: Paul, the witness to the risen Christ, stands before a king (Agrippa), a governor (Festus), and the assembled rulers 'with great pomp.' The scene faintly evokes the psalm's kings and rulers gathered before the LORD's anointed and his messengers — a motif Acts has already cited at 4:25-26. Figural and contested; no verbal borrowing.
sourceText: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,

note: Paul stands trial 'for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers.' The covenant promise to the patriarchs — that in Abraham's seed all nations would be blessed — is the substance of that hope. Acts repeatedly anchors the promise to the patriarchs (cf. Acts 3:25; 13:32-33), and the language 'made to our fathers' points back to the Genesis covenant cycle.
sourceText: All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your seed, because you have obeyed my voice.”

note: 'Our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain' it. The 'twelve tribes' is the constitutive self-designation of restored Israel, rooted in the blessing of Jacob's sons; Paul presents the resurrection hope as the goal of the whole covenant people.
sourceText: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his blessing.

note: 'Why is it judged incredible with you, if God does raise the dead?' Daniel 12:2 is the clearest OT statement of bodily resurrection ('many of those who sleep in the dust shall awake'), the very Pharisaic hope Paul defends here and the hope shared by the twelve tribes.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: The resurrection hope of v.8 resonates with Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones revived — Israel's national hope cast as God raising the dead, which dovetails with Paul's framing of resurrection as the consummation of the covenant promise to the tribes.
sourceText: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]

note: The doubled vocative 'Saul, Saul' from heaven mirrors the theophanic double-address by which God calls his chosen agents — 'Moses, Moses' from the burning bush. The pattern (light/fire, voice, prostration, commission) frames Paul's conversion as a prophetic call-narrative.
sourceText: When Yahweh saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the midst of the bush, and said, “Moses! Moses!” He said, “Here I am.”

note: 'Samuel, Samuel' — the doubled name by which the LORD summons the boy Samuel to prophetic service reinforces the call-form behind 'Saul, Saul,' another reluctant or unwitting hearer drafted into divine commission.
sourceText: Yahweh came, and stood, and called as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” Then Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.”

note: Paul and his companions 'had all fallen to the earth' before a heavenly light and then heard a voice — exactly Ezekiel's response to the glory of the LORD: 'I fell upon my face, and I heard a voice of one that spoke.' The vision-then-voice sequence is the prophetic theophany template.
sourceText: As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh’s glory. When I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard a voice of one that spoke.

note: Daniel falls in a deep sleep with his face to the ground at the blinding appearance of the heavenly man, then is addressed and raised — the same overwhelmed prostration before a radiant figure that Paul reports on the Damascus road.
sourceText: Yet heard I the voice of his words; and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I fallen into a deep sleep on my face, with my face toward the ground.

note: The 'light from the sky, brighter than the sun' faintly recalls the eschatological intensification of light in Isaiah, where the light of the sun is sevenfold in the day of restoration — supernatural radiance as a sign of God's saving intervention.
sourceText: Moreover the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be seven times brighter, like the light of seven days, in the day that Yahweh binds up the fracture of his people, and heals the wound they were struck with.

note: 'It is hard for you to kick against the goads' is a proverb of Greek provenance, but some hear an echo of Jeshurun who 'kicked' against the LORD after being fattened — futile rebellion against God by the well-fed. The verbal link is slight and the source debated.
sourceText: But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked. You have grown fat. You have grown thick. You have become sleek. Then he abandoned God who made him, and rejected the Rock of his salvation.

note: 'But arise, and stand on your feet' verbally reproduces the LORD's words to Ezekiel ('Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I will speak to you... I send you to the children of Israel'). The commission of Paul is cast as a prophetic sending in Ezekiel's idiom.
sourceText: He said to me, Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you. The Spirit entered into me when he spoke to me, and set me on my feet; and I heard him who spoke to me. He said to me, Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, to a nation of rebels who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me even to this very day.

note: The heavenly messenger tells the prostrate Daniel to 'stand upright' to receive a revelation — the same raising-up-to-be-commissioned motif behind 'stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose.'
sourceText: He said to me, Daniel, you man greatly beloved, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright; for am I now sent to you. When he had spoken this word to me, I stood trembling.

note: 'Delivering you from the people, and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you' closely tracks Jeremiah's call: 'to all that I shall send you, you shall go... be not afraid of their faces: for I am with you to deliver you.' Both the sending and the promise of rescue are drawn from the prophet's commission.
sourceText: But Yahweh said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak. Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh.

note: 'To open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light' is lifted from the Servant's mandate: 'to open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house.' Paul's mission is the Servant's mission extended.
sourceText: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: 'Turn from darkness to light' echoes Isaiah 42:16, 'I will make darkness light before them' — the LORD leading the blind by a way they knew not, the same darkness-to-light transformation Paul is sent to effect.
sourceText: I will bring the blind by a way that they don’t know. I will lead them in paths that they don’t know. I will make darkness light before them, and crooked places straight. I will do these things, and I will not forsake them.

note: 'To appoint you a servant and a witness' draws on the Servant Song's 'Behold my servant... I have put my Spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.' Paul is appointed a servant in the Servant's pattern, with a Gentile commission.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.

note: 'A witness... of the things which you have seen' echoes 'You are my witnesses, says the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen' — the conjunction of 'servant' and 'witness' in Paul's call matches Isaiah's pairing exactly.
sourceText: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.

note: 'To open their eyes' resonates with the eschatological promise 'then the eyes of the blind shall be opened' — the restoration of sight as a sign of God's coming salvation, here applied to spiritual illumination of Jews and Gentiles.
sourceText: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.

note: 'Turn from darkness to light' recalls 'the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light; they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them has the light shined' — the prophetic image of light dawning on those in darkness.
sourceText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: The cluster 'open their eyes... receive remission of sins' faintly recalls the Servant-Anointed's mission to proclaim liberty to captives and opening of the prison — release and forgiveness as the substance of the sent one's task.
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

note: 'An inheritance among those who are sanctified' echoes the deuterocanonical 'how is he numbered among the children of God, and his lot is among the saints (holy ones)' — the lot/inheritance among the sanctified as the believer's destiny.
sourceText: How was he counted among sons of God? And how is his lot among saints?

note: 'Saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen' invokes Moses as a witness to the coming Christ; the Mosaic promise of a prophet 'like me' whom Israel must heed stands behind the appeal to 'Moses' as testifying to the suffering and risen Messiah.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.

note: 'How the Christ must suffer' rests on the Suffering Servant — 'a man of sorrows... wounded for our transgressions.' The necessity of the Messiah's suffering, which Paul says the prophets foretold, is grounded chiefly in this song.
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.

note: 'How the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead' pairs suffering with vindication, matching 'he shall see of the travail of his soul... my righteous servant shall justify many' — the Servant's anguish followed by life and fruitfulness.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

note: 'He would be first to proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles' draws directly on 'I will also give you for a light to the Gentiles, that you may be my salvation unto the end of the earth' — the same Servant text Paul cites programmatically at Acts 13:47.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: 'Light both to these people and to the Gentiles' echoes 'I will give you for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles' — the Servant as light to both Israel and the nations, exactly Paul's twofold audience.
sourceText: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations;

note: 'Proclaim light... to the Gentiles' resonates with Zion's dawning glory drawing the nations: 'the Gentiles shall come to your light' — the eschatological light to which the nations are summoned, here realized in the risen Christ's proclamation.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

note: 'By the resurrection of the dead, he would be first' rests on 'you will not leave my soul in Sheol; neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption' — the psalm Acts uses (2:27-31; 13:35) to prove the Messiah's resurrection.
sourceText: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.

note: The opening of the sea-voyage sets up the psalm's tableau of those who 'go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters'; here the verbal contact is minimal (mere embarkation and difficult sailing), so the echo is faint and anticipatory, gathering force only when the storm breaks. Thematic coherence is real but volume is near zero at this stage.
sourceText: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their […]

note: Like Jonah, who 'found a ship' and boarded for a sea-passage toward a distant destination, Paul is put aboard ship after ship bound westward; the framing of a divinely-directed man embarking on a fraught Mediterranean voyage primes the Jonah typology that the storm scene activates. Verbal borrowing is slight, so this is a low-confidence narrative resonance.
sourceText: But Jonah rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of Yahweh. He went down to Joppa, and found a ship going to Tarshish; so he paid its fare, and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish from the presence of Yahweh.

note: Luke dates the danger by noting 'the Fast had now already gone by' — the Day of Atonement, whose fixed autumn date (the tenth of the seventh month) Leviticus prescribes as a day of self-affliction. The detail is a calendar marker rather than a theological citation, but it presupposes the Levitical institution and places the voyage in the perilous post-Atonement sailing season.
sourceText: “It shall be a statute to you forever: in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict your souls, and shall do no kind of work, the native-born, or the stranger who lives as a foreigner among you: for on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. It is a Sabbath of solemn rest to you, and you shall afflict your souls. It is a statute forever.

note: A second locus for the Day of Atonement 'Fast' that Luke's temporal note assumes; the same calendrical institution underlies the warning that the voyage has become dangerous. Offered as an alternate scriptural anchor for the same allusion.
sourceText: “However on the tenth day of this seventh month is the day of atonement: it shall be a holy convocation to you, and you shall afflict yourselves; and you shall offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh. You shall do no kind of work in that same day; for it is a day of atonement, to make atonement for you before Yahweh your God. For whoever it is who shall not deny himself in that same day; shall be cut off from his people.

note: The closest narrative parallel: a violent wind hurled upon the sea, a ship in danger of breaking, terrified mariners, and the casting of cargo overboard to lighten the vessel — all of which recur here (Euroclydon, reinforcing the hull, jettisoning cargo and tackle). The shared storm-script and the act of throwing freight into the sea give real thematic and motif coherence, though Luke borrows the type, not the words.
sourceText: But Yahweh sent out a great wind on the sea, and there was a mighty storm on the sea, so that the ship was likely to break up. Then the mariners were afraid, and every man cried to his god. They threw the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten the ship. But Jonah had gone down into the innermost parts of the ship, and he was laying down, and was fast asleep.

note: The psalm's seafarers meet a 'stormy wind' that lifts the waves, so that 'they reel to and fro, and are at their wits' end' — answering precisely to the driven, rudderless ship and the loss of all hope of being saved. The progression from tempest to despair tracks the psalm's movement and is the chapter's strongest figural backbone for the storm.
sourceText: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end.

note: Ezekiel's dirge over Tyre depicts the merchant ship driven into the heart of the seas by the east wind and broken, its mariners and cargo sinking — a literary type of the freighted vessel undone by wind that resonates with the Alexandrian grain ship overwhelmed here. Verbal contact is minimal; the link is thematic.
sourceText: Your rowers have brought you into great waters: the east wind has broken you in the heart of the seas. Your riches, and your wares, your merchandise, your mariners, and your pilots, your repairers of ship seams, and the dealers in your merchandise, and all your men of war, who are in you, with all your company which is in your midst, shall fall into the heart of the seas in the day of your ruin.

note: 'Thou breakest the ships of Tarshish with an east wind' supplies a compact scriptural image of a great fleet-vessel shattered by an east wind, matching Euroclydon (the east-northeast gale). A brief, low-volume motif echo rather than a developed allusion.
sourceText: With the east wind, you break the ships of Tarshish.

note: The angel's nocturnal 'Don't be afraid' to Paul echoes the formula of the divine reassurance oracle that recurs across the OT, of which God's night-word to Abram ('Fear not... I am thy shield') is the paradigm. The salvation-oracle form (night setting, fear-not, promise of protection and destiny) is well attested; the specific verbal tie is to the formula, not this verse alone.
sourceText: After these things Yahweh’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.”

note: Isaiah's 'Fear not... when thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee' fuses the fear-not oracle with the motif of preservation through the deep — exactly Paul's situation: assured deliverance through the storm, with no loss of life. The combination of formula and water-rescue gives this strong thematic coherence.
sourceText: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned, and flame will not scorch you.

note: An angelic night visitation that opens with 'Fear not, Daniel' and conveys a divine message of assurance furnishes a close formal parallel to the angel standing by Paul at night saying 'Don't be afraid.' The angelophany-plus-reassurance pattern matches; verbal overlap is the shared fear-not formula.
sourceText: Then he said to me, Don’t be afraid, Daniel; for from the first day that you set your heart to understand, and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard: and I have come for your words’ sake.

note: Paul's confident promise that all aboard will be preserved anticipates the psalm's resolution — the distressed cry, God stilling the storm, and the survivors brought safe to harbor. The assurance that 'it will be just as it has been spoken to me' embodies the providential rescue the psalm celebrates.
sourceText: Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their distress. He makes the storm a calm, so that its waves are still. Then they are glad because it is calm, so he brings them to their desired haven.

note: The mariners' nighttime effort to reach land — taking soundings, dropping anchors, and the sailors' attempt to escape in the boat — recalls Jonah's sailors rowing hard to bring the ship to shore against the storm. A faint narrative resonance of seamen straining toward land amid tempest; little verbal contact.
sourceText: Nevertheless the men rowed hard to get them back to the land; but they could not, for the sea grew more and more stormy against them.

note: Paul's pledge that 'not a hair will perish from any of your heads' reproduces the OT idiom of total preservation — Israel's oath over Jonathan that 'there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground' — used to guarantee that no life will be lost. The proverbial formula is distinctive and its sense (life entirely safeguarded) is exactly Paul's.
sourceText: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God this day!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.

note: The same hyperbole of inviolable safety — 'there shall not one hair of thy son fall to the earth' — secured by oath; an alternate locus for the 'not a hair shall perish' assurance Paul gives. Offered as a parallel attestation of the idiom.
sourceText: Then she said, “Please let the king remember Yahweh your God, that the avenger of blood destroy not any more, lest they destroy my son.” He said, “As Yahweh lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the earth.”

note: Paul's taking bread, giving thanks to God before all, breaking and eating it draws on the OT practice of blessing God over food — 'thou shalt eat and be full, and thou shalt bless the LORD thy God.' The act of thanksgiving over bread before a meal coheres with this command, though here it is a custom evoked rather than a text cited.
sourceText: You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless Yahweh your God for the good land which he has given you.

note: The chapter's denouement realizes the psalm's climax: after the tempest, God 'bringeth them unto their desired haven' — here all 276 aboard 'escaped safely to the land.' The bringing of every imperiled person out of the storm to dry land is the psalmist's pattern of deliverance enacted in narrative.
sourceText: Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their distress. He makes the storm a calm, so that its waves are still. Then they are glad because it is calm, so he brings them to their desired haven.

note: Jonah's storm ends with the sea ceasing from its raging and the ship's company spared; likewise the wreck resolves with the violent sea finally beaching the vessel and every soul brought through alive. A typological resonance of storm-to-rescue, with the righteous man's presence proving the means of others' preservation.
sourceText: So they took up Jonah, and threw him into the sea; and the sea ceased its raging. Then the men feared Yahweh exceedingly; and they offered a sacrifice to Yahweh, and made vows.

note: Paul gathers sticks, a viper fastens on his hand, yet he shakes it off unharmed. The promise that the righteous one 'will tread on the adder' and trample serpent and viper without harm (LXX Ps 90:13) is the closest scriptural template for the scene: deadly snake, divine protection, no injury. The vocabulary of viper/serpent and the motif of the protected servant give strong thematic coherence at the book's climax.

Reversal of the primal serpent-bite is figurally apt for the apostle's vindication.
