note: 2:6 'according to works' is closely paralleled by Sirach 16:12-14, 'he judges a man according to his deeds... he makes room for every act of mercy; everyone receives according to his deeds' — Second Temple crystallization of the same recompense doctrine.
sourceText: As his mercy is great, so is his correction also: He judges a man according to his works. The sinner will not escape with his plunder; And the perseverance of the godly will not be frustrated. He will make room for every work of mercy; Each man will find according to his works.

note: 2:11 'no partiality' is anticipated by Sirach 35:12-13 (LXX 35:15-16), 'the Lord is the judge, and with him is no partiality; he will not show partiality to the poor' — Second Temple restatement of the impartiality formula in a judgment context.
sourceText: Think not to corrupt with gifts; for he will not receive them: And set not your mind on an unrighteous sacrifice; For the Lord is judge, And with him is no respect of persons. He will not accept any person against a poor man; And he will listen to the prayer of him that is wronged.

note: 2:13 'the doers of the law will be justified' echoes the Torah principle 'the person who does them shall live by them' — the do-and-live logic (which Paul cites directly at 10:5; Gal 3:12) standing behind 'doers' over 'hearers.'
sourceText: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.

note: 2:13 hearing-versus-doing reflects Moses' charge to 'listen (hear) to the statutes... and do them, that you may live,' the Deuteronomic pairing of shema and asah that Paul splits to indict mere hearers.
sourceText: Now, Israel, listen to the statutes and to the ordinances, which I teach you, to do them; that you may live, and go in and possess the land which Yahweh, the God of your fathers, gives you.

note: 2:14-15 Gentiles 'a law to themselves' with the law's work 'in their hearts' faintly recalls Deut 30:11-14, 'the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it' — the nearness/internality of the commandment (Paul quotes this at 10:6-8), here generalized to conscience.
sourceText: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]

note: 2:15 'the work of the law written in their hearts' verbally echoes the new-covenant promise 'I will put my law within them, and on their hearts I will write it' — though Paul applies the imagery to Gentiles' moral intuition rather than Israel's eschatological renewal, the borrowing is deliberate and ironic.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:

note: 2:16 'God will judge the secrets of men' draws on Qoheleth's conclusion, 'God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil' — secret-deed judgment as the climax of the wisdom tradition.
sourceText: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.

note: 2:16 judging 'the secrets of men' echoes Ps 44:21 (LXX 43:22), 'would not God discover this? For he knows the secrets of the heart' — divine knowledge of hidden things grounding the verdict.
sourceText: won’t God search this out? For he knows the secrets of the heart.

note: 2:16 'judge the secrets' parallels Wisdom of Solomon 1:6-9, 'God is witness of his inmost feelings... a hearing reaches the Lord... and the report of his words comes to the Lord to convict him of his lawless deeds' — Second Temple scrutiny of inner thoughts at judgment.
sourceText: For wisdom is a spirit that loves man, And she will not hold a blasphemer guiltless for his lips; Because God bears witness of his reins, And is a true overseer of his heart, And a hearer of his tongue: Because the spirit of the Lord has filled the world, And that which holds all things together has knowledge of every voice. Therefore no man that utters unrighteous things will be unseen; Neither will Justice, when it convicts, pass him by. For in the […]

note: 2:16 God judging hidden 'secrets' resonates with 'man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart' — the principle of inward divine sight underlying Paul's contrast between outward and inward (developed at 2:28-29).
sourceText: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

note: 2:16 secret-judgment overlaps with Jer 17:10, 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind' — heart-searching paired with works-recompense, already noted at 2:6 and reinforcing the pericope's frame.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: 2:24 'the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, just as it is written' is an explicit formula-citation of Isa 52:5 LXX, 'because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations' — Paul's clinching scriptural proof of the indictment.
sourceText: “Now therefore, what do I do here,” says Yahweh, “seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Those who rule over them mock,” says Yahweh, “and my name continually all the day is blasphemed.

note: 2:24 the profaning of God's name among the nations is reinforced by Ezek 36:20-23, 'they profaned my holy name... wherever they came among the nations' — the same prophetic logic (Israel's conduct dishonoring God before the Gentiles), and Ezek 36's heart/spirit renewal also feeds 2:29.
sourceText: When they came to the nations, where they went, they profaned my holy name; in that men said of them, These are the people of Yahweh, and are gone out of his land. But I had respect for my holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations, where they went. Therefore tell the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: I don’t do this for your sake, house of Israel, but for my holy name, which you have profaned among the nations, where […]

note: 2:21-22 'you who teach another, don't you teach yourself? You who preach don't steal, do you steal?... commit adultery?' closely mirrors Ps 50:16-21 (LXX 49), 'what right have you to recite my statutes...? you keep company with thieves... and with adulterers' — God's rebuke of the hypocrite who recites the law while breaking it.
sourceText: But to the wicked God says, “What right do you have to declare my statutes, that you have taken my covenant on your lips, since you hate instruction, and throw my words behind you? When you saw a thief, you consented with him, and have participated with adulterers. “You give your mouth to evil. Your tongue frames deceit. You sit and speak against your brother. You slander your own mother’s son. You have done these things, and I kept silent. You thought […]

note: 2:19 'a guide of the blind, a light to those in darkness' draws on the Servant's vocation 'a light to the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out... those who sit in darkness' — Israel's self-understanding as light to the Gentiles, which Paul ironizes.
sourceText: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations; to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: 2:19 'a light to those in darkness' also echoes Isa 49:6, 'I will make you a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' — the Servant-Israel light-to-Gentiles motif Paul invokes only to expose the teacher's failure.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: 2:19 the irony deepens with Isa 42:19, 'who is blind but my servant... who is blind as the dedicated one?' — the would-be guide of the blind is himself the blind servant; a faint counter-echo within the same Isaianic context.
sourceText: Who is blind, but my servant? Or who is as deaf as my messenger whom I send? Who is as blind as he who is at peace, and as blind as Yahweh’s servant?

note: 2:22 'you who abhor idols, do you rob temples?' reflects Deut 7:25-26, 'the carved images of their gods you shall burn... you shall utterly abhor it (bdelysse), for it is an abomination' — the very verb of abhorring idols (bdelyssomenos) Paul uses, sharpening the charge of temple-robbing inconsistency.
sourceText: You shall burn the engraved images of their gods with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them, nor take it for yourself, lest you be snared in it; for it is an abomination to Yahweh your God. You shall not bring an abomination into your house, and become a devoted thing like it. You shall utterly detest it, and you shall utterly abhor it; for it is a devoted thing.

note: 2:29 'circumcision is that of the heart' directly echoes Moses' command 'circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn' — the foundational text spiritualizing circumcision (note the proximity to Deut 10:17's impartiality, used at 2:11).
sourceText: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.

note: 2:29 heart-circumcision in the Spirit draws on Deut 30:6, 'the LORD your God will circumcise your heart... so that you will love the LORD' — the promised divine (eschatological, Spirit-effected) circumcision, matching Paul's 'in the spirit not the letter.'
sourceText: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.

note: 2:29 'circumcision of the heart' echoes Jer 4:4, 'circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts' — prophetic demand for inward circumcision lest wrath go forth, fitting Paul's wrath-and-heart argument.
sourceText: Circumcise yourselves to Yahweh, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go out like fire, and burn so that no one can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.

note: 2:25-29 the worthlessness of fleshly circumcision without obedience reflects Jer 9:25-26, 'I will punish all who are circumcised merely in the flesh... for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart' — exactly Paul's leveling of circumcised and uncircumcised by the heart criterion.
sourceText: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will punish all those who are circumcised in uncircumcision: Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that have the corners of their hair cut off, who dwell in the wilderness; for all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart.

note: 2:29 inward circumcision recalls Lev 26:41, 'if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled and they make amends for their iniquity' — the Holiness Code's notion of an uncircumcised heart needing humbling, a Torah basis for the heart/flesh distinction.
sourceText: I also walked contrary to them, and brought them into the land of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled, and they then accept the punishment of their iniquity;

note: 2:25-29 the pairing 'uncircumcised in heart and flesh' appears in Ezek 44:7-9 barring those 'uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh' from the sanctuary — the dual (heart/flesh) circumcision distinction Paul exploits.
sourceText: in that you have brought in foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary, to profane it, even my house, when you offer my bread, the fat and the blood, and they have broken my covenant, to add to all your abominations. You have not performed the duty of my holy things; but you have set performers of my duty in my sanctuary for yourselves. Thus says the Lord Yahweh, No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and […]

note: 2:29 'in the spirit, not in the letter' echoes the new-heart promise, 'I will give you a new heart... and put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes' — Spirit-wrought interior obedience over external observance.
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: 2:25-29 the whole argument presupposes and reinterprets the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision in the flesh (Gen 17, 'every male shall be circumcised... in your flesh an everlasting covenant') — Paul figurally relocates the 'everlasting covenant' sign from flesh to heart/Spirit.
sourceText: God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he […]

note: 2:29 'whose praise is not from men but from God' likely plays on the etymology of 'Jew' (Judah/Yehudah), named in Gen 29:35 when Leah says 'this time I will praise the LORD' — the true Jew is the one of genuine praise, a Hebrew wordplay (Judah = praise; cf. Gen 49:8).
sourceText: She conceived again, and bore a son. She said, “This time will I praise Yahweh.” Therefore she named him Judah. Then she stopped bearing.

note: Verbatim citation introduced by 'as it is written' in 3:4: 'that you might be justified in your words, and might prevail when you come into judgment' = LXX Psalm 50:6, David's confession in the Miserere. Paul deploys it to vindicate God's righteousness against human faithlessness: God is justified (proven right) precisely when humans are shown liars.
sourceText: Against you, and you only, have I sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight; that you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge.
lxxText: Against thee only have I sinned, and done evil before thee: that thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged.

note: The 'advantage of the Jew' and being 'entrusted with the oracles of God' (3:1-2) echoes Israel's unique covenantal privilege of possessing God's statutes and nearness, the defining boast of Deuteronomy 4:7-8. Paul concedes this advantage before relativizing it.
sourceText: For what great nation is there, that has a god so near to them, as Yahweh our God is whenever we call on him? What great nation is there, that has statutes and ordinances so righteous as all this law, which I set before you this day?

note: Israel as guardian of 'the oracles/words of God' (3:2) faintly recalls Levi keeping God's word and covenant; the 'logia tou theou' language draws on the deposit-of-the-law tradition.
sourceText: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.

note: 'Let God be found true, but every man a liar' (3:4) restates Balaam's axiom that God is not a man that he should lie; the contrast between divine truthfulness and human falsehood is the same theological commitment.
sourceText: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?

note: 'Every man a liar' (3:4) is the psalmist's verbatim verdict, 'all men are liars' (LXX Psalm 115:2). Paul fuses it with the Psalm 51 citation to dramatize the truth-of-God / lie-of-humanity antithesis.
sourceText: I said in my haste, “All men are liars.”

note: 'How will God judge the world?' (3:6) invokes Abraham's appeal to the Judge of all the earth who must do right; God's universal judicial competence is the unquestionable premise that secures his righteousness.
sourceText: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”

note: The faithfulness-of-God-despite-Israel's-faithlessness theme (3:3) anticipates the Hosea citations Paul will marshal in Romans 9; God's covenant fidelity outlasts the people's apistia.
sourceText: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’

note: Head of the catena (3:10-12): 'There is none righteous... none who understands... none who seeks God; all have turned aside, together become worthless; none does good, not one.' This is a near-verbatim chain from LXX Psalm 13:1-3, the fool who says there is no God. Paul opens his 'as it is written' string here.
sourceText: The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt. They have done abominable works. There is no one who does good. Yahweh looked down from heaven on the children of men, to see if there were any who understood, who sought after God. They have all gone aside. They have together become corrupt. There is no one who does good, no, not one.

note: 'There is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins' supplies the same universal-sin thesis as the catena's opening 'none righteous... none does good' (3:10-12); a wisdom-tradition reinforcement of the Psalm 14 verdict.
sourceText: Surely there is not a righteous man on earth, who does good and doesn’t sin.

note: Catena member at 3:13a: 'Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they have practiced deceit' = LXX Psalm 5:10, verbatim. Begins the catena's catalogue of speech-organs (throat, tongue, lips, mouth).
sourceText: For there is no faithfulness in their mouth. Their heart is destruction. Their throat is an open tomb. They flatter with their tongue.

note: Catena member at 3:13b: 'The poison of asps/vipers is under their lips' = LXX Psalm 139:4, verbatim. Continues the speech catalogue from lips.
sourceText: They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent. Viper’s poison is under their lips. Selah.

note: Catena member at 3:14: 'whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness' draws on LXX Psalm 9:28 (Psalm 10:7 MT), 'his mouth is full of cursing and deceit and oppression.' Completes the mouth-cursing item of the speech catalogue.
sourceText: His mouth is full of cursing, deceit, and oppression. Under his tongue is mischief and iniquity.

note: Catena member at 3:15-17: 'Their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways; and the way of peace they have not known' = Isaiah 59:7-8, the prophet's indictment that justice and peace are absent. The lone prophetic link in the otherwise psalmic chain; shifts from speech to feet/ways.
sourceText: Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood: their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; desolation and destruction are in their paths. The way of peace they don’t know; and there is no justice in their goings: they have made them crooked paths; whoever goes therein does not know peace.

note: 'Their feet run to evil and make haste to shed blood' parallels 3:15 ('their feet are swift to shed blood') and overlaps Isaiah 59:7; some hold Proverbs 1:16 contributes to or doubles the source of the feet-shedding-blood clause.
sourceText: for their feet run to evil. They hurry to shed blood.

note: Catena's climactic capstone at 3:18: 'There is no fear of God before their eyes' = LXX Psalm 35:2, verbatim. The chain closes by returning the indictment to its root (fear of God / eyes), inclusio with the opening 'none seeks God.'
sourceText: An oracle is within my heart about the disobedience of the wicked: “There is no fear of God before his eyes.”

note: 3:20: 'by works of the law no flesh will be justified in his sight' adapts LXX Psalm 142:2, 'do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no living one shall be justified.' Paul adds 'by works of the law' but the 'no flesh justified before you' core is verbatim from the psalmist.
sourceText: Don’t enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no man living is righteous.

note: 'All have turned aside, together become corrupt/worthless' (3:12) faintly recalls the Flood verdict that all flesh had corrupted its way on earth; both render a totalizing 'all flesh' depravity.
sourceText: God saw the earth, and saw that it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth.

note: Beyond the quoted 59:7-8, the wider Isaiah 59 oracle ('none calls for justice... they conceive mischief') colors the catena's portrait; Paul likely has the whole indictment-of-no-righteousness pericope in view.
sourceText: No one sues in righteousness, and no one pleads in truth: they trust in vanity, and speak lies; they conceive mischief, and give birth to iniquity.

note: 'How can a man be righteous before God?' anticipates 3:20's 'no flesh justified in his sight'; the forensic impossibility of human self-justification before God is a shared wisdom premise.
sourceText: “Truly I know that it is so, but how can man be just with God?

note: The thesis of 'righteousness of God through faith' (3:21-22) carries forward the programmatic citation of 1:17, 'the righteous shall live by faith'; the faith-righteousness axis here is governed by Habakkuk even without re-quotation.
sourceText: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.

note: 'A righteousness of God has been revealed' (3:21) echoes Deutero-Isaiah's repeated proclamation that God's righteousness/salvation 'draws near' and 'is revealed'; the apocalyptic unveiling of divine sedaqah is Isaianic.
sourceText: My righteousness is near, my salvation has gone out, and my arms shall judge the peoples; the islands shall wait for me, and on my arm shall they trust. Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished. “Listen to me, […]

note: 'The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations' is a close template for 3:21-22: God's righteousness now revealed to all who believe, Jew and Gentile alike.
sourceText: Yahweh has made known his salvation. He has openly shown his righteousness in the sight of the nations.

note: Christ set forth as 'hilasterion' / atoning sacrifice 'in his blood' (3:25) typologically fulfills the Day of Atonement mercy seat (kapporeth, LXX hilasterion) sprinkled with blood; the temple atonement apparatus prefigures the cross.
sourceText: and he shall put the incense on the fire before Yahweh, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is on the testimony, so that he will not die. He shall take some of the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy seat on the east; and before the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times. “Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering, that is for the people, and bring his blood […]

note: The 'hilasterion' of 3:25 is the very term LXX uses for the mercy seat / cover of the ark where God meets Israel; Paul presents Christ as the eschatological place of propitiation, fulfilling the ark typology.
sourceText: You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold. Two and a half cubits shall be its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth. You shall make two cherubim of hammered gold. You shall make them at the two ends of the mercy seat. Make one cherub at the one end, and one cherub at the other end. You shall make the cherubim on its two ends of one piece with the mercy seat. The cherubim shall spread out their wings upward, covering the mercy seat with their wings, […]

note: Justification 'freely by his grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus' and the atoning-blood demonstration of righteousness (3:24-25) echoes the Servant who 'makes many righteous' by bearing sin; the vicarious sin-bearing undergirds Paul's atonement language.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: 'There is one God who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith' (3:30) grounds itself in the Shema's 'the LORD is one'; Paul turns Israel's monotheistic confession into the warrant for one way of justification for Jew and Gentile.
sourceText: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.

note: The circumcised/uncircumcised distinction relativized in 3:29-30 presupposes the Abrahamic circumcision covenant; Paul prepares the ground for Romans 4's argument that Abraham was reckoned righteous before circumcision.
sourceText: God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he […]

note: God's 'forbearance' and 'passing over of former sins' (3:25-26) draws on the covenant formula of the LORD slow to anger, forgiving iniquity yet not clearing the guilty; Paul shows how God can pass over sins and still be just.
sourceText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth, keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”

note: 'Where then is boasting? It is excluded' (3:27) echoes Jeremiah's prohibition of boasting in wisdom, might, or riches, allowing boasting only in knowing the LORD who does righteousness; Paul transposes the anti-boast theme to works of law.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.

note: 'A righteous God and a Savior... in the LORD all the offspring of Israel shall be justified,' with every nation turning to the one God, undergirds 3:26-30: God just and justifier, one God of Jews and Gentiles.
sourceText: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other. I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every […]

note: 'Justified by faith apart from works of the law' (3:28) anticipates and is governed by the Abraham-reckoned-righteous text Paul will quote in 4:3; the faith-reckoning principle is already operative here.
sourceText: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.

note: The governing text of the entire chapter, quoted verbatim in 4:3 ('Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness'). Paul launches a sustained midrash on this single verse, returning to its key term 'accounted/reckoned' (LXX elogisthe) throughout. Maximum volume and recurrence.
sourceText: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.

note: Quoted verbatim in 4:7-8 ('Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven... Blessed is the man whom the Lord will by no means charge with sin'). Paul attributes it to David and links it to Genesis 15:6 by gezerah shawah on the shared verb 'reckon/charge' (logizomai): the man to whom the Lord does NOT reckon sin = the man to whom God reckons righteousness apart from works.
sourceText: Blessed is he whose disobedience is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man to whom Yahweh doesn’t impute iniquity, in whose spirit there is no deceit.

note: Paul's argument from 'reward' (misthos) in 4:4 ('to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace') draws on the immediate context of Genesis 15:6, where God tells Abraham in 15:1 'your reward shall be very great.' Paul reads the surrounding promise narrative, not just the proof-text.
sourceText: After these things Yahweh’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.”

note: God's self-description as one who 'justifies the ungodly' (4:5) deliberately inverts the legal maxim of Exodus 23:7 LXX, 'you shall not justify the ungodly' (ou dikaioseis ton asebe). Paul scandalously predicates of God the very act forbidden to human judges, signaling that justification is grace, not legal verdict on merit.
sourceText: “Keep far from a false charge, and don’t kill the innocent and righteous: for I will not justify the wicked.

note: Reinforces the same forensic reversal: Proverbs 17:15 calls 'he who justifies the wicked' an abomination to the Lord. Paul's phrase 'justifies the ungodly' (4:5) is a calculated provocation against this wisdom commonplace. Thematically coherent but verbally less direct than Exodus 23:7; marked contested.
sourceText: He who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the righteous, both of them alike are an abomination to Yahweh.

note: Second Temple reception of Abraham: 'Abraham was the great father of a multitude of nations... he kept the law of the Most High... therefore the Lord assured him by an oath that nations would be blessed through his offspring.' Sirach reads Abraham's righteousness as covenant-keeping/Torah-obedience, the very reading Paul argues against. A contested background echo: Paul writes with such Second Temple Abraham-as-law-keeper tradition in view.
sourceText: Abraham was a great father of a multitude of nations; And there was none found like him in glory; Who kept the law of the Most High, And was taken into covenant with him: In his flesh he established the covenant; And when he was proved, he was found faithful. Therefore he assured him by an oath, That the nations should be blessed in his seed; That he would multiply him as the dust of the earth, And exalt his seed as the stars, And cause them to inherit […]

note: 1 Maccabees 2:52 ('Was not Abraham found faithful when tested, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness?') itself cites Genesis 15:6 but fuses it with the Aqedah (Genesis 22) to make faith = proven works/faithfulness under testing. This is the foil for Paul's whole argument that the reckoning preceded and excluded works. Strong verbal overlap with the catchphrase 'reckoned... as righteousness'; marked contested as reception-background rather than source.
sourceText: Was not Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness?

note: 'Abraham, our forefather' (4:1) may echo Isaiah 51:2, 'Look to Abraham your father... for he was but one when I called him,' a text about Abraham as progenitor of a numerous people from a single ancestor — the theme Paul develops in 4:16-18. Faint; thematic only.
sourceText: Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, and I blessed him, and made him many.

note: Paul's argument that Abraham 'received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith' (4:11) directly invokes Genesis 17:10-11, where circumcision is instituted as 'a sign of the covenant.' Paul takes the Genesis term 'sign' and subordinates it to the faith of Genesis 15, which chronologically preceded it.
sourceText: This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you.

note: The pericope hangs entirely on the chronology of Genesis: faith reckoned (15:6) came BEFORE circumcision (chapter 17). 4:9-10 re-quotes 'faith was accounted to Abraham for righteousness' and asks whether the reckoning happened in circumcision or uncircumcision — recurrence of the governing text used as a temporal argument.
sourceText: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.

note: 'That he might be the father of all those who believe' (4:11) and 'the father of circumcision' (4:12) anticipate the quotation of Genesis 17:5 in 4:17, reading Abraham's universal fatherhood out of the Genesis covenant promise. The 'father of many nations' motif governs the circumcised/uncircumcised dual fatherhood here.
sourceText: Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.

note: 'The promise to Abraham and to his seed that he should be heir of the world' (4:13) universalizes the land-inheritance promises of Genesis (17:8 'I will give to you and your offspring... all the land of Canaan for an everlasting possession'; cf. 13:15; 15:7). Paul expands the territorial 'land' to 'the world' (kosmos), a move grounded in the cosmic scope of the promise.
sourceText: I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”

note: The promise to Abraham 'and to his seed' (4:13) echoes the oath of Genesis 22:17-18, 'I will multiply your seed... and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed,' which links seed, multiplication, and universal blessing — the basis for 'heir of the world.' The word 'seed' (sperma) is the Genesis catchword Paul foregrounds.
sourceText: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies. All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your seed, because you have obeyed my voice.”

note: The 'heir of the world' expansion has a Second Temple precedent in Sirach 44:21, where God promises Abraham 'to give them an inheritance from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth' — already enlarging the land to global scope. A contested background echo for Paul's kosmos language.
sourceText: Therefore he assured him by an oath, That the nations should be blessed in his seed; That he would multiply him as the dust of the earth, And exalt his seed as the stars, And cause them to inherit from sea to sea, And from the River to the utmost part of the earth.

note: Genesis 15:7 ('I am the Lord who brought you out... to give you this land to inherit it'), within the same chapter as 15:6, supplies the inheritance vocabulary Paul universalizes in 'heir of the world.' Faint; reinforces that Paul reads the whole Genesis 15 unit.
sourceText: He said to him, “I am Yahweh who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give you this land to inherit it.”

note: Quoted verbatim with the introductory formula 'As it is written' in 4:17: 'I have made you a father of many nations' (Genesis 17:5 LXX, 'patera pollon ethnon tetheika se'). Paul reads the perfect tense ('I HAVE made') as already-accomplished divine speech that calls the not-yet into being.
sourceText: Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.

note: Quoted verbatim in 4:18: 'So will your seed be' (Genesis 15:5 LXX, 'houtos estai to sperma sou'), the star-promise spoken immediately before Genesis 15:6. Paul binds the two halves of Genesis 15 together: the promise (v.5) and Abraham's believing response reckoned as righteousness (v.6).
sourceText: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So will your seed be.”

note: 'He being about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah's womb' (4:19) draws directly on Genesis 17:17, where Abraham, told he will have a son, says 'Shall a child be born to him who is a hundred years old? And shall Sarah, who is ninety, bear?' Paul reuses the numeric detail and the implied biological impossibility.
sourceText: Then Abraham fell on his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, “Will a child be born to him who is one hundred years old? Will Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”

note: 'The deadness of Sarah's womb' and Abraham's 'body already worn out' (4:19) echo Genesis 18:11-12: 'it had ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women,' and Sarah's words 'After I am worn out (LXX katetribe), shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?' Paul's 'worn out' (nenekromenon/already dead) language tracks the Genesis 18 description of both spouses' exhaustion.
sourceText: Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age. Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?”

note: Abraham 'being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform' (4:21) answers the rhetorical question of Genesis 18:14, 'Is anything too hard for the Lord? At the appointed time I will return... and Sarah shall have a son.' Paul converts the LORD's question into Abraham's confident assent — God's power over the impossible.
sourceText: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”

note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) draws on the scriptural confession of God as life-giver, e.g. 1 Samuel 2:6 (Hannah), 'The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.' This is the standard OT idiom Paul applies to both Isaac's miraculous conception and the resurrection.
sourceText: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.

note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) also resonates with Deuteronomy 32:39, 'I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal,' a foundational text for God's sole power over death and life. Reinforces the same divine attribute Paul predicates.
sourceText: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.

note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) may figurally echo Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, where the Spirit raises a dead Israel to life — a paradigm of resurrection-as-restoration. Thematically coherent with Paul's resurrection horizon; verbally faint, marked contested.
sourceText: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]

note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) figurally echoes the creation account, where God's word summons being out of nonbeing ('Let there be... and there was'). Paul pairs creation (calling the nonexistent) with resurrection (giving life to the dead) as twin marks of the God Abraham believed.
sourceText: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) has its closest Second Temple parallel in 2 Maccabees 7:28, where the mother urges her son to recognize 'that God did not make them out of things that existed' — an early articulation of creation from nothing, paired (as in Romans 4) with resurrection hope. Contested background echo.
sourceText: I beseech you, my child, to lift your eyes to the heaven and the earth, and to see all things that are therein, and thus to recognize that God made them not of things that were, and that the race of men in this wise comes into being.

note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) may echo the Isaianic creator who 'calls' the heavens and earth into existence (Isaiah 48:13; 41:4; 44:24), where divine calling is creative summons. Faint verbal link via the verb 'call'; marked contested.
sourceText: Yes, my hand has laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand has spread out the heavens: when I call to them, they stand up together.

note: The pericope closes in 4:22 by re-quoting the governing text: 'Therefore it also was reckoned to him for righteousness.' Recurrence of Genesis 15:6 as the inclusio binding the demonstration of Abraham's faith back to its scriptural anchor.
sourceText: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.

note: 'Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone, but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted' (4:23-24) explicitly thematizes the act of reading Genesis 15:6 as Scripture written for the church. The verb 'accounted/reckoned' is carried forward one last time, applied now to believers in the God who raised Jesus.
sourceText: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.

note: 'Who was delivered up for our trespasses' (4:25) echoes Isaiah 53 LXX, especially 53:6 ('the Lord delivered him up for our sins,' paredoken auton tais hamartiais hemon) and 53:12 ('he was delivered up because of their sins'). Paul's verb 'delivered up' (paredothe) plus 'for our trespasses' is verbatim Servant-song language, identifying the crucified Jesus as the suffering Servant.
sourceText: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: 'And was raised for our justification' (4:25) draws on Isaiah 53:11 LXX, 'the righteous one will justify the many (dikaiosai dikaion... tois pollois), and he shall bear their sins.' The pairing of the Servant's vindication with the justification 'of many' undergirds Paul's resurrection-justification clause, linking the Abraham-righteousness midrash to the Servant's righteousness.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: "Justified by faith" (5:1) is the conclusion Paul has just drawn from Abraham (Romans 4), and ultimately rests on Genesis 15:6, "Abram believed the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness." The faith-righteousness link governing 5:1 is verbally and conceptually the Genesis 15:6 logic carried forward into this pericope's opening clause.
sourceText: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.

note: "The righteous shall live by faith" is Paul's thesis text (Romans 1:17) and stands behind "being justified by faith" (5:1). The faith-life pairing of Habakkuk 2:4 resonates in the move from justification by faith to being "saved by his life" (5:10), though no verbal quotation appears here.
sourceText: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.

note: "Peace with God" (5:1) and reconciliation through Christ's death (5:10-11) echo the Suffering Servant whose "chastisement brought us peace, and with his stripes we are healed." Isaiah 53 supplies the template of one man's death securing peace and healing for the many that drives the whole passage.
sourceText: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.

note: "While we were yet sinners/ungodly" Christ died for us (5:6, 5:8): "All we like sheep have gone astray... and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all." The Servant bearing the iniquity of the straying matches Paul's "Christ died for the ungodly."
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: "He poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many" stands behind "Christ died for us" while sinners (5:8) and "justified by his blood" (5:9). The Servant's vicarious death for "many" anticipates the many/one structure Paul develops.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: "Justified by his blood" (5:9): "the life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that makes atonement." Paul's atoning-blood language draws on the Levitical principle that blood effects expiation, already invoked at Romans 3:25 (hilasterion).
sourceText: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.

note: "Justified by his blood" (5:9) may faintly recall the blood of the covenant Moses dashed on the people, sealing the relationship with God. Disputed as a deliberate echo here versus general sacrificial background.
sourceText: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”

note: "We rejoice in hope of the glory of God" and "rejoice in God" (5:2, 5:11): "let all who take refuge in you rejoice; let them ever sing for joy... let those who love your name exult in you." The pattern of those justified/sheltered by God rejoicing/exulting in him is a recurrent Psalmic posture Paul takes up.
sourceText: But let all those who take refuge in you rejoice, Let them always shout for joy, because you defend them. Let them also who love your name be joyful in you.

note: "Hope does not put us to shame" (5:5): "they trusted in you and were not put to shame." The Psalmic confession that trust in God does not end in shame is the verbal-conceptual root of Paul's claim that hope ou kataischynei.
sourceText: They cried to you, and were delivered. They trusted in you, and were not disappointed.

note: "Hope does not put us to shame" (5:5): "none who wait for you shall be put to shame." Psalm 25 (vv. 3, 20) repeatedly grounds the assurance that hope in God is not disappointed, matching Paul's claim about hope.
sourceText: Yes, no one who waits for you shall be shamed. They shall be shamed who deal treacherously without cause.

note: "Hope does not put us to shame" (5:5): "whoever believes will not be put to shame" (LXX). Paul quotes this very verse at Romans 9:33 and 10:11; the same shame/faith formula colors his statement here that hope does not disappoint.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: "God's love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (5:5): "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh." The verb "pour out" (ekcheo) applied to the Spirit is the prophetic eschatological-outpouring idiom; Paul quotes Joel 2:32 at Romans 10:13, showing the passage is in view.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.

note: "God's love poured out... through the Holy Spirit" (5:5): "I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring." The same Spirit-outpouring promise, paired with water/blessing imagery, undergirds Paul's image of love flooding the heart by the Spirit.
sourceText: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:

note: "Poured out into our hearts... the Holy Spirit who was given to us" (5:5): "I will give you a new heart... I will put my Spirit within you." The new-covenant promise of God's Spirit placed within the heart matches Paul's interiorized gift of the Spirit and love.
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: "Suffering produces perseverance, and perseverance proven character" (5:3-4): "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing... for gold is tested in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation." A Second Temple wisdom commonplace that trials refine and prove the faithful, closely parallel to Paul's chain suffering->endurance->proven character.
sourceText: My son, if you come to serve the Lord, Prepare your soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure, And make not haste in time of calamity. Cleave to him, and depart not, That you may be increased at your latter end. Accept whatever is brought upon you, And be longsuffering when you passest into humiliation. For gold is tried in the fire, And acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation.

note: "Suffering works perseverance... proven character; and proven character, hope" (5:3-4): "Having been disciplined a little, they will receive great good, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself; like gold in the furnace he tried them." Second Temple parallel linking testing/discipline to being proven worthy and to hope of glory (cf. Wisdom 3:4, hope full of immortality).
sourceText: And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and found them worthy of himself. As gold in the furnace he proved them, And as a whole burnt offering he accepted them.

note: "Peace with God" through righteousness (5:1): "the work of righteousness shall be peace." The prophetic linkage of righteousness and peace faintly underlies Paul's pairing of justification with peace, though no verbal borrowing is evident.
sourceText: The work of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.

note: "Peace with God" (5:1): "righteousness and peace kiss each other." The Psalm's union of righteousness and peace as God's salvific gift resonates faintly with Paul's justification-yields-peace claim. Disputed as a deliberate echo.
sourceText: I will hear what God, Yahweh, will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, his saints; but let them not turn again to folly. Surely his salvation is near those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land. Mercy and truth meet together. Righteousness and peace have kissed each other.

note: "Peace with God" for the reconciled (5:1, 5:10-11): "Peace, peace, to the far and the near, says the LORD; and I will heal him." The prophetic announcement of peace and healing to estranged people faintly anticipates peace and reconciliation language. Contested.
sourceText: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”

note: "Sin entered into the world through one man" (5:12) figurally reads the Eden narrative: Adam's single transgression in eating the forbidden fruit is the entry point of sin into the cosmos. Paul explicitly types Adam as "a foreshadowing of him who was to come" (5:14, typos), making the fall the controlling figure for the Adam-Christ antithesis.
sourceText: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]

note: "Death through sin... death passed to all" (5:12): "in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." The divine sentence binding death to the one prohibited act is the textual basis for Paul's claim that death entered through the one man's transgression.
sourceText: but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”

note: "Death passed to all men" and "death reigned" (5:12, 5:14, 5:17): "cursed is the ground because of you... you are dust, and to dust you shall return." Adam's curse universalizing death is figurally taken up as the reign of death over all humanity that Christ's act of righteousness reverses.
sourceText: To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life. It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, […]

note: "Through the one man's disobedience many were made sinners" (5:19): "she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband, and he ate." Adam's specific act of disobedient eating is the trespass/parakoe Paul opposes to Christ's obedience (hypakoe).
sourceText: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate; and she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.

note: "Adam's disobedience" / "the one man's disobedience" (5:14, 5:19): "Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?" God's interrogation frames Adam's act precisely as disobedience to a command, supplying the parakoe Paul contrasts with Christ's obedience.
sourceText: God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”

note: "Death reigned from Adam until Moses" (5:14): the tolling refrain "and he died" through the Sethite genealogy (Genesis 5) concretizes the unbroken reign of death over the generations between Adam and the giving of the law. Paul's historical span presupposes this litany of mortality.
sourceText: Adam lived one hundred thirty years, and became the father of a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he became the father of other sons and daughters. All the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, then he died. Seth lived one hundred five years, then became the father of Enosh. Seth lived after he became the father of Enosh eight […]

note: "Through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin" (5:12): "God created man for incorruption... but through the devil's envy death entered the world." The closest Second Temple parallel, sharing the precise idiom "death entered the world" (eiselthen... thanatos) and tracing universal death to a primeval cause. Paul localizes the cause in Adam's trespass rather than the devil's envy.
sourceText: Because God created man for incorruption, And made him an image of his own proper being; But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, And those who are of his portion make trial thereof.

note: "Through one... death" passed to all (5:12, 5:15): "From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die." A Second Temple text tracing universal death to the primeval transgression in Eden, structurally parallel to Paul (though Ben Sira blames Eve, Paul Adam). Strong thematic overlap on death-through-one.
sourceText: From a woman was the beginning of sin; And because of her we all die.

note: "Death reigned from Adam until Moses" and "the law came in besides" (5:14, 5:20): the Sinai law-giving through Moses is the temporal boundary and the "law that came in" so that the trespass might increase. Paul presupposes the Mosaic legislation (Exodus 20 / the Decalogue) as the entry of nomos into his salvation-history scheme.
sourceText: God spoke all these words, saying, “I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. “You shall have no other gods before me. “You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the […]

note: "Grace... reign through righteousness to eternal life" (5:21): the tree of life in Eden (Genesis 2:9; 3:22-24), forfeited at the fall, faintly stands behind the restoration of "eternal life" through the second Adam. A disputed figural undertone rather than a verbal echo.
sourceText: Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

note: "As through one trespass... all condemned" (5:18): "like Adam they transgressed the covenant" (one reading of Hosea 6:7) treats Adam as the archetypal covenant-breaker. A faint and textually disputed possible precedent for Paul's Adam-as-transgressor typology.
sourceText: But they, like Adam, have broken the covenant. They were unfaithful to me, there.

note: To Cain: sin 'is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.' Paul's 'do not let sin reign (basileueto) in your mortal body' (6:12) personifies Sin as a power seeking to master a person who must instead exercise dominion over it. The shared image of Sin as an external would-be ruler the believer must refuse to obey is striking; many read 6:12 against this primal scene.
sourceText: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”

note: Redemption-from-bondage language: God brings Israel 'out from under the burdens' and 'redeems' them from slavery. Romans 6:6 ('no longer in bondage to sin', douleuein) and 6:7 ('freed from sin') run the exodus slavery/liberation pattern onto sin as the new Pharaoh. The slavery-redemption typology is strong thematically though the verbal contact here is diffuse; the fuller slavery exposition comes in 6:15-23.
sourceText: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:

note: The valley of dry bones: God brings the dead up from their graves to new life by his Spirit. Paul's death-and-burial-then-'newness of life' (6:4) and 'alive from the dead' (6:13) share the figural movement of resurrection-as-new-existence, though Paul grounds it christologically rather than nationally.
sourceText: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]

note: New heart and new spirit enabling obedience; 'newness of life' (6:4, kainotes zoes) coheres with the prophetic promise of interior renewal. Faint and disputed verbal contact, but the renewal/new-walk theme is shared.

note: 'The pangs of childbirth come for him' as an image of judgment and impending deliverance resonates faintly with the cosmic travail of v.22.
sourceText: The sorrows of a travailing woman will come on him. He is an unwise son; for when it is time, he doesn’t come to the opening of the womb.

note: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' as eschatological down-payment resonates with 'the first fruits of the Spirit' (v.23), the Spirit as the firstfruits/guarantee of the coming redemption.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.

note: 'The first fruits of the Spirit' (v.23) draws on the cultic firstfruits offering that consecrates and pledges the full harvest; the Spirit is the consecrating pledge of the redeemed body.
sourceText: The first of the first fruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of Yahweh your God. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.

note: The lament's 'why do you sleep?... our soul is bowed down... redeem us' anticipates the groaning, waiting, and hoped-for redemption (vv.23-25); the same psalm is quoted at v.36.
sourceText: Wake up! Why do you sleep, Lord? Arise! Don’t reject us forever. Why do you hide your face, and forget our affliction and our oppression? For our soul is bowed down to the dust. Our body clings to the earth. Rise up to help us. Redeem us for your loving kindness’ sake.

note: 'All my longing is before you; my groaning is not hidden from you' resonates with the inarticulate groaning the Spirit voices before 'him who searches the hearts' (vv.26-27).
sourceText: Lord, all my desire is before you. My groaning is not hidden from you.

note: 'The LORD looks on the heart' undergirds 'he who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit's mind' (v.27); God's heart-discerning gaze validates the wordless intercession.
sourceText: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

note: 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind' supplies the precise epithet 'he who searches the hearts' (v.27); the heart-searcher reads the Spirit's unutterable groanings.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: 'O LORD, you have searched me and known me... you discern my thoughts from afar' resonates with God searching the hearts and knowing the Spirit's mind (v.27).
sourceText: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar.

note: Being 'conformed to the image of his Son' (v.29) reworks humanity's creation in the image of God; the restored image is now christological, the Son as the prototype to which the predestined are refashioned.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: 'I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth' grounds 'that he might be the firstborn among many brothers' (v.29); the Davidic-messianic firstborn title is extended to the Son who heads a redeemed family.
sourceText: I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.

note: 'Israel is my firstborn son' reinforces the 'firstborn among many brothers' (v.29): the firstborn-son status, once Israel's, belongs to the Son who incorporates many siblings.
sourceText: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,

note: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you... I appointed you' supplies the foreknowing-and-appointing pattern of vv.29-30; divine foreknowledge as elective purpose precedes calling.
sourceText: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”

note: The Servant 'called from the womb,' named before birth, resonates with the chain of foreknowing, predestining, and calling in vv.29-30.
sourceText: Listen, islands, to me; and listen, you peoples, from far: Yahweh has called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother has he made mention of my name:

note: 'You meant evil... but God meant it for good' faintly underlies 'all things work together for good for those who love God' (v.28); divine providence turning suffering toward good.
sourceText: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.

note: 'Showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments' supplies the covenantal designation 'those who love God' (v.28), the loving-God-and-being-blessed pattern.
sourceText: and showing loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.

note: v.36 cites verbatim with the formula 'even as it is written': 'For your sake we are killed all day long; we were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.' The lament psalm of the righteous suffering for God's sake interprets the believers' affliction (v.35).
sourceText: Yes, for your sake we are killed all day long. We are regarded as sheep for the slaughter.

note: The Servant's courtroom taunt 'He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me?... It is the Lord GOD who helps me; who will declare me guilty?' is reworked into 'Who could bring a charge against God's chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns?' (vv.33-34); the forensic question-and-answer pattern is shared.
sourceText: He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord Yahweh will help me; who is he who shall condemn me? Behold, all they shall wax old as a garment, the moth shall eat them up.

note: 'He who didn't spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all' (v.32) echoes the Aqedah, where God says to Abraham 'you have not withheld (spared) your son, your only son'; God now does for all what Abraham was prepared to do, the Father not sparing his own Son.
sourceText: He said, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy, neither do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.”

note: 'Because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son' reinforces v.32; the Septuagint's verb for 'spare/withhold' (pheidomai) is the same word Paul uses, strengthening the Aqedah allusion.
sourceText: and said, “I have sworn by myself, says Yahweh, because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son,

note: 'The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all' and the Servant 'delivered up' (LXX paradidomi, 53:6,12) stands behind 'delivered him up for us all' (v.32); the handing-over of the Servant for the many.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: The Servant 'poured out his soul to death... bore the sin of many and makes intercession for the transgressors' resonates with Christ who 'makes intercession for us' (v.34); both join self-giving death with ongoing intercession.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: 'Sit at my right hand' grounds 'who is at the right hand of God' (v.34); the enthronement of the exalted Lord secures his advocacy and the impossibility of any condemnation.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: 'The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?' supplies the rhetorical shape of 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (v.31); the same God-for-me-therefore-fearless logic.
sourceText: Yahweh is on my side. I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?

note: 'The LORD is with us; do not fear them' resonates with 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (v.31); divine presence nullifies opposing power.
sourceText: Only don’t rebel against Yahweh, neither fear the people of the land; for they are bread for us. Their defense is removed from over them, and Yahweh is with us. Don’t fear them.”

note: 'This I know, that God is for me' is a near-verbal antecedent to 'God is for us' (v.31), the confidence that God's siding with the petitioner routs adversaries.
sourceText: Then my enemies shall turn back in the day that I call. I know this, that God is for me.

note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?... though war arise against me, yet I will be confident' resonates with the catalogue of perils that cannot prevail (vv.35,37-39).
sourceText: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers came at me to eat up my flesh, even my adversaries and my foes, they stumbled and fell. Though an army should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear. Though war should rise against me, even then I will be confident.

note: 'There is no god besides me... I kill and I make alive' underlies the totalizing pairing 'neither death, nor life' (v.38) as the extremes wholly within God's sovereign love.
sourceText: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.

note: The catalogue of deprivations (failed crops, no flock) followed by 'yet I will rejoice in the LORD' parallels the list of hardships in v.35 that cannot separate from God's love, culminating in triumphant confidence (v.37).
sourceText: For though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines; the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food; the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in Yahweh. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!

note: The three youths' confidence that 'our God whom we serve is able to deliver us' amid fire and sword resonates with believers as 'more than conquerors' through perils including 'sword' (vv.35-37).
sourceText: If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king.

note: 'The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them... having been disciplined a little they will receive great good' parallels the assurance that no affliction separates from God's love (vv.35-39); the righteous tested 'like gold in the furnace' and found worthy.
sourceText: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality; And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and […]

note: 'The righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord... they will receive a glorious crown' resonates with being 'more than conquerors' and inseparable from God's love (vv.37-39).
sourceText: But the righteous live forever, And in the Lord is their reward, And the care for them with the Most High. Therefore will they receive the crown of royal dignity And the diadem of beauty from the Lord’s hand; Because with his right hand will he cover them, And with his arm will he shield them.

note: The martyr-mother and seven sons, killed 'all day long' for covenant faithfulness yet confident of resurrection, resonate with 'for your sake we are killed all day long' read as triumphant martyrdom (vv.36-37).
sourceText: And it came to pass that seven kindred also with their mother were at the king’s command taken and shamefully handled with scourges and cords, to compel them to taste of the abominable swine’s flesh. But one of them made himself the spokesman and said, What would you ask and learn of us? for we are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers. And the king fell into a rage, and commanded to heat pans and caldrons: and when these forthwith […]

note: 'In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword' enumerates perils paralleling v.35's famine, sword, and danger, with God's protection through them.
sourceText: He will deliver you in six troubles; yes, in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death; in war, from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, neither shall you be afraid of destruction when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, neither shall you be afraid of the animals of the earth.

note: Paul's wish in v.3 that he himself were 'accursed (anathema) from Christ' for his kinsmen echoes Moses' intercession after the golden calf: 'blot me out of your book' rather than destroy Israel. Both are intercessors offering self-substitution/self-curse to spare the people; the Exodus 32 setting also frames the whole chapter's mercy-language (33:19 quoted at v.15).
sourceText: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”

note: The catalogue of Israel's privileges (adoption, glory, covenants, law-giving, service, promises, fathers) in vv.4-5 draws on the Deuteronomic election traditions naming Israel as God's chosen, holy people set above the nations.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.

note: 'Whose is the adoption (huiothesia)' (v.4) recalls the sonship of Israel: 'Israel is my firstborn son.' Israel's national adoption is the OT root of the privilege Paul lists.
sourceText: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,

note: 'The glory' (doxa, v.4) evokes the Shekinah glory of the LORD that appeared to Israel in the wilderness and dwelt in tabernacle/temple — a covenant privilege belonging to Israel.
sourceText: As Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, Yahweh’s glory appeared in the cloud.

note: 'The covenants' and 'the promises' (vv.4) point to the patriarchal covenant with Abraham and his seed, the seed-theme Paul immediately develops in vv.6-9.
sourceText: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.

note: 'The giving of the law' (nomothesia) as a unique privilege of Israel echoes the psalm's boast that God 'declares his word to Jacob... He has not dealt so with any nation.'
sourceText: He shows his word to Jacob; his statutes and his ordinances to Israel. He has not done this for just any nation. They don’t know his ordinances. Praise Yah!

note: Formula-marked citation in v.7: 'In Isaac will your seed be called' is verbatim from God's word to Abraham concerning Ishmael and Isaac. Paul uses it to prove that physical descent does not equal the elect 'seed' — only the line of promise counts.
sourceText: God said to Abraham, “Don’t let it be grievous in your sight because of the boy, and because of your handmaid. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice. For from Isaac will your seed be called.

note: v.9 'At the appointed time I will come, and Sarah will have a son' explicitly named 'a word of promise.' Conflates the LXX of Genesis 18:10 ('I will return to you at this season') with the promise of a son; the miraculous, promise-born birth of Isaac grounds Paul's 'children of the promise' argument.
sourceText: He said, “I will certainly return to you when the season comes round. Behold, Sarah your wife will have a son.” Sarah heard in the tent door, which was behind him.

note: v.12 'The elder will serve the younger' is verbatim from the oracle to Rebekah about Jacob and Esau in the womb. Paul cites it to show election precedes birth and works ('being not yet born, neither having done good or bad').
sourceText: Yahweh said to her, “Two nations are in your womb. Two peoples will be separated from your body. The one people will be stronger than the other people. The elder will serve the younger.”

note: v.13 'as it is written, Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' is a formula-cited verbatim quotation of Malachi's oracle, which itself reflects back on the Genesis Jacob/Esau election. Caps the argument that God's elective love is unmerited and prior.
