sourceText: “I have loved you,” says Yahweh. Yet you say, “How have you loved us?” “Wasn’t Esau Jacob’s brother?” says Yahweh, “Yet I loved Jacob; but Esau I hated, and made his mountains a desolation, and gave his heritage to the jackals of the wilderness.”

note: The 'appointed time' clause of v.9 also echoes Genesis 18:14, 'Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return... and Sarah shall have a son,' reinforcing that Isaac is born by divine power, not by natural descent.
sourceText: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”

note: v.10 'Rebekah also conceived by one' alludes to the narrative of Isaac and Rebekah; Paul stresses both twins share one father and one conception to isolate election as the only differentiator.
sourceText: Isaac entreated Yahweh for his wife, because she was barren. Yahweh was entreated by him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.

note: v.15 'he said to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion' is a verbatim LXX quotation of God's self-revelation to Moses. Grounds divine freedom in mercy and answers the charge of unrighteousness.
sourceText: He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.”

note: v.17 'the Scripture says to Pharaoh, For this very purpose I caused you to be raised up, that I might show in you my power, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth' is a formula-marked quotation. Pharaoh is the foil to Moses: God's freedom both to show mercy and to harden.
sourceText: but indeed for this cause I have made you stand: to show you my power, and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth;

note: v.18 'he hardens whom he desires' draws on the recurring Exodus motif that the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 4:21; 7:3; 9:12; 14:4). Paul generalizes the hardening theme from the plague narrative.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “When you go back into Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders which I have put in your hand, but I will harden his heart and he will not let the people go.

note: The mercy/compassion pairing of v.15 resonates with the divine-name proclamation that follows in Exodus 34:6, 'merciful and gracious,' the immediate sequel to 33:19 — the same theophanic context Paul mines.
sourceText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,

note: v.20 'Will the thing formed ask him who formed it, Why did you make me like this?' echoes Isaiah's rebuke of the clay that questions the potter, 'Shall the thing made say of him who made it, He did not make me?' Paul's potter/clay rebuttal is built on this prophetic protest-against-protest.
sourceText: You turn things upside down! Should the potter be thought to be like clay; that the thing made should say about him who made it, “He didn’t make me”; or the thing formed say of him who formed it, “He has no understanding?”

note: v.20-21 also draws on Isaiah 45:9, 'Woe to him who strives with his Maker... shall the clay say to him who fashions it, What are you making?' The 'who are you to reply against God' (antapokrinomenos) directly answers Isaiah's woe against the clay that contends with the potter.
sourceText: Woe to him who strives with his Maker— a clay pot among the clay pots of the earth! Shall the clay ask him who fashions it, ‘What are you making?’ or your work, ‘He has no hands?’

note: v.21 'has not the potter a right over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?' alludes to Jeremiah's potter's-house oracle: 'as the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.' Supplies the sovereign-potter image and the right to remake.
sourceText: House of Israel, can’t I do with you as this potter? says Yahweh. Behold, as the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel.

note: v.25, formula-marked ('As he says also in Hosea'): 'I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, who was not beloved' quotes Hosea's reversal of Lo-Ammi/Lo-Ruhamah. Paul applies the restoration of unfaithful Israel to the calling of Gentiles.
sourceText: I will sow her to me in the earth; and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy; and I will tell those who were not my people, ‘You are my people;’ and they will say, ‘My God!’”

note: v.26 'in the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, there they will be called children of the living God' is a verbatim quotation of Hosea 1:10 (LXX 2:1), continuing the Lo-Ammi reversal that Paul reads as the inclusion of the Gentiles among God's children.
sourceText: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’

note: v.27-28, formula-marked ('Isaiah cries concerning Israel'): 'If the number of the children of Israel are as the sand of the sea, it is the remnant who will be saved; for He will finish the work and cut it short in righteousness' quotes Isaiah's remnant oracle. Establishes the remnant theology central to ch.9-11.
sourceText: For though your people, Israel, are like the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness. For the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will make a full end, and that determined, in the midst of all the earth.

note: v.29, formula-marked ('As Isaiah has said before'): 'Unless the Lord of Armies had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and would have been made like Gomorrah' is a verbatim LXX quotation. Reinforces that survival rests entirely on God's gracious preservation of a remnant 'seed.'
sourceText: Unless Yahweh of Armies had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom; we would have been like Gomorrah.

note: The 'finishing/cutting short' decisive-action language of v.28 also draws on Isaiah 28:22, 'a full end, decreed upon the whole earth,' blended with 10:22-23; both stand behind Paul's compressed remnant-judgment formula.
sourceText: Now therefore don’t be scoffers, lest your bonds be made strong; for I have heard a decree of destruction from the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, on the whole earth.

note: 'As the sand of the sea' (v.27) verbally re-sounds the Abrahamic promise that the seed would be as numberless as the sand; Paul ironically juxtaposes the vast promised multitude with the saved remnant.
sourceText: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies.

note: The 'Sodom and Gomorrah' comparison cited in v.29 carries the figural weight of the destroyed cities of Genesis 19; the remnant 'seed' is what spares Israel from total annihilation like the cities of the plain.
sourceText: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky.

note: The Sodom/Gomorrah overthrow as a type of complete divine judgment (Isaiah 13:19, of Babylon) reinforces the destruction-imagery behind the Isaiah 1:9 quotation in v.29.
sourceText: Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldeans’ pride, will be like when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.

note: v.33, formula-marked ('as it is written'): 'Behold, I lay in Zion... a stone... and no one who believes in him will be disappointed/put to shame' quotes Isaiah's cornerstone oracle. Paul fuses it with Isaiah 8:14 to make the laid stone both foundation and stumbling block.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: v.33 'a stumbling stone and a rock of offense' is quoted from Isaiah 8:14, where the LORD himself becomes 'a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' to both houses of Israel. Paul conflates it with 28:16 to explain why Israel stumbled while Gentiles attained righteousness by faith.
sourceText: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

note: v.31-32 Israel 'pursuing/following after' a law of righteousness faintly echoes Isaiah's address to 'you who pursue righteousness, who seek the LORD,' inverted: Israel pursued by works, not faith, and so failed to attain it.
sourceText: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from.

note: The stumbling-stone/Zion-stone complex of v.32-33 belongs to the broader 'stone' testimonia tradition that also includes 'the stone the builders rejected'; Paul's stone Christology participates in this cluster though he cites only the Isaiah texts here.
sourceText: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.

note: 'You who pursue righteousness, who seek the LORD' — the verb pair pursue/seek righteousness underlies Paul's diagnosis that Israel 'sought to establish their own righteousness.' Thematic resonance with Isaianic righteousness language but no verbal quotation; disputed.
sourceText: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from.

note: Moses warns Israel not to say 'in their heart' that their own righteousness has earned the land — the seed of the 'establish their own righteousness' motif. The 'do not say in your heart' formula recurs verbatim in 10:6, so its conceptual root here (self-righteousness vs. God's gift) is a plausible anticipatory echo.
sourceText: Don’t say in your heart, after Yahweh your God has thrust them out from before you, saying, “For my righteousness Yahweh has brought me in to possess this land”; because Yahweh drives them out before you because of the wickedness of these nations. Not for your righteousness, or for the uprightness of your heart, do you go in to possess their land; but for the wickedness of these nations Yahweh your God does drive them out from before you, and that he may […]

note: The chapter's terminal quotation (cited at 10:20-21) describes a people zealous yet disobedient; Israel's 'zeal for God but not according to knowledge' here anticipates that Isaianic portrait of a contrary people. Forward-pointing thematic echo binding the pericope to the chapter's close.
sourceText: “I am inquired of by those who didn’t ask; I am found by those who didn’t seek me: I said, See me, see me, to a nation that was not called by my name. I have spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts;

note: telos/'end of the law' language; for Paul elsewhere love-of-neighbor is the law's fulfillment. Faint and disputed connection to the meaning of Christ as the law's goal; included for maximal coverage.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: Formula-cited: 'Moses writes about the righteousness of the law' introduces 'The one who does them will live by them' — a near-verbatim quotation of Leviticus 18:5 ('which if a man do, he shall live in them'). Paul makes it the voice of law-righteousness over against faith-righteousness. Also quoted at Galatians 3:12; high recurrence in Paul.
sourceText: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.

note: Formula-introduced ('the righteousness of faith says'): 'Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven... Who will descend into the abyss... The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart' — a sustained verbatim quotation of Deuteronomy 30:12-14, reworked christologically (ascend = bring Christ down; descend into the abyss = bring Christ up from the dead). High volume, the structural backbone of the pericope.
sourceText: It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.

note: The opening 'Do not say in your heart' in 10:6 conflates Deuteronomy 30:12 with the warning formula of Deuteronomy 9:4 ('Do not say in your heart... my righteousness'), which directly concerns self-righteousness. Strong verbal borrowing that splices the anti-self-righteousness warning onto the faith-word quotation. Widely recognized double allusion.
sourceText: Don’t say in your heart, after Yahweh your God has thrust them out from before you, saying, “For my righteousness Yahweh has brought me in to possess this land”; because Yahweh drives them out before you because of the wickedness of these nations.

note: The immediately preceding verse — 'this commandment is not too hard for you, nor is it far off' — sets up the not-in-heaven/not-beyond-the-sea contrast Paul exploits. Borrowed context for the 'word is near' argument even though only vv.12-14 are quoted.
sourceText: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant.

note: 'They mount up to heaven, they go down to the depths (abyss)' — the heaven/abyss merism for cosmic extremity. Paul's pairing 'ascend into heaven / descend into the abyss' may draw on this stock idiom; Deut 30 itself says 'beyond the sea,' so the 'abyss' wording suggests a secondary scriptural idiom. Disputed.
sourceText: They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble.

note: Formula-cited: 'the Scripture says, Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame/disappointed' — a quotation of Isaiah 28:16 (the precious cornerstone in Zion). Paul adds the universalizing 'whoever' (pas). Recurs at Romans 9:33, knitting chapters 9-10 together; high volume and recurrence.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: Formula-cited climax: 'Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved' — verbatim quotation of Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5). Paul reads kyrios as the risen Jesus (10:9, 'Jesus is Lord'), grounding the Jew-Greek universalism of 10:12. Also cited in Acts 2:21; high recurrence.
sourceText: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.

note: The 'mouth... heart' pairing of the Deut quotation is redeployed by Paul in 10:9-10 (confess with the mouth, believe in the heart). This is an exegetical extension of the quoted text — Paul mines the very words 'mouth/heart' to structure confession and faith. Strong internal echo of the source just cited.
sourceText: But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.

note: 'You shall... not be put to shame' in Joel 2:27, just before the quoted v.32, shares the not-ashamed motif Paul draws from Isaiah 28:16. Possible reinforcing echo from the Joel context Paul is already mining. Disputed.
sourceText: You will know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am Yahweh, your God, and there is no one else; and my people will never again be disappointed.

note: 'the abyss' (abyssos) as primeval deep; Paul's substitution of 'abyss' for Deut's 'beyond the sea' carries cosmic/death overtones (= realm of the dead, whence Christ is raised). Faint scriptural background for the abyss imagery. Disputed.
sourceText: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.

note: Formula-cited ('as it is written'): 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things' — quotation of Isaiah 52:7 (the herald announcing 'Your God reigns'). Paul reads the herald's gospel of return-from-exile as the apostolic gospel. High volume; central to the chain on hearing/preaching.
sourceText: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

note: 'Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good tidings, who proclaims peace' — closely parallels Isaiah 52:7 and may be conflated in Paul's wording (feet + good tidings + peace). Possible secondary scriptural source for the same image. Disputed.
sourceText: Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.

note: Formula-cited: 'Isaiah says, Lord, who has believed our report?' — verbatim quotation of Isaiah 53:1, the opening of the Servant Song. Paul uses Israel's unbelief at the Servant's message to explain why 'they did not all heed the gospel.' The 'report' (akoe) is punningly tied to 'faith comes by hearing (akoe)' in 10:17. High volume and theological weight.
sourceText: Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?

note: Separate echo: 10:17 ('faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ') exploits the LXX term akoe ('report/what is heard') from the Isaiah 53:1 quotation just given. Paul's whole hearing→faith chain is generated by the double sense of akoe in the source text. Verbal-exegetical echo distinct from the bare quotation.
sourceText: Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?

note: Formula-introduced rhetorically ('did they not hear? Yes...'): 'Their sound went out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world' — verbatim quotation of Psalm 19:4 (LXX 18:5). Paul transfers the cosmic witness of the heavens to the universal proclamation of the gospel, answering whether Israel has heard. High volume.
sourceText: Their voice has gone out through all the earth, their words to the end of the world. In them he has set a tent for the sun,

note: Formula-cited ('First Moses says'): 'I will provoke you to jealousy with that which is no nation; with a nation void of understanding I will make you angry' — verbatim quotation of Deuteronomy 32:21 from the Song of Moses. Grounds Paul's jealousy motif (cf. 11:11,14): Gentile inclusion provokes Israel. High recurrence in Paul's argument across chs. 9-11.
sourceText: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

note: Beyond the quotation, the Song of Moses (Deut 32) as a whole — Israel's faithlessness, God's turn to a foolish nation, eventual mercy — supplies the deep structure of Romans 9-11. The 'no-people/no-understanding' framing echoes through Paul's Gentile argument. Recurrence-based echo of the broader source context.
sourceText: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

note: Formula-cited ('Isaiah is very bold and says'): 'I was found by those who did not seek me; I was revealed to those who did not ask for me' — quotation of Isaiah 65:1, applied to the Gentiles who found God without seeking. High volume; pairs antithetically with the next verse on Israel.
sourceText: “I am inquired of by those who didn’t ask; I am found by those who didn’t seek me: I said, See me, see me, to a nation that was not called by my name.

note: Formula-cited ('But as to Israel he says'): 'All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people' — verbatim quotation of Isaiah 65:2, the chapter's climactic indictment of Israel's disobedience. Paired with 65:1 to contrast believing Gentiles and resistant Israel; high volume, the rhetorical capstone of ch. 10.
sourceText: I have spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts;

note: 'Why, when I came, was there no one? ... Is my hand shortened?' — the motif of God's outstretched/extended hand meeting no response resonates with 'all day long I stretched out my hands.' Faint reinforcing Isaianic echo. Disputed.
sourceText: Why, when I came, was there no man? when I called, was there no one to answer? Is my hand shortened at all, that it can’t redeem? or have I no power to deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a wilderness: their fish stink, because there is no water, and die for thirst.

note: The fuller Psalm 19 context — the heavens declaring God's glory with speech that has 'no words... yet their voice goes out' — undergirds Paul's claim that the gospel proclamation reaches everyone. Background of the quoted v.4. Disputed as to intentional reach.
sourceText: The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge. There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard.

note: Paul's opening 'God did not reject his people' (v.1-2) verbally tracks the psalm's promise 'the LORD will not reject his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.' Same verb of rejection, same object 'his people'; it functions almost as an embedded near-quotation grounding the whole argument.
sourceText: For Yahweh won’t reject his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.

note: Samuel: 'the LORD will not forsake his people for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself.' Paul's denial of rejection draws on this covenant-fidelity formula; pairs with Ps 94:14 as the scriptural backbone of v.1-2 'God did not reject his people.'
sourceText: For Yahweh will not forsake his people for his great name’s sake, because it has pleased Yahweh to make you a people to himself.

note: Paul's self-identification as 'a descendant of Abraham' (v.1) leans on the Abrahamic covenant promise to the seed; faint, but it grounds his claim that membership in the people persists by descent and election.
sourceText: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you. I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”

note: Verbatim of Elijah's complaint at Horeb: 'they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars; I alone am left, and they seek my life.' Paul cites it formulaically ('don't you know what the Scripture says about Elijah... how he pleads with God against Israel') to introduce the remnant theme (v.3).
sourceText: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

note: Elijah's complaint is repeated verbatim in 1 Kgs 19:14 (the second utterance to the LORD); Paul's v.3 reproduces this doubled lament. Listed separately because the source occurs at both v.10 and v.14 (recurrence within the source narrative).
sourceText: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

note: Formula-cited divine answer (v.4): 'I have reserved for myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to Baal.' Verbatim of the LORD's reply to Elijah; the foundational proof-text for Paul's doctrine of a preserved remnant 'according to the election of grace' (v.5).
sourceText: Yet will I leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth which has not kissed him.”

note: The remnant motif of v.5 ('a remnant according to the election of grace') draws on Isaiah's remnant theology ('though your people be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return'), a text Paul has already quoted in Rom 9:27-28. Strong conceptual borrowing of the 'remnant' (leimma/hypoleimma) word-field.
sourceText: For though your people, Israel, are like the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness. For the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will make a full end, and that determined, in the midst of all the earth.

note: Formula-cited ('as it is written') in v.8: 'God gave them a spirit of stupor (pneuma katanyxeos)' is verbatim from Isa 29:10 LXX, 'the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep.' Supplies the head phrase of the conflated citation about Israel's hardening.
sourceText: For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers.

note: The continuation of v.8 — 'eyes that they should not see and ears that they should not hear, to this very day' — is verbatim from Deut 29:4 ('the LORD has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day'). Paul fuses it with Isa 29:10 into a single formula-introduced quotation; 'to this very day' is the Deuteronomy tag.
sourceText: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.

note: The 'eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear' hardening language of v.8 also resonates with Isaiah's commissioning oracle ('hearing you will hear and not understand; seeing you will see and not perceive'), the classic hardening text. Reinforces the conflated citation's theme even if Deut 29:4 supplies the closer wording.
sourceText: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: Attributed quotation (v.9-10, 'David says'): 'Let their table be made a snare and a trap... Let their eyes be darkened that they may not see, and bow down their back always.' Verbatim of Ps 69:22-23 LXX. A psalm of the righteous sufferer Paul reads imprecatorily against the hardened; pairs the 'darkened eyes' with the Isaiah/Deut citation of v.8.
sourceText: Let their table before them become a snare. May it become a retribution and a trap. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they can’t see. Let their backs be continually bent.

note: The 'snare/trap' imprecation of v.9 also echoes the wider psalmic curse tradition ('let destruction come upon him unawares, and let his net that he hid catch himself'). Faint reinforcement of the Ps 69 citation.
sourceText: Let destruction come on him unawares. Let his net that he has hidden catch himself. Let him fall into that destruction.

note: 'to provoke them to jealousy' (v.11, again v.14) borrows directly from the Song of Moses: 'they have moved me to jealousy... I will provoke them to jealousy by those who are not a people.' Paul already quoted Deut 32:21 at Rom 10:19; here he deploys its key verb (parazeloo) as the engine of his Gentiles-to-Israel argument. Strong verbal borrowing with recurrence.
sourceText: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

note: 'If the first fruit is holy, so is the lump' (v.16) draws on the dough/firstfruit offering of Num 15: a portion of the first of the dough (aparche) is given so the whole batch is sanctified. Paul applies the cultic logic of consecration-by-firstfruit to the patriarchs and Israel.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘When you come into the land where I bring you, then it shall be that when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall offer up a wave offering to Yahweh. Of the first of your dough you shall offer up a cake for a wave offering. As the wave offering of the threshing floor, so you shall heave it. Of the first of your dough, you shall give to Yahweh a wave offering throughout […]

note: The olive-tree image for Israel (v.17-24, 'the root and the richness of the olive tree') borrows Jeremiah's figure: 'The LORD called your name, A green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit'—followed there by branches broken and burned for unbelief. Supplies both the olive-tree identification of Israel and the broken-branches judgment motif.
sourceText: Yahweh called your name, A green olive tree, beautiful with goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he has kindled fire on it, and its branches are broken.

note: Hosea's restoration oracle pictures renewed Israel: 'his branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be like the olive tree.' Paul's olive-tree-with-spreading-branches and hope of regrafting (v.23-24) coheres with this restoration imagery alongside Jer 11:16.
sourceText: His branches will spread, and his beauty will be like the olive tree, and his fragrance like Lebanon.

note: 'I am like a green olive tree in the house of God' — the righteous flourishing as an olive planted by God resonates faintly with Paul's cultivated 'good olive tree' (v.24) into which branches are grafted.
sourceText: But as for me, I am like a green olive tree in God’s house. I trust in God’s loving kindness forever and ever.

note: 'Don't boast over the branches... Don't be conceited, but fear' (v.18, 20) echoes 'Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and depart from evil.' The pairing of not-being-wise-in-self with fear is distinctive; recurs at v.25 ('wise in your own conceits').
sourceText: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.

note: 'Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes' undergirds Paul's warning against Gentile conceit (v.18-20, 25). Faint thematic reinforcement of the Prov 3:7 admonition.
sourceText: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!

note: 'You stand by your faith' (v.20) faintly recalls Isaiah's word to Ahaz: 'If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established (stand firm).' The standing-by-faith / falling-by-unbelief antithesis coheres, though the verbal link is thin.
sourceText: and the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son. If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established.’”

note: 'Their acceptance... life from the dead' (v.15) reads Israel's future restoration typologically as resurrection, the figure of the valley of dry bones where dead Israel is raised and replanted in its land. Typological rather than verbal.
sourceText: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]

note: Formula-cited ('as it is written') in v.26-27: 'There will come out of Zion the Deliverer, and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.' Verbatim core from Isa 59:20-21 LXX ('the Deliverer will come for Zion's sake, and turn away ungodliness from Jacob'), with the 'covenant' clause flowing from 59:21. The backbone citation of the 'all Israel will be saved' climax.
sourceText: “A Redeemer will come to Zion, and to those who turn from disobedience in Jacob,” says Yahweh. “As for me, this is my covenant with them,” says Yahweh. “My Spirit who is on you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, nor out of the mouth of your seed, nor out of the mouth of your seed’s seed,” says Yahweh, “from henceforth and forever.”

note: 'This is my covenant to them, when I will take away their sins' (v.27b) supplies the sin-removal clause via Isa 27:9 LXX: 'this is his blessing, when I take away his sin.' Paul conflates it with Isa 59:20-21; the phrase 'take away their sins' is the Isa 27:9 contribution to the composite citation.
sourceText: Therefore by this the iniquity of Jacob will be forgiven, and this is all the fruit of taking away his sin: that he makes all the stones of the altar as chalk stones that are beaten in pieces, so that the Asherah poles and the incense altars shall rise no more.

note: 'This is my covenant to them, when I will take away their sins' (v.27) also draws the new-covenant formula from Jer 31:33-34 ('this is the covenant I will make... I will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more'). The 'covenant + forgiveness of sins' pairing is distinctively Jeremianic; Paul fuses it into the Isaianic Deliverer oracle.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin […]

note: 'Out of Zion' as the source of deliverance (v.26) resonates with Zion-centered eschatology ('out of Zion shall go forth the law'). Faint thematic backdrop to the quoted Isa 59:20.
sourceText: Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.

note: 'A partial hardening has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in' (v.25) sustains the Isaianic hardening motif of the chapter (cf. the Isa 29:10 citation at v.8). The temporal 'until' frames the hardening as the bounded judicial blindness of Isaiah's commission.
sourceText: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: 'concerning the election, they are beloved for the fathers' sake' (v.28) draws on Deuteronomy's election theology: 'because the LORD loved you... and because he would keep the oath which he swore to your fathers.' The love-of-Israel-for-the-fathers'-sake is the Deuteronomic ground Paul invokes.
sourceText: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

note: 'The LORD had a delight in your fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them' directly undergirds v.28's 'beloved for the fathers' sake' and v.29's irrevocable calling. Pairs with Deut 7:7-8 as the election-of-the-patriarchs source.
sourceText: Only Yahweh had a delight in your fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them, even you above all peoples, as at this day.

note: 'The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable' (v.29) coheres with Balaam's oracle that God 'is not a man, that he should lie... has he said, and will he not do it?'—the unchangeableness of God's word toward Israel. Faint thematic support.
sourceText: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?

note: Verbatim quotation (v.34): 'For who has known the mind of the LORD? Or who has been his counselor?' from Isa 40:13 LXX ('who has known the mind of the LORD, and who has been his counselor that he might instruct him?'). Caps the doxology on the unsearchability of God's wisdom.
sourceText: Who has directed the Spirit of Yahweh, or has taught him as his counselor?

note: Quotation (v.35): 'Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?' rendering Job 41:11 ('who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is mine'). Paul follows a Hebrew-leaning form (the LXX differs), asserting God's unindebted sovereignty.
sourceText: Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Everything under the heavens is mine.

note: 'How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out' (v.33) borrows Isaiah's 'my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways... as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways.' The inscrutable 'ways' of God is the shared figure, and Isa 40-55 supplies the doxology's whole register.
sourceText: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways,” says Yahweh. “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.

note: 'Who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number' resonates with v.33's 'unsearchable judgments... past tracing out.' Coheres with the Job-framed doxology that closes with the Job 41:11 citation.
sourceText: who does great things that can’t be fathomed, marvelous things without number;

note: 'Who does great things past finding out, yes, marvelous things without number' parallels v.33's untraceable ways of God. Faint reinforcement of the Joban wisdom backdrop to the doxology.
sourceText: He does great things past finding out; yes, marvelous things without number.

note: 'Have you heard the secret counsel of God?'—the rhetorical challenge to anyone claiming to be God's counselor—anticipates v.34's 'who has been his counselor?' alongside the primary Isa 40:13 quotation.
sourceText: Have you heard the secret counsel of God? Do you limit wisdom to yourself?

note: 'For what man can know the counsel of God? Or who can conceive what the Lord wills?' (deuterocanonical) closely parallels v.34's question and likely stands in the same wisdom-doxology stream Paul draws on; some see it as a mediating source for the Isa 40:13 citation.
sourceText: For what man will know the counsel of God? Or who will conceive what the Lord willeth?

note: 'Who has stood in the council of the LORD, that he should perceive and hear his word?' faintly underlies v.34's 'who has been his counselor?'—the prophetic topos of no human admittance to the divine council.
sourceText: For who has stood in the council of Yahweh, that he should perceive and hear his word? who has marked my word, and heard it?

note: "Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God" reuses the technical cultic vocabulary of the burnt offering, which must be presented/brought 'acceptable before the LORD' (LXX dekton). Paul figurally transposes the Levitical offering from animal victim to the embodied self.
sourceText: “‘If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without defect. He shall offer it at the door of the Tent of Meeting, that he may be accepted before Yahweh. He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.

note: The Psalm's claim that God does not delight in animal sacrifice but in 'a broken spirit' anticipates Paul's redefinition of true worship (logike latreia) as the offering of the whole self rather than the slain victim.
sourceText: For you don’t delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.

note: 'To obey is better than sacrifice' belongs to the prophetic stream that internalizes and ethicizes cult; Paul's 'reasonable/spiritual service' redirects sacrifice toward obedient self-presentation in the same key.
sourceText: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.

note: 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice' is part of the prophetic critique that grounds Paul's reframing of worship as embodied, merciful obedience rather than ritual offering.
sourceText: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

note: Micah's rhetorical rejection of burnt offerings in favor of doing justice and walking humbly parallels Paul's contrast between cultic sacrifice and 'living sacrifice' as the true service God requires.
sourceText: How shall I come before Yahweh, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will Yahweh be pleased with thousands of rams? With tens of thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience? The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

note: The promise of a 'new heart and a new spirit' stands behind 'be transformed by the renewing of your mind'; the eschatological interior renewal of the prophets is here applied to the believing community.
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.

note: The new-covenant law written on the heart/mind (LXX dianoia) coheres with the 'renewing of the mind' that enables one to discern God's will; faint verbal contact via mind/heart-renewal.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:

note: Discerning and doing 'the good and acceptable and perfect will of God' echoes Deuteronomy's insistence that God's commandment is knowable and doable, internalized in heart and mouth — a theme Paul invokes nearby in Romans 10.
sourceText: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]

note: 'Not to think of himself more highly than he ought' draws on the wisdom warning 'Be not wise in your own eyes'; the same maxim returns explicitly at 12:16, framing the pericope's call to sober self-estimation.
sourceText: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.

note: 'Do you see a man wise in his own conceit? There is more hope for a fool' supplies the proverbial backdrop for Paul's exhortation against inflated self-regard ('think reasonably').
sourceText: Do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.

note: Sirach's wisdom that 'pride is hateful before the Lord and before men' is a Second Temple parallel to Paul's call not to over-rate oneself but to measure by the faith God apportions.
sourceText: Pride is hateful before the Lord and before men; And in the judgement of both will unrighteousness err.

note: 12:19 cites with the formula 'it is written': 'Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.' The wording reflects the Song of Moses (with a form closer to the Targum/Hebrew than LXX), making divine retribution the ground for renouncing personal revenge.
sourceText: Vengeance is mine, and recompense, at the time when their foot slides; for the day of their calamity is at hand. Their doom rushes at them.”

note: 12:20 quotes nearly verbatim: 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so you will heap coals of fire on his head.' Paul takes over the LXX wisdom saying whole as the positive counterpart to renounced vengeance.
sourceText: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.

note: 'You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge... you shall love your neighbor' is the holiness-code substratum of the whole love-section: 'let love be without hypocrisy,' 'do not avenge yourselves,' and the love of brothers all draw on this command Paul elsewhere makes the summary of the law (13:9).
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'Abhor that which is evil; cling to that which is good' (12:9) closely renders the prophetic imperative 'Hate evil and love good'; the antithetical evil/good pairing matches Amos's covenant ethics.
sourceText: Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts. It may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”

note: 'Depart from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it' underlies both 'abhor evil... cling to good' (12:9) and 'be at peace with all men' (12:18); the twin evil-shunning and peace-pursuing maxims are reflected together.
sourceText: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.

note: 'You who love the LORD, hate evil' offers a further scriptural pairing of love and abhorrence of evil behind 12:9.
sourceText: You who love Yahweh, hate evil. He preserves the souls of his saints. He delivers them out of the hand of the wicked.

note: 'Do not be wise in your own conceits' (12:16) reproduces 'Be not wise in your own eyes' (LXX), the same proverb that grounded 12:3; here it caps the call to humble association with the lowly.
sourceText: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.

note: 'Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes' reinforces the prophetic condemnation of self-conceit that Paul forbids in 12:16.
sourceText: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!

note: 'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD and he will save you' is the wisdom source for 'Repay no one evil for evil' (12:17) joined to leaving wrath to God (12:19) — the Proverb already links non-retaliation with reliance on divine vindication.
sourceText: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.

note: 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done' directly parallels the prohibition of returning evil for evil in 12:17.
sourceText: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”

note: 'Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men' (12:17) echoes 'find favor and good repute in the sight of God and man' (LXX Prov 3:4), the wisdom ideal of conduct visibly good before others.
sourceText: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.

note: 'God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble' undergirds 'associate with the humble; do not be high-minded' (12:16); the humility motif is the same wisdom orientation James and 1 Peter also draw from this verse.
sourceText: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
lxxText: The Lord resists the proud; but he gives grace to the humble.

note: 'Do not fail those who weep, but mourn with those who mourn' is a strikingly close Second Temple parallel to 'weep with those who weep' (12:15); a wisdom maxim of empathetic solidarity rather than a quotation.
sourceText: Be not lacking to those who weep; And mourn with those who mourn.

note: 'Did I not weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the poor?' anticipates the compassionate mourning-with-the-mourner of 12:15.
sourceText: Didn’t I weep for him who was in trouble? Wasn’t my soul grieved for the needy?

note: The psalmist's mourning and prayer for his persecutors ('I afflicted myself... I went about as one who laments for his mother') parallels both 'weep with those who weep' (12:15) and 'bless those who persecute you' (12:14).
sourceText: But as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth. I afflicted my soul with fasting. My prayer returned into my own bosom. I behaved myself as though it had been my friend or my brother. I bowed down mourning, as one who mourns his mother.

note: The command to love the resident alien 'as yourself' grounds the welcome of strangers behind 'given to hospitality' (12:13) within the same holiness-code love ethic that governs the pericope.
sourceText: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.

note: Abraham's hospitality to the three visitors is the paradigm narrative of welcome that informs the early-Christian virtue 'given to hospitality' (12:13).
sourceText: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]

note: 'The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself... what is committed to you, attend to in humility' parallels 'do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble' (12:16) as Second Temple humility instruction.
sourceText: The greater you are, humble yourself the more, And you will find favor before the Lord. For great is the potency of the Lord, And he is glorified of those who are lowly.

note: 'O LORD, God of vengeance' confirms that retribution belongs to God alone — the theological premise of 12:19 that Paul anchors in Deuteronomy 32:35; possible secondary resonance.
sourceText: Yahweh, you God to whom vengeance belongs, you God to whom vengeance belongs, shine out.

note: David's refusal to harm Saul — 'May the LORD avenge me on you, but my hand shall not be against you' — is a narrative enactment of leaving vengeance to God and not repaying evil for evil (12:17, 19).
sourceText: May Yahweh judge between me and you, and may Yahweh avenge me of you; but my hand shall not be on you.

note: Paul's axiom 'there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God' restates Daniel's hymn that God 'changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings.' Strong thematic and conceptual borrowing: the establishment and deposing of rulers is God's act, the theological ground for v.1.
sourceText: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;

note: 'The Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will' (cf. 4:25, 4:32) is the Danielic doctrine that earthly dominion is conferred by God, directly underwriting 'ordained by God' and 'a servant of God.'
sourceText: The sentence is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones; to the intent that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.

note: Wisdom declares 'By me kings reign, and rulers decree justice; by me princes rule.' The claim that legitimate rule derives from God and exists to commend the good (v.3) closely tracks this sapiential formula.
sourceText: By me kings reign, and princes decree justice. By me princes rule; nobles, and all the righteous rulers of the earth.

note: Address to rulers: 'your dominion was given you from the Lord, and your sovereignty from the Most High, who will search out your works.' This Second Temple text gives the nearest verbal-conceptual parallel to vv.1-4 (authority delegated by God; rulers accountable as God's ministers). Many read Romans 13 as engaging precisely this Hellenistic-Jewish political theology.
sourceText: Hear therefore, you kings, and understand; Learn, you judges of the ends of the earth: Give ear, you that have dominion over much people, And make your boast in multitudes of nations. Because your dominion was given you from the Lord, And your sovereignty from the Most High; Who will search out your works, And will make inquisition of your counsels:

note: Rulers are called 'servants/ministers of his kingdom' who will be judged for failing to govern rightly — parallel to Paul's repeated 'servant of God' (diakonos/leitourgos, vv.4,6) and the threat of wrath upon wrongdoers.
sourceText: Because being officers of his kingdom you did not judge aright, Neither kept you law, nor walked after the counsel of God. Awfully and swiftly will he come upon you; Because a stern judgement befalleth those who are in high place:

note: 'The government of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and over it he will raise up the right leader for the time' — Ben Sira's statement that political authority and its incumbents are God-appointed coheres tightly with vv.1-2.
sourceText: In the hand of the Lord is the authority of the earth; And in due time he will raise up over it one that is profitable.

note: God: 'I have made the earth... and I give it to whomever it seems right to me. Now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar... my servant.' A pagan king is called God's 'servant' and his rule is divinely ordained — striking precedent for calling the (Roman) ruler 'a servant of God' (vv.4,6).
sourceText: I have made the earth, the men and the animals that are on the surface of the earth, by my great power and by my outstretched arm; and I give it to whom it seems right to me. Now have I given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant; and the animals of the field also have I given him to serve him.

note: 'Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you... and pray to the LORD on its behalf' — the exilic posture of submission to and cooperation with a foreign government anticipates Paul's counsel of subjection, taxes, and honor (vv.5-7).
sourceText: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it; for in its peace you shall have peace.

note: 'My son, fear the LORD and the king' pairs reverence for God with honor due the ruler — directly behind the closing exhortation to render 'respect to whom respect, honor to whom honor' (v.7).
sourceText: My son, fear Yahweh and the king. Don’t join those who are rebellious:

note: 'Keep the king's command... whoever keeps a command will not experience harm' — wisdom on prudent obedience to royal authority parallels Paul's 'be in subjection... do good and you will have praise' (vv.3-5).
sourceText: I say, “Keep the king’s command!” because of the oath to God. Don’t be hasty to go out of his presence. Don’t persist in an evil thing, for he does whatever pleases him, for the king’s word is supreme. Who can say to him, “What are you doing?” Whoever keeps the commandment shall not come to harm, and his wise heart will know the time and procedure.

note: 'You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people' — Torah pairs honoring God with not dishonoring the civil authority, an antecedent to 'he who resists the authority withstands the ordinance of God' (v.2) and 'honor to whom honor' (v.7).
sourceText: “You shall not blaspheme God, nor curse a ruler of your people.

note: 'Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed' — the foundational warrant for human authority to execute lethal justice stands behind 'he does not bear the sword in vain... an avenger for wrath' (v.4).
sourceText: Whoever sheds man’s blood, his blood will be shed by man, for God made man in his own image.

note: 'It is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another' — God's sovereignty over the rise and fall of rulers undergirds 'those who exist are ordained by God' (v.1).
sourceText: But God is the judge. He puts down one, and lifts up another.

note: David's doxology: 'Yours is the kingdom, O LORD... power and might are in your hand.' The conviction that all rule belongs to and flows from God is the broader scriptural matrix for vv.1-2.
sourceText: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all. Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all; and in your hand is power and might; and it is in your hand to make great, and to give strength to all.

note: God names the Persian Cyrus 'his anointed' and uses a pagan emperor as instrument of his purposes — a figural precedent for treating the Roman magistrate as 'God's servant' (vv.4,6) without the ruler's knowledge of God.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have held, to subdue nations before him, and strip kings of their armor; to open the doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut:

note: Verbatim citation of the second-table Decalogue commandments: 'You shall not commit adultery,' 'You shall not murder,' 'You shall not steal,' 'You shall not covet.' Paul lists adultery before murder, following the Septuagint order of Deuteronomy 5 (and Exodus 20 LXX manuscripts).
sourceText: “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”

note: The Deuteronomic recension of the same commandments; the LXX of Deuteronomy 5 places adultery before murder, matching Paul's sequence in v.9, so this is the likely proximate text.
sourceText: “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. Neither shall you desire your neighbor’s house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor’s.”

note: Explicit verbatim quotation: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' which Paul names as the saying in which all the commandments are 'summed up.' The interpretive move (love of neighbor as the epitome of the law) recurs in Romans (cf. 13:10) and Galatians 5:14.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: v.10 'Love does no harm to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law' continues to expound the same Levitical command, drawing out its negative corollary as the substance of all the prohibitions just cited.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head' — the divine-warrior imagery of donning protective armor underlies 'put on the armor of light' (v.12) and 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' (v.14). Paul develops this same Isaianic armor motif at Ephesians 6 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8.
sourceText: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.

note: 'He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, and wear impartial justice as a helmet' — this Second Temple reworking of Isaiah 59:17 stands in the same stream feeding Paul's 'put on the armor of light' (v.12).
sourceText: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet; He will take holiness as an invincible shield,

note: 'Arise, shine, for your light has come... darkness shall cover the earth... but the LORD will arise upon you' — the dawning of eschatological light dispelling darkness parallels 'the night is far gone, the day is near' and the light/darkness antithesis of vv.12-13.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

note: 'Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments' — combines the summons to wake and the imperative to 'put on,' both present in Paul's 'awaken out of sleep' (v.11) and 'put on the armor of light' / 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' (vv.12,14).
sourceText: Awake, awake, put on your strength, Zion; put on your beautiful garments, Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean.

note: 'Rouse yourself, rouse yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem' — the prophetic call to awaken to the hour of salvation parallels 'it is already time for you to awaken out of sleep' (v.11).
sourceText: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.

note: 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' — the night-to-day, darkness-to-light reversal of vv.12-13 resonates with this classic salvation-light oracle.
sourceText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: 'He has clothed me with the garments of salvation... as a bridegroom decks himself' — the salvific 'putting on' of clothing as a figure for new status anticipates 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' (v.14).
sourceText: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings' — the dawning day of salvation coheres with 'the day is near' (v.12) and the nearness of salvation (v.11).
sourceText: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.

note: 'Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust' — eschatological awakening from sleep/death as a figure of salvation faintly parallels 'awaken out of sleep' (v.11).
sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

note: Those who 'rebel against the light' and work evil under cover of night/darkness anticipate 'the works of darkness' (v.12) contrasted with walking properly 'as in the day' (v.13).
sourceText: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths. The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief. The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face. In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light. For the morning is to all of them like thick […]

note: 'Be not among drunkards... for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty' — sapiential warning against carousing and drunkenness behind 'not in reveling and drunkenness' (v.13).
sourceText: Don’t be among ones drinking too much wine, or those who gorge themselves on meat: for the drunkard and the glutton shall become poor; and drowsiness clothes them in rags.

note: Woe to those who 'run after strong drink... till wine inflames them' — prophetic censure of revelry and drunkenness parallels the vice-list of v.13.
sourceText: Woe to those who rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; who stay late into the night, until wine inflames them!

note: Paul's explicit formula-citation in 14:11 ('it is written, As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee will bow, every tongue will confess to God') quotes Isaiah 45:23 LXX. In Isaiah the universal bowing and swearing/confessing is rendered to YHWH alone as the only God and Savior; Paul deploys it to ground the certainty of universal accountability at the divine judgment seat. The same verse recurs at Philippians 2:10-11, showing Pauline thematic recurrence.
sourceText: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.

note: The introductory divine-oath formula 'As I live, says the Lord' (zōn egō legei kyrios) prefixed to the Isaiah 45 quotation is not in Isaiah 45:23 itself; it is the LXX oath formula 'as I live' (ζῶ ἐγώ) characteristic of Numbers 14:21,28 and Ezekiel. Paul (or his Vorlage) conflates the oath formula with the Isaiah quotation to heighten its solemnity as a guarantee of universal judgment.
sourceText: but in very deed, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with Yahweh’s glory;

note: An alternative/complementary source for the prefixed oath 'As I live, says the Lord': Isaiah 49:18 ('As I live, says the LORD') stands within the same section of Isaiah as 45:23, making it a plausible internal-Isaianic source for the conflated formula rather than the Numbers/Ezekiel oath stock.
sourceText: Lift up your eyes all around, and see: all these gather themselves together, and come to you. As I live,” says Yahweh, “you shall surely clothe yourself with them all as with an ornament, and dress yourself with them, like a bride.

note: Ezekiel is the densest concentration of the 'As I live, says the Lord' oath (Ezekiel 5:11; 14:16; 16:48; 33:11, etc.). The recurrence of the formula there may stand behind the LXX phrasing Paul attaches to the Isaiah citation; faint and not pointed to a single verse.
sourceText: Therefore as I live, says the Lord Yahweh, surely, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things, and with all your abominations, therefore will I also diminish you; neither shall my eye spare, and I also will have no pity.

note: The 'weak' eating only vegetables (lachana, 14:2) recalls the original Edenic vegetarian diet granted to humanity (Genesis 1:29, every seed-bearing plant for food). The contrast of vegetable-only vs. eating-all-things may evoke the pre-Noahic dietary order; thematic and faint, not verbal.
sourceText: God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.

note: The position that 'one has faith to eat all things' (panta phagein, 14:2) echoes the post-flood Noahic grant: 'Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you; as the green plants I gave you everything' (Genesis 9:3). Paul's 'all things are clean' (14:14,20) presupposes this universal grant of food over against later dietary restriction.
sourceText: Every moving thing that lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green herb, I have given everything to you.

note: The clean/unclean food dispute underlying 14:1-12 (and explicit in 14:14,20, 'nothing is unclean of itself... all things indeed are clean') directly engages the Levitical purity code distinguishing clean from unclean animals (Leviticus 11; cf. Deuteronomy 14). The 'weak' likely keep these distinctions; Paul's verdict that nothing is koinon in itself overturns the categorical force of Leviticus 11 for those in Christ.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]

note: Deuteronomy's parallel dietary legislation ('You shall not eat any abominable thing') reinforces the Levitical clean/unclean backdrop to the eating dispute. The 'weak in faith' who eat only vegetables may be observing scruples derived from this Torah food law (and/or avoiding marketplace meat of uncertain provenance).
sourceText: You shall not eat any abominable thing. These are the animals which you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the chamois. Every animal that parts the hoof, and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, that may you eat. Nevertheless these you shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of those who have the hoof cloven: the camel, the hare, and the […]

note: Daniel and his companions refuse the king's rich food and wine, eating only vegetables (LXX lachana / ospria) and water to avoid defilement (Daniel 1:12,16). This is the closest Scriptural antecedent to a diaspora Jew eating 'only vegetables' (14:2) out of purity scruple in a Gentile environment, providing a likely model for the 'weak.'
sourceText: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself. Now God made Daniel to find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs. The prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel, I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse […]

note: Paul's axiom 'none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself... we are the Lord's' (14:7-8) reflects the creational logic that life is a gift wholly owed to its Giver (cf. Genesis 2:7, the breath of life from God). Faint thematic resonance of creaturely belonging rather than verbal borrowing.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: 'We are the Lord's' (tou kyriou esmen, 14:8) echoes the creational ownership confessed in Psalm 24:1 ('The earth is the LORD's and its fullness'), which Paul cites elsewhere at 1 Corinthians 10:26 in a closely parallel food-and-conscience argument. The lordship grounding here is conceptually linked though not quoted.
sourceText: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell therein.

note: 'Each one of us will give account of himself to God' (14:12) coheres with the Wisdom expectation that 'God will bring every deed into judgment' (Ecclesiastes 12:14). Thematic accountability before the divine Judge; faint and conceptual.
sourceText: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.

note: The motif of individual rendering of account to God who judges (14:10,12) resonates with Psalm 62:12 ('you will render to each according to his work'), a verse Paul invokes for judgment-according-to-works at Romans 2:6. The shared judgment-recompense logic links the chapters.
sourceText: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.

note: 'We will all stand before the judgment seat of God/Christ' (14:10) carries the prophetic Day-of-the-LORD note of standing before the dread Judge (cf. Joel 2:11, 'who can endure it?'), reframed by Paul christologically. Very faint thematic echo.
sourceText: Yahweh thunders his voice before his army; for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of Yahweh is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?

note: Paul's declaration 'nothing is unclean of itself... all things indeed are clean' (14:14,20) directly engages and relativizes the Levitical clean/unclean food code (Leviticus 11). The very term koinon ('common/unclean') is the purity vocabulary of the dietary law; Paul affirms the law's categories exist only for the one who reckons a thing unclean.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]

note: 'All things indeed are clean' (panta kathara, 14:20) restates the universal Noahic food grant (Genesis 9:3, everything that lives given as food). Paul grounds Christian liberty regarding food in the creation/Noahic order that precedes and outranks the Levitical restriction.
sourceText: Every moving thing that lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green herb, I have given everything to you.

note: The command not to 'put a stumbling block in his brother's way' (proskomma, 14:13) draws on the Holiness Code prohibition: 'You shall not put a stumbling block before the blind' (Leviticus 19:14 LXX, proskomma / skandalon). Paul transposes the literal physical stumbling-block into the moral injury of causing a fellow believer to fall.
sourceText: “‘You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear your God. I am Yahweh.

note: 'If your brother is grieved because of food, you walk no longer in love' (14:15) applies the love-of-neighbor command (Leviticus 19:18) that Paul has just made the fulfillment of the law in 13:8-10. The 'brother' (adelphos) language and the priority of love over one's own right enact Leviticus 19:18 directly.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'Don't let your good be slandered/blasphemed' (mē blasphēmeisthō, 14:16) echoes the prophetic concern that God's name/people be 'blasphemed among the nations' (Isaiah 52:5 LXX), a verse Paul cites at Romans 2:24. The fear that the gospel-given 'good' becomes an occasion of blasphemy reuses this prophetic anxiety.
sourceText: “Now therefore, what do I do here,” says Yahweh, “seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Those who rule over them mock,” says Yahweh, “and my name continually all the day is blasphemed.

note: 'Let us follow after things which make for peace' (ta tēs eirēnēs diōkōmen, 14:19) closely echoes Psalm 34:14 LXX ('seek peace and pursue it,' zētēson eirēnēn kai diōxon autēn). The verb 'pursue' (diōkō) with 'peace' as object is the distinctive shared phrasing.
sourceText: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.

note: The build-up vs. tear-down language ('build one another up,' 14:19; 'don't overthrow God's work,' 14:20, katalye) resonates with the Jeremianic commission to 'pluck up and break down... to build and to plant' (Jeremiah 1:10). The oikodomē/kataluō opposition is a recurring prophetic idiom for God's constructive work among his people.
sourceText: Behold, I have this day set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”

note: 'The Kingdom of God is... righteousness, peace, and joy' (14:17) coheres with the prophetic vision that 'the work of righteousness shall be peace' (Isaiah 32:17), where dikaiosynē and eirēnē are paired as the fruit of the Spirit poured out (32:15). Thematic resonance of the Spirit-wrought eschatological order.
sourceText: The work of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.

note: The triad 'peace and joy' as marks of the inbreaking Kingdom (14:17) faintly echoes the Isaianic new-exodus promise 'you shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace' (Isaiah 55:12), where joy and peace characterize redeemed life under God's reign. Faint thematic.
sourceText: For you shall go out with joy, and be led out with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break out before you into singing; and all the trees of the fields shall clap their hands.

note: 'It is good not to eat meat, drink wine...' (14:21) — the renunciation of wine for the sake of another — has a faint sapiential backdrop in wisdom warnings about wine (Proverbs 23:31, 'do not look at wine when it is red'). Here, however, abstinence is for the brother's sake, not self-discipline; the link is thematic and weak.
sourceText: Don’t look at the wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup, when it goes down smoothly.

note: Ben Sira's measured counsel on wine and food at table (Sirach 31:25-31), weighing one's conduct for the sake of fellow diners, offers a Second Temple sapiential parallel to Paul's 'it is good not to eat meat or drink wine' where another stumbles (14:21). Conceptual, not verbal.
sourceText: Show not yourself valiant in wine; For wine has destroyed many. The furnace proves the temper of steel by dipping; So does wine prove hearts in the quarreling of the proud. Wine is as good as life to men, If you drink it in its measure: What life is there to a man that is without wine? And it has been created to make men glad. Wine drunk in season and to satisfy Is joy of heart, and gladness of soul: Wine drunk largely is bitterness of soul, With […]

note: The blessing 'Happy is he who doesn't judge himself in that which he approves' (14:22) faintly resonates with the Qoheleth beatitude on eating one's bread and drinking one's wine with a clear conscience before God (Ecclesiastes 9:7, 'God has already approved your works'). Thematic resonance of approved, untroubled enjoyment.
sourceText: Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
