note: 'As we have borne the image of those made of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly' (v.49) invokes the creation of humanity 'in the image of God,' now patterned after the heavenly Man. The image (eikon) language is distinctively Gen 1:26-27 (cf. 5:3); coherence with Paul's Adam Christology supports a medium allusion.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: The graded 'glory' of sun, moon, and differing stars applied to the resurrection body (vv.40-42) echoes 'those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars.' Daniel's astral imagery of the risen righteous gives the star-glory analogy its resurrection coherence; verbal overlap on stars/glory grounds the allusion.
sourceText: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: 'To each seed a body of its own' and the distinct kinds of flesh (vv.38-39) faintly echo the creation account where plants bear seed 'each according to its kind' and creatures are made by kinds. The echo is conceptual, supporting Paul's argument that God assigns distinct bodies; volume is low, hence a faint echo.
sourceText: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so. The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.

note: 'Death is swallowed up in victory' (v.54) quotes Isaiah's eschatological banquet oracle, 'he will swallow up death forever.' Paul follows a reading (cf. Theodotion/Aquila) giving 'in victory'; the citation formula 'then shall come to pass the word that is written' marks maximal volume. The text is the OT charter for death's defeat.
sourceText: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.

note: 'Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?' (v.55) quotes Hosea's taunt, 'O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your destruction?' (LXX). Volume is high (verbatim apostrophe to Death), and Paul fuses it with Isaiah 25:8 to climax the resurrection argument. Secure quotation.
sourceText: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.

note: 'The dead will be raised incorruptible, and we will be changed' (v.52) draws on 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake, some to everlasting life.' The sleep-then-awake resurrection schema and the transformation of the raised cohere with Daniel's two-outcome resurrection; recurrence of the 'sleep' motif (vv.6,18,51) supports the allusion.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: 'At the last trumpet... the trumpet will sound' (v.52) echoes the eschatological 'great trumpet' that gathers the scattered to worship. The trumpet as signal of the end-time ingathering of God's people coheres with the resurrection summons; among trumpet texts this is the most eschatologically specific, hence medium.
sourceText: It will happen in that day that a great trumpet will be blown; and those who were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and those who were outcasts in the land of Egypt, shall come; and they will worship Yahweh in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

note: 'Blow the trumpet in Zion... for the day of the LORD is coming' is part of the prophetic Day-of-the-LORD trumpet tradition behind 'the last trumpet' (v.52). Volume is low and the motif is diffuse across several prophets, so this is a faint echo alongside Isaiah 27:13 and Zechariah 9:14.
sourceText: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of Yahweh comes, for it is close at hand:

note: 'The Lord GOD will sound the trumpet' in the theophanic deliverance oracle contributes to the eschatological-trumpet background of v.52. The echo is faint and one of several trumpet texts; included to map the cluster of OT trumpet imagery Paul compresses into 'the last trumpet.'
sourceText: Yahweh will be seen over them; and his arrow will go flash like lightning; and the Lord Yahweh will blow the trumpet, and will go with whirlwinds of the south.

note: The Sinai theophany 'trumpet blast' that summons Israel before God may stand at the headwaters of the eschatological trumpet of v.52. Volume is low and the link is typological rather than verbal, so this is a faint echo of the trumpet-of-divine-presence tradition.
sourceText: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled.

note: 'This mortal must put on immortality' (vv.53-54) resonates with the deuterocanonical hope that 'the souls of the righteous... their hope is full of immortality.' Availability as second-temple text is secure; the verbal link on immortality (athanasia) is real but the conceptual frame differs (Paul stresses bodily transformation), so a low, contested echo.
sourceText: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality;

note: Paul directs each one to save 'as he may prosper'—an almost verbatim conceptual match to Deuteronomy's pilgrim-feast rule that each give 'as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God which he has given you.' The volume is high at the level of the proportional-giving principle, and the festal-collection setting (cf. Pentecost in v.8) increases coherence.
sourceText: Every man shall give as he is able, according to Yahweh your God’s blessing which he has given you.

note: The weekly setting-aside of gifts on the first day evokes the agricultural firstfruits/ingathering offerings of the festal calendar. The link is thematic (sanctified periodic giving) rather than verbal, so volume is low and it is partly carried by Paul's later 'firstfruits' language in v.15.
sourceText: And the feast of harvest, the first fruits of your labors, which you sow in the field; and the feast of ingathering, at the end of the year, when you gather in your labors out of the field.

note: 'Honor the LORD with your substance and with the firstfruits of all your produce' undergirds Paul's appeal to set aside wealth for sacred use. Verbal contact is faint and the proverb is one of several wisdom sources for proportional generosity, so confidence stays low.
sourceText: Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase:

note: Paul's 'a great and effective door has opened to me' may draw on the prophetic 'door of hope' that the LORD opens for renewed mission. The metaphor of a divinely-opened door for fruitful action has OT antecedents, but the contact is conceptual not verbal and the open-door image is broadly diffuse, so it is contested.
sourceText: I will give her vineyards from there, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope; and she will respond there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.

note: 'Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the LORD' is the closest verbal and structural parallel to Paul's paired imperatives 'be courageous, be strong.' Volume is high (LXX andrizesthe/krataiousthe vocabulary matches), and the exhortation-to-the-faithful setting gives strong coherence.
sourceText: Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who hope in Yahweh.

note: The repeated divine charge 'be strong and courageous' to Joshua is the canonical fountainhead of the formula Paul echoes. The LXX renders it with the same andrizou/ischye verbs Paul uses, giving high volume and strong recurrence across the courage-tradition.
sourceText: “Be strong and courageous; for you shall cause this people to inherit the land which I swore to their fathers to give them. Only be strong and very courageous, to observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded you. Don’t turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may […]

note: Moses' twofold 'be strong and courageous' to Israel and to Joshua belongs to the same exhortation cluster, sharing LXX vocabulary with Paul's imperatives. It is one of several courage-formula texts, so it ranks just below the Joshua/Psalm 31 parallels in distinctiveness.
sourceText: Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or scared of them; for Yahweh your God himself is who goes with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.” Moses called to Joshua, and said to him in the sight of all Israel, “Be strong and courageous, for you shall go with this people into the land which Yahweh has sworn to their fathers to give them; and you shall cause them to inherit it.

note: Joab's battle exhortation 'Be strong, and let us be courageous for our people' supplies the martial coloring of 'act like men' (andrizesthe). The military-valor sense reinforces coherence with Paul's call to firm faith, though it is one node in a recurring formula.
sourceText: Be courageous, and let us be strong for our people, and for the cities of our God; and Yahweh do that which seems good to him.”

note: 'Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage' is a near-twin of Psalm 31:24 and feeds the same exhortation tradition Paul reuses. High recurrence within the Psalter strengthens the case, though it overlaps heavily with the Psalm 31 parallel.
sourceText: Wait for Yahweh. Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yes, wait for Yahweh.

note: Calling the household of Stephanas 'the firstfruits of Achaia' applies the Deuteronomic firstfruits rite—the first of the produce consecrated to God—figurally to the first converts of a region. Volume rests on the loaded term 'firstfruits' (aparche), and the consecration-of-the-first logic gives genuine coherence.
sourceText: that you shall take some of the first of all the fruit of the ground, which you shall bring in from your land that Yahweh your God gives you. You shall put it in a basket, and shall go to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there.

note: The firstfruits-to-God motif of Proverbs reinforces Paul's honorific use of 'firstfruits' for the Stephanas household and their dedicated service. The link is thematic and secondary to the Deuteronomic rite, so confidence is low.
sourceText: Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase:

note: Paul's 'let him be accursed' (anathema) on whoever does not love the Lord reflects the Deuteronomic covenant-curse liturgy, where the assembly pronounces 'cursed' on covenant-breakers. The setting—a closing covenantal sanction against the disloyal—gives coherence, though the conceptual rather than verbal contact keeps it medium.
sourceText: ‘Cursed is the man who makes an engraved or molten image, an abomination to Yahweh, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and sets it up in secret.’ All the people shall answer and say, ‘Amen.’ ‘Cursed is he who dishonors his father or his mother.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’ ‘Cursed is he who removes his neighbor’s landmark.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’ ‘Cursed is he who leads the blind astray on the road.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’ […]

note: 'Maranatha / Come, Lord!' invokes the eschatological coming of the Lord, of which Malachi's 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple' is a prime OT expectation. The contact is thematic (the awaited advent that judges the disloyal), pairing naturally with the preceding curse, so it is offered low and contested.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'He comes to judge the earth' frames the Lord's advent that Paul's Maranatha petitions, joining curse and coming in a judgment horizon. Diffuse OT advent-language and absence of verbal markers keep this faint and contested.
sourceText: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.

note: The epistolary salutation 'Grace to you and peace' conjoins gift and shalom in a way that echoes the Aaronic blessing, where YHWH's gracious face and the gift of peace are invoked over Israel. The pairing of favor and peace as a divine bestowal is the priestly benediction's structure, and Paul speaks as one mediating God's blessing to the assembly. Volume is low and the wording is Paul's own formula, so this is a faint liturgical echo rather than a citation.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: Paul's wish of 'peace from God' to the gathered saints resonates with the psalm's close, where YHWH gives strength and blesses his people with peace. The thematic coherence is the divine grant of peace to the covenant assembly. The echo is faint and competes with the broader Greco-Roman/Jewish letter convention, hence contested.
sourceText: Yahweh will give strength to his people. Yahweh will bless his people with peace.

note: The titulature 'God of all comfort' who 'comforts us in all our affliction' draws directly on the programmatic 'Comfort, comfort my people' that opens Second Isaiah. The verbal density of comfort-language (parakaleo/paraklēsis) matches Isaiah's nacham/LXX parakaleite, and the consolation of an afflicted people awaiting redemption is the precise thematic field Paul occupies. High volume and recurrence across Isaiah make this the controlling text.
sourceText: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.

note: Isaiah declares that YHWH 'has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted,' coupling consolation with mercy toward the afflicted exactly as Paul's 'Father of mercies and God of all comfort who comforts us in all our affliction.' The mercy/comfort/affliction triad is distinctive of the Servant-era consolation oracles, satisfying volume and thematic coherence.
sourceText: Sing, heavens; and be joyful, earth; and break out into singing, mountains: for Yahweh has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his afflicted.

note: Isaiah promises that YHWH 'will comfort Zion, will comfort all her waste places,' a refrain of repeated comfort that Paul's piled-up paraklēsis vocabulary mirrors. The pattern of God comforting the desolate so they overflow with gladness coheres with Paul's logic that comfort received is comfort passed on. Recurrence of the comfort motif across Isaiah 51 strengthens availability.
sourceText: For Yahweh has comforted Zion; he has comforted all her waste places, and has made her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of Yahweh; joy and gladness shall be found therein, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.

note: 'I, even I, am he who comforts you' identifies God himself as the comforter of the afflicted and fearful, which is exactly Paul's confession that we 'are comforted by God.' The emphatic self-identification of God as comforter undergirds the title 'God of all comfort.' Strong thematic coherence and verbal overlap.
sourceText: “I, even I, am he who comforts you: who are you, that you are afraid of man who shall die, and of the son of man who shall be made as grass;

note: 'As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem' supplies the maternal-divine consolation image that Paul universalizes as the 'God of all comfort.' The promise that the comforted will themselves be settled and consoled coheres with Paul's chain of comfort flowing through sufferers to others. High volume of the comfort motif.
sourceText: As one whom his mother comforts, so will I comfort you; and you will be comforted in Jerusalem.”

note: 'Break forth into joy... for YHWH has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem' ties comfort to redemption and corporate joy, paralleling Paul's link between shared suffering and shared comfort/salvation. The recurrence of the comfort-redemption pairing in Second Isaiah supports availability, though the verbal contact is lighter than 49:13 or 51:12.
sourceText: Break out into joy, sing together, you waste places of Jerusalem; for Yahweh has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.

note: The shepherd-God who gathers and gently carries the flock extends the consolation oracle's pastoral tenderness that 'Father of mercies' evokes. The echo is thematic rather than verbal and is subsidiary to the louder 40:1 contact.
sourceText: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.

note: 'When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul' offers the closest psalmic parallel to comfort multiplying amid affliction, matching Paul's claim that as sufferings abound so comfort abounds. The psalm's vocabulary of divine consolation (LXX paraklēseis) gives verbal as well as thematic contact.
sourceText: In the multitude of my thoughts within me, your comforts delight my soul.

note: 'YHWH is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit' coheres with Paul's God who draws near to comfort the afflicted. The psalm belongs to the deliverance-of-the-righteous-sufferer tradition Paul inhabits across the pericope, satisfying thematic coherence though the wording is comfort-adjacent rather than identical.
sourceText: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

note: 'This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life' fuses comfort, affliction, and life-giving promise in one verse, the same cluster Paul develops here and into 1:9-10. The shared comfort-in-affliction formula gives reasonable volume; the psalm's consolation idiom was readily available in Greek.
sourceText: This is my comfort in my affliction, for your word has revived me.

note: 'Your rod and your staff, they comfort me' provides the archetypal image of divine comfort in the midst of mortal danger, resonating with Paul's comfort amid sufferings. Volume is low and the contact is conceptual, so it is a faint supporting echo.
sourceText: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.

note: Zion's lament 'there is none to comfort her' frames the absence Paul's 'God of all comfort' answers; the consolation oracles of Isaiah respond to exactly this Lamentations cry. The echo works intertextually with Isaiah rather than directly, hence low confidence and contested.
sourceText: Her filthiness was in her skirts; she didn’t remember her latter end; therefore is she come down wonderfully; she has no comforter: see, Yahweh, my affliction; for the enemy has magnified himself.

note: Ben Sira's counsel that the one who would serve God should prepare for testing and endure affliction, trusting that God will help, parallels Paul's pairing of sufferings with steadfast hope and patient endurance. As a Second-Temple wisdom text it meets availability and offers thematic coherence on suffering-then-comfort, though no verbal quotation.
sourceText: My son, if you come to serve the Lord, Prepare your soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure, And make not haste in time of calamity. Cleave to him, and depart not, That you may be increased at your latter end. Accept whatever is brought upon you, And be longsuffering when you passest into humiliation. For gold is tried in the fire, And acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation. Put your trust in him, and he will help you: […]

note: Paul's confession of trust in 'God who raises the dead' draws on the canonical resurrection hope, of which Isaiah 26:19 ('your dead shall live, the dwellers in the dust shall awake') is a foundational text. Having received 'the sentence of death,' Paul grounds rescue in the God whose signature act is raising the dead, a distinctively Jewish-apocalyptic confession. Strong thematic coherence with the resurrection tradition.
sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

note: The hope in the God 'who raises the dead' rests on the explicit resurrection promise that 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake.' Daniel is the clearest OT articulation of bodily resurrection and was central to Second-Temple resurrection faith, making it readily available as the conceptual source for Paul's title. High availability and thematic coherence.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: 'To deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine' matches Paul's 'delivered us out of so great a death, and does deliver,' the same verb-cluster of rescue from death. The psalm's confidence that God delivers from death rather than human strength parallels Paul's refusal to 'trust in ourselves.' Reasonable verbal and thematic contact.
sourceText: to deliver their soul from death, to keep them alive in famine.

note: 'You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling' is a thanksgiving for rescue from mortal peril that closely tracks Paul's deliverance 'out of so great a death.' Psalm 116 is a deliverance-thanksgiving in which the rescued one calls on God and pays vows publicly, paralleling Paul's expectation of corporate thanksgiving (v. 11). Good thematic coherence.
sourceText: For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling.

note: 'The cords of death encompassed me... in my distress I called upon YHWH... and he heard' supplies the deliverance-from-death-through-prayer pattern Paul reproduces: mortal peril, reliance on God, rescue, and the role of supplication (v. 11). Recurrence of this lament-to-rescue schema across the Psalter supports availability.
sourceText: The cords of death surrounded me. The floods of ungodliness made me afraid. The cords of Sheol were around me. The snares of death came on me. In my distress I called on Yahweh, and cried to my God. He heard my voice out of his temple. My cry before him came into his ears.

note: 'O YHWH, you brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit' frames rescue from death as a near-resurrection, mirroring Paul's link between deliverance from 'so great a death' and the God who raises the dead. Thematic coherence with the rescue-as-resurrection motif is strong.
sourceText: Yahweh, you have brought up my soul from Sheol. You have kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit.

note: Hannah's confession that 'YHWH kills and makes alive; he brings down to Sheol and raises up' grounds Paul's title 'God who raises the dead' in Israel's earliest doxology of divine life-and-death sovereignty. The bringing-down-then-raising movement matches Paul's death-sentence-then-deliverance experience. Good thematic coherence.
sourceText: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.

note: 'I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal, and there is none that can deliver out of my hand' is the Song of Moses' claim of exclusive power over death and rescue, underwriting Paul's confidence in God's deliverance against self-reliance. The kill/make-alive + deliver vocabulary aligns closely. Reasonable volume.
sourceText: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.

note: 'He will deliver you in six troubles... in famine he will redeem you from death' offers a wisdom statement of repeated divine rescue from death matching Paul's 'delivered... and does deliver... will still deliver.' The triple-tense reliance on future rescue gives thematic coherence, though verbal contact is modest.
sourceText: He will deliver you in six troubles; yes, in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death; in war, from the power of the sword.

note: The contrast between the cursed who 'trust in man' and the blessed who 'trust in YHWH' undergirds Paul's purpose 'that we should not trust in ourselves but in God.' The trust-not-in-self / trust-in-God antithesis is the conceptual spine here, though Paul does not cite Jeremiah's wording. Faint but coherent.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh: Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from Yahweh. For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good comes, but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, a salt land and not inhabited. Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose trust Yahweh is.

note: 'I will not trust in my bow... but you have saved us from our foes' parallels Paul's renunciation of self-reliance in favor of the God who delivers. Thematic coherence with the not-in-self-but-in-God logic; low volume of verbal contact.
sourceText: For I will not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me. But you have saved us from our adversaries, and have shamed those who hate us.

note: 'You have power over life and death; you lead down to the gates of Hades and back again' is a Second-Temple statement of God's authority to rescue from death that closely parallels Paul's God who raises the dead and delivers. As deuterocanonical it meets availability and offers a near-resurrection idiom, though verbal contact with Paul is loose.
sourceText: For you have authority over life and death, And you lead down to the gates of Hades, and lead up again.

note: The martyr's hope that 'the King of the universe will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life' is a Second-Temple confession of God raising the dead amid suffering unto death, the same resurrection faith Paul invokes when under a death sentence. Availability is strong in the martyrological milieu; the contact is conceptual, not verbal.
sourceText: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.

note: Paul's 'boasting' grounded not in 'fleshly wisdom' but in God echoes Jeremiah's oracle that one should not boast in wisdom or might but boast in knowing YHWH. The wisdom-versus-true-boasting antithesis is precisely Jeremiah's, and Paul elsewhere cites this very passage, raising availability. Good thematic coherence despite no full quotation here.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.

note: The wisdom counsel against self-boasting ('let another praise you, not your own mouth') informs Paul's careful, conscience-tested form of boasting. The contact is the moral evaluation of boasting rather than verbal, so it remains a faint wisdom echo.
sourceText: Don’t boast about tomorrow; for you don’t know what a day may bring. Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.

note: 'I hold fast my righteousness... my heart does not reproach me for any of my days' is the classic appeal to a clear conscience that matches Paul's boast in 'the testimony of our conscience' to integrity of conduct. Job's self-defense by an unaccusing heart provides the closest OT analogue to Paul's conscience-language. Reasonable thematic coherence.
sourceText: I hold fast to my righteousness, and will not let it go. My heart shall not reproach me so long as I live.

note: 'Judge me, O YHWH, according to my righteousness and the integrity that is in me' parallels Paul's confidence before God in his holiness and sincerity of conduct. The appeal to inward integrity as the basis for vindication is shared, though Paul does not quote the psalm. Faint echo.
sourceText: Yahweh administers judgment to the peoples. Judge me, Yahweh, according to my righteousness, and to my integrity that is in me.

note: 'Love righteousness... think of the Lord in goodness and seek him in sincerity (haplotēs) of heart' shares Paul's distinctive pairing of 'holiness and sincerity of God.' The sincerity/single-heartedness vocabulary is at home in Hellenistic-Jewish wisdom, satisfying availability; the contact is lexical-thematic rather than a citation.
sourceText: Love righteousness, you that be judges of the earth, Think you of the Lord with a good mind, And in singleness of heart seek you him;

note: Paul's claim that the promises find their 'Yes' and 'Amen' in Christ 'to the glory of God' draws on Isaiah's 'God of Amen/truth,' where one blesses and swears by the God of truth (LXX/Heb 'God of Amen'). The unusual liturgical 'Amen' tied to God's reliability points to this text as the lexical source for divine faithfulness sealing the promises. High thematic coherence with God's truthfulness.
sourceText: so that he who blesses himself in the earth shall bless himself in the God of truth; and he who swears in the earth shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten, and because they are hidden from my eyes.

note: 'Know that YHWH your God is the faithful God who keeps covenant' grounds Paul's 'as God is faithful' and the certainty that all God's promises are confirmed (Yes/Amen). The covenant-keeping faithfulness of God is the theological basis for Paul's argument that his word, mirroring God's, is not equivocating Yes-and-No. Good thematic coherence.
sourceText: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,

note: 'God is not a man that he should lie... has he said, and will he not do it?' directly supports Paul's contrast between human fickleness and God's reliable Yes to his promises. The denial of divine vacillation undergirds the Yes/Amen argument. Reasonable verbal-thematic contact on God keeping his word.
sourceText: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?

note: Paul's 'he... anointed us' draws on the anointing tradition in which Samuel anoints David and 'the Spirit of YHWH came mightily upon him.' The conjunction of anointing with the gift of the Spirit (v. 22) maps onto this royal-prophetic anointing pattern. Good thematic coherence between anointing and Spirit-endowment.
sourceText: Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brothers: and the Spirit of Yahweh came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up, and went to Ramah.

note: The holy anointing oil that consecrates priests and the tent supplies the consecration imagery behind 'he... anointed us... and gave us the Spirit.' Anointing as a setting-apart for God's service coheres with Paul's claim that God establishes, anoints, and seals believers. Availability is strong though the application is figural.
sourceText: You shall make it a holy anointing oil, a perfume compounded after the art of the perfumer: it shall be a holy anointing oil. You shall use it to anoint the Tent of Meeting, the ark of the testimony, the table and all its articles, the lamp stand and its accessories, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin with its base. You shall sanctify them, that they may be most holy. Whatever touches them shall be holy. […]

note: 'I will make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you' offers the OT 'seal' image of God designating and securing his chosen one, behind Paul's 'who also sealed us.' The signet/seal as a mark of ownership and guaranteed status matches Paul's sealing tied to the Spirit-down-payment. Reasonable thematic coherence.
sourceText: In that day, says Yahweh of Armies, will I take you, Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel,’ says Yahweh, ‘and will make you as a signet, for I have chosen you,’ says Yahweh of Armies.”

note: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' is the eschatological Spirit-gift that Paul claims as already given 'in our hearts' as a down payment. The lavish outpouring of the Spirit on God's people in the last days underwrites Paul's arrabon language. Good availability and thematic coherence with Spirit-as-pledge.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.

note: 'I will put my Spirit within you' supplies the promise of the indwelling Spirit that Paul says God 'gave... in our hearts.' The new-covenant gift of an internal Spirit, paired with a new heart, coheres precisely with Paul's sealing and down-payment of the Spirit in the heart. Strong thematic coherence.
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: 'I will put my law within them and write it on their hearts' provides the new-covenant interiorization motif behind Paul's Spirit given 'in our hearts' as guarantee. The heart as the locus of God's confirming work coheres with Paul's establishing/sealing language. Recurrence with Ezekiel 36 strengthens the new-covenant background.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:

note: The covenant in which God guarantees his promise to Abraham models the down-payment/pledge logic that the promises are sure and confirmed (Yes/Amen). The arrabon as a first installment securing the whole resonates with God's covenant guarantee. Conceptual rather than verbal, hence low.
sourceText: He said, “Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?” He said to him, “Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.” He brought him all of these, and divided them in the middle, and laid each half opposite the other; but he didn’t divide the birds. The birds of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them away. When the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on […]

note: 'He remembers his covenant forever... which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute' restates the reliability of God's promises that Paul affirms as Yes in Christ. The motif of God establishing/confirming his promise to many generations parallels 'establishes us... in Christ.' Faint thematic echo.
sourceText: He has remembered his covenant forever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations, the covenant which he made with Abraham, his oath to Isaac, and confirmed the same to Jacob for a statute; to Israel for an everlasting covenant,

note: The pledge (Heb erabon, the Semitic source of Greek arrabon) Judah leaves with Tamar is the lexical background for Paul's 'down payment of the Spirit.' The shared erabon/arrabon term marks the Spirit as a deposit guaranteeing full payment to come. Contact is lexical-etymological, so low confidence and contested.
sourceText: He said, “I will send you a young goat from the flock.” She said, “Will you give me a pledge, until you send it?” He said, “What pledge will I give you?” She said, “Your signet and your cord, and your staff that is in your hand.” He gave them to her, and came in to her, and she conceived by him.

note: 'The Spirit of YHWH shall rest upon him' (the anointed messianic shoot) extends the anointing-with-Spirit pattern that Paul applies to believers in Christ ('anointed us... gave us the Spirit'). The messianic anointing background coheres figurally; verbal contact with Paul is light.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: 'I will not violate my covenant or alter the word that went forth from my lips... his line shall endure forever' affirms God's unalterable, faithful word that Paul echoes in 'God is faithful, our word was not Yes and No.' The non-vacillation of the divine promise coheres with Paul's argument. Faint echo.
sourceText: I will not break my covenant, nor alter what my lips have uttered. Once have I sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David. His seed will endure forever, his throne like the sun before me. It will be established forever like the moon, the faithful witness in the sky.” Selah.

note: Paul's solemn 'I call God for a witness to my soul' echoes Job's appeal, 'even now, behold, my witness is in heaven,' invoking God as the guarantor of one's truthfulness. The recourse to God-as-witness in self-defense against suspicion is the shared rhetorical move. Reasonable thematic coherence with the heavenly-witness motif.
sourceText: Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven. He who vouches for me is on high.

note: Samuel's 'YHWH is witness against you... that you have found nothing in my hand' is a formal oath calling God to attest the speaker's integrity, paralleling Paul's calling God as witness to his motives. The covenant-lawsuit form of invoking God as witness is well attested and available. Good thematic coherence.
sourceText: He said to them, “Yahweh is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found anything in my hand.” They said, “He is witness.”

note: 'God is witness between you and me' in the Laban-Jacob covenant supplies the oath-formula of summoning God to witness sincerity of intent, the same form Paul uses. The contact is to the conventional witness-oath rather than to specific wording, hence low and contested.
sourceText: If you afflict my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters, no man is with us; behold, God is witness between me and you.”

note: The command to fear God and 'swear by his name' frames the legitimacy of calling God to witness an oath, which Paul does regarding his change of travel plans. The contact is to the sanctioned practice of God-invoking oaths rather than to the verse's wording. Faint echo.
sourceText: You shall fear Yahweh your God; and you shall serve him, and shall swear by his name.

note: 'YHWH was witness between you' uses the same God-as-witness formula Paul employs to attest the truth of his conduct toward the Corinthians. The prophetic deployment of the witness-oath shows the idiom's availability; verbal contact with Paul is conventional. Low confidence.
sourceText: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant.

note: Paul writes 'with many tears' out of 'much affliction and anguish of heart,' grieving over a community he loves. Jeremiah's wish that his head were waters to weep day and night for his people supplies the prophetic prototype of the leader who weeps over those under his charge. Coherence is strong (Paul's self-presentation as a suffering apostle); volume is low since there is no shared diction.
sourceText: Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a spring of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!

note: 'I wrote to you with many tears' resonates with the lament psalmist who floods his bed with weeping. The motif of tears poured out in anguish of heart is a stock Psalter idiom Paul would have internalized. Faint and diffuse, marked low for lack of verbal anchor.
sourceText: I am weary with my groaning. Every night I flood my bed. I drench my couch with my tears.

note: 'Anguish of heart' (v.4) matches the psalmist's 'the troubles of my heart are enlarged.' The Greek thlipsis/synochē kardias language draws on LXX heart-distress vocabulary. Volume is low; recorded as an available Septuagintal coloring of Paul's affliction language.
sourceText: The troubles of my heart are enlarged. Oh bring me out of my distresses.

note: Paul urges the church to 'forgive him and comfort (parakaleō) him' lest he be overwhelmed. The comfort/paraklēsis vocabulary that saturates 2 Corinthians is rooted in Isaiah 40's 'Comfort, comfort my people,' the LXX charter text for eschatological consolation. Coherence with the letter's comfort theme is high; verbal echo is real but generic, hence medium.
sourceText: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.

note: The offender risks being 'swallowed up' (katapinō) by excessive sorrow. The lament psalmist prays not to be swallowed by the flood or have the pit close its mouth over him; the verb katapinō is the LXX term for being engulfed/overwhelmed. Volume is moderate through the shared swallowing imagery applied to a person drowning in grief.
sourceText: Don’t let the flood waters overwhelm me, neither let the deep swallow me up. Don’t let the pit shut its mouth on me.

note: 'Swallowed up' (katepothē) is the repeated verb of Lamentations for the Lord engulfing Zion in sorrow. Paul fears the penitent will be similarly engulfed by grief. The figural link is to overwhelming communal sorrow; low because the LXX term is common and the referent differs.
sourceText: The Lord has become as an enemy, he has swallowed up Israel; He has swallowed up all her palaces, he has destroyed his strongholds; He has multiplied in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation.

note: Paul guards against 'Satan' gaining advantage, 'for we are not ignorant of his schemes.' The figure of ha-satan operating against the faithful, testing and seeking advantage before God, is established in the Job prologue (and Job 2:1-7). Availability and coherence are strong: Satan as the adversarial accuser is a Second-Temple development of this OT scene.
sourceText: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]

note: Satan's 'schemes' to gain advantage echo the satan standing at God's right hand to accuse Joshua the high priest, only to be rebuked. The accuser seeking legal advantage over God's people informs Paul's worry about being outwitted. Medium: thematically apt accuser imagery without verbal overlap.
sourceText: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”

note: 'We are not ignorant of his schemes (noēmata)' recalls the serpent who was 'more crafty/subtle' than any beast, the archetypal deceiver of God's people. Paul elsewhere (2 Cor 11:3) makes this Eden-craftiness link explicit, raising the recurrence weight here. The scheming-deceiver coherence is strong; verbal volume low.
sourceText: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”

note: Satan 'incited' David to a course that brought ruin, a parade case of the adversary gaining advantage over a leader. Paul's anxiety not to give Satan an opening fits this pattern. Low confidence: thematic only, one of several OT satan-scenes available.
sourceText: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to number Israel.

note: 'I had no relief for my spirit' (ouk eschēka anesin tō pneumati) echoes the covenant-curse condition of finding 'no rest for the sole of your foot' and an 'anxious/trembling heart.' Paul's restlessness over Titus is colored by this LXX no-rest idiom. Low: diffuse mood-echo, no quotation.
sourceText: Among these nations you will find no ease, and there will be no rest for the sole of your foot; but Yahweh will give you there a trembling heart, failing of eyes, and pining of soul.

note: 'A door was opened to me in the Lord' may resonate with Hosea's 'door of hope' (petach tiqvah) opened in the wilderness as a gateway to renewed mission. The image of a divinely opened door of opportunity is faint and contested, as the Roman idiom of an 'open door' for preaching may be independent. Marked low.
sourceText: I will give her vineyards from there, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope; and she will respond there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.

note: 'The sweet aroma (osmē euōdias)' Paul and his ministry spread is the exact LXX sacrificial formula for the burnt offering: 'an offering by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.' Paul casts apostolic ministry as a sacrifice whose fragrance ascends. Volume is high on the set phrase osmē euōdias; medium overall because the phrase recurs across the whole sacrificial system rather than one verse.
sourceText: but its innards and its legs he shall wash with water. The priest shall burn all of it on the altar, for a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.

note: The first 'pleasing aroma' (osmē euōdias) is Noah's offering, which God 'smelled' and was reconciled. Paul's fragrance imagery for a ministry that mediates reconciliation draws on this foundational pleasing-odor scene. Medium: shares the precise LXX formula but is one instance among several aroma texts.
sourceText: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.

note: The ordination ram offered as 'a pleasing aroma, an offering by fire to the LORD' supplies priestly-consecration coloring to Paul's self-presentation as a fragrant offering in service of God. The ordination context coheres with Paul's apostolic vocation. Medium on shared formula.
sourceText: You shall burn the whole ram on the altar: it is a burnt offering to Yahweh; it is a pleasant aroma, an offering made by fire to Yahweh.

note: 'As a pleasing aroma I will accept you when I bring you out from the peoples' applies the sacrificial-fragrance formula to God's restored people gathered from the nations. Paul, spreading the aroma 'in every place' among saved and perishing, picks up this universalized, gathering sense of the pleasing odor. Medium.
sourceText: As a pleasant aroma will I accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples, and gather you out of the countries in which you have been scattered; and I will be sanctified in you in the sight of the nations.

note: 'In every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering; for my name is great among the nations.' Paul's aroma of the knowledge of God spread 'in every place' strikingly combines fragrant offering + worldwide diffusion among the nations, matching Malachi's vision. Coherence with Paul's Gentile mission is high; medium for the inexact wording.
sourceText: For from the rising of the sun even to the going down of the same, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the nations,” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Personified Wisdom says she gave forth fragrance 'like cinnamon and aromatic balm... like choice myrrh... like the fragrance of incense in the tabernacle,' spreading her aroma. Paul's 'fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place' transposes Wisdom's self-diffusing aroma onto the knowledge of God in Christ. Strong thematic coherence (fragrance = diffused divine knowledge); medium for deuterocanonical, non-verbal link.
sourceText: As cinnamon and aspalathus, I have given a scent of perfumes; And as choice myrrh, I spread abroad a pleasant odour; As galbanum, and onyx, and stacte, And as the fume of frankincense in the tabernacle.

note: 'Your anointing oils are fragrant; your name is oil poured out, therefore the maidens love you' offers the erotic-devotional register of a fragrant, beloved name. Paul's aroma of Christ that draws (or repels) may glance at this beloved-name fragrance. Low: evocative but lacks verbal contact and the sacrificial frame dominates.
sourceText: Your oils have a pleasing fragrance. Your name is oil poured out, therefore the virgins love you.

note: Paul spreads 'the knowledge of him in every place,' which resonates with the eschatological promise that 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD.' The universal diffusion of divine knowledge is the shared note. Low/medium: thematic, mediated through the aroma metaphor.
sourceText: They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth will be full of the knowledge of Yahweh, as the waters cover the sea.

note: 'God always leads us in triumph (thriambeuō)' uses the Roman triumphal-procession image, but its OT analogue is the divine warrior who 'ascended on high, leading captives in your train.' Paul figures himself among those led in God's victory train. Low: the primary background is Greco-Roman, not OT, so this is a faint figural overlay.
sourceText: You have ascended on high. You have led away captives. You have received gifts among men, yes, among the rebellious also, that Yah God might dwell there.

note: 'Who is sufficient for these things?' echoes Moses' protest of inadequacy at his call ('I am not eloquent... I am slow of speech'), the paradigm of human insufficiency for a divine commission answered by God's enabling. Paul's rhetorical question and his later 'our sufficiency is from God' (3:5) make the call-narrative resonance coherent. Medium.
sourceText: Moses said to Yahweh, “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.”

note: 'Who is sufficient/who can endure it?' (tis estai hikanos / tis hypoisei) matches the prophetic exclamation before the overwhelming Day of the LORD. Paul's 'who is sufficient (hikanos) for these things?' may pick up this LXX idiom of human inadequacy before God's awesome work. Low: shared rhetorical form, divergent context.
sourceText: Yahweh thunders his voice before his army; for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of Yahweh is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?

note: Paul condemns those 'peddling (kapēleuō) the word of God,' the verb for a huckster/tavern-keeper who adulterates wares. Isaiah's indictment 'your wine is mixed with water' (LXX: tavern-keepers diluting wine) is the prophetic image of corrupting/cheapening what is holy for profit. Coherence with Paul's charge of adulterating God's word is good; low because the link is conceptual, not quoted.
sourceText: Your silver has become dross, your wine mixed with water.

note: The contrast 'not on tablets of stone' deliberately evokes the stone tablets God gave Moses, which Exodus 24:12 first announces ('the tables of stone, and the law, and the commandment, which I have written'). Volume is high (verbal 'tablets of stone') and the whole chapter is a sustained reading of the Sinai narrative, satisfying coherence and availability.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Come up to me on the mountain, and stay here, and I will give you the stone tablets with the law and the commands that I have written, that you may teach them.”

note: Paul's 'tablets of stone written... with the Spirit of the living God' inverts Exodus 31:18, where the two tables of testimony were 'tables of stone, written with the finger of God.' The Spirit/finger-of-God substitution is a precise figural play, and the phrase 'tablets of stone' is near-quotation.
sourceText: He gave to Moses, when he finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets, written with God’s finger.

note: Exodus 32:15-16 stresses that the tables were 'written on both their sides' and that 'the writing was the writing of God, graven upon the tables.' Paul's antithesis of divine writing on stone versus writing by the Spirit on hearts draws on this stone-tablet imagery; slightly lower volume than 31:18 since the verbal anchor is shared across the cluster.
sourceText: Moses turned, and went down from the mountain, with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand; tablets that were written on both their sides; on the one side and on the other they were written. The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tables.

note: Exodus 34:1 ('Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first') supplies the renewed-covenant tablets that frame the very Exodus 34 narrative Paul exposits across the chapter. Coherence with the chapter's overall theme is strong, though the specific stone-tablet phrase is drawn from the whole cluster.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Chisel two stone tablets like the first: and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.

note: 'Written... on tablets of human hearts' echoes Jeremiah 31:33, where God promises to 'put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.' Recurrence is strong: Paul names a 'new covenant' (3:6) directly from Jer 31:31, making the heart-inscription allusion here mutually reinforcing and high-confidence.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:

note: 'Hearts of flesh' as the surface of inscription, contrasted with stone, directly takes up Ezekiel 36:26: 'I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.' The stone/flesh-heart antithesis is verbally exact and thematically central, scoring high on volume and coherence.
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.

note: Ezekiel 11:19 ('I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh') is the parallel oracle to 36:26 and joined to the gift of a 'new spirit,' which coheres with Paul's 'Spirit of the living God' writing on hearts of flesh. Recurrence across Ezekiel strengthens the allusion.
sourceText: I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them a heart of flesh;

note: Jeremiah 17:1 says Judah's sin is 'graven... upon the table of their heart' with a pen of iron — the inverse image of God's good writing on hearts. Paul may echo this 'table of the heart' idiom; volume is modest and the valence is reversed, so it is faint and contested.
sourceText: The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of your altars;

note: Proverbs 3:3 urges writing mercy and truth 'upon the table of thine heart,' a sapiential idiom for internalized teaching that Paul's heart-tablet language may draw on. The verbal overlap ('table of the heart') is real but the source is more plausibly the prophetic new-covenant texts, so this is a contested secondary echo.
sourceText: Don’t let kindness and truth forsake you. Bind them around your neck. Write them on the tablet of your heart.

note: Proverbs 7:3 ('write them upon the table of thine heart') repeats the same sapiential heart-tablet idiom and reinforces its availability in Paul's scriptural vocabulary. Faint and contested for the same reason as 3:3; listed for recurrence of the idiom.
sourceText: Bind them on your fingers. Write them on the tablet of your heart.

note: Deuteronomy 5:22 recalls the Decalogue 'written... in two tables of stone' delivered at Horeb, part of the broad stone-tablet tradition behind Paul's antithesis. Lower volume than the Exodus passages, so a faint corroborating echo.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke these words to all your assembly on the mountain out of the midst of the fire, of the cloud, and of the thick darkness, with a great voice. He added no more. He wrote them on two stone tablets, and gave them to me.

note: 'Servants of a new covenant' (3:6) is a direct appropriation of Jeremiah 31:31, the only OT text to name a 'new covenant.' Volume and distinctiveness are very high, and it anchors the heart-writing allusions of 3:3 and the whole chapter's covenant theology.
sourceText: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:

note: The new-covenant promise that the law would be inward 'Spirit not letter' depends on Jeremiah 31:33 ('I will write it in their hearts'). Recurrence with 3:3 and 3:6's covenant language makes this a coherent, high-confidence allusion to the same oracle.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:

note: Paul's 'Spirit gives life' against the death-dealing 'letter' draws on Ezekiel 36:27, 'I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes' — the Spirit internalizing the law. This pairs with Jer 31 to ground the letter/Spirit antithesis and scores high on coherence.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: 'The Spirit gives life' echoes the valley-of-bones promise, Ezekiel 37:14: 'I shall put my spirit in you, and ye shall live.' The life-giving function of the Spirit is verbally and thematically tight, and Ezekiel's spirit-life motif coheres with Paul's new-covenant argument.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.

note: Ezekiel 37:5-6 ('I will cause breath/spirit to enter into you, and ye shall live') reinforces the Spirit-vivifies-the-dead imagery behind 'the Spirit gives life.' Recurrence within Ezekiel 37 strengthens the allusion cluster; slightly lower volume than v.14.
sourceText: Thus says the Lord Yahweh to these bones: Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you shall live.

note: The life-giving Spirit/breath that animates dead matter may echo Genesis 2:7, where God breathes the breath of life and man becomes a living soul. Plausible figural backdrop to 'the Spirit gives life,' but volume is low and the Ezekiel new-covenant texts are the nearer source, so contested.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: Deuteronomy 30:6 ('the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart... that thou mayest live') anticipates the inward, life-giving renewal Paul ascribes to the Spirit over against the letter. A faint coherence-driven echo to the heart-circumcision tradition behind new-covenant interiority.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.

note: 'The children of Israel could not look steadfastly on the face of Moses for the glory of his face' is a close paraphrase of Exodus 34:29-30, where Moses' face shone and Aaron and Israel 'were afraid to come nigh him.' This is the interpretive center of the whole pericope; volume and coherence are maximal.
sourceText: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him. When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him.

note: Exodus 34:35 ('the children of Israel saw the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face shone') supplies the shining-face datum Paul reads as a fading glory. Recurrence across 34:29-35 and verbal overlap ('face of Moses... shone/glory') make this a strong allusion.
sourceText: The children of Israel saw Moses’ face, that the skin of Moses’ face shone: and Moses put the veil on his face again, until he went in to speak with him.

note: 'The service of death, written engraved on stones' identifies the Mosaic ministry with the stone tablets of the renewed covenant in Exodus 34:1. The 'engraved on stones' phrase links the glory of Moses' face specifically to the inscribed Decalogue, a figural reading of the Exodus 34 tablets.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Chisel two stone tablets like the first: and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.

note: 'Written engraved on stones' recalls the tables 'written with the finger of God' (Exodus 31:18), the same tablets Paul names a 'ministry of death.' Reinforces the stone-tablet motif from 3:3; medium because the stone-tablet phrasing is shared across the Sinai cluster.
sourceText: He gave to Moses, when he finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets, written with God’s finger.

note: Deuteronomy 9:10 describes 'two tables of stone written with the finger of God' bearing the commandments — the engraved-on-stone law Paul calls the ministry of death/condemnation. A faint corroborating echo of the stone-engraving tradition.
sourceText: Yahweh delivered to me the two stone tablets written with the finger of God On them were all the words which Yahweh spoke with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire in the day of the assembly.

note: 'Moses, who put a veil on his face' directly cites Exodus 34:33: 'till Moses had done speaking with them, he put a vail on his face.' The veil is the load-bearing image of Paul's argument; verbal volume and coherence are maximal.
sourceText: When Moses was done speaking with them, he put a veil on his face.

note: Exodus 34:35 ('Moses put the vail upon his face again, until he went in to speak with him') gives the repeated veiling Paul reinterprets as concealing the glory's end. Recurrence with 34:33 strengthens the allusion; Paul's 'reading of the old covenant' makes the Sinai veil a hermeneutical figure.
sourceText: The children of Israel saw Moses’ face, that the skin of Moses’ face shone: and Moses put the veil on his face again, until he went in to speak with him.

note: The Israelites' inability to gaze (v.13, 'wouldn't look steadfastly on the end of that which was passing away') recalls their fear before Moses' shining face in Exodus 34:30. Coherent continuation of the shining-face motif into the veil pericope.
sourceText: When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him.

note: 'Their minds were hardened' and a veil 'on their heart' resonate with Isaiah 6:10's hardening of heart so the people cannot perceive — a stock prophetic hardening motif Paul applies to Israel's reading of Moses. Faint and contested, since the immediate frame is the Exodus veil.
sourceText: Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: Deuteronomy 29:4 ('the LORD hath not given you an heart to perceive, and eyes to see... unto this day') parallels Paul's 'until this very day... a veil remains' and 'minds were hardened.' The 'unto this day' obduracy idiom is a plausible faint source; contested against the Exodus veil frame.
sourceText: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.

note: 'Whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away' rewrites Exodus 34:34: 'when Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he took the vail off.' Paul transposes Moses' going-in-to-the-Lord into the believer's turning to the Lord; near-quotation with high volume and coherence.
sourceText: But when Moses went in before Yahweh to speak with him, he took the veil off, until he came out; and he came out, and spoke to the children of Israel that which he was commanded.

note: 'With unveiled face' (3:18) inverts Exodus 34:35, where Israel saw Moses re-veil his shining face; now all believers behold with face unveiled. The veil/unveiled antithesis depends directly on the Exodus 34 veiling scene.
sourceText: The children of Israel saw Moses’ face, that the skin of Moses’ face shone: and Moses put the veil on his face again, until he went in to speak with him.

note: 'Beholding/seeing the glory of the Lord... transformed into the same image from glory to glory' figurally generalizes Moses' transformation in Exodus 34:29, where his face shone from speaking with the LORD. Paul makes the Sinai theophany the pattern of Christian transfiguration; strong coherence with the chapter.
sourceText: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him.

note: 'Transformed into the same image' draws on the creation of humanity 'in the image of God' (Genesis 1:26-27); the glory once on Moses' face is being restored as the divine image in believers. A figural creation/new-creation reading; medium because 'image' could be primarily Christological.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: Psalm 8:5 ('crowned him with glory and honour') articulates humanity's glory, which Paul sees restored as believers go 'from glory to glory.' A faint thematic echo of the glory-of-the-image tradition; contested and low volume.
sourceText: For you have made him a little lower than God, and crowned him with glory and honor.

note: 'Seeing the glory of the Lord' uses the Exodus theophanic formula 'the glory of the LORD' (e.g., Exodus 16:7; 24:16-17; 40:34-35), the glory that settled on Sinai and the tabernacle. A faint availability echo of the wilderness glory tradition behind Paul's Sinai exposition.
sourceText: and in the morning, then you shall see Yahweh’s glory; because he hears your murmurings against Yahweh. Who are we, that you murmur against us?”

note: 'As in a mirror' beholding glory and being transformed into the image may echo Wisdom 7:26, where Wisdom is 'the unspotted mirror of the power of God, and the image of his goodness.' A Second-Temple availability echo linking mirror, image, and divine glory; faint and contested.
sourceText: For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.

note: Paul's 'craftiness' (panourgia) echoes the LXX description of the serpent as panourgos in Genesis 3:1, a link he makes explicit at 2 Cor 11:3. Coherence is decent (Paul's recurring serpent/deception polemic) but volume here is faint, so the verbal contact is best treated as a thematic echo.
sourceText: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”

note: 'Handling the word of God deceitfully' versus 'manifestation of the truth' replays the wisdom contrast between deceitful counsels and honest speech. The link is generic to the sapiential tradition rather than to a single verse, hence low volume.
sourceText: The thoughts of the righteous are just, but the advice of the wicked is deceitful.

note: The 'god of this world has blinded the minds' so they cannot see the light recasts Isaiah's hardening commission, where eyes are made blind 'lest they see.' High recurrence in Paul (Rom 11:8) and strong coherence with the veiling theme of ch. 3 support a deliberate allusion.
sourceText: Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: Deuteronomy's lament that the LORD had 'not given a heart to know, eyes to see' supplies the unbelief-as-imposed-blindness motif Paul fuses with Isaiah. Paul cites this very verse in Rom 11:8, raising its availability and coherence here.
sourceText: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.

note: The Servant's task to 'open blind eyes' frames Paul's gospel as the light that should dawn; 42:19's 'blind servant' sharpens the irony of unbelieving blindness. Volume is moderate but coherence with the Isaianic light/blindness cluster Paul is mining is strong.
sourceText: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.

note: Calling Christ 'the image of God' reads the creation of humanity in God's image figurally, with Christ as the true eikon. The pairing of image (4:4) and the creation of light (4:6) keys the whole pericope to Genesis 1, making this a deliberate new-creation typology.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”

note: Wisdom as 'image of his goodness' and radiance of glory is the Second-Temple lexicon for Christ as 'image of God' and 'glory of Christ.' Availability and coherence are high; volume rests on shared eikon/glory vocabulary rather than a quotation.
sourceText: For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.

note: 'God who said, Light will shine out of darkness' rewords the creation fiat, presenting conversion as a new act of creation in the heart. The volume is high (clear verbal evocation of the fiat lux) and coherent with the Genesis 1 image motif of 4:4.
sourceText: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

note: 'The light of the knowledge of the glory of God' closely tracks Habakkuk's promise that the earth will be filled with 'the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.' The triple chain knowledge-glory-LORD is distinctive enough to register as more than coincidence.
sourceText: For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of Yahweh’s glory, as the waters cover the sea.

note: Light shining on those in darkness echoes Isaiah's people who 'walked in darkness' seeing a great light, reinforcing the gospel-as-dawn imagery. Coherent with the Isaianic light theme already in play, though the verbal contact is general.
sourceText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: 'The glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ' continues ch. 3's contrast with the glory on Moses' face, transferring the shining-face motif to Christ. Recurrence from the immediately prior argument makes the Exodus glory narrative the controlling subtext.
sourceText: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him.

note: 'Precious sons of Zion' reckoned as 'earthen pots, the work of the potter' supplies the exact pairing of priceless worth held in cheap clay vessels that Paul exploits. The treasure/earthen-vessel antithesis gives this strong coherence and notable volume.
sourceText: The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, How are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter!

note: The 'clay vessel' housing divine power evokes the human creature formed from dust and animated by God's breath, so the frailty is constitutive of creaturehood. Figural rather than verbal, but it grounds Paul's 'not from ourselves' in the dust-origin of humanity.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: 'We are the clay, you our potter' establishes the creature-as-vessel theme that Paul presses to magnify God's power over human weakness. Availability and coherence are strong within Paul's potter/clay usage (Rom 9:21).
sourceText: But now, Yahweh, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you our potter; and we all are the work of your hand.

note: Those who 'dwell in houses of clay' and are easily crushed parallel the fragility of the clay vessel motif. Volume is faint and the contact is conceptual, so it functions only as a supporting echo.
sourceText: How much more, those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed before the moth!

note: Gideon's torches hidden in clay jars, broken to flash God's deliverance, joins the light of 4:6 to the clay vessels of 4:7: divine power shines precisely when the fragile jar is shattered. The shared jar+light+power configuration gives this a striking coherence.
sourceText: He divided the three hundred men into three companies, and he put into the hands of all of them trumpets, and empty pitchers, with torches within the pitchers.

note: 'Struck down, yet not destroyed' closely matches the psalmist's 'the LORD has chastened me severely, but has not given me over to death.' The structure of severe affliction stopped just short of destruction is the same, supplying good volume for the climactic clause.
sourceText: Yah has punished me severely, but he has not given me over to death.

note: 'Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down, for the LORD upholds his hand' mirrors the not-forsaken/not-destroyed paradox of the righteous sufferer. Coherent with Paul's hardship-catalog theology of divine sustenance.
sourceText: Though he stumble, he shall not fall, for Yahweh holds him up with his hand.

note: 'Pursued, yet not forsaken' echoes the covenant assurance that God 'will not leave you nor forsake you.' The phrase is widespread, so volume is low and the link is a general scriptural commonplace.
sourceText: Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or scared of them; for Yahweh your God himself is who goes with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.”

note: 'Always delivered to death for Jesus' sake' anticipates the very verse ('we are killed all day long') Paul quotes at Rom 8:36, casting apostolic suffering as the lot of the faithful slain for God. Recurrence in Paul lends the echo weight.
sourceText: Yes, for your sake we are killed all day long. We are regarded as sheep for the slaughter.

note: Carrying 'the putting to death of Jesus' so that 'life may be revealed' loosely figures the Servant whose death yields life and offspring. The contact is thematic and contested, with no verbal tether, hence figural and low.
sourceText: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand.

note: 'I believed, and therefore I spoke' is an explicit citation (introduced by 'according to that which is written') of the LXX of Psalm 115:1 (MT 116:10). The marked quotation formula and verbatim wording make this an unambiguous quotation.
sourceText: I believed, therefore I said, “I was greatly afflicted.”

note: 'He who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also' draws on the OT hope that 'your dead shall live,' the Scriptural seedbed of bodily resurrection. The link is conceptual and shared with Daniel 12:2, so low volume.
sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

note: The 'eternal weight of glory' puns on the Hebrew kabod, which means both 'weight' and 'glory,' the very glory Moses asked to see. Paul's running engagement with the Exodus glory theme (chs. 3-4) makes the wordplay plausible, though no verse is quoted.
sourceText: He said, “Please show me your glory.”

note: 'The things which are seen are temporal, but the unseen are eternal' echoes Isaiah's contrast that the heavens and earth 'will vanish away' while God's salvation 'shall be forever.' The transient-visible versus everlasting antithesis aligns well, giving moderate coherence.
sourceText: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.

note: The 'inward man renewed day by day' against the decaying outward man faintly echoes the renewal of youth 'like the eagle's.' The contact is thematic and weak, so it serves only as a low-confidence supporting echo.
sourceText: who satisfies your desire with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.
