note: 'Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all' frames Paul's catalog of sufferings as the lot of the righteous sufferer whom God preserves. The peristasis list reads as an enactment of this psalmic maxim, coherent with Paul's boast 'in weakness.' Volume is thematic.
sourceText: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.

note: The covenant-curse list of serving 'in hunger, thirst, nakedness, and want of all things' supplies the lexical cluster behind Paul's 'hunger and thirst... cold and nakedness.' Paul ironically wears the curse-catalog as apostolic credential. Volume is low and the wording is common to affliction lists; flagged contested.
sourceText: therefore you will serve your enemies whom Yahweh sends against you, in hunger, in thirst, in nakedness, and in lack of all things. He will put an iron yoke on your neck, until he has destroyed you.

note: The beating and imprisonment of the persecuted prophet Jeremiah typifies the suffering true messenger over against false prophets, the very contrast Paul presses against the 'super-apostles.' The link is figural, conforming Paul to the prophetic sufferer rather than citing a text. Marked low and contested.
sourceText: Now Pashhur, the son of Immer the priest, who was chief officer in Yahweh’s house, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things. Then Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper gate of Benjamin, which was in Yahweh’s house.

note: 'A night and a day in the deep,' perils of waters and being engulfed, resonate with the lament psalmist sinking in deep waters where the floods overwhelm him, a classic image of the righteous sufferer's distress. Volume is faint and the danger is literal for Paul, so flagged low and contested.
sourceText: Save me, God, for the waters have come up to my neck! I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold. I have come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.

note: 'If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness' inverts ordinary boasting along the lines of Jeremiah's oracle that the wise, mighty, and rich must not boast in their strength but only in knowing the LORD. Paul's recurring 'boast in the Lord' motif (cf. 10:17) makes this the controlling subtext for his weakness-boast. Coherence is strong across the letter.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.

note: The escape from Damascus, 'let down in a basket through a window by the wall,' replays Rahab lowering the spies by a rope through her window in the city wall. The shared escape-through-the-wall-window motif suggests Paul casts his flight in the idiom of the rescued/rescuing agent. Volume rests on the distinctive window-and-wall lowering.
sourceText: Then she let them down by a cord through the window; for her house was on the side of the wall, and she lived on the wall.

note: Michal lets David down through a window so he escapes the king who seeks his life, a close structural parallel to Paul evading King Aretas's governor. The persecuted-servant-lowered-through-a-window motif coheres, though Paul does not cite it. Offered as an alternative/companion source to the Rahab episode; flagged low.
sourceText: So Michal let David down through the window. He went, fled, and escaped.

note: 'The God and Father... who is blessed forever more' follows the berakah pattern of the psalter's doxologies ('Blessed be the LORD... forever and ever, Amen'). Paul's eulogy formula is liturgically shaped by such blessings. Volume is formulaic and low; flagged contested.
sourceText: Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting and to everlasting! Amen and amen.

note: Paul opens his account of ascent with the rubric 'visions and revelations of the Lord,' echoing the prophetic-apocalyptic technical language for throne and merkabah experience inaugurated by Ezekiel's 'I saw visions of God' (Ezek 1:1). The recurrence of such opening formulae across Ezekiel and Daniel makes this the native idiom Paul reworks; coherence is high since the whole pericope is a heavenly vision.
sourceText: Now in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth of the month, as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.

note: The apocalyptic 'visions' frame and the motif of being shown heavenly realities draw on Danielic seer-vision conventions, where Daniel beholds the divine throne 'in the visions of the night.' Faint and generic; flagged because Paul's vocabulary of revelation belongs to the Danielic apocalyptic stream that was available in the Second-Temple period.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: Paul says the man was 'caught up into Paradise' (paradeisos), the LXX word for the garden 'God planted in Eden.' The localization of Paradise in the highest heaven is a Second-Temple development from the Eden narrative; volume is moderate because the loaded term Paradise is a direct lexical link to the Genesis garden as rendered by the LXX.
sourceText: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed.

note: Ezekiel's oracle places a figure 'in Eden, the garden of God,' fusing Eden with a glorious cosmic-mountain sanctuary, a trajectory that feeds the heavenly-Paradise of Paul's account. Coherence is strong because Ezekiel already relocates Eden into visionary, throne-adjacent space, the very move Paul presupposes when he equates the third heaven with Paradise.
sourceText: You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone adorned you: ruby, topaz, emerald, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and beryl. Gold work of tambourines and of pipes was in you. In the day that you were created they were prepared.

note: Paul's repeated uncertainty 'whether in the body or out of the body' and the verb 'caught up' recall prophetic rapture, as when the spirit 'lifted me up between earth and heaven' and brought Ezekiel in visions to Jerusalem. Faint but coherent: the motif of bodily-or-spiritual transport in vision is a prophetic precedent Paul reflexively invokes.
sourceText: He stretched out the form of a hand, and took me by a lock of my head; and the Spirit lifted me up between earth and the sky, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem, to the door of the gate of the inner court that looks toward the north; where there was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy.

note: The 'unspeakable words which it is not lawful to utter' loosely participates in the OT topos of an ineffable divine encounter, as at Horeb where the LORD passes by in a silence beyond the wind, earthquake, and fire. Very faint and contested; offered only because the apophatic restraint around theophany has OT roots, though Paul's secrecy is closer to apocalyptic sealing conventions.
sourceText: He said, “Go out, and stand on the mountain before Yahweh.” Behold, Yahweh passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains, and broke in pieces the rocks before Yahweh; but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake.

note: The notion that what was heard 'is not lawful for a man to utter' resonates with the Sinai principle that direct apprehension of God's glory exceeds human bearing ('no man shall see me and live'). Faint; flagged because the unspeakable/unbearable quality of the highest revelation traces to the Mosaic theophany tradition Paul elsewhere engages closely (2 Cor 3).
sourceText: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”

note: The 'thorn in the flesh' draws on the LXX idiom for a persistent God-permitted affliction, where unexpelled inhabitants become 'thorns in your sides.' Volume and coherence are good: the metaphor of a thorn/goad lodged in the body as an ongoing scourge is precisely the OT figure Paul reworks into a personal torment.
sourceText: “But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those you let remain of them will be as pricks in your eyes and as thorns in your sides, and they will harass you in the land in which you dwell.

note: Ezekiel promises Israel relief from 'a pricking brier and a grieving thorn' from hostile neighbors, the same skolops/thorn imagery for a chronic harassment. The recurrence of this exact figure (Num, Josh, Ezek) for a divinely-tolerated irritant strengthens the case that Paul's 'thorn' is biblical metaphor, not merely medical.
sourceText: There shall be no more a pricking brier to the house of Israel, nor a hurting thorn of any that are around them, that scorned them; and they shall know that I am the Lord Yahweh.

note: Joshua warns that the remaining nations will be 'scourges in your sides and thorns in your eyes,' pairing thorn with scourge exactly as Paul pairs his thorn with a tormenting 'messenger of Satan.' The combined thorn-and-scourge motif, recurring across the conquest texts, gives strong intertextual coherence to Paul's affliction language.
sourceText: know for a certainty that Yahweh your God will no longer drive these nations from out of your sight; but they shall be a snare and a trap to you, a scourge in your sides, and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from off this good land which Yahweh your God has given you.

note: Paul's 'messenger of Satan to torment me' closely mirrors the prologue of Job, where the LORD permits the Satan to strike Job's flesh with sore boils. The structural parallel is strong: a faithful servant afflicted in the body by Satan under divine permission for a higher purpose, which frames Paul's theodicy of the thorn.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life.” So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.

note: Paul's resolve to 'take pleasure in weaknesses... for Christ's sake' and to receive affliction without rebellion echoes Job's acceptance, 'shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?' Coherence is high because both texts make Satanic bodily affliction the arena of tested faithfulness rather than divine abandonment.
sourceText: But he said to her, “You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. What? Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” In all this Job didn’t sin with his lips.

note: The divine word 'my power is made perfect in weakness' and 'when I am weak, then am I strong' enact Isaiah's promise that God 'gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength.' Volume is moderate but thematic coherence is strong: strength supplied precisely at the point of human exhaustion is Isaiah's consolation reapplied to apostolic suffering.
sourceText: He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might.

note: Paul's paradox that weakness is the condition of renewed power restates Isaiah's 'they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength.' Recurrence within the same Isaianic passage (40:29-31) and Paul's documented dependence on Isaiah in 2 Corinthians strengthen the link beyond a generic strength-theme.
sourceText: But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

note: The principle that God's work advances through human weakness rather than human force recalls Zechariah's oracle, 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.' Coherence is strong: both deny that strength is the basis of God's accomplishment, locating efficacy in divine power, though Paul's wording is his own.
sourceText: Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is Yahweh’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.

note: Paul's confession that grace suffices when his own flesh fails echoes the psalmist's 'My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart.' The shared move from bodily failure to God as one's sustaining strength gives good thematic coherence to the grace-in-weakness motif.
sourceText: My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

note: The promise that grace is sufficient and Christ's power rests on the weak loosely reflects the psalmic conviction that 'the LORD is near to those of a broken heart.' Faint and generic; included because Paul's grace-to-the-afflicted theology participates in the psalter's nearness-to-the-lowly tradition.
sourceText: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

note: The phrase that 'the power of Christ may rest on me' (lit. 'tabernacle/dwell upon me,' episkenoo) faintly evokes the glory that 'filled the tabernacle' and overshadowed it at its consecration. Faint but offered because Paul's verb is cognate to tabernacle/skene, suggesting the indwelling Shekinah-glory now resting on the apostle's weak body.
sourceText: Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle.

note: The 'power of Christ' resting upon the apostle distantly echoes the Spirit of the LORD that 'shall rest upon' the messianic shoot. Faint; flagged because the resting of divine power/Spirit upon a chosen agent is an Isaianic figure, here transferred from Messiah to the one who bears Christ's power in weakness.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: Paul appeals to 'signs and wonders and mighty works' as the credentials of an apostle, using the fixed OT formula for God's authenticating acts, as when the LORD multiplied 'my signs and my wonders' in Egypt. Faint but coherent: the sign-and-wonder pairing is the Deuteronomistic vocabulary of divine accreditation that Paul transfers to apostolic ministry.
sourceText: I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.

note: The triad 'signs and wonders and mighty works' echoes Deuteronomy's recital of how God took Israel 'by signs, and by wonders... and by a mighty hand.' Recurrence of this credal formula across Deuteronomy strengthens the case that Paul deliberately borrows the language of God's saving demonstrations to mark genuine apostleship.
sourceText: Or has God tried to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, by war, by a mighty hand, by an outstretched arm, and by great terrors, according to all that Yahweh your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?

note: Paul's maxim 'the parents should save up for the children, not the children for the parents' inverts and applies the proverbial principle that 'a good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children.' Coherence is good because Paul reasons from the accepted wisdom convention of parental provision to justify his refusal to burden his spiritual children.
sourceText: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, but the wealth of the sinner is stored for the righteous.

note: The assumption that fathers lay up substance for their offspring also reflects 'house and riches are an inheritance from fathers.' Faint and overlapping with Prov 13:22; included to register the broader wisdom topos of inherited parental provision that undergirds Paul's analogy.
sourceText: House and riches are an inheritance from fathers, but a prudent wife is from Yahweh.

note: Paul's feared catalog of communal sins (strife, jealousy, anger, slander, whisperings) echoes the prophetic indictments of Israel's social corruption, as in Jeremiah's complaint that the tongue 'speaks deceit... one speaks peaceably to his neighbour with his mouth, but in his heart he lays his wait.' Faint and diffuse, but coherent with the prophetic tradition of cataloguing the sins that fracture the covenant community.
sourceText: Their tongue is a deadly arrow; it speaks deceit: one speaks peaceably to his neighbor with his mouth, but in his heart he lays wait for him.

note: Paul's vice-list culminating in one who 'sows discord' parallels the wisdom catalog of things the LORD hates, which ends with 'one who sows discord among brothers' and includes a lying tongue and a false witness. The shared form of an enumerated list of community-destroying sins gives modest coherence, though Paul's specific terms are his own.
sourceText: There are six things which Yahweh hates; yes, seven which are an abomination to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood; a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that are swift in running to mischief, a false witness who utters lies, and he who sows discord among brothers.

note: Paul's fear that God 'would humble me before you' and that he must mourn over the unrepentant draws on the covenantal pattern wherein the people's 'uncircumcised heart' is humbled until they repent. Faint; flagged because the humbling-then-mourning-over-sin sequence reflects the Levitical/Deuteronomic logic of covenant discipline.
sourceText: I also walked contrary to them, and brought them into the land of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled, and they then accept the punishment of their iniquity;

note: Paul's lament over 'the uncleanness and sexual immorality and lustfulness' of the unrepentant echoes Ezekiel's prophetic language of Israel's lewdness and uncleanness for which the people must be judged and turned. Faint and thematic; included because Paul's grief over sexual impurity in the congregation belongs to the prophetic idiom of denouncing covenantal 'uncleanness.'
sourceText: Thus will I cause lewdness to cease out of the land, that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness.

note: Paul cites the two-or-three-witnesses rule verbatim ('At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established'), a direct LXX-form quotation governing judicial proof. Volume is maximal: explicit citation formula and near-verbatim wording. Coherence is strong since Paul frames his three visits as the requisite testimony before disciplinary action.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: The same Deuteronomic two-or-three-witnesses principle appears here in a capital-case context, part of the legal tradition Paul invokes. The wording overlaps with Deut 19:15, the primary source, so this is a parallel attestation of the rule rather than the citation's lemma. Recurrence within the Torah strengthens the availability of the witness-tradition.
sourceText: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.

note: Numbers also codifies that a person shall be put to death only on the testimony of witnesses, reinforcing the multi-witness legal tradition Paul deploys. It is a secondary attestation alongside Deut 17:6 rather than the quoted text. The cluster shows the rule's standing as established Torah jurisprudence.
sourceText: “‘Whoever kills any person, the murderer shall be slain at the mouth of witnesses; but one witness shall not testify against any person that he die.

note: Christ 'crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God' echoes the Servant who is afflicted and humbled yet exalted and vindicated by God. Volume is faint and no verbal citation occurs, so the link rests on the conceptual coherence of suffering-then-power. Contested because the weakness/power dialectic is broadly Pauline and not demonstrably keyed to Isaiah here.
sourceText: Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed? For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and […]

note: Paul's 'Test your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves' resonates with the psalmist's 'Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; test my heart and my mind.' Volume is moderate through shared testing/proving vocabulary in the self-scrutiny tradition. Coherence is high since both concern verifying genuine standing before God.
sourceText: Examine me, Yahweh, and prove me. Try my heart and my mind.

note: The summons to be searched and tested to see whether any wicked way is present parallels Paul's call to self-examination 'whether you are in the faith.' The introspective testing tradition supplies the conceptual frame for Paul's appeal. No verbal quotation, so this is an allusion within a recurrent biblical motif.
sourceText: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.

note: 'Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD' supplies a corporate self-examination motif close to Paul's command to test oneself. Volume is faint with no shared diction in Greek, so the echo is thematic. Coherence is supported by the repentance/restoration aim of the surrounding verses (perfecting, doing no evil).
sourceText: Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to Yahweh.

note: 'The refining pot is for silver... but the LORD tests the hearts' belongs to the wisdom tradition of divine testing that informs Paul's language of approval and being 'reprobate/disqualified' (adokimos). The link is conceptual rather than verbal and competes with the Psalms as a closer source. Marked contested for its faintness.
sourceText: The refining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold, but Yahweh tests the hearts.

note: 'Live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you' echoes the Aaronic benediction's 'the LORD... give you peace,' the foundational peace-blessing of Israel. Volume is moderate via the shared peace-and-presence formula closing the letter. Coherence is strong since Paul is pronouncing a farewell blessing, the benediction's native function.
sourceText: Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: The full priestly blessing (grace/favor, the LORD's face, peace) stands behind Paul's closing of peace and divine presence and anticipates the triune benediction in v.14. The threefold structure of grace, love, and fellowship loosely mirrors the threefold Aaronic form. Marked allusion rather than quotation given the absence of verbatim wording.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: The divine title 'the God of love and peace' faintly recalls covenantal peace-name traditions such as Gideon's altar 'The LORD is Peace' (YHWH-shalom). The connection is purely thematic with no verbal overlap, so it is a faint echo. Contested and secondary to the Aaronic blessing as the operative source.
sourceText: Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

note: The closing triune benediction ('the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit') functions as Paul's Christianized Aaronic blessing, its threefold grace/presence/peace structure refracted into a threefold divine formula. Volume rests on the shared benedictory genre and triadic shape rather than diction. Coherence is high: a letter-closing priestly-style blessing invoking grace and the divine presence 'with you all.'
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: 'The love of God' draws on the covenant self-revelation of the LORD as abounding in steadfast love (hesed), the wellspring of Israel's confidence in divine favor. The echo is conceptual, supplying the OT substrate for 'love of God,' with no verbal citation. Contested because 'love of God' is a generic Pauline phrase not demonstrably keyed to this text.

Volume is moderate, thematic coherence high (vicarious death), and the Servant is firmly available in Second-Temple use.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: The self-giving sin-offering ('when you make his soul an offering for sin') undergirds 'gave himself for our sins.' Coheres with Isa 53:6 as a Servant matrix Paul presupposes; counted distinctly because the offering-language adds the cultic note. Contested only as to which Servant verse is primary.
sourceText: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand.

note: 'that he might deliver us out of this present evil age' draws on the Exodus deliverance vocabulary (rescue from bondage by God's act). The age-from-which-rescued substitutes for Egypt; faint and figural, but the deliverance verb-frame is a deep OT staple. Marked low/contested as a generic redemption motif.

note: 'Grace to you and peace' may stylize the Aaronic blessing's pairing of favor ('be gracious') and peace (shalom). The epistolary greeting is Paul's formula, so volume is low, but the grace-and-peace dyad has a plausible priestly-blessing background. Contested as a possible coincidence of common cultic terms.
sourceText: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you.

note: 'to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen' reproduces the closing-doxology pattern of the Psalter's book-seams ('Blessed be the LORD... forever and ever. Amen and Amen'). Recurrence across Pss 41, 72, 89, 106 makes the liturgical formula securely available; Paul Christianizes it.
sourceText: Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting and to everlasting! Amen and amen.

note: David's ascription 'Yours is the glory... forever' is a candidate liturgical source for the doxology in v.5. Overlaps with the Psalter doxologies; listed for recurrence of the 'the glory belongs to God forever' template. Low because the Psalter forms are the likelier proximate model.
sourceText: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.

note: 'I marvel that you are so quickly deserting' echoes 'they have turned aside quickly out of the way' at the golden calf; LXX uses tachu ('quickly') as Paul does (tacheos). Apostasy-after-deliverance is thematically apt for Galatians, and the speed-of-defection lexeme strengthens the link.
sourceText: They have turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them. They have made themselves a molten calf, and have worshiped it, and have sacrificed to it, and said, ‘These are your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt.’”

note: The hypothetical preacher of a counterfeit message who must be cursed mirrors the prophet/dreamer who urges other gods and is to be purged; even 'an angel from heaven' fits the 'though he gives a sign' test. The death-sentence on the seducer coheres with Paul's anathema.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul. note: 'let him be cursed' (anathema/epikataratos) draws the covenant-curse formulary of the Ebal liturgy where the people ratify 'Cursed be' on covenant-breakers. The repeated curse-pronouncement (vv.8-9) mimics the antiphonal recurrence of Deut 27, anchoring availability of the curse-genre.
sourceText: ‘Cursed is the man who makes an engraved or molten image, an abomination to Yahweh, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and sets it up in secret.’ All the people shall answer and say, ‘Amen.’

note: The anathema may carry the cherem ('devoted to destruction') sense from Jericho, where what is accursed is set apart for God's judgment and contaminates the camp. Coheres with treating the false gospel as defiling, but the curse-formulary of Deuteronomy is the nearer source, so low/contested.
sourceText: The city shall be devoted, even it and all that is in it, to Yahweh. Only Rahab the prostitute shall live, she and all who are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent.

note: 'am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God?' rests on the contrast that man judges by outward appearance while the LORD looks on the heart. The man-versus-God antithesis of approval is thematically coherent with Paul's defense of divine commissioning over human applause.

sourceText: There they were in great fear, where no fear was, for God has scattered the bones of him who encamps against you. You have put them to shame, because God has rejected them.

note: Paul's insistence that his gospel is 'not according to man' but by revelation contrasts the true prophetic word with prophets who 'speak a vision of their own heart, not from the mouth of the LORD.' Coheres with the prophetic claim to mediated, not self-generated, message; low because no shared wording.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh of Armies, Don’t listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you: they teach you vanity; they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of Yahweh.

note: 'it came to me through revelation' fits the prophetic axiom that the Lord reveals his secret (sod) to his servants the prophets. Supports Paul casting his call as prophetic disclosure rather than tradition; faint and thematic only, hence low/contested.
sourceText: Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.

note: 'being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers' while persecuting evokes Phinehas, the paradigm of zeal who slays the covenant-breaker and is rewarded with a covenant. Second-Temple Judaism made Phinehas the model of violent zeal Paul once embodied; thematic coherence high.

sourceText: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

sourceText: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

sourceText: Yahweh will strike you with madness, with blindness, and with astonishment of heart.

Verbal volume is low; the link is conceptual via the promised-Spirit theme that culminates in v.14. Contested.

note: Verbatim LXX citation: 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.' This is the foundational proof-text of Paul's whole justification-by-faith argument, repeated at Romans 4:3 and James 2:23, satisfying recurrence and high volume. Availability and coherence are maximal.
sourceText: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.

sourceText: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”

sourceText: All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your seed, because you have obeyed my voice.”

note: Verbatim LXX citation: 'Cursed is everyone who doesn't continue in all things written in the book of the law, to do them.' Paul adds 'all' (pasin) emphasizing total obedience. This is a formal proof-text from the Shechem curse-liturgy, high in volume and coherence.
sourceText: ‘Cursed is he who doesn’t uphold the words of this law by doing them.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’”

note: 'The righteous will live by faith' cites Hab 2:4, a programmatic text Paul also uses at Romans 1:17 (and Hebrews 10:38), giving strong recurrence. Paul follows a form close to the LXX but drops the possessive pronoun. The faith/life antithesis is the hinge of his argument.
sourceText: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.

note: 'The man who does them will live by them' cites Lev 18:5 (LXX), set in deliberate antithesis to Hab 2:4. Paul reuses the same text at Romans 10:5, establishing recurrence; it embodies the law's do-and-live principle he contrasts with faith. High volume.
sourceText: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.

This is the resolution of the citation chain begun in v.8, so the recurrence within the chapter is strong. Allusive recapitulation rather than fresh quotation.
sourceText: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”

note: 'The promise of the Spirit' (v.14) may echo the prophetic promise of the poured-out Spirit (Joel 2:28-29; cf. Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 36:27). Paul does not cite a text, but the eschatological-Spirit-promise tradition stands behind the phrase. Contested and diffuse.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.

note: 'To your seed' (v.16) cites the recurring promise to Abraham 'and to your seed' in Gen 13:15 (cf. 17:8; 24:7). Paul's argument turns on the singular collective noun 'seed' (sperma) read messianically as Christ. The verbal anchor is exact and central to the pericope.
sourceText: for all the land which you see, I will give to you, and to your offspring forever.

sourceText: I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”

note: Gen 24:7 ('to your seed I will give this land') is a further instance of the singular-seed land-promise underlying v.16. Listing these reinforces that Paul's 'not seeds but seed' rests on a real and recurrent Genesis formula. High coherence.
sourceText: Yahweh, the God of heaven, who took me from my father’s house, and from the land of my birth, who spoke to me, and who swore to me, saying, ‘I will give this land to your seed.’ He will send his angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there.

note: The '430 years' (v.17) between promise and law derives from Exod 12:40 LXX, which dates Israel's sojourn at 430 years. Paul uses the figure to prove the law came later and cannot annul the prior covenant. The specific number makes the allusion strong despite no quoted clause.
sourceText: Now the time that the children of Israel lived in Egypt was four hundred thirty years.

note: Paul's framing of the Abrahamic 'covenant' (diatheke) confirmed by God draws on the covenant-cutting of Gen 15:18 (cf. Gen 17). The covenant concept rather than wording is in view, undergirding the legal analogy of v.15. Faint and conceptual.
sourceText: In that day Yahweh made a covenant with Abram, saying, “To your seed I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:

note: 'Ordained through angels' (v.19) reflects the Second-Temple tradition that the law was mediated by angels at Sinai, grounded in Deut 33:2 LXX ('at his right hand angels with him') and reflected in Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2. The angelic-mediation reading is available in the LXX and intertestamental sources. Medium volume.
sourceText: He said, “Yahweh came from Sinai, and rose from Seir to them. He shone from Mount Paran. He came from the ten thousands of holy ones. At his right hand was a fiery law for them.

note: Ps 68:17 (LXX 67:18), 'the chariots of God are myriads... the Lord among them at Sinai,' contributed to the tradition of angelic hosts at the Sinai law-giving behind v.19. The link is part of a cluster of texts, not a single source; verbal contact is slight. Contested.
sourceText: The chariots of God are tens of thousands and thousands of thousands. The Lord is among them, from Sinai, into the sanctuary.

note: 'If there had been a law given which could make alive' (v.21) replays the do-and-live principle of Lev 18:5 cited in v.12, now denied as a means of life. The intra-chapter recurrence of the life-by-law motif makes the allusion coherent though not re-quoted.
sourceText: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.

note: 'The Scripture imprisoned all things under sin' (v.22) summarizes the universal-sinfulness verdict Paul elsewhere proves with a catena including Ps 14:1-3 (cf. Rom 3:9-19). No clause is quoted here, but the scriptural confinement-under-sin theme draws on that tradition. Contested and diffuse.
sourceText: They have all gone aside. They have together become corrupt. There is no one who does good, no, not one.

note: Ps 143:2 ('no one living is righteous before you'), which Paul cites at Gal 2:16 and Rom 3:20, stands behind the 'all under sin' verdict of v.22. The echo continues the justification argument from the previous chapter. Faint; offered as an alternative scriptural ground.
sourceText: Don’t enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no man living is righteous.

note: 'There is neither... male nor female' (v.28) verbally echoes Gen 1:27 LXX 'male and female he created them' (arsen kai thely), the only place this exact pairing occurs. Paul's shift from 'nor/nor' to 'and' marks the deliberate citation; the new creation in Christ relativizes the created distinction. Medium-high volume on the specific phrase.
sourceText: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: 'You are Abraham's seed and heirs according to promise' (v.29) recapitulates the singular-seed promise of Gen 13:15/17:8 expounded in v.16, now extended to all who are Christ's. This closes the chapter's inclusio on seed/promise/inheritance with strong intra-chapter recurrence.
sourceText: for all the land which you see, I will give to you, and to your offspring forever.

note: The heirs-of-promise climax (v.29) realizes the seed-and-nations blessing of Gen 22:18, gathering Gentile believers into Abraham's offspring. It reprises the citation chain (vv.8, 16) and so coheres with the chapter's argument, though without fresh wording. Medium.
sourceText: All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your seed, because you have obeyed my voice.”

note: 'Put on Christ' (v.27) may echo the clothing-with-salvation imagery of Isa 61:10 ('he has clothed me with garments of salvation') and the robing motif of Zechariah 3:4. The metaphor of investiture is available in the prophets but the contact is thematic, not verbal. Contested and faint.
sourceText: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

note: "God sent out his Son, born to a woman" (v.4) faintly evokes the protoevangelium's promise of the woman's seed who undoes the serpent. Coherence with Paul's redemption-of-the-enslaved theme is real but the verbal volume is thin; the phrase 'born of woman' is a common idiom (cf. Job). Marked low and contested.
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: The cluster of sonship/adoption/firstborn language (vv.5-7, 'receive the adoption,' 'no longer a bondservant but a son,' 'heir') recalls God's claim 'Israel is my son, my firstborn.' Coherence is high in a redemption-from-bondage argument that runs on Exodus categories; Recurrence of son/heir terms supports it. Verbal volume is moderate, hence allusion not quotation.
sourceText: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,

note: 'Out of Egypt I called my son' supplies the same divine sonship motif undergirding 'God sent out his Son' and the adoption of children. The link is conceptual rather than verbal in Galatians; availability and coherence hold but volume is low. Contested as a deliberate echo.
sourceText: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.

note: 'That he might redeem those who were under the law' (v.5) draws on the Exodus vocabulary of God redeeming a people from slavery (cf. Exod 6:6, 15:13). The redemption-from-bondage frame coheres tightly with Paul's slave/son contrast, but no single Exodus verse is quoted, so this is a diffuse echo.
sourceText: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:

note: 'You observe days, months, seasons, and years' (v.10) maps onto the creation luminaries appointed 'for signs and for seasons and for days and years,' the calendrical basis of Israel's festal observance Paul deprecates. The four-term sequence is a strong verbal/structural match; coherence with the 'elemental principles' (stoicheia, vv.3,9) reinforces it.
sourceText: God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years;

note: The 'days, months, seasons' Paul names are the appointed feasts, sabbaths, and new moons codified in the festal calendar of Lev 23. Coherence is high since the agitators urge Torah calendar observance; the allusion is to the institution as a whole rather than to a single quoted clause.
sourceText: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘The set feasts of Yahweh, which you shall proclaim to be holy convocations, even these are my set feasts.

note: Paul's wariness of 'new moons and sabbaths' calendar piety echoes Isaiah's prophetic critique of 'new moon and sabbath' observance that God comes to loathe. The polemical stance coheres, but Galatians supplies no shared wording, so this is a faint echo at best.
sourceText: Bring no more vain offerings. Incense is an abomination to me; new moons, Sabbaths, and convocations: I can’t bear with evil assemblies.

note: 'You received me as an angel/messenger of God' (v.14) may glance at the messenger-of-the-Lord motif (Mal 2:7; cf. Zech) where a human envoy is welcomed as God's representative. The wording is generic and the link is weak; marked low and contested.
sourceText: For the priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth; for he is the messenger of Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'Abraham had two sons, one by the handmaid' (v.22) directly recounts Hagar bearing Ishmael to Abraham. This is the foundational narrative Paul allegorizes; the citation is explicit ('it is written') and figurally load-bearing for the whole pericope.
sourceText: Hagar bore a son for Abram. Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.

note: 'One by the free woman' born 'through promise' (vv.22-23) recounts Sarah bearing Isaac at the appointed time God had promised. Volume and coherence are maximal; Paul builds the free-woman/promise half of the allegory directly on this Genesis event.
sourceText: Sarah conceived, and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.

note: 'The son by the free woman was born through promise' (v.23) rests on God's explicit promise that Sarah would bear a son and become 'mother of nations.' Coherence with Paul's promise/flesh antithesis is exact; the promise to Sarah is the textual hinge of the contrast.
sourceText: I will bless her, and moreover I will give you a son by her. Yes, I will bless her, and she will be a mother of nations. Kings of peoples will come from her.”

note: The 'born through promise' language (v.23) echoes the annunciation 'I will surely return to you, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.' This is the verbal source of the divine promise of Isaac that Paul treats as paradigmatic; recurrence with 17:16 strengthens it.
sourceText: He said, “I will certainly return to you when the season comes round. Behold, Sarah your wife will have a son.” Sarah heard in the tent door, which was behind him.

note: 'The son by the handmaid was born according to the flesh' (v.23) recalls the merely human stratagem of Gen 16, where Sarai gives Hagar to Abram to bear a child by ordinary means. Coherence with Paul's flesh/Spirit antithesis is strong; supplies the 'according to the flesh' pole.
sourceText: Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bore him no children. She had a handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar.

note: V.27 quotes Isaiah 54:1 almost verbatim (LXX): 'Rejoice, you barren who don't bear... more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband.' Highest volume; the barren-now-fruitful Zion is mapped onto the free Jerusalem above and Sarah. Explicit 'it is written.'
sourceText: “Sing, barren, you who didn’t bear; break out into singing, and cry aloud, you who did not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife,” says Yahweh.

note: 'One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children to bondage, which is Hagar' (v.24-25) keys the whole covenant typology to the Hagar narrative. The figural identification of Hagar with Sinai/present Jerusalem in slavery is the interpretive core of the pericope.
sourceText: Hagar bore a son for Abram. Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.

note: 'One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children to bondage' (v.24) presupposes the Sinai covenant/law-giving (Exod 19-20) which Paul recategorizes as enslaving. Coherence with the two-covenants argument is high; the allusion is to the Sinai event as institution.
sourceText: In the third month after the children of Israel had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that same day they came into the wilderness of Sinai.

note: 'The Jerusalem that is above is free, the mother of us all' (v.26) draws on the prophetic exaltation of Zion as the mother-city to which nations stream. Conceptual availability is strong (heavenly/eschatological Zion) but Galatians supplies no shared wording, so low/contested.
sourceText: Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.

note: The 'Jerusalem above... mother of us all' (v.26) coheres with Zion as the mother of whom it is said 'this one and that one were born in her.' The maternal-Zion motif is apt but verbally faint in Galatians; marked low and contested.
sourceText: Yes, of Zion it will be said, “This one and that one was born in her”; the Most High himself will establish her.

note: 'We, brothers, as Isaac was, are children of promise' (v.28) identifies believers with Isaac, the son born by promise (Gen 21:1-2). Coherence with the promise/flesh allegory is exact; Isaac is the explicit figural type.
sourceText: Sarah conceived, and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.

note: 'He who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit' (v.29) draws on Ishmael 'mocking/playing with' Isaac (Gen 21:9), read in Jewish tradition as persecution. Strong coherence; supplies the persecution motif Paul applies to the agitators.
sourceText: Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, mocking.

note: V.30 quotes Gen 21:10 (Sarah's words): 'Throw out the handmaid and her son, for the son of the handmaid will not inherit with the son of the free woman.' High verbal volume; the inheritance/exclusion ruling is Paul's clinching scriptural warrant, marked 'what does the Scripture say.'
sourceText: Therefore she said to Abraham, “Cast out this handmaid and her son! For the son of this handmaid will not be heir with my son, Isaac.”

note: 'We are not children of a handmaid, but of the free woman' (v.31) closes the allegory by reasserting the Hagar/Sarah identification. The figural reading of the slave-woman narrative governs the concluding antithesis.
sourceText: Hagar bore a son for Abram. Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.

note: Paul's 'yoke of bondage/slavery' inverts the exodus formula where God 'broke the bars of your yoke' and made Israel walk upright after Egyptian slavery. Volume is fair (the yoke-of-slavery image is distinctively exodus/covenant) and coheres with Paul's whole exodus-from-law typology in Galatians. The redemptive-liberation logic matches closely.
sourceText: I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, that you should not be their slaves. I have broken the bars of your yoke, and made you go upright.

note: The Jubilee proclamation of 'liberty (deror) throughout the land' may underlie Paul's stress on the freedom for which Christ liberated. Coherence is real (release from debt-servitude) but volume is faint; the verbal link runs through the LXX language of eleutheria rather than direct citation.
sourceText: You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.

note: The Servant's anointing 'to proclaim liberty to the captives' is a Second-Temple touchstone for eschatological release that Paul's freedom language may draw upon. Faint volume and no verbal quotation, but the messianic-liberty theme coheres with Christ as the agent who 'made us free.'
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

note: Jeremiah's sign-act of the broken/iron yoke (chs. 27-28) gives the prophetic vocabulary of a yoke as imposed servitude that is broken or re-imposed. Coherence is moderate but recurrence is weak; the image is generic enough that direct dependence is uncertain.
sourceText: Thus speaks Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, saying, I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.

note: Paul's whole argument about receiving circumcision presupposes the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision as the sign binding one to the law. Availability and volume are strong as the institutional backdrop, even though Paul does not cite the words. The figural reversal (circumcision now profits nothing) depends on the reader knowing this text.
sourceText: This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised.

note: Being 'a debtor to do the whole law' restates the Deuteronomic curse on everyone who does not confirm all the words of the law to do them, which Paul quotes explicitly at 3:10. Recurrence within Galatians is high, making the echo here coherent and deliberate.
sourceText: ‘Cursed is he who doesn’t uphold the words of this law by doing them.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’”

note: The demand to 'do the whole law' resonates with the Levitical maxim that the one who does these statutes shall live by them, which Paul cites at 3:12. Volume is moderate but the verbal contact here is thematic rather than lexical.
sourceText: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.

note: 'Through the Spirit, by faith we wait for the hope of righteousness' recalls the prophetic axiom that the righteous shall live by faith, which Paul cites at 3:11. The faith-righteousness pairing coheres strongly, though here it is allusive rather than quoted.
sourceText: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.

note: 'A little yeast leavens the whole lump' draws on the Passover/Unleavened Bread command to purge all leaven from the house, where leaven functions as a spreading defilement. Volume and availability are high; the agricultural proverb is freighted with the cultic logic of total removal that fits Paul's warning about the agitators.
sourceText: “‘Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even the first day you shall put away yeast out of your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel.

note: The reinforcing command that no leaven be seen in all your borders during the feast undergirds the same purity image. Recurrence across the Exodus leaven texts strengthens the figural force of contamination spreading through the community.
sourceText: Unleavened bread shall be eaten throughout the seven days; and no leavened bread shall be seen with you, neither shall yeast be seen with you, in all your borders.

note: Paul's wish that the circumcisers would 'cut themselves off' (mutilate/emasculate) trades on the law excluding the emasculated from the assembly of the LORD, a bitterly ironic inversion: those zealous for circumcision are told to go further and be excluded. Coherence and wordplay are strong though the dependence is contested versus a generic castration gibe.
sourceText: He who is emasculated by crushing or cutting shall not enter into Yahweh’s assembly.

note: 'The stumbling block of the cross' echoes the prophetic stone of stumbling and rock of offense, a Second-Temple testimony Paul uses elsewhere. Volume is faint here and the link is thematic; the contact may run through shared early-Christian stone testimonia.
sourceText: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

note: Paul cites verbatim 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' declaring the whole law fulfilled in this one word. This is an explicit LXX quotation with the highest volume and availability; it is the interpretive center of the pericope.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'If you bite and devour one another' echoes the psalmist's enemies who draw near 'to eat up my flesh,' supplying the predatory cannibal imagery for internal strife. Volume is modest and the metaphor is conventional, so dependence is plausible but uncertain.
sourceText: When evildoers came at me to eat up my flesh, even my adversaries and my foes, they stumbled and fell.

note: Micah's indictment of leaders who 'eat the flesh of my people' and tear their skin matches Paul's imagery of mutual consuming as social predation. The prophetic backdrop coheres with the moral charge, though the image is widespread enough to be only an echo.
sourceText: who also eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them, and break their bones, and chop them in pieces, as for the pot, and as flesh within the cauldron.

note: The wisdom portrait of a generation whose teeth are swords 'to devour the poor' reinforces the same devouring-one-another trope. Faint volume; offered as a maximal candidate within the predatory-mouth field.
sourceText: There is a generation whose teeth are like swords, and their jaws like knives, to devour the poor from the earth, and the needy from among men.

note: 'Walk by the Spirit' and being 'led by the Spirit' echo the new-covenant promise that God will put his Spirit within and cause his people to walk in his statutes. Coherence is strong with Paul's Spirit-versus-law contrast, and availability is high in Second-Temple Spirit-endowment hope.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: 'Let your good Spirit lead me on level ground' supplies the rare motif of the divine Spirit as the agent of moral guidance behind Paul's 'led by the Spirit.' Volume is low but the verbal pairing of Spirit and leading is distinctive.
sourceText: Teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Your Spirit is good. Lead me in the land of uprightness.

note: The exodus retrospect where the Spirit of the LORD gave Israel rest and led the people gives a prophetic precedent for Spirit-leading. Faint and contested, but it coheres with Paul's exodus-shaped Spirit theology.
sourceText: As the livestock that go down into the valley, the Spirit of Yahweh caused them to rest; so you led your people, to make yourself a glorious name.

note: The vice 'sorcery' (pharmakeia) names a practice condemned in the Deuteronomic catalog of diviners and sorcerers, signaling that Paul's list draws the flesh's works partly from Torah's prohibited paganisms. Coherence with idolatry (next item) strengthens the covenantal framing.
sourceText: There shall not be found with you anyone who makes his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, one who uses divination, one who practices sorcery, or an enchanter, or a sorcerer,

note: 'Idolatry' as the head of the cultic vices echoes the Decalogue's first/second commandments against other gods and images. Availability and recurrence are high; idolatry is the paradigmatic covenant breach the prophets repeatedly indict.
sourceText: “You shall have no other gods before me.

note: Hosea's catalog of swearing, lying, killing, stealing, and adultery breaking out is a prophetic vice-list precedent for Paul's enumerated 'works of the flesh.' The form-critical parallel coheres, though Paul's specific items are largely Hellenistic, so the dependence is a structural echo rather than citation.
sourceText: There is cursing, lying, murder, stealing, and committing adultery; they break boundaries, and bloodshed causes bloodshed.

note: The deuterocanonical vice-catalog spawned by idolatry (bloodshed, deceit, corruption, disorder, sexual confusion) is a close Second-Temple analogue to Paul's idolatry-rooted list. Availability is strong and the genre match is notable, supporting a Hellenistic-Jewish background for the form.
sourceText: And all things confusedly are filled with blood and murder, theft and deceit, Corruption, faithlessness, tumult, perjury,

note: The 'fruit of the Spirit' yielding peace and righteousness recalls Isaiah's vision of the Spirit poured from on high making the wilderness fruitful so that the effect of righteousness is peace. The agricultural Spirit-fruit-peace cluster coheres closely with Paul's metaphor.
sourceText: Until the Spirit is poured on us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is considered a forest.

note: The sevenfold endowment resting on the messianic shoot (wisdom, counsel, knowledge, fear of the LORD) is the OT prototype of Spirit-borne virtue catalogs that Paul's nine-fold list develops. Volume is faint and the items differ, so this is an underlying conceptual echo of Spirit-given character.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: 'If we live by the Spirit' resonates with Ezekiel's promise 'I will put my Spirit in you and you shall live,' the new-covenant linkage of Spirit and resurrection-life. Coherence is good with Paul's Spirit-life theme, though here it is a faint thematic echo without verbal citation.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.

note: The pairing of Spirit/breath and life behind 'live by the Spirit' may distantly invoke the creation account where God's breath makes the human a living being, now read pneumatologically. Very faint volume; offered as a maximal figural candidate.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (v.2) recapitulates Paul's reading of Lev 19:18 as the whole law's summation, already explicit in Gal 5:14. Volume and recurrence within Galatians are high; the burden-bearing of v.2 specifies the neighbor-love command in concrete mutual care. The clearest OT substrate for "fulfill the law" here.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: Restoring the one "caught in some fault" and mutual responsibility may faintly evoke Cain's "Am I my brother's keeper?" as the negative foil. Volume is thin and there is no verbal contact; offered as a contested figural counterpoint to communal accountability.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”

note: "Restore such a one" and the duty not to ignore the stumbling brother resonates with the sapiential charge to rescue those being led to ruin. Coherence with Paul's communal ethic is moderate but verbal availability is weak; marked contested.
sourceText: Rescue those who are being led away to death! Indeed, hold back those who are staggering to the slaughter! If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this”; doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not render to every man according to his work?

note: "Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap" (v.7) draws on the wisdom maxim of moral retribution stated in Job 4:8, "those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same." The sowing/reaping figure is a stock OT idiom; volume is high and coherence with Paul's flesh-vs-Spirit harvest (v.8) is strong.
sourceText: According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity, and sow trouble, reap the same.

note: Hosea's "they sow the wind and reap the whirlwind" is the prophetic locus for inexorable sowing-reaping judgment, closely matching Gal 6:7-8's certainty that the harvest answers the seed. Recurrence of the agricultural-judgment topos across the prophets supports availability; coherence with reaping corruption is high.
sourceText: For they sow the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind. He has no standing grain. The stalk will yield no head. If it does yield, strangers will swallow it up.

note: Hosea 10:12-13 opposes sowing righteousness/steadfast love and reaping accordingly versus plowing iniquity and reaping injustice, the same antithetical structure as Paul's sowing to the flesh vs. to the Spirit (v.8). The two-way harvest imagery makes this among the strongest prophetic substrates for the pericope.
sourceText: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you. You have plowed wickedness. You have reaped iniquity. You have eaten the fruit of lies, for you trusted in your way, in the multitude of your mighty men.

note: "Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity" supplies the sapiential form of the maxim Paul cites in v.7. Volume is moderate and the proverb belongs to the same cluster as Job 4:8; coherence is high though no single source is quoted verbatim.
sourceText: He who sows wickedness reaps trouble, and the rod of his fury will be destroyed.
lxxText: He that sows wickedness shall reap troubles; and shall fully receive the punishment of his deeds. God loves a cheerful and liberal man; but a man shall fully prove the folly of his works.

note: "Whoever sows righteousness gets a sure reward" matches the positive pole of Paul's harvest ("sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life," v.8) and the promise of v.9 that doing good will reap in due season. Part of the wisdom sowing-cluster; offered as a corroborating echo rather than a single source.
sourceText: Wicked people earn deceitful wages, but one who sows righteousness reaps a sure reward.

note: "Do not sow in the furrows of injustice, lest you reap them sevenfold" is the Second-Temple form of the maxim, demonstrating its currency in Paul's milieu (availability). Volume is moderate; it strengthens the case that v.7 cites a proverbial commonplace rather than one prophet.
sourceText: My son, sow not upon the furrows of unrighteousness, And you shall not reap them sevenfold.

note: "We will reap in due season" (v.9) may faintly recall the covenant promise of rain and harvest "in its season" for obedience. Coherence with eschatological reaping is partial and the verbal link is thin; marked contested.
sourceText: that I will give the rain of your land in its season, the former rain and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain, your new wine, and your oil.

note: "Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy" parallels v.9's encouragement not to grow weary because reaping comes in due season if one does not give up. The consolatory sowing-reaping reversal coheres with Paul's exhortation, though there is no verbal citation; contested.
sourceText: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.

note: "God is not mocked" (v.7) resonates with the Song of Moses' rebuke of the people who treat the LORD with contempt and with the broader OT motif that God will not be derided. Volume is low and no single text is in view; offered as a faint contested backdrop.
sourceText: Is this the way you repay Yahweh, foolish and unwise people? Isn’t he your father who has bought you? He has made you and established you.

note: "Neither circumcision... but a new creation" (v.15) draws on Isaiah's "new heavens and a new earth," the prophetic announcement of God's eschatological re-creation. Recurrence of the new-creation theme across Isaiah and coherence with Paul's crucified-world (v.14) make this the primary OT source for kaine ktisis.
sourceText: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.

note: Isaiah 66:22's "new heavens and new earth" that shall remain reinforces 65:17 as the scriptural matrix for the abiding "new creation" of v.15. The pairing supplies recurrence within Isaiah; coherence with Paul's contrast between old marks-in-the-flesh and new creation is strong.
sourceText: “For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me,” says Yahweh, “so your seed and your name shall remain.

note: "Do not remember the former things... I am doing a new thing" frames the new creation as the displacement of what is old, paralleling Paul's relegation of circumcision/uncircumcision to nothing (v.15). Volume is moderate and the theme is part of Isaiah's new-exodus cluster.
sourceText: “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.

note: The promise of a "new heart" and "new spirit" undergirds Paul's interior new-creation reality over against fleshly circumcision (vv.12-15). Coherence with the flesh/Spirit antithesis of the chapter is high, though the language is anthropological rather than cosmic; corroborating echo.
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.

note: Jeremiah's oracle that God will punish all who are "circumcised yet uncircumcised"—Israel being uncircumcised in heart—anticipates Paul's devaluing of fleshly circumcision in favor of inward transformation (vv.12-15). Volume is moderate; the prophetic relativizing of physical circumcision strongly coheres with Paul's argument.
sourceText: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will punish all those who are circumcised in uncircumcision: Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that have the corners of their hair cut off, who dwell in the wilderness; for all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart.

note: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart" supplies the Torah's own move from fleshly to inward circumcision, the trajectory Paul completes with "new creation" (v.15). Coherence is high and the motif recurs (Deut 30:6); offered as a corroborating echo of the heart-circumcision tradition.
sourceText: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.

note: "Peace... on God's Israel" (v.16) echoes the psalm's closing benediction "Peace be upon Israel," a liturgical blessing Paul redirects to those who walk by the rule of new creation. Volume and the formulaic shape (peace-upon-Israel) are high; coherence with a closing benediction is exact.
sourceText: But as for those who turn aside to their crooked ways, Yahweh will lead them away with the workers of iniquity. Peace be on Israel.

note: Psalm 128:6 likewise ends "Peace be upon Israel," reinforcing v.16 as a deliberate echo of the Psalter's pilgrimage benediction. Recurrence of the exact phrase across Pss 125 and 128 strengthens availability; Paul invokes the blessing while redefining its recipients.
sourceText: Yes, may you see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel.

note: The Aaronic benediction—"the LORD... give you peace"—is the liturgical fountainhead for pronouncing peace and mercy upon Israel (v.16). Volume of the peace-blessing motif is high though the verbal contact is thematic; coherence with a closing apostolic blessing is strong.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: "I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body" (v.17) evokes the protective mark (taw) set on the foreheads of the faithful who are spared the slaughter. The marking that distinguishes God's own coheres with Paul's stigmata as the true seal over against circumcision; verbal contact is figural but apt.
sourceText: Yahweh said to him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark on the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry over all the abominations that are done in its midst. To the others he said in my hearing, Go through the city after him, and strike: don’t let your eye spare, neither have pity; kill utterly the old man, the young man and the virgin, and little children and women; but don’t come near any man on whom is […]

note: Isaiah's image of one who "writes on his hand, 'The LORD's,'" marking belonging to God, parallels Paul's bodily "marks of Jesus" (v.17) as a sign of ownership. Coherence with the slave-brand/belonging motif is good; volume is moderate and the link is figural.
sourceText: One will say, ‘I am Yahweh’s;’ and another will be called by the name of Jacob; and another will write with his hand ‘to Yahweh,’ and honor the name of Israel.”

note: The high-priestly gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD" worn on the body has been proposed as background for Paul's engraved marks of Jesus (v.17). The cultic-engraving association is suggestive but verbally remote; offered as a contested, low-volume echo.
sourceText: “You shall make a plate of pure gold, and engrave on it, like the engravings of a signet, ‘HOLY TO YAHWEH.’ You shall put it on a lace of blue, and it shall be on the sash; on the front of the sash it shall be. It shall be on Aaron’s forehead, and Aaron shall bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall make holy in all their holy gifts; and it shall be always on his forehead, that they may be accepted before Yahweh.

note: The Torah's prohibition of cutting marks in the flesh forms an ironic backdrop to Paul's embrace of the "marks of Jesus" (v.17) as honorable wounds. The connection is conceptual rather than citational and runs by contrast; marked contested.
sourceText: “‘You shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor tattoo any marks on you. I am Yahweh.

note: The epistolary salutation 'Grace to you and peace from God our Father' echoes the structure of the Aaronic blessing, which couples divine favor ('be gracious') with peace ('give you peace'). Recurrence: peace-from-God greetings pervade Pauline openings, drawing on the priestly benediction available in the LXX. Thematic coherence is real but the volume is faint, since the salutation is a fixed Pauline formula rather than a direct citation.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ' reproduces the Jewish berakah formula 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel,' which closes Book I of the Psalter. Volume is high (verbatim opening 'Blessed be the God'); recurrence across the Psalter (41:13; 72:18; 106:48) and Israel's liturgy makes the form availably and thematically coherent as the native idiom of doxological praise.
sourceText: Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting and to everlasting! Amen and amen.

note: The eulogetos opening directly imitates the doxological berakah 'Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel,' another Psalter book-closing blessing. Recurrence with 41:13 and 106:48 establishes the form as a standing liturgical pattern Paul Christologically reworks ('the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ'). Thematic coherence with the eulogetos genre is exact.
sourceText: Praise be to Yahweh God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds.

note: Melchizedek's 'Blessed be God Most High' is the patriarchal prototype of the berakah Paul deploys. Availability and thematic coherence (blessing the God who delivers and gives) support the link, though the volume is lower than the Psalter parallels, since the verbal overlap is only the opening 'Blessed be God.'
sourceText: and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Abram gave him a tenth of all.

note: 'He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy' transposes Israel's election: 'the LORD has chosen you to be a people for his own possession... holy.' Volume is strong (the verb 'chose' + the purpose 'holy'); recurrence in Deuteronomy's election theology and thematic coherence (gratuitous love, not merit) make this the controlling OT subtext for predestination language.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth. Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, […]

note: 'The LORD has chosen you to be a people for his own possession... a holy people' supplies both the election verb and the 'holy/possession' pairing that Ephesians 1:4 and 1:14 develop. Recurrence with Deut 7:6 reinforces a settled Deuteronomic formula; thematic coherence with adoption and inheritance is high.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God, and Yahweh has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.

note: 'Holy and without defect before him' draws on the Holiness Code's 'You shall be holy, for I... am holy,' and the sacrificial demand that an offering be 'without blemish' (Lev 1:3; 22:21). Thematic coherence (Israel/offering presented blameless to God) is strong; the volume is diffuse because two strands of Levitical holiness merge.
sourceText: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.

note: 'Adoption as children' (huiothesia) presupposes Israel's sonship: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn.' Volume is conceptual rather than verbal, but recurrence (Hos 11:1; Jer 31:9) and thematic coherence with election and inheritance make Israel's adoptive sonship the OT matrix Paul universalizes in Christ.
sourceText: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,

note: 'When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son' ties adoption to redemptive love and election, the same cluster Ephesians 1:4-6 fuses ('in love... adoption'). Recurrence with Exod 4:22 strengthens the sonship motif; the volume is thematic, marked medium because Ephesians does not cite the wording.
sourceText: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.

note: 'The Beloved' (en to egapemeno) evokes Isaac, 'your son, your only son, whom you love,' the beloved offered son — apt for a passage moving toward 'redemption through his blood.' Thematic coherence (beloved son, sacrifice) is good; the volume is moderate because 'Beloved' also draws on Psalm 2 and Isaiah 5 traditions.
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: Isaiah's Song 'for my beloved' (to egapemeno LXX) is one of the LXX loci where ho egapemenos functions almost titularly, a possible reservoir for Ephesians' 'in the Beloved.' Availability is genuine, but volume and thematic coherence are weak here, so the echo is marked low and contested.
sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill.

note: The royal decree 'You are my son; today I have begotten you,' read messianically in Second-Temple Judaism, undergirds the 'Beloved' Son in whom believers are adopted as sons. Recurrence of Psalm 2 in NT sonship texts and thematic coherence (divine sonship grounding adoption) support a medium-confidence echo.
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
