note: Verses 2-3 quote the Decalogue commandment verbatim from the LXX: 'Honor your father and mother, that it may be well with you and that you may live long.' Volume is maximal (explicit citation formula 'which is the first commandment with a promise'). Paul reads the Sinai command as still binding catechesis for Christian households.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.

note: The Deuteronomic recension of the Fifth Commandment is the more exact verbal parallel: it adds 'that it may be well with you' (eu soi genetai), which Eph 6:3 reproduces against Exodus' shorter form. The dual availability of both Decalogue versions explains Paul's conflated wording; Deuteronomy supplies the well-being clause.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.

note: The charge to fathers to 'nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord' (6:4) coheres with the Shema's command to teach the commandments diligently to one's children. The thematic link (paternal catechesis) is strong but verbal contact is faint, so an echo rather than allusion.
sourceText: and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

note: Fatherly 'discipline and instruction of the Lord' (paideia... kyriou, 6:4) echoes the wisdom tradition's language of the Lord's paideia of a son. Recurrence of paideia across Proverbs LXX supports coherence, though no single verse is quoted.
sourceText: My son, don’t despise Yahweh’s discipline, neither be weary of his reproof: for whom Yahweh loves, he reproves; even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.
lxxText: My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loves, he rebukes, and scourges every son whom he receives.

note: The instruction not to 'provoke children to wrath' but to nurture them tempers the wisdom theme of disciplined child-rearing found in Proverbs. The connection is conceptual coherence within the household-instruction tradition, hence a faint, contested echo.
sourceText: One who spares the rod hates his son, but one who loves him is careful to discipline him.

note: Sirach's extended meditation on honoring father and mother, with its promise of long life and atonement, stands in the Second-Temple stream that mediated the Decalogue command into household ethics. Availability (deuterocanon) and thematic coherence are real, but Paul cites the Decalogue directly, so Sirach is background not source.
sourceText: Hear me your father, O my children, And do thereafter, that you may be saved. For the Lord has given the father glory as touching the children, And has confirmed the judgement of the mother as touching the sons. He that honors his father will make atonement for sins: And he that gives glory to his mother is as one that lays up treasure. Whoso honors his father will have joy of his children; And in the day of his prayer he will be heard. He that gives […]

note: The assurance that the heavenly Master shows 'no partiality' (prosopolempsia, 6:9) draws on the LXX formula 'God... does not show partiality' (ou thaumazei prosopon). Volume is high via the distinctive divine-impartiality idiom; Paul applies the courtroom maxim to dissolve master/slave status before God.
sourceText: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.

note: Jehoshaphat's charge to judges grounds impartial justice in the fact that 'with the LORD our God there is no... partiality' (ouk estin... lempsis prosopou). The same theologoumenon underlies 6:9; recurrence of the formula across the OT strengthens coherence, though Deuteronomy is the primary verbal source.
sourceText: Now therefore let the fear of Yahweh be on you. Take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with Yahweh our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes.”

note: Masters told to 'give up threatening' (6:9) coheres with the Holiness Code's prohibition on ruling over a fellow Israelite 'with harshness/rigor,' grounded likewise in fear of God. The ethical shape matches but no verbal quotation occurs, so a faint echo.
sourceText: You shall not rule over him with harshness, but shall fear your God.

note: Job's refusal to despise the case of his servant, because the same God made both master and slave in the womb, anticipates Eph 6:9's leveling of master and slave before their common heavenly Master. Coherence is strong; verbal dependence is absent, so a contested echo.
sourceText: “If I have despised the cause of my male servant or of my female servant, when they contended with me; What then shall I do when God rises up? When he visits, what shall I answer him? Didn’t he who made me in the womb make him? Didn’t one fashion us in the womb?

note: The opening exhortation 'be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might' (6:10) echoes the repeated divine charge to Joshua 'be strong and courageous' (ischye kai andrizou) as he takes the land. The martial 'stand firm' framing of the whole passage coheres with the conquest setting, though the wording is a stock LXX encouragement formula.
sourceText: “Be strong and courageous; for you shall cause this people to inherit the land which I swore to their fathers to give them. Only be strong and very courageous, to observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded you. Don’t turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may […]

note: 'In the strength of his might' (en to kratei tes ischyos autou, 6:10) resonates with Isaiah's promise that those who wait on the Lord 'shall renew their strength.' The verbal contact is thematic (divine strengthening of the weak) rather than lexical, so a faint echo.
sourceText: But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

note: The cosmic conflict 'not against flesh and blood but against the principalities... rulers of the darkness' (6:12) coheres with Daniel's angelic 'princes' (archontes) of Persia and Greece who war in the heavens. Second-Temple angelology of national powers supplies availability; the connection is conceptual, hence a contested echo.
sourceText: But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days; but, behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me: and I remained there with the kings of Persia.

note: The command to 'put on the whole armor of God' (endysasthe... panoplian tou theou, 6:11,13) draws its core image from Isaiah's Divine Warrior who 'put on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation,' and from Wisdom's elaboration of God arming creation. The arming verb endysasthai and the panoply frame derive from this Divine-Warrior tradition before the individual pieces are named.
sourceText: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.

note: Wisdom expands Isaiah 59:17 into a full panoply: the Lord 'will take his zeal as a panoply (panoplian) and arm creation,' donning righteousness as breastplate and impartial judgment as helmet. Paul's distinctive word panoplia and the assembled set of pieces show direct dependence on this Second-Temple development, not Isaiah alone.
sourceText: He will take his jealousy as complete armor, And will make the whole creation his weapons for vengeance on his enemies: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet; He will take holiness as an invincible shield, And he will sharpen stern wrath for a sword: And the world will go forth with him to fight against his insensate foes.

note: 'The belt of truth buckled around your waist' (6:14) draws on the messianic shoot of Jesse who wears 'righteousness as the belt of his waist and faithfulness/truth the belt of his loins.' Volume is high: the girdle imagery and the pairing with truth/righteousness are distinctive to Isaiah 11, and Paul redistributes its terms across belt and breastplate.
sourceText: Righteousness will be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his waist.

note: 'The breastplate of righteousness' (6:14) is a direct lift of the Divine Warrior who 'put on righteousness as a breastplate' (enedysato dikaiosynen hos thoraka). The lexical match (thorax dikaiosynes) is exact, making this a high-volume allusion; the believer is clothed in God's own armor.
sourceText: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.

note: Wisdom's reworking of Isaiah ('he will put on righteousness as a breastplate') is the proximate Second-Temple form Paul knows, reinforcing the breastplate piece. Recurrence of the Isaiah image through Wisdom strengthens coherence even where Isaiah is the ultimate source.
sourceText: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet;

note: 'Feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace' (6:15) alludes to Isaiah's herald, 'how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news... who proclaims peace.' The triad feet + euangelizomenos + peace is distinctive to this verse; the 'shoes' piece evangelizes the warrior's stance.
sourceText: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

note: Nahum 2:1 LXX (1:15 EVV) repeats Isaiah's herald motif: 'behold upon the mountains the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace.' Its near-identical wording strengthens the 'gospel of peace' shoe imagery, though Isaiah 52:7 is the primary source.
sourceText: Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.

note: The 'shield of faith' that quenches 'all the flaming darts of the evil one' (6:16) coheres with the Psalmist's image of God making his arrows into 'flaming/fiery shafts.' The unusual 'flaming darts' (belos pepyromena) motif has its nearest OT background here, though the attacker is reversed; a faint echo.
sourceText: He has also prepared for himself the instruments of death. He makes ready his flaming arrows.

note: The 'shield of faith' (thyreos tes pisteos, 6:16) may evoke the LORD's word to Abram, 'I am your shield,' the foundational pairing of shield and faith (Abram 'believed'). Coherence with the faith motif is suggestive but the lexical contact is generic, so a low-confidence echo.
sourceText: After these things Yahweh’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.”

note: 'Take the helmet of salvation' (perikephalaian tou soteriou, 6:17) is a verbatim borrowing from the Divine Warrior who set 'a helmet of salvation on his head' (perikephalaian soteriou). The exact lexical match makes this among the clearest pieces of Isaianic armor; God's saving victory becomes the believer's headgear.
sourceText: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.

note: Wisdom 5:18 also gives the warrior 'impartial judgment as a helmet,' confirming the Second-Temple currency of the helmet image alongside Isaiah. Recurrence supports coherence though Isaiah supplies the exact 'helmet of salvation.'
sourceText: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet;

note: 'The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God' (6:17) draws on the Servant who says God 'made my mouth like a sharp sword.' The fusion of sword + the spoken word of God is distinctive to this Servant Song; the believer wields the prophetic word as weapon.
sourceText: and he has made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand, he has hidden me: and he has made me a polished shaft; in his quiver has he kept me close:

note: The messianic shoot strikes the earth 'with the rod of his mouth' and slays the wicked 'with the breath (pneumati) of his lips,' joining sword/word with Spirit (pneuma) precisely as Eph 6:17 ('sword of the Spirit... word of God'). The Spirit-word-judgment cluster strengthens the allusion alongside Isaiah 49:2.
sourceText: but with righteousness he will judge the poor, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked.

note: God's killing/hewing of the people 'by the words of my mouth' provides a further prophetic precedent for the word of God as a slaying weapon, supporting the sword image. The contact is thematic recurrence rather than verbal dependence, hence a faint echo.
sourceText: Therefore I have cut them to pieces with the prophets; I killed them with the words of my mouth. Your judgments are like a flash of lightning.

note: 'Praying at all times in the Spirit... in all perseverance' (6:18) coheres with the OT pattern of unceasing, regular prayer exemplified by Daniel's thrice-daily petition. The connection is to a devotional topos rather than a specific text, so a faint echo.
sourceText: When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.

note: The summons to constant 'prayer and requests... at all times' (6:18) resonates with the Psalmist's plea that prayer rise continually like incense. Thematic coherence with perpetual supplication supports a low-confidence, contested echo.
sourceText: Let my prayer be set before you like incense; the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice.

note: Paul's request that 'utterance may be given me in opening my mouth' to make known the mystery with boldness (6:19) echoes the prophetic call in which God opens the prophet's mouth to speak his word. The mouth-opening / divinely given speech motif coheres with prophetic commissioning, though no single verse is quoted.
sourceText: But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall tell them, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: He who hears, let him hear; and he who forbears, let him forbear: for they are a rebellious house.

note: The closing benediction 'Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith... Grace be with all' (6:23-24) stands in the stream of the Aaronic blessing's peace-and-grace formula. The contact is to a liturgical convention rather than a quotation, so a faint, contested echo.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: The salutation 'Grace to you, and peace' may carry the cadence of the Aaronic blessing, whose climax is shalom ('peace'). Volume is faint and the formula is Paul's standard epistolary opening, so coherence with the Numbers benediction is real but diffuse; availability of the priestly blessing in Second-Temple liturgy supports a soft echo, not a citation.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: 'Saints' (hagioi) for the addressed community draws on the OT designation of God's holy/set-apart people (qedoshim), used of the assembly and the heavenly host in psalmody and Daniel. Recurrence across the LXX is high but the term is so naturalized in Paul that any single referent is weak; marked contested.
sourceText: a very awesome God in the council of the holy ones, to be feared above all those who are around him?

note: 'Servants of Jesus Christ' echoes the OT honorific 'servant of the LORD' borne by Moses, Joshua, and the prophets, now transferred to Christ as the divine master. Coherence with Paul's self-designation elsewhere is strong, but volume here is thin and the title is conventional; faint figural transfer.
sourceText: Now after the death of Moses the servant of Yahweh, Yahweh spoke to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses’ servant, saying,

note: 'He who began a good work in you will complete it' rests on the OT confidence that God finishes what he starts: LXX Ps 137:8 'the LORD will accomplish/perfect (epitelesei) on my behalf... do not forsake the works of your hands.' The shared verb-idea of God perfecting his own work, plus the appeal to divine faithfulness, gives real coherence; volume is moderate, so allusion rather than quotation.
sourceText: Yahweh will fulfill that which concerns me; your loving kindness, Yahweh, endures forever. Don’t forsake the works of your own hands.

note: 'The day of Jesus Christ' (also 1:10) christologizes the prophetic 'day of the LORD,' a fixed eschatological topos in Joel, Amos, and Zephaniah. Recurrence of the motif across the prophets and its centrality to Paul's eschatology give strong coherence; the transfer of YHWH's day to Christ is the load-bearing figural move.
sourceText: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: Supplementary witness to the 'day of the LORD' background behind 'the day of Jesus Christ.' Lower than Joel/Amos because the verbal contact is generic; included for recurrence of the motif.
sourceText: The great day of Yahweh is near. It is near, and hurries greatly, the voice of the day of Yahweh. The mighty man cries there bitterly.

note: Paul's longing 'in the tender mercies (splanchna) of Christ Jesus' draws on OT compassion language (rachamim/oiktirmoi) characteristically predicated of God. The affective vocabulary coheres with the divine-mercy tradition, but the Greek splanchna is not the usual LXX term, so the echo is faint.
sourceText: Yahweh is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and of great loving kindness.

note: 'Filled with the fruits of righteousness' draws on the wisdom/prophetic image where righteousness yields fruit: 'the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life.' Coherence with the agricultural righteousness-fruit metaphor is strong and recurrent across wisdom and prophets; volume moderate.
sourceText: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life. He who is wise wins souls.

note: Amos's rhetorical 'you have turned... the fruit of righteousness into wormwood' is a candidate source for the precise phrase 'fruit of righteousness.' The exact word-pair appears here, raising volume, but the contexts differ sharply (judgment vs. blessing), weakening coherence; offered as a contested verbal parallel.
sourceText: Do horses run on the rocky crags? Does one plow there with oxen? But you have turned justice into poison, and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness;

note: The vineyard song where God looks for 'righteousness' as fruit stands behind the broader prophetic expectation of righteous fruit. Thematic coherence is good but verbal contact is indirect; faint echo supporting the fruit-of-righteousness cluster.
sourceText: For the vineyard of Yahweh of Armies is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for justice, but, behold, oppression; for righteousness, but, behold, a cry of distress.

note: 'Sow for yourselves righteousness, reap the fruit of steadfast love' supplies the same sowing/reaping-of-righteousness logic. Recurrence within the prophetic fruit-of-righteousness motif justifies inclusion at low confidence.
sourceText: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.

note: 'Sincere and without offense to the day of Christ' pairs the day-of-the-LORD motif with purity/refining language reminiscent of Malachi's refiner who purifies until offerings are presented in righteousness. The contact is thematic, not verbal; faint.
sourceText: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and refine them as gold and silver; and they shall offer to Yahweh offerings in righteousness.

note: 'The things which happened to me have turned out rather to the progress of the gospel' resonates figurally with Joseph's 'you meant evil... but God meant it for good,' the paradigm of imprisonment turned to providential benefit. Coherence with Paul's providential reading of his chains is suggestive; verbal contact is absent, so this is a contested typological echo.
sourceText: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.

note: 'This will turn out to my salvation' reproduces LXX Job 13:16 verbatim ('touto moi apobesetai eis soterian'). The exact wording, the shared situation of a righteous sufferer confident of vindication before God, and Job's surrounding 'I will not be put to shame' all yield maximal volume and coherence; this is the chapter's one near-citation.
sourceText: This also shall be my salvation, that a godless man shall not come before him.

note: 'My earnest expectation and hope, that I will in no way be put to shame' echoes the recurrent psalmic confidence 'in you I trust, let me not be put to shame' (LXX Ps 24:2-3,20). The shame/hope-in-God vocabulary is dense in the Psalter and coheres tightly with Paul's vindication theme; allusion to the topos rather than one verse.
sourceText: My God, I have trusted in you. Don’t let me be shamed. Don’t let my enemies triumph over me. Yes, no one who waits for you shall be shamed. They shall be shamed who deal treacherously without cause.

note: The Servant's 'I shall not be put to shame... I have set my face like flint' supplies the suffering-yet-unashamed confidence behind Paul's 'I will in no way be disappointed (shamed)... with all boldness.' Coherence with the vindicated-Servant pattern is strong; verbal contact (shame + boldness) is moderate.
sourceText: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.

note: 'Christ will be magnified (megalynthesetai) in my body' echoes the psalmic call to magnify the LORD (LXX Ps 33:4 'megalynate ton kyrion'); Ps 34 also supplies the adjacent 'those who look to him are radiant, never put to shame.' The shared verb of magnifying and the linked shame motif give good coherence; christological transfer of God's magnification to Christ is the figural pivot.
sourceText: Oh magnify Yahweh with me. Let us exalt his name together.

note: 'You are my servant... in whom I will be glorified' undergirds the idea that God/Christ is glorified-magnified in his servant's body and life-or-death faithfulness. Thematic coherence with the Servant being the locus of glorification is good, but verbal contact is faint.
sourceText: and he said to me, “You are my servant; Israel, in whom I will be glorified.”

note: Paul's desire 'to depart and be with Christ' may faintly draw on the OT hope of being taken to be with God, paradigmatically Enoch who 'was not, for God took him,' and the psalmic 'you will receive me to glory' (Ps 73:24). The contact is conceptual; low and contested.
sourceText: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.

note: 'In nothing frightened by the adversaries' resonates with the psalmist's fearlessness before foes ('though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear'). The shared courage-before-enemies posture coheres with Paul's exhortation; verbal contact is generic, so a faint echo.
sourceText: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers came at me to eat up my flesh, even my adversaries and my foes, they stumbled and fell. Though an army should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear. Though war should rise against me, even then I will be confident.

note: Paul's call to do nothing through conceit and to count others better than oneself coheres with the wisdom warning 'Be not wise in your own eyes,' a recurrent sapiential theme of self-abasement. Volume is faint (no shared vocabulary in WEB) and the thought is a commonplace, so this is a contested low-confidence echo of the humility tradition rather than a pointed allusion.
sourceText: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.

note: 'The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself' supplies a Second-Temple Jewish backdrop for Paul's 'in humility each counting others better than himself.' Availability and coherence are strong (Sirach's humility ethic was widely read), but the verbal overlap is thematic rather than lexical, marking this a faint contested echo.
sourceText: The greater you are, humble yourself the more, And you will find favor before the Lord.

note: Christ 'existing in the form of God' (en morphe theou) evokes humanity made in the image/likeness of God, the foundational image-of-God text, setting up the Adam/Christ contrast that runs through the hymn. Coherence is high with Pauline image-of-God theology (cf. 2 Cor 4:4; Col 1:15), though 'form' is not the LXX 'image,' so this remains an allusion of medium volume.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”

note: That Christ 'didn't consider equality with God a thing to be grasped' is widely read as an inverse of Adam and Eve's grasping to 'be like God' at the serpent's prompting. The Adam-Christ antithesis (humility undoing the primal grasp) gives high coherence with Pauline theology; the allusion is conceptual rather than verbal, hence medium confidence and a recognized scholarly debate.
sourceText: for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

note: 'Emptied himself, taking the form of a servant' echoes the Suffering Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and was 'numbered with the transgressors,' the Servant's self-emptying obedience unto death. Volume is strong given the servant/slave (doulos) language plus the death motif, and recurrence is high since the hymn climaxes in an explicit Isaiah citation (45:23), grounding availability and coherence.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: The downward arc 'he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death' sets up the Servant who, though abased, 'shall be exalted and lifted up,' which v.9 then fulfills. The pairing of the Servant's humiliation here and exaltation in 2:9 mirrors Isa 52:13's own movement, giving strong coherence and recurrence within the hymn.
sourceText: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.

note: 'Becoming obedient to death, yes, the death of the cross' resonates with the Servant 'cut off out of the land of the living,' the violent, undeserved death of the righteous sufferer. The echo strengthens the broader Isa 53 matrix already active in the hymn, though the specific 'death' wording is generic, keeping confidence medium.
sourceText: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?

note: The righteous one condemned 'to a shameful death' who tests God's claim coheres with Christ's obedient death on the cross and subsequent vindication. Wisdom 2-5 was available and shares the suffering-then-vindicated righteous pattern, but lexical overlap with Philippians is thin, so this is a faint contested echo.
sourceText: With outrage and torture let us put him to the test, That we may learn his gentleness, And may prove his patience under wrong. Let us condemn him to a shameful death; For he will be visited according to his words.

note: 'That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow... and every tongue should confess' is a direct citation of 'to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear,' a monotheistic oracle of universal homage. Volume is maximal (near-verbatim of the LXX with knee-bow and tongue-confess parallelism), and Paul redeploys the same text in Rom 14:11, giving high recurrence; the staggering move is applying YHWH's exclusive worship to Jesus.
sourceText: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.

note: 'Therefore God also highly exalted him' answers Isa 52:13's promise that the Servant 'shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.' The Greek hyperhypsoo intensifies the LXX's verbs of exaltation, and the Servant frame from 2:7-8 makes this the climactic vindication, yielding strong coherence and volume.
sourceText: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.

note: The confession 'Jesus Christ is Lord' draws its monotheistic force from the surrounding oracle ('there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Savior'), the very context of the quoted 45:23. Including the immediate co-text strengthens availability and coherence, supporting the bold identification of Jesus with the one Lord.
sourceText: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me.

note: 'The name which is above every name' evokes the divine Name revealed to Moses, the ineffable Tetragrammaton/'I AM,' which bowing and confession honor. Coherence is high since the bestowed 'name' that draws universal worship is best read as the divine Name (kyrios = YHWH), though Exodus is not verbally cited, so confidence is medium and the precise referent is debated.
sourceText: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.

note: The cosmic scope 'those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth' resonates with Deutero-Isaiah's Creator who 'formed the earth' and rules all spheres, the universal-sovereignty context of the cited oracle. The three-tier cosmos language is conventional, so this is a faint contested echo bolstering the 45:23 citation's totality.
sourceText: For thus says Yahweh who created the heavens, the God who formed the earth and made it, who established it and didn’t create it a waste, who formed it to be inhabited: “I am Yahweh; and there is no other.

note: 'Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling' echoes 'Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling,' the posture of reverent obedience before God's enthroned king. The phobos kai tromos pairing is a recurrent LXX idiom Paul favors (1 Cor 2:3; 2 Cor 7:15; Eph 6:5), giving coherence; the Psalm 2 royal context coheres with the Lordship theme of 2:9-11, supporting medium confidence.
sourceText: Serve Yahweh with fear, and rejoice with trembling.

note: 'It is God who works in you both to will and to work' faintly recalls Isaiah's confession 'we have... wrought no deliverance in the earth' apart from God, the theme that salvation is God's effective working, not human achievement. The conceptual overlap (God as the one who works salvation) is thin verbally, so this is a low-confidence contested echo.
sourceText: We have been with child. We have been in pain. We gave birth, it seems, only to wind. We have not worked any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen.

note: 'Do all things without murmurings' evokes Israel's wilderness murmuring against the LORD over manna, the paradigmatic rebellion of God's people. The gongysmos word-group is the LXX term for these episodes, and Paul casts the Philippians as a wilderness generation to be unlike, giving coherence and recurrence across the Exodus-Numbers complex.
sourceText: and in the morning, then you shall see Yahweh’s glory; because he hears your murmurings against Yahweh. Who are we, that you murmur against us?” Moses said, “Now Yahweh shall give you meat to eat in the evening, and in the morning bread to satisfy you; because Yahweh hears your murmurings which you murmur against him. And who are we? Your murmurings are not against us, but against Yahweh.” Moses said to Aaron, “Tell all the congregation of the children of […]

note: The congregation that 'murmured against Moses and against Aaron' and was condemned to die in the wilderness models the grumbling Paul forbids, sharpening the contrast with becoming 'blameless children of God.' Recurrence of the murmuring motif (Num 14, 16, 17) and shared gongysmos vocabulary support a medium-confidence allusion.
sourceText: All the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, “We wish that we had died in the land of Egypt, or that we had died in this wilderness!

note: Aaron's rod episode aims to 'make to cease... the murmurings... against me,' reinforcing the wilderness grumbling background of 2:14. The echo is part of the cumulative Numbers murmuring matrix rather than a discrete allusion, hence low confidence.
sourceText: It shall happen, that the rod of the man whom I shall choose shall bud. I will make the murmurings of the children of Israel, which they murmur against you, cease from me.”

note: 'Children of God without defect in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation' lifts the Song of Moses' indictment of Israel as 'a perverse and crooked generation,' but inverts it: the church are now the faithful children. Volume is high (skolios kai diestrammenos plus 'children/not his children' from the same verse), and the Song of Moses is a recurrent NT source, giving strong availability and coherence.
sourceText: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.

note: 'You are seen as lights in the world' draws on the eschatological promise that 'those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament,' the luminous vindication of the faithful at the end. Coherence is high with Paul's 'day of Christ' framing in v.16, and the shining-luminary imagery (phosteres) gives strong volume for an allusion.
sourceText: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: Within the same Song of Moses, God's complaint about 'a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faith' reinforces the 32:5 quotation and the 'children of God' contrast. The echo deepens the Deuteronomy 32 backdrop already active, so it is a low-confidence supporting echo.
sourceText: He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.

note: 'That I didn't run in vain nor labor in vain' resonates with the Servant's lament 'I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing,' the worry of fruitless toil later vindicated by God. The 'in vain' (eis kenon / kenos) labor motif and the Servant context (already active in the hymn) give a faint coherent echo, kept low for thin verbal overlap.
sourceText: But I said, “I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely the justice due to me is with Yahweh, and my reward with my God.”

note: 'If I am poured out on the sacrifice and service of your faith' draws on the cultic drink offering (spende) poured out beside the sacrifice, casting Paul's possible martyrdom as a libation. The spendomai imagery is precise to the tamid libation legislation, and 'sacrifice and service' (thysia, leitourgia) is sacrificial vocabulary, giving medium-to-strong coherence.
sourceText: Its drink offering shall be the fourth part of a hin for the one lamb. You shall pour out a drink offering of strong drink to Yahweh in the holy place.

note: The daily burnt offering's prescribed drink offering of wine poured out supplies the same libation image behind Paul's 'poured out.' Together with Num 28:7 this gives recurrence within the sacrificial-libation tradition, supporting a medium-confidence allusion to the drink offering rite.
sourceText: and with the one lamb a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour mixed with the fourth part of a hin of beaten oil, and the fourth part of a hin of wine for a drink offering.

note: Epaphroditus 'risking his life' (paraboleusamenos te psyche) near to death for the work of Christ faintly recalls the proverb 'skin for skin, all that a man has will he give for his life,' the valuation of life staked in service. The overlap is thematic (life imperiled for a higher cause), not lexical, so this is a faint contested echo.
sourceText: Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will renounce you to your face.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life.”

note: Paul's imperative 'rejoice in the LORD' verbally echoes the Psalter's recurrent summons 'Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, you righteous' (Ps 32:11). The phrase 'in the Lord/in YHWH' as the ground of joy is a Septuagintal idiom; Paul gives it eschatological force in Christ. Recurrence across the Psalms strengthens the resonance.
sourceText: Be glad in Yahweh, and rejoice, you righteous! Shout for joy, all you who are upright in heart!

note: 'Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous' (LXX Ps 32:1) supplies the liturgical pattern Paul reuses. The collocation of 'rejoice' with the divine name as object of joy is distinctively Psalmic and coheres with Philippians' larger joy motif.
sourceText: Rejoice in Yahweh, you righteous! Praise is fitting for the upright.

note: 'Be glad and rejoice in the LORD your God' (Joel 2:23) is a prophetic instance of the same idiom Paul deploys. Faint and one of many possible Septuagintal sources, so marked contested.
sourceText: “Be glad then, you children of Zion, and rejoice in Yahweh, your God; for he gives you the former rain in just measure, and he causes the rain to come down for you, the former rain and the latter rain, as before.

note: Paul's pejorative 'the dogs' inverts the Torah's exclusion of the 'dog' (cult prostitute's wage) from the sanctuary; the unclean outsider epithet is reapplied to Judaizing opponents in a deliberate reversal. Coherence with the circumcision polemic that follows supports the link, though the metaphor is widespread.
sourceText: You shall not bring the hire of a prostitute, or the wages of a male prostitute, into the house of Yahweh your God for any vow; for both of these are an abomination to Yahweh your God.

note: Isaiah's 'dumb dogs' / 'greedy dogs' for faithless watchmen of Israel provides the prophetic stock for Paul's insult against false teachers within the covenant community. The transfer of 'dog' from Gentile to errant Israelite leader matches Paul's polemical reversal.
sourceText: His watchmen are blind, they are all without knowledge; they are all mute dogs, they can’t bark; dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber. Yes, the dogs are greedy, they can never have enough; and these are shepherds who can’t understand: they have all turned to their own way, each one to his gain, from every quarter.

note: 'We are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit' draws on the promise that the LORD will 'circumcise your heart' so you love him. Paul claims this interior, Spirit-wrought circumcision as the believers' true identity over against physical 'mutilation.' High volume and strong coherence with the surrounding argument.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.

note: 'Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, remove the foreskin of your hearts' is the prophetic locus for heart-circumcision that Paul presupposes when he denies 'confidence in the flesh.' The contrast between fleshly and heart circumcision is exactly Paul's antithesis here.
sourceText: Circumcise yourselves to Yahweh, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go out like fire, and burn so that no one can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.

note: Jeremiah threatens to punish those 'circumcised in the flesh' yet 'uncircumcised in heart,' leveling Israel with the nations. Paul's relativizing of fleshly circumcision and elevation of inward worship coheres with this oracle.
sourceText: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will punish all those who are circumcised in uncircumcision: Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that have the corners of their hair cut off, who dwell in the wilderness; for all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart.

note: The covenant curse turns on the 'uncircumcised heart' being humbled; the trope of heart-circumcision as the true requirement undergirds Paul's claim that Spirit-worship, not flesh, marks the covenant people.
sourceText: I also walked contrary to them, and brought them into the land of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled, and they then accept the punishment of their iniquity;

note: Ezekiel bars the 'uncircumcised in heart and flesh' from the sanctuary; Paul reworks the temple-purity logic so that true 'worship' belongs to those circumcised in spirit. Fainter and one of a cluster, so marked contested.
sourceText: Thus says the Lord Yahweh, No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter into my sanctuary, of any foreigners who are among the children of Israel.

note: 'Circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn' is a further Deuteronomic source for the heart-circumcision motif Paul invokes against 'confidence in the flesh.' Recurrence across Deuteronomy and Jeremiah strengthens the whole cluster.
sourceText: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.

note: Isaiah's warning that the 'uncircumcised and unclean' shall no more enter Zion supplies background for Paul's reversal of who constitutes the holy, worshiping community. Faint.
sourceText: Awake, awake, put on your strength, Zion; put on your beautiful garments, Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean.

note: 'Circumcised the eighth day' directly invokes the Abrahamic covenant statute that every male be circumcised at eight days old. Paul cites his impeccable conformity to this Torah marker as the leading item of fleshly 'confidence' he renounces. High volume and verbal precision.
sourceText: He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed.

note: The legal restatement 'on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised' reinforces the same eighth-day statute Paul claims. A secondary witness to the precept behind his pedigree.
sourceText: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.

note: 'Of the tribe of Benjamin' points to Rachel's son Benjamin, named at Genesis 35:18; Paul's tribal claim asserts descent from a fully Israelite, non-proselyte lineage. Identity-marker allusion rather than verbal quotation.
sourceText: As her soul was departing (for she died), she named him Benoni, but his father named him Benjamin.

note: 'Of the stock of Israel' evokes the renaming of Jacob as Israel, the patronym of the chosen people Paul claims as his birthright. Faint background to the ethnic boast.
sourceText: He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.”

note: 'As to zeal, persecuting the church' casts Paul in the line of Phinehas, whose 'zeal' (LXX zelos) for God by violent action averted wrath and won a covenant of priesthood. Paul reads his pre-Christian persecuting as this paradigmatic zeal, now reassessed as loss. Strong thematic coherence; 'zeal' is the operative catchword.
sourceText: “Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I didn’t consume the children of Israel in my jealousy.

note: Elijah's 'I have been very zealous for the LORD' supplies the second exemplar of biblical zeal that frames Paul's self-description as a zealot-persecutor. The Phinehas–Elijah zeal tradition was a live Second-Temple ideal, available to Paul.
sourceText: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

note: Mattathias's deathbed roll names 'Phinehas our father, because he was zealous with great zeal,' the proximate Second-Temple charter for the violent-zeal ideal Paul embodied as persecutor. Availability within the deuterocanon and thematic fit are strong; included as a Maccabean development of the zeal motif.
sourceText: Phinehas our father, for that he was zealous exceedingly, obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.

note: Mattathias acts 'as Phinehas did,' showing 'zeal for the law' expressed in killing apostates — precisely the persecuting zeal Paul claims and renounces. Faint, supplementary to 1 Macc 2:54.
sourceText: And he was zealous for the law, even as Phinehas did to Zimri the son of Salu.

note: The Psalter reckons Phinehas's intervention to him 'as righteousness' forever; Paul's pairing of zealous persecution with 'righteousness in the law, blameless' may trade on this Phinehas-righteousness link. Faint and contested.
sourceText: Then Phinehas stood up, and executed judgment, so the plague was stopped. That was credited to him for righteousness, for all generations to come.

note: 'That I may know him' and the renunciation of every fleshly ground of boasting answers Jeremiah's oracle: let no one boast in wisdom, might, or riches, but only that 'he understands and knows me, the LORD.' Paul transmutes covenant 'knowledge of God' into 'the excellency of the knowledge of Christ.' Strong coherence and Pauline recurrence (cf. 1 Cor 1:31).
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.

note: 'Let us know, let us press on to know the LORD... on the third day he will raise us up' links 'knowing' God to resurrection — exactly Paul's sequence of 'know him and the power of his resurrection.' The verbal pairing of knowledge and rising is distinctive.
sourceText: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him. Let us acknowledge Yahweh. Let us press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.”

note: 'The righteousness which is from God by faith,' set against the law's righteousness, restates Paul's governing text 'the righteous shall live by faith' (cf. Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11). The faith/law antithesis here is the same justification doctrine Habakkuk anchors.
sourceText: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.

note: Righteousness 'from God by faith' rather than 'of my own from the law' is the Abrahamic credo 'he believed the LORD, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness,' Paul's standard proof that righteousness is faith-reckoned, not works-earned. High coherence with Pauline usage.
sourceText: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.

note: 'This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is from me, says the LORD' is a Septuagintal source for a 'righteousness from God' that is gift, not achievement — Paul's exact phrase. Verbal overlap with 'righteousness from God' supports the echo.
sourceText: No weapon that is formed against you will prevail; and you will condemn every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of Yahweh, and their righteousness which is of me,” says Yahweh.

note: 'If by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead' depends on Daniel's promise that 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake,' the principal OT text for bodily resurrection. Paul's hope of out-resurrection presupposes this Danielic apocalyptic frame. High availability and coherence.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: 'Your dead shall live; the dwellers in the dust shall awake and sing' is the prophetic companion to Daniel 12 for resurrection hope, undergirding Paul's 'resurrection from the dead.' Recurrence of the resurrection motif strengthens the link.
sourceText: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

note: The martyrs' confidence that 'the King of the world will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life' is the Second-Temple development of resurrection hope Paul shares. Faint and supplementary to Daniel, so contested.
sourceText: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.

note: The Servant 'set his face' and is vindicated by God who 'justifies' him; Paul's 'fellowship of his sufferings... conformed to his death' followed by resurrection vindication may echo the suffering-then-vindicated Servant pattern. Faint, figural.
sourceText: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed. He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord Yahweh will help me; who is he who shall condemn me? Behold, all they shall wax old as a garment, the moth shall eat them up.

note: 'Pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD' offers a Septuagintal background of pressing/pursuing after a goal that resonates with Paul's 'I press on toward the goal.' Faint, athletic-pursuit imagery is widespread.
sourceText: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from.

note: 'Seek peace and pursue it' supplies the verb of strenuous pursuit Paul reuses in 'I press on/pursue toward the goal.' One of several possible Septuagintal sources for the diolko motif, hence contested.
sourceText: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.

note: 'Whose glory is in their shame' reflects the prophetic reversal 'I will change their glory into shame' (Hos 4:7), where Israel's boast becomes its disgrace. Paul applies the same glory/shame inversion to the enemies of the cross.
sourceText: As they were multiplied, so they sinned against me. I will change their glory into shame.

note: 'You will be filled with shame instead of glory' is a prophetic glory-for-shame exchange that may stand behind Paul's 'their glory is in their shame.' Faint and one of a pair, so contested.
sourceText: You are filled with shame, and not glory. You will also drink, and be exposed! The cup of Yahweh’s right hand will come around to you, and disgrace will cover your glory.

note: 'Whose god is the belly' may echo the wilderness craving where Israel's 'lust' for food provokes judgment, a type of appetite-driven apostasy. Faint thematic figure of the rebellious 'belly.'
sourceText: The mixed multitude that was among them lusted exceedingly: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, “Who will give us flesh to eat?

note: The 'greedy dogs' who 'cannot be satisfied' and seek their own gain anticipate Paul's belly-serving, earthly-minded enemies, tying this verse back to the 'dogs' polemic of 3:2. Faint.
sourceText: Yes, the dogs are greedy, they can never have enough; and these are shepherds who can’t understand: they have all turned to their own way, each one to his gain, from every quarter.

note: The transformation of 'the body of our humiliation' into the likeness of Christ's 'body of glory' draws on Daniel's promise that the wise 'shall shine like the brightness of the firmament... like the stars forever.' Paul's glorified resurrection body realizes this astral glorification. Strong coherence with the resurrection hope of 3:11.
sourceText: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: 'By which he is able even to subject all things to himself' quotes the verbal substance of 'you have put all things under his feet' (Ps 8:6), Paul's standard text for Christ's universal subjection of all things (cf. 1 Cor 15:27). High volume and Pauline recurrence.
sourceText: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:

note: Christ's power to 'subject all things to himself' also resonates with the enthronement oracle 'sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool,' the dominant NT subjection text paired with Ps 8. Recurrence in early Christian use supports the echo.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: The heavenly 'citizenship' and expectation of a transforming Savior may faintly echo Zion-restoration oracles where the LORD comes to clothe and gather his people in glory. Faint and diffuse, so contested.
sourceText: Lift up your eyes all around, and see: all these gather themselves together, and come to you. As I live,” says Yahweh, “you shall surely clothe yourself with them all as with an ornament, and dress yourself with them, like a bride.

note: 'Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you' supplies a glory-transformation backdrop for the bodies of the lowly being conformed to Christ's glory. Faint, supplementary to Daniel 12:3.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you.

note: Paul's calling the Philippians his 'crown' (stephanos) echoes the prophetic image of a crown laid up as a memorial and reward in the temple, and more broadly the OT crown-of-glory motif (Isaiah 28:5; 62:3). Volume is faint and the metaphor is conventional, but coherence with the eschatological reward imagery available in the prophets supports a low-grade echo.
sourceText: The crowns shall be to Helem, and to Tobijah, and to Jedaiah, and to Hen the son of Zephaniah, for a memorial in Yahweh’s temple.

note: 'You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the LORD' supplies the figural background for Paul's 'my joy and crown,' where a redeemed community is the eschatological adornment of its caretaker. Recurrence of the crown-of-glory image across Isaiah (28:5; 62:3) makes it available, though the volume here is low and the trope generic.
sourceText: You shall also be a crown of beauty in the hand of Yahweh, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.

note: The exhortation to 'stand firm in the Lord' draws on the OT contrast between the stable righteous, planted and unmoved, and the chaff-like wicked. Coherence with the steadfastness motif (Psalm 1:3; 112:6) is real, but the volume is faint and 'stand firm' is too diffuse to anchor a single source, so this is a contested echo.
sourceText: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;

note: Paul's claim that his fellow workers' 'names are in the book of life' alludes directly to Moses' plea to be blotted out of 'the book you have written,' the founding OT text of the heavenly register. Volume is high (the explicit book-of-life image), availability is secure in the Torah, and coherence with Paul's confidence in the Philippians' salvation is strong.
sourceText: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”

note: 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not enrolled among the righteous' provides the precise phrase 'book of life/living' that Paul reverses into a positive assurance. High volume on the shared lexeme, strong recurrence of the register motif across the Psalter and prophets, and thematic coherence with the contrast of the saved versus the lost.
sourceText: Let them be blotted out of the book of life, and not be written with the righteous.

note: Daniel's eschatological promise that 'everyone whose name is found written in the book' shall be delivered supplies the apocalyptic deliverance sense Paul gives the image. Availability in Second-Temple apocalyptic and coherence with the resurrection hope of Philippians 3 make this a strong contributor to Paul's 'book of life.'
sourceText: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.

note: 'A book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD' offers the motif of a heavenly ledger recording the faithful by name, coherent with Paul's naming of co-laborers whose names stand recorded. Volume is moderate (remembrance-book rather than 'book of life'), but recurrence within the register tradition supports the link.
sourceText: Then those who feared Yahweh spoke one with another; and Yahweh listened, and heard, and a book of memory was written before him, for those who feared Yahweh, and who honored his name.

note: 'Are they not in your book?' adds another instance of the divine record motif, reinforcing the availability and recurrence of the heavenly-book tradition Paul invokes. Low volume and no shared 'life' lexeme make it a faint contributing echo rather than a primary source.
sourceText: You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren’t they in your book?

note: 'Rejoice in the LORD always' echoes the recurrent Psalter imperative 'Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, you righteous' (32:11; cf. 33:1; 97:12). Recurrence is strong across the Psalter and coherence with Paul's joy theme is high; volume is moderate because Paul universalizes 'always' beyond any single psalm.
sourceText: Be glad in Yahweh, and rejoice, you righteous! Shout for joy, all you who are upright in heart!

note: 'Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous' supplies the same divine-object joy imperative that Paul doubles for emphasis. The Psalter's habitual call to rejoice in the LORD is available and coherent, though the volume of any single verse is moderate given the formula's diffusion.
sourceText: Be glad in Yahweh, you righteous people! Give thanks to his holy Name.

note: 'The Lord is at hand' (ho kyrios engys) most closely matches 'The LORD is near to all who call on him' (engys kyrios), grounding Paul's nearness claim and its link to prayer in v.6. High lexical volume on engys, coherence with the prayer/petition context, and availability in the LXX Psalter make this the strongest source for the phrase.
sourceText: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth.

note: 'The LORD is near to the brokenhearted' reinforces the 'Lord is near' motif with the same engys idiom, and Psalm 34 broadly underwrites Paul's confidence in deliverance. Recurrence of the nearness formula with Psalm 145 strengthens coherence, though volume per verse is moderate.
sourceText: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

note: 'The day of the LORD is at hand/near' supplies the eschatological-imminence sense of 'The Lord is at hand,' if Paul means the Lord's coming rather than his presence. Availability in the prophetic day-of-the-Lord tradition and coherence with Philippians' Parousia hope (3:20) support this, though it competes with the Psalter nearness reading.
sourceText: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests.

note: 'You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you' parallels Paul's 'peace of God which surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts,' linking divine peace, the mind, and protective keeping. Coherence is strong on the guarding-peace-of-the-mind motif; volume is moderate because Paul does not quote the phrasing verbatim.
sourceText: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.

note: 'In peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety' offers the OT pairing of divine peace with security from anxiety that underlies 'do not be anxious... and the peace of God will guard you.' Volume is low and the link thematic, so this is a contributing echo.
sourceText: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety.

note: 'Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you' parallels Paul's remedy for anxiety: hand your requests to God in prayer rather than carry them. Coherence with the anti-anxiety-through-petition logic is strong; volume is moderate since Paul shares the idea, not the wording.
sourceText: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.

note: 'Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad' supplies a wisdom backdrop for Paul's 'in nothing be anxious.' Volume and verbal overlap are slight, but the heart-anxiety theme is available in the sapiential tradition, making this a faint echo.
sourceText: Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad.

note: Paul's virtue catalogue (true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report) draws on the sapiential ideal of the pure heart and gracious speech that wins favor. Recurrence of these virtue terms in Proverbs and the wider Hellenistic-Jewish moral tradition supplies availability, but the volume of any one verse is low.
sourceText: He who loves purity of heart and speaks gracefully is the king’s friend.

note: Wisdom's praise of the cardinal virtues ('she teaches self-control and prudence, justice and courage') models the Hellenistic-Jewish virtue list Paul adapts, especially the terms for 'just' and the framing of virtue (arete) itself, which Paul uses uniquely here. Coherence with the Wisdom tradition's moral catalogues makes this a plausible deuterocanonical source.
sourceText: And if a man loves righteousness, The fruits of wisdom’s labor are virtues, For she teaches soberness and understanding, righteousness and courage; And there is nothing in life for men more profitable than these.

note: 'So you will find favor and good repute (LXX: good things) in the sight of God and man' parallels Paul's 'whatever is of good report' and the appeal to public commendation. Volume is low and the link conceptual, but the good-repute motif is available in the sapiential tradition.
sourceText: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.

note: 'The God of peace will be with you' continues the divine-peace motif of v.7 and resonates with Isaiah's promise that God keeps in peace those whose minds are fixed on him. Volume is faint here and the title 'God of peace' is Paul's own, so this is a low-grade continuation echo of the peace tradition.
sourceText: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.

note: Gideon's altar 'The LORD is peace' (YHWH-shalom) offers an OT antecedent for naming God by his peace, loosely behind Paul's 'the God of peace.' The volume is very low and the connection figural, but it documents the availability of associating God's name with shalom.
sourceText: Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

note: Agur's prayer 'give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful' supplies the wisdom ideal of contentment in either abundance or want that Paul claims to have learned (filled or hungry, abound or be in need). Coherence is strong on the sufficiency-in-any-state theme; volume is moderate since Paul reworks rather than cites.
sourceText: Remove far from me falsehood and lies. Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me; lest I be full, deny you, and say, ‘Who is Yahweh?’ or lest I be poor, and steal, and so dishonor the name of my God.

note: Sirach's counsel to master one's appetites and not be enslaved to want or excess models the disciplined self-sufficiency (autarkeia) Paul describes learning. Availability in the deuterocanonical wisdom tradition and coherence with the 'secret of contentment' make this a credible source for Paul's Stoic-tinged but scripturally rooted contentment.
sourceText: Go not after your lusts; And refrain yourself from your appetites. If you give fully to your soul the delight of her desire, She will make you the laughing stock of your enemies. Make not merry in much luxury; Neither be tied to the expense thereof. Be not made a beggar by banqueting upon borrowing, When you have nothing in your purse.

note: Qoheleth's acceptance of one's lot, finding contentment in whatever portion God gives, parallels Paul's learning 'in whatever state I am, to be content.' Volume is low and verbal overlap slight, but the contentment-with-one's-portion theme is available in the sapiential tradition.
sourceText: Behold, that which I have seen to be good and proper is for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy good in all his labor, in which he labors under the sun, all the days of his life which God has given him; for this is his portion. Every man also to whom God has given riches and wealth, and has given him power to eat of it, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labor—this is the gift of God.

note: 'He gives power to the faint... they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength' grounds Paul's 'I can do all things through him who strengthens me,' where divine empowerment supplies endurance to the weak. Coherence with the strength-from-God-in-weakness theme is strong; volume is moderate because Paul states the principle without quoting.
sourceText: He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might. Even the youths faint and get weary, and the young men utterly fall; But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

note: 'The God who equipped me with strength' (LXX: ho theos ho perizonnuon me dynamin) supplies the divine-empowerment idiom behind 'him who strengthens (endynamounti) me.' Recurrence of God-as-strengthener language across the Psalter (18:1, 32, 39) makes it available and coherent with Paul's claim, though volume per verse is moderate.
sourceText: the God who arms me with strength, and makes my way perfect?

note: 'I will strengthen you, I will help you' adds to the prophetic strengthening tradition Paul draws on for 'who strengthens me.' Volume is low for any single verse, but recurrence of the divine-strengthening promise in Isaiah reinforces availability and coherence.
sourceText: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.

note: 'God, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer's' offers another instance of the LORD as the believer's enabling strength in adversity, coherent with Paul's confidence amid abundance and want. Volume is faint, so this functions as a corroborating echo within the divine-strength tradition.
sourceText: Yahweh, the Lord, is my strength. He makes my feet like deer’s feet, and enables me to go in high places. For the music director, on my stringed instruments.

note: Paul calls the Philippians' gift 'a sweet-smelling fragrance, an acceptable and well-pleasing sacrifice to God,' adopting the cultic formula 'a pleasing aroma, an offering by fire to the LORD' from the sacrificial law. Volume is high on the pleasing-aroma + acceptable-sacrifice language, and coherence is strong as Paul recasts material aid as acceptable cultic offering.
sourceText: You shall burn the whole ram on the altar: it is a burnt offering to Yahweh; it is a pleasant aroma, an offering made by fire to Yahweh.

note: 'The LORD smelled the pleasing aroma' of Noah's offering establishes the foundational 'pleasing aroma' (osme euodias) idiom Paul applies to the Philippians' gift. Availability in the Torah and recurrence of the formula in the sacrificial system make it coherent, though Exodus 29 supplies the fuller 'acceptable' phrasing.
sourceText: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.

note: 'As a pleasing aroma I will accept you' applies the sacrifice formula to persons God receives, paralleling Paul's transfer of cultic acceptability from animal offerings to the gift and givers. Coherence with the figural extension of sacrificial acceptance is strong; volume is moderate as one instance of the recurring aroma motif.
sourceText: As a pleasant aroma will I accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples, and gather you out of the countries in which you have been scattered; and I will be sanctified in you in the sight of the nations.

note: 'A burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD' is the prototypical instance of the formula Paul quotes, reinforcing availability and recurrence of the 'pleasing aroma' sacrificial language across the Levitical code. Volume is moderate; it corroborates Exodus 29 as the cultic backdrop.
sourceText: but its innards and its legs he shall wash with water. The priest shall burn all of it on the altar, for a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.

note: 'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want' underwrites Paul's 'My God will supply every need of yours,' the assurance that God provides so the faithful lack nothing. Coherence with the divine-provision theme is strong; volume is moderate since Paul echoes the concept of no-lack rather than the shepherd image.
sourceText: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.

note: 'Those who seek the LORD lack no good thing... the young lions suffer want, but those who fear the LORD lack nothing' closely parallels 'My God will supply every need of yours.' Recurrence of the no-lack-for-the-faithful promise (with v.18 already echoed above) strengthens coherence; volume is moderate.
sourceText: Oh fear Yahweh, you his saints, for there is no lack with those who fear him. The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger, but those who seek Yahweh shall not lack any good thing.

note: 'No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly' adds to the divine-provision tradition behind Paul's promise that God will supply every need. Volume is low and the link thematic, but recurrence reinforces availability of the God-withholds-no-good-thing motif.
sourceText: For Yahweh God is a sun and a shield. Yahweh will give grace and glory. He withholds no good thing from those who walk blamelessly.

note: Paul's doxology 'to our God and Father be the glory forever and ever, Amen' reproduces the eulogy-plus-'forever'-plus-'Amen' pattern that closes the books of the Psalter ('Blessed be the LORD... forever and ever. Amen and Amen'). Coherence with Jewish berakah doxology is strong; volume is moderate as a formal rather than verbal match.
sourceText: Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting and to everlasting! Amen and amen.

note: 'Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen' supplies the glory-forever-Amen doxological form Paul uses. Volume is low and the form conventional, but the Psalter doxologies are available and coherent with Paul's closing ascription of glory.
sourceText: Blessed be his glorious name forever! Let the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and amen.

note: The closing benediction 'The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you all' echoes the Aaronic blessing's structure of invoking God's grace and presence upon the people ('the LORD be gracious to you... the LORD be with you'). Volume is faint and the formula is a fixed Pauline close, but coherence with the priestly grace-and-presence benediction is real.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: The epistolary blessing 'Grace to you and peace' channels the Aaronic benediction's pairing of divine favor and shalom (the LORD make his face shine... and give you peace). Volume is low and the formula is conventionally Pauline, but the coherence with the priestly grace/peace dyad and its availability in the Torah make it a plausible faint figural backdrop.
sourceText: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: The gospel 'bearing fruit and growing... in all the world' (v.6) replays the creation/Edenic mandate 'be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.' The paired participles fruit-bearing + increasing, set worldwide, deliberately recast the protological blessing as the spread of the word, a Genesis-creation coherence the hymn that follows will make explicit.
sourceText: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”

note: The post-flood renewal of the be-fruitful-and-multiply command (also 9:7) reinforces the Genesis fruitfulness lexeme behind v.6's worldwide growth of the gospel. Recurrence of the same blessing-formula in Genesis strengthens availability; lower volume than 1:28 since the wording is the same mandate repeated.
sourceText: God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, “Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.

note: The 'word of the truth of the gospel' that 'has come to you' and is fruitful in all the world echoes Isaiah's word that goes out from God's mouth and does not return empty but accomplishes and prospers, like rain making the earth bring forth and sprout. Coherence is strong: a divine word personified as agriculturally fruitful and unfailingly effective.
sourceText: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: Jeremiah's promise that the gathered remnant 'shall be fruitful and multiply' fuses the Genesis blessing with restoration hope; Colossians' worldwide fruitful word may stand in this prophetic stream of fruitfulness-as-restoration. Faint and overlapping with the Genesis echoes, hence contested.
sourceText: I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they shall be fruitful and multiply.

note: The motif of 'all the world' / earth filled (here with the fruitful word) faintly recalls Isaiah's eschatological 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea,' which also surfaces in the knowledge-language of v.9-10. Low volume, flagged contested.
sourceText: They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth will be full of the knowledge of Yahweh, as the waters cover the sea.

note: The prayer to be 'filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding' (v.9) draws on the messianic endowment of Isaiah 11:2, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and knowledge. The triad wisdom/understanding/knowledge clusters in both texts, a coherent Spirit-given cognition of God's will.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: Being 'filled with' wisdom and understanding (v.9) echoes Bezalel filled with the Spirit of God 'in wisdom, in understanding, and in knowledge' for the work of the sanctuary. The fullness-of-Spirit-wisdom idiom and the same three faculties make this a strong lexical parallel; availability in Exodus is secure.
sourceText: and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,
