note: Solomon's prayer that Wisdom be sent to teach 'what is pleasing' to God and to guide him to 'walk' rightly parallels v.9-10's prayer for knowledge of God's will so as to 'walk worthily... pleasing him.' The walk/please/wisdom cluster is Wisdom-tradition coherent, though diffuse.
sourceText: And with you is wisdom, which knows your works, And was present when you were making the world, And which understands what is pleasing in your eyes, And what is right according to your commandments. Send her forth out of the holy heavens, And from the throne of your glory bid her come, That being present with me she may toil with me, And that I may learn what is well-pleasing before you. For she knows all things and has understanding thereof, And in my […]

note: The 'inheritance of the saints in light' (v.12) faintly recalls Daniel's promise that the wise will 'rest and stand in your allotted inheritance at the end of days' and shine like the brightness of the firmament (12:3). The lot/inheritance of the holy ones in light is apocalyptic-coherent. Faint, contested.
sourceText: But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.

note: 'The inheritance of the saints in light' (v.12) resonates with Wisdom 5:5, where the righteous are numbered 'among the sons of God' and their 'lot is among the saints/holy ones.' Shared lot-among-the-holy-ones language gives modest coherence with Second-Temple beatific-portion expectation.
sourceText: How was he counted among sons of God? And how is his lot among saints?

note: Being delivered 'out of the power of darkness' and translated into the kingdom (v.13) draws on Isaiah's people walking in darkness who see a great light and the dawning kingdom of the messianic son (9:6-7). Light/darkness reversal plus an established kingdom of a royal son cohere tightly.
sourceText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: 'The kingdom of the Son of his love' (v.13) evokes the royal-adoption oracle 'You are my Son'; with v.15-18's firstborn language it situates Christ in the Davidic sonship of Psalm 2. Volume here is thematic (beloved royal son enthroned over a kingdom) rather than verbal.
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.

note: 'The Son of his love' / the Beloved (v.13) carries the Aqedah resonance of Isaac, 'your son, your only son, whom you love,' a beloved-son figure offered up. Coherence with the redemption-through-death theme that immediately follows (v.14, v.20) strengthens the figural reading of the beloved son.
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: 'Son of his love' (v.13) may faintly echo Isaiah's 'song of my beloved' for the vineyard; the LXX agapetos vocabulary links beloved-son and beloved-vineyard traditions. Low volume and contested against the stronger Psalm 2 / Genesis 22 candidates.
sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill.

note: 'In whom we have our redemption' after being delivered out of the domain of darkness (v.13-14) replays the exodus pattern: God redeems (apolytrosis/lytrosis) Israel out of bondage with an outstretched arm. The deliverance-then-redemption sequence and transfer into God's kingdom map onto the exodus from Egypt's darkness.
sourceText: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:

note: 'Our redemption, the forgiveness of sins' (v.14) resonates with Isaiah's 'I have redeemed you, I have called you by name, you are mine,' and 43:25's blotting out of transgressions. Redemption coupled with forgiveness is a second-exodus motif; volume modest, flagged contested.
sourceText: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine.

note: The 'power of darkness' from which we are delivered (v.13) may glance at the plague of palpable darkness over Egypt that the exodus undoes, reinforcing the deliverance-from-darkness-into-kingdom exodus typology. Faint and contested.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.”

note: 'The image of the invisible God' (v.15) directly invokes the creation of humanity in the image and likeness of God. Christ is presented as the true eikon in whom the protological image is realized, and the hymn's creation framing (v.16) confirms the Genesis 1 backdrop. High volume and coherence.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: 'Image of the invisible God' (v.15) and the fullness/glory motifs draw on Wisdom personified as 'a breath of the power of God,' 'a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty,' 'a spotless mirror... and an image (eikon) of his goodness.' The eikon-of-the-invisible-God predicate is a near-direct Wisdom borrowing.
sourceText: For she is a breath of the power of God, And a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; Therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.

note: 'The firstborn of all creation' who is 'before all things' (v.15,17) recasts Wisdom, whom 'the LORD created/possessed as the beginning (arche) of his way, before his works of old.' The hymn maps Christ onto pre-existent Wisdom as the principle and firstfruit of creation; v.18 even calls him arche.
sourceText: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old.

note: 'For by/in him all things were created' and 'in him all things hold together' (v.16-17) draws on Wisdom present when God established the heavens, the deep, and the foundations, beside him as the agent/craftsman of creation. Wisdom-as-cosmic-mediator coherence is strong across the whole hymn.
sourceText: When he established the heavens, I was there; when he set a circle on the surface of the deep, when he established the clouds above, when the springs of the deep became strong, when he gave to the sea its boundary, that the waters should not violate his commandment, when he marked out the foundations of the earth; then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him,

note: 'The firstborn (prototokos) of all creation' (v.15) and 'firstborn from the dead' (v.18) draw on the Davidic oracle 'I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.' Firstborn as a title of supreme rank and primacy ('that he might be preeminent') matches Psalm 89's royal exaltation exactly.
sourceText: I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.

note: 'By him all things were created, in heaven and on earth' (v.16) is a deliberate restatement of 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth,' with the merism heaven/earth and the verb create binding the hymn to Genesis 1. Christ is the agent through whom the Genesis creation comes to be.
sourceText: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

note: 'By him all things were created... all things have been created through him' (v.16) echoes 'By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth.' Creation-by-the-word coherence supports the Logos/Wisdom agency Colossians ascribes to Christ.
sourceText: By Yahweh’s word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth.

note: 'In him all things hold together' (v.17) parallels Sirach's cosmological 'by his word all things hold together' (en logo autou sygkeitai ta panta), the sustaining of the cosmos by the divine word. The cohesion verb and the all-things object make this a strong Second-Temple sapiential parallel.
sourceText: By reason of him his end has success, And by his word all things consist.

note: 'In him all things hold together' (v.17) resonates with Wisdom's 'the spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which holds all things together (to synechon ta panta) knows every word.' Wisdom as the cosmic glue that fills and binds the universe undergirds the hymn's sustaining-Christ claim.
sourceText: Because the spirit of the Lord has filled the world, And that which holds all things together has knowledge of every voice.

note: 'He is before all things, and in him all things hold together' (v.17) echoes 'Wisdom reaches mightily from one end of the earth to the other, and orders all things well.' Wisdom's pervasive cosmic ordering supports Christ's pre-eminence and sustaining role.
sourceText: But she reaches from one end of the world to the other with full strength, And ordereth all things graciously.

note: 'For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell' (v.19) faintly echoes the mountain that God 'desired for his dwelling,' where the LORD will dwell forever, transferring the chosen-dwelling motif onto Christ as the locus where God is pleased to dwell. Volume low; the eudokia/katoikein dwelling logic is the link.
sourceText: Why do you look in envy, you rugged mountains, at the mountain where God chooses to reign? Yes, Yahweh will dwell there forever.

note: 'All the fullness was pleased to dwell in him' (v.19) draws on the glory (kabod) filling the temple so that it could not be contained, the divine presence taking up bodily dwelling. Christ becomes the new temple in whom the full divine presence indwells; the dwelling/fullness/glory cluster (cf. v.27) coheres.
sourceText: so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for Yahweh’s glory filled Yahweh’s house.

note: 'The fullness was pleased to dwell in him' (v.19) resonates with the LORD's choice of Zion: 'this is my resting place forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it.' The desire/pleasure-to-dwell verb aligns; faint and overlapping with the 1 Kings 8 temple-glory echo.
sourceText: For Yahweh has chosen Zion. He has desired it for his habitation. “This is my resting place forever. Here I will live, for I have desired it.

note: 'To reconcile all things to himself... making peace through the blood of his cross' (v.20) reframes the Day of Atonement reconciliation accomplished by blood. The blood-effecting-reconciliation logic is Levitical; volume low because Colossians universalizes it cosmically rather than cultically.
sourceText: for on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh.

note: 'Making peace through the blood of his cross' (v.20) faintly recalls the Servant whose chastisement brought 'peace' (shalom) and whose wounds bring healing. The peace-through-suffering-death linkage is coherent; flagged contested given the diffuse wording.
sourceText: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.

note: To 'present you holy and without defect/blameless before him' (v.22) borrows the sacrificial standard that an offering must be 'without blemish (amomos) to be accepted.' Believers are presented as a perfected, unblemished cultic offering, the holiness/without-defect language taken directly from the sacrificial code.
sourceText: Whoever offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to Yahweh to accomplish a vow, or for a freewill offering, of the herd or of the flock, it shall be perfect to be accepted. It shall have no defect.

note: 'Without defect and blameless' (v.22) echoes the Passover lamb requirement 'your lamb shall be without blemish.' The amomos qualifier and the presentation-before-God of an acceptable victim cohere with the paschal/sacrificial backdrop, reinforcing the blood-of-the-cross atonement just stated.
sourceText: Your lamb shall be without defect, a male a year old. You shall take it from the sheep, or from the goats:

note: Being presented 'blameless' (amomos/teleios) before God (v.22) faintly recalls the covenant charge 'walk before me and be blameless.' The blameless-walk-before-God ideal coheres with v.10's 'walk worthily,' though the volume is low.
sourceText: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless.

note: 'The mystery (mysterion) which has been hidden for ages... but now has been revealed' (v.26) draws on Daniel's God 'who reveals mysteries' and 'made known what will be in the latter days.' The technical hidden-then-revealed mystery apocalyptic vocabulary derives from Daniel 2 (cf. 2:19,28,47).
sourceText: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:

note: 'The mystery now revealed' (v.26) resonates with Daniel's 'he reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him,' joining the revealed-mystery motif with the light/darkness imagery of v.12-13. Coherent but lower volume than Daniel 2:28.
sourceText: he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.

note: The disclosure of a previously hidden divine plan now 'revealed to his saints' (v.26) faintly echoes 'the Lord God does nothing without revealing his secret (sod) to his servants the prophets.' The hidden-counsel-now-disclosed prophetic motif is coherent though diffuse.
sourceText: Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.

note: The mystery's content 'among the Gentiles' (v.27) resonates with the Servant given 'as a light to the nations' so salvation reaches the ends of the earth. The Gentile-inclusion-as-revealed-glory theme coheres with Colossians' worldwide gospel (v.6,23). Faint, contested.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: 'In all wisdom... that we may present every man perfect (teleios)' (v.28) resonates with Wisdom-tradition pedagogy that leads to maturity/perfection. The teaching-in-wisdom-toward-perfection aim coheres with the sapiential framing of the whole chapter; volume modest.
sourceText: Wisdom is radiant and fades not away; And easily is she saw those who love her, And found of those who seek her. She forestalleth those who desire to know her, making herself first known. He that rises up early to seek her will have no toil, For he will find her sitting at his gates. For to think upon her is perfectness of understanding, And he that watches for her sake will quickly be free from care. Because she goes about, herself seeking those who are […]

note: The treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ closely tracks Proverbs 2, where one cries out for understanding and searches for it as for hidden treasures, and the LORD gives wisdom and knowledge. Volume is high (shared lexis: wisdom, knowledge, hidden, treasure) and the coherence with Paul's epistemology of revelation is strong.
sourceText: Yes, if you call out for discernment, and lift up your voice for understanding; If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures: then you will understand the fear of Yahweh, and find the knowledge of God. For Yahweh gives wisdom. Out of his mouth comes knowledge and understanding.

note: The treasures of darkness and hidden riches given to Cyrus so that he may know the LORD supplies the motif of concealed treasure tied to knowledge of God, matching Paul's 'treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden' that yield the knowledge of God's mystery. Recurrence of the hidden-treasure-leading-to-knowledge pattern supports the echo.
sourceText: I will give you the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that you may know that it is I, Yahweh, who call you by your name, even the God of Israel.

note: Daniel's hymn praises God who reveals deep and hidden things, gives wisdom and knowledge, and discloses mysteries; Paul's 'mystery of God' in whom are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge draws on this apocalyptic vocabulary where mystery, revelation, wisdom, and knowledge cluster (Daniel 2:28-30, 47). The Second-Temple availability and shared mystery-language ground the link.
sourceText: Daniel answered, Blessed be the name of God forever and ever; for wisdom and might are his. He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him. I thank you, and praise you, you God of my fathers, who have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known […]

note: Ben Sira's saying that in the treasuries of wisdom are parables of knowledge offers a near-verbal Second-Temple parallel to 'treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden.' Availability and shared sapiential idiom make this a plausible faint echo, though contested given the diffuse wisdom topos.
sourceText: A parable of knowledge is in the treasures of wisdom; But godliness is an abomination to a sinner.

note: The messianic Spirit of wisdom and knowledge resting on the shoot of Jesse may stand behind Christ as the one in whom wisdom and knowledge are concentrated; the coherence with Paul's Christ-as-locus-of-wisdom is suggestive but the verbal volume is thin.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: The warning against being deluded by persuasiveness of speech recalls the seductress of Proverbs 7 who with much fair speech caused him to yield; the wisdom motif of smooth/persuasive words leading astray is shared. Faint and contested given the commonplace.
sourceText: With persuasive words, she led him astray. With the flattering of her lips, she seduced him.

note: 'After the tradition of men' (and the precepts of men in v.22) echoes Isaiah's indictment that the people's fear of God is a commandment of men taught by rote, the locus classicus for human tradition supplanting God's word. Recurrence within the chapter (v.22) and coherence with the polemic against the 'philosophy' strengthen the allusion.
sourceText: The Lord said, “Because this people draws near with their mouth and with their lips to honor me, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught;
lxxText: And the Lord has said, This people draw nigh to me with their mouth, and they honour me with their lips, but their heart is far from me: but in vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men.

note: The customs of the peoples are vain/futile in Jeremiah 10 supplies the language of 'vain deceit' rooted in worthless human practice and false worship of created things, coherent with 'elements of the world' as enslaving cosmic powers. Volume is moderate via the LXX 'vain' vocabulary.
sourceText: For the customs of the peoples are vanity; for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman with the ax.

note: Being 'rooted and built up' and 'established' draws on the planted-tree imagery of the righteous in Psalm 1 (and Jeremiah 17:8), a stock figure for stability through walking rightly. Coherence with 'walk in him' supports a faint echo.
sourceText: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.

note: The man planted by water whose roots reach the stream parallels Paul's horticultural metaphor 'rooted... abounding,' reinforcing the OT trope of the rooted and fruitful righteous. Faint and contested.
sourceText: For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and shall not fear when heat comes, but its leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.

note: That 'the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily' in Christ recasts the OT theme of God choosing to dwell on the mountain/sanctuary where the LORD will abide forever; Christ becomes the true locus of divine indwelling. The figural transfer of dwelling-glory is coherent though verbally faint.
sourceText: Why do you look in envy, you rugged mountains, at the mountain where God chooses to reign? Yes, Yahweh will dwell there forever.

note: The temple vision where the whole earth is full of the LORD's glory underlies the language of divine 'fullness' now resident bodily in Christ; the fullness/glory motif coheres with Colossians 1:19 and the indwelling theme. Contested and diffuse.
sourceText: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”

note: Circumcision 'not made with hands' in 'the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh' draws directly on Deuteronomy's promise that the LORD will circumcise the heart so you will love him and live, the foundational text for an internal, divinely-wrought circumcision. Volume, coherence, and recurrence in the heart-circumcision tradition are all strong.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.

note: The command to circumcise yourselves to the LORD and remove the foreskin of the heart provides the prophetic call to true (inward) circumcision over against fleshly circumcision, exactly the antithesis Paul presses. Strong coherence with v.11's contrast between hand-made and Christ's circumcision.
sourceText: Circumcise yourselves to Yahweh, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go out like fire, and burn so that no one can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.

note: Circumcise the foreskin of your heart and be no longer stiff-necked supplies the same heart-circumcision idiom; its recurrence alongside Deut 30:6 and Jer 4:4 confirms a stable tradition standing behind Paul's spiritualized circumcision.
sourceText: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.

note: Ezekiel's denunciation of the uncircumcised in heart and flesh entering the sanctuary supplies the paired heart/flesh circumcision categories Paul deploys ('uncircumcision of your flesh', v.13). The shared dual idiom supports the echo, though it is less verbally direct.
sourceText: in that you have brought in foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary, to profane it, even my house, when you offer my bread, the fat and the blood, and they have broken my covenant, to add to all your abominations. You have not performed the duty of my holy things; but you have set performers of my duty in my sanctuary for yourselves. Thus says the Lord Yahweh, No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and […]

note: The institution of circumcision in the flesh as the covenant sign is the background Paul transcends with 'circumcision not made with hands'; the polemical contrast presupposes the Abrahamic rite. Coherence is high but it is presupposed background rather than a quoted echo.
sourceText: You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you.

note: Being 'made alive together with him' while dead in trespasses resonates with Ezekiel's vision of God opening graves and putting his Spirit in the dead so they live; the death-to-life raising motif coheres with vv.12-13's burial-and-resurrection. Faint and contested.
sourceText: Therefore prophesy, and tell them, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people; and I will bring you into the land of Israel. note: God 'wiping out the handwriting' and forgiving all trespasses echoes Isaiah's 'I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake,' the divine erasure of the record of sin. The blotting-out vocabulary and forgiveness theme give moderate volume and strong coherence.
sourceText: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.

note: The plea to blot out my transgressions according to your mercy supplies the same image of erasing the written debt of sin that stands against the sinner. Coherent but diffuse, hence a faint echo.
sourceText: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.

note: The disarming and public shaming of the powers while bearing sin to the cross may draw on the Servant who was numbered with transgressors yet divided the spoil with the strong, a victory-through-suffering pattern. The triumph-out-of-humiliation coherence is real but the verbal link is thin and contested.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: The peg/nail fastened in a sure place that is then cut down and the burden hung on it falls, in Isaiah 22, offers a faint backdrop to 'nailing it to the cross'; the imagery of fastening a burden to a peg coheres loosely. Highly contested.

I will break the doors of brass in pieces, and cut apart the bars of iron.

note: The Song of the Sea celebrating the LORD as warrior who shatters the enemy in triumph supplies the archetype of God's public victory parade over hostile powers that Paul reapplies to the cross ('made a show of them openly, triumphing'). Coherent but figural and faint.

sourceText: You have ascended on high. You have led away captives. You have received gifts among men, yes, among the rebellious also, that Yah God might dwell there.

High verbal volume in the same ordered list and coherence with Paul relativizing the festal calendar make this the primary source.
sourceText: I will also cause all her celebrations to cease: her feasts, her new moons, her Sabbaths, and all her solemn assemblies.

note: The prince's obligation at 'the feasts, the new moons, and the sabbaths' lists the same three calendrical categories Paul names, confirming a stock OT triad of appointed times. Recurrence across Hosea, Ezekiel, and Chronicles strengthens the allusion.
sourceText: It shall be the prince’s part to give the burnt offerings, and the meal offerings, and the drink offerings, in the feasts, and on the new moons, and on the Sabbaths, in all the appointed feasts of the house of Israel: he shall prepare the sin offering, and the meal offering, and the burnt offering, and the peace offerings, to make atonement for the house of Israel.

note: Offerings on 'the sabbaths, the new moons, and the set feasts' gives the same three-term cultic calendar, part of the recurring biblical formula that Paul's 'feast, new moon, sabbath' draws on. Moderate volume via the fixed triad.
sourceText: and to offer all burnt offerings to Yahweh, on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and on the set feasts, in number according to the ordinance concerning them, continually before Yahweh;

note: The festal legislation prescribing offerings for the daily, sabbath, new-moon, and appointed-feast cycle, together with their associated food and drink offerings, undergirds Paul's pairing of 'eating, or drinking' with 'feast, new moon, sabbath.' The food-and-drink plus calendar coherence supports the allusion.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Command the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘See that you present my offering, my food for my offerings made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to me, in their due season.’ You shall tell them, ‘This is the offering made by fire which you shall offer to Yahweh: male lambs a year old without defect, two day by day, for a continual burnt offering. note: That these observances are 'a shadow of the things to come' but the body is Christ's draws on the type/copy logic; while the wording 'shadow' (Exodus 25:40's pattern tradition) is the better backdrop, the prophetic theme of the present cult as provisional resonates faintly. Contested.

note: The command to make the tabernacle after the pattern shown on the mountain founds the OT copy/shadow-versus-true-reality schema that Paul invokes with 'a shadow of the things to come, but the body is Christ's.' Coherence with the type/antitype theology is strong though the lexical contact is indirect.
sourceText: See that you make them after their pattern, which has been shown to you on the mountain.

note: The dietary laws governing clean/unclean 'eating' stand behind the food-judgments Paul forbids others to impose; the broader Levitical kashrut backdrop coheres with 'judge you in eating, or in drinking.' Faint, presupposed background.

note: The 'worshiping of the angels' and 'dwelling in the things which he has not seen' may engage the apocalyptic vision world of myriads of angelic attendants around the throne (Daniel 7), against which Paul polemicizes excessive angel-veneration. sourceText: A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.

note: The visionary 'dwelling in the things which he has not seen' evokes merkavah/throne-vision speculation such as Ezekiel's chariot vision that fed Second-Temple angelology; Paul critiques those who enter such visions and so worship angels. Faint, contested.

note: Enoch's heavenly ascent and vision of angelic hosts before the throne typifies the visionary, angel-focused piety Paul opposes ('worshiping of the angels... things which he has not seen'). Pseudepigraphal availability warrants noting the milieu, but the link is general and contested.

High verbal volume and recurrence (cf. v.8) make this a near-quotation.

sourceText: Of their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch; they are unclean to you.

note: 'Touch no unclean thing' offers a purity-touch idiom standing behind the ascetic 'do not touch' rule Paul deflates as mere 'severity to the body.' Coherent with the food/purity theme but verbally faint and contested.
sourceText: Depart, depart, go out from there, touch no unclean thing! Go out of the midst of her! Cleanse yourselves, you who bear the vessels of Yahweh.

note: "Where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God" verbally echoes the LXX of Ps 110:1 ("Sit at my right hand"), the most-cited OT verse in the NT. High volume of distinctive language (right hand, seated, exaltation) and strong recurrence make the session at God's right hand the dominant figure for the exalted Christ. Coherence with Colossians' cosmic Christology is exact.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: The exalted Christ glorified and revealed in heavenly session may faintly invoke Daniel's Son of Man given dominion and glory before the Ancient of Days. Low volume since no distinctive vocabulary is reproduced; the echo rests on the shared schema of heavenly enthronement and future revelation "in glory" (v.4).
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: "Your life is hidden with Christ in God" coheres with the psalmist's hope that God is his portion and will receive him to glory, the hidden security of life bound to God. Faint and contested; rests on thematic coherence (hiddenness, glory, God as the believer's life) rather than verbal contact.
sourceText: You will guide me with your counsel, and afterward receive me to glory. Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

note: "Evil desire" and the inventory of corrupt members recall the prophetic-Pentateuchal diagnosis that the inclination of the human heart is only evil continually. Faint; the vice list is a Hellenistic-Jewish form and contact is conceptual (the earthly members, depraved passion) rather than lexical.
sourceText: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.

note: "Covetousness, which is idolatry" presupposes the Decalogue's prohibition of coveting, the climactic command that exposes disordered desire. The identification of greed with idolatry draws on Israel's covenant logic where craving what is not one's own is functionally false worship; coherent with Second-Temple Jewish moralizing of pleonexia.
sourceText: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”

note: Naming covetousness "idolatry" invokes the first commandment's exclusive worship and the prohibition of other gods. The equation of greed with idol-service is a recurring Second-Temple move (cf. Testament traditions) grounded in the Decalogue's opening; coheres with the wrath-of-God indictment that follows.

sourceText: Remember, and don’t forget, how you provoked Yahweh your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day that you left the land of Egypt, until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against Yahweh.

note: Linking sexual immorality and idolatry, followed by divine wrath, echoes the Baal-Peor episode where harlotry with Moab and idol-worship together kindle God's anger. Faint; contact is the recurrent OT pairing of porneia with idolatry under wrath rather than verbal citation.

sourceText: “‘You shall not steal. “‘You shall not lie. “‘You shall not deceive one another.

note: "The new man, being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator" directly reworks the creation of humanity in God's image. High volume (image, Creator, the making of man) and exact coherence: the new self is re-creation according to the imago Dei, recapitulating Gen 1. Availability and recurrence in Pauline new-creation theology are strong.

note: "After the image of his Creator" also resonates with the toledot statement that God made man in his likeness, the verse that reasserts the image after the fall. Supports the renewal-of-the-image reading; medium because Gen 1:26-27 is the primary lexical source and 5:1 is the secondary, reinforcing one.
