sourceText: Give thanks to Yahweh! Call on his name! Make his doings known among the peoples.

note: "Wives, be in subjection to your husbands" may invoke the post-fall ordering of the woman to her husband. Low/contested; the household-code form is shared with Hellenistic moral philosophy, so direct dependence on Gen 3:16 is uncertain.
sourceText: To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. In pain you will bear children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

note: "Children, obey your parents in all things, for this pleases the Lord" rests on the Decalogue's command to honor father and mother. Medium coherence; obedience-to-parents framed as pleasing God draws directly on the fifth commandment, the one OT command structuring filial duty.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.

note: The Deuteronomic recension of "honor your father and mother" equally underlies the children's clause and its promise of well-being. Reinforces the Exod 20:12 link; the obey-and-it-goes-well-with-you logic coheres with "for this pleases the Lord."
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.

note: "Fathers, don't provoke your children" tempers the wisdom tradition of paternal discipline; the inversion presupposes Proverbs' instruction on raising children. Faint; contact is conceptual (the father-child formation theme) rather than a cited proverb.
sourceText: Don’t withhold correction from a child. If you punish him with the rod, he will not die. Punish him with the rod, and save his soul from Sheol.

note: "There is no partiality" reproduces the Deuteronomic confession that God is not partial and takes no bribe, the OT root of the no-respect-of-persons formula. High coherence: divine impartiality grounds the just recompense of the wrongdoer (v.25); strong recurrence of this attribute across the law and prophets.
sourceText: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.

note: Jehoshaphat's charge that with the LORD there is no injustice, partiality, or bribe-taking reinforces "there is no partiality." Medium/supporting; Deut 10:17 is the controlling text, with 2 Chr 19:7 a recurrence applying impartiality to just judgment, exactly the context here.
sourceText: Now therefore let the fear of Yahweh be on you. Take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with Yahweh our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes.”

note: "He who does wrong will receive again for the wrong he has done" tracks the wisdom maxim that God repays each according to his deeds. Medium coherence; the recompense formula (rendering to a man according to his work) is the OT principle behind both the servant's reward (v.24) and the wrongdoer's payback.
sourceText: If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this”; doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not render to every man according to his work?

note: "You render to each according to his work" supplies the same recompense principle informing v.25's repayment of the wrongdoer. Reinforces Prov 24:12; the recurrence of "render according to works" across psalm and proverb shows an available, well-attested formula.
sourceText: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.

note: The address to servants and masters with assurance of just recompense faintly recalls Deuteronomy's protection of the hired servant and his wages before God. Low/contested; thematic coherence (labor, fair reward, God as guarantor) without verbal citation.
sourceText: You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates. In his day you shall give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down on it; for he is poor, and sets his heart on it; lest he cry against you to Yahweh, and it be sin to you.

note: Masters must treat slaves 'justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven' — the appeal grounds earthly authority in the impartial heavenly Judge. Deut 10:17 names God as 'God of gods and Lord of lords' who 'is not partial and takes no bribe,' the standard text for divine impartiality that levels the master/slave relation. Volume is high on the theme of God showing no partiality; coherence is strong with Paul's recurring 'no partiality' (Eph 6:9 reflex) rooted in this OT motif.
sourceText: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.

note: The command that masters render what is 'just and equal' echoes the Holiness Code's restraint on slaveholders: 'You shall not rule over him with rigor, but shall fear your God.' Both texts curb the master's power by invoking the fear of the divine Lord. The Jubilee slave legislation (Lev 25) is the most concrete OT availability for an ethic of fair treatment tied to God's overlordship.
sourceText: You shall not rule over him with harshness, but shall fear your God.

note: Job's defense of justice toward his servants — 'Did not he who made me in the womb make him?' — grounds fair treatment in a shared Maker and a final reckoning before God, matching the logic of a heavenly Master who judges masters. Faint and thematic rather than verbal; flagged contested because the link is conceptual coherence, not citation.
sourceText: “If I have despised the cause of my male servant or of my female servant, when they contended with me; What then shall I do when God rises up? When he visits, what shall I answer him? Didn’t he who made me in the womb make him? Didn’t one fashion us in the womb?

note: 'Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful' may draw on the watchman motif: Isaiah's watchmen 'all the day and all the night... shall never be silent,' giving God no rest until Zion is established. The image of unceasing, vigilant intercession coheres with Paul's call to persevere wakefully in prayer. Verbal contact is faint, so marked contested.
sourceText: I have set watchmen on your walls, Jerusalem; they shall never hold their peace day nor night: you who call on Yahweh, take no rest,

note: The prayer for an open door 'to speak the mystery (mystērion) of Christ' picks up the apocalyptic vocabulary of Daniel 2, where 'there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries' and discloses hidden things. Daniel LXX is the principal Second-Temple source for mystērion as divine secret now unveiled, coherent with Paul's 'mystery' language throughout Colossians. Conceptual rather than quotational.
sourceText: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:

note: 'Let your speech... be gracious, seasoned with salt' evokes the 'covenant of salt' required on every grain offering: 'with all your offerings you shall offer salt.' Salt as a sign of permanence, fidelity, and covenant fellowship gives the metaphor of salted speech its OT depth. Volume is moderate and coherence good, since salt elsewhere figures preservation and bond (cf. the next entries).
sourceText: Every offering of your meal offering you shall season with salt; neither shall you allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be lacking from your meal offering. With all your offerings you shall offer salt.

note: Reinforces the 'covenant of salt' background for 'seasoned with salt' — 'a covenant of salt forever before the LORD.' Salt symbolizes an inviolable, perpetual bond, fitting speech meant to build and preserve relationship with outsiders. Faint, recurrence-based support for the Lev 2:13 allusion rather than an independent source.
sourceText: All the wave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer to Yahweh, have I given you, and your sons and your daughters with you, as a portion forever. It is a covenant of salt forever before Yahweh to you and to your seed with you.”

note: 'We eat the salt of the palace' uses salt as a figure of loyalty and shared allegiance, a Near-Eastern idiom that may color the social sense of 'speech seasoned with salt' toward outsiders. Very faint and contested; offered only for the recurrence of salt-as-fidelity imagery in the OT.
sourceText: Now because we eat the salt of the palace, and it is not appropriate for us to see the king’s dishonor, therefore have we sent and informed the king;

note: 'Making the best use of the time' (exagorazomenoi ton kairon, 'redeeming the time') resembles the idiom in Daniel 2:8 LXX, where the king says the magi are 'buying time' (kairon... exagorazete). The shared kairos-redemption phrasing toward 'those outside' suggests a possible verbal echo, though the sense differs and the link is contested.
sourceText: The king answered, I know of a certainty that you would gain time, because you see the thing is gone from me.

note: The counsel to 'walk in wisdom toward outsiders' with speech that is gracious and apt to answer each one reflects the wisdom tradition's prizing of gracious, well-timed speech: 'he who loves purity of heart and whose speech is gracious will have the king as his friend.' Sapiential coherence is strong as a milieu, but no single proverb is quoted; faint and contested.
sourceText: He who loves purity of heart and speaks gracefully is the king’s friend.

note: Paul's epistolary 'Grace to you and peace' fuses a Greek salutation with the Hebrew shalom; the doubled blessing of grace/favor and peace recalls the Aaronic benediction where YHWH makes his face shine (grace) and gives peace. Volume is low and the wording is Pauline convention, so the echo is faint, but Availability and Coherence with a Jewish blessing idiom support a thin resonance.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: The triad work-of-faith, labor-of-love, and 'patience (endurance) of hope' before God resonates with Isaiah's posture of waiting for YHWH's name in the path of his judgments, the soul's desire and hope. The conceptual overlap (steadfast hope directed toward God) is real but the verbal volume is minimal, so this is a contested coherence-driven echo.
sourceText: Yes, in the way of your judgments, Yahweh, have we waited for you. Your name and your renown are the desire of our soul.

note: 'Brothers loved by God, that you are chosen' transposes Israel's covenant election directly: Deuteronomy says YHWH chose Israel not for their merit but because he loved them (agapan/eklegesthai LXX), the exact pairing of divine love and choosing Paul applies to gentile believers. Volume and Coherence are strong, and Recurrence of the election theme through 1 Thess makes this a programmatic allusion.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth. Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, […]

note: 'Blessed is the nation whose God is YHWH, the people he has chosen for his own inheritance' supplies the same election idiom Paul extends to the Thessalonian assembly. The LXX exelexato matches Paul's vocabulary of being chosen; Volume is moderate and the allusion reinforces the Deuteronomic election frame.
sourceText: Blessed is the nation whose God is Yahweh, the people whom he has chosen for his own inheritance.

note: 'Beloved of YHWH' (Benjamin) as a covenant epithet underlies Paul's address 'brothers loved by God.' The phrase is a stock Septuagintal way of naming the elect community; faint by itself but coherent with the surrounding election language.
sourceText: About Benjamin he said, “The beloved of Yahweh will dwell in safety by him. He covers him all day long. He dwells between his shoulders.”

note: 'Israel my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, offspring of Abraham my beloved... I have chosen you and not cast you off' clusters chosenness and divine love exactly as Paul does. The dense overlap of election + beloved makes this a plausible secondary source alongside Deuteronomy 7.
sourceText: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend, You whom I have taken hold of from the ends of the earth, and called from its corners, and said to you, ‘You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you away;’

note: The gospel coming 'not in word only, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit' echoes the Spirit-anointed proclamation of good news (the LXX euangelisasthai with the Spirit of the Lord upon the herald). Coherence with Paul's evangel-in-Spirit is strong; verbal volume is moderate, supporting an echo of the Isaianic herald.
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

note: 'I am full of power by the Spirit of YHWH' pairs power and Spirit as the equipment of true proclamation, the same coupling Paul uses to validate his preaching against mere word. The dyad is suggestive but the link is contested given how common power/Spirit language is.
sourceText: But as for me, I am full of power by the Spirit of Yahweh, and of judgment, and of might, to declare to Jacob his disobedience, and to Israel his sin.

note: 'Received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit' resonates with the prophetic motif of drawing joy from God amid distress (e.g., joy from the wells of salvation). The eschatological-Spirit joy-in-affliction pattern is broadly Septuagintal; volume is low, so this is a faint coherence echo.
sourceText: Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation.

note: 'From you the word of the Lord has been declared... in every place' echoes the Zion oracle in which the word of YHWH goes forth from Jerusalem to the nations. Paul recasts the believing community as a new radiating center for the logos kyriou; Coherence with the mission-of-the-word theme is strong though the geography is reapplied.
sourceText: Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.

note: YHWH's word that 'goes out' from his mouth and does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose underlies the image of the word of the Lord sounding forth and bearing fruit everywhere. The 'going out' verb and effectual-word theology cohere, but the verbal contact is modest.
sourceText: so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: 'Their voice has gone out into all the earth' is the classic text for a proclamation diffusing universally (cited at Romans 10:18). The 'gone out into every place' phrasing of Paul's report shares this diffusion imagery; faint but availability and coherence warrant noting.
sourceText: Their voice has gone out through all the earth, their words to the end of the world. In them he has set a tent for the sun,

note: 'In every place' offerings are made to YHWH's name 'from the rising of the sun to its setting' supplies the universalizing 'in every place' formula Paul uses for the spread of faith toward God. The phrase is a Septuagintal marker of the name's worldwide honor; contested given its commonness.
sourceText: For from the rising of the sun even to the going down of the same, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the nations,” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'A living and true God' set against 'idols' renders Jeremiah's contrast: 'YHWH is the true God; he is the living God' over against the worthless idols of the nations. Jeremiah 10 is the locus classicus of the idol-polemic Paul compresses; Volume, Coherence, and the living/true pairing make this a strong allusion.
sourceText: But Yahweh is the true God; he is the living God, and an everlasting King: at his wrath the earth trembles, and the nations are not able to withstand his indignation.

note: 'You turned to God from idols' draws on the satire of manufactured idols (silver and gold, the work of human hands, with mouths that cannot speak) versus the living God. The turning-from-idols-to-serve-God movement is the Psalm's polemic inverted into conversion language; high coherence and strong Septuagintal availability.
sourceText: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.

note: Isaiah's extended mockery of idol-makers who fashion lifeless gods is the deutero-Isaianic counterpart Paul presupposes in 'turned to God from idols.' The dead-idols vs. living-God antithesis is the engine of the verse; Recurrence of this polemic across Second-Temple Judaism strengthens the allusion.
sourceText: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]

note: Darius's decree that all should fear 'the living God... who endures forever' supplies the 'living God' confession that gentiles are summoned to serve. The phrase 'living God' is the verbal anchor; Daniel's gentile-king acknowledgment coheres with Paul's report of gentile turning to the living and true God.
sourceText: I make a decree, that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel; for he is the living God, and steadfast forever, His kingdom that which shall not be destroyed; and his dominion shall be even to the end.

note: 'To serve a living and true God' picks up the Shema-context command to fear YHWH and serve (latreuein) him only, the exclusive-service demand that idolatry violates. The Deuteronomic 'serve him alone' is the positive correlate of turning from idols; coherence is strong, volume moderate.
sourceText: You shall fear Yahweh your God; and you shall serve him, and shall swear by his name.

note: 'For a long time Israel was without the true God' uses the precise phrase 'true God' that Paul applies to the object of conversion. A faint but genuine Septuagintal source for 'true God' alongside Jeremiah 10.
sourceText: Now for a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law.

note: 'The wrath to come' from which Jesus delivers draws on the Day of YHWH as 'a day of wrath' (the orge of the Lord); Zephaniah 1:15,18 is the densest concentration of day-of-wrath language Paul presupposes for the coming eschatological judgment. Coherence with Pauline orge and Recurrence of the wrath motif in 1 Thess (2:16; 5:9) make this a primary allusion.
sourceText: That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,

note: 'In the day of YHWH's wrath... the whole earth shall be consumed' supplies the universal, future, fiery character of 'the wrath to come.' Reinforces 1:15 as the Day-of-the-Lord matrix from which deliverance is needed.
sourceText: Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them in the day of Yahweh’s wrath, but the whole land will be devoured by the fire of his jealousy; for he will make an end, yes, a terrible end, of all those who dwell in the land.

note: 'The day of YHWH is great and very terrible; who can endure it?' frames the coming wrath as the dreadful Day from which one must be rescued. Joel's rhetorical question about enduring the Day undergirds Paul's promise that Jesus 'delivers us'; coherence is strong, verbal volume moderate.
sourceText: Yahweh thunders his voice before his army; for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of Yahweh is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?

note: 'The day of YHWH comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the earth a desolation' is a paradigmatic Day-of-wrath oracle feeding Paul's 'wrath to come.' The eschatological orge directed at the nations coheres with the deliverance of believers; a solid secondary source for the wrath motif.
sourceText: Behold, the day of Yahweh comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger; to make the land a desolation, and to destroy its sinners out of it.

note: 'Who can endure the day of his coming?' couples the coming (the One who comes) with refining judgment, resonating with waiting for the Son who delivers from the coming wrath. The 'who can endure' topos and the link of advent + judgment make this a coherent echo within the Day-of-the-Lord cluster.
sourceText: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap;

note: 'Hide yourselves... until the wrath (orge) is past, for YHWH comes out to punish' offers the motif of being sheltered from passing wrath, paralleling deliverance 'from the wrath to come.' Faint verbal contact but apt coherence with rescue-from-wrath; contested.
sourceText: Come, my people, enter into your rooms, and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourself for a little moment, until the indignation is past. For, behold, Yahweh comes out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity. The earth also will disclose her blood, and will no longer cover her slain.

note: 'To wait for his Son from heaven' reads the enthroned royal Son ('You are my Son') figurally of the risen Jesus whose advent executes divine judgment, the Psalm whose next verses warn the nations of the Son's wrath. The Son-language plus impending judgment coheres figurally, though Paul does not cite it here; marked low and contested.
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.

note: Waiting for the Son to come 'from heaven' to deliver at the judgment evokes the one like a son of man coming with the clouds to receive dominion at the eschatological assize. The heavenly-advent-and-judgment pattern is figurally apposite, though the explicit Son-of-Man title is absent here; faint, contested.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: Paul says God 'tests our hearts' (dokimazonti tas kardias), nearly verbatim the LXX language of Jeremiah's confessions where the Lord 'tests the hearts and reins' (dokimazon kardias kai nephrous). The forensic image of God assaying the inner person to validate the prophet's integrity is the controlling thought of vv. 3-4. High volume and coherence: Paul casts apostolic ministry in the mold of the persecuted-but-vindicated prophet.
sourceText: But, Yahweh of Armies, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, I shall see your vengeance on them; for to you have I revealed my cause.

note: A recurrence of the Jeremianic heart-testing motif: 'you have tried my heart toward you' (dedokimakas ten kardian mou). The repetition across Jeremiah (11:20; 12:3; 17:10) strengthens the Recurrence criterion and shows a settled idiom Paul could draw on for the tested servant of God.
sourceText: But you, Yahweh, know me; you see me, and try my heart toward you: pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and prepare them for the day of slaughter.

note: 'I the Lord search the heart and test (dokimazon) the reins, to give to each according to his ways.' The phrase fuses heart-testing with eschatological recompense, matching Paul's claim that he speaks to please God who weighs the heart rather than men. Coheres with the wider Jeremiah cluster.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: 'You have tried my heart; you have visited me by night; you have tested (epyrosas/edokimasas) me and found no unrighteousness in me.' The psalmist's protest of integrity under divine examination parallels Paul's denial of error, impurity, and deceit (v. 3). Strong thematic coherence with the heart-testing topos.
sourceText: You have proved my heart. You have visited me in the night. You have tried me, and found nothing. I have resolved that my mouth shall not disobey.

note: 'The refining pot is for silver and the furnace for gold, but the Lord tests hearts (kardias dokimazei).' Supplies the metallurgical sense behind dokimazo and may stand behind Paul's 'approved/tested' (dokimasmetha) in v. 4. Faint and contested as a direct source, but it reinforces the availability of the heart-assaying idiom.
sourceText: The refining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold, but Yahweh tests the hearts.

note: Paul likens himself to a nurse cherishing her children (v. 7), echoing Moses' complaint, 'Did I conceive all this people... that you should say to me, Carry them in your bosom as a nurse (trophos) carries the nursing child?' The maternal-nurse metaphor for the leader bearing a fledgling people is a distinctively Mosaic image; coherence is high since Paul casts apostolic care as Mosaic burden-bearing.
sourceText: Have I conceived all this people? Have I brought them out, that you should tell me, ‘Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing infant, to the land which you swore to their fathers?’

note: 'Can a woman forget her nursing child... ?' supplies the tender maternal-nursing imagery that informs Paul's self-comparison to a trophos cherishing her own children. Faint verbal contact but coherent with the nurturing-mother topos drawn from Israel's prophets.
sourceText: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!

note: 'As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you.' The motherly consolation that God promises Zion may color Paul's affectionate maternal self-portrait (vv. 7-8); the same passage stands near 66:14 imagery he uses elsewhere. Contested and faint.
sourceText: As one whom his mother comforts, so will I comfort you; and you will be comforted in Jerusalem.”

note: Paul exhorts 'as a father his own children' (v. 11), echoing 'the Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his son (hos ei tis trophophoresei... huion).' Deuteronomy's paternal image of God forming Israel through the wilderness coheres with Paul's claim to have fathered a people and called them to walk worthily (v. 12). Pairs with the maternal-nurse figure of v. 7.
sourceText: and in the wilderness, where you have seen how that Yahweh your God bore you, as a man does bear his son, in all the way that you went, until you came to this place.”

note: 'As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him.' Reinforces the fatherly-tenderness simile of v. 11. Faint verbal tie but strongly coherent with the divine-father topos Paul applies to his own pastoral role.
sourceText: Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him.

note: 'For whom the Lord loves he reproves, even as a father the son in whom he delights.' Supplies the father-exhorting-son pattern behind Paul's 'exhorting and encouraging' each one as a father (v. 11). Contested, but it belongs to the available paternal-discipline idiom.
sourceText: for whom Yahweh loves, he reproves; even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.

note: God 'calls you into his own kingdom and glory' (v. 12) draws on the OT hope that the saints receive the kingdom; Daniel 7:18 ('the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom') is the seedbed of that eschatological kingdom-and-glory language. Faint and contested as a specific source.
sourceText: But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.

note: Paul charges that they 'killed... their own prophets' (v. 15), the classic Deuteronomistic prophet-killing tradition stated programmatically in Nehemiah's confession: 'they were disobedient... and slew your prophets who testified against them.' High coherence: Paul's polemic is a compressed restatement of this historiographical theme of Israel's persecution of God's messengers.
sourceText: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.

note: 'They mocked the messengers of God... till the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy.' This verse uniquely binds prophet-rejection to the inescapable wrath that 'came upon them to the uttermost' (v. 16), matching both halves of Paul's statement (killing prophets + final wrath). Very strong coherence and volume.
sourceText: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.

note: 'Your own sword has devoured your prophets like a destroying lion.' A concrete instance of the prophet-killing charge that Paul generalizes in v. 15. Recurrence of the motif across the prophets strengthens its presence here.
sourceText: “I have struck your children in vain. They received no correction. Your own sword has devoured your prophets, like a destroying lion.

note: The narrative of the prophet Uriah, pursued and 'slain with the sword' by the king, is a paradigmatic OT account of killing a prophet who spoke God's word. It supplies historical substance to Paul's 'killed... their own prophets' and the driving-out theme ('drove us out', v. 15).
sourceText: There was also a man who prophesied in Yahweh’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: and when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt: and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son […]

note: 'To fill up their sins always' (v. 16) echoes the measure-of-iniquity motif: 'the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (anapeplerontai).' The notion that sin must reach a fixed full measure before judgment falls coheres precisely with Paul's logic that wrath comes when sins are 'filled up.'
sourceText: In the fourth generation they will come here again, for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.”

note: 'When the transgressors have reached their full measure (pleroumenon ton hamartion), a king... shall arise.' Daniel applies the filling-up-of-sins idea to an eschatological crisis preceding wrath, matching Paul's 'fill up their sins always... wrath has come.' Reinforces Genesis 15:16 within a second-temple judgment framework.
sourceText: In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up.

note: Explains that God waits 'until they have reached the full measure of their sins' before punishing — a deuterocanonical articulation of the same measure-of-iniquity theology behind v. 16. Faint as a direct source but confirms the idea's currency in second-temple Judaism (Availability criterion).
sourceText: For in the case of the other nations the Sovereign Lord does with longsuffering forbear, until that he punish them when they have attained to the full measure of their sins; but not so judged he as touching us,

note: 'The days of visitation have come, the days of recompense have come' supplies the prophetic 'the wrath/days have come' formula behind v. 16 ('wrath has come upon them to the uttermost'). Coherent with the prophetic wrath topos; contested as a specific source.
sourceText: The days of visitation have come. The days of reckoning have come. Israel will consider the prophet to be a fool, and the man who is inspired to be insane, because of the abundance of your sins, and because your hostility is great.

note: 'Now I will shortly pour out my wrath upon you, and accomplish my anger against you.' Ezekiel 7's repeated 'the end has come... wrath' announcement is a candidate background for Paul's compressed 'wrath has come upon them at last.' Faint, contested, but it belongs to the available prophetic-wrath idiom.
sourceText: Now will I shortly pour out my wrath on you, and accomplish my anger against you, and will judge you according to your ways; and I will bring on you all your abominations.

note: The pseudepigraphal phrase 'the wrath of God came upon them to the uttermost (eis telos)' is strikingly close to Paul's wording in v. 16 and is often cited as the nearest verbal parallel. Warranted as a faint, contested second-temple echo illuminating the fixed formula Paul deploys.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: Paul calls the Thessalonians his 'crown of rejoicing/boasting' (v. 19), echoing 'you shall be a crown of beauty (stephanos kallous) in the hand of the Lord.' Isaiah's image of a redeemed people as God's crown of glory coheres with Paul presenting his converts as his eschatological crown and glory (v. 20).
sourceText: You shall also be a crown of beauty in the hand of Yahweh, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.

note: 'I put a beautiful crown (stephanon) upon your head' — God adorning Jerusalem as his cherished bride. Supplies the crown-as-glory-of-a-beloved-people imagery behind Paul's 'crown of boasting.' Faint and contested but thematically coherent.
sourceText: I put a ring on your nose, and earrings in your ears, and a beautiful crown on your head.

note: 'Gray hair is a crown of glory (stephanos kauchaseos)' — the LXX phrase 'crown of boasting' is nearly identical to Paul's stephanos kaucheseos (v. 19). Strong verbal contact at the idiom level even though the application differs; flagged contested because the sense is proverbial rather than borrowed.
sourceText: Gray hair is a crown of glory. It is attained by a life of righteousness.

note: 'The fear of the Lord is glory and exultation (kauchema), and gladness and a crown of rejoicing (stephanos agalliamatos).' This deuterocanonical line couples crown + rejoicing/boasting just as Paul does, attesting the idiom's second-temple currency (Availability). Faint and contested as a direct source.
sourceText: The fear of the Lord is glory, and exultation, And gladness, and a crown of rejoicing.

note: 'Be wise, my son, that you may make my heart glad, that I may answer him who reproaches me.' The pattern of a teacher's vindication-before-others through the conduct of his children may underlie Paul's hope of presenting the Thessalonians 'before our Lord at his coming' (v. 19). Faint, contested.
sourceText: Be wise, my son, and bring joy to my heart, then I can answer my tormentor.

note: Paul names "the tempter" (ho peirazon) who might have "tempted" the Thessalonians and rendered his labor vain. The figure of a heavenly adversary who tests the faith of the righteous draws on the satan of Job's prologue, who is permitted to afflict Job precisely to see whether his fidelity will hold. The cluster of testing, affliction, and the danger of falling away mirrors Job's ordeal.
sourceText: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]

note: "The tempter" who could lure the converts away echoes the serpent who seduces in Eden, the archetypal scene of temptation leading to the undoing of the faithful. Paul elsewhere reads the serpent's deception figurally for the church (2 Cor 11:3), and the same Edenic background plausibly stands behind the worry that the tempter's work would make his labor "in vain."
sourceText: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]

note: Paul's fear that "our labor would have been in vain" reaches for the Septuagintal idiom of laboring fruitlessly (eis kenon), prominent in the Servant's lament "I have labored in vain." Isaiah's promise that such labor is finally not wasted is the same hope Paul expresses for his missionary toil.
sourceText: But I said, “I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely the justice due to me is with Yahweh, and my reward with my God.”

note: Paul insists believers "are appointed" to affliction, having foretold that "we are to suffer." The Psalter's axiom that "many are the afflictions of the righteous" supplies the scriptural conviction that suffering is the appointed lot of the faithful rather than a sign of abandonment.
sourceText: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.

note: Paul's overflowing "what thanksgiving can we render again to God for you" echoes the psalmist's "What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits toward me?" Both pose the rhetorical question of an adequate return of gratitude to God for received good, framed as thanksgiving rendered before God.
sourceText: What will I give to Yahweh for all his benefits toward me?

note: "At the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints" closely reproduces Zechariah's "the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him," a key text for the eschatological advent accompanied by the heavenly host. Paul applies the prophecy of the Lord's theophanic arrival with his holy ones directly to the parousia of Jesus.
sourceText: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*

note: The advent of the Lord "with all his saints/holy ones" draws on the Sinai theophany where the LORD "came with myriads of holy ones," the foundational image of God arriving attended by his angelic host. The same verse stands behind the developed expectation of the divine coming surrounded by the holy ones.
sourceText: He said, “Yahweh came from Sinai, and rose from Seir to them. He shone from Mount Paran. He came from the ten thousands of holy ones. At his right hand was a fiery law for them.

note: The myriads of "holy ones" attending the Lord's coming evoke Daniel's throne vision, where thousands of thousands serve and ten thousand times ten thousand stand before the Ancient of Days. This apocalyptic court of attendants feeds the picture of Jesus arriving with all his holy ones.
sourceText: A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.

note: "All his saints" recalls the heavenly "assembly of the holy ones" who praise and surround the LORD, the council of holy ones before whom God is feared. Paul's holy retinue at the parousia shares this picture of the angelic congregation accompanying the divine presence.
sourceText: The heavens will praise your wonders, Yahweh; your faithfulness also in the assembly of the holy ones. For who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of the heavenly beings is like Yahweh, a very awesome God in the council of the holy ones, to be feared above all those who are around him?

note: The Lord coming "with all his saints" faintly recalls the chariots of God, "twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands," the LORD among them as at Sinai. The motif of God advancing amid innumerable heavenly hosts overlaps with the parousia escort.
sourceText: The chariots of God are tens of thousands and thousands of thousands. The Lord is among them, from Sinai, into the sanctuary.

note: The coming of the Lord "with all his holy ones" parallels the Enochic oracle that "the Lord will come with his holy myriads to execute judgment," itself an expansion of Deuteronomy 33:2. This pseudepigraphal text (cited in Jude 14-15) attests the same first-century expectation of the Lord's advent attended by his holy ones that Paul invokes.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: The prayer that God "direct our way to you" (kateuthynai) uses the Septuagintal vocabulary of God making straight one's paths, as in "he will direct your paths." The petition entrusts the missionaries' route to divine guidance in the manner of the wisdom tradition.
sourceText: In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.

note: The goal that God "establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God" echoes the covenantal charge to "walk before me and be blameless." The pairing of blamelessness with standing before God recalls the patriarchal call to integrity in the divine presence.
sourceText: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless.

note: "Establish your hearts" (sterixai tas kardias) echoes the Septuagint's description of the righteous whose "heart is established/steadfast," unafraid. The image of an inwardly fixed, unshakable heart underlies Paul's prayer for hearts confirmed in holiness.
sourceText: His heart is established. He will not be afraid in the end when he sees his adversaries.

note: Paul's call to abstain from sexual immorality as the content of sanctification draws on the Holiness Code's catalog of forbidden sexual relations, which there too distinguishes Israel from 'the nations.' The structural logic (holiness = sexual self-control over against Gentile practice) is Levitical.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them, ‘I am Yahweh your God. You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt, where you lived: and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, where I am bringing you; neither shall you walk in their statutes. You shall do my ordinances, and you shall keep my statutes, and walk in them: I am Yahweh your God. You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man […]

note: 'God called us... in sanctification' and the refrain of holiness echo the Holiness Code's foundational imperative, 'You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.' The grounding of ethical holiness in the holy character of the God who calls is Levitical.
sourceText: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.

note: 'Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy' immediately follows prohibitions of sexual sin, matching Paul's pairing of consecration (sanctification, honor) with abstaining from porneia. Reinforces the Holiness Code substrate.
sourceText: “‘Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am Yahweh your God.

note: 'the Gentiles who don't know God' verbally matches Jeremiah's 'the nations that do not know you,' a stock LXX characterization of pagans as ignorant of the true God. Paul applies the same idiom to ground sexual ethics in covenantal knowledge of God.
sourceText: Pour out your wrath on the nations that don’t know you, and on the families that don’t call on your name: for they have devoured Jacob, yes, they have devoured him and consumed him, and have laid waste his habitation.

note: Parallel to Jeremiah 10:25, 'the nations that do not know you,' the same formula identifying Gentiles by their ignorance of God. The two texts are nearly identical and both stand behind Paul's phrase 'who don't know God.'
sourceText: Pour out your wrath on the nations that don’t know you; on the kingdoms that don’t call on your name;

note: 'the Lord is an avenger in all these things' draws on the Song of Moses, 'Vengeance is mine, and recompense.' Paul invokes the divine prerogative of vengeance to enforce sexual justice toward a wronged brother, as he does explicitly in Romans 12:19.
sourceText: Vengeance is mine, and recompense, at the time when their foot slides; for the day of their calamity is at hand. Their doom rushes at them.”

note: 'O LORD, God of vengeance' (LXX Ps 93:1) supplies the divine title 'avenger' that Paul applies. The psalm's plea for God to requite oppressors parallels Paul's warning that the Lord avenges the defrauded.
sourceText: Yahweh, you God to whom vengeance belongs, you God to whom vengeance belongs, shine out.

note: 'God, who has also given his Holy Spirit to you' echoes Ezekiel's new-covenant promise, 'I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes.' The gift of the indwelling Spirit as the enabling power of holiness undergirds Paul's claim that rejecting his teaching rejects the Spirit-giving God.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: 'I will put my Spirit in you' restates the promise of 36:27, linking the Spirit's indwelling to new covenant life. Reinforces the Ezekielian background for God 'who gives his Holy Spirit.'
sourceText: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.

note: Wisdom links the Gentiles' ignorance of God to idolatry and the resulting sexual corruption ('defiling of souls... sexual perversion'), the very chain Paul compresses in 'the passion of lust, even as the Gentiles who don't know God.' Deuterocanonical; the conceptual sequence (no knowledge of God -> disordered desire) is shared.
sourceText: Afterward it was not enough for them to go astray as touching the knowledge of God; But also, while they live in sore conflict through ignorance of him. That multitude of evils they call peace. note: 'all men... were ignorant of God' is the premise that Gentiles fail to know God from creation; a faint deuterocanonical parallel to 'who don't know God.' Contested as direct dependence versus shared topos.
sourceText: For verily all men by nature were but vain who had no perception of God, And from the good things that are seen they gained not power to know him that is, Neither by giving heed to the works did they recognize the architect;

note: If 'possess his own vessel' means controlling one's body, the cultic 'vessels of the young men are holy' offers a faint lexical analogy of vessels as sanctified bodies. Highly contested; the meaning of skeuos (body vs. wife) is itself disputed.
sourceText: David answered the priest, and said to him, “Truly, women have been kept from us about these three days. When I came out, the vessels of the young men were holy, though it was but a common journey. How much more then today shall their vessels be holy?”

note: Ben Sira's denunciation of the man enslaved to lustful passion and the adulterer who profanes sanctity parallels Paul's contrast of lustful passion with sanctification and honor. Deuterocanonical wisdom on sexual self-mastery; thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: Two sorts of men multiply sins, And the third will bring wrath: A hot mind, as a burning fire, will not be quenched till it be consumed: A fornicator in the body of his flesh will never cease till he has burned out the fire. All bread is sweet to a fornicator: He will not leave off till he die. A man that goes astray from his own bed, Saying in his heart, Who sees me? Darkness is round about me, and the walls hide me, And no man sees me; of whom am I […]

note: 'you yourselves are taught by God' (theodidaktoi) echoes the eschatological promise that 'all your children shall be taught by the LORD.' Paul claims this Isaianic restoration is realized among the Thessalonians, who need no human instruction in love.
sourceText: All your children shall be taught of Yahweh; and great shall be the peace of your children.

note: The new-covenant promise of the law written on hearts so that 'they shall all know me' undergirds 'taught by God to love one another.' Internal, Spirit-given instruction replacing external teaching is the Jeremianic hope Paul presupposes.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin […]

note: Paul's theme of philadelphia, loving one another, rests on the foundational command 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself,' which he elsewhere calls the law's summation. The mutual-love ethic is its application within the community.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'you shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands' commends self-supporting manual labor as blessing, paralleling Paul's exhortation to 'work with your own hands' and lack nothing. Wisdom-of-labor background.
sourceText: For you will eat the labor of your hands. You will be happy, and it will be well with you.

note: The sluggard reproof, urging diligent work to avoid want, parallels Paul's call to industrious self-sufficiency so as to 'have need of nothing.' Proverbial labor ethic; thematic only.
sourceText: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.

note: Eating bread 'by the sweat of your face' establishes manual labor as the human vocation, faintly resonant with Paul's dignity-of-handwork charge. Very faint and contested.
sourceText: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

note: The promise that at the end 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake' grounds Paul's hope for 'those who have fallen asleep' rising. The deliverance of God's people and the resurrection/awakening sequence is the clearest scriptural matrix for vv. 14-16.
sourceText: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book. Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: Being 'caught up together... in the clouds, to meet the Lord' draws on the vision of one like a son of man coming 'with the clouds of heaven.' The cloud imagery of glorious eschatological encounter is Danielic.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

note: The Sinai theophany, with the LORD descending, thick cloud, and a very loud trumpet blast, supplies the template for the Lord descending from heaven with God's trumpet and a shout. Paul recasts covenant theophany as parousia.
sourceText: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. note: 'the Lord GOD will sound the trumpet' as the divine warrior appears closely matches 'with God's trumpet' at the Lord's descent. The eschatological trumpet of divine advent is shared.
sourceText: Yahweh will be seen over them; and his arrow will go flash like lightning; and the Lord Yahweh will blow the trumpet, and will go with whirlwinds of the south.

note: 'Blow the trumpet in Zion... for the day of the LORD is coming' associates the trumpet blast with the day of the Lord, the framework for Paul's trumpet and parousia. Continues into 1 Thess 5's 'day of the Lord.'
sourceText: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of Yahweh comes, for it is close at hand:

sourceText: It will happen in that day that a great trumpet will be blown; and those who were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and those who were outcasts in the land of Egypt, shall come; and they will worship Yahweh in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

note: 'Your dead shall live... awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust' is a primary OT resurrection text behind 'the dead in Christ will rise.' The awakening of the dead at the LORD's coming directly informs Paul's hope against grief.

note: 'the LORD is coming forth out of his place, and will come down' provides the descent imagery of God leaving heaven to act, echoed in 'the Lord himself will descend from heaven.' Theophanic descent.
sourceText: For, behold, Yahweh comes out of his place, and will come down and tread on the high places of the earth.

note: 'God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet' uniquely pairs a loud shout with a trumpet blast, the precise combination in 'with a shout... and with God's trumpet.' Direction is reversed (ascent vs. descent) but the acclamation imagery is striking.
sourceText: God has gone up with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a trumpet.

note: 'the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him' parallels 'God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep' and the Lord's coming accompanied by his people. Often cited behind the parousia retinue.
sourceText: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*

note: The silver trumpets that summon the assembly and signal God's remembrance offer a cultic backdrop to the eschatological trumpet gathering the saints. Faint and thematic.
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Make two trumpets of silver. You shall make them of beaten work. You shall use them for the calling of the congregation, and for the journeying of the camps. When they blow them, all the congregation shall gather themselves to you at the door of the Tent of Meeting. If they blow just one, then the princes, the heads of the thousands of Israel, shall gather themselves to you. When you blow an alarm, the camps that lie on the […]

note: 'a day of trumpet blast' for the day of the LORD reinforces the trumpet-of-judgment-and-advent motif. Faint, part of the cluster of day-of-the-LORD trumpet texts.
sourceText: a day of the trumpet and alarm, against the fortified cities, and against the high battlements.

note: Elijah's being 'taken up' bodily to heaven, like Enoch (Gen 5:24), figurally anticipates the living being 'caught up' to meet the Lord without death. Typological rather than verbal.
sourceText: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

note: Enoch, who 'was not, for God took him,' prefigures the rapture of the living to be with the Lord forever. Faint figural precedent for translation without death.
sourceText: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.

note: The phrase 'the day of the Lord' (5:2) draws directly on the prophetic Day-of-the-Lord tradition, of which Joel is a primary witness: a day of darkness and gloom announced with alarm. Paul assumes his readers know the concept without explanation, presupposing the prophetic background.
sourceText: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of Yahweh comes, for it is close at hand: A day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness. As the dawn spreading on the mountains, a great and strong people; there has never been the like, neither will there be any more after them, even to the years of many generations.

note: Amos memorably reframes the day of the Lord as darkness and not light, an inversion that Paul exploits when he contrasts the children of light/day with those overtaken in darkness (5:4-5). The thematic pairing of the Day with darkness and sudden doom is shared.
sourceText: “Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! Why do you long for the day of Yahweh? It is darkness, and not light. Even very dark, and no brightness in it?

note: Zephaniah describes the day of the Lord as near, hastening, a day of wrath, distress, and ruin coming suddenly. Paul's 'sudden destruction' and the appointment 'not to wrath' (5:3, 9) echo this Day-of-the-Lord wrath vocabulary.
sourceText: The great day of Yahweh is near. It is near, and hurries greatly, the voice of the day of Yahweh. The mighty man cries there bitterly. That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,

note: Malachi's coming day burning like an oven that overtakes the wicked contributes to the burning, inescapable judgment color of Paul's Day-of-the-Lord imagery (5:2-3). Faint and one of several Day texts standing behind the motif.
sourceText: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

note: Paul's 'Peace and safety, then sudden destruction' (5:3) inverts the false-prophet slogan 'Peace, peace, when there is no peace.' Jeremiah condemns those who heal the wound lightly by crying peace; Paul makes the same false security the prelude to sudden ruin.
sourceText: They have healed also the hurt of my people superficially, saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ when there is no peace.

note: A near-doublet of Jer 6:14, again denouncing 'Peace, peace, when there is no peace.' It reinforces the false-peace background of the 'Peace and safety' slogan in 5:3.
sourceText: They have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.

note: Ezekiel likewise indicts prophets who say 'Peace' when there is no peace, whitewashing a flimsy wall that will fall. The deceptive cry of peace followed by sudden collapse parallels Paul's 'Peace and safety, then sudden destruction' (5:3).
sourceText: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there is no peace; and when one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash:

note: Paul compares the sudden destruction to 'birth pains on a pregnant woman' (5:3). Isaiah's oracle on the day of the Lord against Babylon uses the same labor-pang simile for inescapable terror, tying the metaphor directly to a Day-of-the-Lord context.
sourceText: They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame.

note: Isaiah pictures a pregnant woman writhing and crying out in her labor pains as an image of distress, a standard prophetic figure that informs Paul's labor-pain simile for sudden destruction (5:3).
sourceText: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh.

note: Jeremiah describes anguish and pain 'like a woman in labor' on hearing of coming disaster, in the same context as the false-peace slogan of 6:14. The shared labor-pang imagery for sudden, inescapable calamity stands behind 5:3.
sourceText: We have heard its report; our hands become feeble: anguish has taken hold of us, and pains as of a woman in labor.

note: The armor metaphor 'breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation' (5:8) reworks Isaiah's portrait of the Divine Warrior who 'put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head.' Paul transfers God's own armor to the believer and recasts the virtues.
sourceText: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.

note: Wisdom, itself dependent on Isa 59:17, depicts the Lord taking 'holiness as an invincible shield' and putting on righteousness as a breastplate, arming creation against enemies. It is a likely mediating deuterocanonical witness for Paul's armor imagery in 5:8.
sourceText: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet;

note: Isaiah's call to 'walk in the light of the LORD' offers a faint background for Paul's 'children of light... children of the day' (5:5) language of belonging to the light rather than darkness. Contested and one of several light/darkness texts.
sourceText: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of Yahweh.

note: Isaiah's eschatological light shining on God's people while darkness covers the nations supplies a faint backdrop to the light/day versus night/darkness antithesis of 5:4-5. Faint and figural rather than verbal.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

note: 'See that no one returns evil for evil' (5:15) restates the Holiness Code's prohibition of vengeance and grudge-bearing, the verse that culminates in 'love your neighbor as yourself.' Paul's command not to retaliate but to pursue the good for one another draws on this foundational text.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'Don't say, I will repay evil' in Proverbs is the closest sapiential parallel to Paul's 'no one returns evil for evil' (5:15), commending waiting on the Lord rather than retaliating.
sourceText: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.

note: 'Don't say, I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work' parallels Paul's prohibition of repaying evil for evil (5:15), reinforcing the wisdom-tradition rejection of tit-for-tat retaliation.
sourceText: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”

note: 'Whoever rewards evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house' shares the evil-for-good/evil-for-evil idiom that Paul negates in 5:15. Faint and contested against the stronger Prov 20:22 and Lev 19:18.
sourceText: Whoever rewards evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house.

note: 'Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it' resonates with Paul's clustered exhortations to 'always follow after that which is good' and 'be at peace among yourselves' (5:13, 15). A possible sapiential backdrop, faint.
sourceText: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.

note: Elihu's 'Let us choose for ourselves that which is right; let us know among ourselves what is good' offers a faint sapiential parallel to Paul's 'Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good' (5:21), the discernment of good from its counterfeit.
sourceText: Let us choose for us that which is right. Let us know among ourselves what is good.

note: 'Doesn't the ear try words, even as the palate tastes its food?' supplies a testing/discernment image akin to Paul's command to test everything (5:21). Faint and figural.
sourceText: Doesn’t the ear try words, even as the palate tastes its food?

note: 'Taste and see that the LORD is good' parallels the discern-the-good motif of 'Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good' (5:21). Faint and contested.
sourceText: Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.

note: 'Hate the evil, love the good' parallels Paul's paired commands to 'hold firmly that which is good' and 'abstain from every form of evil' (5:21-22). A faint prophetic-ethical backdrop.
sourceText: Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts. It may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”

note: 'You who love the LORD, hate evil' resonates with the good/evil antithesis of 'hold firmly that which is good... abstain from every form of evil' (5:21-22). Faint.
sourceText: You who love Yahweh, hate evil. He preserves the souls of his saints. He delivers them out of the hand of the wicked.

note: 'I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth' offers a faint backdrop to the continual praise and thanksgiving commanded in 'Rejoice always... In everything give thanks' (5:16-18). Faint and contested.
sourceText: I will bless Yahweh at all times. His praise will always be in my mouth.

note: The prayer that the believer's 'whole spirit, soul, and body' be preserved blameless (5:23) reflects an anthropology rooted in Genesis, where God breathes the breath of life into the body so that the man becomes a living soul. Faint and figural.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: The Shema's command to love God with heart, soul, and might gives a faint background to Paul's whole-person sanctification of 'spirit, soul, and body' (5:23). Contested as a verbal source.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: The divine title 'the God of peace' (5:23) draws on Israel's covenantal naming of God with peace, as where Gideon names the altar 'The LORD is Peace.' A faint backdrop to Paul's recurring peace-of-God title.
sourceText: Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

note: The Aaronic blessing's climactic gift of peace ('the LORD... give you peace') stands faintly behind the benedictory 'God of peace' and the wish for blameless preservation in the closing prayer (5:23). Faint and figural.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: 'Know therefore that the LORD your God... is the faithful God' undergirds Paul's assurance 'He who calls you is faithful' (5:24). A faint covenantal echo of God's reliability to fulfill his word.
sourceText: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,

note: 'A God of faithfulness who does no wrong' resonates with 'He who calls you is faithful, who will also do it' (5:24). Faint and one of several covenant-faithfulness texts.
sourceText: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.

note: The epistolary salutation 'Grace to you and peace' draws on the Aaronic blessing, where the LORD's gracious face and the gift of peace (shalom) are pronounced over Israel. Paul reworks the priestly benediction into a christological greeting that names both Father and Lord Jesus as its source. The link is formulaic and contested as a deliberate allusion.
sourceText: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: Paul's 'boast about you in the assemblies of God' inverts Jeremiah's prohibition against boasting in wisdom, might, or wealth, redirecting glorying toward what God has wrought in the believers' faith. The motif of legitimate versus illegitimate boasting is a Pauline staple rooted in this oracle. Faint and contested here, since the object of boasting differs.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.

note: The endurance of the assembly under 'persecutions and afflictions' resonates with Daniel's vision of the little horn making war on and wearing out the holy ones before their vindication. The apocalyptic pattern of saints suffering prior to the kingdom undergirds the whole chapter. The verbal contact is thematic rather than lexical.
sourceText: I saw, and the same horn made war with the saints, and prevailed against them; until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom. Thus he said, The fourth animal shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be diverse from all the kingdoms, and shall devour the whole earth, and shall tread it down, and break it in pieces. As for the ten horns, out of this […]

note: The phrase 'righteous judgment of God' echoes the psalmic confession that the LORD has established his throne for judgment and will judge the world in righteousness. Paul reads present suffering as evidence that this just verdict is already operative. The righteousness-of-judgment language is pervasive in the Psalter (cf. Psalm 96:13; 98:9).
sourceText: But Yahweh reigns forever. He has prepared his throne for judgment. He will judge the world in righteousness. He will administer judgment to the peoples in uprightness.

note: Being 'counted worthy of the Kingdom of God, for which you also suffer' draws on Daniel's promise that the holy ones of the Most High shall receive and possess the kingdom after the beast's oppression. The pairing of present affliction with future royal vindication is distinctively Danielic. Cf. Daniel 7:22, 27.
sourceText: But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.

note: The idea that suffering is the means by which believers are 'counted worthy' of the kingdom parallels Wisdom's teaching that the righteous, though chastened and tested like gold in the furnace, are found worthy of God and accepted. This deuterocanonical theodicy of vindication-through-affliction closely matches Paul's logic in 1:5. A strong conceptual echo.
sourceText: For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality; And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and found them worthy of himself. As gold in the furnace he proved them, And as a whole burnt offering he accepted them.

note: The martyr-theology that suffering for God qualifies one for the kingdom and resurrection vindication has its narrative archetype in the deaths of Eleazar and the seven brothers. Paul's framing of persecution as a 'sign' pointing to just recompense shares this martyrological worldview. Thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: and when he was at the point to die with the stripes, he groaned aloud and said, To the Lord, that has the holy knowledge, it is manifest that, whereas I might have been delivered from death, I endure sore pains in my body by being scourged; but in soul I gladly suffer these things for my fear of him. So this man also died after this manner, leaving his death for an ensample of nobleness and a memorial of virtue, not only to the young but also to the […]

note: 'A righteous thing with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you' enacts the lex talionis of the Song of Moses, where vengeance and recompense belong to the LORD. Paul grounds eschatological retribution in this Torah principle of divine, not human, requital. Cf. the same passage cited at Romans 12:19.
sourceText: Vengeance is mine, and recompense, at the time when their foot slides; for the day of their calamity is at hand. Their doom rushes at them.”

note: Isaiah's 'voice of the LORD that renders recompense to his enemies' supplies the recompense-on-the-afflicters logic of 1:6, and the surrounding oracle (66:5-16) frames the whole 2 Thessalonians 1 scenario of relief for the oppressed and fiery requital for foes. This is the chapter's controlling intertext. High confidence given the dense cluster of contacts across 1:6-10.
sourceText: A voice of tumult from the city, a voice from the temple, a voice of Yahweh that renders recompense to his enemies.

note: 'When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven... in flaming fire' renders Isaiah's theophany: the LORD will come in fire, his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury and his rebuke with flames of fire. Paul transfers this divine advent to the revealed Lord Jesus. The combination of coming, fire, and recompense is verbally and conceptually tight.
sourceText: For, behold, Yahweh will come with fire, and his chariots shall be like the whirlwind; to render his anger with fierceness, and his rebuke with flames of fire.

note: The pairing of vengeance on oppressors with rescue ('relief') for the afflicted matches Isaiah's promise that God will come with vengeance, with divine recompense, to save you. Paul's antithesis of affliction-for-afflicters and relief-for-the-afflicted reflects this two-sided day of the LORD. A genuine but less verbally specific contact.
sourceText: Tell those who have a fearful heart, “Be strong. Don’t be afraid. Behold, your God will come with vengeance, God’s retribution. He will come and save you.

note: The repayment formula 'to repay affliction to those who afflict you' resonates with the imprecatory blessing on whoever repays Babylon what she has done to Zion. The measure-for-measure justice is shared, though Paul reserves the act to God's eschatological judgment rather than human agents. Contested as a direct source.
sourceText: Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction, he will be happy who rewards you, as you have served us.

note: 'Revealed from heaven with his mighty angels' draws on Zechariah's day-of-the-LORD coming, when the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him. The retinue of accompanying holy ones is a standard feature of the parousia that Paul applies to Jesus. Cf. Deuteronomy 33:2.
sourceText: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*

note: The fiery apparatus of judgment — a stream of fire issuing before the Ancient of Days while thousands of angels attend — informs the 'flaming fire' and 'mighty angels' of the Lord's revelation. Daniel's heavenly courtroom supplies both the fire and the angelic host of the judgment scene. Combined with the Son of Man advent of 7:13.
sourceText: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.

note: Isaiah's portrait of the name of the LORD coming from afar, burning with anger, his tongue a devouring fire, with flame and tempest, parallels the fiery, wrathful advent of 1:7-8. The shared imagery of divine arrival in consuming fire to judge the nations supports a faint echo. Contested as a distinct source amid the Isaianic cluster.
sourceText: Behold, Yahweh’s name comes from far away, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke. His lips are full of indignation, and his tongue is as a devouring fire. His breath is as an overflowing stream that reaches even to the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of destruction; and a bridle that leads to ruin will be in the jaws of the peoples. You will have a song, as in the night when a holy feast is kept; and gladness of heart, as when one […]

note: The Sinai theophany — the LORD descending in fire amid smoke and trembling — stands behind the biblical grammar of God revealed in 'flaming fire.' Paul's parousia language is colored by this foundational fire-theophany even where no single verse is quoted. Faint and diffuse.
sourceText: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lower part of the mountain.
