Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked […]

note: 'Giving vengeance to those who don't know God' echoes Jeremiah's prayer that God pour out his wrath on the nations that know him not and on the peoples that do not call on his name. Paul takes up this categorization of the godless as those who 'do not know God' as the object of eschatological vengeance. Closely paralleled by Psalm 79:6.
sourceText: Pour out your wrath on the nations that don’t know you, and on the families that don’t call on your name: for they have devoured Jacob, yes, they have devoured him and consumed him, and have laid waste his habitation.

note: The plea to 'pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that do not call on your name' is the closest Psalter parallel to 1:8's vengeance on 'those who don't know God.' Together with Jeremiah 10:25 it supplies the formulaic designation of the wicked. High confidence as a shared source.
sourceText: Pour out your wrath on the nations that don’t know you; on the kingdoms that don’t call on your name;

note: Isaiah's indictment of those who, when God called, did not answer and did not obey but did evil, undergirds 1:8's 'those who don't obey the Good News.' The Isaiah 66 oracle thus frames both halves of 1:8 — not knowing God and not obeying. Reinforces the chapter's saturation in Isaiah 66.
sourceText: I also will choose their delusions, and will bring their fears on them; because when I called, no one answered; when I spoke, they didn’t listen; but they did that which was evil in my eyes, and chose that in which I didn’t delight.”

note: 'Eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might' renders Isaiah's refrain: hide in the rock from before the terror of the LORD and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth. The double phrase 'face/terror of the Lord' and 'glory of his might/majesty' is a near-quotation. The thrice-repeated refrain anchors the verse.
sourceText: Enter into the rock, and hide in the dust, from before the terror of Yahweh, and from the glory of his majesty.

note: The repetition at 2:19 (and 2:21) — fleeing to caves from before the terror of the LORD and the glory of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth — supplies the exclusionary 'from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might' in 1:9. The refrain's threefold form makes the dependence especially secure.
sourceText: Men shall go into the caves of the rocks, and into the holes of the earth, from before the terror of Yahweh, and from the glory of his majesty, when he arises to shake the earth mightily.

note: 'Glorified in his saints' and 'admired' draws on the picture of a God greatly feared in the council of the holy ones and awesome above all around him. The parousia in which Christ is glorified amid his holy ones reflects this assembly of the heavenly host marveling at God. Cf. Psalm 68:35.
sourceText: a very awesome God in the council of the holy ones, to be feared above all those who are around him?

note: 'To be glorified in his saints' echoes the Servant oracle, 'You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified.' Paul applies the motif of God being glorified in his people to the eschatological revelation of the Lord Jesus in his believers. A genuine but transposed contact.
sourceText: and he said to me, “You are my servant; Israel, in whom I will be glorified.”

note: Isaiah 66:5's promise that the LORD will appear to the joy of the persecuted faithful while their mockers are put to shame matches 1:10's vindicating appearance 'glorified in his saints.' The same oracle's reversal — glory for the oppressed, judgment for oppressors — pervades 2 Thessalonians 1. Consistent with the chapter's Isaiah 66 frame.
sourceText: Hear Yahweh’s word, you who tremble at his word: “Your brothers who hate you, who cast you out for my name’s sake, have said, ‘Let Yahweh be glorified, that we may see your joy;’ but it is those who shall be disappointed.

note: The eschatological tag 'in that day,' when 'the LORD alone will be exalted,' colors 1:10's 'in that day' when Christ is glorified and admired. Isaiah 2:11,17 supplies the day-of-the-LORD formula of exclusive divine exaltation that Paul reads christologically. Faint, given how conventional the phrase is.
sourceText: The lofty looks of man will be brought low, the haughtiness of men will be bowed down, and Yahweh alone will be exalted in that day.

note: The prayer 'that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him' continues the Isaiah 66 motif of the LORD being glorified before and within his vindicated people. The mutual glorification reflects the oracle's promise that God will show his glory to the faithful. Faint within the chapter's broader Isaianic frame.
sourceText: Hear Yahweh’s word, you who tremble at his word: “Your brothers who hate you, who cast you out for my name’s sake, have said, ‘Let Yahweh be glorified, that we may see your joy;’ but it is those who shall be disappointed.

note: 'That the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified' resonates with Malachi's oracle that God's name will be great among the nations, from the rising of the sun to its setting. Paul transfers the magnification of the divine name to the name of the Lord Jesus. Thematic and contested as a deliberate source.
sourceText: For from the rising of the sun even to the going down of the same, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the nations,” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: The glorifying of the Lord's name among believers echoes the psalmist's expectation that all nations will come, worship, and glorify God's name. The eschatological honoring of the name underlies 1:12. A faint, diffuse contact within a common biblical topos.
sourceText: All nations you have made will come and worship before you, Lord. They shall glorify your name.

note: The eschatological 'day of the Lord' (here 'day of Christ/the Lord') that Paul corrects the Thessalonians about derives its weight from the prophetic Day-of-the-Lord tradition, of which Joel is a primary witness. Joel sounds the alarm that the day is near and dreadful.
sourceText: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of Yahweh comes, for it is close at hand:

note: The 'great and awesome day of the Lord' with cosmic signs feeds the apocalyptic timetable Paul is addressing. The Thessalonians' panic that the day had already come presupposes this prophetic frame.
sourceText: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: Amos's reversal of the Day of the Lord into darkness rather than light is foundational to the NT's sober expectation of that day. Paul's warning against premature certainty draws on this prophetic gravity.
sourceText: “Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! Why do you long for the day of Yahweh? It is darkness, and not light. As if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him; Or he went into the house and leaned his hand on the wall, and a snake bit him. Won’t the day of Yahweh be darkness, and not light? Even very dark, and no brightness in it?

note: Zephaniah's 'day of the Lord is near' with wrath and distress contributes to the prophetic Day-of-the-Lord matrix behind Paul's eschatology.
sourceText: The great day of Yahweh is near. It is near, and hurries greatly, the voice of the day of Yahweh. The mighty man cries there bitterly. That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,

note: Isaiah's 'day of the Lord' coming as destruction from the Almighty is part of the broad prophetic stream informing Paul's 'day of Christ.'
sourceText: Wail; for the day of Yahweh is at hand! It will come as destruction from the Almighty. Therefore all hands will be feeble, and everyone’s heart will melt. They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame. Behold, the day of Yahweh comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger; to make the land a desolation, and to destroy its […]

note: The burning day of the Lord in Malachi belongs to the prophetic Day tradition that frames Paul's correction; faint and diffuse.
sourceText: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

note: Paul's 'our gathering together to him' (episynagoge) echoes the prophetic hope of God gathering scattered Israel one by one at the trumpet. The ingathering of the elect is a stock eschatological motif rooted here.
sourceText: It will happen in that day, that Yahweh will thresh from the flowing stream of the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt; and you will be gathered one by one, children of Israel. It will happen in that day that a great trumpet will be blown; and those who were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and those who were outcasts in the land of Egypt, shall come; and they will worship Yahweh in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

note: The promise that the Lord will gather the dispersed from the ends of the heavens undergirds the eschatological 'gathering together to him.' This is the seedbed of the NT gathering-of-the-elect language.
sourceText: If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of the heavens, from there Yahweh your God will gather you, and from there he will bring you back.

note: Zechariah's call to the scattered people belongs to the ingathering hope behind episynagoge; faint.
sourceText: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.

note: 'Gather my faithful ones to me' offers a verbal-conceptual parallel to the assembling of believers to the Lord, though Paul does not cite it.
sourceText: “Gather my saints together to me, those who have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.”

note: The deuterocanonical hope that God will 'gather his people together' (episynagoge cognate) when mercy comes parallels Paul's gathering-to-him language. Possible shared eschatological idiom.
sourceText: But when Jeremiah perceived it, he blamed them, saying, Yes and the place shall be unknown until God gather the people again together, and mercy come:

note: The man of sin who 'opposes and exalts himself against all that is called God' closely tracks Daniel's king who 'shall do as he wills, exalt himself above every god, and speak astonishing things against the God of gods.' This is the principal scriptural template for the figure.
sourceText: The king shall do according to his will; and he shall exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak marvelous things against the God of gods; and he shall prosper until the indignation be accomplished; for that which is determined shall be done.

note: Daniel's profanation of the sanctuary and setting up the abomination underlies Paul's 'sits as God in the temple of God.' The desecration-of-the-temple motif is drawn directly from Daniel's depiction of the eschatological tyrant.
sourceText: Forces shall stand on his part, and they shall profane the sanctuary, even the fortress, and shall take away the continual burnt offering, and they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.

note: The 'abomination that makes desolate' set up in the temple grounds Paul's image of the lawless one seating himself in God's temple. Daniel's desolating abomination is the prototype of the temple usurpation.
sourceText: From the time that the continual burnt offering shall be taken away, and the abomination that makes desolate set up, there shall be one thousand two hundred ninety days.

note: The covenant-breaker who sets the abomination on a wing of the temple feeds the temple-defilement element of Paul's portrait of the man of lawlessness.
sourceText: He shall make a firm covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease; and on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate; and even to the full end, and that determined, shall wrath be poured out on the desolate.

note: The little horn that 'speaks words against the Most High' and exalts itself supplies the blasphemous self-deification of the man of sin.
sourceText: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.

note: The little horn that grows great, casts down the host, magnifies itself against the prince and takes away the regular sacrifice prefigures the lawless one's assault on God and his sanctuary.
sourceText: Out of one of them came out a little horn, which grew exceeding great, toward the south, and toward the east, and toward the glorious land. It grew great, even to the army of the sky; and some of the army and of the stars it cast down to the ground, and trampled on them. Yes, it magnified itself, even to the prince of the army; and it took away from him the continual burnt offering, and the place of his sanctuary was cast down. The army was given over to […]

note: The horn that magnifies himself and 'rises up against the Prince of princes' contributes to the self-exalting opposition to God that defines the man of lawlessness.
sourceText: Through his policy he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand; and he shall magnify himself in his heart, and he shall destroy many in their security. He shall also stand up against the prince of princes; but he shall be broken without hand.

note: The prince of Tyre who says 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of gods' is a close conceptual and verbal parallel to the man of sin 'setting himself up as God' and sitting in God's temple. The blasphemous claim to deity and the enthroned posture both resonate.
sourceText: Son of man, tell the prince of Tyre, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Because your heart is lifted up, and you have said, I am a god, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet you are man, and not God, though you set your heart as the heart of God—

note: The king of Babylon's boast, 'I will ascend... I will make myself like the Most High,' is a primary source for the self-exaltation of the man of lawlessness 'against all that is called God.' The hubristic ascent against the divine is the shared core.
sourceText: You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!”

note: The rebuke that the self-deifying prince is 'a man and not a god' continues the Tyre oracle's exposure of blasphemous self-deification, paralleling the man of sin's pretension to godhood.
sourceText: therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh: Because you have set your heart as the heart of God, therefore, behold, I will bring strangers on you, the terrible of the nations; and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom, and they shall defile your brightness. They shall bring you down to the pit; and you shall die the death of those who are slain, in the heart of the seas. Will you yet say before him who kills you, I am God? but you are […]

note: The king who 'pays no heed to any god, for he magnifies himself above all' extends the self-exaltation directly behind Paul's description of opposition to every object of worship.
sourceText: Neither shall he regard the gods of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor regard any god; for he shall magnify himself above all.

note: The rise of a bold king 'when transgressors have reached their full measure' may inform Paul's sequence of the rebellion/apostasy preceding the lawless one's revelation.
sourceText: In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up.

note: Antiochus's setting up of the 'abomination of desolation' on the altar is the historical realization of Daniel's prophecy and a deuterocanonical witness to the temple-desecration imagery behind Paul's man of sin.
sourceText: And on the fifteenth day of Chislev, in the hundred and forty and fifth year, they built an abomination of desolation upon the altar, and in the cities of Judah on every side they built idol altars.

note: The wider Maccabean apostasy narrative, where many abandon the law, can stand behind Paul's 'departure/rebellion' that comes first; faint and analogical.
sourceText: and many of Israel consented to his worship, and sacrificed to the idols, and profaned the Sabbath.

note: The vision that 'awaits its appointed time' and will not delay may inform Paul's notion of the lawless one being revealed 'in his own season' and the present restraint. Conceptual parallel of an appointed eschatological moment.
sourceText: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
lxxText: For the vision is yet for a time, and it shall shoot forth at the end, and not in vain: though he should tarry, wait for him; for he will surely come, and will not tarry.

note: Daniel's testing 'until the time of the end, for it is yet for the appointed time' parallels the idea that the revelation of the lawless one waits for its set season.
sourceText: Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.

note: The clause 'till the indignation is accomplished, for what is determined shall be done' supplies a sense of restraint until an appointed limit, paralleling Paul's restrainer holding back until the set time.
sourceText: The king shall do according to his will; and he shall exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak marvelous things against the God of gods; and he shall prosper until the indignation be accomplished; for that which is determined shall be done.

note: 'The Lord will kill with the breath of his mouth' draws almost verbatim on the messianic ruler who 'with the breath of his lips shall kill the wicked.' Paul applies Isaiah's portrait of the slaying breath of the Branch directly to Christ's destruction of the lawless one.
sourceText: but with righteousness he will judge the poor, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked.

note: 'By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed' parallels destruction by the divine breath. A complementary source for the slaying-breath image.
sourceText: By the breath of God they perish. By the blast of his anger are they consumed.

note: The Lord's breath like an overflowing stream and devouring fire executing judgment resonates with destruction by the breath of his mouth; faint.
sourceText: Behold, Yahweh’s name comes from far away, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke. His lips are full of indignation, and his tongue is as a devouring fire. His breath is as an overflowing stream that reaches even to the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of destruction; and a bridle that leads to ruin will be in the jaws of the peoples.

note: The breath of the Lord kindling the pyre for the king (Topheth) parallels the breath that destroys the eschatological tyrant.
sourceText: For his burning place has long been ready. Yes, for the king it is prepared. He has made its pyre deep and large with fire and much wood. Yahweh’s breath, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.

note: 'By the breath of his mouth all the host' were made; here the same creative-destroying breath of the mouth is turned to judgment. Verbal echo of 'breath of his mouth.'
sourceText: By Yahweh’s word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth.

note: The false prophet who performs 'signs and wonders' to lead people astray, sent as a test, closely informs the lawless one's coming 'with all power and signs and lying wonders' and the resulting deception. Deuteronomy's framework of God permitting deceptive signs to test loyalty is foundational.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.

note: Pharaoh's magicians counterfeiting Moses' signs is the paradigm of 'lying wonders' opposing God's truth, standing behind Satan's deceptive power in the lawless one.
sourceText: Then Pharaoh also called for the wise men and the sorcerers. They also, the magicians of Egypt, did the same thing with their enchantments. For they each cast down their rods, and they became serpents: but Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods.

note: The magicians replicating the sign 'by their secret arts,' hardening resistance to God, parallels the counterfeit signs that deceive those who reject the truth.
sourceText: The magicians of Egypt did the same thing with their enchantments; and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them; as Yahweh had spoken.

note: The horn that destroys 'by his cunning' and prospers through deceit parallels the lawless one operating with deception and false wonders.
sourceText: His power shall be mighty, but not by his own power; and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper in what he does; and he shall destroy the mighty ones and the holy people. Through his policy he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand; and he shall magnify himself in his heart, and he shall destroy many in their security. He shall also stand up against the prince of princes; but he shall be broken without hand.

note: God's judicial hardening so that the people hear but do not understand underlies Paul's 'God sends them a working of error, that they should believe a lie.' The motif of divinely-sent blindness on those who reject truth is central.
sourceText: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”

note: The Lord pouring out a 'spirit of deep sleep,' closing eyes, parallels the strong delusion God sends so that they believe what is false. Judicial stupefaction is the shared idea.
sourceText: For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers.

note: The 'lying spirit' the Lord puts in the mouth of the prophets to entice Ahab to his doom is a close parallel to God sending a 'working of error' so they believe a lie unto judgment. God's sovereign use of deception against the condemned is the shared logic.
sourceText: Yahweh said to him, ‘How?’ He said, ‘I will go out and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ He said, ‘You will entice him, and will also prevail. Go out and do so.’ Now therefore, behold, Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; and Yahweh has spoken evil concerning you.”

note: 'If the prophet is deceived... I the Lord have deceived that prophet' supplies the same theology of divinely-sent delusion upon those who turn from God, directly paralleling Paul's God-sent error.
sourceText: If the prophet is deceived and speak a word, I, Yahweh, have deceived that prophet, and I will stretch out my hand on him, and will destroy him from the midst of my people Israel.

note: The parallel account of the lying spirit permitted by the Lord to deceive Ahab's prophets reinforces the source for God sending a delusion that leads to judgment.
sourceText: “He said, ‘I will go, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ “He said, ‘You will entice him, and will prevail also. Go and do so.’ “Now therefore, behold, Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets; and Yahweh has spoken evil concerning you.”

note: The Lord hardening Pharaoh's heart so he will not believe parallels God sending a working of error so that they believe the lie and are condemned. The Pharaoh-hardening pattern stands behind judicial delusion.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “When you go back into Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders which I have put in your hand, but I will harden his heart and he will not let the people go.

note: 'I will harden Pharaoh's heart' continues the hardening motif that informs the God-sent delusion upon unbelievers; faint and analogical.
sourceText: I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.

note: The idolaters whose eyes are shut so they cannot understand, feeding on ashes and a 'deluded heart,' parallels those who believe the lie; faint.
sourceText: They don’t know, neither do they consider: for he has shut their eyes, that they can’t see; and their hearts, that they can’t understand. No one thinks, neither is there knowledge nor understanding to say, “I have burned part of it in the fire. Yes, I have also baked bread on its coals. I have roasted meat and eaten it. Shall I make the rest of it into an abomination? Shall I bow down to a tree trunk?” He feeds on ashes. A deceived heart has turned him […]

note: God 'chose you' not for your numbers but in love is the election language behind 'God chose you from the beginning for salvation.' Paul transposes Israel's election to the believing community.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth. Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples:

note: The Lord taking Israel as his treasured, holy people set high for praise and glory parallels the choosing for salvation and obtaining glory. The covenant-election frame with firstfruits context (Deut 26) resonates.
sourceText: Yahweh has declared this day that you are a people for his own possession, as he has promised you, and that you should keep all his commandments. He will make you high above all nations that he has made, in praise, in name, and in honor; and that you may be a holy people to Yahweh your God, as he has spoken.

note: A textual variant of v.13 reads 'as firstfruits' (aparchen) rather than 'from the beginning'; the firstfruits offering commanded here would then stand behind believers chosen as firstfruits for salvation.
sourceText: that you shall take some of the first of all the fruit of the ground, which you shall bring in from your land that Yahweh your God gives you. You shall put it in a basket, and shall go to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there.

note: Israel as 'the firstfruits of his harvest, holy to the Lord' parallels the firstfruits-for-salvation reading of v.13. Supports the variant in which believers are God's elect firstfruits.
sourceText: Israel was holiness to Yahweh, the first fruits of his increase. All who devour him shall be held guilty. Evil shall come on them,”’ says Yahweh.”

note: 'The Lord has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession' reinforces the election language behind God's choosing the Thessalonians for salvation.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God, and Yahweh has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.

note: 'Israel, my chosen... I have chosen you and not cast you off' parallels Paul's 'God chose you... for salvation' through calling. The prophetic election-and-call pattern is applied to the church.
sourceText: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend, You whom I have taken hold of from the ends of the earth, and called from its corners, and said to you, ‘You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you away;’

note: The promise of a new spirit causing the people to walk in God's statutes parallels 'sanctification of the Spirit' as the means of salvation; faint and conceptual.
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: 'Consecrate yourselves... I am the Lord who sanctifies you' parallels sanctification as God's work in setting apart his people; faint.
sourceText: “‘Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am Yahweh your God. You shall keep my statutes, and do them. I am Yahweh who sanctifies you.

note: 'Stand firm and see the salvation of the Lord' offers a verbal-conceptual parallel to Paul's exhortation to 'stand firm,' though Paul's idiom is broadly Septuagintal.
sourceText: Moses said to the people, “Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today: for the Egyptians whom you have seen today, you shall never see them again.

note: 'I, I am he who comforts you' lies behind 'God our Father... who gave us eternal comfort.' The divine self-designation as the comforter of his people resonates with Paul's benediction.
sourceText: “I, even I, am he who comforts you: who are you, that you are afraid of man who shall die, and of the son of man who shall be made as grass;

note: 'Comfort, comfort my people' establishes the prophetic theme of divine consolation that informs 'eternal comfort and good hope.'
sourceText: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.

note: 'The Lord has comforted his people' continues the Isaianic consolation motif behind God's gift of eternal comfort; faint.
sourceText: Sing, heavens; and be joyful, earth; and break out into singing, mountains: for Yahweh has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his afflicted.

note: 'As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you' parallels the divine comfort Paul invokes; faint.
sourceText: As one whom his mother comforts, so will I comfort you; and you will be comforted in Jerusalem.”

note: 'His heart is established/steady' parallels the prayer that God 'establish your hearts.' A possible Septuagintal verbal echo (sterizo/heart).
sourceText: His heart is established. He will not be afraid in the end when he sees his adversaries.

note: Paul asks that 'the word of the Lord may spread rapidly (lit. run) and be glorified.' The psalm pictures God sending his command to the earth, his word running swiftly. The shared image of the divine word personified as a swift runner is striking and likely deliberate.
sourceText: He sends out his commandment to the earth. His word runs very swiftly.

note: Isaiah's word that goes out from God's mouth and does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose underlies Paul's confidence that the gospel word will run and be glorified. The efficacious, mission-accomplishing word is the conceptual backdrop.
sourceText: so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: Paul's plea to be 'delivered from unreasonable and evil men' echoes the psalmist's prayer to be rescued from evil and violent men. A common lament idiom rather than a specific citation.
sourceText: Deliver me, Yahweh, from the evil man. Preserve me from the violent man;

note: 'But the Lord is faithful' draws on the covenantal confession that the Lord is the faithful God who keeps covenant. The predicate 'faithful' (pistos) of God is rooted in this Deuteronomic and broader OT formula of divine covenant fidelity.
sourceText: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,

note: 'The Lord... will guard you from the evil one' echoes the psalm's promise that the Lord will keep/guard you from all evil and will keep your life. The verb of divine guarding (phylasso) against evil is the shared note; Paul personalizes 'evil' as 'the evil one.'
sourceText: Yahweh will keep you from all evil. He will keep your soul.

note: 'May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God' recalls David's prayer that the Lord direct/establish the hearts of the people toward himself. The idiom of God directing the human heart toward devotion is the link.
sourceText: Yahweh, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Israel, our fathers, keep this forever in the imagination of the thoughts of the heart of your people, and prepare their heart for you;

note: The notion that the Lord 'directs' a person's heart/steps, while the human plans, lies behind Paul's wish that the Lord direct their hearts. A wisdom commonplace about divine guidance of the inner life.
sourceText: A man’s heart plans his course, but Yahweh directs his steps.

note: 'If anyone will not work, neither let him eat' rests on the primeval verdict that by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread. The post-Eden link between toil and bread is the theological ground of Paul's labor rule, including his own working night and day for his bread.
sourceText: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

note: The wisdom contrast between the slack/idle hand bringing poverty and the diligent hand bringing wealth underlies Paul's rebuke of those who refuse to work. Proverbs' sustained ethic of diligence vs. sloth shapes his command.
sourceText: He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth.

note: The sluggard sent to the ant, who provides her food by labor, and the warning that poverty comes on the lazy, parallels Paul's portrait of the idle who refuse to work. A central sloth-condemning passage in the wisdom tradition.
sourceText: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.

note: 'Idleness casts into a deep sleep, and the slack person will go hungry' closely mirrors Paul's pairing of idleness with not eating. A pointed wisdom maxim on the cost of laziness.
sourceText: Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep. The idle soul shall suffer hunger.

note: 'Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty' echoes Paul's bread-and-work logic and his complaint about busybodies pursuing nothing useful.
sourceText: One who works his land will have an abundance of food; but one who chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty.

note: Ben Sira urges putting an idle servant to work lest idleness teach mischief, since idleness breeds trouble. This deuterocanonical labor wisdom is close in spirit to Paul's treatment of the idle who become busybodies.
sourceText: Send him to labor, that he be not idle; For idleness teaches much mischief. Set him to work, as is fit for him; And if he obey not, make his fetters heavy.

note: 'Don't be weary in doing well' may echo Isaiah's promise that those who wait on the Lord will renew strength, run and not be weary, walk and not faint. The shared vocabulary of not growing weary is suggestive but the Isaian context is endurance, not active well-doing.
sourceText: But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

note: 'Don't count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother' enacts the Holiness Code command not to hate your brother in your heart but to reason with/reprove your neighbor. The pattern of corrective rebuke that preserves fraternal love is the same.
sourceText: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.

note: 'May the Lord of peace himself give you peace' draws on the Aaronic blessing, where the Lord lifts up his countenance upon you and gives you peace. Paul reshapes the priestly benediction's gift of shalom into a benediction from the 'Lord of peace.'
sourceText: Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: Gideon's altar named 'The Lord is Peace' (YHWH-shalom) supplies a precedent for the divine title 'Lord of peace.' The naming of God by peace is the conceptual link, though Paul's phrasing is his own.
sourceText: Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

note: 'The Lord be with you all' echoes the customary Israelite greeting/blessing, as when Boaz greets the reapers, 'The Lord be with you.' A liturgical-blessing formula rather than a quotation.
sourceText: Behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and said to the reapers, “Yahweh be with you.” They answered him, “Yahweh bless you.”

note: The title 'God our Savior' draws on the Septuagintal designation of YHWH as the saving God, where Israel forgot 'God his Savior.' Paul transfers the covenantal epithet for God to the gospel framing of the letter. The phrase recurs through 1 Timothy and is rooted in OT salvation language.
sourceText: But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked. You have grown fat. You have grown thick. You have become sleek. Then he abandoned God who made him, and rejected the Rock of his salvation.

note: 'God our Savior' echoes the Psalter's repeated address to the LORD as 'God of my salvation,' grounding the apostolic greeting in Israel's confession. The link is thematic rather than verbal. Marked low/contested as the title is a general OT topos.
sourceText: Guide me in your truth, and teach me, For you are the God of my salvation, I wait for you all day long.

note: The triadic blessing 'grace, mercy, and peace' expands the Aaronic benediction, which invokes the LORD's favor (grace) and peace upon Israel. Paul's epistolary greeting Christianizes the priestly blessing. The added 'mercy' reflects OT covenant-mercy vocabulary.
sourceText: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: The warning against 'endless genealogies' presupposes the OT genealogical literature (the toledoth lists of Genesis) that later speculative interpreters elaborated. Paul rejects the misuse of such material for fruitless dispute. The genealogies of Genesis are the textual seedbed of the practice opposed.
sourceText: This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, he made him in God’s likeness.

note: The 'myths and endless genealogies' likely targets Second Temple genealogical embellishments like those reworking Genesis lineages in Jubilees. Paul opposes this haggadic expansion of the patriarchal lists. Cited as a pseudepigraphal parallel illustrating the practice, not a direct source.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: The goal of the charge, 'love out of a pure heart,' draws on the cultic ideal of the one with 'clean hands and a pure heart' who may ascend the LORD's hill. Paul makes inward purity the aim of sound teaching. The phrase 'pure heart' is a direct OT moral-cultic category.
sourceText: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.

note: 'A pure heart' echoes David's penitential plea, 'Create in me a clean heart, O God.' The renewed, purified heart is the locus of the love that fulfills the law. Paul presupposes this OT theology of inward cleansing.
sourceText: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.

note: Naming love as the 'goal' of the commandment recalls the Torah's own summary command to love the neighbor, which the NT treats as the law's fulfillment. The teachers of the law have missed the law's true telos. The echo grounds Paul's contrast between love and vain dispute.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: Love as the aim of the divine charge resonates with the Shema's command to love God wholeheartedly, the foundational Torah demand. Paul recasts the would-be law-teachers' failure as missing this central love. A thematic echo undergirding the love/law relationship.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: The affirmation 'the law is good' echoes Moses' praise of Israel's righteous statutes as a unique gift among the nations. Paul affirms the law's goodness while qualifying its proper use. The OT background secures the positive valuation of Torah.
sourceText: What great nation is there, that has statutes and ordinances so righteous as all this law, which I set before you this day?

note: 'The law is good' recalls the Psalter's celebration of the LORD's law as perfect, reviving the soul. Paul presumes this OT confession of the law's intrinsic goodness even as he restricts its application. A thematic echo of Torah-piety.
sourceText: Yahweh’s law is perfect, restoring the soul. Yahweh’s testimony is sure, making wise the simple.

note: The vice list of vv. 9-10 tracks the second table of the Decalogue in order: dishonoring parents, killing, sexual sin, stealing (men-stealing), false witness. Paul structures the catalogue of the lawless on the Ten Commandments. The Exodus Decalogue is the organizing template.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.

note: The Deuteronomic recension of the Decalogue equally underlies the vice list's sequence (honor parents, no killing, no adultery, no stealing, no false witness). Paul's catalogue mirrors this commandment order. Cited alongside Exodus 20 as the dual Decalogue source.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.

note: 'Murderers of fathers and mothers' specifically reflects the capital statute against one who strikes father or mother, an intensification of the fifth commandment. Paul names the most flagrant breakers of the parent-honoring command. The Covenant Code furnishes the exact category.
sourceText: “Anyone who attacks his father or his mother shall be surely put to death.

note: 'Slave-traders' (men-stealers) corresponds to the capital law against one who steals and sells a person, the concrete form of the prohibition against stealing. Paul places kidnapping/enslaving at the stealing slot of the Decalogue sequence. The Exodus statute is the legal source.
sourceText: “Anyone who kidnaps someone and sells him, or if he is found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.

note: The man-stealer/slave-trader echoes the Deuteronomic capital law against kidnapping a fellow Israelite to enslave or sell him. This grounds the 'enslavers' entry in the vice list. Cited with Exodus 21:16 as the Torah basis for condemning man-stealing.
sourceText: If a man is found stealing any of his brothers of the children of Israel, and he deals with him as a slave, or sells him; then that thief shall die. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.

note: 'The sexually immoral, homosexuals' draws on the Holiness Code's prohibition of male same-sex intercourse as part of the sexual-purity legislation behind the adultery commandment. Paul's term reflects the Septuagint phrasing of this statute. The Levitical law informs the vocabulary.
sourceText: “‘You shall not lie with a man, as with a woman. That is detestable.

note: The condemnation of homosexual practice also echoes the parallel capital statute of the Holiness Code. The Septuagint wording of these verses is widely held to underlie the NT compound term rendered 'homosexuals.' A lexical echo of Levitical purity law.
sourceText: “‘If a man lies with a male, as with a woman, both of them have committed an abomination: they shall surely be put to death; their blood shall be upon them.

note: 'Liars and perjurers' reflects the Holiness Code's paired prohibitions against lying to one another and swearing falsely by God's name, expressions of the false-witness and name-misuse commandments. Paul groups deceit and false oaths together as the law does. The Levitical statutes shape the entry.
sourceText: “‘You shall not steal. “‘You shall not lie. “‘You shall not deceive one another. “‘You shall not swear by my name falsely, and profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh.

note: 'Perjurers' specifically transgress the commandment against taking the LORD's name in vain by false swearing. Paul's inclusion of oath-breakers reaches back to the third commandment. A targeted echo of the Decalogue's name-honoring command.
sourceText: “You shall not take the name of Yahweh your God in vain, for Yahweh will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.

note: Paul's repeated 'I obtained mercy' draws on the LORD's self-revelation as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, the foundational OT confession of divine compassion. The mercy shown to the chief of sinners enacts this character of God. Exodus 34:6 is the wellspring of biblical mercy language.
sourceText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,

note: Receiving mercy as one formerly outside it echoes Hosea's reversal where 'not pitied' becomes 'pitied' and the unloved become God's people. Paul the persecutor is the paradigm of unexpected mercy. The Hosea motif of mercy granted to the undeserving stands behind the testimony.
sourceText: I will sow her to me in the earth; and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy; and I will tell those who were not my people, ‘You are my people;’ and they will say, ‘My God!’”

note: Paul's mercy receives its texture from the Psalter's restatement of the Exodus 34 formula, 'a God merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love.' The grace that 'abounded exceedingly' resonates with this superabundant covenant mercy. A liturgical echo of the divine attributes.
sourceText: But you, Lord, are a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth.

note: The doxology to 'the King eternal' draws on the Psalter's praise that 'your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom' and the LORD's dominion endures through all generations. Paul ascribes timeless kingship to the only God. Psalm 145 supplies the eternal-king acclamation.
sourceText: Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. Your dominion endures throughout all generations. Yahweh is faithful in all his words, and loving in all his deeds.

note: 'The King eternal' echoes the climactic acclamation of the Song of the Sea, 'The LORD shall reign forever and ever.' Paul's doxology takes up Israel's primal confession of God's everlasting reign. The Exodus hymn underlies the 'forever and ever' of the praise.
sourceText: Yahweh shall reign forever and ever.”

note: Calling God 'invisible' recalls Sinai, where Israel heard the voice but 'saw no form,' the basis of OT aniconism. Paul affirms the unseeable nature of the only God. Deuteronomy's no-form theology grounds the predicate 'invisible.'
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to you out of the midst of the fire: you heard the voice of words, but you saw no form; you only heard a voice.

note: 'The only God' (God who alone is wise / only God) is the Shema's confession that the LORD is one. Paul's monotheistic doxology rests on Israel's foundational creed. The Shema secures the 'only God' acclamation.
sourceText: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.

note: Darius's decree that God 'is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed' parallels Paul's praise of the King eternal and immortal. The Aramaic court tale supplies a Gentile confession of the everlasting, deathless God. A close conceptual model for the doxology.
sourceText: I make a decree, that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel; for he is the living God, and steadfast forever, His kingdom that which shall not be destroyed; and his dominion shall be even to the end.

note: Tobit's hymn, 'Blessed be God who lives forever, for his kingdom lasts throughout all ages,' parallels the doxology's eternal, immortal King. The deuterocanonical doxology shares Paul's vocabulary of everlasting divine reign. Cited as a Second Temple liturgical analogue.
sourceText: And Tobit wrote a prayer for rejoicing, and said, “Blessed is God who lives forever! Blessed is his kingdom!

note: 'He who lives forever created all things together' offers a deuterocanonical parallel to ascribing eternity and sole deity to God. The wisdom tradition's praise of the everliving Creator stands near Paul's doxology. A faint thematic echo from Second Temple piety.
sourceText: He that lives forever created all things in common.

note: 'Christ came to save sinners' resonates with the prophetic invitation in which scarlet sins are made white as snow, the OT promise of cleansing for the guilty. Paul as foremost sinner receives this promised pardon. A contested thematic echo of prophetic forgiveness.
sourceText: “Come now, and let us reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

note: Paul's self-identification as 'foremost' of sinners yet shown mercy recalls the prophetic remnant spared by the LORD's grace despite Sodom-like guilt. The pattern of mercy preserving the unworthy underlies the testimony. Marked low as a diffuse echo.
sourceText: Unless Yahweh of Armies had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom; we would have been like Gomorrah.

note: Handing Hymenaeus and Alexander 'over to Satan' so they may be disciplined echoes the LORD's delivering of Job into Satan's power within set limits for a corrective end. The motif of God permitting satanic affliction for a purpose informs the disciplinary act. Job supplies the pattern of a measured handing-over.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life.”

note: The handing of the blasphemers to Satan also recalls the first heavenly grant, where the LORD places Job's possessions in Satan's hand. The bounded delegation of the accuser's power undergirds Paul's act of church discipline. A secondary echo of the Job prologue.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don’t stretch out your hand.” So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh.

note: The figure of Satan as adversary against whom the LORD rebukes and from whom a 'brand' is plucked offers an OT backdrop to delivering offenders to Satan for their ultimate restoration. The corrective rather than destructive aim parallels Paul's intent. A contested figural echo.
sourceText: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”

note: The exhortation to 'wage the good warfare' draws on the OT theme of the LORD's battle, where 'the battle is the LORD's,' transposed into spiritual struggle. Timothy's fight is framed by Israel's holy-war language. A faint metaphorical echo.
sourceText: and that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn’t save with sword and spear: for the battle is Yahweh’s, and he will give you into our hand.”

note: Paul's directive to pray for kings and all in high places that believers may lead a tranquil life echoes Jeremiah's letter urging the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon and pray to the LORD for it, because in its peace they will find peace. Both texts ground intercession for pagan rulers in the community's own well-being under foreign power. The logic of praying for the governing authority's order so that God's people may flourish is structurally identical.
sourceText: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it; for in its peace you shall have peace.

note: The Persian decree provides for sacrifices and prayers 'for the life of the king and his sons,' a precedent for the synagogue practice of intercession for the ruling power that Paul commends to the church. This institutionalized prayer for the Gentile monarch stands behind the apostolic instruction. The continuity of Jewish intercession for kings informs the exhortation.
sourceText: that they may offer sacrifices of pleasant aroma to the God of heaven, and pray for the life of the king, and of his sons.

note: Baruch directs prayer for the life of Nebuchadnezzar and his son Belshazzar, that the exiles may live under their shadow and find favor, mirroring the petition for kings so believers can live quietly. The deuterocanonical text models the very practice of interceding for a foreign sovereign's reign for the sake of the people's peace. It is a close conceptual parallel to verses 1-2.
sourceText: and pray for the life of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and for the life of Baltasar his son, that their days may be as the days of heaven above the earth: and the Lord will give us strength, and lighten our eyes, and we shall live under the shadow of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and under the shadow of Baltasar his son, and we shall serve them many days, and find favor in their sight.

note: The conviction that the king's heart is a watercourse in the LORD's hand, turned wherever he wills, undergirds the rationale for praying for rulers: God can move them toward conditions of peace. Paul's confidence that prayer for kings yields a tranquil life presupposes divine sovereignty over rulers. The link is thematic rather than verbal and is faint.
sourceText: The king’s heart is in Yahweh’s hand like the watercourses. He turns it wherever he desires.

note: God's declared desire that all be saved and come to knowledge of the truth echoes the LORD's protest that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn and live. Both passages assert a universal divine will for life and salvation rather than condemnation. Verse 32 of the same chapter reinforces this with the appeal to turn and live.
sourceText: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? says the Lord Yahweh; and not rather that he should return from his way, and live?

note: The oath 'As I live, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live' restates the divine saving desire that Paul invokes in saying God wills all people to be saved. The emphatic divine self-witness to a will for repentance and life parallels Paul's theology of God our Savior. It complements the Ezekiel 18 echo.
sourceText: Tell them, As I live, says the Lord Yahweh, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn, turn from your evil ways; for why will you die, house of Israel?

note: The call 'Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth, for I am God and there is no other' fuses the universal saving will with strict monotheism, precisely the pairing Paul makes in 'who desires all to be saved' and 'there is one God.' Isaiah's universal salvation offer grounded in the oneness of God stands directly behind this passage. The verbal and theological overlap is strong.
sourceText: “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.

note: 'There is one God' restates the Shema's confession that the LORD is one, the foundational monotheistic creed of Israel. Paul reframes the Shema christologically by adding the one mediator, but the bedrock affirmation of divine oneness is directly drawn from Deuteronomy. This is the clearest scriptural anchor of verse 5.
sourceText: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.

note: 'Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?' offers a parallel monotheistic confession linked to the unity of humanity, resonant with Paul's 'one God' grounding the universality of salvation. The pairing of divine oneness with the common bond of all people overlaps with the passage. The connection is thematic and secondary to the Shema.
sourceText: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?

note: Job's lament that 'there is no umpire between us, who might lay his hand on us both' articulates the need for a mediator between God and man that Paul declares fulfilled in the one mediator Christ Jesus. The longing for an arbitrator standing between God and humanity is answered in verse 5. The conceptual correspondence to 'one mediator' is notable though not verbal quotation.
sourceText: There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both.

note: Moses standing between the LORD and the people, offering himself to make atonement for their sin, typifies the role of the one mediator that Paul ascribes to Christ. The Mosaic mediation at Sinai is the paradigmatic Old Testament instance of a man interceding between God and men. Christ as mediator is read against this figural background.
sourceText: On the next day, Moses said to the people, “You have sinned a great sin. Now I will go up to Yahweh. Perhaps I shall make atonement for your sin.” Moses returned to Yahweh, and said, “Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made themselves gods of gold. Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”

note: Moses' statement that he stood between the LORD and the people to declare the word, because they feared the fire, presents him as mediator of the covenant, prefiguring the one mediator language. The Mosaic mediatorial office informs Paul's category. The link is figural and faint.
sourceText: (I stood between Yahweh and you at that time, to show you Yahweh’s word: for you were afraid because of the fire, and didn’t go up onto the mountain;) saying,

note: The atonement money, a ransom for each life given at the census so that no plague befall them, supplies the cultic background for Christ giving himself as 'a ransom for all.' The Hebrew kopher / lytron concept of a redemptive price for life stands behind Paul's ransom language. The universalizing 'for all' extends the Exodus ransom to all humanity.
sourceText: “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.

note: The Servant who makes his life an offering for sin and bears the sin of many provides the scriptural template for Christ giving himself as a ransom for all. The substitutionary self-offering 'for many' is universalized by Paul to 'for all.' The Servant Song is a primary source for the ransom theology of verse 6.
sourceText: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]

note: The psalm's note that no one can by any means ransom another or give to God a price for his life sets up, by contrast, the ransom that Christ alone provides 'for all.' Paul's ransom claim answers the human impossibility the psalm laments. The link is conceptual and contrastive.
sourceText: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough,

note: The summons to 'lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD' is the posture Paul prescribes when he calls men to pray 'lifting up holy hands.' The gesture of uplifted hands in worship is a fixed Old Testament image of prayer. Paul's qualifier 'holy' draws on the cultic demand for purity in the hands that are raised.
sourceText: Lift up your hands in the sanctuary. Praise Yahweh!

note: 'Hear the voice of my supplications when I lift up my hands toward your holy sanctuary' directly models the praying posture of uplifted hands. The coupling of supplication with raised hands matches Paul's instruction. It is among the closest verbal parallels to the gesture in verse 8.
sourceText: Hear the voice of my petitions, when I cry to you, when I lift up my hands toward your Most Holy Place.

note: 'I will lift up my hands in your name' expresses the same gesture of prayer and blessing that Paul commends. The psalmist's lifted hands in devotion parallel the men's lifted holy hands. It reinforces the conventional posture echoed here.
sourceText: So I will bless you while I live. I will lift up my hands in your name.

note: 'Let the lifting up of my hands be as the evening sacrifice' ties uplifted hands to acceptable worship, matching Paul's vision of prayer with holy hands. The equation of raised hands with pleasing sacrifice undergirds the call to pray rightly. It complements the other Psalm parallels.
sourceText: Let my prayer be set before you like incense; the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice.

note: The LORD's refusal to hear when 'you spread out your hands' because they are 'full of blood' supplies the negative counterpart to Paul's demand that hands be 'holy... without anger.' Lifted hands stained by violence are rejected; lifted holy hands are required. The condition of moral purity behind acceptable prayer is drawn from this oracle.
sourceText: When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you. Yes, when you make many prayers, I will not hear. Your hands are full of blood.

note: The requirement of 'clean hands and a pure heart' to ascend the LORD's hill informs Paul's insistence on 'holy hands without anger and doubting.' The cultic standard of pure hands for approaching God shapes the qualification on prayer. The moral-ritual purity link is the point of contact.
sourceText: Who may ascend to Yahweh’s hill? Who may stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.

note: 'Let us lift up our heart with our hands to God in the heavens' offers another instance of the uplifted-hands prayer posture, with an added inward orientation paralleling Paul's concern for the disposition behind the gesture. The combined outward gesture and inner attitude resonates with verse 8. The parallel is supportive and faint.
sourceText: Let us lift up our heart with our hands to God in the heavens.

note: Abram's 'I have lifted up my hand to the LORD' shows the raised hand as a gesture of solemn appeal to God, a background image for the praying hands. The connection is to gesture-vocabulary rather than to the worship setting and is faint. It is offered maximally.
sourceText: Abram said to the king of Sodom, “I have lifted up my hand to Yahweh, God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth,

note: The oracle against the haughty daughters of Zion with their finery, ornaments, headdresses, and jewelry, stripped away in judgment, stands behind Paul's call that women not adorn themselves with braided hair, gold, and costly attire. The catalogue of external feminine ornament condemned by Isaiah parallels Paul's list. The prophetic critique of ostentatious adornment shapes the instruction.
sourceText: Moreover Yahweh said, “Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with outstretched necks and flirting eyes, walking to trip as they go, jingling ornaments on their feet; therefore the Lord brings sores on the crown of the head of the women of Zion, and Yahweh will make their scalps bald.” In that day the Lord will take away the beauty of their anklets, the headbands, the crescent necklaces, the earrings, the bracelets, the veils, the […]

note: 'Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD shall be praised' contrasts outward appearance with godly character exactly as Paul opposes external adornment to 'good works' becoming women professing godliness. The valued woman is praised for fearing God, not for looks, matching verse 10. The wisdom ideal of inner piety over display informs the passage.
sourceText: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a woman who fears Yahweh, she shall be praised.

note: The capable woman 'clothed with strength and dignity' offers the image of inner moral clothing that Paul prefers to braided hair and gold. The metaphor of being adorned with virtue rather than ornament parallels 'adorn... with good works.' It reinforces the wisdom contrast underlying verses 9-10.
sourceText: Strength and dignity are her clothing. She laughs at the time to come.

note: The gold nose-ring and bracelets given to Rebekah illustrate the gold ornamentation Paul names, providing a narrative instance of the adornment vocabulary. The link is to the items listed rather than to any critique. It is offered maximally and is faint.
sourceText: As the camels had done drinking, the man took a golden ring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold,

note: Ben Sira's praise of a wife whose true beauty is her modesty and good character, more than physical charm, parallels Paul's preference for good works over outward adornment. The deuterocanonical wisdom contrast between modest virtue and external display resonates with verses 9-10. The connection is thematic.
sourceText: The grace of a wife will delight her husband; And her knowledge will fatten his bones. A silent woman is a gift of the Lord; And there is nothing so much worth as a well-instructed soul. A shamefast woman is grace upon grace; And there is no price worthy of a continent soul. As the sun when it arises in the highest places of the Lord, So is the beauty of a good wife in the ordering of a man’s house. As the lamp that shineth upon the holy candlestick, So […]

note: Paul's argument 'Adam was first formed' rests on the account of the LORD God forming the man from the dust and breathing life into him. The verb and the priority of Adam's formation are taken directly from the creation narrative. This is the scriptural basis for 'Adam was first formed, then Eve.'
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: The making of the woman from the man's side as a helper, after the man, supplies the order of formation Paul invokes ('then Eve'). The sequence of creation, with woman fashioned after and from Adam, is the load-bearing premise of his appeal. The passage is quoted in substance.
sourceText: Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.” Out of the ground Yahweh God formed every animal of the field, and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. Whatever the man called every living creature became its name. The man gave names to all livestock, and to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for man there was not found a helper […]

note: Eve's seeing, taking, and eating the fruit grounds Paul's claim that 'the woman, being deceived, has fallen into disobedience.' The narrative of her being drawn in by the fruit is the event Paul interprets. It anchors the deception-and-transgression argument of verse 14.
sourceText: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate; and she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.

note: Eve's confession 'the serpent deceived me, and I ate' is the direct source of Paul's 'the woman, being deceived, has fallen into disobedience.' The motif of the woman's deception is lifted from her own words in the Fall account. This is the closest verbal dependence in the pericope.
sourceText: Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

note: The sentence on the woman, 'in pain you shall bring forth children,' and the rule of the husband over her, underlies both 'saved through her childbearing' and the call to subjection. Paul reads the curse of painful childbearing as the very sphere of the woman's salvation. The verse is central to verse 15.
sourceText: To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. In pain you will bear children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

note: The protoevangelium promising the woman's seed who will crush the serpent's head can stand behind 'saved through childbearing' if 'the childbearing' is read as the bearing of the promised seed. The hope of redemption arising from the woman's offspring frames the saving childbearing. The reading is figural and contested.
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: Adam naming his wife Eve, 'because she was the mother of all living,' resonates with the elevation of childbearing as the woman's vocation and avenue of salvation. The link between Eve and life-giving motherhood supports verse 15. The connection is faint and thematic.
sourceText: The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living.

note: The creation of humanity male and female in God's image offers an alternative creation datum that some weigh against the formation-order argument; Paul, however, builds on the Genesis 2 sequence rather than the simultaneous creation of Genesis 1. It is noted as a relevant background text. The relation is contrastive and faint.
sourceText: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: Jethro's criteria for appointing leaders over Israel — capable, God-fearing, trustworthy men who hate dishonest gain — supply the scriptural template for the qualified overseer. The cluster of 'without reproach,' 'not greedy for money,' and good character closely tracks this paradigm of vetted communal leadership.
sourceText: Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

note: Moses' charge to select 'wise, understanding, and respected men' as heads parallels the demand that the overseer be sensible and have good testimony. A secondary witness to the same leader-selection topos as Exodus 18.
sourceText: Take wise men of understanding and well known according to your tribes, and I will make them heads over you.”

note: 'Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall' underwrites the warning that a new convert, being puffed up, may 'fall into the same condemnation as the devil.' The pride-then-fall logic is the wisdom commonplace Paul deploys.
sourceText: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.

note: The fall of the Day Star, brought down to Sheol for his self-exalting ambition, lies behind 'the condemnation of the devil' when read through later traditions identifying this figure with Satan's primal pride. Contested because Isaiah's oracle targets the king of Babylon; the diabolical reading is a development.
sourceText: How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.

note: The counsel that rulers should not crave wine lest they pervert judgment resonates with 'not a drinker' among qualifications for one who governs God's household. A faint thematic link within the broader wisdom critique of drunken leadership.
sourceText: It is not for kings, Lemuel; it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes to say, ‘Where is strong drink?’ lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the justice due to anyone who is afflicted.

note: Abraham is chosen precisely because he will 'command his children and his household' to keep the way of the LORD — a faint figural anticipation of the principle that one who rules his own house well is fit to care for the assembly of God.
sourceText: For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of Yahweh, to do righteousness and justice; to the end that Yahweh may bring on Abraham that which he has spoken of him.”

note: The 'snare of the fowler' from which God delivers feeds the imagery of 'the snare of the devil' into which the disreputable overseer may fall. Faint; 'snare' is a common metaphor shared with Proverbs 29:25.
sourceText: For he will deliver you from the snare of the fowler, and from the deadly pestilence.

note: Ben Sira's warning against being called 'double-tongued' (dilogos / the slanderer's two-faced speech) directly parallels the deacon requirement 'not double-tongued.' The deuterocanonical wisdom tradition is the nearest verbal antecedent for this rare moral term.
sourceText: Be not called a whisperer; And lie not in wait with your tongue: For upon the thief there is shame, And an evil condemnation upon him that has a double tongue.

note: 'A gossip betrays a confidence, but the trustworthy keep a secret' undergirds both 'not double-tongued' for deacons and 'not slanderers' for the women. The contrast of the talebearer against the faithful person is the wisdom backdrop.
sourceText: One who brings gossip betrays a confidence, but one who is of a trustworthy spirit is one who keeps a secret.

note: The 'not greedy for money' (lit. 'not greedy for dishonest gain') required of deacons echoes Jethro's stipulation that leaders 'hate bribes/dishonest gain,' extending the same integrity standard from overseers to assistants.
sourceText: Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

note: 'The living God' — a recurring covenant epithet first voiced at Horeb ('who has heard the voice of the living God?') — names the church as 'the assembly of the living God.' The phrase carries the Sinai contrast between Israel's true God and lifeless idols.
sourceText: For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?

note: Solomon's two bronze pillars Jachin ('he establishes') and Boaz ('in him is strength') at the temple porch supply the architectural image behind the church as 'the pillar and ground of the truth.' The temple/pillar metaphor casts the assembly as the structure that upholds revealed truth.
sourceText: He set up the pillars at the porch of the temple: and he set up the right pillar, and called its name Jachin; and he set up the left pillar, and called its name Boaz.

note: Wisdom 'has built her house, she has hewn her seven pillars' lends a sapiential resonance to 'house of God' as a pillared structure of truth. Faint and secondary to the temple-pillar imagery.
sourceText: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars.

note: 'You ascended on high, leading captives' stands behind the hymn's closing 'received up in glory,' the standard OT ascent-text in early Christian exaltation language. Faint because the verbal contact is thematic (ascent/glory) rather than quotation.
sourceText: You have ascended on high. You have led away captives. You have received gifts among men, yes, among the rebellious also, that Yah God might dwell there.

note: The one like a son of man presented before the Ancient of Days and given dominion, served by 'all peoples, nations, and languages,' figurally anticipates the hymn's arc — seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, received up in glory. A heavenly enthronement pattern rather than a citation.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: The Servant before whom nations and kings are startled, who is 'proclaimed' where unheard, faintly underlies 'preached among the nations, believed on in the world.' A thin link to the Isaianic mission-to-the-nations motif.
sourceText: so shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they understand.

note: The Spirit's prediction that 'in later times some will fall away from the faith' draws on Danielic apocalyptic, where a refining apostasy precedes 'the time of the end' (Dan 11:35; 12:1, 4). The pattern of a foretold falling-away in the last days shapes the Pastoral's eschatological framing.
sourceText: Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.
