note: The rise of deceptive, conscience-seared teachers in the latter time may echo Daniel's vision of a deceitful power arising 'at the latter end' of the apostasy who works ruin by cunning. A faint structural parallel rather than a verbal one.
sourceText: In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up. His power shall be mighty, but not by his own power; and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper in what he does; and he shall destroy the mighty ones and the holy people. Through his policy he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand; and he shall magnify himself in his heart, and he shall […]

note: 'Doctrines of demons' and 'seducing spirits' resonate with the Song of Moses, where Israel 'sacrificed to demons (shedim), not God, to gods they had not known.' The apostate teaching is figured as worship of demonic powers behind false religion.
sourceText: They sacrificed to demons, not God, to gods that they didn’t know, to new gods that came up recently, which your fathers didn’t dread.

note: The idea of devotion redirected to demons recalls the psalmist's indictment that Israel 'sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons.' A reinforcing echo of the OT motif of demonic deception lying behind false cult.
sourceText: Yes, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.

note: 'Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected' directly recalls God's verdict over creation, 'God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.' Paul grounds the rejection of food asceticism in the original goodness of all created things.
sourceText: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.

note: The claim that God created foods 'to be received with thanksgiving' echoes the post-flood grant, 'Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you; as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything.' This universal grant of food undergirds the rejection of forbidden-food asceticism.
sourceText: Every moving thing that lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green herb, I have given everything to you.

note: The divine provision of foods 'which God created to be received' recalls the original grant of every seed-bearing plant and tree for food. The created order itself is the warrant for eating with thanksgiving.
sourceText: God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.

note: The reception of food 'with thanksgiving' and its sanctification 'through prayer' draws on the command, 'You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you.' The blessing/thanksgiving over food is the OT practice presupposed.
sourceText: You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless Yahweh your God for the good land which he has given you.

note: The condemnation of those 'forbidding marriage' implicitly appeals to God's own institution of marriage, 'It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper.' Asceticism that bans marriage contradicts the Creator's design.
sourceText: Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

note: Forbidding marriage runs against the creational blessing, 'Be fruitful and multiply.' A faint echo grounding the polemic against marriage-prohibition in the goodness of the procreative mandate.
sourceText: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”

note: That food is 'sanctified through the word of God' may echo creation by divine word ('And God said... and it was so'); what the word made good, the word also makes holy. A theological rather than verbal echo.
sourceText: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

note: Being 'nourished in the words of the faith' figurally recalls the lesson of the wilderness, that 'man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.' Spiritual nourishment by the word stands behind the metaphor.
sourceText: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.

note: The summons to 'exercise yourself toward godliness' and refuse profane fables echoes the wisdom tradition's contrast between the fear of the LORD and the folly that 'despises wisdom and instruction.' Godliness here functions much as the OT 'fear of the LORD.'
sourceText: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.

note: Godliness 'having the promise of the life which is now and that which is to come' draws on the Deuteronomic offer of life through covenant fidelity, 'I have set before you life and good... that you may live.' The promise-of-life motif is reframed in two-age terms.
sourceText: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil.

note: 'The living God' is a fixed OT title for Yahweh as distinct from lifeless idols, e.g. 'the voice of the living God.' The Pastoral deploys it against dead asceticism and false teaching.
sourceText: For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?

note: 'The living God, who is the Savior of all men' draws on Deutero-Isaiah's universal salvation oracle, 'a righteous God and a Savior; there is none besides me. Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.' The 'Savior of all' claim universalizes Isaiah's offer.
sourceText: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.

note: God as 'Savior of all men' may echo the psalm's confession that 'you save man and beast, O LORD,' broadening salvation to the whole creation. A faint support for the universal scope of God's saving care.
sourceText: Your righteousness is like the mountains of God. Your judgments are like a great deep. Yahweh, you preserve man and animal.

note: The title 'Savior' applied to the living God resonates with 'I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior.' The Pastoral confesses Yahweh's exclusive saving identity now extended to all peoples.
sourceText: I myself am Yahweh; and besides me there is no savior.

note: 'Let no man despise your youth' recalls Jeremiah's commissioning, where he protests 'I am only a youth' and the LORD answers 'Do not say, I am only a youth.' Timothy's youthful commission is patterned on the prophetic call to speak despite young age.
sourceText: Then I said, “Ah, Lord Yahweh! Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” But Yahweh said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak.

note: The charge to 'pay attention to reading, to exhortation, and to teaching' reflects the model of Ezra's assembly, where the Book of the Law was read aloud, interpreted, and the sense given so the people understood. Public reading plus exposition is the OT template for Timothy's liturgical duty.
sourceText: All the people gathered themselves together as one man into the broad place that was before the water gate; and they spoke to Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which Yahweh had commanded to Israel. Ezra the priest brought the law before the assembly, both men and women, and all who could hear with understanding, on the first day of the seventh month. He read therein before the broad place that was before the water gate from early […]

note: The 'reading' Timothy is to attend to echoes the Deuteronomic mandate, 'you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing,' the foundational command for public reading of Scripture in the assembly. This institutes the practice the Pastoral continues.
sourceText: when all Israel has come to appear before Yahweh your God in the place which he will choose, you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing.

note: 'The gift... given to you by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands' draws on Moses commissioning Joshua, taking 'a man in whom is the Spirit' and laying his hands on him before the assembly to invest him with authority. Timothy's ordination reenacts this hand-laying transfer of office.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]

note: The 'gift that is in you' conveyed by 'laying on of hands' echoes 'Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him.' The endowment of a Spirit-gift through imposition of hands is the direct OT precedent.
sourceText: Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as Yahweh commanded Moses.

note: The gift conferred amid 'the elders' (presbytery) recalls the seventy elders on whom the LORD put the Spirit that was on Moses. A faint background to communal, Spirit-endowed eldership behind the ordination scene.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, that they may stand there with you. I will come down and talk with you there. I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you not bear it yourself alone.

note: 'You will save both yourself and those who hear you' echoes the watchman charge, 'if you warn the wicked... you will have saved your life.' The minister's vigilance secures both his own and his hearers' deliverance.
sourceText: Nevertheless, if you warn the wicked of his way to turn from it, and he doesn’t turn from his way; he shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.

note: Persevering teaching that saves 'those who hear you' faintly recalls 'those who turn many to righteousness' shining like the stars. A possible eschatological coloring of the teacher's saving role.
sourceText: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: The charge not to rebuke an older man but to exhort him 'as a father' reflects the Holiness Code's command to rise before the gray head and honor the face of an old man. Paul translates the Torah's reverence for the aged into pastoral conduct within the household of faith.
sourceText: “‘You shall rise up before the gray head, and honor the face of an old man, and you shall fear your God. I am Yahweh.

note: Treating older men as fathers and older women as mothers extends the Decalogue's command to honor father and mother to the wider church family. The familial honor owed to parents becomes the template for intergenerational respect in the congregation.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.

note: The careful, non-shaming manner of correction ('do not rebuke... exhort') may echo the Holiness Code's directive to reason frankly with a neighbor rather than incur sin through hatred. The aim of rebuke without harshness reflects the Torah's regulated form of fraternal reproof.
sourceText: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.

note: Treating younger men as brothers and younger women as sisters 'in all purity' evokes the command to love one's neighbor as oneself within a familial frame. The kinship language fits the Levitical ethic of treating the community as one's own people.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'Honor widows who are widows indeed' rests on the pervasive Torah concern for the widow, here grounded in God who 'executes justice for the fatherless and the widow.' The church's obligation to honor genuine widows continues God's own care for the defenseless.
sourceText: He does execute justice for the fatherless and widow, and loves the foreigner, in giving him food and clothing.

note: The duty to provide for and protect true widows reflects the covenant prohibition, 'You shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child,' enforced by divine sanction. Paul's regulation of widow-care assumes this foundational Torah safeguard for the vulnerable.
sourceText: “You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child.

note: The insistence on justice for the widow who is truly desolate echoes the command not to deprive the sojourner or fatherless of justice, nor take a widow's garment in pledge. The church inherits the Deuteronomic charge to shield the widow from neglect.
sourceText: You shall not deprive the foreigner or the fatherless of justice, nor take a widow’s clothing in pledge;

note: The duty of children and grandchildren to 'repay their parents' and show piety to their own family applies the Decalogue's command to honor father and mother. Caring for an aged widowed parent is the concrete fulfillment of filial honor that pleases God.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.

note: The privileging of the widow as object of communal duty resonates with the prophetic summons to 'bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause.' Right religion before God includes the defense of the widow, which Paul codifies for the assembly.
sourceText: Learn to do well. Seek justice. Relieve the oppressed. Judge the fatherless. Plead for the widow.”

note: The widow 'desolate' who sets her hope on God recalls God as 'father of the fatherless and protector of widows in his holy habitation.' Her continual prayer night and day rests on the psalmist's portrait of God as the widow's defender.
sourceText: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.

note: The genuine widow's persistent petitions 'night and day' echo Ben Sira's assurance that the Lord does not ignore the supplication of the widow whose tears run down. Her uninterrupted prayer is the very plea Sirach promises God will hear.
sourceText: He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall?

note: The widow who 'gives herself to pleasure is dead while she lives' draws on wisdom's warning that 'whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man.' Self-indulgent dissipation is figured as a living death, the opposite of the prayerful hope set on God.
sourceText: He who loves pleasure shall be a poor man. He who loves wine and oil shall not be rich.

note: The motif of luxury and indulgence ruining a person undergirds the saying that the wanton widow is 'dead while she lives.' Ben Sira's warnings that wine and dissipation destroy understanding inform the wisdom backdrop of spiritual death-in-life.
sourceText: Wine and women will make men of understanding to fall away: And he that cleaves to harlots will be the more reckless. Moths and worms will have him to heritage; And a reckless soul will be taken away.

note: The paradox 'dead while she lives' may faintly echo the Edenic verdict that death attends the life lived for self apart from God. The wisdom-tinged idea of life forfeited through misdirected desire stands behind the aphorism.
sourceText: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

note: The demand that believers 'provide for their own household' may reflect Isaiah's true-fast call to share bread and not hide from one's own flesh. Failing one's kin is precisely the neglect of 'your own flesh' that the prophet condemns.
sourceText: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?

note: The enrolled widow commended for having 'washed the saints' feet' evokes Abraham's hospitality, where water is brought to wash the feet of the visiting strangers. Foot-washing as a token of welcome to guests reaches back to the patriarchal ideal of hospitality.
sourceText: Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.

note: Being 'hospitable to strangers' as a mark of the approved widow recalls Abraham and Sarah's reception of the three visitors at Mamre. The patriarchal scene became the paradigm of welcoming strangers that Paul lists among the widow's good works.
sourceText: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]

note: The praise of the hospitable widow who lodges strangers echoes Job's testimony that 'the sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler.' Hospitality to the stranger is a recognized mark of righteousness in the wisdom tradition.
sourceText: (the foreigner has not lodged in the street, but I have opened my doors to the traveler);

note: The widow approved for relieving the afflicted reflects Job's oath that he never withheld from the poor, the widow, or the needy but warmed them. The catalog of good works for the enrolled widow mirrors the patriarch's self-vindication in deeds of mercy.
sourceText: “If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (no, from my youth he grew up with me as with a father, her have I guided from my mother’s womb); if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or that the needy had no covering; if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been warmed with my sheep’s fleece;

note: Washing the feet of others as humble service recalls Abigail's offer to wash the feet of David's servants. The act signifies lowly, devoted hospitality, the disposition Paul commends in the enrolled widow.
sourceText: She arose, and bowed herself with her face to the earth, and said, “Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”

note: The counsel that younger widows 'marry, bear children, rule the household' reflects the creational mandate to be fruitful and multiply and to govern the domestic sphere. Paul roots his pastoral preference in the created good of marriage and childbearing.
sourceText: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”

note: Directing the younger to marry rather than remain idle assumes the Edenic judgment that 'it is not good that the man should be alone.' Marriage is presented as the fitting state guarding against the dangers of an unanchored life.
sourceText: Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

note: The portrait of the good wife who 'rules the household' may echo Ben Sira's praise of the silent, well-ordered, home-keeping wife as a gift from the Lord. The domestic ideal Paul commends overlaps with the wisdom tradition's picture of the virtuous spouse.
sourceText: The grace of a wife will delight her husband; And her knowledge will fatten his bones. A silent woman is a gift of the Lord; And there is nothing so much worth as a well-instructed soul. A shamefast woman is grace upon grace; And there is no price worthy of a continent soul. As the sun when it arises in the highest places of the Lord, So is the beauty of a good wife in the ordering of a man’s house.

note: The idle younger widows 'going about from house to house... gossips and busybodies' recall the wandering, restless woman of Proverbs whose feet do not stay at home. The wisdom warning against the roving, undisciplined woman colors Paul's caution.
sourceText: She is loud and defiant. Her feet don’t stay in her house. Now she is in the streets, now in the squares, and lurking at every corner.

note: Paul cites verbatim, 'You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain,' introduced as 'the Scripture says,' to justify material support for laboring elders. The Torah's provision for the working animal becomes the warrant for compensating those who labor in word and teaching.
sourceText: You shall not muzzle the ox when he treads out the grain.

note: The principle that 'the laborer is worthy of his wages' reflects the Levitical command not to keep back the wages of a hired worker overnight. The just and timely payment of the laborer undergirds the double honor owed to elders.
sourceText: “‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.

note: The maxim about the laborer's wages aligns with the Deuteronomic command to pay the poor hired worker each day before sunset, lest he cry out to the Lord. The principle of due reward for labor stands behind Paul's argument for supporting elders.
sourceText: You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates. In his day you shall give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down on it; for he is poor, and sets his heart on it; lest he cry against you to Yahweh, and it be sin to you.

note: Supporting elders who labor in teaching echoes the provision that the Levites may eat the tithe as 'your wages in return for your service.' Sacred ministry warrants material support, a principle drawn from the priestly portion in the Torah.
sourceText: You may eat it anywhere, you and your households, for it is your reward in return for your service in the Tent of Meeting.

note: The rule that no accusation against an elder be received 'except at the word of two or three witnesses' directly applies the Torah's evidentiary standard that a charge is established only on two or three witnesses. Paul transfers the judicial safeguard into church discipline of leaders.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: The two-or-three-witnesses requirement also draws on the capital-case statute that no one be put to death on the testimony of a single witness. The double attestation needed before disciplining an elder mirrors this Deuteronomic protection against false accusation.
sourceText: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.

note: The insistence on multiple witnesses echoes the law that a murderer be executed only on the evidence of witnesses, never one alone. The same principle restraining hasty condemnation governs accusations against elders.
sourceText: “‘Whoever kills any person, the murderer shall be slain at the mouth of witnesses; but one witness shall not testify against any person that he die.

note: The charge to observe these things 'without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality' reflects the Holiness Code's command to do no injustice in judgment, neither favoring the poor nor deferring to the great. Impartial judgment is the Levitical standard Paul imposes on church discipline.
sourceText: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.

note: Acting 'without prejudice' and refusing partiality echoes Moses' charge to judges: 'You shall not be partial in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike.' The impartiality demanded of Israel's judges becomes the rule for Timothy's oversight.
sourceText: You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be afraid of the face of man, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.”

note: Reproving open sinners 'in the sight of all, that the rest also may be in fear' echoes the Deuteronomic rationale for public punishment, that 'all Israel shall hear and fear.' Visible discipline as deterrent reflects the Torah's pedagogy of communal fear.
sourceText: That prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death, because he has spoken rebellion against Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to draw you aside out of the way which Yahweh your God commanded you to walk in. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.

note: The aim that public reproof make 'the rest also be in fear' parallels the law's purpose that 'the rest shall hear and fear, and shall never again commit such evil.' The deterrent function of open correction is drawn from this witness statute.
sourceText: Those who remain shall hear, and fear, and will never again commit any such evil in your midst.

note: The demand to judge without partiality may echo Jehoshaphat's charge that with the Lord there is 'no injustice or partiality or taking of bribes.' Impartial oversight images the character of the God in whose sight Paul places the command.
sourceText: Now therefore let the fear of Yahweh be on you. Take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with Yahweh our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes.”

note: The warning to 'lay hands hastily on no one' presupposes the OT rite of commissioning by the laying on of hands, as Moses laid hands on Joshua before the assembly. Ordination's gravity, derived from this transfer of office, demands caution against premature appointment.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]

note: The charge against careless laying on of hands recalls that Joshua was full of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. The efficacy and seriousness of hand-laying for office lie behind Paul's exhortation to restraint.
sourceText: Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as Yahweh commanded Moses.

note: The observation that 'some men's sins are evident... and some also follow later' echoes the psalmist's awareness that God sets our secret sins in the light of his presence. Hidden sins that will eventually appear reflect the OT conviction that all deeds come to judgment.
sourceText: You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence.

note: The maxim that sins and good works alike cannot finally be hidden reflects Qoheleth's conclusion that God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing. The eventual exposure of all conduct draws on this wisdom certainty.
sourceText: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.

note: The saying that concealed sins and good works 'can't be hidden' resonates with the proverb that crooked ways will be found out while integrity walks securely. Wisdom's confidence that character is eventually disclosed informs the chapter's closing aphorism.
sourceText: He who walks blamelessly walks surely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.

note: Slaves are to honor masters 'that the name of God and the doctrine not be blasphemed.' The motif of God's name being blasphemed among outsiders on account of his people echoes Isaiah 52:5 LXX, 'because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations,' which Paul cites explicitly at Romans 2:24. The conduct of the covenant community before observers determines whether God's name is honored or reviled.
sourceText: “Now therefore, what do I do here,” says Yahweh, “seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Those who rule over them mock,” says Yahweh, “and my name continually all the day is blasphemed.

note: Ezekiel develops the same theme that Israel 'profaned my holy name among the nations' so that God acts to vindicate it. The Pastoral concern that believing slaves not cause God's name to be blasphemed by outsiders draws on this prophetic logic of the name's holiness being bound to the people's behavior. Closely paired with Isaiah 52:5 as the wellspring of the 'name blasphemed' tradition.
sourceText: When they came to the nations, where they went, they profaned my holy name; in that men said of them, These are the people of Yahweh, and are gone out of his land. But I had respect for my holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations, where they went. Therefore tell the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: I don’t do this for your sake, house of Israel, but for my holy name, which you have profaned among the nations, where […]

note: The grave sin of 'blaspheming the Name' is codified in the Holiness legislation on the blasphemer. The Pastoral fear that misconduct leads outsiders to blaspheme God's name may faintly trade on this background sense of the Name's sanctity, though the verbal link is general rather than specific.
sourceText: The son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the Name, and cursed; and they brought him to Moses. His mother’s name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan. They put him in custody, until Yahweh’s will should be declared to them. Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Bring out of the camp him who cursed; and let all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and let all the congregation stone him. You shall speak to the children of Israel, […]

note: The portrait of the conceited teacher 'obsessed with arguments' who breeds 'envy, strife, insulting' recalls wisdom's contrast between the greedy/proud who stir up strife and the trusting who prosper. The catalogue of social vices arising from pride and contention reflects the sapiential pattern rather than any one quotation.
sourceText: One who is greedy stirs up strife; but one who trusts in Yahweh will prosper.

note: 'By pride comes only contention' supplies the wisdom commonplace standing behind the picture of the conceited heretic who produces disputes and word-battles. The link is thematic, illustrating the proverbial association of arrogance with quarreling.
sourceText: Pride only breeds quarrels, but with ones who take advice is wisdom.

note: The charge that the false teachers 'suppose that godliness is a means of gain' anticipates the chapter's critique of money-driven religion and resonates with wisdom's warning against wearing oneself out to be rich. A faint forward link to the avarice motif developed in vv.9-10.
sourceText: Don’t weary yourself to be rich. In your wisdom, show restraint. Why do you set your eyes on that which is not? For it certainly sprouts wings like an eagle and flies in the sky.

note: 'We brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can't carry anything out' closely renders Job's confession, 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return there.' The shared logic of human poverty at birth and at death grounds the call to contentment and is the primary scriptural source for v.7.
sourceText: He said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh’s name.”

note: 'As he came from his mother's womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor.' Qoheleth's meditation on the impossibility of carrying wealth out of life is a direct conceptual parallel to v.7 and reinforces the Job allusion. The pairing forms the wisdom backbone of the contentment teaching.
sourceText: As he came out of his mother’s womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, which he may carry away in his hand.

note: 'For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not descend after him.' The psalm's reflection that the rich take nothing in death directly parallels the claim that we 'can't carry anything out.' A strong supporting witness to the same death-and-dispossession tradition.
sourceText: For when he dies he shall carry nothing away. His glory shall not descend after him.

note: Ben Sira warns against relying on wealth and saying 'I have enough,' urging the reader not to follow heart and strength after riches. The deuterocanonical wisdom on the futility of trusting possessions undergirds the contentment ethic of vv.6-8 and the warnings of vv.9-10.
sourceText: Set not your heart upon your goods; And say not, They are sufficient for me. Follow not your own mind and your strength, To walk in the desires of your heart; And say not, Who will have dominion over me? For the Lord will surely take vengeance on you. Say not, I sinned, and what happened to me? For the Lord is longsuffering. Concerning atonement, be not without fear, To add sin upon sins: And say not, His compassion is great; He will be pacified for the […]

note: Agur's prayer, 'feed me with the food that is needful for me,' seeking neither poverty nor riches, supplies the ideal of sufficiency behind 'having food and clothing, we will be content.' The wisdom request for daily necessities is the closest sapiential parallel to v.8.
sourceText: Remove far from me falsehood and lies. Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me; lest I be full, deny you, and say, ‘Who is Yahweh?’ or lest I be poor, and steal, and so dishonor the name of my God.

note: Jacob's vow asks God for 'bread to eat and clothing to wear,' the same minimal pairing of food and clothing that defines contentment in v.8. The verbal pairing may stand behind Paul's formula, though it is a common biblical idiom of basic provision.
sourceText: Jacob vowed a vow, saying, “If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and clothing to put on,

note: The wilderness lesson that God provided manna and that clothing did not wear out teaches dependence on God for daily food and covering. This forms a faint background to the food-and-clothing sufficiency that the believer is to rest content in.
sourceText: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth. Your clothing didn’t grow old on you, neither did your foot swell, these forty years.

note: 'He who is greedy for gain troubles his own house.' The maxim that avarice brings ruin upon the grasping person directly underwrites 'the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' and the picture of those who 'pierced themselves through with many sorrows.' A core wisdom source for v.10.
sourceText: He who is greedy for gain troubles his own house, but he who hates bribes will live.

note: 'Many have sinned for the sake of profit, and he who seeks to multiply gain will turn his eye away.' Ben Sira's aphorism that the pursuit of money is itself a cause of sin is the closest known parallel to 'the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.' Strong deuterocanonical antecedent for v.10.
sourceText: Many have sinned for a thing indifferent; And he that seeks to multiply gain will turn his eye away.

note: 'He who loves gold will not be justified... Gold has been a stumbling block to many, and their destruction has met them face to face. It is a snare to those who are devoted to it.' The imagery of gold as a snare causing ruin parallels both the 'snare' of v.9 and the 'root of evil' of v.10. A remarkably close sapiential model.
sourceText: He that loves gold shall not be justified; And he that follows destruction shall himself have his fill of it. Many have been given over to ruin for the sake of gold; And their perdition meets them face to face. It is a stumbling block to those who sacrifice to it; And every fool shall be taken therewith.

note: 'He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver, nor he who loves abundance with increase.' Qoheleth's insight into the insatiability of money-love directly parallels the diagnosis of those 'determined to be rich' and 'the love of money.' A direct wisdom witness to the avarice critique.
sourceText: He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.

note: 'Don't weary yourself to be rich... riches certainly sprout wings.' The warning against straining to be wealthy maps onto 'those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation and a snare.' The fleeting, ensnaring character of riches grounds vv.9-10.
sourceText: Don’t weary yourself to be rich. In your wisdom, show restraint. Why do you set your eyes on that which is not? For it certainly sprouts wings like an eagle and flies in the sky.

note: 'A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn't know that poverty waits for him.' The proverb that the avaricious rush toward wealth only to meet ruin parallels the trajectory of those who 'fall into... ruin and destruction.' Supporting wisdom source.
sourceText: A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn’t know that poverty waits for him.

note: 'So are the ways of everyone who is greedy for gain. It takes away the life of its owners.' Wisdom's claim that greed is self-destructive, ambushing the very ones who seek it, parallels those who in greed 'pierced themselves through with many sorrows.' A self-harm motif resonant with v.10.
sourceText: but these lay wait for their own blood. They lurk secretly for their own lives. So are the ways of everyone who is greedy for gain. It takes away the life of its owners.

note: 'If you pursue, you will not overtake... and you will not escape by fleeing.' Ben Sira's counsel against frenetic pursuit of gain resonates with those 'determined to be rich' who fall into a snare. A faint deuterocanonical parallel.
sourceText: My son, be not busy about many matters: For if you meddle much, you will not be unpunished; And if you pursue, you will not overtake; And you will not escape by fleeing.

note: The address 'man of God' is the standard Hebrew Bible title for a prophet or authorized servant of God, applied to Moses ('the man of God') and frequently to figures like Elijah and Elisha. Timothy is cast in this prophetic-leadership lineage, charged to embody covenant virtue.
sourceText: This is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death.

note: Samuel is repeatedly called 'the man of God,' establishing the title as a designation for a trusted seer who speaks for the Lord. The Pastoral epithet for Timothy draws on this same OT usage of the authorized divine spokesman.
sourceText: He said to him, “See now, there is in this city a man of God, and he is a man who is held in honor. All that he says comes surely to pass. Now let us go there. Perhaps he can tell us concerning our journey whereon we go.”

note: 'He who follows after righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor.' The exhortation to 'follow after righteousness... and gentleness' and so 'lay hold of eternal life' resonates with wisdom's promise that pursuing righteousness leads to life. A thematic virtue-pursuit parallel.
sourceText: He who follows after righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor.

note: 'You give life to all of them' praises the one God who made and sustains all things. The charge before 'God, who gives life to all things' (v.13) echoes this confession of the Creator as life-giver to the whole creation. A direct conceptual parallel to the life-giving formula.
sourceText: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.

note: 'I kill and I make alive... there is no god with me.' God's exclusive prerogative over life and death undergirds 'God, who gives life to all things' and the doxology's stress that he 'alone has immortality.' Supports both the life-giver and sole-sovereign motifs of vv.13-16.
sourceText: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.

note: 'For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods and Lord of lords.' The doxology's title 'King of kings, and Lord of lords' (v.15) directly takes up this Deuteronomic confession of God's supremacy over all powers. The clearest verbal source for the title.
sourceText: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.

note: 'Give thanks to the God of gods... to the Lord of lords.' The liturgical pairing of these superlatives reinforces the 'Lord of lords' title of v.15 and its hymnic, doxological setting. A strong secondary witness alongside Deuteronomy 10:17.
sourceText: Give thanks to the God of gods; for his loving kindness endures forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords; for his loving kindness endures forever:

note: Nebuchadnezzar confesses Daniel's God as 'God of gods, and Lord of kings.' The royal-supremacy formula praising the God who is over all kings parallels 'King of kings, and Lord of lords.' Reflects the apocalyptic vocabulary of divine kingship behind v.15.
sourceText: The king answered to Daniel, and said, Of a truth your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, since you have been able to reveal this secret.

note: 'You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.' The doxology's 'whom no man has seen, nor can see' (v.16) directly echoes God's word to Moses on the impossibility of beholding the divine face. A primary scriptural source for the invisibility motif.
sourceText: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”

note: God is 'covered with light as with a garment.' 'Dwelling in unapproachable light' (v.16) draws on this hymnic image of God clothed in light. The closest scriptural antecedent for the light-dwelling description.
sourceText: He covers himself with light as with a garment. He stretches out the heavens like a curtain.

note: The glory of the Lord appeared 'like a devouring fire' on the mountain, inaccessible to the people. The unapproachable, blazing presence informs the 'unapproachable light' in which God dwells. A faint Sinai-theophany resonance.
sourceText: The appearance of Yahweh’s glory was like devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the eyes of the children of Israel.

note: 'For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light.' The association of God with life and with light loosely supports the doxology's coupling of the life-giver (v.13) with the God of unapproachable light (v.16). A thematic resonance rather than a citation.
sourceText: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.

note: 'Yahweh will be your everlasting light.' The eschatological depiction of God as light may faintly inform the doxology's 'unapproachable light.' A distant resonance secondary to Psalm 104:2.
sourceText: The sun shall be no more your light by day; neither for brightness shall the moon give light to you: but Yahweh will be to you an everlasting light, and your God your glory.

note: 'If riches increase, don't set your heart on them.' The charge that the rich not 'have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches' closely matches the psalm's warning against fixing the heart on growing wealth. A primary source for v.17.
sourceText: Don’t trust in oppression. Don’t become vain in robbery. If riches increase, don’t set your heart on them.

note: 'He who trusts in his riches will fall.' The contrast between trusting riches and the alternative directly parallels the command not to hope in 'the uncertainty of riches' but on the living God. A core wisdom antecedent for v.17.
sourceText: He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous shall flourish as the green leaf.

note: Riches 'certainly sprout wings, like an eagle they fly toward the sky.' The fleeting, unreliable nature of wealth grounds the phrase 'the uncertainty of riches.' A vivid wisdom image of money's instability.
sourceText: Why do you set your eyes on that which is not? For it certainly sprouts wings like an eagle and flies in the sky.

note: 'Don't let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he... knows me.' The redirection of the wealthy from boasting in riches to glorying in God parallels the charge that the rich not be haughty but hope on the living God. A strong source for the structure of v.17.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.

note: 'Beware lest you say... My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth. But you shall remember Yahweh your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth.' The warning against pride in self-made riches and the reminder that God is the giver parallels the charge against the haughty rich and the God 'who richly provides us with everything.'
sourceText: and lest you say in your heart, “My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth.” But you shall remember Yahweh your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth; that he may establish his covenant which he swore to your fathers, as at this day.

note: 'He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.' The exhortation that the rich 'be rich in good works, ready to distribute,' 'laying up in store... a good foundation against the time to come' echoes the wisdom principle that generosity to the needy is treasure stored with God. Grounds the storing-up imagery of v.19.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

note: 'Give alms from your possessions... you will be laying up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity.' Tobit's almsgiving counsel that charity stores up a treasure for the day of need is a remarkably close parallel to 'laying up in store... a good foundation against the time to come' (v.19). A strong deuterocanonical source.
sourceText: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]

note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments... and it will profit you more than gold. Store up almsgiving in your treasury, and it will rescue you from all affliction.' Ben Sira's image of almsgiving as treasure that delivers in the future directly parallels the rich laying up a good foundation against the time to come. Close sapiential antecedent for v.19.
sourceText: Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all affliction:

note: Agur's prayer against riches that lead one to deny God and against poverty that leads to theft frames wealth as spiritually perilous. This wisdom ambivalence about riches faintly supports the warning that the rich not be haughty nor trust their wealth.
sourceText: Remove far from me falsehood and lies. Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me; lest I be full, deny you, and say, ‘Who is Yahweh?’ or lest I be poor, and steal, and so dishonor the name of my God.

note: 'Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.' The command 'guard that which is committed to you' draws on the wisdom ideal of vigilant safekeeping of what is precious. A thematic resonance with the keeping/guarding motif.
sourceText: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

note: 'Stay away from a foolish man, for you won't find knowledge on his lips.' The injunction to turn away from 'the empty chatter and oppositions of the knowledge falsely so called' resonates with wisdom's warning to avoid the fool's pseudo-knowledge. A faint sapiential parallel to the rejection of false gnosis.
sourceText: Stay away from a foolish man, for you won’t find knowledge on his lips.

note: Paul styles his apostleship as serving 'the promise of the life which is in Christ Jesus.' The Deuteronomic covenant blessing frames clinging to the LORD as the source of 'life and length of days,' an OT matrix for the promise-of-life language Paul Christologizes here.
sourceText: to love Yahweh your God, to obey his voice, and to cling to him; for he is your life, and the length of your days; that you may dwell in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them.

note: The 'promise' according to which Paul is sent recalls the patriarchal covenant promise to Abraham and his seed; Pauline 'promise' theology consistently roots in this Genesis covenant. Faint here, marked contested.
sourceText: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.

note: The greeting 'Grace, mercy, and peace' echoes the Aaronic priestly blessing, where the LORD is asked to 'be gracious' and to 'give peace.' The triad of grace and peace in Paul's salutations draws on this benedictory form.
sourceText: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: Serving God 'as my forefathers did' with a 'pure conscience' presents Paul's gospel as continuous with ancestral Jewish piety; 2 Maccabees praises the high priest Onias as a man of upright conscience and ancestral devotion. Deuterocanonical conscience language is faint background.
sourceText: And the vision of that dream was this: He saw Onias, him that was high priest, a noble and good man, reverend in bearing, yet gentle in manner and well-spoken, and exercised from a child in all points of virtue, with outstretched hands invoking blessings on the whole body of the Jews:

note: The 'pure conscience' with which Paul serves echoes the OT ideal of the 'pure heart and clean hands' required to stand before God. The psalm's purity-of-heart standard underlies the conscience language transposed into Pauline interiority.
sourceText: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.

note: The plea for a 'clean heart' and right spirit parallels Paul's claim to serve God with a pure conscience; the conscience motif develops the OT clean-heart ideal. Faint, marked contested.
sourceText: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.

note: Paul's 'unceasing memory' and remembering 'night and day' draws on the OT idiom of a fragrant memorial / remembrance before God; Genesis introduces the 'pleasing aroma' the LORD remembers. The remembrance language is faint.
sourceText: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.

note: The 'sincere faith' that lived first in grandmother Lois and mother Eunice and now in Timothy enacts the Shema's command to bind covenant faith on the heart and teach it diligently to children across generations. The intergenerational transmission of faith is the Deuteronomic catechetical ideal.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might. These words, which I command you this day, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

note: The chain of faith from grandmother to mother to son mirrors the psalm's mandate that fathers teach the next generation so that children yet unborn would set their hope in God. Timothy's inherited 'sincere faith' embodies this generational handing-down.
sourceText: For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a teaching in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children; that the generation to come might know, even the children who should be born; who should arise and tell their children, that they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments,

note: The faith received specifically through grandmother and mother recalls the wisdom tradition's appeal to heed 'your mother's teaching.' The maternal pedagogy motif faintly underlies the naming of Lois and Eunice.
sourceText: My son, listen to your father’s instruction, and don’t forsake your mother’s teaching:

note: Stirring up 'the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands' recalls Moses commissioning Joshua by the laying on of hands so that he was filled with the spirit of wisdom. The ordination-by-imposition-of-hands motif is rooted in this Mosaic succession.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]

note: Joshua was 'full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him,' the precise pattern Paul invokes: a spiritual gift conferred through imposition of hands by the predecessor. Strongly parallels Timothy's reception of the charisma.
sourceText: Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as Yahweh commanded Moses.

note: The Spirit God gives, 'of power, love, and self-control' rather than fear, recalls the messianic endowment of the Spirit of wisdom, counsel, and might resting on the shoot of Jesse. The enumerated Spirit-qualities echo Isaiah's catalog of the Spirit's gifts.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: 'God didn't give us a spirit of fear' answers the LORD's charge to Joshua, 'be strong and courageous; do not be afraid,' precisely as Timothy steps into a Joshua-like succession of leadership. The not-fearing-but-strong commission undergirds the whole exhortation.
sourceText: Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid, neither be dismayed: for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.”

note: The 'spirit of power' contrasted with fear echoes 'not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit'; the divine Spirit as the true source of effective strength. Faint conceptual link, marked contested.
sourceText: Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is Yahweh’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'Don't be afraid, for I am with you... I will strengthen you' parallels Paul's denial that God gives a spirit of fear and his assertion of a spirit of power. Isaiah's salvation-oracle formula of fearlessness-through-divine-strength stands behind the verse.
sourceText: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.

note: 'Don't be ashamed of the testimony' draws on the Servant's resolve: 'I have set my face like a flint, and I know I will not be put to shame.' The vindication-of-the-unashamed-witness motif shapes Paul's appeal to Timothy to embrace suffering without shame.
sourceText: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.

note: 'I will speak of your testimonies before kings, and will not be put to shame' directly anticipates Paul's call not to be ashamed of the testimony and of his chains. The unashamed public confession before rulers is the psalmist's posture.
sourceText: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.

note: 'He who believes will not be put to shame' is a recurrent Pauline shame-text; here it faintly informs the unashamed-testimony theme even without citation. Marked contested.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: God 'saved us and called us... not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace' restates the Deuteronomic logic of election: the LORD set his love on Israel not because of their numbers or merit but because he loved them and kept his oath. Election by sheer gracious purpose is the OT root.
sourceText: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

note: Christ 'who abolished death' echoes the eschatological promise that the LORD 'will swallow up death forever.' The abolition-of-death motif is the climactic Isaianic hope now realized in the Savior's appearing.
sourceText: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.

note: Christ 'brought life and immortality to light' resonates with Wisdom's claim that God created humanity for incorruption, in the image of his own eternity. The deuterocanonical immortality/incorruption vocabulary directly underlies Paul's athanasia language.
sourceText: Because God created man for incorruption, And made him an image of his own proper being;

note: The hope that 'the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God' and their 'hope is full of immortality' parallels the life-and-immortality brought to light through the gospel. Wisdom's immortality theology is the closest Second-Temple antecedent.
sourceText: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality;

note: 'I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death' provides an OT oracle of death's defeat behind Christ's abolishing of death. Faint, overlapping with Isaiah 25:8.
sourceText: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.

note: The disclosure of 'life and immortality' resonates with Daniel's resurrection hope of awaking to everlasting life. The apocalyptic immortality promise is a faint backdrop to the gospel's bringing of imperishable life to light.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

note: Paul's appointment as 'a teacher of the Gentiles' enacts the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations,' that salvation might reach the ends of the earth. His Gentile herald-role fulfills Isaiah's light-to-the-nations mandate.
sourceText: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

note: 'Yet I am not ashamed' in the midst of suffering reprises the Servant's flint-faced confidence that he will not be put to shame. The Servant's unashamed endurance models Paul's own.
sourceText: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.

note: 'I know whom I have believed, and... he is able to guard that which I have committed to him' echoes 'Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me.' The committing/entrusting of oneself to the faithful God parallels the psalmist's deposit. Marked contested.
sourceText: Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth.

note: 'In God I trust; I will not be afraid' parallels Paul's confident 'I know whom I have believed' and lack of shame. Faint trust-formula resonance.
sourceText: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you. In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?

note: Holding 'the pattern of sound words' and guarding 'that good thing committed to you' draws on the Deuteronomic charge to add nothing and take nothing from the commanded word but to keep it. The deposit-of-teaching motif reflects covenant-word preservation.
sourceText: You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it, that you may keep the commandments of Yahweh your God which I command you.

note: 'Guard' the good deposit through the Spirit echoes the command to lay up God's words in heart and soul, binding and teaching them. The entrusted-treasure-of-the-word imagery is rooted in Deuteronomy's commands to keep and transmit the torah.
sourceText: Therefore you shall lay up these my words in your heart and in your soul. You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes. You shall teach them your children, talking of them, when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

note: 'Take hold of instruction; do not let go; keep her, for she is your life' closely parallels 'hold the pattern of sound words' and 'guard' the deposit. The wisdom command to grip and guard saving instruction undergirds Paul's exhortation.
sourceText: Take firm hold of instruction. Don’t let her go. Keep her, for she is your life.

note: Receiving words and 'treasuring up' commandments parallels the entrusted good deposit to be guarded. Faint wisdom-deposit link, marked contested.
sourceText: My son, if you will receive my words, and store up my commandments within you;

note: 'All who are in Asia turned away from me' echoes the lament of abandonment by close associates, as the psalmist's familiar friend turns against him. The desertion-by-companions motif colors Paul's account, marked contested.
sourceText: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

note: Paul's prayer that the Lord 'grant mercy to the house of Onesiphorus' for kindness shown echoes Naomi's blessing that the LORD deal kindly with those who showed kindness (chesed) to the living and the dead. The reciprocal-kindness-blessing formula is the OT antecedent.
sourceText: Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, “Go, return each of you to her mother’s house: Yahweh deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead, and with me.

note: 'May the LORD reward you well for what you have done' parallels Paul's wish that the Lord repay Onesiphorus's refreshing kindness with mercy. The petition-for-divine-recompense-of-mercy is faintly present.
sourceText: For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away unharmed? Therefore may Yahweh reward you good for that which you have done to me this day.

note: Asking that Onesiphorus 'find mercy from the Lord in that day' invokes the Judge of all the earth doing right at the eschatological judgment. The day-of-the-LORD judgment frame behind 'that day' is rooted in OT theophany. Marked contested.
sourceText: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”

note: Onesiphorus 'often refreshed me' and the prayer for his reward echoes 'whoever refreshes others will be refreshed.' The one-who-refreshes-will-be-refreshed proverb closely matches the language and logic of Paul's blessing.
sourceText: The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.

note: 'Let your kindness extend to all the living, and do not withhold kindness even from the dead' resonates with Paul's prayer of mercy for the absent (possibly deceased) Onesiphorus and his household. Deuterocanonical kindness-to-the-departed ethic faintly informs the petition.
sourceText: A gift has grace in the sight of every man living; And for a dead man keep not back grace.

note: Entrusting the deposit to 'faithful men' who can teach others recalls the OT ideal of the trustworthy servant, paradigmatically Moses who is 'faithful in all my house.' The transmission-by-faithful-stewards motif underlies Paul's chain of witnesses.
sourceText: My servant Moses is not so. He is faithful in all my house.

note: The soldier who must not be 'entangled in the affairs of life' so he can please his commander echoes the holy-war muster law, which exempts the man who has built a house, planted a vineyard, or betrothed a wife so that the army on campaign is undistracted. The single-minded enlisted soldier is the shared image.
sourceText: The officers shall speak to the people, saying, “What man is there who has built a new house, and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man dedicate it. What man is there who has planted a vineyard, and has not used its fruit? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man use its fruit. What man is there who has pledged to be married a wife, and has not taken her? […]

note: The 'farmers who labor must be first to get a share of the crops' draws on the Torah principle that the one who plants the vineyard rightly enjoys its fruit. The labor-then-reward logic runs through the soldier/athlete/farmer triad.
sourceText: What man is there who has planted a vineyard, and has not used its fruit? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man use its fruit.

note: 'He who tends a fig tree will eat its fruit' is the closest sapiential parallel to the laboring farmer who earns the first share. Paul applies the proverb's reward-for-tending logic to gospel ministry.
sourceText: Whoever tends the fig tree shall eat its fruit. He who looks after his master shall be honored.

note: The right of the agricultural laborer to a share of the produce echoes the ox-treading-grain principle Paul elsewhere applies to ministry support. Faint but thematically continuous with the farmer image.
sourceText: You shall not muzzle the ox when he treads out the grain.

note: 'Jesus Christ... of the seed of David' invokes the Davidic covenant promise that God will raise up David's offspring and establish his kingdom forever. Paul reads the resurrection as the fulfillment of the dynastic promise of an everlasting seed.
sourceText: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom.

note: The Davidic-seed Christology resonates with the shoot from the stump of Jesse, the messianic branch of David's line. Combined with v.10's root of Jesse, it grounds the title in prophetic messianism.
sourceText: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.

note: The 'root of Jesse' standing as a banner to which the nations rally undergirds the risen seed of David proclaimed in Paul's gospel for the chosen ones. Reinforces the Davidic-messiah background.
sourceText: It will happen in that day that the nations will seek the root of Jesse, who stands as a banner of the peoples; and his resting place will be glorious.

note: 'The fruit of your body I will set on your throne' restates the sworn promise of a Davidic heir behind 'of the seed of David.' A liturgical witness to the covenant Paul presupposes.
sourceText: Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it: “I will set the fruit of your body on your throne.

note: 'If we are faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself' echoes the Song of Moses' confession of God as the faithful Rock, without iniquity, just and upright. Divine constancy despite human failure is the shared theology.
sourceText: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.

note: 'He cannot deny himself' restates Balaam's oracle that God is not a man that he should lie, nor change his mind; what he has said he will do. The immutability of God's own word grounds the faithful saying.
sourceText: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?

note: Paul's endurance 'for the chosen ones' sake' picks up Isaiah's promise that God's chosen/elect will inherit and possess. The remnant-election vocabulary colors the eschatological 'salvation with eternal glory.'
sourceText: I will bring a seed out of Jacob, and out of Judah an inheritor of my mountains; and my chosen shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there.

note: 'But God's word isn't chained' faintly echoes the promise that the word going out from God's mouth will not return empty but accomplishes its purpose. The irrepressible, effective word is the common motif against Paul's chains.
sourceText: so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.

note: 'The Lord knows those who are his' quotes Moses' answer to Korah's rebellion, when the Lord makes known who is his and who is holy. Paul stamps this as the first half of the seal on God's firm foundation amid the disruption of false teachers (Hymenaeus, Philetus) — a deliberate Korah typology of schism within the covenant community.
sourceText: He said to Korah and to all his company, “In the morning, Yahweh will show who are his, and who is holy, and will cause him to come near to him. Even him whom he shall choose, he will cause to come near to him.

note: 'Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness' draws directly on Moses' command to depart from the tents of the wicked men (Korah, Dathan, Abiram) lest one be swept away in their sins. The Korah scene supplies both halves of the v.19 double seal: God knows his own, and the faithful must separate from the rebels.
sourceText: He spoke to the congregation, saying, “Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest you be consumed in all their sins!”

note: 'Everyone who names the name of the Lord' echoes Isaiah's confession that only your name we acknowledge/invoke, contrasting the true God with other lords who ruled. Supplies the naming-the-Name half of the citation alongside the Korah command.
sourceText: Yahweh our God, other lords besides you have had dominion over us, but by you only will we make mention of your name.

note: 'Depart from unrighteousness' resonates with the exodus-from-Babylon summons, 'Depart, depart, touch no unclean thing... be clean, you who bear the vessels of the Lord.' The separation-and-purity demand (and the vessel imagery picked up in vv.20-21) makes this a strong secondary source for the seal.
sourceText: Depart, depart, go out from there, touch no unclean thing! Go out of the midst of her! Cleanse yourselves, you who bear the vessels of Yahweh.

note: 'Depart from unrighteousness/iniquity' parallels Elihu's word that God commands them to return from iniquity. A sapiential analogue to the moral-separation clause.
sourceText: He also opens their ears to instruction, and commands that they return from iniquity.

note: 'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity' supplies a Psalter idiom of separation from the wicked that the v.19 seal recasts as an imperative on those who name the Name. Faint and one of several possible backgrounds.
sourceText: Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for Yahweh has heard the voice of my weeping.

note: The potter who from the same clay molds both vessels for clean uses and their opposites, deciding the use of each, is the closest antecedent to the great house with vessels for honor and dishonor. Strong deuterocanonical parallel for the honorable/dishonorable distinction.
sourceText: For a potter, kneading soft earth, Laboriously mouldeth each several vessel for our service: Nay, out of the same clay does he fashion Both the vessels that minister to clean uses, and those of a contrary sort, All in like manner; But what shall be the use of each vessel of either sort, The craftsman himself is the judge.

note: The potter reworking the clay 'as it seemed good to him,' with God's sovereign right over the house of Israel like clay in the potter's hand, underlies the vessels-for-honor-or-dishonor image and the call to be made fit for the master's use.
sourceText: The word which came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying, Arise, and go down to the potter’s house, and there I will cause you to hear my words. Then I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work on the wheels. When the vessel that he made of the clay was marred in the hand of the potter, he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it. Then Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, House of Israel, can’t I do with you as […]

note: 'Shall the thing made say of its maker, He did not make me?' frames the made vessel's subordination to its fashioner, the conceptual ground for a vessel cleansing itself for honorable use under the master.
sourceText: You turn things upside down! Should the potter be thought to be like clay; that the thing made should say about him who made it, “He didn’t make me”; or the thing formed say of him who formed it, “He has no understanding?”

note: 'Woe to him who strives with his Maker... shall the clay say to the potter, What are you making?' reinforces the potter-and-clay sovereignty motif behind the honor/dishonor vessels. Pairs with 29:16 as the prophetic clay backdrop.
sourceText: Woe to him who strives with his Maker— a clay pot among the clay pots of the earth! Shall the clay ask him who fashions it, ‘What are you making?’ or your work, ‘He has no hands?’

note: As clay is in the potter's hand to mold as he pleases, so humanity is in the hand of the Maker who appoints some for honor and some for dishonor — verbal and conceptual proximity to vessels for honor and dishonor in a household.
sourceText: And all men are from the ground, And Adam was created of earth. In the abundance of his knowledge the Lord distinguished them, And made their ways various: Some of them he blessed and exalted, And some of them he hallowed and brought near to himself: Some of them he cursed and brought low, And overthrew them from their place. As the clay of the potter in his hand, All his ways are according to his good pleasure; So men are in the hand of him that made […]

note: Belshazzar's praise of gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone supplies the closest OT catalogue of vessel materials (here gold, silver, wood, clay). The list of materials, not the theology, is the link.
sourceText: Belshazzar, while he tasted the wine, commanded to bring the golden and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem; that the king and his lords, his wives and his concubines, might drink from them. Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of God’s house which was at Jerusalem; and the king and his lords, his wives and his concubines, drank from them. They drank wine, and […]

note: The purity rules distinguishing vessels of wood and clay and requiring cleansing or breaking faintly inform 'if anyone purges himself... he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified.' The clean-vessel cultic background colors the sanctification language.
sourceText: On whatever any of them falls when they are dead, it shall be unclean; whether it is any vessel of wood, or clothing, or skin, or sack, whatever vessel it is, with which any work is done, it must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it will be clean. Every earthen vessel, into which any of them falls, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it.
