note: Calling on the Lord 'out of a pure heart' echoes the ascent liturgy's requirement of clean hands and a pure heart to stand in God's holy place. The pure-heart qualification for approaching God is the shared demand.
sourceText: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.

note: 'Those who call on the Lord' draws on the promise that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved, the OT formula for the worshipping covenant people. Paul restricts it to those who call from a pure heart.
sourceText: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.

note: 'Pursue righteousness... and peace' echoes the wisdom imperative to depart from evil, do good, and seek peace and pursue it. The verb 'pursue' applied to peace is a notable verbal contact.
sourceText: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.

note: 'Pursue righteousness' resonates with Isaiah's address to those who pursue righteousness and seek the Lord. A secondary prophetic backdrop to the chain of virtues to pursue.
sourceText: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from.

note: 'The Lord's servant must not quarrel but be gentle... patient' echoes the Servant of the Lord who will not cry out or lift up his voice in the street and will not break a bruised reed. The non-contentious, gentle servant typology shapes the ideal teacher.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations. He will not shout, nor raise his voice, nor cause it to be heard in the street. He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick. He will faithfully bring justice.

note: 'Flee youthful lusts' faintly recalls the verdict that the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth. The youth-as-locus-of-sinful-impulse motif lies behind the warning.
sourceText: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.

note: Recovering 'out of the devil's snare' having been 'taken captive' echoes deliverance from the snare of the fowler. The trap-and-rescue imagery supplies the OT coloring for the diabolical snare.
sourceText: For he will deliver you from the snare of the fowler, and from the deadly pestilence.

note: God's giving 'repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth' parallels the affirmation that God judges gradually and gives room/opportunity for repentance. A deuterocanonical analogue to the divine grant of repentance.
sourceText: But judging them by little and little you gave them a place of repentance, Not being ignorant that their nature by birth was evil, and their wickedness inborn, And that their manner of thought would in no wise ever be changed,

note: The catalog of human depravity in the 'last days' draws on the antediluvian corruption tradition, where the wickedness of mankind was great and every imagination of the heart was only evil continually. The eschatological intensification of vice echoes the primeval flood-generation's total moral collapse.
sourceText: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.

note: The earth corrupted and filled with violence before the flood furnishes a scriptural type for the moral degeneration of the last days. 'Corrupted in mind' (v. 8) verbally recalls the corruption motif of the Genesis flood narrative.
sourceText: The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. God saw the earth, and saw that it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth.

note: 'Disobedient to parents' inverts the fifth commandment to honor father and mother. The vice catalog functions in part as a reversal of the Decalogue, listing the breaking of commands as a sign of last-days lawlessness.
sourceText: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.

note: The portrait of the proud, boastful, God-denying wicked who oppress and prosper resembles the psalmist's description of the arrogant oppressor who says God has forgotten. The cluster of pride, greed, and contempt for the holy parallels this lament's indictment.
sourceText: In arrogance, the wicked hunt down the weak. They are caught in the schemes that they devise. For the wicked boasts of his heart’s cravings. He blesses the greedy, and condemns Yahweh. The wicked, in the pride of his face, has no room in his thoughts for God. His ways are prosperous at all times. He is haughty, and your laws are far from his sight. As for all his adversaries, he sneers at them. He says in his heart, “I shall not be shaken. For generations […]

note: The wicked who has no fear of God, flatters himself, and devises mischief parallels the impostors who hold a form of godliness while denying its power. The self-deceiving, God-ignoring wickedness matches the vice list's portrait.
sourceText: An oracle is within my heart about the disobedience of the wicked: “There is no fear of God before his eyes.” For he flatters himself in his own eyes, too much to detect and hate his sin. The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit. He has ceased to be wise and to do good. He plots iniquity on his bed. He sets himself in a way that is not good. He doesn’t abhor evil.

note: 'Holding a form of godliness, but having denied its power' echoes the prophetic indictment of those who honor God with their lips while their heart is far from him, whose worship is merely a commandment of men. The hollow, powerless piety is the prophets' charge against false religion.
sourceText: The Lord said, “Because this people draws near with their mouth and with their lips to honor me, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught;
lxxText: And the Lord has said, This people draw nigh to me with their mouth, and they honour me with their lips, but their heart is far from me: but in vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men.

note: Jannes and Jambres who 'opposed Moses' are the unnamed Egyptian magicians who matched Aaron's signs with their secret arts before Pharaoh. The names derive from Jewish tradition (Targums, CD, the lost book of Jannes and Jambres); the canonical referent is the Exodus contest of the magicians.
sourceText: Then Pharaoh also called for the wise men and the sorcerers. They also, the magicians of Egypt, did the same thing with their enchantments.

note: The magicians of Egypt did the same with their enchantments, opposing Moses by replicating the plague of blood and hardening Pharaoh's resistance to the truth. This is part of the Exodus magician cycle that Paul invokes by the names Jannes and Jambres.
sourceText: The magicians of Egypt did the same thing with their enchantments; and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them; as Yahweh had spoken.

note: The magicians brought up frogs with their enchantments, again imitating the sign and resisting Moses. This continues the contest tradition Paul compresses into the named opposition of Jannes and Jambres.
sourceText: The magicians did the same thing with their enchantments, and brought up frogs on the land of Egypt.

note: The magicians could not produce the gnats and confessed 'This is the finger of God'; their failure marks the limit of their power. 'Their folly will be evident to all' (v. 9) alludes to this public exposure of the magicians' impotence before God's true work.
sourceText: The magicians tried with their enchantments to produce lice, but they couldn’t. There were lice on man, and on animal. Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God:” and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them; as Yahweh had spoken.

note: The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, the climactic public defeat of those who opposed him. This caps the magician tradition behind Jannes and Jambres, whose 'folly became evident.'
sourceText: The magicians couldn’t stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boils were on the magicians, and on all the Egyptians.

note: Paul names the two Egyptian magicians from a developed extrabiblical tradition (the pseudepigraphal book of Jannes and Jambres, the Damascus Document, and the Targums) rather than from the bare Exodus text. The pseudepigraphal source supplies the names absent from the canonical narrative.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: The picture of those who 'creep into houses and take captive gullible women loaded down with sins, led away by various lusts' faintly recalls the seduction tradition; some see a generalized echo of household predation. The connection is thematic and contested.
sourceText: He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he ate. Joseph was well-built and handsome. After these things, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph; and she said, “Lie with me.” But he refused, and said to his master’s wife, “Behold, my master doesn’t know what is with me in the house, and he has put all that he has into my hand. He isn’t greater in this house than I, neither has he kept […]

note: 'The Lord delivered me out of them all' closely echoes the psalm's 'Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all.' The verbal correspondence of the righteous sufferer rescued from all troubles is strong.
sourceText: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.

note: The trust that God delivers those who cry to him, who were not put to shame, parallels Paul's testimony of rescue from persecution. The righteous-sufferer-vindicated pattern resonates faintly.
sourceText: Our fathers trusted in you. They trusted, and you delivered them. They cried to you, and were delivered. They trusted in you, and were not disappointed.

note: The end-time deceivers who 'grow worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived' and the refining persecution of those who know God resemble Daniel's apocalyptic scenario of flatterers, deceit, and the testing of the wise in the latter days. The eschatological framing of persecution and deception aligns.
sourceText: Such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he pervert by flatteries; but the people who know their God shall be strong, and take action. Those who are wise among the people shall instruct many; yet they shall fall by the sword and by flame, by captivity and by plunder, many days. Now when they shall fall, they shall be helped with a little help; but many shall join themselves to them with flatteries. Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine […]

note: The 'holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation' echoes 'the law of the LORD is perfect... making wise the simple.' The conviction that God's word imparts saving wisdom is rooted in this psalm's praise of Torah.
sourceText: Yahweh’s law is perfect, restoring the soul. Yahweh’s testimony is sure, making wise the simple.

note: The commandments that make the psalmist 'wiser than my enemies' and give more understanding than teachers stand behind the claim that Scripture makes one wise. The lifelong formation in the word echoes this Torah-wisdom motif.
sourceText: Your commandments make me wiser than my enemies, for your commandments are always with me. I have more understanding than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation. I understand more than the aged, because I have kept your precepts.

note: The charge to keep, teach, and not forget the statutes which are the people's wisdom, passing them to children, undergirds 'from infancy you have known the holy Scriptures.' The intergenerational transmission of God's law as wisdom is the Deuteronomic pattern.
sourceText: Behold, I have taught you statutes and ordinances, even as Yahweh my God commanded me, that you should do so in the midst of the land where you go in to possess it. Keep therefore and do them; for this is your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples, who shall hear all these statutes, and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” For what great nation is there, that has a god so near to them, as Yahweh our God […]

note: The command to teach God's words diligently to children from earliest years grounds Timothy's knowing the sacred writings 'from infancy.' The household catechesis of Scripture reflects the Shema's instruction.
sourceText: These words, which I command you this day, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

note: 'All Scripture is God-breathed' (theopneustos) evokes the creative breath of God that animated the man, who became a living being when God breathed into him. Scripture's life-giving divine breath parallels the breath of life at creation.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: 'Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD' stands behind the conviction that the God-breathed word sustains and equips life. Scripture as the word from God's mouth animating the believer reflects this manna lesson.
sourceText: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.

note: 'By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth' offers a creation-by-divine-breath background for 'God-breathed' Scripture. The pairing of word and breath of God's mouth resonates with theopneustos.
sourceText: By Yahweh’s word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth.

note: God's good Spirit given to instruct his people, and the law taught for their instruction, parallels Scripture's profit 'for teaching... for instruction in righteousness.' The motif of the inspired word teaching the people of God resonates faintly.
sourceText: You gave also your good Spirit to instruct them, and didn’t withhold your manna from their mouth, and gave them water for their thirst.

note: The precepts of the LORD that are right, the commandment pure enlightening the eyes, and the word more to be desired than gold, by which the servant is warned, parallel Scripture's profit for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. The functional benefits of God's word match closely.
sourceText: Yahweh’s precepts are right, rejoicing the heart. Yahweh’s commandment is pure, enlightening the eyes. The fear of Yahweh is clean, enduring forever. Yahweh’s ordinances are true, and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, yes, than much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and the extract of the honeycomb. Moreover by them is your servant warned. In keeping them there is great reward.

note: The charge to meditate on the book of the law to do all written in it, so as to be prosperous and successful, parallels Scripture equipping the man of God 'for every good work.' The word-formed competence for faithful action resonates.
sourceText: This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.

note: Ben Sira's identification of the law of Moses with wisdom that fills people with understanding and instruction offers a deuterocanonical analogue to Scripture making one wise for salvation. The Torah-as-wisdom theme parallels Paul's claim.
sourceText: All these things are the book of the covenant of the Most High God, Even the law which Moses commanded us for a heritage to the assemblies of Jacob. It is he that makes wisdom abundant, as Pishon, And as Tigris in the days of new fruits; That makes understanding full as Euphrates, And as Jordan in the days of harvest; That makes instruction to shine forth as the light, As Gihon in the days of vintage. The first man knew her not perfectly; And in like […]

note: The reference to the God who 'inspired him with an active soul and breathed into him a living spirit' connects the breath of God with life and knowledge, a deuterocanonical background for the God-breathed (theopneustos) word. The divine inbreathing motif resonates faintly.
sourceText: Because he was ignorant of him that moulded him, And of him that inspired into him an active soul, And breathed into him a vital spirit.

note: The solemn charge invokes God and Christ as the one 'who will judge the living and the dead at his appearing.' The motif of the LORD coming to 'judge the earth' is a refrain of the enthronement psalms, supplying the eschatological-judgment frame Paul adapts to Christ's appearing.
sourceText: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.

note: Joel's vision of the LORD seated to judge all the nations gathered in the valley of decision lies behind the forensic image of universal judgment of 'the living and the dead.' The Day-of-the-LORD assize is the conceptual reservoir for the charge given before the coming Judge.
sourceText: “Let the nations arouse themselves, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat; for there will I sit to judge all the surrounding nations.

note: The portrait of people who 'will not listen to the sound doctrine' but want teachers 'after their own lusts' and 'turn away their ears from the truth' closely mirrors Isaiah's rebellious people who tell seers, 'Prophesy not to us right things, speak unto us smooth things.' The refusal of true instruction in favor of pleasing words is the same indictment.
sourceText: For it is a rebellious people, lying children, children who will not hear Yahweh’s law; who tell the seers, “Don’t see!” and to the prophets, “Don’t prophesy to us right things. Tell us pleasant things. Prophesy deceits. Get out of the way. Turn aside from the path. Cause the Holy One of Israel to cease from before us.”

note: Jeremiah's lament that 'the prophets prophesy falsely... and my people love to have it so' parallels the hearers who heap up teachers to suit their own desires. The collusion between corrupt teachers and a people who prefer to be flattered underlies Paul's warning about itching ears.
sourceText: The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority; and my people love to have it so. What will you do in the end of it?

note: Micah pictures a people who would welcome a lying prophet who preaches of wine and strong drink as 'the prophet of this people.' The image of an audience that selects teachers appealing to its appetites resonates with the itching-ears congregation gathering pleasing instructors.
sourceText: If a man walking in a spirit of falsehood lies: “I will prophesy to you of wine and of strong drink”; he would be the prophet of this people.

note: Ahab's preference for prophets who tell him good rather than Micaiah who tells the truth typifies the pattern Paul names: hearers turning from truth toward voices that gratify them. A faint Old Testament instance of choosing flattering teachers over sound doctrine.
sourceText: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of Yahweh, Micaiah the son of Imlah; but I hate him; for he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.” Jehoshaphat said, “Don’t let the king say so.”

note: Paul says 'I am already being offered' (poured out as a drink offering), drawing on the sacrificial libation prescribed in the Mosaic cult. The image of life poured out like the wine offering at the altar gives his coming death a cultic, sacrificial coloring.
sourceText: In this way you shall offer daily, for seven days, the food of the offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh. It shall be offered in addition to the continual burnt offering, and its drink offering.

note: The 'crown of righteousness' which the righteous Judge will award echoes Wisdom's promise that the righteous 'shall receive a glorious kingdom and a beautiful crown from the Lord's hand.' The eschatological reward of a crown from God's hand to the righteous is shared imagery.
sourceText: Therefore will they receive the crown of royal dignity And the diadem of beauty from the Lord’s hand; Because with his right hand will he cover them, And with his arm will he shield them.

note: The title 'the righteous judge' who will give the crown 'on that day' reuses the enthronement-psalm refrain that the LORD comes to judge the world in righteousness. The forensic epithet is colored by the Old Testament confession of God as righteous judge of all.
sourceText: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.

note: The laying-up of a crown for the faithful may faintly recall the crowns set in the temple of the LORD as a memorial in Zechariah. The notion of a crown stored and later bestowed offers a remote Old Testament background to the crown reserved for Paul.
sourceText: Yes, take silver and gold, and make crowns, and set them on the head of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest; and speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple; even he shall build Yahweh’s temple; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule on his throne; and he shall be a priest on his throne; and the counsel of peace […]

note: The note that Demas deserted, 'having loved this present world,' may faintly draw on the psalmist's contrast between those who love vanity and the upright who walk in integrity. The framing of misplaced love for the world against faithfulness has a sapiential-psalmic ring, though no specific text is quoted.
sourceText: I have not sat with deceitful men, neither will I go in with hypocrites.

note: 'The Lord will repay him according to his works' reproduces the psalm's confession that God 'renders to every man according to his work.' Paul applies the principle of just recompense to Alexander, leaving vengeance to God rather than himself.
sourceText: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.

note: Proverbs asks whether God who weighs the heart will not 'render to every man according to his works,' the same recompense formula Paul invokes against Alexander the coppersmith. The wisdom maxim of divine repayment by deeds underwrites Paul's restraint.
sourceText: If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this”; doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not render to every man according to his work?

note: David's word that 'the LORD shall reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness' parallels Paul committing Alexander's recompense to God. A narrative instance of deferring vengeance to the LORD's just repayment.
sourceText: I am this day weak, though anointed king; and these men the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for me. May Yahweh reward the evildoer according to his wickedness.”

note: 'I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion' draws directly on the psalmist's cry, 'Save me from the lion's mouth.' Paul casts his rescue at the first defense in the language of the suffering righteous one delivered from the predatory lion.
sourceText: Save me from the lion’s mouth! Yes, from the horns of the wild oxen, you have answered me.

note: Deliverance 'out of the mouth of the lion' evokes Daniel, whose God 'sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths' so the beasts did not hurt him. The archetype of the faithful servant rescued from the lions stands behind Paul's testimony of standing firm and being delivered.
sourceText: My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me; because as before him innocence was found in me; and also before you, O king, have I done no hurt.

note: Mattathias's catalogue of the faithful recalls that 'Daniel for his innocency was delivered from the mouth of the lions,' the very phrase echoed in Paul's rescue. The deuterocanonical retelling shows the lions'-mouth deliverance already proverbial for divine rescue of the righteous.
sourceText: Daniel for his innocency was delivered from the mouth of lions.

note: The plea lest the enemy 'tear my soul like a lion' contributes to the stock image of the lion as deadly adversary from which the righteous is delivered. A supporting psalmic source for the lion-of-the-mouth rescue motif.
sourceText: lest they tear apart my soul like a lion, ripping it in pieces, while there is no one to deliver.

note: 'The Lord stood by me and strengthened me' resonates with the psalm's assurance that the LORD 'shall stand at the right hand of the poor' to save him. The image of God standing beside the abandoned righteous one as defender underlies Paul's account of his lonely first defense.
sourceText: For he will stand at the right hand of the needy, to save him from those who judge his soul.

note: The Lord standing by Paul amid mortal danger faintly recalls the fourth figure standing with the three in the furnace, a deliverance narrative paired with Daniel's lions. The motif of divine presence rescuing the faithful from death rounds out the Danielic background.
sourceText: He answered, Look, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are unharmed; and the aspect of the fourth is like a son of the gods.

note: The promise that the Lord 'will deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me' echoes the psalm of protection, where God delivers from the snare and preserves the one who trusts him. The confidence of comprehensive deliverance and preservation has a psalmic protective texture.
sourceText: For he will deliver you from the snare of the fowler, and from the deadly pestilence.

note: The closing benediction 'The Lord be with your spirit' echoes the Old Testament greeting formula 'The LORD be with you,' as exchanged by Boaz and his reapers. The liturgical wish of the LORD's presence frames Paul's farewell.
sourceText: Behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and said to the reapers, “Yahweh be with you.” They answered him, “Yahweh bless you.”

note: The clause that God 'can't lie' (1:2) draws on Balaam's oracle that 'God is not a man, that he should lie.' The divine veracity grounds the promise of eternal life made 'before time began.' Shared vocabulary and theology of God's unbreakable word make this the primary background.
sourceText: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?

note: Samuel's declaration that 'the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent' reinforces the same axiom of divine truthfulness behind 'God, who can't lie.' Often paired with Numbers 23:19 as a doublet on the immutability of God's word.
sourceText: Also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent; for he is not a man, that he should repent.”

note: God's oath 'I have sworn by my holiness; I will not lie to David' supplies a covenantal instance of the same axiom undergirding a promise 'before time began.' Faint and contested, offered as a thematic parallel rather than verbal source.
sourceText: Once have I sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David.

note: Jethro's counsel to select 'able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness' to lead supplies the OT template of vetted, blameless leaders appointed over the people. Titus's charge to appoint elders who are above reproach and not greedy echoes this qualification list.
sourceText: Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

note: Moses' instruction to take 'wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes' to be made heads parallels the appointment of recognized, reputable elders 'in every city.' The figural pattern of qualified communal leadership stands behind the overseer requirements.
sourceText: Take wise men of understanding and well known according to your tribes, and I will make them heads over you.”

note: The command to appoint judges and officers 'in all your gates' who shun a bribe and dishonest gain echoes both the city-by-city appointing of elders and the 'not greedy for dishonest gain' qualification. Faint and contested as a direct source.
sourceText: You shall make judges and officers in all your gates, which Yahweh your God gives you, according to your tribes; and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment. You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality. You shall not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise, and perverts the words of the righteous. You shall follow that which is altogether just, that you may live, and inherit the land which Yahweh your God gives […]

note: The priestly requirement that one who draws near be 'without blemish' offers an OT background to the demand that the overseer be 'blameless.' Contested, since the moral 'above reproach' of Titus differs from Levitical physical wholeness; logged as a faint figural resonance.
sourceText: “Say to Aaron, ‘None of your seed throughout their generations who has a defect may approach to offer the bread of his God. For whatever man he is that has a defect, he shall not draw near: a blind man, or a lame, or he who has a flat nose, or any deformity, or a man who has an injured foot, or an injured hand, or hunchbacked, or a dwarf, or one who has a defect in his eye, or an itching disease, or scabs, or who has damaged testicles. No man of the seed […]

note: The wisdom warning that rulers should not be 'given to wine' lest they pervert justice resonates with the overseer being 'not given to wine.' Faint and contested verbal echo within the leadership-qualification cluster.
sourceText: It is not for kings, Lemuel; it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes to say, ‘Where is strong drink?’ lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the justice due to anyone who is afflicted.

note: Isaiah's indictment of shepherds who are 'greedy dogs… they all look to their own way, every one for his gain' stands behind the deceivers who teach 'for dishonest gain's sake.' The portrait of mercenary false leaders is a stock prophetic type Titus applies to the Cretan teachers.
sourceText: Yes, the dogs are greedy, they can never have enough; and these are shepherds who can’t understand: they have all turned to their own way, each one to his gain, from every quarter.

note: Micah condemns leaders who 'teach for hire' and prophets who 'divine for money,' the same fusion of teaching and shameful gain leveled at the deceivers in 1:11. The prophetic critique of religious profiteering is the conceptual source.
sourceText: Her leaders judge for bribes, and her priests teach for a price, and her prophets of it tell fortunes for money: yet they lean on Yahweh, and say, “Isn’t Yahweh in the midst of us? No disaster will come on us.”

note: Micah's prophets who 'make my people err' for food reinforce the picture of deceivers leading whole houses astray for gain. Logged as a supporting faint parallel within the greedy-false-prophet cluster.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh concerning the prophets who lead my people astray; for those who feed their teeth, they proclaim, “Peace!” and whoever doesn’t provide for their mouths, they prepare war against him:

note: Ezekiel's princes 'like wolves… to get dishonest gain' parallel those teaching for dishonest gain and overthrowing households. A faint reinforcing prophetic echo of rapacious leadership.
sourceText: Her princes in its midst are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.

note: Jeremiah's charge that 'every one is given to covetousness… from the prophet even to the priest every one deals falsely' echoes the deceivers who teach for gain. Faint and contested, offered as a parallel within the same prophetic topos.
sourceText: “For from their least even to their greatest, everyone is given to covetousness; and from the prophet even to the priest, everyone deals falsely.

note: The maxim 'to the pure, all things are pure' (1:15) presupposes the creation verdict that God saw all that he had made 'and behold, it was very good.' The goodness of all created things grounds Paul's rejection of the ascetic/ritual purity demands of the teachers.
sourceText: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.

note: Haggai's priestly ruling that one defiled by a corpse renders what he touches unclean, applied to 'this people… so is every work of their hands,' lies behind 'to those who are defiled… nothing is pure' and 'their mind and conscience are defiled.' Contagion of defilement is reversed/transposed onto inward corruption.
sourceText: Then Haggai said, “If one who is unclean by reason of a dead body touch any of these, will it be unclean?” The priests answered, “It will be unclean.” Then Haggai answered, “‘So is this people, and so is this nation before me,’ says Yahweh; ‘and so is every work of their hands. That which they offer there is unclean.

note: The generation 'pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness' parallels those who profess purity yet are inwardly defiled in mind and conscience. A pointed wisdom echo on self-deceived impurity.
sourceText: There is a generation that is pure in their own eyes, yet are not washed from their filthiness.

note: Isaiah's people who 'draw near with their mouth… but have removed their heart far from me,' teaching 'the commandment of men,' stands behind both 'commandments of men who turn away from the truth' (1:14) and 'they profess that they know God, but by their works they deny him' (1:16). Lip-profession contradicted by life is the shared indictment.
sourceText: The Lord said, “Because this people draws near with their mouth and with their lips to honor me, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught;
lxxText: And the Lord has said, This people draw nigh to me with their mouth, and they honour me with their lips, but their heart is far from me: but in vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men.

note: God's complaint that the wicked are 'near in their mouth, and far from their reins' parallels professing to know God while denying him by works. A faint contested echo overlapping with Isaiah 29:13.
sourceText: You have planted them, yes, they have taken root; they grow, yes, they produce fruit: you are near in their mouth, and far from their heart.

note: The clean/unclean food distinctions of the holiness code form the implicit ritual background that 'to the pure all things are pure' relativizes. Contested as a direct source rather than a conceptual foil for the purity dispute.
sourceText: For I am Yahweh your God. Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am holy: neither shall you defile yourselves with any kind of creeping thing that moves on the earth. For I am Yahweh who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy. “‘This is the law of the animal, and of the bird, and of every living creature that moves in the waters, and of every creature that creeps on the earth, to make […]

note: The portrait of the older and younger women — reverent, loving their households, 'workers at home,' kind and industrious — draws on the ideal of the worthy woman whose works praise her. The household-management language coheres with the Septuagintal woman of Proverbs 31. Thematic volume and availability are strong even without verbal quotation.
sourceText: Who can find a worthy woman? For her price is far above rubies. The heart of her husband trusts in her. He shall have no lack of gain. She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life. She seeks wool and flax, and works eagerly with her hands. She is like the merchant ships. She brings her bread from afar. She rises also while it is yet night, gives food to her household, and portions for her servant girls. She considers a field, and buys it. […]

note: 'Workers at home' (v.5) recalls the worthy woman who 'looks well to the ways of her household.' A faint domestic-management echo within the broader Proverbs 31 frame.
sourceText: She looks well to the ways of her household, and doesn’t eat the bread of idleness.

note: Older women 'not enslaved to much wine' (v.3) echoes the wisdom warning against intoxication, where wine is unfit for those who must judge and govern. Reinforced by Proverbs 23:20-21. Contested as generic moral commonplace.
sourceText: It is not for kings, Lemuel; it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes to say, ‘Where is strong drink?’ lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the justice due to anyone who is afflicted. Give strong drink to him who is ready to perish; and wine to the bitter in soul: Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more.

note: 'That God's word may not be blasphemed' (v.5; cf. the name not reviled) reworks Isaiah's lament that 'my name continually all the day is blasphemed' among the nations because of Israel. Paul transfers the prophetic concern about Gentiles reviling God's name to the conduct of believers in the household.
sourceText: “Now therefore, what do I do here,” says Yahweh, “seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Those who rule over them mock,” says Yahweh, “and my name continually all the day is blasphemed.

note: The motif that God's people may cause his name to be profaned/blasphemed among the nations underlies v.5 and v.10 ('that they may adorn the doctrine of God'). Ezekiel pairs the profaning of the name with God's resolve to vindicate his holy name, the same logic of witness Paul applies.
sourceText: When they came to the nations, where they went, they profaned my holy name; in that men said of them, These are the people of Yahweh, and are gone out of his land. But I had respect for my holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations, where they went. Therefore tell the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: I don’t do this for your sake, house of Israel, but for my holy name, which you have profaned among the nations, where […]

note: The instruction that wives be 'in subjection to their own husbands' (v.5) may faintly echo the post-fall ordering of marriage. Contested, since the household-code material is more directly Hellenistic-Jewish ethical convention than a Genesis citation.
sourceText: To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. In pain you will bear children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

note: 'The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men' (v.11) and the 'appearing of the glory' (v.13) draw on the revelation of the LORD's glory which 'all flesh shall see together.' The universal scope of salvation/glory revealed is Isaianic.
sourceText: Yahweh’s glory shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together; for the mouth of Yahweh has spoken it.”

note: Salvation 'to all men' (v.11) echoes the bared arm of the LORD by which 'all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.' A faint universal-salvation echo supporting v.11.
sourceText: Yahweh has made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.

note: Grace 'instructing/training us' (paideuō, v.12) to renounce ungodliness invokes the divine discipline tradition: the LORD chastens/instructs the one he loves as a father his son. The pedagogical grace of Titus is framed in this wisdom-discipline idiom.
sourceText: My son, don’t despise Yahweh’s discipline, neither be weary of his reproof: for whom Yahweh loves, he reproves; even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.
lxxText: My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loves, he rebukes, and scourges every son whom he receives.

note: The training/disciplining work of grace (v.12) echoes 'as a man chastens his son, so the LORD your God chastens you.' Reinforces the paideia background alongside Proverbs 3.
sourceText: You shall consider in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so Yahweh your God disciplines you.

note: 'The appearing of the glory of our great God' (v.13) draws on the glory of the LORD that rises and is seen upon his people while darkness covers the earth. An eschatological epiphany-of-glory source.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you.

note: 'The LORD shall appear in his glory' undergirds the 'blessed hope and appearing of the glory' (v.13). The verb of divine appearing in glory matches the epiphany expectation.
sourceText: For Yahweh has built up Zion. He has appeared in his glory.

note: The sudden coming of the Lord to his temple, and the question 'who shall abide the day of his appearing,' resonates with the awaited appearing in glory (v.13) and the purifying purpose of v.14. Contested, faint volume.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap;

note: 'Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity' (v.14) closely tracks 'he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.' The pairing of redemption with deliverance from all iniquity/lawlessness is a near-verbal dependence.
sourceText: He will redeem Israel from all their sins.

note: 'Purify for himself a people for his own possession' (v.14) draws on 'you shall be my treasured possession (peculiar people) above all peoples.' The covenant election of a treasured people is reapplied to the church redeemed by Christ.
sourceText: Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine;

note: 'A people for his own possession' (v.14) echoes Israel as 'a holy people unto the LORD, a peculiar people unto himself, above all peoples.' Part of the Deuteronomic treasured-people cluster behind v.14.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.

note: Restates the election of Israel as a 'peculiar people' / treasured possession, directly informing the 'people for his own possession' language of v.14.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God, and Yahweh has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.

note: 'The LORD has avouched you this day to be a peculiar people unto himself' supplies the covenant-possession formula reused in v.14, here tied to keeping his commandments (cf. 'zealous for good works').
sourceText: Yahweh has declared this day that you are a people for his own possession, as he has promised you, and that you should keep all his commandments.

note: 'Purify for himself a people' (v.14) echoes 'I will cleanse them... so they shall be my people, and I will be their God.' The cleansing-to-be-a-people motif of the new covenant underlies the purifying purpose of redemption.
sourceText: neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things, nor with any of their transgressions; but I will save them out of all their dwelling places, in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them: so shall they be my people, and I will be their God.

note: The promise to sprinkle clean water and cleanse from all uncleanness reinforces the 'purify a people' language of v.14 within the same Ezekielian new-covenant cleansing complex. Faint, secondary to 37:23.
sourceText: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.

note: 'They shall be mine, my treasured possession (peculiar treasure)' on the day God acts supports the 'people for his own possession' of v.14, joining the treasured-people motif to an eschatological day, fitting the appearing of v.13.
sourceText: They shall be mine,” says Yahweh of Armies, “my own possession in the day that I make, and I will spare them, as a man spares his own son who serves him.

note: 'Zealous for good works' (v.14) may evoke Phinehas, who 'was zealous for his God,' the paradigm of covenant zeal rewarded with an everlasting covenant. Contested, since Paul's 'zeal for good works' may be generic rather than a Phinehas allusion.
sourceText: “Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I didn’t consume the children of Israel in my jealousy. Therefore say, ‘Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace. It shall be to him, and to his seed after him, the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was jealous for his God, and made atonement for the children of […]

note: 'Redeem us' (lytroō, v.14) echoes the exodus redemption language: the LORD 'redeemed you from the house of bondage.' A faint redemption-vocabulary echo behind v.14, reinforced by Exodus 6:6.
sourceText: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

note: 'Exhort and reprove with all authority; let no man despise you' (v.15) faintly recalls the prophetic commissioning, where the young prophet is told not to fear, for God will be with him. A contested echo of prophetic emboldening, since the charge fits general pastoral exhortation.
sourceText: But Yahweh said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak. Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh.

note: The charge to fear the LORD and the king, and not to join with the rebellious, stands behind Paul's instruction to be subject to rulers and authorities. The wisdom tradition links reverence for God with submission to civic authority, the same dual loyalty Titus urges.
sourceText: My son, fear Yahweh and the king. Don’t join those who are rebellious:

note: Qoheleth counsels keeping the king's command, framed by an oath before God, mirroring the obedience to rulers Titus enjoins. The Septuagint vocabulary of obeying royal authority overlaps conceptually with subjection to those in power.
sourceText: I say, “Keep the king’s command!” because of the oath to God.

note: Jeremiah's letter tells the exiles to seek the welfare of the city and pray for it, the model of constructive subjection to a pagan order. Titus' call to be ready for every good work toward all extends this exilic posture of civic good toward the surrounding society.
sourceText: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it; for in its peace you shall have peace.

note: Wisdom literature counsels prudent, peaceable deference to those who hold power. The disposition of gentleness and avoidance of contention toward rulers echoes the sapiential ideal of pacifying authority.
sourceText: The king’s wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise man will pacify it.

note: A soft answer turns away wrath underlies the exhortation to speak evil of no one and to be gentle, showing all humility. The sapiential ethic of gentle, non-contentious speech is the backdrop for these virtues.
sourceText: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

note: The confession that we were once deceived recalls the primal pattern of being led astray, the serpent's deception of Eve. The catalogue of human bondage to lust and malice traces back to the Edenic fall as the origin of disordered desire.
sourceText: Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

note: All we like sheep have gone astray, each to his own way, lies behind the description of being deceived and serving various lusts. The motif of straying and being saved not by works but by mercy resonates with the Servant who bears wandering humanity.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: The Wisdom vice-list portrays idolaters living in malice, envy, deceit, and disordered passions, the same cluster Titus uses for the unredeemed past. Both texts diagnose pre-conversion humanity as enslaved to corrupt desire and mutual hatred born of false worship.
sourceText: Afterward it was not enough for them to go astray as touching the knowledge of God; But also, while they live in sore conflict through ignorance of him. That multitude of evils they call peace. For either slaughtering children in solemn rites, or celebrating secret mysteries, Or holding frantic revels of strange ordinances, No longer do they guard either life or purity of marriage, But one brings upon another either death by treachery, or anguish by […]

note: The new-covenant promise to sprinkle clean water for cleansing and to put a new spirit within stands directly behind the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit. The pairing of water-cleansing with Spirit-renewal is the structural template of Titus' soteriology.
sourceText: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: The promise that God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh underlies the statement that he poured out the Spirit on us richly. The verb of outpouring is the prophetic signature for the eschatological gift of the Spirit appropriated here.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.

note: God's pledge that I have poured out my Spirit on the house of Israel reinforces the outpouring language of verse 6. The prophetic image of lavish Spirit-effusion grounds Paul's emphasis on the Spirit poured out richly.
sourceText: neither will I hide my face any more from them; for I have poured out my Spirit on the house of Israel, says the Lord Yahweh.

note: I will pour water on the thirsty and my Spirit on your offspring fuses water and Spirit exactly as Titus fuses the washing with the renewing of the Holy Spirit. The double pouring of water and Spirit is the prophetic matrix for the regenerating bath.
sourceText: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:

note: Purge me and I shall be clean, wash me and I shall be whiter than snow voices the cleansing-by-washing that Titus names the washing of regeneration. The penitential plea for inward purity prefigures the saving bath grounded in mercy, not works.
sourceText: Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.

note: Create in me a clean heart and renew a right spirit within me supplies the language of renewal by the Spirit. The Davidic prayer joins cleansing and inward renewing precisely as Titus joins washing and renewing of the Holy Spirit.
sourceText: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.

note: I will put my Spirit in you and you shall live undergirds the link between Spirit-indwelling and the hope of eternal life in verse 7. The vivifying gift of the Spirit that raises the dead nation prefigures regeneration unto life.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.

note: The ritual sprinkling of the water of purification to cleanse defilement informs the cultic background of the washing of regeneration. The Mosaic lustration provides the ceremonial idiom later spiritualized into the saving bath.
sourceText: “For the unclean, they shall take of the ashes of the burning of the sin offering; and running water shall be poured into a vessel. A clean person shall take hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle it on the tent, on all the vessels, on the persons who were there, and on him who touched the bone, or the slain, or the dead, or the grave. The clean person shall sprinkle on the unclean on the third day, and on the seventh day. On the seventh day, he shall […]

note: The recital of the LORD's lovingkindnesses and the multitude of his mercies frames God's saving action as kindness and love, echoed in the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind. Salvation is grounded in covenant mercy rather than desert.
sourceText: I will make mention of the loving kindnesses of Yahweh and the praises of Yahweh, according to all that Yahweh has bestowed on us, and the great goodness toward the house of Israel, which he has bestowed on them according to his mercies, and according to the multitude of his loving kindnesses.

note: The self-revelation of the LORD as merciful, gracious, and abounding in steadfast love stands behind the appearance of the kindness and love of God who saves according to his mercy. The grace-formula of Sinai is the theological ground for salvation not by works.
sourceText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,

note: With the LORD is steadfast love and plenteous redemption colors the claim that salvation rests on mercy and issues in justification by grace. The psalm's hope in abundant redemption parallels the hope of eternal life made the believer's inheritance.
sourceText: Israel, hope in Yahweh, for with Yahweh there is loving kindness. With him is abundant redemption.

note: The promise that whoever calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved follows the Spirit-outpouring oracle and undergirds the language of being saved according to mercy. The Joel context links Spirit and salvation as Titus does.
sourceText: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.

note: The beginning of strife is like releasing water, so abandon a quarrel before it breaks out, undergirds the command to shun strife and disputes and to avoid the factious man. Wisdom counsels disengaging from contention before it spreads, as Titus instructs.
sourceText: The beginning of strife is like breaching a dam, therefore stop contention before quarreling breaks out.

note: It is to a man's honor to keep aloof from strife, while every fool is quick to quarrel, parallels the avoidance of foolish questionings and disputes. The sapiential praise of those who refrain from quarreling shapes Paul's verdict that strife is unprofitable and vain.
sourceText: It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife; but every fool will be quarreling.

note: As charcoal kindles fire, a contentious man kindles strife, illuminating the warning against the factious person who must be avoided. The wisdom portrait of the quarrel-feeder informs the directive to reject the divisive after two warnings.
sourceText: As coals are to hot embers, and wood to fire, so is a contentious man to kindling strife.

note: Ben Sira warns against contending with the powerful and against quarreling with the loud-mouthed and contentious, advice that parallels shunning disputes and the factious man. The deuterocanonical counsel to avoid futile contention reinforces Titus' rejection of vain wrangling.
sourceText: Contend not with a mighty man, Lest haply you fall into his hands. Strive not with a rich man, lest haply he overweigh you: For gold has destroyed many, And turned away the hearts of kings. Contend not with a man that is full of tongue, And heap not wood upon his fire.

note: Refrain from strife and you will lessen sins, for a hasty quarrel kindles fire, echoes the diagnosis that the factious man sins and is self-condemned. Ben Sira treats quarreling as sin-producing, matching the moral framing of strife as unprofitable and corrupting.
sourceText: Abstain from strife, and you will diminish your sins: For a passionate man will kindle strife; And a man that is a sinner will trouble friends, And will make debate among those who are at peace. As is the fuel of the fire, so will it burn; And as the stoutness of the strife is, so will it burn: As is the strength of the man, so will be his wrath; And as is his wealth, so will he exalt his anger. A contention begun in haste kindles a fire; And a hasty […]

note: Conviction on the evidence of two or three witnesses, then purging the evil from the midst, lies behind the pattern of a first and second warning followed by rejecting the divisive person. The Mosaic procedure of repeated testimony then removal supplies the disciplinary template.
sourceText: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death. The hand of the witnesses shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.

note: The requirement that a matter be established by two or three witnesses informs the first-and-second-warning structure preceding the rejection of the factious man. The legal norm of repeated attestation underlies the procedural fairness of two admonitions.
sourceText: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.

note: The Aaronic blessing's bestowal of the LORD's grace and peace lies faintly behind the closing benediction, grace be with you all. The epistolary grace-greeting draws on the priestly tradition of invoking divine favor upon the congregation.
sourceText: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: Paul says the hearts (literally bowels/inward parts) of the saints have been 'refreshed' through Philemon. Proverbs likens a faithful messenger to the cold of snow that 'refreshes the soul' of his masters, the nearest sapiential parallel to this language of inward refreshment. The link is verbal and thematic rather than a citation, and Paul develops it more pointedly at v20.
sourceText: As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.

note: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus 'no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother.' The Holiness Code forbids treating an impoverished Israelite who sells himself as a slave, requiring instead that he be held as a hired worker and a brother, not ruled over harshly. Paul effectively extends this Israelite kinship-over-bondage principle to a Christian master and his returning slave.
sourceText: “‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you; you shall not make him to serve as a slave. As a hired servant, and as a temporary resident, he shall be with you; he shall serve with you until the Year of Jubilee: then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and shall return to his own family, and to the possession of his fathers. For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be […]

note: The Deuteronomic slave law mandates release of a Hebrew bondservant and generous provision out of remembered solidarity ('you were a slave in Egypt'). Paul's reconfiguring of Onesimus from slave to beloved brother, no longer held under necessity, resonates with this manumission-and-fraternity ethic, though Paul never cites the statute.
sourceText: If your brother, a Hebrew man, or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, and serves you six years; then in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you. When you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty. You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your wine press. As Yahweh your God has blessed you, you shall give to him. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and […]

note: The law forbids returning an escaped slave to his master and requires letting him dwell freely where he chooses. Paul's careful handling of the fugitive Onesimus, sending him back only as a free brother and asking Philemon not to reclaim him as property, stands in deliberate tension and dialogue with this provision. Many read the whole letter as Paul navigating around the spirit of this command.
sourceText: You shall not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place which he shall choose within one of your gates, where it pleases him best. You shall not oppress him.

note: 'Perhaps he was separated from you for a while, that you would have him forever' echoes Joseph's providential reading of his own separation from his family: 'God sent me before you to preserve life... it was not you who sent me here, but God.' Paul, like Joseph, reframes a painful parting as hidden divine purpose that yields a greater, lasting reunion.
sourceText: Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life. For these two years the famine has been in the land, and there are yet five years, in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest. God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant in the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance. So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God, and he has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord […]

note: Joseph's summary, 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good,' undergirds Paul's 'perhaps' of v15, where Onesimus's wrong and flight are recast as occasion for good. The thematic kinship is strong even though Paul borrows no wording.
sourceText: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.

note: Onesimus is now to be received as a brother 'both in the flesh and in the Lord.' Laban's welcome of Jacob, 'surely you are my bone and my flesh,' is the paradigmatic Hebrew idiom for kinship recognition that overrides prior status. The connection is faint and conceptual.
sourceText: Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.” He lived with him for a month.

note: 'If he has wronged you or owes you anything, put that to my account... I will repay it' enacts the role of surety. Judah pledges himself for Benjamin: 'I will be surety for him; of my hand you shall require him.' Paul stands as personal guarantor for Onesimus exactly as Judah does for his brother, assuming the debt against himself.
sourceText: I’ll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him. If I don’t bring him to you, and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever,

note: Judah restates his suretyship before Joseph, 'I became surety for the boy to my father,' offering to bear the consequence in the brother's place. Paul's handwritten pledge to absorb Onesimus's debt and stand in his stead closely parallels this self-substituting guarantee for a kinsman.
sourceText: For your servant became collateral for the boy to my father, saying, ‘If I don’t bring him to you, then I will bear the blame to my father forever.’

note: Proverbs repeatedly treats the giving of surety for another as a weighty, self-binding act ('if you have struck your hands in pledge for a stranger... you are snared by the words of your mouth'). Paul knowingly takes on precisely this binding pledge for Onesimus, inverting the proverb's caution into voluntary love.
sourceText: My son, if you have become collateral for your neighbor, if you have struck your hands in pledge for a stranger; You are trapped by the words of your mouth. You are ensnared with the words of your mouth. Do this now, my son, and deliver yourself, since you have come into the hand of your neighbor. Go, humble yourself. Press your plea with your neighbor.

note: 'He who is surety for a stranger will suffer for it.' Paul's assumption of Onesimus's liability deliberately embraces the cost the proverb warns against, making the sapiential surety-language a backdrop for his act of intercession.
sourceText: He who is collateral for a stranger will suffer for it, but he who refuses pledges of collateral is secure.

note: 'Refresh my heart in the Lord' picks up the language of inward refreshment from v7. Proverbs' image of the faithful messenger who 'refreshes the soul of his masters' is the closest wisdom parallel to this petition for refreshment as the fruit of obedient love.
sourceText: As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.

note: 'Prepare a guest room for me' faintly recalls the Shunammite woman who prepares a small upper room for Elisha so the man of God may lodge with her. The shared motif is hospitality of a lodging readied for an honored servant of God, though Paul uses ordinary travel language without scriptural signal.
sourceText: It fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread. She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, that passes by us continually. Please let us make a little room on the wall. Let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. It shall be, when he comes to us, that he […]

note: ‘Sat down on the right hand of the Majesty’ (v. 3) is a low-volume echo of Ps 110:1, planted before the catena begins and paid off as its explicit climax at 1:13. Hays' recurrence test: the same source surfaces twice, so even the faint first instance earns credence.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’

note: ‘When he had by himself purified us of our sins’ (v. 3) quotes nothing, yet figurally invokes the Day of Atonement cult that chapters 9–10 will expound — the book's central typology. No verbal volume; high figural coherence (Hays, Reading Backwards).
sourceText: For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. (Leviticus 16:30)

note: The marquee echo of the chapter. ‘Radiance of his glory… the very image of his substance’ (v. 3) reproduces the rare term apaugasma and the eikōn/glory pairing of Wis 7:25–26 — high verbal volume against a Second Temple text most scholars (Hays, Attridge, Beale & Carson) name as the direct source. Hebrews transfers what Wisdom says of personified Sophia to the Son. Confidence kept high despite low text-field availability, since bible-api serves only the Protestant canon.
sourceText: For she is a breath of the power of God, and a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, and an unspotted mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. (Wisdom of Solomon 7:25–26)

note: ‘Through whom also he made the worlds’ (v. 2) draws on the Wisdom-as-agent-of-creation tradition that runs from Prov 8:22–31 into Wisdom and Sirach. Thematic coherence (Wisdom christology) more than verbal volume; the LXX of Prov 8:22 (‘the Lord created me’) fed the patristic debates this verse anticipates.
sourceText: Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was there; when he set a circle on the surface of the deep, when he established the clouds above, when the springs of the deep became strong, when he gave to the sea its boundary, that the waters should not violate his commandment, when he marked out the foundations of the earth; then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him, rejoicing in his whole world. My delight was with the sons of men.

note: ‘Whom he appointed heir of all things’ (v. 2) sounds the inheritance grant of Ps 2:8 — the same psalm quoted outright at 1:5. Recurrence (Hays): Ps 2 is demonstrably available and re-used, so the inheritance language is heard as its anticipatory echo.
sourceText: Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance, the uttermost parts of the earth for your possession.

note: ‘Heir of all things’ and the universal, unending dominion granted the one ‘like a son of man’ (Dan 7:14) share thematic coherence with the Son's inheritance and session. Faint, contested — no verbal volume — but a stock messianic substrate scholars note behind the exaltation language.
sourceText: Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom that which will not be destroyed.

note: ‘Upholding all things by the word of his power’ (v. 3) ascribes to the Son the sole-creator role Isa 44:24 reserves to YHWH — a faint conceptual echo that prepares the bolder Ps 102 transfer at 1:10–12. Low volume; coherence with the creation theme of the prologue.
sourceText: Yahweh, your Redeemer, and he who formed you from the womb says: ‘I am Yahweh, who makes all things; who alone stretches out the heavens; who spreads out the earth by myself;’

note: ‘Having become so much better than the angels’ (v. 4) faintly recalls the incomparability formula of Ps 89:6, which sets YHWH above the ‘sons of the heavenly beings.’ A dashed echo seeding the angel-comparison the catena exists to make; Ps 89 recurs at 1:6 (‘firstborn’).
sourceText: For who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of the heavenly beings is like Yahweh,

note: The royal-enthronement decree, applied to the Son. Verbatim (high volume) and recurrent — Ps 2 returns at Heb 5:5. The first link in the chain.
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, ‘You are my son. Today I have become your father.’

note: Nathan's dynastic oracle to David, read messianically and welded to Ps 2:7 by shared father/son language — a classic gezerah shavah (linking two texts by a common phrase). The author silently drops the clause about iniquity.
sourceText: I will be his father, and he will be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;

note: Ps 89:26–27 reworks the Nathan oracle into ‘You are my Father… I will appoint him my firstborn,’ the same father/firstborn nexus Hebrews exploits across 1:5–6. The verbatim text-field shows Ps 89:6 (what bible-api returns for psalm+89:6); the relevant 26–27 wording is quoted inline. Medium volume, strong thematic coherence linking this verse to 1:6's prōtotokos.
sourceText: For who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of the heavenly beings is like Yahweh, (Psalm 89:6; vv. 26–27: ‘He will call to me, “You are my Father, my God, and the rock of my salvation.” I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.’)

note: The clause immediately preceding the quoted 7:14 promises an everlasting throne — the dynastic-permanence note Hebrews develops into the eternal Son (cf. ‘your throne… forever’ at 1:8). A contiguous echo riding on the formal citation.
sourceText: He will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.

note: The Chronicler's parallel of the Nathan oracle drops the conditional ‘if he commits iniquity,’ giving the unconditioned father/son form Hebrews actually uses. A faint witness that the author's tradition already read the oracle as Hebrews does; low independent volume.
sourceText: I will be his father, and he will be my son. I will not take my loving kindness away from him, as I took it from him that was before you;

note: A textual fork. The Hebrew of Deut 32:43 (‘Rejoice, you nations, with his people…’) has no such line; the clause exists only in the Septuagint the author read. Hays' first test — availability — in action: the Scripture available to him was the Greek Bible, and that is the text he quotes.
sourceText: Rejoice, you nations, with his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants. He will take vengeance on his adversaries, and will make atonement for his land and for his people.
lxxText: Rejoice, ye heavens, with him, and let all the angels of God worship him; rejoice ye Gentiles, with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen themselves in him; for he will avenge the blood of his sons, and he will render vengeance, and recompense justice to his enemies, and will reward them that hate him; and the Lord shall purge the land of his people.

note: ‘The firstborn’ (prōtotokos) carries the Davidic-king title of Ps 89:27 — a verbal allusion, not a formal citation, transferring the king's rank to the Son.
sourceText: I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.

note: The LXX of Ps 97:7 renders the Hebrew ‘all you gods (elohim)’ as ‘all his angels,’ giving the very clause Hebrews cites — hence many (Beale & Carson, NA28 margin) read Ps 97:7 LXX, not Deut 32:43, as the primary source. The WEB (Hebrew) shown here lacks the angelic wording; the divergence is the whole contest. A theophany-of-judgment psalm bent to the enthronement of the firstborn.
sourceText: Let all them be shamed who serve engraved images, who boast in their idols. Worship him, all you gods!
lxxText: Let all that worship graven images be ashamed, who boast of their idols; worship him, all ye his angels.

note: The Masoretic Hebrew of Deut 32:43 (shown here) shows what the Greek expanded: no command to worship and no angels. Included to mark the Hebrew-vs-LXX gap figurally — the Song of Moses' eschatological vindication is the frame into which the Greek tradition inserted the angelic homage Hebrews needs. Low volume; contested.
sourceText: Rejoice, you nations, with his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants. He will take vengeance on his adversaries, and will make atonement for his land and for his people.
lxxText: Rejoice, ye heavens, with him, and let all the angels of God worship him; rejoice ye Gentiles, with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen themselves in him; for he will avenge the blood of his sons, and he will render vengeance, and recompense justice to his enemies, and will reward them that hate him; and the Lord shall purge the land of his people.

note: A creation psalm. The Hebrew (here, WEB) reads ‘makes winds his messengers’; Hebrews follows the Greek word order — ‘makes his angels winds’ — bending the line toward angelology. The same reversible ambiguity the argument needs: angels are mutable servants, the Son is enthroned.
sourceText: He makes his messengers winds; his servants flames of fire.
lxxText: Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire.

note: The picture of wind and fire as God's compliant agents (‘stormy wind, fulfilling his word’) shares the mutable-creature theme Hebrews presses against the angels. A faint thematic echo, no verbal volume — listed for the maximal inventory.
sourceText: lightning and hail, snow and clouds; stormy wind, fulfilling his word;

note: A royal wedding psalm in which the king is addressed as ‘God.’ Hebrews reads the vocative christologically — the figural payload (the Son addressed as God) rides on a high-volume, verbatim quotation.
sourceText: Your throne, God, is forever and ever. A scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness, and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.

note: The same psalm opens by setting the king ‘above the sons of men,’ matching ‘above your fellows’ (v. 9). A contiguous echo from the immediate context of the citation, reinforcing the Son's surpassing rank (recurrence within one source).
sourceText: You are the most excellent of the sons of men. Grace has anointed your lips, therefore God has blessed you forever.

note: ‘Has anointed you with the oil of gladness’ (v. 9) draws on the messianic-anointing register that Isa 61:1 made canonical for the title ‘Christ/anointed.’ Faint, no verbal volume — thematic coherence with the Son's anointing above his fellows.
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;
