note: James cites 'Do not commit adultery' (v.11) from the Decalogue, Exodus 20:14. The pairing of adultery and murder is a formal scriptural citation establishing that breaking one point makes one a transgressor of all.
sourceText: “You shall not commit adultery.

note: The Decalogue's murder prohibition also appears at Deuteronomy 5:17; James's citation draws on the Decalogue in either form. Listed as an alternate source for the murder commandment quoted in v.11.
sourceText: “You shall not murder.

note: The adultery prohibition also stands at Deuteronomy 5:18; James's quotation reflects the Decalogue. Provided as the Deuteronomic parallel to the Exodus citation in v.11.
sourceText: “You shall not commit adultery.

note: 'Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered.' James 2:13 says 'judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy.' The lex talionis of mercy/mercilessness is closely paralleled.
sourceText: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.

note: '...to do justice, and to love mercy (hesed), and to walk humbly with your God.' James's exaltation of mercy as triumphing over judgment (v.13) draws on the prophetic prizing of mercy as the heart of covenant obedience.
sourceText: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

note: 'Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy... do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor.' James links impartial judgment with mercy toward the poor in the same breath. Strong thematic correspondence.
sourceText: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother. Don’t oppress the widow, nor the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor; and let none of you devise evil against his brother in your heart.’

note: Ben Sira: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned... Does anyone harbor anger against another, and expect healing from the Lord?' James 2:13's principle that the merciless receive merciless judgment closely parallels this deuterocanonical wisdom on reciprocal mercy.
sourceText: He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins. Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins?

note: Tobit's almsgiving counsel: 'give alms from your possessions... almsgiving delivers from death.' James's coupling of mercy/almsgiving with deliverance at judgment (v.13) resonates with this deuterocanonical theology of merciful deeds. Conceptual echo.
sourceText: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]

note: 'Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.' Background to James's mercy-rewarded-at-judgment principle. Faint wisdom echo within the mercy cluster.
sourceText: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.

note: 'You believe that God is one' (v.19) cites the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4, 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.' James affirms monotheism then notes even demons hold it and shudder, making the point that bare belief without works is insufficient.
sourceText: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.

note: 'Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar' (v.21) refers directly to the Aqedah, Genesis 22:9-12, where Abraham binds Isaac on the altar and the angel stays his hand. The binding is James's proof that Abraham's faith was completed by works.
sourceText: They came to the place which God had told him of. Abraham built the altar there, and laid the wood in order, bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar, on the wood. Abraham stretched out his hand, and took the knife to kill his son. Yahweh’s angel called to him out of the sky, and said, “Abraham, Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy, neither do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, since you have not […]

note: Formal citation: 'the Scripture was fulfilled which says, "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him as righteousness"' (v.23). This is a verbatim quotation of Genesis 15:6, here read as fulfilled in the Aqedah.
sourceText: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.

note: 'He was called the friend of God' (v.23). Isaiah 41:8 calls Israel the offspring of 'Abraham my friend' (LXX: 'whom I loved'). This title for Abraham, not stated in Genesis, is James's scriptural warrant for naming him God's friend.
sourceText: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend,

note: Jehoshaphat's prayer recalls God giving the land to the descendants of 'Abraham your friend forever.' Together with Isaiah 41:8 this is the scriptural basis for James 2:23's 'friend of God' epithet. Listed as parallel source.
sourceText: Didn’t you, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it to the seed of Abraham your friend forever?

note: 'Rahab the prostitute also justified by works, in that she received the messengers, and sent them out another way' (v.25) refers to Joshua 2, where Rahab hides the Israelite spies and lets them down by another route. Her hospitable, faith-driven deed is James's second exemplum of justifying works.
sourceText: Joshua the son of Nun secretly sent two men out of Shittim as spies, saying, “Go, view the land, including Jericho.” They went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab, and slept there. The king of Jericho was told, “Behold, men of the children of Israel came in here tonight to spy out the land.” The king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, “Bring out the men who have come to you, who have entered into your house; for they have come to […]

note: Joshua 6:17,22-25 records Rahab and her household being spared at Jericho's fall because she hid the messengers. James 2:25's commendation of Rahab presupposes this deliverance as the vindication of her works. Supplies the outcome of the act James cites.
sourceText: The city shall be devoted, even it and all that is in it, to Yahweh. Only Rahab the prostitute shall live, she and all who are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent.

note: God's deliberation, 'Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?', reflects the intimacy underlying the 'friend of God' tradition. Faint background echo to James 2:23's friendship motif; the explicit title comes from Isaiah/Chronicles.
sourceText: Yahweh said, “Will I hide from Abraham what I do, since Abraham has surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth will be blessed in him? For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of Yahweh, to do righteousness and justice; to the end that Yahweh may bring on Abraham that which he has spoken of him.”

note: 'Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.' This obedience tradition supports James's claim that Abraham's faith was perfected by works (v.22). Conceptual echo of Abraham as the man whose faith issued in obedience.
sourceText: because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my requirements, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.”

note: Mattathias's deathbed exhortation: 'Was not Abraham found faithful when tested, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness?' This deuterocanonical text already fuses Genesis 15:6 with the Aqedah-as-test (Genesis 22), exactly the synthesis James makes in vv.21-23. Strong evidence James draws on this interpretive tradition.
sourceText: Was not Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness?

note: Ben Sira's praise of Abraham: 'kept the law of the Most High... when tested he was found faithful,' linking covenant, testing, and reckoned righteousness. James's works-completing-faith reading of Abraham stands in this Second Temple tradition. Deuterocanonical interpretive parallel.
sourceText: Abraham was a great father of a multitude of nations; And there was none found like him in glory; Who kept the law of the Most High, And was taken into covenant with him: In his flesh he established the covenant; And when he was proved, he was found faithful. Therefore he assured him by an oath, That the nations should be blessed in his seed; That he would multiply him as the dust of the earth, And exalt his seed as the stars, And cause them to inherit […]

note: The angel's oath after the binding, 'because you have done this... I will surely bless you,' grounds the reward of Abraham's obedient act. Reinforces James's point (v.22) that faith was perfected through the work of offering Isaac. Faint extension of the Aqedah citation.
sourceText: and said, “I have sworn by myself, says Yahweh, because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son, that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies. All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your seed, because you have obeyed my voice.”

note: True fasting is 'to share your bread with the hungry... when you see the naked, to cover him.' James 2:15-16's example of a brother 'naked and in lack of daily food' whom one fails to clothe and feed echoes this prophetic critique of empty piety divorced from deeds of mercy. Faint thematic echo.
sourceText: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?

note: Job's defense: 'if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing... if his body has not blessed me for warming him with the fleece of my sheep.' James's hollow 'be warmed and filled' (v.16) without provision inverts Job's actual care for the naked and cold. Faint wisdom echo.
sourceText: if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or that the needy had no covering; if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been warmed with my sheep’s fleece;

note: 'You shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother, but open your hand to him.' James 2:15-16 rebukes the empty word that withholds 'the things the body needs' from a needy brother. Faint Torah echo of obligatory open-handedness.
sourceText: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks.

note: James's warning that teachers face a heavier judgment and that the one who does not stumble in word is perfect rests on the wisdom axiom that 'when words are many, transgression is not lacking.' Volume is conceptual rather than verbal, but the coherence with James's whole tongue-theme is high.
sourceText: In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.

note: Ben Sira's beatitude, 'Blessed is the one who does not blunder with his lips,' is the nearest Second-Temple parallel to 'if anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man.' Recurrence in the sapiential stream James draws on raises the confidence.
sourceText: Blessed is the man that has not slipped with his mouth, And is not pricked with sorrow for sins.

note: The image of bridling the mouth/body is voiced in the Psalter: 'I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I will bridle my mouth.' James reuses the same controlling-the-tongue metaphor that the psalm applies to speech, transferring it to the bit-and-bridle figure.
sourceText: I said, “I will watch my ways, so that I don’t sin with my tongue. I will keep my mouth with a bridle while the wicked is before me.”

note: The horse curbed with bit and bridle so it will not stray is the psalm's image for the need of restraint; James literalizes it ('we put bits into the horses' mouths') to argue the small member governs the whole body.
sourceText: Don’t be like the horse, or like the mule, which have no understanding, who are controlled by bit and bridle, or else they will not come near to you.

note: Ben Sira's extended denunciation of 'the third tongue' that 'has destroyed strong cities' and is a scourge of fire is the closest antecedent to James's 'the tongue is a fire… a restless evil.' The shared fire-imagery and the theme of the untamable, ruinous tongue make this the controlling Second-Temple subtext.
sourceText: Curse the whisperer and double-tongued: For he has destroyed many that were at peace. A third person’s tongue has shaken many, And dispersed them from nation to nation; And it has pulled down strong cities, And overthrown the houses of great men. A third person’s tongue has cast out brave women, And deprived them of their labors. He that hearkens to it will not find rest, Nor shall he dwell quietly. The stroke of a whip makes a mark in the flesh; But the […]

note: 'A worthless man… his speech is like a scorching fire' supplies the proverbial root of James's tongue-as-fire. The volume is moderate but the figure is distinctive.
sourceText: A worthless man devises mischief. His speech is like a scorching fire.

note: 'They make their tongue sharp as a serpent's; adder's poison is under their lips' stands behind James's 'full of deadly poison.' The pairing of the tongue with serpent venom is rare enough to mark a genuine echo.
sourceText: They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent. Viper’s poison is under their lips. Selah.

note: The deceitful tongue answered with 'glowing coals of the broom tree' shares the tongue-and-fire association, a fainter contributory echo.
sourceText: Deliver my soul, Yahweh, from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue. What will be given to you, and what will be done more to you, you deceitful tongue? Sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper.

note: 'Every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature is tamed by mankind' recalls the creation grant of dominion over the beasts; James turns the trope ironically — humanity tames the beasts but cannot tame its own tongue.
sourceText: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”

note: Cursing 'men, who are made in the image of God' depends directly on the creation of humanity in God's image; the inconsistency of blessing God and cursing his image-bearers is the moral force of the passage.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: 'In the likeness of God he made him' reinforces the image-of-God ground; Genesis 9:6 ('whoever sheds man's blood… for God made man in his own image') is the same principle applied to harming the image-bearer.
sourceText: This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, he made him in God’s likeness.

note: 'The fruit discloses the cultivation of a tree; so the expression of a thought discloses the heart' is the sapiential source of James's fig-tree/vine and spring analogies, where the source determines the fruit.
sourceText: The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man.

note: 'Death and life are in the power of the tongue' undergirds the blessing-and-cursing antithesis as a faint background echo.
sourceText: Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

note: The catalog of wisdom's qualities — 'intelligent, holy, … pure, … beneficent, … unhampered' — is the closest model for James's 'wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle… full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.' The list-form and the heavenly origin of wisdom align closely.
sourceText: For she that is the architect of all things taught me, even wisdom. For there is in her a spirit quick of understanding, holy, Alone in kind, manifold, Subtil, freely moving, Clear in utterance, unpolluted, Distinct, unharmed, Loving what is good, keen, unhindered, Beneficent, loving toward man, Stedfast, sure, free from care, All-powerful, all-surveying, And penetrating through all spirits That are quick of understanding, pure, most subtle: For wisdom is […]

note: 'The Lord gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding' grounds James's distinction of a wisdom that 'comes down from above' against an earthly counterfeit.
sourceText: For Yahweh gives wisdom. Out of his mouth comes knowledge and understanding.

note: 'The effect of righteousness will be peace' stands directly behind 'the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace,' linking righteousness and shalom as James does.
sourceText: The work of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.

note: 'Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love' supplies the agricultural metaphor of sowing-and-reaping righteousness that James applies to peacemakers.
sourceText: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.

note: 'One who sows righteousness gets a sure reward' (cf. 11:30, 'the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life') reinforces the harvest-of-righteousness figure.
sourceText: Wicked people earn deceitful wages, but one who sows righteousness reaps a sure reward.

note: Ben Sira's teaching that all wisdom is from the Lord and poured out on the faithful is the wider sapiential horizon for James's heavenly wisdom.
sourceText: All wisdom comes from the Lord, And is with him forever. The sand of the seas, and the drops of rain, And the days of eternity, who shall count? The height of the heaven, and the breadth of the earth, And the deep, and wisdom, who shall search them out? Wisdom has been created before all things, And the understanding of prudence from everlasting. To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed? And who has known her shrewd counsels? There is one wise, […]

note: Amos's complaint that the people 'have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood' is the prophetic inverse of James's peaceful harvest of righteousness — a faint contrastive echo.
sourceText: Do horses run on the rocky crags? Does one plow there with oxen? But you have turned justice into poison, and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness;

note: 'You lust and do not have; you kill, covet, and cannot obtain' traces the chain of conflict to covetous desire, the disorder the tenth commandment forbids. The volume is thematic but coheres with James's diagnosis of war from within.
sourceText: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”

note: The progression from frustrated desire to murder ('you kill, covet') echoes Cain, whose envy of his brother led to the first killing; James 3-4 elsewhere leans on the genealogy of sin from desire.
sourceText: but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell. Yahweh said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen? If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.” Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, […]

note: 'You adulterers and adulteresses! friendship with the world is hostility toward God' deploys the prophetic figure of Israel's covenant-breaking as spiritual adultery, of which Hosea's marriage to Gomer is the paradigm. The single vocative 'adulteresses' presupposes the whole prophetic marriage-metaphor.
sourceText: Yahweh’s word that came to Hosea the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel. When Yahweh spoke at first by Hosea, Yahweh said to Hosea, “Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitution and children of unfaithfulness; for the land commits great adultery, forsaking Yahweh.” So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived, and bore him a […]

note: 'The Spirit who dwells in us yearns jealously' rests on the self-revelation of the LORD as 'a jealous God'; the divine jealousy that brooks no rival is exactly what makes friendship with the world enmity. Exodus 34:14 ('the LORD, whose name is Jealous') is the same datum.
sourceText: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,

note: James cites it with a formula ('therefore it says'): 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble' reproduces the Septuagint of Proverbs 3:34 nearly verbatim (the Greek reads 'the Lord opposes the arrogant'). The same verse is cited at 1 Peter 5:5.
sourceText: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
lxxText: The Lord resists the proud; but he gives grace to the humble.

note: The Song of Moses, where Israel 'made me jealous with what is no god,' is part of the jealousy-of-God background to v.5.
sourceText: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

note: 'I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy' supplies a prophetic restatement of the divine jealousy James invokes for the indwelling Spirit.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh of Armies: “I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath.”

note: 'Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you' restates the covenant promise 'Return to me… and I will return to you.' The reciprocal-approach formula is distinctive to this prophetic call to repentance.
sourceText: Therefore tell them: Thus says Yahweh of Armies: ‘Return to me,’ says Yahweh of Armies, ‘and I will return to you,’ says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'Return to me, and I will return to you' is the same drawing-near formula; Malachi's setting of repentance and cleansing matches James's summons to sinners and the double-minded.
sourceText: From the days of your fathers you have turned aside from my ordinances, and have not kept them. Return to me, and I will return to you,” says Yahweh of Armies. “But you say, ‘How shall we return?’

note: 'Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean' lies behind 'cleanse your hands, you sinners,' the prophetic call to moral purification.
sourceText: Wash yourselves, make yourself clean. Put away the evil of your doings from before my eyes. Cease to do evil.

note: 'Clean hands and a pure heart' is the temple-entrance requirement that James fuses with Isaiah: 'cleanse your hands… purify your hearts.' The pairing of hands and heart is verbally close.
sourceText: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.

note: 'When they are humbled you say, It is because of pride; but he saves the lowly' anticipates 'humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.' The humbling-then-exalting reversal is the same.
sourceText: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.

note: 'One's pride will bring him low, but the lowly in spirit will obtain honor' is the proverb James restates as 'humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.'
sourceText: A man’s pride brings him low, but one of lowly spirit gains honor.

note: 'Return to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning' supplies the lament-and-mourning summons ('let your laughter be turned to mourning').
sourceText: “Yet even now,” says Yahweh, “turn to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.” Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity.

note: 'There is one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy' echoes the Song of Moses, 'I kill and I make alive… there is none who can deliver out of my hand' — the sole divine prerogative over life and death.
sourceText: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.

note: 'The LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us' is the nearest verbal antecedent to James's 'one lawgiver and judge… able to save.' The triad judge/lawgiver/savior is distinctive.
sourceText: For Yahweh is our judge. Yahweh is our lawgiver. Yahweh is our king. He will save us.

note: 'You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people' grounds 'do not speak against one another,' part of the same Holiness-Code love-of-neighbor James reads as the royal law.
sourceText: “‘You shall not go up and down as a slanderer among your people. “‘You shall not endanger the life of your neighbor. I am Yahweh.

note: 'Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring' is the proverb James expands into the rebuke of merchants who plan a year's trade 'whereas you do not know what tomorrow will bring.'
sourceText: Don’t boast about tomorrow; for you don’t know what a day may bring.

note: 'Man is a mere breath… a man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather' stands behind 'you are a vapor that appears for a little time and then vanishes,' the breath-brevity figure applied to acquisitive boasting.
sourceText: Behold, you have made my days hand breadths. My lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely every man stands as a breath.” Selah. “Surely every man walks like a shadow. Surely they busy themselves in vain. He heaps up, and doesn’t know who shall gather.

note: Ben Sira's rich man who says 'I have found rest, now I shall feast on my goods' yet does not know that death is near is the wisdom prototype of James's presumptuous merchant.
sourceText: There is that waxes rich by his wariness and pinching, And this is the portion of his reward: When he says, I have found rest, And now will I eat of my goods; Yet he knows not what time will pass, And he will leave them to others, and die.

note: 'Remember that my life is a breath' contributes to the mist-and-vapor brevity-of-life motif.
sourceText: Oh remember that my life is a breath. My eye shall no more see good.

note: 'Come now, you rich, weep and howl' opens with the prophetic woe-cry, 'Wail, for the day of the LORD is near.' The same howling-summons announces eschatological judgment on the complacent.
sourceText: Wail; for the day of Yahweh is at hand! It will come as destruction from the Almighty.

note: Amos's woe on those 'at ease… who lie on beds of ivory and eat lambs from the flock' and 'are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph' is the prophetic template for James's denunciation of the luxurious rich who have 'lived delicately on the earth.' The coherence of theme and the day-of-slaughter motif are strong.
sourceText: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel come! Go to Calneh, and see; and from there go to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. are they better than these kingdoms? or is their border greater than your border? Those who put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near; Who lie on beds of […]

note: 'You shall give him his wages… lest he cry against you to the LORD' is the law James indicts the rich for breaking: 'the wages of the laborers you kept back by fraud cry out.' The crying-out-to-God of withheld wages is verbally and legally precise.
sourceText: You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates. In his day you shall give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down on it; for he is poor, and sets his heart on it; lest he cry against you to Yahweh, and it be sin to you.

note: 'The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning' is the Holiness-Code companion to Deuteronomy 24, prohibiting exactly the withholding James condemns.
sourceText: “‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.

note: The LORD comes in judgment 'against those who oppress the hired worker in his wages,' a prophetic restatement of the offense and the cry that reaches God.
sourceText: I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against the perjurers, and against those who oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and who deprive the foreigner of justice, and don’t fear me,” says Yahweh of Armies.

note: 'The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground' is the archetype of injustice that cries out to God, behind 'the cries… have entered the ears of the Lord of Hosts.'
sourceText: Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.

note: 'Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten' contributes the corrosion-and-moth imagery of decaying wealth (cf. Isaiah 50:9; 51:8).
sourceText: though I am decaying like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.

note: The wicked who 'oppress the righteous poor man' and resolve to 'condemn him to a shameful death' is the Second-Temple righteous-sufferer scene behind 'you have condemned, you have murdered the righteous one. He does not resist you.'
sourceText: Let us oppress the righteous poor; Let us not spare the widow, Nor reverence the hairs of the old man gray for length of years. But let our strength be to us a law of righteousness; For that which is weak is found to be of no service. But let us lie in wait for the righteous man, Because he is of disservice to us, And is contrary to our works, And upbraids us with sins against the law, And lays to our charge sins against our discipline. He professes to […]

note: 'I will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the later rain' is the covenant promise James invokes for the patient farmer who waits 'until it receives the early and late rain.' The early/late-rain pair is distinctive.
sourceText: that I will give the rain of your land in its season, the former rain and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain, your new wine, and your oil.

note: 'He has given the early rain… the early and the latter rain' restates the same agricultural promise as a sign of restoration, reinforcing the patient-farmer figure.
sourceText: “Be glad then, you children of Zion, and rejoice in Yahweh, your God; for he gives you the former rain in just measure, and he causes the rain to come down for you, the former rain and the latter rain, as before.

note: 'Let us fear the LORD… who gives the rain in its season, the autumn and the spring rains' supplies a further early/late-rain antecedent.
sourceText: Neither do they say in their heart, ‘Let us now fear Yahweh our God, who gives rain, both the former and the latter, in its season; who preserves to us the appointed weeks of the harvest.’

note: 'You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and seen the outcome of the Lord' depends on the Job narrative — his endurance under loss without sin, and the restored 'outcome' of Job 42. James makes Job the type of patient endurance.
sourceText: He said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh’s name.” In all this, Job did not sin, nor charge God with wrongdoing.

note: 'How the Lord is full of compassion and mercy' reproduces the LORD's self-revelation, 'merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love' — the formula echoed across the Psalter (103:8; 111:4).
sourceText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,

note: 'Do not swear… let your yes be yes' rests on 'you shall not swear by my name falsely,' the Holiness-Code regulation of oaths that James radicalizes into avoiding oaths altogether.
sourceText: “‘You shall not swear by my name falsely, and profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh.

note: The law on vows — that one must perform what is sworn and that refraining from vowing is no sin — is the legal background to James's counsel against swearing.
sourceText: When you vow a vow to Yahweh your God, you shall not be slack to pay it; for Yahweh your God will surely require it of you; and it would be sin in you. But if you refrain from making a vow, it shall be no sin in you. You shall observe and do that which has gone out of your lips. Whatever you have vowed to Yahweh your God as a freewill offering, which you have promised with your mouth, you must do.

note: 'Do not accustom your mouth to oaths… a man who swears many oaths is full of iniquity' is the wisdom counsel against swearing that most closely parallels James.
sourceText: Accustom not your mouth to an oath; And be not accustomed to the naming of the Holy One. For as a servant that is continually scourged will not lack a bruise, So he also that swears and names God continually will not be cleansed from sin. A man of many oaths will be filled with iniquity; And the scourge will not depart from his house: If he shall offend, his sin will be upon him; And if he disregard it, he has sinned doubly; And if he has sworn in vain, […]

note: 'Heaven is my throne and the earth is my footstool' grounds the prohibition of swearing 'by heaven or by earth,' since both belong to God.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what kind of house will you build to me? and what place shall be my rest?

note: 'Elijah… prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it did not rain' draws directly on Elijah's word that 'there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.' James reads the drought as answered prayer.
sourceText: Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the foreigners of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”

note: 'He prayed again, and the sky gave rain' depends on Elijah on Carmel bowing to the ground in prayer until the rain came. The two-part drought-and-rain narrative is the backbone of James's example of the righteous person's prayer.
sourceText: Elijah said to Ahab, “Get up, eat and drink; for there is the sound of abundance of rain.” So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he bowed himself down on the earth, and put his face between his knees. He said to his servant, “Go up now, look toward the sea.” He went up, and looked, and said, “There is nothing.” He said, “Go again” seven times. On the seventh time, he said, “Behold, a small cloud, like a man’s hand, […]

note: 'The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous, and his ears toward their cry' grounds 'the insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.'
sourceText: Yahweh’s eyes are toward the righteous. His ears listen to their cry.

note: 'The prayer of the upright is acceptable to him' (cf. 15:29, 'he hears the prayer of the righteous') is the proverbial basis for the efficacy of the righteous person's prayer.
sourceText: The sacrifice made by the wicked is an abomination to Yahweh, but the prayer of the upright is his delight.

note: Ben Sira's praise of Elijah, who 'shut up the heavens' and 'brought down fire,' is the Second-Temple reception of the drought-prayer that James presupposes.
sourceText: Also there arose Elijah the prophet as fire, And his word burned like a torch: Who brought a famine upon them, And by his zeal made them few in number. By the word of the Lord he shut up the heaven: Thrice did he thus bring down fire.

note: 'Love covers all offenses' stands behind 'he who turns a sinner… will cover a multitude of sins,' the proverb of love covering sin applied to restoring the wanderer.
sourceText: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.

note: The watchman who warns the wicked to turn 'will have saved his life' is the prophetic logic behind saving a soul from death by turning the sinner back (cf. Ezekiel 3:18-21).
sourceText: When I tell the wicked, O wicked man, you shall surely die, and you don’t speak to warn the wicked from his way; that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood will I require at your hand. Nevertheless, if you warn the wicked of his way to turn from it, and he doesn’t turn from his way; he shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.

note: 'Those who turn many to righteousness' shine like the stars — a faint echo behind turning a sinner from the error of his way.
sourceText: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: 'Dispersion' (diaspora) is the LXX term for Israel scattered among the nations as covenant curse; Peter recasts the addressees' geographic scatter across Asia Minor as the eschatological diaspora of God's people. High thematic coherence; recurrence of diaspora language across the Deuteronomic curses.
sourceText: Yahweh will cause you to be struck before your enemies. You will go out one way against them, and will flee seven ways before them. You will be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth.

note: The gathering of the 'dispersed of Judah from the four corners' supplies the restoration backdrop to which 'elect exiles of the dispersion' alludes; faint verbal contact via diaspora, strong thematic coherence with Isaian return-from-exile.
sourceText: He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

note: Prayer to 'gather together our dispersion' shows Second Temple use of diaspora as a theological-not-merely-geographic category, the same move Peter makes; Second Temple recurrence supports the reading though no verbal borrowing beyond the term.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: Abraham's self-description as a 'stranger and sojourner' (paroikos) is the patriarchal template for the resident-alien identity Peter assigns his readers; the same paroikos/parepidemos word-pair recurs in 1 Peter 2:11. Volume modest, recurrence within the letter high.
sourceText: “I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you. Give me a possession of a burying-place with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.”

note: 'You are strangers and sojourners with me' grounds Israel's tenancy on God's land; Peter universalizes the sojourner status. Faint verbal echo through the sojourner vocabulary, coherent with the letter's pilgrim ecclesiology.
sourceText: “‘The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine; for you are strangers and live as foreigners with me.

note: David's 'we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were' is a near-formulaic sojourner confession standing behind 1:1 and 1:17; low volume, supports recurrence.
sourceText: For we are strangers before you, and foreigners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is no remaining.

note: Election theology—the Most High apportioning peoples and taking Jacob as his allotted portion—underlies 'chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father'; figural/thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the children of men, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel. For Yahweh’s portion is his people. Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.

note: 'Sanctification... that you may obey... and be sprinkled with his blood' fuses the two halves of Sinai covenant ratification: Israel's pledge 'all that the LORD has spoken we will do and obey' (24:7) and Moses sprinkling the blood of the covenant on the people (24:8). High volume via the obey+blood-sprinkling sequence; thematic coherence with covenant inauguration.
sourceText: He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, “All that Yahweh has spoken will we do, and be obedient.” Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”

note: The sprinkling that purifies the unclean (water of the red-heifer ash) is a secondary purification background for 'sprinkled with his blood'; lower volume than Exodus 24, contested as the primary referent.
sourceText: A clean person shall take hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle it on the tent, on all the vessels, on the persons who were there, and on him who touched the bone, or the slain, or the dead, or the grave. The clean person shall sprinkle on the unclean on the third day, and on the seventh day. On the seventh day, he shall purify him. He shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water, and shall be clean at evening. But the man who shall be unclean, […]

note: 'I will sprinkle clean water on you... and put my Spirit within you' joins sprinkling with the gift of the Spirit—exactly Peter's pairing of 'sanctification of the Spirit' and 'sprinkled with his blood.' Strong thematic coherence; sprinkling+Spirit recurrence.
sourceText: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: Moses sprinkling blood to consecrate the priests supports the priestly-consecration overtone of 'sanctification... sprinkled with his blood,' anticipating the royal priesthood of 2:9. Faint, figural.
sourceText: Moses took some of the anointing oil, and some of the blood which was on the altar, and sprinkled it on Aaron, on his garments, and on his sons, and on his sons’ garments with him, and sanctified Aaron, his garments, and his sons, and his sons’ garments with him.

note: 'Peace be multiplied to you' (also Daniel 4:1) is the verbatim Aramaic-letter greeting Peter expands to 'grace and peace be multiplied.' Distinctive verbal borrowing of the 'be multiplied' epistolary formula.
sourceText: Then king Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages, who dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you.

note: 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel' is the berakah doxology Peter Christianizes as 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.' Distinctive opening-blessing form recurring across the Psalter's book-seams.
sourceText: Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting and to everlasting! Amen and amen.

note: David's 'Blessed are you, O LORD, the God of Israel our father' supplies both the eulogy form and the Father-language behind 1:3; coherent with the inheritance theme that follows (29:11-16).
sourceText: Therefore David blessed Yahweh before all the assembly; and David said, “You are blessed, Yahweh, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever.

note: 'According to your great mercy' echoes the Psalter's 'according to the abundance of your mercy'; low volume but a fixed liturgical collocation.
sourceText: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.

note: 'The LORD is my portion and my inheritance... a goodly heritage' reframes inheritance from land to God himself, the move behind an 'inheritance kept in heaven.' Thematic coherence high; the imperishable heavenly inheritance transposes the Levitical land-allotment.
sourceText: Yahweh assigned my portion and my cup. You made my lot secure. The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places. Yes, I have a good inheritance.

note: The priests have no land-inheritance because 'I am your portion and inheritance'; Peter's heavenly, unfading inheritance figurally fulfills this priestly pattern (cf. royal priesthood, 2:9). Figural, low verbal volume.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Aaron, “You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the children of Israel.

note: 'The righteous live forever... they will receive a glorious crown... from the Lord's hand' parallels the imperishable, heaven-reserved inheritance and the 'praise, glory, and honor' of 1:7; Second Temple thematic coherence.
sourceText: But the righteous live forever, And in the Lord is their reward, And the care for them with the Most High. Therefore will they receive the crown of royal dignity And the diadem of beauty from the Lord’s hand; Because with his right hand will he cover them, And with his arm will he shield them.

note: 'The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but the LORD tests hearts' is the proverbial matrix for faith 'tested by fire... more precious than gold.' High thematic coherence; gold-tested-by-fire is a stock wisdom topos Peter applies to faith.
sourceText: The refining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold, but Yahweh tests the hearts.

note: 'I will refine them as one refines silver and test them as gold is tested,' set in an eschatological remnant-purification, supplies the trial-as-refinement frame of 1:6-7; verbal contact (refine/test, gold) plus eschatological coherence.
sourceText: I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”

note: 'When he has tested me, I shall come forth as gold' is the closest first-person analogue: testing through suffering yielding vindicated, gold-like faith. Strong thematic coherence, moderate volume.
sourceText: But he knows the way that I take. When he has tried me, I shall come out like gold.

note: 'My child, when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing... for gold is tested in the fire, and those found acceptable in the furnace of humiliation.' The fullest pre-Christian template: discipleship + fiery testing + gold + acceptance, mirroring 1:6-7. Second Temple recurrence and high thematic coherence.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: 'Having been disciplined a little... like gold in the furnace he tried them' joins brief affliction ('a little while', cf. 1:6) with gold-furnace testing of the righteous souls; strong thematic coherence with 1:6-9.
sourceText: And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and found them worthy of himself. As gold in the furnace he proved them, And as a whole burnt offering he accepted them.

note: Daniel 'heard but did not understand' and sought the meaning, told the words were 'sealed until the time of the end'—the paradigm for prophets who 'searched diligently... what time the Spirit pointed to' (1:10-11). Distinctive prophet-seeks-yet-defers motif.
sourceText: I heard, but I didn’t understand: then I said, my lord, what shall be the issue of these things? He said, Go your way, Daniel; for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end.

note: 'The Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets' undergirds 'to them it was revealed' that they served a later generation (1:12); thematic, low verbal volume.
sourceText: Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.

note: 'The sufferings of Christ and the glories that follow' (1:11) tracks the Servant's affliction-then-vindication arc (Isaiah 52:13-53:12); Peter's signature suffering/glory pattern, faint here but recurrent in the letter.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

note: 'Gird up the loins of your mind' literalizes the Passover posture—'your loins girded, your sandals on, in haste'—readiness for imminent deliverance, fitting the redemption-by-the-lamb imagery of 1:18-19. High volume on the distinctive idiom plus contextual Passover coherence.
sourceText: This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.

note: 'Gird up your loins like a man' (also 40:7) is the summons to brace for an encounter with God; supplies the metaphorical (mental readiness) sense Peter intends. Moderate verbal volume; the idiom recurs as a call to resolve.
sourceText: Brace yourself like a man, for I will question you, then you answer me!

note: 'Gird up your loins; stand and speak' commissions the prophet to fearless action; reinforces the gird-loins call but is a secondary witness to the idiom. Low distinctiveness.
sourceText: “You therefore put your belt on your waist, arise, and speak to them all that I command you. Don’t be dismayed at them, lest I dismay you before them.

note: Formula-marked citation ('because it is written, You shall be holy, for I am holy'). Leviticus 11:44-45 supplies the holiness ground anchored in the exodus ('I am the LORD who brought you up out of Egypt to be your God'), matching Peter's redemption framing. Highest volume—explicit quotation.
sourceText: For I am Yahweh your God. Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am holy: neither shall you defile yourselves with any kind of creeping thing that moves on the earth. For I am Yahweh who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.

note: 'You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy' is the most verbally exact source of 1:16 and heads the Holiness Code chapter Peter draws on repeatedly (love of neighbor, impartiality). Co-primary with Leviticus 11:44-45.
sourceText: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.

note: 'The God of gods... who is not partial and takes no bribe' is the locus classicus for 'judges impartially, without respect of persons' (1:17). Distinctive 'shows no partiality' formula; high thematic coherence.
sourceText: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.

note: 'You repay each according to his work' supplies the second half of 1:17 (judges 'according to each one's work'); a fixed retributive formula. Moderate volume, recurs widely.
sourceText: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.

note: 'I the LORD... give to each according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds' parallels the judge-by-works formula; secondary witness, low distinctiveness.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: 'The Lord is judge, and with him there is no partiality' shows the impartial-judge formula in Second Temple piety, supporting the recurrence of 1:17's idea; minimal verbal borrowing.
sourceText: Think not to corrupt with gifts; for he will not receive them: And set not your mind on an unrighteous sacrifice; For the Lord is judge, And with him is no respect of persons. He will not accept any person against a poor man; And he will listen to the prayer of him that is wronged.

note: 'You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money' stands behind 'redeemed, not with silver or gold' (1:18)—redemption explicitly not monetary. Distinctive silver/gold-vs-true-redemption contrast.
sourceText: For thus says Yahweh, “You were sold for nothing; and you shall be redeemed without money.”

note: 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm' is the exodus redemption verb Peter applies to ransom 'from the futile ways inherited from your fathers'—a new exodus from ancestral bondage. Thematic coherence high.
sourceText: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:

note: 'Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things (vanity) in which there is no profit' closely matches 'the futile ways inherited from your fathers' (1:18)—ancestral idolatry as vanity. Notable verbal contact (inherited+vain+fathers).
sourceText: Yahweh, my strength, and my stronghold, and my refuge in the day of affliction, to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, vanity and things in which there is no profit.

note: 'Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old' is the Passover-lamb specification behind 'a lamb without blemish or spot' (1:19), reinforcing the redemption/exodus matrix of the pericope. High volume on the without-blemish lamb.
sourceText: Your lamb shall be without defect, a male a year old. You shall take it from the sheep, or from the goats:

note: 'Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter... he opened not his mouth' supplies the suffering-Servant lamb whose blood ransoms; Peter fuses Passover lamb with Isaian Servant (cf. the dense Isaiah 53 citation in 2:22-25). High thematic coherence and recurrence in the letter.
sourceText: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.

note: The sacrificial requirement that an offering be 'without blemish... no defect' generalizes the spotless-lamb language of 1:19 across the cult. Supports volume of the blemish-free motif.
sourceText: that you may be accepted, you shall offer a male without defect, of the bulls, of the sheep, or of the goats. But whatever has a defect, that you shall not offer; for it shall not be acceptable for you.

note: 'My servant shall be exalted and lifted up' grounds 'raised him from the dead and gave him glory' (1:21)—the Servant's vindication. Faint, figural, but coherent with Peter's suffering-then-glory pattern.
sourceText: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.

note: 'Love one another earnestly from the heart' (1:22) draws on the Holiness Code command 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself'—the same Leviticus 19 chapter Peter quotes for holiness in 1:16. Recurrence within the source chapter supports the link though Peter rephrases.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'Living and abiding word of God' resonates with oaths by 'him who lives forever'; faint, the enduring/living quality is better anchored in the Isaiah 40 citation that follows.
sourceText: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished.

note: Verbatim, formula-introduced citation ('For, All flesh is like grass... the grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of the Lord endures forever'). Peter quotes the LXX of Isaiah 40:6-8 to ground the imperishable seed/word; highest volume. Isaiah's word-of-comfort frames the whole exile-and-restoration ecclesiology of the letter.
sourceText: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”

note: 'As for man, his days are like grass; he flourishes like a flower of the field; the wind passes over it and it is gone' is a parallel grass/flower-frailty topos reinforcing the Isaiah 40 quotation. Moderate volume; same withering-flower imagery.
sourceText: As for man, his days are like grass. As a flower of the field, so he flourishes. For the wind passes over it, and it is gone. Its place remembers it no more.

note: 'Why are you afraid of mortal man... who fades like grass?' is a nearby Isaian grass-frailty saying within the same comfort-of-Zion section, supporting the Isaiah 40 recurrence. Low distinctiveness on its own.
sourceText: “I, even I, am he who comforts you: who are you, that you are afraid of man who shall die, and of the son of man who shall be made as grass;

note: Humanity 'like grass that is renewed in the morning... in the evening it fades and withers' is another grass-mortality witness underlining the perishable-vs-enduring contrast of 1:23-25. Faint, thematic.
sourceText: You sweep them away as they sleep. In the morning they sprout like new grass. In the morning it sprouts and springs up. By evening, it is withered and dry.

note: "if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious" (2:3) closely reworks Psalm 34:8 LXX (33:9), "taste and see that the Lord is good (chrēstos)." The verb 'tasted' plus the divine predicate is a strong verbal borrowing; the wordplay chrēstos/Christos prepares the turn to the living stone. Psalm 34 recurs across 1 Peter (cf. 3:10-12 quoting Ps 34:12-16), raising recurrence and volume.
sourceText: Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.

note: "long for the pure milk of the Word" (2:2) picks up the 'word' (logos/rhēma) by which the readers were reborn (1:23-25, where Isa 40:6-8 is just quoted); the abiding word of God is the nourishment metaphor here, an echo carried over from the immediately preceding citation.
sourceText: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”

note: "Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen, and precious: He who believes in him will not be disappointed" (2:6) is a formula-introduced citation ("it is contained in Scripture") of Isaiah 28:16 LXX. Verbatim: tithēmi en Siōn lithon... eklekton entimon, and the believer not being put to shame. The keywords 'chosen/precious' also reach back to v.4-5 ('chosen by God, precious').
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: "The stone which the builders rejected, has become the chief cornerstone" (2:7) is a verbatim quotation of Psalm 118:22 LXX (117:22). Part of the stacked stone-testimonia catena; the same text is a primary early-Christian Christological proof (cf. Mark 12:10; Acts 4:11). 'Rejected'/'builders' ties to the rejection theme of v.4.
sourceText: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.

note: "a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense" (2:8) quotes Isaiah 8:14, lithos proskommatos kai petra skandalou. Third member of the stone catena, applied to the disobedient who stumble at the word; combined here (as in Rom 9:33) with Isa 28:16.
sourceText: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

note: "a royal priesthood... a holy nation" (2:9) draws directly on Exodus 19:6 LXX, basileion hierateuma kai ethnos hagion, the Sinai vocation of Israel now applied to the church. High volume; the priesthood theme also undergirds v.5 ('holy priesthood... spiritual sacrifices').
sourceText: and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation.’ These are the words which you shall speak to the children of Israel.”

note: "a chosen race... a people for God's own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him" (2:9) is woven from Isaiah 43:20-21 LXX, 'my chosen race (genos eklekton)... my people whom I preserved to declare my excellencies (aretas).' The distinctive phrase 'proclaim the excellencies/aretas' is verbatim from Isa 43:21 and not from Exod 19, marking this as a separate source fused into the title-collage.
sourceText: The animals of the field shall honor me, the jackals and the ostriches; because I give water in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, to give drink to my people, my chosen, the people which I formed for myself, that they might declare my praise.

note: "a people for God's own possession" (2:9) renders laos eis peripoiēsin, echoing the 'peculiar treasure/possession' (laos periousios / segullah) of Exodus 19:5; reinforces the Sinai covenant frame alongside Exod 19:6, and resonant with Mal 3:17 / Isa 43:21.
sourceText: Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine;

note: "who in time past were no people, but now are God's people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy" (2:10) reworks Hosea 2:23 (LXX 2:25), 'I will say to Not-my-people, You are my people' and 'I will have mercy on Not-pitied.' The double not-people/people and not-mercy/mercy antithesis is the signature of Hosea, also taken up in Rom 9:25.
sourceText: I will sow her to me in the earth; and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy; and I will tell those who were not my people, ‘You are my people;’ and they will say, ‘My God!’”

note: "were no people, but now are God's people" (2:10) also draws on Hosea 1:9-10, the naming of Lo-ammi ('not my people') and the reversal 'you are sons of the living God.' Companion source to Hos 2:23 supplying the 'not a people' title; high recurrence within the Hosea reversal oracle.
sourceText: He said, “Call his name Lo-Ammi; for you are not my people, and I will not be yours. Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’

note: "coming to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God" (2:4) anticipates and conditions the catena: the 'rejected by men / chosen by God' contrast frames the stone testimonia of vv.6-8 and the figural identification of Christ as the temple cornerstone before any is formally cited.
sourceText: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

note: "chosen by God, precious" (2:4) pre-echoes Isaiah 28:16's eklekton entimon ('chosen and precious'), the very words cited in v.6; Peter introduces the catena's keywords narratively before quoting, a deliberate framing device.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: "rejected indeed by men" (2:4) anticipates 'the stone which the builders rejected' of Ps 118:22 (v.7); apodedokimasmenon shares the rejection motif, weaving the psalm into the opening description of Christ as living stone.
sourceText: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.

note: "as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices" (2:5) is a typological reading of the Zion-stone oracle: believers become the new temple founded on Christ the cornerstone, a priesthood offering spiritual (not Levitical) sacrifices. The figural new-temple/new-Israel construal organizes the whole pericope.
sourceText: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

note: "For you who believe therefore is the honor" (2:7) plays on Isa 28:16's 'precious/honor' (entimon/timē) as the antithesis to the builders' rejection of Ps 118:22, binding the two quotations into a single believe/disbelieve contrast.
sourceText: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.

note: "I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims" (2:11) echoes the sojourner self-designation paroikos kai parepidēmos of Genesis 23:4 LXX (Abraham), also Psalm 39:12 (LXX 38:13). Reinforces the letter's elect-exile theme (1:1, 1:17); the patriarchal alien status is figurally applied to the diaspora church.
sourceText: “I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you. Give me a possession of a burying-place with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.”

note: "foreigners and pilgrims" (2:11) also recalls Psalm 39:12 (LXX 38:13), 'I am a sojourner (paroikos) with you and a pilgrim (parepidēmos), as all my fathers were' — the precise LXX pairing of both nouns, supplying the alien-on-earth posture.
sourceText: “Hear my prayer, Yahweh, and give ear to my cry. Don’t be silent at my tears. For I am a stranger with you, a foreigner, as all my fathers were.

note: "they may by your good works... glorify God in the day of visitation" (2:12) uses 'day of visitation' (hēmera episkopēs), the LXX phrase of Isaiah 10:3 ('what will you do in the day of visitation?'); the Gentiles' eventual glorifying of God when God visits frames the eschatological reckoning behind honorable conduct.
sourceText: What will you do in the day of visitation, and in the desolation which will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth?

note: "having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you" (2:12) inverts Isaiah 52:5 LXX, 'my name is continually blasphemed among the nations (ethnesin)' — where Israel's conduct caused God's name to be reviled, the church's good works among the nations cause it to be glorified.
sourceText: “Now therefore, what do I do here,” says Yahweh, “seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Those who rule over them mock,” says Yahweh, “and my name continually all the day is blasphemed.

note: "glorify God" through the witness of conduct 'among the nations' (2:12) resonates with Ezekiel 36:23, God sanctifying his name profaned among the nations so that the nations know him; a faint thematic parallel to the vindication-of-the-name motif.
sourceText: I will sanctify my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, which you have profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am Yahweh, says the Lord Yahweh, when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes.

note: "Fear God. Honor the king" (2:17) closely mirrors Proverbs 24:21 LXX, 'Fear God, my son, and the king (phobou ton theon... kai basilea)' — the paired imperatives toward God and king are a near-verbatim wisdom borrowing structuring the closing quatrain.
sourceText: My son, fear Yahweh and the king. Don’t join those who are rebellious:

note: Submission 'to the king as supreme' and to governors (2:13-14) reflects the wisdom counsel to keep the king's command (Eccl 8:2-5); a faint thematic backdrop to honoring civil authority.
sourceText: I say, “Keep the king’s command!” because of the oath to God. Don’t be hasty to go out of his presence. Don’t persist in an evil thing, for he does whatever pleases him, for the king’s word is supreme. Who can say to him, “What are you doing?” Whoever keeps the commandment shall not come to harm, and his wise heart will know the time and procedure.

note: "who did not sin, 'neither was deceit found in his mouth'" (2:22) quotes Isaiah 53:9 LXX, 'he did no lawlessness, nor was deceit (dolos) found in his mouth.' Verbatim citation of the Servant; anchors the Christ-as-suffering-Servant exemplum.
sourceText: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

note: "when he was cursed, didn't curse back. When he suffered, didn't threaten" (2:23) interprets Isaiah 53:7, 'he was afflicted yet opened not his mouth; like a lamb led to slaughter... he opens not his mouth.' The Servant's silent non-retaliation is the model for unjustly suffering servants.
sourceText: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.

note: "who his own self bore our sins in his body on the tree" (2:24) draws on Isaiah 53:4 LXX, 'he bears our sins (houtos tas hamartias hēmōn pherei),' fused with 53:12. The vicarious sin-bearing is the theological core of the Servant application.
sourceText: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.

note: "bore our sins in his body" (2:24) also reflects Isaiah 53:12, 'he bore the sins of many (autos hamartias pollōn anēnegken)' — the verb anapherō ('bore/bore up') matches 53:12 LXX, making this a distinct source-clause alongside 53:4.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: "by whose stripes you were healed" (2:24) is a near-verbatim citation of Isaiah 53:5 LXX, 'by his bruise (tō mōlōpi autou) we were healed.' Distinctive rare word mōlōps marks high volume.
sourceText: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.

note: "For you were going astray like sheep; but now have returned" (2:25) reworks Isaiah 53:6 LXX, 'all we like sheep have gone astray (planēthēmen).' The verb 'gone astray' + 'sheep' is verbatim from the Servant song; the 'returned' supplies the gospel reversal.
sourceText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: "returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls" (2:25) draws on the divine-shepherd oracle of Ezekiel 34, where God himself seeks and gathers the scattered sheep; the straying-sheep/returning-to-shepherd movement of Isa 53:6 is completed with Ezekiel's restoring shepherd imagery.
sourceText: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]

note: "the Shepherd... of your souls" (2:25) faintly recalls the Lord-as-shepherd of Psalm 23:1; a thematic resonance of God's pastoral care behind the title applied to Christ.
sourceText: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.

note: "that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness" (2:24) resonates with Isaiah 53:11, the Servant who 'makes many righteous (dikaiōsai dikaion)'; the righteousness outcome of sin-bearing parallels the Servant's justifying work.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

note: The pattern of patient unjust suffering held up as example (2:19-21) reflects the despised-and-rejected Servant of Isaiah 53:3, conditioning the whole exemplum before the formal citations begin.
sourceText: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.

note: Sarah's submission and her calling Abraham 'lord' (kyrios in LXX) is the explicit verbal anchor for 3:6 'as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord.' In Genesis 18:12 Sarah laughs and says 'after I am grown old shall I have pleasure, my lord (kyrios) being old also.' Peter borrows the LXX address-title 'kyrios' as the proof-text for the submissive yet honored wife.
sourceText: Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?”

note: 'Whose children you now are' (3:6) extends the Abrahamic-promise logic: Gentile believing wives become daughters of Sarah/children of the Abrahamic covenant, echoing the promise that Abraham would father a people. Faint and dependent on the Sarah link.
sourceText: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Get out of your country, and from your relatives, and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you. I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”

note: Sarah as the matriarch who 'hoped in God' and bore Isaac in old age informs the portrait of 'the holy women before who hoped in God' (3:5). Thematic, not verbal.
sourceText: Sarah said, “God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.” She said, “Who would have said to Abraham, that Sarah would nurse children? For I have borne him a son in his old age.”

note: 'Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised' undergirds the contrast in 3:3-4 between outward adornment (braided hair, gold, fine clothing) and the inner adornment of 'a gentle and quiet spirit' fearing God. Strong thematic coherence with the Proverbs ideal of the praiseworthy woman.
sourceText: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a woman who fears Yahweh, she shall be praised.

note: Isaiah's catalogue of women's outward finery — braided/ornamental hair, jewelry, fine garments — that God will strip away may color Peter's list of external adornments in 3:3. Faint, list-of-finery parallel.
sourceText: In that day the Lord will take away the beauty of their anklets, the headbands, the crescent necklaces, the earrings, the bracelets, the veils, the headdresses, the ankle chains, the sashes, the perfume bottles, the charms, the signet rings, the nose rings, the fine robes, the capes, the cloaks, the purses, the hand mirrors, the fine linen garments, the tiaras, and the shawls. It shall happen that instead of sweet spices, there shall be rottenness; […]

note: 'Joint heirs of the grace of life' (3:7), with husband and wife as co-heirs, faintly echoes the equal-dignity creation of male and female in the image of God. Disputed and thematic only.
sourceText: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: The longest OT quotation in 1 Peter (3:10-12) reproduces Psalm 34:12-16 (LXX 33:13-17) nearly verbatim: 'He who would love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil... let him turn away from evil and do good, let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and his ears open to their prayer, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.' Psalm 34 saturates 1 Peter (cf. 2:3 'you have tasted that the Lord is good' = Ps 34:8); Peter mines it as a charter for the righteous-suffering community. Formal quotation, no introductory formula but verbatim citation.
sourceText: Who is someone who desires life, and loves many days, that he may see good? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking lies. Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it. Yahweh’s eyes are toward the righteous. His ears listen to their cry. Yahweh’s face is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth.

note: 'Whoever returns evil for good, evil will not depart from his house' lies behind 3:9 'not rendering evil for evil.' The non-retaliation ethic of repaying evil with blessing draws on the wisdom prohibition of returning evil.
sourceText: Whoever rewards evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house.

note: 'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD and he will deliver you' directly grounds the non-retaliation command of 3:9 ('not rendering evil for evil... but instead blessing'), entrusting vindication to God rather than self.
sourceText: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.

note: 'You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge... but love your neighbor as yourself' underlies the cluster of 3:8-9 — brotherly love, tender-heartedness, and refusal to retaliate. The love-command tradition stands behind the communal virtue list.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'That you may inherit a blessing' (3:9) sounds the Abrahamic blessing-inheritance theme — those who bless rather than curse inherit the promised blessing. Faint, thematic.
sourceText: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”
