note: 'Speak the truth to one another... do not devise evil in your hearts... love no false oath' parallels the call to keep the tongue from evil and lips from deceit (3:10) and to seek peace (3:11). Faint, may be mediated through Psalm 34.
sourceText: These are the things that you shall do: speak every man the truth with his neighbor. Execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates, and let none of you devise evil in your hearts against his neighbor, and love no false oath: for all these are things that I hate,” says Yahweh.

note: 1 Peter 3:14-15 quotes Isaiah 8:12-13: 'Do not fear what they fear, neither be troubled (Isa 8:12), but sanctify the LORD of hosts (Isa 8:13)' — Peter christologizes it to 'sanctify the Lord [Christ] God in your hearts.' The Isaianic 'do not fear, do not be in dread, but the LORD of hosts him you shall regard as holy' becomes the charter for fearless witness under hostility. Formal quotation woven into the exhortation.
sourceText: “Don’t say, ‘A conspiracy!’ concerning all about which this people say, ‘A conspiracy!’ neither fear their threats, nor be terrorized. Yahweh of Armies is who you must respect as holy. He is the one you must fear. He is the one you must dread.

note: The immediately following Isaianic 'stone of stumbling and rock of offense' (echoed in 1 Pet 2:8) suggests Peter has the whole Isaiah 8 context in view; the suffering-righteous who fear God not man inhabit that sanctuary-vs-stumbling frame. Contextual echo.
sourceText: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”

note: 'Be zealous for / imitators of that which is good' and 'suffer for righteousness' sake' (3:13-14) continue the Psalm 34 program just quoted ('depart from evil and do good'); the do-good ethic flows directly out of the citation, a recurrence binding the pericopes.
sourceText: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.

note: The Servant's confident 'the Lord GOD helps me... who will declare me guilty?' parallels 3:13 'who is he who will harm you, if you become imitators of that which is good?' — vindication of the righteous sufferer. Faint, thematic.
sourceText: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed. He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord Yahweh will help me; who is he who shall condemn me? Behold, all they shall wax old as a garment, the moth shall eat them up.

note: The flood narrative is invoked typologically: 'the days of Noah while the ship was being built' (3:20). Peter reads the wickedness and judgment of the antediluvian world (Gen 6) as the backdrop against which the ark/baptism deliverance is the antitype (antitypos, 3:21). The flood's saving-through-water becomes the type fulfilled in baptism — explicitly figural.
sourceText: When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives. Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.” The Nephilim were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when God’s sons came in to men’s daughters and had children […]

note: 'Few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water' (3:20) cites the ark deliverance of Genesis 7 (Noah, his wife, three sons and their wives = eight). The salvation 'through water' is the explicit antitype of baptism in 3:21 — the flood-water that destroyed the disobedient world saves the elect remnant in the ark. Typological/figural reading of the flood as baptism.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Noah, “Come with all of your household into the ship, for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation. You shall take seven pairs of every clean animal with you, the male and his female. Of the animals that are not clean, take two, the male and his female. Also of the birds of the sky, seven and seven, male and female, to keep seed alive on the surface of all the earth. In seven days, I will cause it to rain on the earth for […]

note: God's 'waiting patiently in the days of Noah' (3:20) reflects the long patience while the ark was built and the flood receded (Gen 8); the divine forbearance toward the disobedient generation undergirds the patience motif. Recurrence within the Noah cycle.
sourceText: God remembered Noah, all the animals, and all the livestock that were with him in the ship; and God made a wind to pass over the earth. The waters subsided. The deep’s fountains and the sky’s windows were also stopped, and the rain from the sky was restrained. The waters continually receded from the earth. After the end of one hundred fifty days the waters decreased. The ship rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on Ararat’s […]

note: 'My Spirit shall not abide in man forever... his days shall be 120 years' — the limited span of divine patience before the flood — directly informs '(God) waited patiently in the days of Noah' (3:20), the period of forbearance before judgment.
sourceText: Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”

note: The 'disobedient' spirits/generation 'who before were disobedient in the days of Noah' (3:19-20) echo the corruption and violence that filled the earth (Gen 6:11-13). Faint, depends on identifying the 'spirits in prison' with the Noahic generation.
sourceText: The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. God saw the earth, and saw that it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth. God said to Noah, “I will bring an end to all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them and the earth.

note: The 'sons of God' who transgressed before the flood (Gen 6:1-4) feed the Second-Temple Watchers tradition (1 Enoch) widely thought to lie behind 'the spirits in prison' to whom Christ preached (3:19). Contested: whether the spirits are fallen angels (Watchers) or the human dead of Noah's generation.
sourceText: When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives. Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.” The Nephilim were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when God’s sons came in to men’s daughters and had children […]

note: 'Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous' (3:18) draws on the Servant who 'bore the sin of many' and 'the righteous one, my servant, shall make many to be accounted righteous.' The vicarious righteous-for-unrighteous formula extends 1 Peter's sustained use of Isaiah 53 (cf. 2:22-25).
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: The Servant who is 'exalted and lifted up' parallels the exaltation of the suffering-then-glorified Christ 'at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven' (3:22). Faint, part of the Isaiah 52-53 Servant arc.
sourceText: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.

note: 'Who is at the right hand of God' (3:22) cites the enthronement formula of Psalm 110:1 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.' The subjection of 'angels and authorities and powers' to the exalted Christ realizes the footstool-of-enemies motif. The most-cited royal psalm for Christ's exaltation.
sourceText: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”

note: 'Put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit' (3:18) and Christ's descent/proclamation faintly echo the Psalm of resurrection hope ('you will not abandon my soul to Sheol'), a text early Christians applied to Christ's vindication from death. Faint, thematic.
sourceText: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.

note: The exaltation of the suffering one to heavenly dominion over 'angels and authorities and powers' (3:22) recalls the Son of Man given everlasting dominion and all powers subjected to him. Faint, thematic cosmic-subjection parallel.
sourceText: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: "Christ suffered for us in the flesh" (4:1) reprises the Suffering Servant who suffered/bore in his body, the controlling christological frame of 1 Peter (cf. 2:21-25). Sets up the believer's call to share that mindset.
sourceText: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t […]

note: "Arm yourselves" (hoplisasthe, 4:1) may echo the divine warrior who puts on righteousness/salvation as armor; the military arming metaphor recurs in early Christian paraenesis. Faint and disputed.
sourceText: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.

note: The vice catalog of 4:3 (lewdness, drunken binges, orgies, "abominable idolatries") follows the Hellenistic-Jewish topos that Gentile idolatry breeds sexual and social corruption, classically developed in Wisdom's indictment of idol-worship. Deuterocanonical.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: "Abominable idolatries" (4:3) and the catalog of "desire of the Gentiles" recall the Holiness Code's warning against the abominations of the nations that defile the land; shared abomination-of-the-Gentiles framing. Thematic, contested.
sourceText: “‘Don’t defile yourselves in any of these things: for in all these the nations which I am casting out before you were defiled. The land was defiled: therefore I punished its iniquity, and the land vomited out her inhabitants. You therefore shall keep my statutes and my ordinances, and shall not do any of these abominations; neither the native-born, nor the stranger who lives as a foreigner among you; (for all these abominations have the men of the land […]

note: Drunkenness, whoredom, and idolatry chained together as the religion of the nations parallels the moral logic of the 4:3 vice list. Faint.
sourceText: Prostitution, wine, and new wine take away understanding. My people consult with their wooden idol, and answer to a stick of wood. Indeed the spirit of prostitution has led them astray, and they have been unfaithful to their God. They sacrifice on the tops of the mountains, and burn incense on the hills, under oaks and poplars and terebinths, because its shade is good. Therefore your daughters play the prostitute, and your brides commit adultery. I will […]

note: God "ready to judge the living and the dead" (4:5) draws on the OT confession that the LORD comes to judge the earth/the peoples; cf. Psalm 98:9. Generic judgment-theophany echo.
sourceText: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.

note: "Him who is ready to judge" (4:5) reflects the standing title of God as Judge of all the earth who renders account. Faint topical echo.
sourceText: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”

note: "The end of all things is near" (4:7) strongly recalls Ezekiel's emphatic oracle, "An end! The end has come... the end is upon you," the prophetic announcement of imminent eschatological judgment. Shared end (telos) language and nearness.
sourceText: You, son of man, thus says the Lord Yahweh to the land of Israel, An end: the end has come on the four corners of the land. Now is the end on you, and I will send my anger on you, and will judge you according to your ways; and I will bring on you all your abominations. My eye shall not spare you, neither will I have pity; but I will bring your ways on you, and your abominations shall be in your midst: and you shall know that I am Yahweh. Thus says the […]

note: "Love covers a multitude of sins" (4:8) verbatim-quotes Proverbs 10:12 ("love covers all transgressions"), closer to the Hebrew/proverbial sense than LXX. Foundational maxim of the pericope; cf. James 5:20.
sourceText: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.

note: The call to hospitality (4:9) and stewardship of gifts toward one another resonates with the prophetic ideal of sharing bread and shelter with the needy. Thematic, faint.
sourceText: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?

note: "He who covers a transgression seeks love" offers a near-parallel proverb to 4:8, reinforcing the love-covers-sin tradition; possible secondary source alongside Proverbs 10:12.
sourceText: He who covers an offense promotes love; but he who repeats a matter separates best friends.

note: The "fiery trial... to test you" (4:12) draws on the wisdom/prophetic metaphor of the crucible refining metal as God tests his people; cf. the smelting imagery the verse shares with Proverbs 17:3.
sourceText: The crucible is for silver, and the furnace for gold; but man is refined by his praise.

note: The refining fire that purifies (4:12) echoes the Lord's coming as a refiner's fire who purges the sons of Levi; this same Malachi context (judgment beginning at the temple) also feeds 4:17.
sourceText: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and refine them as gold and silver; and they shall offer to Yahweh offerings in righteousness.

note: "I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and try them as gold" closely parallels the testing-by-fire of God's remnant in 4:12. Strong thematic and verbal coherence.
sourceText: I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”

note: "You, God, have tested us; you have refined us as silver is refined" supplies the same trial-as-refining figure behind 4:12. Faint, one of several refining texts.
sourceText: For you, God, have tested us. You have refined us, as silver is refined.

note: "The Spirit of glory and of God rests on you" (4:14) reworks "the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him" (the messianic endowment), transferring the resting Spirit from the Messiah to the reproached believer. Verbal "rests/Spirit" link.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: Being "insulted for the name of Christ" (4:14) evokes the psalmist bearing the reproach of God's servants and of the LORD's anointed; shared reproach-for-the-name motif. Cf. Psalm 69:9.
sourceText: Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants, how I bear in my heart the taunts of all the mighty peoples, With which your enemies have mocked, Yahweh, with which they have mocked the footsteps of your anointed one.

note: "Judgment to begin with the household of God" (4:17) draws directly on the command to begin the slaughter "at my sanctuary," i.e., judgment commencing with God's own house before the wider world. Core source for the verse's logic.
sourceText: kill utterly the old man, the young man and the virgin, and little children and women; but don’t come near any man on whom is the mark: and begin at my sanctuary. Then they began at the old men that were before the house.

note: "I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name, and should you go utterly unpunished?" supplies the a fortiori structure of 4:17 (if it begins with us, what of the disobedient?). Strong conceptual parallel.
sourceText: For, behold, I begin to work evil at the city which is called by my name; and should you be utterly unpunished? You shall not be unpunished; for I will call for a sword on all the inhabitants of the earth, says Yahweh of Armies.

note: The Lord suddenly coming to his temple to judge begins purifying judgment at the house of God (4:17), reinforcing Ezekiel 9; the same passage's refining fire underlies 4:12.
sourceText: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and […]

note: "You only have I known... therefore I will punish you" expresses the same principle that election intensifies rather than exempts from judgment, undergirding 4:17. Thematic.
sourceText: “You only have I chosen of all the families of the earth. Therefore I will punish you for all of your sins.”

note: "If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will happen to the ungodly and the sinner?" (4:18) cites Proverbs 11:31 in its LXX form verbatim (the LXX renders the Hebrew as a saved/scarcely-saved a fortiori). Formula-cited proverb.
sourceText: Behold, the righteous shall be repaid in the earth; how much more the wicked and the sinner!
lxxText: If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?

note: "Entrust their souls to him" (4:19) echoes "Into your hand I commit my spirit," the psalm of committing oneself to God amid suffering (also on Christ's lips, Luke 23:46). Verbal commit-to-God parallel.
sourceText: Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth.

note: "A faithful Creator" (4:19) draws on the prophetic confession of God as the faithful Creator and Redeemer of his people who can be trusted in trial. Faint, supports the entrusting-to-Creator theme.
sourceText: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine.

note: The command to 'shepherd the flock of God,' with the rebuke of leaders who lord it over and feed themselves rather than the sheep, draws directly on Ezekiel 34's oracle against the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and ruled harshly, and on God's promise to shepherd his flock himself. The motifs of oversight, not domineering, and the contrast of true vs. self-serving shepherds are densely shared.
sourceText: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and tell them, even to the shepherds, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, and you clothe yourself with the wool, you kill the fatlings; but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither […]

note: Jeremiah's woe against shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep, and God's promise to set faithful shepherds over the flock who will tend them, supplies the same prophetic shepherd critique standing behind the charge to elders to tend God's flock rightly.
sourceText: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]

note: The Lord-as-shepherd image and the flock's care undergird the 'chief Shepherd' designation; the underlying Davidic shepherd theology resonates even if not verbally borrowed.
sourceText: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.

note: 'He will feed his flock like a shepherd, gathering the lambs in his arms' colors the tender-shepherd ideal that the elders are to embody and that the chief Shepherd fulfills.
sourceText: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.

note: The worthless shepherd who does not care for the flock furnishes another prophetic backdrop for the warning against shepherding for dishonest gain rather than the sheep's good.
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]

note: The prayer for a leader so the congregation 'be not as sheep without a shepherd' lies behind the biblical pattern of appointed shepherds over God's people that the elders here continue.
sourceText: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”

note: The promise that the wise 'shall shine... like the stars forever' parallels the imperishable 'crown of glory' awarded the faithful shepherds at the chief Shepherd's revealing.
sourceText: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: The righteous receiving 'a glorious crown' and 'beautiful diadem' from the Lord's hand parallels the unfading crown of glory, a Second Temple development of the reward motif.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: 'God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble' is a near-verbatim citation of Proverbs 3:34 LXX (which reads 'God' for MT 'he'/'the Lord'), introduced with proverbial authority; the same LXX form is quoted at James 4:6.
sourceText: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
lxxText: The Lord resists the proud; but he gives grace to the humble.

note: 'When they are cast down... the humble person he saves' (LXX: God 'will save the one of lowly eyes') feeds the humility-then-exaltation logic of 'humble yourselves... that he may exalt you.'
sourceText: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.

note: 'The mighty hand of God' is the fixed exodus idiom for God's powerful, delivering action (the 'mighty hand' that brought Israel out of Egypt); here it frames the suffering exiles' submission under and rescue by that same hand.
sourceText: I know that the king of Egypt won’t give you permission to go, no, not by a mighty hand. I will reach out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders which I will do in its midst, and after that he will let you go.

note: The recurrent Deuteronomic formula of God acting 'by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm' establishes 'the mighty hand of God' as a deliverance idiom underlying 5:6.
sourceText: Or has God tried to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, by war, by a mighty hand, by an outstretched arm, and by great terrors, according to all that Yahweh your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?

note: 'I will bring you out... with a mighty hand' applies the exodus 'mighty hand' to a restoration-from-exile context, fitting 1 Peter's address to elect exiles under God's hand.
sourceText: and I will bring you out from the peoples, and will gather you out of the countries in which you are scattered, with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out;

note: 'Casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you' closely renders 'Cast your burden on the Lord, and he will sustain you' (LXX Ps 54:23), the clearest scriptural source for the anxiety-casting exhortation.
sourceText: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.

note: 'Commit your way to the Lord; trust in him, and he will act' offers a parallel trust-and-cast-upon-God motif reinforcing Psalm 55:22 behind 5:7.
sourceText: Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this:

note: The enemies 'open wide their mouths at me, like a ravening and roaring lion' supplies the 'roaring lion seeking to devour' image for the devil; the suffering-righteous-one context of Psalm 22 fits the persecuted readers.
sourceText: They open their mouths wide against me, lions tearing prey and roaring.

note: 'The satan' as the accusing adversary who roams the earth (Job 1:7; 2:2) and tests the righteous stands behind 'your adversary, the devil, walks around... seeking whom he may devour,' and behind the call to withstand him steadfast in faith.
sourceText: There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job. That man was blameless and upright, and one who feared God, and turned away from evil. There were born to him seven sons and three daughters. His possessions also were seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred female donkeys, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the children of the east. His sons went and held a feast in the […]

note: 'Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people' contributes the roaring-lion image of a predatory oppressor, apt for the persecuting power the devil energizes.
sourceText: As a roaring lion or a charging bear, so is a wicked ruler over helpless people.

note: 'Lest like a lion they tear my soul apart' adds to the stock of lament psalms portraying the enemy as a devouring lion behind 5:8.
sourceText: lest they tear apart my soul like a lion, ripping it in pieces, while there is no one to deliver.

note: Satan standing to accuse the high priest, and the Lord rebuking him, reinforces the adversary/accuser background to the devil whom believers are to resist.
sourceText: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”

note: Daniel's faithful endurance in the lions' den, delivered by God, is a possible typological resonance for steadfastly withstanding the roaring lion amid suffering.
sourceText: Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. The king spoke and said to Daniel, Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you. A stone was brought, and laid on the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel. Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting; neither were instruments of music […]

note: 'She who is in Babylon' uses Babylon as a cryptonym for Rome, the imperial power; Jeremiah's oracles against Babylon as the place of exile and judgment supply the typology by which the church in Rome is figured as God's people in 'Babylon.'
sourceText: Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and save every man his life; don’t be cut off in her iniquity: for it is the time of Yahweh’s vengeance; he will render to her a recompense. Babylon has been a golden cup in Yahweh’s hand, who made all the earth drunken: the nations have drunk of her wine; therefore the nations are mad. Babylon is suddenly fallen and destroyed: wail for her; take balm for her pain, if so be she may be healed.

note: Daniel's depiction of faithful exiles living under Babylon's empire establishes 'Babylon' as the type of the dominating pagan power among whom the elect sojourn, supporting the Babylon=Rome cryptonym.
sourceText: In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to Jerusalem, and besieged it. The Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God; and he carried them into the land of Shinar to the house of his god: and he brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god. The king spoke to Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring in some of the children of […]

note: 'By the rivers of Babylon... we wept' crystallizes Babylon as the archetypal land of exile, resonating with 1 Peter's framing of its readers as elect exiles greeted from 'Babylon.'
sourceText: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down. Yes, we wept, when we remembered Zion.

note: Isaiah's burden against Babylon contributes to the prophetic Babylon-as-doomed-imperial-power tradition that makes Babylon an apt cryptonym for Rome.
sourceText: The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw: Set up a banner on the bare mountain! Lift up your voice to them! Wave your hand, that they may go into the gates of the nobles. I have commanded my consecrated ones; yes, I have called my mighty men for my anger, even my proudly exulting ones. The noise of a multitude is in the mountains, as of a great people; the noise of an uproar of the kingdoms of the nations gathered together! Yahweh of Armies […]

note: Becoming 'partakers of the divine nature' having escaped corruption draws on the creation of humanity in God's image and likeness — the restoration of the image is the goal of the divine promises.
sourceText: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

note: 'I said, you are gods, sons of the Most High' is the scriptural datum behind the deifying participation language of v.4.
sourceText: I said, “You are gods, all of you are sons of the Most High.

note: Wisdom's sorites, ascending from desire of instruction to love and incorruption that 'brings one near to God,' is the closest Second-Temple model for Peter's chain of virtues beginning here and listed in vv.5-7.
sourceText: For her true beginning is desire of discipline; And the care for discipline is love of her; And love of her is observance of her laws; And to give heed to her laws confirmeth incorruption; And incorruption brings near to God; So then desire of wisdom promoteth to a kingdom.

note: The graded virtue-chain ('in faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge…') follows the sapiential sorites-form most fully developed in Wisdom 6, where one virtue leads to the next and finally to nearness to God.
sourceText: For her true beginning is desire of discipline; And the care for discipline is love of her; And love of her is observance of her laws; And to give heed to her laws confirmeth incorruption; And incorruption brings near to God; So then desire of wisdom promoteth to a kingdom.

note: The contrast of being 'not idle nor unfruitful' versus barrenness recalls the prophetic vineyard expected to bear fruit; a faint coherence with the fruitfulness theme.
sourceText: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]

note: 'Make your calling and election sure' presupposes Israel's election as a chosen people, the covenant language Peter applies to the church's assurance.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.

note: 'As long as I am in this tent… the putting off of my tent comes swiftly' uses the body-as-tent figure of Hezekiah's lament, 'my dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent.'
sourceText: My dwelling is removed, and is carried away from me like a shepherd’s tent. I have rolled up, like a weaver, my life. He will cut me off from the loom. From day even to night you will make an end of me.

note: 'The perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthy tent burdens the mind' is the Hellenistic-Jewish source of the tent-of-the-body image Peter uses for his approaching death.
sourceText: For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, And the earthy frame lies heavy on a mind that is full of cares.

note: The Transfiguration voice 'This is my beloved Son' fuses the royal-enthronement decree 'You are my Son' with the beloved-son language; Peter cites it as eyewitness confirmation of Christ's majesty.
sourceText: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.

note: 'In whom I am well pleased' reflects the Servant call, 'my chosen, in whom my soul delights,' the second strand woven into the heavenly voice.
sourceText: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.

note: 'Your son, your only son… whom you love' supplies the 'beloved Son' resonance, with the Aqedah lurking behind the Father's word over Jesus.
sourceText: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

note: 'The holy mountain' and the voice from 'the Majestic Glory' recall Sinai, where the glory of the LORD settled on the mountain and God spoke from the cloud.
sourceText: Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain. Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud. The appearance of Yahweh’s glory was like devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the eyes of the children of Israel.

note: 'A lamp shining in a dark place' applies the psalm's 'your word is a lamp to my feet' to the prophetic word the readers do well to heed until the day dawns.
sourceText: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.

note: 'The morning star arises in your hearts' draws on Balaam's oracle, 'a star shall come out of Jacob,' the messianic star of dawn (cf. Malachi 4:2, the sun of righteousness).
sourceText: I see him, but not now. I see him, but not near. A star will come out of Jacob. A scepter will rise out of Israel, and shall strike through the corners of Moab, and break down all the sons of Sheth.

note: 'No prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men spoke being moved by the Holy Spirit' rests on David's claim, 'The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue' — the model of Spirit-carried prophecy.
sourceText: “The Spirit of Yahweh spoke by me. His word was on my tongue.

note: Balaam, on whom 'the Spirit of God came,' uttering the oracle of 'one who hears the words of God,' is a further instance of prophecy that comes not by human will but by the Spirit.
sourceText: Balaam lifted up his eyes, and he saw Israel dwelling according to their tribes; and the Spirit of God came on him. He took up his parable, and said, “Balaam the son of Beor says, the man whose eyes are open says; he says, who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down, and having his eyes open:

note: 'False prophets arose among the people, as false teachers will be among you' presupposes the Mosaic law on the prophet who entices Israel after other gods and must be purged — the Deuteronomic category of the false prophet.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul. […]

note: Jeremiah's false prophets who 'speak visions of their own minds' and lead the people astray supply the prophetic backdrop to the destructive teachers with their 'deceptive words.'
sourceText: Thus says Yahweh of Armies, Don’t listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you: they teach you vanity; they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of Yahweh. They say continually to those who despise me, Yahweh has said, You shall have peace; and to everyone who walks in the stubbornness of his own heart they say, No evil shall come on you.

note: Ezekiel's foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and whitewash the wall add to the false-prophet portrait.
sourceText: Thus says the Lord Yahweh, Woe to the foolish prophets, who follow their own spirit, and have seen nothing! Israel, your prophets have been like foxes in the waste places. You have not gone up into the gaps, neither built up the wall for the house of Israel, to stand in the battle in the day of Yahweh. They have seen falsehood and lying divination, who say, Yahweh says; but Yahweh has not sent them: and they have made men to hope that the word would be […]

note: 'God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them down to Tartarus' draws on the sons of God who took human wives before the flood, read in Second-Temple tradition as the rebellion of the Watchers.
sourceText: When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives. note: The binding of the sinful angels in 'pits of darkness, reserved for judgment' follows the Enochic account of the Watchers chained in the valleys of the earth until the day of judgment — the explicit source of the imprisonment imagery (pseudepigraphal; cf. Jude 6).

note: 'He did not spare the ancient world but preserved Noah with seven others… when he brought a flood' rests on the flood narrative and the eight souls saved in the ark.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Noah, “Come with all of your household into the ship, for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation.

note: 'Turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah into ashes, condemned them… an example' draws directly on the destruction of the cities by fire and sulfur as a paradigm of judgment.
sourceText: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky. He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground.

note: 'Delivered righteous Lot, distressed by the lustful life of the wicked' depends on Lot's rescue from Sodom; Peter reads him as the righteous man tormented among the lawless.
sourceText: He said, “Please, my brothers, don’t act so wickedly. See now, I have two virgin daughters. Please let me bring them out to you, and you may do to them what seems good to you. note: Wisdom's account that she 'rescued a righteous man when the ungodly were perishing' as fire fell on Pentapolis is the Second-Temple reading of Lot as the rescued righteous one.
sourceText: While the ungodly were perishing, wisdom delivered a righteous man, When he fled from the fire that descended out of heaven on Pentapolis.

note: 'The LORD knows how to deliver the godly… and to keep the unrighteous under punishment' restates the psalm's confidence that the LORD delivers the righteous out of all their afflictions.
sourceText: The righteous cry, and Yahweh hears, and delivers them out of all their troubles. Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit. Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.

note: That even angels 'do not bring a railing judgment' against the dignitaries before the Lord parallels the rebuke 'The LORD rebuke you, O Satan' — the restraint of the angel before God that Jude 9 makes explicit.
sourceText: Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”

note: 'Like unreasoning animals, born natural creatures to be taken and destroyed' echoes the psalm's 'man… is like the beasts that perish,' the bestial-and-doomed figure for those without understanding.
sourceText: But man, despite his riches, doesn’t endure. He is like the animals that perish.

note: 'They followed the way of Balaam… who loved the wages of wrongdoing, but was rebuked… a mute donkey spoke with a man's voice and stopped the madness of the prophet' depends directly on Balaam and the speaking donkey of Numbers 22.
