God’s anger was kindled because he went; and Yahweh’s angel placed himself in the way for an adversary against him. Now he was riding on his donkey, and his two servants were with him. The donkey saw Yahweh’s angel standing in the way, with his sword drawn in his hand; and the donkey turned aside out of the way, and went into the field. Balaam struck the donkey, to […]

note: Balaam's later role in enticing Israel to sin at Peor ('loved the wages of wrongdoing') deepens the indictment of the false teachers' greed (cf. Deuteronomy 23:4-5).
sourceText: Behold, these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against Yahweh in the matter of Peor, and so the plague was among the congregation of Yahweh.

note: 'Wells without water' inverts the prophetic image of the LORD as 'the fountain of living waters' whom the people forsook for 'broken cisterns that can hold no water' — the false teachers promise water and give none.
sourceText: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

note: Peter cites it as a 'true proverb': 'The dog turns to his own vomit again' reproduces Proverbs 26:11, 'like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly.' The washed-sow saying is paired with it as a popular proverb.
sourceText: As a dog that returns to his vomit, so is a fool who repeats his folly.

note: The broader proverbial portrait of the fool incorrigible in folly stands behind the double proverb of the dog and the sow.
sourceText: A whip is for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools!

note: The mockers' taunt 'Where is the promise of his coming?' echoes the scoffers of Jeremiah, 'Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come!' — the derision of a delayed divine word.
sourceText: Behold, they tell me, Where is Yahweh’s word? let it come now.

note: 'Let him be quick… that we may know it' — the mockers who dare God's purpose to hurry — is the prophetic prototype of those who scoff at the deferred day of the Lord.
sourceText: Who say, “Let him make speed, let him hasten his work, that we may see it; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, that we may know it!”

note: 'The days grow long, and every vision comes to nothing' is the proverb of delay Ezekiel must refute, parallel to 'all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation.'
sourceText: Son of man, what is this proverb that you have in the land of Israel, saying, The days are prolonged, and every vision fails?

note: 'By the word of God… an earth formed out of water and amid water' draws on the creation, where God's word separated the waters and gathered them so dry land appeared.
sourceText: God said, “Let there be an expanse in the middle of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.” God made the expanse, and divided the waters which were under the expanse from the waters which were above the expanse; and it was so. God called the expanse “sky”. There was evening and there was morning, a second day. God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered together to one place, and let the dry land appear”; and it was so.

note: 'By the word of the LORD the heavens were made' grounds Peter's insistence that the heavens existed 'by the word of God,' the same creative word that now reserves them for fire.
sourceText: By Yahweh’s word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth.

note: 'The world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished' depends on the flood that destroyed the ancient world — the precedent for a coming judgment, now by fire.
sourceText: In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on the same day all the fountains of the great deep were burst open, and the sky’s windows were opened. It rained on the earth forty days and forty nights. In the same day Noah, and Shem, Ham, and Japheth—the sons of Noah—and Noah’s wife and the three wives of his sons with them, entered into the ship— they, and every animal after its kind, all the […]

note: 'One day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day' restates the psalm's 'a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past' — God's time is not man's, answering the charge of delay.
sourceText: For a thousand years in your sight are just like yesterday when it is past, like a watch in the night.

note: 'Not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance' reflects the LORD's declaration, 'Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked… and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?'
sourceText: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? says the Lord Yahweh; and not rather that he should return from his way, and live?

note: 'The Lord is not slow concerning his promise' answers the vision that 'awaits its appointed time… if it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come.'
sourceText: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
lxxText: For the vision is yet for a time, and it shall shoot forth at the end, and not in vain: though he should tarry, wait for him; for he will surely come, and will not tarry.

note: God 'gracious and merciful, slow to anger… and relents over disaster' grounds the patience that defers judgment for repentance (cf. Jonah 4:2).
sourceText: Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity.

note: 'The heavens will pass away… the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll' is the prophetic dissolution of the heavens behind 'the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will be dissolved.'
sourceText: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.

note: 'The mountains will melt… like wax before the fire' supplies the melting-by-fire imagery of the day of the Lord.
sourceText: The mountains melt under him, and the valleys split apart, like wax before the fire, like waters that are poured down a steep place.

note: 'New heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells' draws directly on 'I create new heavens and a new earth,' the prophetic promise of a renewed creation.
sourceText: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.

note: 'The new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me' is the companion promise behind Peter's hope of the abiding new creation where righteousness is at home.
sourceText: “For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me,” says Yahweh, “so your seed and your name shall remain.

note: 'The heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment… but my salvation will be forever' frames the dissolution-and-enduring-righteousness contrast Peter draws.
sourceText: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.

note: 'In the fire of his jealousy all the earth shall be consumed' is a further day-of-the-LORD-by-fire antecedent for the burning heavens and melting elements.
sourceText: Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them in the day of Yahweh’s wrath, but the whole land will be devoured by the fire of his jealousy; for he will make an end, yes, a terrible end, of all those who dwell in the land.

note: Being found 'without defect and blameless' uses the cultic language of the unblemished offering applied to the readers' moral state at the coming.
sourceText: Whoever offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to Yahweh to accomplish a vow, or for a freewill offering, of the herd or of the flock, it shall be perfect to be accepted. It shall have no defect.

note: The opening phrase 'that which was from the beginning' deliberately echoes the Septuagint's 'en arche' of Genesis 1:1. The author frames the proclamation in cosmogonic terms, locating the Word of life at the primordial beginning of all things.
sourceText: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

note: The creative divine word that calls light into being ('Let there be light') resonates faintly with the 'Word of life' that is manifested. The juxtaposition of beginning, word, and life recalls the spoken creation of Genesis.
sourceText: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

note: 'By the word of the LORD the heavens were made' supplies the background for a life-giving creative word. The Word of life that was from the beginning draws on the tradition of God's word as the agent of creation and vivification.
sourceText: By Yahweh’s word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth.

note: Personified Wisdom, 'possessed from the beginning, before the earth was,' provides a conceptual matrix for a pre-existent Word that was from the beginning with the Father. The 1 John prologue shares the sapiential vocabulary of primordial origin.
sourceText: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed.

note: The manifested 'life' that the witnesses heard, saw, and touched may recall God breathing the breath of life into the human, the originating gift of life. The link is thematic rather than verbal.
sourceText: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

note: Wisdom as a 'tree of life' to those who lay hold of her loosely parallels the 'eternal life' that the witnesses lay hold of and touch with their hands. A faint sapiential resonance.
sourceText: She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her. Happy is everyone who retains her.

note: The LORD as 'your life and the length of your days' undergirds the Johannine equation of God/Word with life itself. The eternal life that was with the Father echoes the covenantal life found in God.
sourceText: to love Yahweh your God, to obey his voice, and to cling to him; for he is your life, and the length of your days; that you may dwell in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them.

note: Wisdom as 'a pure emanation' and 'reflection of eternal light' with God supplies a deuterocanonical bridge for the pre-existent life that was with the Father and was manifested. Shares the language of a divine reality made visible.
sourceText: For she is a breath of the power of God, And a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; Therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.

note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' grounds the declaration that 'God is light.' The metaphor of God as the believer's light is a fixed OT motif that 1 John condenses into a definitional statement.
sourceText: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?

note: 'In your light we see light' joins divine light to the source of life, matching the prologue's pairing of light and the Word of life. The verse provides a close conceptual parallel to God as unmixed light.
sourceText: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.

note: 'The LORD will be your everlasting light' and the sun's light will be superseded by God himself. This eschatological vision of God as undiminished light supports the claim that in him is no darkness at all.
sourceText: The sun shall be no more your light by day; neither for brightness shall the moon give light to you: but Yahweh will be to you an everlasting light, and your God your glory.

note: The theophany where God's brightness 'was like the light' and rays flashed from his hand offers an OT image of divine radiance. A faint background to the absolute light of 1 John.
sourceText: His splendor is like the sunrise. Rays shine from his hand, where his power is hidden.

note: God 'covers himself with light as with a garment' presents the deity clothed in light. This supports the predication 'God is light' as native to Israel's praise of the Creator.
sourceText: He covers himself with light as with a garment. He stretches out the heavens like a curtain.

note: 'He knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him' pairs God with light over against darkness, mirroring 1 John's light/darkness antithesis. A contested but apt verbal resonance.
sourceText: he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.

note: God who forms light and creates darkness establishes the sovereignty over both realms; 1 John sharpens this into God being pure light with no darkness. The relationship is dialectical rather than direct.
sourceText: I form the light, and create darkness. I make peace, and create calamity. I am Yahweh, who does all these things.

note: 'Come, let us walk in the light of the LORD' supplies the ethical idiom of walking in light that 1 John opposes to walking in darkness. The summons to conduct oneself in God's light is directly echoed.
sourceText: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of Yahweh.

note: The contrast of 'the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn' with 'the way of the wicked is like deep darkness' frames walking in light versus darkness as the two ways. This is the closest sapiential parallel to 1 John's antithesis.
sourceText: But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light, that shines more and more until the perfect day. The way of the wicked is like darkness. They don’t know what they stumble over.

note: Those who 'walk about in darkness' without knowledge depict moral and spiritual blindness, paralleling the one who claims fellowship yet walks in darkness. A faint background image.
sourceText: They don’t know, neither do they understand. They walk back and forth in darkness. All the foundations of the earth are shaken.

note: On the Day of Atonement 'you shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins' through the sacrificial blood, undergirding the claim that the blood cleanses from all sin. 1 John transposes the cultic purgation onto the blood of Jesus.
sourceText: for on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh.

note: 'The life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that makes atonement' establishes the atoning, cleansing power of blood that 1 John applies to Jesus' blood. The sacrificial logic of cleansing-by-blood is foundational.
sourceText: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.

note: 'A fountain opened... to cleanse from sin and uncleanness' anticipates a definitive cleansing from sin, matching the blood that cleanses from all sin. The eschatological purification motif resonates.
sourceText: “In that day there will be a spring opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness.

note: 'Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow' voices the cultic cleansing from sin that 1 John ascribes to the blood. The plea for thorough purification is echoed.
sourceText: Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.

note: The blood of the covenant sprinkled on the people seals the relationship and consecrates them, a background for the cleansing blood that secures fellowship. A faint covenantal resonance.
sourceText: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”

note: 'Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?' directly anticipates the rebuke of those who claim to have no sin. The rhetorical question denies the possibility of sinlessness that 1 John condemns as self-deception.
sourceText: Who can say, “I have made my heart pure. I am clean and without sin?”

note: 'There is no one who does not sin' establishes the universality of sin that exposes the false claim to have no sin. Solomon's prayer provides the scriptural axiom underlying 1 John's warning.
sourceText: If they sin against you (for there is no man who doesn’t sin), and you are angry with them, and deliver them to the enemy, so that they carry them away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near;

note: 'There is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins' restates the universal sinfulness that makes the claim to be without sin self-deceptive. A close sapiential parallel.
sourceText: Surely there is not a righteous man on earth, who does good and doesn’t sin.

note: 'No one living is righteous before you' grounds the impossibility of sinlessness before God. The verse supports 1 John's insistence that to deny sin is to lack the truth.
sourceText: Don’t enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no man living is righteous.

note: 'What is man, that he should be clean?' voices the rhetorical denial of human purity, echoing the futility of claiming to have no sin. A faint wisdom-tradition resonance.
sourceText: What is man, that he should be clean? What is he who is born of a woman, that he should be righteous?

note: Israel's claim 'I am innocent... I have not sinned' is rebuked by God, paralleling the self-deception of those who say they have no sin. The prophetic indictment of denied guilt resonates.
sourceText: “Yet you said, ‘I am innocent. Surely his anger has turned away from me.’ “Behold, I will judge you, because you say, ‘I have not sinned.’

note: 'Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy' is the closest OT parallel to the promise that confession brings forgiveness. 1 John echoes the proverb's logic of confession leading to mercy.
sourceText: He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.

note: 'I acknowledged my sin to you... and you forgave the iniquity of my sin' provides the experiential template for confession resulting in divine forgiveness. The verse matches both the act of confessing and the assurance of pardon.
sourceText: I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn’t hide my iniquity. I said, I will confess my transgressions to Yahweh, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin. Selah.

note: 'Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity... I acknowledge my transgressions' joins confession of sin to the plea for cleansing, matching the dual promise to forgive and to cleanse from all unrighteousness. The penitential pattern is closely paralleled.
sourceText: Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.

note: The LORD 'merciful and gracious... forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin' supplies the character ground for God being faithful and just to forgive. The covenant name-formula underwrites divine reliability in pardon.
sourceText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth, keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”

note: God who 'pardons iniquity' and 'will tread our iniquities underfoot' delighting in steadfast love supports the faithfulness and justice of God in forgiving. The prophetic confidence in pardon resonates.
sourceText: Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity, and passes over the disobedience of the remnant of his heritage? He doesn’t retain his anger forever, because he delights in loving kindness. He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

note: 'To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness, though we have rebelled' joins corporate confession to assured forgiveness, echoing the confession-forgiveness dynamic. A faint background from penitential prayer.
sourceText: To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness; for we have rebelled against him;

note: 'You are just in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt faithfully' pairs God's justice and faithfulness in dealing with sin, echoing the 'faithful and just' predication. A contested resonance from covenantal confession.
sourceText: However you are just in all that has come on us; for you have dealt truly, but we have done wickedly;

note: The cleansing 'from all your sins' on the Day of Atonement underlies the promise to cleanse from all unrighteousness. The cultic language of total purgation reappears alongside confession.
sourceText: for on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh.

note: 'God is not a man, that he should lie' establishes that to contradict God is to make him out a liar, which is what claiming sinlessness does. 1 John inverts the axiom: denying sin effectively calls the truthful God a liar.
sourceText: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?

note: 'There is no one who does not sin' makes the claim 'we have not sinned' a denial of revealed truth. The verse grounds the charge that such a claim makes God a liar.
sourceText: If they sin against you (for there is no man who doesn’t sin), and you are angry with them, and deliver them to the enemy, so that they carry them away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near;

note: 'They have all turned aside... there is none who does good, not even one' affirms universal sin, so denying one's sin contradicts God's own verdict. The psalm's indictment supports the charge of making God a liar.
sourceText: They have all gone aside. They have together become corrupt. There is no one who does good, no, not one.

note: Israel's protest 'I have not sinned' provokes God's judgment, paralleling the self-condemning denial in 1 John. A faint prophetic echo of denied guilt.
sourceText: “Yet you said, ‘I am innocent. Surely his anger has turned away from me.’ “Behold, I will judge you, because you say, ‘I have not sinned.’

note: 'Though I am in the right... my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, he would prove me perverse' captures the futility of self-justification before God. A contested wisdom resonance with denying one's sin.
sourceText: Though I am righteous, my own mouth shall condemn me. Though I am blameless, it shall prove me perverse.

note: 'The Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man' reinforces God's truthfulness, making the denial of sin an implicit charge of falsehood against him. A faint parallel to Numbers 23:19.
sourceText: Also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent; for he is not a man, that he should repent.”

note: Christ as the "atoning sacrifice for our sins" draws on the Day of Atonement, the single day on which atonement is made for all the sins of the people. The hilasmos language of propitiation is rooted in the Levitical cult that cleanses Israel before the LORD. John universalizes the rite to encompass the whole world.
sourceText: for on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh.

note: "It is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life" supplies the sacrificial logic behind calling Jesus the propitiation for sins. The atoning-blood theology of Leviticus underlies the claim that his death covers the guilt of the world.
sourceText: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.

note: The Servant who makes his life an offering for sin and bears the sin of many stands behind the idea of Christ as atoning sacrifice for the whole world. "Not for ours only" extends the Servant's vicarious suffering beyond Israel. The righteous one who justifies many parallels "Jesus Christ, the righteous."
sourceText: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]

note: "The righteous one, my servant" who shall make many to be accounted righteous may color the epithet "Jesus Christ, the righteous" as advocate. The juxtaposition of righteousness and bearing sins links advocate and atonement.
sourceText: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

note: "My witness is in heaven, and he who vouches for me is on high" supplies an OT image of a heavenly advocate pleading one's case before God. This anticipates the Counselor/advocate (paraklētos) Christians have with the Father.
sourceText: Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven. He who vouches for me is on high.

note: The mediating angel/interpreter who declares to man what is right may stand behind the figure of an advocate with the Father. The intercessory role parallels Christ pleading the believer's cause.
sourceText: “If there is beside him an angel, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to show to man what is right for him;

note: "Whoever keeps his word, God's love has been perfected in him" reframes the Shema's command to love the LORD with all one's heart as something now fulfilled in the obedient believer. Keeping the commandments as proof of love directly recalls Deuteronomy's covenant logic.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: The promise that the LORD will circumcise the heart so that Israel may love him with all the heart undergirds the claim that God's love is perfected in those who keep his word. The interiorized, completed love answers Deuteronomy's eschatological hope.
sourceText: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.

note: "You shall love the LORD your God and keep his charge and his commandments" pairs love with commandment-keeping exactly as John does. Knowing God is shown by keeping his commandments in both texts.
sourceText: Therefore you shall love Yahweh your God, and keep his instructions, his statutes, his ordinances, and his commandments, always.

note: Israel is tested to know whether they would keep his commandments; John makes keeping the commandments the test of whether one truly knows God. The verbal link of knowing and keeping commandments connects the passages.
sourceText: You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments, or not.

note: "If you walk in my statutes and keep my commandments" frames covenant fidelity as walking and keeping, language John echoes in walking as Christ walked and keeping his commandments. The covenant blessing depends on this obedience.
sourceText: “‘If you walk in my statutes, and keep my commandments, and do them;

note: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" is the substance of the commandment John calls both old and new. To love one's brother and not hate him is the Holiness Code's command (cf. Leviticus 19:17, "You shall not hate your brother in your heart"). The "old commandment from the beginning" is this Levitical love-command.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" stands directly behind John's contrast between loving and hating one's brother. The man who hates his brother walks contrary to this explicit prohibition.
sourceText: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.

note: "The path of the righteous is like the light of dawn" while "the way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know over what they stumble" closely parallels John's contrast of the one in light versus the one in darkness who does not know where he goes. The blinding darkness and lack of knowing the way are shared.
sourceText: But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light, that shines more and more until the perfect day. The way of the wicked is like darkness. They don’t know what they stumble over.

note: The new covenant in which God writes the law on the heart explains how an "old commandment" can be "new" and "true in him and in you." The interiorized commandment of the new covenant is the love that John says is now realized.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:

note: The promise of a new heart and a new spirit illumines the "new commandment" that becomes true in the believer as the darkness passes and the true light shines. The eschatological renewal makes the old command newly possible.
sourceText: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.

note: "We wait for light, but behold, darkness... we grope for the wall like the blind" parallels the brother-hater who is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes because the darkness has blinded his eyes. Both depict moral blindness as physical groping in the dark.
sourceText: Therefore is justice far from us, neither does righteousness overtake us: we look for light, but, behold, darkness; for brightness, but we walk in obscurity. We grope for the wall like the blind; yes, we grope as those who have no eyes: we stumble at noonday as in the twilight; among those who are lusty we are as dead men.

note: The curse that one shall "grope at noonday, as the blind grope in darkness" supplies the image of being blinded so as not to find one's way. John applies this blinded groping to the one who hates his brother.
sourceText: You will grope at noonday, as the blind gropes in darkness, and you shall not prosper in your ways. You will only be oppressed and robbed always, and there will be no one to save you.

note: "The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light" anticipates the true light already shining and the darkness passing away. The dawning eschatological light frames John's claim about the new commandment.
sourceText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.

note: "Arise, shine, for your light has come" and the receding of darkness over the earth may color the assertion that the darkness is passing and the true light already shines. The dawning of divine light marks the new age.
sourceText: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

note: "Great peace have those who love your law, and nothing causes them to stumble" parallels the one who loves his brother in whom there is no cause of stumbling. Love and freedom from stumbling are joined in both.
sourceText: Those who love your law have great peace. Nothing causes them to stumble.

note: "In your light do we see light" may inform the light/darkness antithesis that governs walking rightly. The divine light as the medium of right sight underlies John's imagery.
sourceText: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.

note: "For your name's sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt" parallels "your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake." Forgiveness grounded in the divine name is a Psalter motif John applies to Christ's name.
sourceText: For your name’s sake, Yahweh, pardon my iniquity, for it is great.

note: "Atone for our sins, for your name's sake" closely matches the forgiveness of sins "for his name's sake." The name as the basis of pardon is shared.
sourceText: Help us, God of our salvation, for the glory of your name. Deliver us, and forgive our sins, for your name’s sake.

note: "As far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions" stands behind the assurance that sins are forgiven. The Psalter's confidence in divine pardon undergirds John's address to the little children.
sourceText: As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.

note: The young men who have "overcome the evil one" may echo the protoevangelium's promise of victory over the serpent. The conquest of the satanic adversary fulfills the primordial enmity.
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: "The word of God remains in you" recalls the Shema's charge that these words be on the heart and taught diligently. The indwelling word as a mark of strength parallels Deuteronomy's internalized commandment.
sourceText: These words, which I command you this day, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

note: The triad of "lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" mirrors Eve seeing that the tree was good for food (flesh), a delight to the eyes (eyes), and desirable to make one wise (pride). The fall narrative supplies the anatomy of worldly desire John condemns.
sourceText: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate; and she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.

note: Qoheleth's pursuit of whatever his eyes desired, only to find all is vanity and passing, parallels the lust of the eyes and the world passing away with its desires. The transience of worldly pleasure is shared.
sourceText: Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor. Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.

note: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity" undergirds the assertion that the world and its lusts are passing away. The fleeting emptiness of all under the sun matches John's contrast with the one who abides forever.
sourceText: “Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.”

note: "The eyes of man are never satisfied" stands directly behind "the lust of the eyes" as insatiable craving. Like Sheol that is never full, worldly desire cannot be satisfied.
sourceText: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied; and a man’s eyes are never satisfied.

note: "All flesh is grass... the grass withers, the flower fades... but the word of our God will stand forever" closely matches the world passing away with its lusts while the one who does God's will remains forever. The contrast of transient flesh and abiding word/will of God is the same.
sourceText: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”

note: "Whom have I in heaven but you? ... God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever" parallels the rejection of the world for the abiding portion of God. The enduring versus the fleeting governs both.
sourceText: Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

note: "Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things" parallels the warning against the lust of the eyes and loving the world. The prayer to avert the eyes from vanity matches John's exhortation.
sourceText: Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.

note: The warning not to follow after one's own heart and eyes, which lead one to whore after them, parallels the lust of the eyes that belongs to the world. Eyes as agents of illicit desire connect the texts.
sourceText: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;

note: The king who exalts himself above every god and speaks against the God of gods supplies the antitype behind the Antichrist who denies the Father and the Son. Daniel's blasphemous end-time figure shapes John's expectation of the coming Antichrist.
sourceText: The king shall do according to his will; and he shall exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak marvelous things against the God of gods; and he shall prosper until the indignation be accomplished; for that which is determined shall be done.

note: The horn that speaks words against the Most High and wears out the saints anticipates the antichrist who arises in the last hour to oppose God. Daniel's eschatological adversary informs the figure of many antichrists.
sourceText: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.

note: The bold king of fierce countenance who rises in the latter time and rises against the Prince of princes colors the picture of the Antichrist appearing in the final hour. The deceitful end-time tyrant stands in the background.
sourceText: In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up. His power shall be mighty, but not by his own power; and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper in what he does; and he shall destroy the mighty ones and the holy people. Through his policy he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand; and he shall magnify himself in his heart, and he shall […]

note: The test of prophets who arise to lead Israel astray after other gods parallels the antichrists who go out and seek to lead the faithful astray with lies. The deceiver who departs from true confession is judged by both.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.

note: "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me" stands behind the believers' "anointing from the Holy One." John democratizes the prophetic anointing of the Spirit so that all who abide are taught directly.
sourceText: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

note: "They shall all know me, from the least to the greatest... no longer shall each teach his neighbor" directly underlies "you don't need for anyone to teach you," because the anointing teaches all things. The new-covenant promise of universal divine instruction is fulfilled in the anointing.
sourceText: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin will I remember no more.

note: The outpouring of God's Spirit on all flesh, so that all prophesy, underlies the anointing given to every believer that teaches them all things. The democratized Spirit of the last days matches John's "you all have knowledge."
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.

note: "All your children shall be taught by the LORD" parallels the anointing that teaches the faithful so they need no human teacher. Direct divine instruction of God's children is the shared promise.
sourceText: All your children shall be taught of Yahweh; and great shall be the peace of your children.

note: "I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" parallels the indwelling anointing that abides and teaches obedience. The internal Spirit guiding conduct connects the texts.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: "The LORD is righteous; he loves righteous deeds" parallels knowing that he is righteous and that everyone who practices righteousness is born of him. The link between God's righteousness and the righteous conduct of his people connects the texts.
sourceText: For Yahweh is righteous. He loves righteousness. The upright shall see his face.

note: "Who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears?" colors the call to abide so as to have boldness and not be ashamed at his appearing. The eschatological testing at the divine appearing is shared.
sourceText: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap;

note: The shame of some and the vindication of the wise who shine at the end may inform having boldness and not being ashamed before him at his coming. The contrast of shame and confidence at the eschaton underlies the verse.
sourceText: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.

note: Israel addressed as 'children of the LORD your God' grounds John's astonishment that believers 'should be called children of God.' The divine-sonship status, once Israel's covenant identity, is here extended to the community. John intensifies the relation with the language of bestowed love.
sourceText: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.

note: Hosea promises that those who were 'not my people' will be called 'children of the living God,' the precise idiom of being 'called children of God.' This eschatological renaming of the people supplies John's vocabulary for present sonship. The passage was a standard locus for adoption-into-sonship.
sourceText: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’

note: God commands the gathering of 'my sons' and 'my daughters' from the ends of the earth, framing the people as God's children. The verse reinforces the sonship motif John applies to believers. Faint but congruent with the divine-family theme.
sourceText: I will tell the north, ‘Give them up!’ and tell the south, ‘Don’t hold them back! Bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth—

note: God tells Moses no one may see his face and live, the canonical statement of the unseen God. John's hope that 'we will see him just as he is' deliberately reverses this prohibition as eschatological promise. The tension between present hiddenness and future sight is structured by this Exodus limit.
sourceText: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”

note: The psalmist hopes to 'behold your face in righteousness' and be 'satisfied with your likeness' upon awaking, the classic beatific-vision text and a likeness motif. John's 'we will be like him, for we will see him' closely mirrors this seeing-and-likeness pairing. The awaking imagery resonates with eschatological revelation.
sourceText: As for me, I shall see your face in righteousness. I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with seeing your form.

note: Job hopes that after his skin is destroyed he will 'see God' with his own eyes, an early witness to seeing God beyond death. This undergirds John's confidence that the not-yet-revealed future includes seeing him. The contested textual history of the verse makes the echo suggestive rather than certain.
sourceText: After my skin is destroyed, then in my flesh shall I see God, Whom I, even I, shall see on my side. My eyes shall see, and not as a stranger. “My heart is consumed within me.

note: Moses uniquely beholds the form/likeness of the LORD, an exceptional clear sight of God amid general hiddenness. John universalizes such direct vision as the believers' destiny. A faint background to seeing him 'as he is.'
sourceText: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”

note: The penitential confession of transgression and the plea to blot out lawlessness frame sin as 'lawlessness' (anomia in the Greek tradition). John's definition 'sin is lawlessness' draws on this Septuagintal vocabulary. Faint lexical resonance rather than direct citation.
sourceText: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.

note: The Servant 'had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth,' the sinless one who bears others' iniquity. John's 'in him is no sin' and 'he was revealed to take away our sins' draws on the Servant who removes sin while being himself without it. The pairing of sin-bearing and sinlessness is distinctively Isaianic.
sourceText: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

note: The Servant bears and carries away the sins of the many, the conceptual ground for 'he was revealed to take away our sins.' John's atonement language echoes this vicarious sin-removal. A strong thematic, looser verbal, link.
sourceText: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

note: The serpent who sins/deceives 'from the beginning' stands behind 'the devil has been sinning from the beginning.' The promised crushing of the serpent's head undergirds the Son's appearing 'to destroy the works of the devil.' This is the foundational devil-as-deceiver-from-the-start text.
sourceText: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]

note: The enmity between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed, with the seed who crushes the serpent, frames both 'destroy the works of the devil' and the children-of-God versus children-of-the-devil opposition. The 'seed' language in 3:9 ('his seed remains in him') plays on this protoevangelium. A primary structural source for the whole pericope.
sourceText: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

note: 'Through the devil's envy death entered the world,' an early identification of the Genesis serpent with the devil. This deuterocanonical reading directly supports John's claim that 'he who sins is of the devil.' It bridges Genesis 3 to John's explicit devil terminology.
sourceText: But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, And those who are of his portion make trial thereof.

note: The creation refrain of plants bearing seed 'according to its kind' may color the image of God's 'seed' remaining and producing offspring true to their origin. The begetting/seed motif of 3:9 has a creational backdrop. Faint and contested.
sourceText: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so. The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.

note: Cain rising up and killing his brother Abel is named explicitly as the negative paradigm of brotherly love. John's 'killed his brother' retells the murder and its judgment directly. This is the most explicit OT reference in the chapter.
sourceText: Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him. Yahweh said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground. Now you are cursed because of the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your […]

note: The LORD's regard for Abel's offering but not Cain's, with Cain's evil works contrasted to Abel's accepted righteousness, grounds 'because his works were evil, and his brother's righteous.' John interprets the motive of the murder from this scene. The works-and-acceptance contrast is taken straight from Genesis 4.
sourceText: Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. Yahweh respected Abel and his offering, but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell. Yahweh said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen? If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”

note: Abel's blood crying from the ground and Cain becoming a fugitive informs John's link between murder and the loss of life ('no murderer has eternal life remaining in him'). The Cain narrative ties bloodshed to exclusion from life. A thematic extension of the explicit citation.
sourceText: Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.

note: 'In the day you eat of it you shall surely die' establishes the death that befalls the disobedient, behind 'remains in death' and the passage from death into life. John frames moral failure as abiding in primeval death. The death/life antithesis traces to the Eden warning.
sourceText: but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”

note: The covenant choice set before Israel between life and death, blessing and curse, frames 'passed out of death into life.' Love of the brothers becomes the mark of having chosen life. A strong conceptual parallel to John's death-to-life transition.
sourceText: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]

note: 'In the way of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death,' linking righteousness to life and its opposite to death. This wisdom antithesis colors John's pairing of love/righteousness with life over against abiding in death. Faint sapiential background.
sourceText: In the way of righteousness is life; in its path there is no death.

note: The Servant 'poured out his soul/life unto death' and bore the sin of many, the OT ground for love defined as 'he laid down his life for us.' John reads self-giving death as the measure of love. The Servant's poured-out life is the template.
sourceText: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note: 'You shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother,' but open your hand to his need, directly underlies 'sees his brother in need, and closes his heart of compassion against him.' John's image of the closed heart inverts the command to open hand and heart. The 'brother in need' vocabulary is shared.
sourceText: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks.

note: True fasting is to share bread with the hungry and not hide oneself from one's own flesh, the prophetic demand to meet a needy brother's wants. John's test of love by sharing 'the world's goods' echoes this concrete charity. The 'do not hide from' your kin matches the closed heart John condemns.
sourceText: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?

note: Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will himself cry and not be heard, linking refusal of compassion to severed relationship with God. This grounds John's rhetorical 'how does the love of God remain in him?' A close wisdom parallel to closing the heart against the needy.
sourceText: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.

note: 'Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due when it is in your power to do it' parallels John's rebuke of the one who has goods yet withholds them. The duty to act on present means matches 'has the world's goods.' Faint sapiential resonance.
sourceText: Don’t withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it. Don’t say to your neighbor, “Go, and come again; tomorrow I will give it to you,” when you have it by you.

note: Tobit's counsel to give alms from one's goods, not turning the face from any poor person, parallels the test of love by sharing the world's goods with a brother in need. This deuterocanonical almsgiving ethic mirrors John's 'in deed and truth.' A strong thematic echo of practical charity.
sourceText: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]

note: Sirach warns against defrauding the poor, turning away the needy, or averting the eye from one in want. This closely matches the one who 'sees his brother in need' yet closes his heart. A deuterocanonical parallel to loving in deed not word.
sourceText: My son, deprive not the poor of his living, And make not the needy eyes to wait long. Make not a hungry soul sorrowful; Neither provoke a man in his distress. To a heart that is provoked add not more trouble; And defer not to give to him that is in need. Reject not a suppliant in his affliction; And turn not away your face from a poor man. Turn not away your eye from one that asks of you, And give none occasion to a man to curse you:

note: God searches and knows the heart, discerning thoughts and words before they are spoken, the ground of 'God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.' John reassures the self-condemning conscience by appeal to this divine omniscience. The all-knowing God who weighs the heart is the precise reference.
sourceText: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.

note: Solomon prays that God, who 'alone knows the hearts of all the children of men,' will render to each accordingly. This explicit claim that God alone knows every heart underlies 'God... knows all things.' The heart-knowing God before whom we are persuaded is drawn from this temple prayer.
sourceText: then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive, and do, and render to every man according to all his ways, whose heart you know; (for you, even you only, know the hearts of all the children of men;)

note: A person's ways seem right to himself, but the LORD weighs the heart, juxtaposing human self-judgment with divine assessment. This parallels the contrast between our condemning heart and the God who is greater and knows all. A wisdom echo of the heart-weighing motif.
sourceText: Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but Yahweh weighs the hearts.

note: 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways,' a key heart-searching text. It reinforces John's appeal to the God who knows all things beyond our heart's verdict. Congruent with the omniscience theme.
sourceText: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.

note: Keeping the commandments before the LORD is reckoned as righteousness, undergirding confidence before God grounded in 'we keep his commandments.' John's boldness toward God rests on obedience as in this Deuteronomic logic. Faint background.
sourceText: It shall be righteousness to us, if we observe to do all this commandment before Yahweh our God, as he has commanded us.”

note: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' is the OT command standing behind John's commandment that 'we should... love one another.' John joins this love-command to belief in the Son as the single commandment. The mutual-love mandate is rooted in the Holiness Code.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: The Shema's command to love God and the broader keeping of his commandments frames 'we keep his commandments' and abiding obedience. John's interiorized obedience and indwelling echo the covenant heart-love. A thematic resonance with keeping the commandments.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: God promises to put his Spirit within his people and cause them to keep his statutes, directly behind 'by the Spirit which he gave us' as the proof of indwelling and obedience. John's pairing of the given Spirit with commandment-keeping mirrors this new-covenant gift. The indwelling Spirit enabling obedience is the source idea.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: 'I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live,' the promise of the indwelling life-giving Spirit. This reinforces 'we know that he remains in us, by the Spirit which he gave us.' A strong new-covenant Spirit parallel.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.

note: God's promise to pour out his Spirit on all flesh stands in the background of the Spirit given to the community as the sign of God's abiding. Faint, but part of the prophetic Spirit-gift matrix John draws on. Contested as a specific source.
sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.

note: The new covenant writes the law on the heart so the people keep it from within, undergirding the union of commandment-keeping and mutual indwelling ('he remains in us'). John's interior obedience and abiding reflect this new-covenant interiority. A strong conceptual parallel to keeping his commandments.
sourceText: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:

note: The command to 'test the spirits' whether they are of God draws on the Deuteronomic protocol for evaluating a prophet or dreamer of dreams. There even a sign-working prophet must be rejected if he leads Israel after other gods, establishing doctrinal content (not wonders) as the test. John's many 'false prophets gone out into the world' echoes this category of the deceiving prophet.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul. […]

note: Deuteronomy supplies the explicit criterion for discerning a true from a false prophet ('how shall we know the word the LORD has not spoken?'). John reworks the prophetic-test tradition into a christological confession test, making confession of Jesus come in the flesh the discriminating mark.
sourceText: You may say in your heart, “How shall we know the word which Yahweh has not spoken?” When a prophet speaks in Yahweh’s name, if the thing doesn’t follow, nor happen, that is the thing which Yahweh has not spoken. The prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You shall not be afraid of him.

note: Jeremiah's oracle against the lying prophets who prophesy from their own hearts and not from the LORD undergirds John's warning that false prophets have gone out into the world and 'speak of the world.' The contrast between those who stood in the council of the LORD and those who speak a deceiving spirit parallels the spirit of truth versus the spirit of error.
sourceText: Concerning the prophets. sourceText: Yahweh appeared of old to me, saying, Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love: therefore with loving kindness have I drawn you.

sourceText: For you love all things that are, And abhor none of the things which you did make; For never would you have formed anything if you did hate it.

sourceText: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.

note: 'I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes' grounds John's claim that we know we abide in God 'because he has given us of his Spirit.' The indwelling Spirit as token of covenant intimacy underlies the Johannine mutual-abiding language.
sourceText: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.

note: The summary confession 'God is love' (repeated) again distills the LORD's self-naming as abounding in steadfast love. John makes the Sinai attribute the definitive predicate of the divine being in which the believer abides.

note: 'There is no fear in love; perfect love casts out fear' stands in deliberate tension with the wisdom maxim that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. John transforms the servile fear of judgment into the boldness of perfected love, a development of the biblical fear-of-God tradition.
sourceText: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.

The depiction of fear as inner anguish anticipating judgment resonates with John's contrast of fear and perfected love.
sourceText: For wickedness, condemned by a witness within, is a coward thing, And, being pressed hard by conscience, always forecasts the worst lot: For fear is nothing else but a surrender of the help which reason offers;

note: 'We love him, because he first loved us' restates the Deuteronomic priority of divine election-love that precedes and grounds any human love for God. The prevenient love of the LORD setting his affection on Israel before any response is the template for John's 'he first loved us.'
sourceText: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

note: The charge against one who says 'I love God' yet hates his brother draws on the Holiness Code: 'you shall not hate your brother in your heart... you shall love your neighbor as yourself.' John binds love of God inseparably to love of the visible brother, fulfilling the neighbor command.
sourceText: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him. “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: 'He who loves God should also love his brother' joins the Shema's command to love God with the whole heart to neighbor-love as a single commandment 'we have from him.' John reads the love of God of the Shema as inseparable from the love of brother required by the Holiness Code.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

sourceText: I said in my haste, “All men are liars.”

sourceText: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother. Don’t oppress the widow, nor the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor; and let none of you devise evil against his brother in your heart.’

note: The Shema's command to love God with the whole self stands behind 'when we love God and keep his commandments.' John makes love of God inseparable from obedience, exactly the link Deuteronomy forges. Loving God and keeping commandments are presented as a single covenantal disposition.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

sourceText: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant.

sourceText: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,

sourceText: Haven’t you made a hedge around him, and around his house, and around all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.

sourceText: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.

sourceText: so that he who blesses himself in the earth shall bless himself in the God of truth; and he who swears in the earth shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten, and because they are hidden from my eyes.

note: The greeting to the "chosen (elect) lady and her children" draws on Israel's status as the people the LORD chose for himself out of all peoples. The personified "lady" likely figures the church as the elect community, transferring covenant-election language to it.
sourceText: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.

note: The address to a beloved "lady" personifying the covenant community recalls the OT habit of personifying Zion/Jerusalem as a woman (daughter of Zion, the bride). The figure of the church as an elect woman with children stands in this tradition.
sourceText: For Zion’s sake will I not hold my peace, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteousness go out as brightness, and her salvation as a lamp that burns. The nations shall see your righteousness, and all kings your glory, and you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of Yahweh shall name. You shall also be a crown of beauty in the hand of Yahweh, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God. You shall no more be termed Forsaken; […]

note: The personification of the community as a lady ("the elect lady") echoes the OT convention of figuring the city/people as a woman, as Lamentations personifies Jerusalem as a bereaved lady. Faint and structural rather than verbal.
sourceText: How the city sits solitary, that was full of people! She has become as a widow, who was great among the nations! She who was a princess among the provinces has become tributary!

note: The salutation "Grace, mercy, and peace... from God the Father" stands in the line of the Aaronic blessing, which invokes the LORD's grace and peace upon the people. The conceptual debt is to the priestly benediction even though the wording is recast.
sourceText: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

note: The pairing of "truth" with "love/mercy" that pervades the opening (loved in truth; grace, mercy in truth and love) recalls the steadfast-love-and-faithfulness word-pair characteristic of the Psalter. The covenant virtues hesed and emet underlie the Johannine "love and truth."
sourceText: All the paths of Yahweh are loving kindness and truth to such as keep his covenant and his testimonies.

note: "Walking in truth" renders an OT idiom for fidelity to God; the psalmist asks to be taught the LORD's way so as to walk in his truth. The behavioral sense of "truth" as covenant loyalty, not mere doctrine, is the OT background.
sourceText: Teach me your way, Yahweh. I will walk in your truth. Make my heart undivided to fear your name.

note: Hezekiah's plea that he walked before the LORD "in truth" supplies the same idiom of life-conduct as fidelity. The elder's joy at children "walking in truth" reuses this covenant-walk language.
sourceText: “Remember now, Yahweh, I beg you, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in your sight.” Hezekiah wept bitterly.

note: The commandment "that we love one another," identified as that held "from the beginning," rests on the Torah command to love your neighbor as yourself. The Johannine "new/old commandment" tension presupposes this foundational Levitical law as the love commandment's source.
sourceText: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.

note: "This is love, that we should walk according to his commandments" reflects the Deuteronomic equation of loving/serving God with walking in all his commandments. Love is defined as obedient covenant-walk, the central Deuteronomic logic.
sourceText: You shall walk in all the way which Yahweh your God has commanded you, that you may live, and that it may be well with you, and that you may prolong your days in the land which you shall possess.

note: The fusion of love and commandment-keeping echoes the Shema's call to love the LORD with the commandments laid on the heart in the surrounding verses. The elder's collapse of love into walking in the commandments is thoroughly Deuteronomic.
sourceText: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.

note: Josiah's covenant "to walk after the LORD and keep his commandments... with all his heart" models the formula of love expressed as walking in the commandments. The verbal pairing of walking and keeping commandments parallels v.6.
sourceText: The king stood by the pillar, and made a covenant before Yahweh, to walk after Yahweh, and to keep his commandments, and his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and all his soul, to confirm the words of this covenant that were written in this book: and all the people stood to the covenant.

note: The "many deceivers" who have gone out and lead astray recall the Deuteronomic prophet or dreamer who seduces Israel to falsehood and must be rejected. The category of the deceiver who tests the community's loyalty is Deuteronomic, though John applies it Christologically.
sourceText: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul. […]

note: "Watch yourselves, that we don't lose the things we have accomplished" reuses the recurrent Deuteronomic warning to take heed to oneself lest one forget and fall away. The reflexive self-guarding against loss is a hallmark Deuteronomic exhortation.
sourceText: Only be careful, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things which your eyes saw, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life; but make them known to your children and your children’s children;

note: The same "take heed to yourselves lest you forget the covenant" formula reinforces the warning against losing what has been gained. The self-watch protects the relationship already established with God.
sourceText: Be careful, lest you forget the covenant of Yahweh your God, which he made with you, and make yourselves an engraved image in the form of anything which Yahweh your God has forbidden you.

note: The hope to "receive a full reward" echoes Boaz's blessing that Ruth receive a full reward from the LORD under whose wings she has taken refuge. The image of a complete recompense for faithful conduct supplies the background.
sourceText: May Yahweh repay your work, and a full reward be given you from Yahweh, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”

note: The refusal to receive the false teacher into one's house or greet him parallels the Deuteronomic command to show no pity and not consent to the one who entices to apostasy. The separation from the corrupter to avoid sharing his guilt reflects this Torah severity toward enticement.
sourceText: If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom, or your friend, who is as your own soul, entices you secretly, saying, “Let us go and serve other gods,” which you have not known, you, nor your fathers; of the gods of the peoples who are around you, near to you, or far off from you, from the one end of the earth even to the other end of the earth; you shall not consent to him, nor listen to him; neither […]

note: "He who welcomes him participates in his evil works" recalls the indictment that one who consents to and keeps company with the wicked shares their portion. The principle that fellowship implicates one in another's sin underlies the prohibition.
sourceText: When you saw a thief, you consented with him, and have participated with adulterers.

note: The wish to come and speak "face to face" rather than with paper and ink echoes the OT idiom of direct, mouth-to-mouth speech, as the LORD spoke with Moses plainly and not in riddles. The idiom marks the intimacy of unmediated presence over written communication.
sourceText: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
