note: Contested source for the twenty-four enthroned “elders.” Isaiah envisions Yahweh reigning “before his elders... in glory,” the only OT throne-text that explicitly seats elders in the divine presence-glory (cf. Exod 24:9-10, the seventy elders who see God). Thematic coherence is suggestive — enthroned elders around the reigning LORD — but verbal volume is thin and the number twenty-four (24 priestly/Levitical courses, 1 Chr 24-25; or 12+12) is not from Isaiah. Held at low/contested.
sourceText: Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed; for Yahweh of Armies will reign on Mount Zion, and in Jerusalem; and before his elders will be glory.

note: The “seven Spirits of God” likely also draws on the sevenfold enumeration of the Spirit resting on the Davidic shoot (LXX Isa 11:2 lists seven spirit-gifts, expanding the Hebrew six with an added 'piety'). Coherence with Revelation's seven-Spirits theology is good. NOTE: text supplied from WEB but NOT fetched live (rate-limit avoidance); flagged for verification. The LXX-vs-Hebrew divergence is itself the basis of the 'seven' (Hebrew has six pairs); John's sevenfold count tracks the Greek tradition.
sourceText: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

note: The “four living creatures” (tessara zoa) with the faces of lion, ox/calf, man, and eagle is a direct dependence on Ezekiel's four living creatures (LXX zoa). Volume, distinctiveness, and recurrence are maximal: the very phrase 'living creatures' and the exact four faces are Ezekiel's. John redistributes the faces (Ezekiel: each creature has all four faces; Rev: each creature bears one face) and substitutes 'calf/ox' (Ezek 'ox', moschos in LXX = Rev 'calf'). LXX Ezek 1:10 supplies the lexical set. The cherubic creatures become heavenly worship-leaders in Revelation.
sourceText: Out of its midst came the likeness of four living creatures. This was their appearance: they had the likeness of a man. Everyone had four faces, and each one of them had four wings. Their feet were straight feet; and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf’s foot; and they sparkled like burnished brass. They had the hands of a man under their wings on their four sides; and the four of them had their faces and their wings thus: their wings were […]

note: The Trisagion — “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty” — and the six wings are lifted from Isaiah's seraphim. Distinctiveness and volume are at their peak: the threefold 'Holy' (LXX hagios hagios hagios) and the six wings (hex pteryges) are Isaiah's signature, found nowhere else in this configuration. John conflates Isaiah's six-winged seraphim with Ezekiel's four-faced cherubim (eyes all around) into a single composite order. 'Lord God Almighty' (kyrios ho theos ho pantokrator) renders the Hebrew 'Yahweh of Armies / Yahweh Sabaoth' that LXX often gives as kyrios sabaoth or pantokrator. Echo of glory-filling-the-earth underlies Rev's cosmic doxology.
sourceText: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was […]

note: “Full of eyes before and behind... around and within” draws the eyes-all-around motif from Ezekiel 10:12 (the second cherubim vision), where the creatures' whole bodies and wheels are full of eyes. Distinctiveness is high — bodies covered in eyes is a peculiarly Ezekielan detail. John transfers the eyes from the wheels/bodies (Ezek 1:18; 10:12) onto the wings/bodies of the creatures themselves. Pairs with Ezek 1:18 below as the dual source of the eyes.
sourceText: Their whole body, and their backs, and their hands, and their wings, and the wheels, were full of eyes all around, even the wheels that the four of them had.

note: Companion source to Ezek 10:12 for the “full of eyes” detail; here the eyes are on the rims of the wheels, 'full of eyes all around' (kykloi auton, plereis ophthalmon in LXX). The phrase 'full of eyes all around' (gemonta ophthalmon kyklothen) in Rev 4:8 echoes this Greek closely. Distinctive, recurrent within Ezekiel, and verbally tight.
sourceText: As for their rims, they were high and dreadful; and the four of them had their rims full of eyes all around.

note: “Him who lives forever and ever” (to zonti eis tous aionas ton aionon) is the Danielic divine title for the eternally-living God whom even Nebuchadnezzar blesses (Dan 4:34; cf. Dan 6:26; 12:7). Distinctiveness: this 'the one who lives forever' formula is a hallmark of Daniel and the Second-Temple liturgical vocabulary Revelation inherits. Theodotion Dan 4:34 has zonti eis ton aiona; Rev expands to the plural-of-eternity. Coherent with Revelation's repeated use of the title (1:18; 10:6; 15:7).
sourceText: At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored him who lives forever; for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom from generation to generation.

note: The title “who was and who is and who is to come” paraphrases the divine self-identification of Deutero-Isaiah — 'I, Yahweh, the first... and the last, I am he' — the eternity formula Revelation triples into past-present-future (cf. Isa 44:6; 48:12). Coherence is strong with Revelation's Alpha-and-Omega theology, but the threefold temporal expansion is John's own (likely shaped by Hellenistic-Jewish renderings of the divine Name / Exod 3:14 'I am who I am' tradition). Medium: conceptual, not verbal, dependence on this specific verse.
sourceText: Who has worked and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I, Yahweh, the first, and with the last, I am he.”

note: “Who was and who is and who is to come” is widely read as a temporal paraphrase of the divine Name revealed at the bush — the ehyeh / 'I AM' of Exod 3:14 — expanded across the three tenses in line with Targumic and Hellenistic-Jewish triple-time glosses of the Tetragrammaton. Coherence is high; this is a contested-but-common scholarly identification. NOTE: text supplied from WEB, NOT fetched live (rate-limit avoidance) — flag for verification. LXX Exod 3:14 ego eimi ho on ('the Being One') is itself the ontological reading Rev's formula presupposes.
sourceText: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

note: The creation-doxology — “you created all things... they existed, and were created,” worshiped by the heavenly host — strongly parallels the Levites' confession: 'You alone... made heaven... the earth and all things on it... and the army of heaven worships you.' Coherence and structural agreement are excellent: God as sole Creator of all, adored by the heavenly army, is exactly the logic of Rev 4:11. Distinctive shared move: the worth/worship of God grounded precisely in his having created and preserved all things. LXX 2 Esdras 19:6 supplies the Greek base.
sourceText: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.

note: “Because of your desire they existed, and were created” echoes the creation-by-the-word/will theology of Ps 33 — 'he spoke, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood firm.' The link between God's will/word and things coming into being is the conceptual engine of Rev 4:11b. LXX Ps 32:9 autos eipen kai egenethesan, autos eneteilato kai ektisthesan — note ektisthesan ('they were created'), the very verb Rev 4:11 ends on. Strong verbal coherence in the Greek; God's bare will effecting creation.
sourceText: By Yahweh’s word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth. He gathers the waters of the sea together as a heap. He lays up the deeps in storehouses. Let all the earth fear Yahweh. Let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him. For he spoke, and it was done. He commanded, and it stood firm.

note: Supports the creation-doxology of v.11 — God as the one who 'laid the foundation of the earth' and whose hands made the heavens — part of the OT creator-praise pool (cf. Ps 8; Ps 95:5; Ps 146:6) on which Rev 4:11 draws. Medium because it is general creator-language rather than a pinpoint verbal source; Neh 9:6 and Ps 33:6-9 are the closer parallels. LXX Ps 101:26 kat' archas su... ten gen ethemeliosas.
sourceText: Of old, you laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the work of your hands.

note: Second-Temple parallel: the unsleeping watchers ceaselessly chanting the Trisagion before God's glory — strikingly close to Rev 4:8's creatures who 'have no rest day and night' singing 'Holy, holy, holy.' Demonstrates that John works within a living apocalyptic liturgical tradition (Isa 6 mediated through Enochic worship-scenes), not Isaiah alone. Low confidence by editorial convention (non-canonical, not fetchable in WEB) but historically a high-value coherence parallel for the ceaseless angelic Sanctus. LXX-vs-Hebrew not applicable; Greek/Ethiopic Enoch tradition.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: The throne-and-courtroom setting with multiple thrones (Dan 7:9 'thrones were placed') and the surrounding myriads who serve and worship (Dan 7:10) lies behind the assembled worship of Rev 4:9-11 and the twenty-four thrones of v.4. Coherence with Revelation's pervasive Danielic frame is strong; the plural 'thrones' is distinctive. Medium for this pericope because the explicit creatures/Trisagion are from Ezekiel/Isaiah; Daniel 7 most directly governs the enthronement and the surrounding council. Theodotion Dan 7:9-10 supplies the Greek throne-of-fire imagery.
sourceText: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.

note: Hays: high verbal volume — the rare detail of a scroll 'written inside and outside / within and without' is shared almost verbatim, and the prophetic-call setting (a heavenly hand presenting a written-on-both-sides scroll to the seer) is recurrent. John conflates Ezekiel's two-sided scroll with Daniel's sealing. The double-sided writing signals a complete, fixed decree with no room left to add. WEB Greek 'gegrammenon esōthen kai opisthen' tracks the Hebrew 'written within and without'; LXX Ezekiel renders similarly.
sourceText: When I looked, behold, a hand was stretched out to me; and, behold, a scroll of a book was therein; He spread it before me: and it was written within and without; and there were written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe.

note: Hays: thematic + verbal coherence — the motif of a 'sealed book' (sphragizō / sealed) reserved 'to the time of the end' supplies the eschatological logic of Revelation 5: the sealed scroll contains the end-time decree that only the worthy one may unseal. Daniel 12 is the closest source for sealing a book until the appointed time; cf. also Daniel 8:26; 12:9. Septuagint/Theodotion both use sphragizō, matching Revelation's vocabulary.
sourceText: But you, Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end: many shall run back and forth, and knowledge shall be increased.”

note: Hays: high — explicit messianic title 'the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah' draws directly on Jacob's blessing, the foundational text linking Judah to a lion and to enduring rule ('scepter will not depart'). Early Jewish/Christian reading took 'until he comes to whom it belongs' (Shiloh) messianically. The lion of Judah and the unfailing scepter together yield the conquering ruler John names. LXX 'heōs an elthē ta apokeimena autō' was read messianically in Second Temple sources.
sourceText: Judah is a lion’s cub. From the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down, he crouched as a lion, as a lioness. Who will rouse him up? The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs. To him will the obedience of the peoples be.

note: Hays: high — the second title in 5:5, 'the Root of David,' fuses Isaiah's 'shoot/branch from the stock of Jesse' (11:1) and 'the root of Jesse' to whom 'the nations will seek' (11:10). John transposes 'root of Jesse' to 'Root of David' (cf. Revelation 22:16), keeping the Davidic-messianic 'rizah Iessai' of LXX Isaiah 11:10, which Paul also cites (Romans 15:12). Pairing Lion-of-Judah with Root-of-David binds Genesis 49 and Isaiah 11 into one messianic identity.
sourceText: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.

note: Hays: medium — supplies the precise scene of a sealed book that no one is able to read/open, with the futile search for a reader echoing John's search for one 'worthy to open the book.' Reinforces the Ezekiel/Daniel scroll cluster: revelation is locked until the qualified one breaks the seal. Verbal link is the sealed-book ('sepher chatum') unable to be opened.
sourceText: All vision has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one who is educated, saying, “Read this, please”; and he says, “I can’t, for it is sealed:”

note: Hays: low / contested — lion-of-conquest imagery is widespread (Jer 49:19; 50:44; Hos 11:10; Amos 3:8), so the 'Lion' of 5:5 need not depend on any one beyond Genesis 49. Listed as a faint reinforcing background to the lion motif, not a primary source; Genesis 49 remains the controlling intertext. Marked low because verbal specificity is lacking and the phrase here is not the fetched WEB wording.
sourceText: Behold, he shall come up like a lion from the pride of the Jordan against the strong habitation: for I will suddenly make them run away from it; and whoever is chosen, him will I appoint over it: for who is like me? and who will appoint me a time? and who is the shepherd who will stand before me?

note: Hays: high — 'a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain' draws on the Servant who is silently 'led to the slaughter' like a lamb. The redemptive-by-death logic that grounds the Lamb's worthiness is Isaiah 53's vicarious suffering. Note lexical divergence: Revelation favors 'arnion' for the slain Lamb, while LXX Isaiah 53:7 uses 'probaton/amnos'; the figural link is conceptual (sacrificial slaughter) more than verbatim, which is why the Passover lamb is a co-source.
sourceText: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.

note: Hays: high (figural) — the slain-yet-standing Lamb evokes the Passover lamb slaughtered by 'the whole assembly,' whose blood redeems (Exod 12:13). Combined with 5:9 ('bought us... with your blood, out of every... nation'), the new-exodus/Passover typology is unmistakable. The Lamb's death effects a redemption patterned on Passover deliverance from Egypt.
sourceText: Your lamb shall be without defect, a male a year old. You shall take it from the sheep, or from the goats: and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening.

note: Hays: high — the Lamb's 'seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God, sent out into all the earth' is a near-citation of Zechariah's 'seven... these are Yahweh's eyes, which run... through the whole earth.' John identifies the seven eyes with the sevenfold Spirit, fusing Zechariah's omniscient divine eyes with the lampstand vision (Zech 4:2). Strong verbal recurrence of 'seven' + 'eyes' + 'whole/all the earth.'
sourceText: Indeed, who despises the day of small things? For these seven shall rejoice, and shall see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel. These are the eyes of Yahweh, which run back and forth through the whole earth.”

note: Hays: medium — the wider Zechariah 4 lampstand vision underlies John's identification of the 'seven eyes' with 'the seven Spirits of God': the seven lamps and the explanatory 'by my Spirit' link the sevenfold lamps to the divine Spirit. Reinforces 5:6 and the 'seven Spirits' motif of Revelation 1:4; 3:1; 4:5.
sourceText: He said to me, “What do you see?” I said, “I have seen, and behold, a lamp stand all of gold, with its bowl on the top of it, and its seven lamps on it; there are seven pipes to each of the lamps, which are on the top of it;

note: Hays: medium — the explanatory gloss 'golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints' rests on the established figure equating incense with prayer ascending to God. Psalm 141:2 is the classic verse making prayer = incense; cf. also the temple incense of Exod 30 and Luke 1:10. Conceptual echo rather than verbal quotation.
sourceText: Let my prayer be set before you like incense; the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice.

note: Hays: high — 'They sang a new song' takes up the formulaic 'new song' (shir chadash / asma kainon) of the Psalter, sung in response to God's saving victory. Psalm 98 is the strongest match because the new song celebrates accomplished 'salvation,' paralleling the Lamb's redemptive victory. LXX 'asma kainon' matches Revelation's 'ōdēn kainēn.'
sourceText: Sing to Yahweh a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand, and his holy arm, have worked salvation for him.

note: Hays: high — 'made us kings and priests to our God' (cf. 1:6; 20:6) directly applies Sinai's vocation of Israel as 'a kingdom of priests' to the redeemed of every nation. John democratizes/universalizes the Exodus covenant identity. Note textual variants: Greek tradition splits between 'a kingdom, priests' (cf. LXX 'basileion hierateuma') and 'kings and priests'; WEB here renders 'kings and priests.' The Sinai source is secure; cf. 1 Peter 2:9.
sourceText: and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation.’ These are the words which you shall speak to the children of Israel.”

note: Hays: medium — part of the 'new song' formula cluster (Pss 33:3; 96:1; 144:9; 149:1) that stands behind 5:9. Paired here with the harps of 5:8 ('Play skillfully'), reinforcing the liturgical 'new song' background. Less specific than Ps 98 because it lacks the explicit salvation/redemption note.
sourceText: Sing to him a new song. Play skillfully with a shout of joy!

note: Hays: medium — adds the universal scope ('all the earth') that matches the Lamb's redeemed 'out of every tribe, language, people, and nation' and the closing 'we will reign on the earth.' Member of the new-song formula cluster; reinforces but does not uniquely control 5:9.
sourceText: Sing to Yahweh a new song! Sing to Yahweh, all the earth.

note: Hays: low — included for completeness in the 'new song' + stringed-instrument cluster (cf. the harps of 5:8). The 'ten-stringed lyre' parallels the heavenly harps, but the link is generic; Ps 98 and Ps 96 carry the load. Faint, formulaic echo.
sourceText: I will sing a new song to you, God. On a ten-stringed lyre, I will sing praises to you.

note: Hays: medium — the fourfold 'every tribe, language, people, and nation' echoes Daniel's recurrent 'peoples, nations, and languages' (Dan 3:4; 5:19; 7:14), and the granting of an everlasting 'kingdom' to the son of man undergirds 'made us... and we will reign on the earth.' Daniel 7 supplies both the universal-peoples formula and the kingdom-to-the-saints theme (Dan 7:27).
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: Hays: high — 'ten thousands of ten thousands, and thousands of thousands' is a near-verbatim adoption of Daniel's heavenly-court formula 'thousands of thousands... ten thousand times ten thousand' attending the Ancient of Days. John relocates this innumerable angelic host around the throne and the Lamb. The shared context (heavenly throne-room, opened books/sealed scroll) makes this the controlling intertext for 5:11. LXX/Theodotion 'chiliai chiliades... myriai myriades' matches Revelation's wording.
sourceText: A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.

note: Hays: high — 'every created thing which is in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea' enacts the cosmic, totalizing praise of Psalm 148, which summons every creature of heaven, earth, and sea to praise. John structures the doxology by the same heaven/earth/sea/under-earth merism. The universal sweep of creation's worship is the Psalm's signature.
sourceText: Praise Yahweh from the earth, you great sea creatures, and all depths! Lightning and hail, snow and clouds; stormy wind, fulfilling his word; mountains and all hills; fruit trees and all cedars; wild animals and all livestock; small creatures and flying birds; kings of the earth and all peoples; princes and all judges of the earth; both young men and maidens; old men and children: let them praise Yahweh’s name, for his name alone is exalted. His glory is […]

note: Hays: high — the sevenfold acclamation 'power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing' and the doxology 'blessing, honor, glory, and dominion' draw on David's catalogue of divine attributes ('the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, the majesty... the kingdom'). The piling of abstract honors ascribed to God — now jointly to God and the Lamb — patterns on this temple-dedication doxology. Reinforces the worthiness language of 4:11; 7:12.
sourceText: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.

note: Hays: medium — the ascription of 'the dominion, forever and ever' to the one on the throne and the Lamb echoes Daniel's grant of everlasting 'dominion' and 'glory' to the son of man. Pairs with Dan 7:10 in 5:11; the same chapter supplies both the angelic myriads and the eternal dominion that frame the doxology's climax.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: Hays: low / contested — Second Temple apocalyptic (1 Enoch 39:12–40:1; 60:1; 71:8) shares Revelation's scene of innumerable angelic myriads ceaselessly blessing the enthroned Lord, suggesting a common throne-vision milieu rather than direct dependence. Daniel 7:10 remains the canonical source. Included to register the Enochic background of the angelic-host doxology; not available in WEB, hence marked deuterocanonical/low.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: The four chariots/horses of differing colors (red, black, white, dappled/grey) going out to the four winds of the earth are the master-template for the four horsemen; high verbal volume (colored horses sent out across the earth) plus thematic coherence of patrolling agents of divine judgment. John adapts the imagery to emissaries of conquest, war, famine, and death.
sourceText: Again I lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold, four chariots came out from between two mountains; and the mountains were mountains of brass. In the first chariot were red horses; in the second chariot black horses; in the third chariot white horses; and in the fourth chariot dappled horses, all of them powerful. Then I asked the angel who talked with me, “What are these, my lord?” The angel answered me, “These are the four winds of the sky, which go out […]

note: The night vision of colored horses (red, sorrel, white) that patrol and report that the earth 'sits at rest' supplies the same color-coded equine imagery; recurrence of the Zecharian horse motif strengthens the link, though here the horses bring war rather than report peace.
sourceText: “I had a vision in the night, and behold, a man riding on a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in a ravine; and behind him there were red, brown, and white horses. Then I asked, ‘My lord, what are these?’” The angel who talked with me said to me, “I will show you what these are.” The man who stood among the myrtle trees answered, “They are the ones Yahweh has sent to go back and forth through the earth.” They reported to Yahweh’s […]

note: Ezekiel's four 'severe judgments'—sword, famine, wild beasts, and pestilence—match the fourth seal's quartet (sword, famine, death/pestilence, wild animals of the earth) almost exactly; high verbal volume and thematic coherence make this the clearest source for v. 8.
sourceText: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: How much more when I send my four severe judgments on Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the evil animals, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and animal!

note: The covenant curses—sword, wild beasts that bereave, pestilence, and famine rationed by weight ('bread by weight')—underlie both the fourth seal's plagues and the third seal's scales of scarcity; LXX uses similar judgment vocabulary, reinforcing the covenant-curse coherence.
sourceText: “‘If you walk contrary to me, and won’t listen to me, then I will bring seven times more plagues on you according to your sins. I will send the wild animals among you, which will rob you of your children, destroy your livestock, and make you few in number. Your roads will become desolate. “‘If by these things you won’t be reformed to me, but will walk contrary to me; then I will also walk contrary to you; and I will strike you, even I, seven times for […]

note: Jeremiah's fourfold appointment to death, the sword, famine, and captivity (with dogs, birds, and beasts to devour) parallels the seals' instruments of slaughter; recurrence of the prophetic 'four kinds' formula supports the echo.
sourceText: It shall happen, when they tell you, Where shall we go out? Then you shall tell them, Thus says Yahweh: Such as are for death, to death; and such as are for the sword, to the sword; and such as are for the famine, to the famine; and such as are for captivity, to captivity. I will appoint over them four kinds, says Yahweh: the sword to kill, and the dogs to tear, and the birds of the sky, and the animals of the earth, to devour and to destroy.

note: God riding with horses and chariots of salvation, bow made bare, may faintly color the bow-bearing first rider; verbal overlap is thin (horses, bow) and the contexts differ, so the link is contested.
sourceText: Was Yahweh displeased with the rivers? Was your anger against the rivers, or your wrath against the sea, that you rode on your horses, on your chariots of salvation? You uncovered your bow. You called for your sworn arrows. Selah. You split the earth with rivers.

note: The royal warrior who rides forth victorious with sharp arrows, conquering, may tint the white rider 'conquering and to conquer'; thematic coherence of triumphal advance, but verbal volume is low.
sourceText: Strap your sword on your thigh, mighty one: your splendor and your majesty. In your majesty ride on victoriously on behalf of truth, humility, and righteousness. Let your right hand display awesome deeds. Your arrows are sharp. The nations fall under you, with arrows in the heart of the king’s enemies.

note: The angel's intercessory cry 'O LORD of hosts, how long?' is the proximate model for the martyrs' 'How long, Master, the holy and true?'; high verbal volume in the lament-formula and shared apocalyptic setting (within the same Zecharian horse-vision matrix used in 6:1-8) give strong coherence.
sourceText: Then Yahweh’s angel replied, “O Yahweh of Armies, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which you have had indignation these seventy years?”

note: The plea 'How long, O LORD?... avenge the outpoured blood of your servants' supplies both the 'how long' lament and the explicit appeal to avenge the blood of God's slain servants; very strong thematic and verbal coherence with vv. 10.
sourceText: How long, Yahweh? Will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire? Pour out your wrath on the nations that don’t know you; on the kingdoms that don’t call on your name; For they have devoured Jacob, and destroyed his homeland. Don’t hold the iniquities of our forefathers against us. Let your tender mercies speedily meet us, for we are in desperate need. Help us, God of our salvation, for the glory of your name. Deliver us, and forgive our […]

note: The Song of Moses promises that God will 'avenge the blood of his servants' and render vengeance on adversaries; the verbal core (avenge / blood / servants) is echoed directly in the martyrs' petition. LXX expands the blood-vengeance language, sharpening the parallel.
sourceText: Rejoice, you nations, with his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants. He will take vengeance on his adversaries, and will make atonement for his land and for his people.
lxxText: Rejoice, ye heavens, with him, and let all the angels of God worship him; rejoice ye Gentiles, with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen themselves in him; for he will avenge the blood of his sons, and he will render vengeance, and recompense justice to his enemies, and will reward them that hate him; and the Lord shall purge the land of his people.

note: The psalmist's 'But you, O LORD—how long?' is a stock lament cry that feeds the martyrs' 'how long'; recurrence of the formula across the Psalter (cf. Pss 13:1-2; 35:17; 90:13) makes it a plausible but diffuse source rather than a single quotation.
sourceText: My soul is also in great anguish. But you, Yahweh—how long?

note: Abel's blood crying out from the ground for justice is the typological prototype of righteous martyr-blood that cries for vindication; thematic coherence is strong though there is no direct verbal quotation.
sourceText: Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.

note: The sacrificial blood poured out 'at the base of the altar' grounds the image of the martyrs' souls/lives 'underneath the altar,' since 'the life is in the blood' (Lev 17:11); cultic-sacrificial coherence supports reading the martyrs as poured-out offerings.
sourceText: The priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of sweet incense before Yahweh, which is in the Tent of Meeting; and he shall pour out all of rest of the blood of the bull at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which is at the door of the Tent of Meeting.

note: God bids his people 'hide for a little while until the wrath is past,' for the LORD comes to punish bloodshed and 'the earth will disclose her blood'; the motif of resting/waiting a short while until the full measure of judgment matches v. 11.
sourceText: Come, my people, enter into your rooms, and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourself for a little moment, until the indignation is past. For, behold, Yahweh comes out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity. The earth also will disclose her blood, and will no longer cover her slain.

note: In 4 Ezra (2 Esdras) the souls of the righteous in their chambers ask 'How long are we to remain here?' and are told to wait until the predetermined number of the righteous is complete—an exact conceptual parallel to the martyrs' being told to wait until their full number is filled. Second-Temple apocalyptic coherence is very high.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: The Similitudes describe the blood/prayer of the righteous ascending and the petition that judgment be done for them, with a set number of the righteous to be fulfilled; close Second-Temple parallel to the fifth seal's cry and the waiting for the completed number.
sourceText: [source text not in the World English Bible]

note: The garment of salvation/robe of righteousness may faintly inform the 'long white robe' given to each martyr as vindication; verbal volume is low and white-robe imagery is widespread, so the link is tentative.
sourceText: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

note: 'The sky shall be rolled up like a scroll, and all their host shall fall as a leaf falls from the vine, as figs fall from the fig tree' supplies both the rolled-up scroll of heaven AND the falling stars/figs imagery—the single densest source in this pericope. The LXX 'the heaven shall be rolled up as a scroll' matches John's wording closely.
sourceText: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.

note: 'The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and terrible day of the LORD' is the direct source for the blackened sun and blood-moon of v. 12; high verbal volume and shared 'day of the LORD' framing (cf. v. 17).
sourceText: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

note: 'The earth quakes... the sun and moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining' yokes the earthquake, darkened luminaries, and stars together exactly as Rev 6:12-13 does; recurrence of Joel's cosmic-portent cluster reinforces the link.
sourceText: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.

note: On the day of the LORD against Babylon, 'the stars of heaven and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark... and the moon will not shed its light'—a standard darkened-luminaries oracle behind v. 12; strong thematic coherence with judgment-day cosmology.
sourceText: For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.

note: God will cover the heavens, darken the sun with a cloud, and make the moon not give light, darkening all the bright lights of heaven over the land; another darkened-luminaries oracle contributing to the cumulative cosmic-collapse imagery.
sourceText: When I shall extinguish you, I will cover the heavens, and make its stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of the sky will I make dark over you, and set darkness on your land, says the Lord Yahweh.

note: Jeremiah's vision of cosmic undoing—the heavens without light, and 'the mountains... quaking and all the hills moved to and fro'—stands behind 'every mountain and island were moved out of their places'; thematic coherence of de-creation judgment.
sourceText: I saw the earth, and, behold, it was waste and void; and the heavens, and they had no light. I saw the mountains, and behold, they trembled, and all the hills moved back and forth.

note: 'I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight' is part of the day-of-the-LORD darkening tradition feeding the blackened sun; verbal volume is modest but the motif recurs across the prophets.
sourceText: It will happen in that day,” says the Lord Yahweh, “that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day.

note: 'The mountains quake before him, the hills melt' contributes to the shaken-mountains imagery of v. 14, though the specific 'moved out of their places' wording is closer to Jeremiah and Isaiah.
sourceText: The mountains quake before him, and the hills melt away. The earth trembles at his presence, yes, the world, and all who dwell in it.

note: 'I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land' may faintly underlie the cosmic shaking that moves every mountain and island; thematic coherence with eschatological upheaval but low verbal volume.
sourceText: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;

note: 'I clothe the heavens with blackness and make sackcloth their covering' offers the rare sackcloth-darkened-sky image matching 'the sun became black as sackcloth of hair'; a precise but isolated verbal parallel, hence tentative.
sourceText: I clothe the heavens with blackness, and I make sackcloth their covering.”

note: Men 'enter the caves of the rocks and the holes of the ground from before the terror of the LORD' on the day he rises to terrify the earth—the direct source for hiding in caves and rocks of the mountains from the divine presence; high verbal volume and shared day-of-judgment setting.
sourceText: Men shall go into the caves of the rocks, and into the holes of the earth, from before the terror of Yahweh, and from the glory of his majesty, when he arises to shake the earth mightily. In that day, men shall cast away their idols of silver, and their idols of gold, which have been made for themselves to worship, to the moles and to the bats; To go into the caverns of the rocks, and into the clefts of the ragged rocks, from before the terror of Yahweh, […]

note: 'They shall say to the mountains, Cover us, and to the hills, Fall on us' is quoted almost verbatim in v. 16 ('they told the mountains and the rocks, Fall on us, and hide us'); the closest thing to a formal citation in the pericope. LXX wording aligns tightly.
sourceText: The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, will be destroyed. The thorn and the thistle will come up on their altars. They will tell the mountains, “Cover us!” and the hills, “Fall on us!”

note: 'Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the LORD and the glory of his majesty' parallels hiding 'from the face of him who sits on the throne'; reinforces the Isaiah 2 hiding-from-the-divine-presence motif.
sourceText: Enter into the rock, and hide in the dust, from before the terror of Yahweh, and from the glory of his majesty.

note: 'The day of the LORD is great and very terrible; who can endure it?' supplies the climactic 'the great day of his wrath has come; and who is able to stand?'; near-verbal match in the rhetorical question of endurance.
sourceText: Yahweh thunders his voice before his army; for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of Yahweh is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?

note: 'Who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears?' is a direct parallel to 'who is able to stand?'; strong verbal volume and shared theme of withstanding the day of judgment.
sourceText: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap;

note: 'Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the heat of his anger?' closely matches the closing question about standing before divine wrath; high coherence with the wrath-and-endurance motif.
sourceText: Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the fierceness of his anger? His wrath is poured out like fire, and the rocks are broken apart by him.

note: The 'great day of the LORD' of wrath and distress, against kings, princes, and all classes, from which silver and gold cannot deliver, supplies both the 'great day of wrath' and the social catalogue (kings, princes, rich); strong thematic and structural coherence.
sourceText: The great day of Yahweh is near. It is near, and hurries greatly, the voice of the day of Yahweh. The mighty man cries there bitterly. That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness, a day of the trumpet and alarm, against the fortified cities, and against the high battlements. I will bring distress on men, that they will walk like blind men, because they […]

note: 'You, even you, are to be feared; and who may stand in your sight when once you are angry?' adds to the cumulative 'who can stand before God's wrath' tradition behind v. 17; thematic coherence, moderate verbal overlap.
sourceText: You, even you, are to be feared. Who can stand in your sight when you are angry?

note: 'The kings of the earth set themselves... against the LORD and against his Anointed' lies behind the catalogue headed by 'the kings of the earth' now cowering before the throne and the Lamb; ironic reversal of Ps 2 supports the echo.
sourceText: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,

note: 'For the LORD has a day of vengeance' belongs to the same day-of-wrath oracle (continuous with Isa 34:4 used in 6:12-14) and may reinforce 'the great day of his wrath'; verbal volume here is low.
sourceText: For Yahweh has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.

note: 'Alas! for that day is great, so that none is like it' may faintly color 'the great day of his wrath,' but the wording is generic to day-of-the-LORD rhetoric, so the link is tentative.
sourceText: Alas! for that day is great, so that none is like it: it is even the time of Jacob’s trouble; but he shall be saved out of it.

note: The defining background: an angelic figure sets a mark (Heb. taw) on the foreheads of the faithful before destruction is unleashed, and those marked are spared ("do not touch any on whom is the mark"). John's sealing of the bondservants on the foreheads before harm comes to earth/sea/trees reproduces the structure exactly — protective marking that withholds judgment. Hays' criteria: volume, thematic coherence, and historical availability all strong; the LXX renders Ezekiel's taw with semeion (sign/mark), bridging toward John's sphragis (seal). The strongest single echo in the unit.
sourceText: Yahweh said to him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark on the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry over all the abominations that are done in its midst. To the others he said in my hearing, Go through the city after him, and strike: don’t let your eye spare, neither have pity; kill utterly the old man, the young man and the virgin, and little children and women; but don’t come near any man on whom is […]

note: "The four winds of heaven stirred up the great sea" — the closest verbal parallel for "the four winds" as agents associated with cosmic upheaval and the unleashing of beasts/judgment. Daniel is John's most pervasive single source-book, raising historical-availability and recurrence weight; here the four winds are the very instruments of the eschatological turmoil John's angels restrain. LXX (Theodotion) tessares anemoi tou ouranou matches John's tessaras anemous.
sourceText: Daniel spoke and said, I saw in my vision by night, and, behold, the four winds of the sky broke out on the great sea.

note: The four chariots/spirits are "the four winds of heaven, which go out from standing before the Lord of all the earth" — four winds as commissioned heavenly agents going forth over the earth, echoed in John's four angels stationed at the four quarters who are given power over earth and sea. LXX uses anemoi explicitly. Coherent with John's angelology of restrained, commissioned winds.
sourceText: The angel answered me, “These are the four winds of the sky, which go out from standing before the Lord of all the earth.

note: "I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and will scatter them toward all those winds" — four winds from the four ends/quarters of heaven as instruments of judgment-scattering. Supplies the spatial idiom of winds at the four corners/quarters that John fuses with the corners-of-the-earth motif. LXX = Jer 25:16 LXX (chapter renumbering); table-of-nations resonance. Cited 49:36 as the principal Hebrew verse.
sourceText: On Elam will I bring the four winds from the four quarters of the sky, and will scatter them toward all those winds; and there shall be no nation where the outcasts of Elam shall not come.

note: "An end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land/earth" — supplies the phrase "the four corners of the earth" (Heb. arba kanphot ha-arets) in an oracle of imminent total judgment, matching John's tessaras gonias tes ges and the eschatological-end setting. Coheres with the surrounding Ezekiel-9 sealing material, suggesting deliberate clustering of Ezekiel imagery.
sourceText: You, son of man, thus says the Lord Yahweh to the land of Israel, An end: the end has come on the four corners of the land.

note: "gather... from the four corners of the earth" (arba kanphot ha-arets) — the only other classic occurrence of the four-corners phrase, here in an ingathering (not destruction) context. Faint; supplies idiom shared with Ezek 7:2 and possibly colors the gathering of the sealed remnant by tribe that immediately follows. Contested as direct.
sourceText: He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

note: Passover typology: the destroyer passes over houses bearing the apotropaic blood-mark on the doorposts, sparing the marked. The protective-mark-withholding-the-destroyer pattern stands behind both Ezek 9 and John's sealing. Faint and mediated through Ezekiel rather than direct, but figurally apt (and reinforced by the Lamb/blood imagery later in the chapter).
sourceText: For Yahweh will pass through to strike the Egyptians; and when he sees the blood on the lintel, and on the two door posts, Yahweh will pass over the door, and will not allow the destroyer to come in to your houses to strike you.

note: "the living God" (Aram. elaha chayya) — Daniel's recurrent epithet (also 6:20), one source for John's "the seal of the living God." The title is widespread (cf. Josh 3:10; Ps 42:2; Hos 1:10), so volume is low and attribution to any single verse is uncertain.
sourceText: I make a decree, that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel; for he is the living God, and steadfast forever, His kingdom that which shall not be destroyed; and his dominion shall be even to the end.

note: Triad "earth... sea... trees" as the scope of creation to be spared echoes the created order (land, waters, trees of the garden); faint creation-protection resonance. More plausibly John's own merism than a specific citation.
sourceText: Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

note: The tribe-by-tribe census-roll of the able-bodied men of Israel, numbered for a holy war muster, is the genre and form John reproduces: "of the tribe of X were numbered/sealed N thousand," tribe after tribe. The 144,000 are an eschatological militia mustered tribe-by-tribe — a Numbers war-census transposed. Strong on form, recurrence (Num 1, 2, 26 all share the cadence), and the military-census connotation. Principal verses Num 1:1-46 (cite 1:20 ff. for the per-tribe formula).
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the Tent of Meeting, on the first day of the second month, in the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying, “Take a census of all the congregation of the children of Israel, by their families, by their fathers’ houses, according to the number of the names, every male, one by one; from twenty years old and upward, all who are able to go out to war in Israel. You and Aaron shall […]

note: Jacob's blessing of the twelve sons/tribes is the foundational twelve-tribe roster and explains John's striking placement of Judah first — Judah, not the firstborn Reuben, heads John's list because Gen 49:8-10 gives Judah primacy and the lion/scepter (messianic) prophecy John applies to the Lamb (cf. Rev 5:5). The reordering is interpretive, not careless. High coherence with John's Judah-Christology.
sourceText: Jacob called to his sons, and said: “Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which will happen to you in the days to come. Assemble yourselves, and hear, you sons of Jacob. Listen to Israel, your father. “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength; excelling in dignity, and excelling in power. Boiling over like water, you shall not excel; because you went up to your father’s bed, then defiled it. He went up to my […]

note: The canonical enumeration of the twelve sons of Jacob by their mothers — the master list against which John's idiosyncratic roster is measured. John's omission of Dan and Ephraim and inclusion of both Manasseh and Joseph (to keep twelve) is a deliberate variation on this base list; recognizing the variation requires this source as foil. Medium volume, high diagnostic value.
sourceText: While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel heard of it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve. The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob’s firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. The sons of Bilhah (Rachel’s handmaid): Dan and Naphtali. The sons of Zilpah (Leah’s handmaid): Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob, who were born to him in Paddan Aram.

note: The second wilderness census (the new generation mustered for the conquest) reinforces the muster-for-holy-war reading of the 144,000 and supplies a second instance of the per-tribe "twelve thousand"-style cadence. Coheres with Num 1; together they make the census-form unmistakable.
sourceText: After the plague, Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest, saying, “Take a census of all the congregation of the children of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, by their fathers’ houses, all who are able to go out to war in Israel.” Moses and Eleazar the priest spoke with them in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, “Take a census, from twenty years old and upward; as Yahweh commanded Moses and the children […]

note: Ezekiel's eschatological twelve-tribe roster — the twelve gates of the restored city named for the twelve tribes — stands behind Revelation's tribal lists (cf. Rev 21:12). Ezekiel here also restores Joseph/Levi arrangements in a non-Numbers order, a precedent for John's reshuffling. Thematic coherence with the eschatological-Israel framing; volume moderate.
sourceText: These are the exits of the city: On the north side four thousand and five hundred reeds by measure; and the gates of the city shall be after the names of the tribes of Israel, three gates northward: the gate of Reuben, one; the gate of Judah, one; the gate of Levi, one. At the east side four thousand and five hundred reeds, and three gates: even the gate of Joseph, one; the gate of Benjamin, one; the gate of Dan, one. At the south side four thousand and […]

note: Possible background for the conspicuous OMISSION of Dan from John's list: Dan's blessing ("a serpent in the way") and later association with idolatry (Judg 18; Dan as the apostate sanctuary, cf. 1 Kgs 12:29) generated a patristic tradition linking Dan to the Antichrist. The absence is an argument-from-silence intertext — significant but inferential.
sourceText: “Dan will judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel. Dan will be a serpent on the trail, an adder in the path, That bites the horse’s heels, so that his rider falls backward. I have waited for your salvation, Yahweh.

note: The Blessing of Moses, a second tribal-blessing roster (notably omitting Simeon and ordering tribes distinctively), is a further precedent for variable, theologically-weighted tribe lists. Faint; cited as one more member of the tribal-roster tradition John draws on rather than a specific source.
sourceText: This is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death. He said, “Yahweh came from Sinai, and rose from Seir to them. He shone from Mount Paran. He came from the ten thousands of holy ones. At his right hand was a fiery law for them. Yes, he loves the people. All his saints are in your hand. They sat down at your feet. Each receives your words. Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance for the assembly of […]

note: The Abrahamic promise: "count the stars, if you are able to count them... so shall your offspring be" — the uncountable, innumerable seed. John's "a great multitude, which no man could count" (hon arithmesai auton oudeis edynato) directly fulfills the count-if-you-can promise, now extended beyond Israel to every nation. Strong on volume and on John's larger Abrahamic-fulfillment logic (the multitude completes what the sealed 144,000 represent).
sourceText: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So will your seed be.”

note: Parallel Abrahamic promise: offspring "as the dust of the earth, which if a man can number..." — the explicit "if a man can number" idiom that John negates ("which no man could count"). LXX ei dynatai tis exarithmesai is verbally close to John's clause. Pairs with Gen 15:5 as the twin innumerability promises being eschatologically realized.
sourceText: I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if a man can number the dust of the earth, then your seed may also be numbered.

note: The palm branches (phoinikes) in the multitude's hands evoke the Feast of Tabernacles/Sukkot, where worshipers take "branches of palm trees" and rejoice before the LORD — fitting the booth/tabernacle imagery that immediately follows (7:15, God spreading his tabernacle, skenosei). Festal-joy and ingathering-harvest coherence is strong; the specific lulav connection is the principal reason this is an allusion not a mere echo.
sourceText: You shall take on the first day the fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm trees, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook; and you shall rejoice before Yahweh your God seven days.

note: "all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him" (Aram./Theod. laoi, phylai, glossai) — Daniel's stereotyped fourfold list of the nations is the template for John's recurrent "every nation, tribe, people, and language" formula (cf. Rev 5:9; 13:7). The multitude drawn from all peoples fulfills Daniel's universal dominion of the Son of Man. Recurrence in Revelation strengthens the link.
sourceText: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.

note: Simon's triumphal entry into the Jerusalem citadel "with praise and palm branches (baia)... and with hymns and songs" — Second-Temple precedent for palm branches as the gesture of victory celebration and deliverance, illuminating why the redeemed multitude (victors out of tribulation) bear palms while acclaiming salvation. Confirms the victory-procession nuance alongside the Tabernacles nuance (cf. also 2 Macc 10:7; John 12:13).
sourceText: And he entered into it on the three and twentieth day of the second month, in the hundred and seventy and first year, with praise and palm branches, and with harps, and with cymbals, and with viols, and with hymns, and with songs: because a great enemy was destroyed out of Israel.

note: "Salvation belongs to the LORD" (LXX Ps 3:9, tou kyriou he soteria) — the acclamation "Salvation be to our God" closely mirrors this psalmic confession that deliverance is God's alone. Idiom is common across the Psalter (cf. Ps 37:39; Jonah 2:9), so attribution to a single verse is uncertain, but the verbal shape is closest here.
sourceText: Salvation belongs to Yahweh. Your blessing be on your people. Selah.

note: David's doxology — "Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory... and the majesty... blessing" — a sevenfold-style ascription of attributes to God that stands behind the seven-membered doxology of 7:12 (blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, might). Liturgical-doxological coherence; faint as a specific citation since such ascriptions are formulaic.
sourceText: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.

note: The throne-vision with surrounding heavenly beings prostrate/crying praise underlies the angels, elders, and four living creatures falling before the throne; the living creatures themselves derive from Isa 6 seraphim and Ezek 1/10. Faint here because the throne-room cast is established earlier (Rev 4) rather than newly drawn from Isaiah in this verse.
sourceText: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”

note: "They shall not hunger nor thirst, neither scorching heat nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them" — the densest verbal source in the chapter. John reproduces all four elements in order: no hunger, no thirst, no sun/scorching heat smiting them, and a shepherd-guide leading to springs of water. Hays' criteria max out (volume, recurrence of the Servant-shepherd motif, coherence with the new-exodus ingathering). LXX peinasousin... dipsesousin... kausön... pegas hydaton tracks John closely.
sourceText: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.

note: "He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces" — direct source for "God will wipe away every tear from their eyes" (exaleipsei... pan dakryon). The eschatological consolation at the victory-banquet on the mountain. High verbal volume; recurs at Rev 21:4. Note the MT "swallow up death" vs. LXX katepien ho thanatos ischysas; John follows the tear-wiping clause closely regardless of the textual divergence in the first colon.
sourceText: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.

note: "I will set up over them one shepherd... my servant David, and he shall feed them and be their shepherd" — the messianic Davidic-shepherd promise underlying "the Lamb... shepherds them." Striking oxymoron (the Lamb is the Shepherd) fuses Ezekiel 34's shepherd-king with John's Lamb-Christology. Strong coherence; Ezek 34:23 cited as the principal verse of the chapter-long shepherd oracle.
sourceText: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.

note: "The LORD is my shepherd... he leads me beside still waters" (LXX Ps 22:1-2, hodegesen me epi hydatos anapauseos) — the shepherd-leads-to-water image directly behind "shepherds them, and leads (hodegesei) them to springs of life-giving waters." John's hodegeo echoes the psalm's verb. High volume and coherence with the Isa 49 / Ezek 34 shepherd cluster.
sourceText: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.

note: Judah's blessing: "he washed his garments in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes" — the only OT image of washing a robe in (grape-)blood, giving John the paradoxical "washed their robes... white in the Lamb's blood." Coheres with the Judah/Lion-Lamb Christology and ties pericope 7.4 back to the Judah-first tribal list (7.2). The blood-of-grapes/blood-of-the-Lamb figural link is medium-to-strong on coherence though contested on verbal volume.
sourceText: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.

note: "Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" — the prophetic image of sin-cleansing producing whiteness underlies robes "made white" through the Lamb's blood (cleansing-unto-whiteness). Coheres with the purification motif; medium volume since John supplies the paradoxical agent (blood) absent from Isaiah.
sourceText: “Come now, and let us reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

note: "Many shall purify themselves and make themselves white (LXX leukanthosin) and be refined" through the time of trouble — the closest source for the eschatological making-white of the faithful precisely amid tribulation, matching "made them white" of those who "came out of the great tribulation." Daniel's end-time-refining-whitening is thematically and verbally apt (leukaino).
sourceText: Many shall purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked shall do wickedly; and none of the wicked shall understand; but those who are wise shall understand.

note: "Some of the wise shall stumble, to refine and purify them and to make them white (LXX leukanai), until the time of the end" — companion to Dan 12:10; the wise are whitened/refined through persecution. Reinforces the tribulation-purification reading of the white-robed multitude. Cited alongside 12:10 as the Danielic whitening pair.
sourceText: Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.

note: "there shall be a time of trouble (LXX thlipsis / Theod. hemera thlipseos) such as never has been" — the eschatological great distress that John names "the great tribulation" (tes thlipseos tes megales). Daniel supplies the technical term and the deliver-the-named-remnant frame; coherent with the sealing/deliverance arc of the whole chapter.
sourceText: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.

note: "I will make my dwelling (LXX skenen) among you... and I will walk among you" — the covenant-presence/tabernacling promise behind "He who sits on the throne will spread his tabernacle (skenosei) over them." Part of the dwelling-of-God-with-his-people stream (Ezek 37:27; cf. Rev 21:3). Medium coherence; the skene cognate strengthens it.
sourceText: I will set my tent among you, and my soul won’t abhor you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.

note: "My dwelling place (LXX kataskenosis) shall be with them, and I will be their God" — the eschatological tabernacling-with-the-redeemed promise, near-synonymous with Lev 26:11 and directly echoed in the skenoo of 7:15 (and again Rev 21:3). Reinforces the new-covenant-presence reading.
sourceText: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

note: Over Zion a canopy/booth (LXX skepe) for "shade from the heat" and shelter — combines the tabernacle-spread-over-them and the no-scorching-heat motifs in a single Zion-protection oracle, paralleling 7:15-16. Faint but apposite; possibly part of the cluster behind John's protective-canopy imagery.
sourceText: Yahweh will create over the whole habitation of Mount Zion, and over her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory will be a canopy. There will be a pavilion for a shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a refuge and for a shelter from storm and from rain.

note: "The LORD is your keeper... the sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night" — the sun-shall-not-strike-you protection paralleling "neither will the sun beat on them." Idiomatically close but likely mediated through Isa 49:10, which John follows more fully; cited as a secondary witness.
sourceText: Yahweh is your keeper. Yahweh is your shade on your right hand. The sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night.

note: Faint: white-garment/clean-robe symbolism of the purified Zion-remnant in Isa 4 (the branch made glorious, the survivors called holy) coheres with the white-robed survivors of tribulation; included as a contested ingathering-of-the-holy-remnant resonance rather than a verbal source.
sourceText: Seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, “We will eat our own bread, and wear our own clothing: only let us be called by your name. Take away our reproach.”

note: "the fountain of living waters" (LXX pegen hydatos zoes) — Jeremiah's image of God as the living-water source colors "springs of life-giving waters" (pegas hydaton zoes); the phrase also runs through Ps 36:9, Zech 14:8, and John 4/7. Common idiom, so single-verse attribution is uncertain; cited as the closest verbal match.
sourceText: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

note: Volume + recurrence: the demand for silence before the LORD in his holy temple is the classic prophetic backdrop for the 'silence in heaven.' Satisfies thematic coherence (heavenly throne/temple) and is the most-cited parallel for the eschatological hush preceding judgment.
sourceText: But Yahweh is in his holy temple. Let all the earth be silent before him!”

note: 'Be silent before the Lord GOD, for the day of the LORD is near' — silence as overture to the Day of the LORD, matching the silence that precedes the trumpet-judgments. Strong thematic coherence with Revelation's day-of-wrath sequence; LXX (Soph 1:7) 'eulabeisthe' softens to 'reverence' where MT has 'hush.'
sourceText: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests.

note: 'Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he is roused from his holy habitation' (MT 2:17). Silence before the LORD stirring from his dwelling for judgment; coheres with the angel's altar action that immediately follows.
sourceText: Be silent, all flesh, before Yahweh; for he has roused himself from his holy habitation!”

note: 'Let my prayer be set forth as incense before you' — the explicit equation of prayer with rising incense underlies vv. 3–4 (incense + prayers of the saints ascending before God). Verbal + conceptual correspondence is very close; a recognized fixed idiom in Second-Temple piety.
sourceText: Let my prayer be set before you like incense; the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice.

note: Day of Atonement: the high priest takes a censer of coals from the altar with handfuls of incense, the smoke cloud rising before the mercy seat. Strong correspondence — golden censer, fire from the altar, incense smoke before the throne/mercy seat — supplying the cultic template for vv. 3–5.
sourceText: He shall take a censer full of coals of fire from off the altar before Yahweh, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and bring it within the veil: and he shall put the incense on the fire before Yahweh, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is on the testimony, so that he will not die.

note: The golden altar of incense before the veil/throne, on which incense is offered. Source for 'the golden altar which was before the throne'; coheres with the tabernacle furniture imagery pervading Revelation's heavenly sanctuary.
sourceText: “You shall make an altar to burn incense on. You shall make it of acacia wood. Its length shall be a cubit, and its breadth a cubit. It shall be square, and its height shall be two cubits. Its horns shall be of one piece with it. You shall overlay it with pure gold, its top, its sides around it, and its horns; and you shall make a gold molding around it. You shall make two golden rings for it under its molding; on its two ribs, on its two sides you shall […]

note: The man clothed in linen is told to fill his hands with burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city as judgment. Direct typological model for v. 5 — fire from the altar cast to the earth, transforming intercession into judgment. High recurrence in Revelation scholarship.
sourceText: He spoke to the man clothed in linen, and said, Go in between the whirling wheels, even under the cherub, and fill both your hands with coals of fire from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city. He went in as I watched.

note: Sinai theophany: thunders, lightnings, and trumpet blast on the mountain. The closing storm-theophany formula (thunders, sounds, lightnings, earthquake) replays Sinai and anticipates the trumpet sequence; a recurring Revelation refrain (cf. 4:5; 11:19; 16:18).
sourceText: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lower part of the mountain. Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked […]

note: Aaron runs with a censer of incense and fire from the altar to stand between the dead and the living, staying the plague. Inverts here: censer/incense intercession becomes the launch of plagues. Plausible figural counterpoint; flagged as a contested intertext.
sourceText: Moses said to Aaron, “Take your censer, and put fire from off the altar in it, and lay incense on it, and carry it quickly to the congregation, and make atonement for them; for wrath has gone out from Yahweh! The plague has begun.” Aaron did as Moses said, and ran into the midst of the assembly. Behold, the plague has begun among the people. He put on the incense, and made atonement for the people. He stood between the dead and the living; and the plague […]

note: Heavenly temple vision: altar, burning coal taken with tongs, smoke filling the house, the throne. Atmospheric coherence with the throne-room sanctuary, though no specific verbal hook beyond shared temple furniture.
sourceText: One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke. Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!” Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal […]

note: Seven priests with seven trumpets before the city of Jericho, whose blast brings the walls down. Anticipatory background for the 'seven angels... seven trumpets' (v. 2); figural model of trumpet-blast as instrument of God's judgment.
sourceText: Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams’ horns before the ark. On the seventh day, you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets. It shall be that when they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, and when you hear the sound of the trumpet, all the people shall shout with a great shout; and the wall of the city shall fall down flat, and the people shall go up every man straight before him.”

note: Raphael as one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the saints and enter before the glory of the Holy One. Second-Temple parallel illuminating the angelic mediation of saints' prayers in vv. 3–4 (cf. also 1 Enoch 9; 99:3).
sourceText: I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and go in before the glory of the Holy One.”

note: Angelic agents 'who stand before God' resonates with the court attendants of Daniel's visions; faint, generic angelological background for 'the seven angels who stand before God.'
sourceText: I saw in the vision; now it was so, that when I saw, I was in the citadel of Susa, which is in the province of Elam; and I saw in the vision, and I was by the river Ulai. Then I lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold, there stood before the river a ram which had two horns: and the two horns were high; but one was higher than the other, and the higher came up last.

note: The seventh Egyptian plague: the LORD sends thunder, hail, and fire running down to the earth, striking everything in the field and shattering every tree. Closest correspondence to 'hail and fire... thrown to the earth' and the destruction of trees/vegetation; the trumpet-plagues are explicitly modeled on the Exodus plagues.
sourceText: Moses stretched out his rod toward the heavens, and Yahweh sent thunder, hail, and lightning flashed down to the earth. Yahweh rained hail on the land of Egypt. So there was very severe hail, and lightning mixed with the hail, such as had not been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation. The hail struck throughout all the land of Egypt all that was in the field, both man and animal; and the hail struck every herb of the field, and broke every […]

note: The two silver trumpets sounded to summon, alarm, and signal the LORD's action; alarm-blast for war and the day of gladness. Source of the cultic-military trumpet that signals divine intervention, framing the whole seven-trumpet sequence (vv. 6 ff.).
sourceText: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Make two trumpets of silver. You shall make them of beaten work. You shall use them for the calling of the congregation, and for the journeying of the camps. When they blow them, all the congregation shall gather themselves to you at the door of the Tent of Meeting. If they blow just one, then the princes, the heads of the thousands of Israel, shall gather themselves to you. When you blow an alarm, the camps that lie on the […]

note: 'Blow the trumpet in Zion... for the day of the LORD is coming' — the trumpet as alarm announcing the Day of the LORD and an attendant army; coheres tightly with Revelation's trumpet-judgments and the locust/fire imagery to follow.
sourceText: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of Yahweh comes, for it is close at hand:

note: Judgment on Gog: 'I will rain on him... torrential rains and hailstones, fire and sulfur.' Hail + fire + blood as instruments of eschatological judgment; supplies the apocalyptic-warfare register fused with the Exodus plague.
sourceText: With pestilence and with blood will I enter into judgment with him; and I will rain on him, and on his hordes, and on the many peoples who are with him, an overflowing shower, and great hailstones, fire, and sulfur.

note: The LORD makes heard his majestic voice with cloudburst, tempest, and hailstones, with the flame of a devouring fire. Thematic coherence for storm-fire judgment from heaven; secondary to the Exodus base text.
sourceText: Yahweh will cause his glorious voice to be heard, and will show the descent of his arm, with the indignation of his anger, and the flame of a devouring fire, with a blast, storm, and hailstones.

note: Theophany: hailstones and coals of fire from the brightness before the LORD. Faint storm-theophany resonance with 'hail and fire'; generic and contested.
sourceText: At the brightness before him his thick clouds passed, hailstones and coals of fire. Yahweh also thundered in the sky. The Most High uttered his voice: hailstones and coals of fire.

note: 'Blood and fire and columns of smoke' among the portents of the day of the LORD (MT/LXX 3:3). Possible source for the unusual 'mixed with blood'; faint verbal cluster (blood + fire), flagged contested.
sourceText: I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke.

note: First Egyptian plague: the Nile and the waters of Egypt turn to blood, the fish die, and the water becomes undrinkable. Direct model for 'one third of the sea became blood' and the death of sea-creatures (vv. 8–9); the plague-template governs the second and third trumpets.
sourceText: Moses and Aaron did so, as Yahweh commanded; and he lifted up the rod, and struck the waters that were in the river, in the sight of Pharaoh, and in the sight of his servants; and all the waters that were in the river were turned to blood. The fish that were in the river died; and the river became foul, and the Egyptians couldn’t drink water from the river; and the blood was throughout all the land of Egypt.

note: Against Babylon: 'I am against you, O destroying mountain... I will make you a burnt mountain.' Closest source for the 'great burning mountain' cast down; Babylon-as-mountain hurled to destruction, apt as Revelation prepares its own Babylon. Verbal hook (burnt/burning mountain) is strong.
sourceText: Behold, I am against you, destroying mountain, says Yahweh, which destroys all the earth; and I will stretch out my hand on you, and roll you down from the rocks, and will make you a burnt mountain.

note: 'I will feed this people with wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink' (MT/LXX 9:14). Source for the wormwood + bitter/poisoned waters motif (vv. 10–11); LXX renders the herb 'cholē/wormwood' with 'water of gall,' close to the Apocalypse's pairing of wormwood and lethal water.
sourceText: therefore thus says Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, Behold, I will feed them, even this people, with wormwood, and give them water of gall to drink.

note: Against false prophets: 'I will feed them with wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink.' Parallel wormwood-and-poison-water judgment formula reinforcing v. 11; doubles the Jeremianic 'wormwood' source.
sourceText: Therefore thus says Yahweh of Armies concerning the prophets: Behold, I will feed them with wormwood, and make them drink the water of gall; for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land.

note: Ninth Egyptian plague: thick darkness over the land of Egypt for three days. Source for the darkening of luminaries (v. 12); the plague-cycle supplies the darkness motif, here recast cosmically onto sun/moon/stars.
